en: Learning is the fruit of virtuous conduct and behavior. || 15 ||
O bulls among sages, is your service to the guru bearing fruit? And is your austerity, such as the Cāndrāyaṇa and other penances, productive of results for you? (16)
"O twice-born ones, even though you are omniscient, why do you ask me? O best of sages, listen as I speak according to my own understanding. (17)
Thus addressed, the Brahmins headed by Śatānanda, whose wealth was their asceticism,
bowed with all eight limbs in devotion and spoke with palms joined in reverence.
The sages said:
O Blessed One, you who are the best among yogis and proficient in all scriptures—how is Brahman to be sought after for knowledge, and by what kinds of fixed vows? (19)
"How can there be identity with Brahman, and how is death at the appointed time to be avoided?"—
thus the son of Vibhāṇḍaka spoke to the sages of celebrated vows regarding the true nature of Time and other matters.
Ṛṣyaśṛṅga said:
"I shall speak according to my understanding regarding that which has been respectfully asked by you;
it should be heard with attention and concentration by the best of yogins. (23)
The time taken for the opening and closing of the eyes of humans is called a *nimeṣa*; thirty *nimeṣas* are declared to be a *kāṣṭhā*. (23)
Thirty *kāṣṭhās* are said to be a *kalā*, and sixty of those are known as a *nāḍikā*.
A *muhūrta* consists of the form of a *gaḍī*, and four of those constitute a *yāma*. (24)
Thirty nāḍīs are declared to be a day, and thirty nāḍīs are known as a night;
sixty nāḍīs are declared to be a day, and that indeed is a full day-and-night (mahorātra).
By those fifteen [days], two [fortnights] are called a month;
in each fortnight there is either the full moon day or the new moon day, which are meritorious dates.
Two *yāmas* are declared to be a season (*ṛtu*), while three [seasons] constitute a solstice (*ayana*).
O Brahmins, it is traditionally taught that twelve months make a year (*saṃvatsara*). || 28 ||
A human year is declared to be a single day of the gods;
they say that four thousand years constitute the Kṛta Yuga. (29)
The twilight preceding it lasts for sixty thousand divine years; this is remembered as the Tretā Yuga. (30)
Its twilight period is said to be one hundred times that [length] according to the divine measure;
two thousand years of mortals is declared to be the Dvāpara Yuga.
Its measure is counted as one hundred million. || 32 ||
A thousand times the product of lunar days, yugas, and years is what is proclaimed;
its count is calculated as one hundred million according to the measurement of the gods.
In this manner, a divine yuga is recorded as consisting of twelve thousand [years]. (33)
A Manvantara consists of seventy-one divine Yugas;
a thousand cycles of four Yugas is declared by Hata to be the lifespan of Brahmā.
That night of Brahmā is said to be equal to that [day];
two thousand sets of four yugas are recorded as one day of Brahmā. (35)

In her, the supreme lord Parameṣṭhin, who performs the work of creation, conceived the divisions of fortnights, months, and so forth, according to the previously stated rule, as he who has four faces.
By his own measure, the wise declare that his lifespan is one hundred years;
this constitutes a single day for Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra, which is their supreme lifespan.
For the omnipresent Lord, who is manifest as Nārāyaṇa, the eternal Supreme Self, there is neither day nor night. (37)
Time creates all beings; Time protects all creatures;
Time destroys the universe; this entire world is subject to Time. 38.
Innumerable Brahmās and Haris have gone to dissolution;
innumerable Rudras, rich in asceticism, have also gone to dissolution. (39)
Indeed, it would be impossible even for Śakra and the other gods to calculate the total destruction; what need is there to mention humans, animals, or even the leaders among the spirits? (40)
He was untimely and invincible, the agent of creation and destruction,
devouring the entire world while simultaneously creating the whole universe.
While he protects the entire world, no one is capable of conquering him—
neither through progeny nor even through ritual action— without realizing the reality of Brahman.
Indeed, time cannot be overcome by wealth nor by gifts,
for one who has not heard [the teachings], who has not served the teacher, and who has not realized the conscious self (cidātman).
The great secret of the Brahman-tattva cannot be conquered by Time;
even the father of Time is directly the Lord of Śrī, whose form is Brahman.
Nārāyaṇa is the great yogi, whose nature is consciousness and whose bliss is truth;
he is the supreme Brahman-tattva, manifest as the very self of Nārāyaṇa.
O Sage, for one who knows the truth, there exists no [further] ocean of saṃsāra;
[this is due to the grace] of the Teacher, the embodiment of compassion, who is Nārāyaṇa himself. (46)
The reality of Brahman is to be intensely desired to be known through service over a long period of time;
it is not attained by ablutions, nor by austerities, nor even by bathing in ashes.
For liberation, which consists of the bliss of Brahman, does not come through non-violence;
for even in all the sacred waters such as the Gaṅgā, there are fish, crocodiles, and other creatures.
For those whose wealth is austerity remain even while being crushed; have they been liberated? Fish drink water and remain silent, yet they are not like them. (49)
Though they were liberated by vows such as fasting and were rich in asceticism,
they became like donkeys— afflicted by disease, with bodies smeared with ashes and hair.
Moreover, those best of Brahmins, who were constantly partaking in liberation, wandered about always intent on the dharma of non-violence toward animals. (51)
"O bulls among sages, tell me: could even deer attain liberation?
Therefore, O twice-born ones, by serving the teacher constantly and for a long time," (52)
Having realized the true nature of Brahman, one attains the bliss of Brahman; out of fear of the Supreme Brahman, the wind blows and the sun shines.
Out of fear of Him the sun rises; out of fear of Him the fire blazes;
and by His command alone, even Time creates and destroys the universe.
Having learned of that Supreme Brahman from his compassionate teacher,
he deceived death and overcame all fears.
O you whose wealth is penance, one certainly attains liberation consisting of the bliss of Brahman;
O bulls among Brahmins, this very inquiry into that bliss shall now be explained.
He was endowed with the fullness of having crossed to the further shore of all the young sciences; he was free from disease, always mature and disciplined, and devoted to all duties.
A virtuous wife who is devoted to her husband and a son who is prosperous—having attained universal sovereignty, he enjoys superhuman bliss. (58)
That which has been declared by those learned in the scriptures as the hundredfold joy of humans is said in the Śruti and Smṛti to be equal to a single unit of the joy of the Gandharvas.
O twice-born ones, by the grace of the Teacher, even a knower of Brahman possesses that bliss;
O twice-born one, it is said to be equal to a hundred joys of the human gandharvas.
O best of sages, that bliss which is proclaimed in the Vedas as the joy of gods and gandharvas is but a hundredth part of the divine bliss of the ancestors. (61)
O Ānanda, even for a single Brahmin who knows the reality of Brahman, it is said that there is a hundredth part of the blisses [experienced] from birth until death. (62)
Even among the gods, there is a hundredfold joy born of birth;
yet, even among the principal gods, that [joy] is declared to be but a single unit of bliss. (63)
A hundredfold that bliss is called the bliss of the wise;
a hundredfold that bliss is said by the learned to be the single bliss of Śakra. (64)
One hundred joys of that [world] are said to be one joy of the Guru;
the joy of the Guru is called the joy of the Lord (Īśvara). (65)
Then, a hundredfold the bliss of Prajāpati would be a single bliss;
and a hundredfold the blisses of Hiraṇyagarbha would be the bliss of Viṣṇu and of Śiva.
The bliss of the Virāṭ Puruṣa is declared to be one;
the bliss of the eternal Supreme Self is directly a hundred times that. (67)
But the bliss of Nārāyaṇa—the eternal Brahman, the Supreme Self, the Lord of Śrī—is indeed one [unit] compared to the bliss of Brahmā. || 68 ||
The bliss known as Brahmananda, which is beyond the reach of mind and speech,
belongs to that self-controlled person who is devoted to the service of the feet of the Guru.
Even for that one who knows the reality of Brahman, who has directly realized Nārāyaṇa as the Self,
and who is liberated while living, the bliss of Brahman is declared.
The bliss known as Brahmananda is proclaimed even in the Vedantas; it cannot be attained by the penances of ten million births, nor even by tens of thousands of great gifts.
O you whose wealth is austerity, even by thousands of horse-sacrifices this [Brahman] cannot be attained;
therefore, one should seek to know Brahman from the lotus-like mouth of a teacher. (73)
"Even when one has reached the time of death, he continues to recite [the mantra] incessantly;
thus, O best among the knowers of Brahman, the method of recitation at the time of death has been described. (74)
"O Brahmins, what more remains to be asked? You have revealed that which was well-guarded," [said he] in this work of the son of Daśaratha, which is a compendium of the meaning of all the Vedas.
Thus has this first chapter been declared in the Tantra named Anuttara.
[Thus ends the first chapter in the venerable Anuttara-Brahma-Tattva-Rahasya, the Dāśarathīya Tantra, which is a compendium of the essence of the meaning of the Vedas.]
The sages said:
O Blessed One, best among yogis, husband of Śāntā, O high-minded one!
How is the reality of Brahman to be known, and how should it be heard with reverence?
O storehouse of compassion, how should service to the teacher be performed by those of firm vows?
Tell us all of this in brief.
Ṛṣyaśṛṅga said:
There exists that which is truly beyond Brahman, devoid of beginning, middle, and end;
it is eternal, pure, unmanifest, and indeed composed of perpetual bliss.
Truth is the supreme form of austerity, free from old age and death;
it consists of consciousness and bliss, is eternal, and is beyond the reach of mind and speech.
The light named Nārāyaṇa is established beyond darkness;
it is neither female, nor neuter, nor male, nor dual, but the supreme Greatness.
Infinite, immovable, subtle, and difficult for others to know,
it is well-situated within the cave of the heart, in the lotus of the heart of all living beings.
It is the unsurpassed dispeller of the mass of darkness within and without;
there, neither the sun shines, nor the moon, nor the fire, nor the lightning.
It alone shines; indeed, it alone shines.
Everything shines after it; by its light all this is illumined. (8)
That form of supreme manliness has the Vedas as its delightful domain;
it is the eternal cause of creation, maintenance, and destruction.
The Supreme Lord, who is expressed by the syllable *oṃ*, is the cause of the universe; from Him arises directly the eternal *akāra*, whose essence is *nāda*. || 10 ||
The stainless Brahman-sages said, "I was indeed known by the name Vāsudeva.
From him, Viṇdu came into being; he is the eternal individual soul (jīvātman).
He is proclaimed as Īśvara, the Person (puruṣa) consisting of pure knowledge;
between those two, there arose the supreme Kalā, whose nature is consciousness.
From that [source], the eternal Mātṛkā consisting of fifty letters appeared in person— whom they call the Lord’s power, whose form is the triple Veda (trayī).
She is Śrī, the Supreme Power, the digit of consciousness (citkalā), the Sovereign Goddess;
she is manifest as Nārāyaṇa herself, non-different from Brahman, and of the nature of consciousness.
Therein, the vowels are sixteen, and the consonants are twenty-five;
then the semivowels and the sibilants—thus is the Mātṛkā remembered.

The vowels (*svara*) beginning with *a* and ending with the *visarga* are proclaimed as *ac*; they are thus designated as *ac*, while *ka* and so forth, excluding vowels (*hal*), are called *ahal*. (16)
The supreme power, whose nature is consciousness, takes the form of the sixteen vowels;
the wise know that the consonants are said to begin with 'ka' and end with 'ha'.
The phonemes beginning with *ka* and ending with *kṣa* have Nārāyaṇa as their essence;
therefore, this [Gāyatrī] consists of the syllables beginning with *ka* and ending with *kṣa*. (18)
The Mātṛkā of Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa has been proclaimed;
O twice-born ones, the Mātṛkā is the supreme Śakti, non-different from Brahman. (19)
By the command of Nārāyaṇa, she creates, protects, and destroys the universe;
from her have emerged the eternal Vedas. (20)
The Dharmaśāstras, the Purāṇas, all the Upaniṣads as well, the sixty-four arts and sciences, and also the eighteen branches [of knowledge]. (21)
The entire world, including both the moving and the non-moving, arose from his body;
this was the supreme Lord Brahmā, the Supreme Self, desiring to create.
Then, O twice-born ones, he who was in the form of Brahmā created the Virāj Puruṣa, whose body is the cause of the universe. (23)
Having divided his own body into two parts, he became a male with one half and a female with the other half; into her, the omnipresent Lord created Virāj.
That Great Being who has been proclaimed by me as being of the nature of the Supreme Brahman—He alone is the transcendent, infallible Lord, whose essence is the glorious eight-syllabled mantra. (25)
Known as Nārāyaṇa, he is the sole cause of all the worlds;
he alone is the primordial, eternal Person, the Supreme Self, and the everlasting one.
The eight-syllabled [mantra] is beyond the reach even of the Vedas and Vedāntas.
For him there exists neither effect nor cause; he has no agent, nor indeed any protector.
His supreme power is heard to be manifold indeed, and his knowledge, strength, and action are inherent. 28.
That all-pervading Lord Nārāyaṇa, who became manifest in two forms,
was the woman Śrī, known as Mahālakṣmī, consisting of his other portion.
The lord of that [egg] is the Puruṣa who is called Nārāyaṇa;
this form of male and female belongs to him, the Brahman, the Supreme Self.
The omnipresent Lord Nārāyaṇa, bearing the concealed Śrī— who is of the nature of consciousness— known as Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa, is eternal.
The omnipresent Lord, the master of the three worlds, who is non-different from consciousness at all times,
is heard of even by the Vedas and Vedāntas which assume embodied forms.
The eternal source of all treasures, whose essence consists of the glorious eight syllables, when at the time of creation assumed the stainless form of both male and female; || 33 ||
The one named Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa is seen in two ways by the eternal ones;
He is denoted by that twelve-syllable mantra as Brahman, higher than the highest.
This Supreme Lord, whose self is Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa and who consists of Nārāyaṇa,
created the Virāj Puruṣa at the time of creation and so forth.
The self of phenomenal manifestation, whose form is time, the existent one, the leader of all, is declared to be the Puruṣa, the cause of all causes. (36)
The all-pervading Lord, who assumes the form of the Gāyatrī consisting of twenty-four principles, whom they call the Supreme Lord and the cause of all the worlds. || 37 ||
From the mouth of Savitṛ— the unborn, pure, eternal, and ancient soul of time— there manifested the eternal and imperishable Praṇava.
The wise know that which is the seed of all rites to be the form of Brahman;
thereafter comes the Vyāhṛti "Bhūḥ," and the pair "Bhuvaḥ" and "Suvaḥ. (39)
From the Gāyatrī, which has become manifest as Virāj, arose the Great Person, austerity, and truth;
this indeed is the great universe, the supreme form of Virāj. || 40 ||
The Blessed One is the very essence of time, the Supreme Brahman;
he is the Sun, the one of universal form, the Virāṭ Puruṣa, the Lord.
They call him Hiraṇyagarbha, the pervasive Pradhānapuruṣa;
he alone creates, protects, and destroys this entire world.
He is Time itself, the one who transcends time, manifest as Nārāyaṇa;
he is [united] with the Gāyatrī, who takes the form of the Sun and the nature of Time.
That golden one, the Sun, who is the soul of time and consists of the Vedas, by whom this entire world exists, is praised directly as the Supreme Person. (44)
That moving and unmoving world, having arisen, was protected by the Supreme Self;
from Him, he then milked forth the Vedas and the three mystical utterances (vyāhṛtis) beginning with Bhūḥ.
Furthermore, from all four Vedas arose sacrifices accompanied by their constituent parts and sacrificial fees, which bestow upon all people the attainment of goals both in this world and the next.
He who is Virāṅmaya, Vāsudeva himself, the Lord of the world, Nārāyaṇa, unborn and eternal, the Great Person, the Sovereign. || 47 ||
That Great Being, the Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati), desiring to bring about creation,
at the very beginning of the creation emitted his vital energy.
Then that golden egg, possessing the brilliance of a thousand suns and a hundredfold luster, was born;
within it arose Vidhi, Brahmā, known as Svayambhū, according to the Śruti.
The waters are called *nārāḥ*, for the waters are indeed the birthplace of *nara*;
since they were his primary abode (*ayana*), he is therefore remembered as Nārāyaṇa. (50)
Hiraṇyagarbha, the soul of the universe, the self-existent, the blessed Lord, [endured] for the sake of the continuous, most great darkness. (51)
Then, pleased by his austerity, the eternal Supreme Self,
Nārāyaṇa— the Puruṣa who is dark and tawny— appeared before the Brāhmaṇa.
[He saw] the Self-born [Brahmā], bowed down with shame and unable himself to perform the work of creation, during the task of the initial emission. 53.
Then, having seen him, the Lord gave him the Vedas together with the Sāvitrī, according to the procedure prescribed in the Śruti, saying, "Perform the creation. (54)
Thus has been described [the path] for the sake of accomplishing the direct realization of the Blessed One’s form;
furthermore, for the sake of attaining the Blessed One’s splendor, there are these very great [practices]. (55)
Then, at that time, the Blessed One, having become a Great Being, shook off all wealth and attachment, and ascended onto the chariot of the sun. (56)
He spoke to the Creator, the sinless Prajāpati.
The Blessed Lord said: "O, O Vra...pitāṃha, who is he that belongs to you?"
"I have been directly perceived by you; I am satisfied with your austerity, O Creator!
I alone am the Supreme Brahman, the eternal Supreme Self. (58)
I am the father even of the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*), which consists of time;
I am Vāsudeva, Viṣṇu, the golden Virāṭ-form. || 59 ||
I am the inner controller of all beings, the individual soul, and the Lord of the three worlds; I am composed of consciousness, I am infinite, and I am devoid of beginning, middle, or end.
I am that which is denoted by the syllable Om, yet I am beyond the scope of even the Vedas;
I am the Self of the universe, the one whose form is the universe, the all-pervading Lord who is to be known through the Vedānta.
I am composed of knowledge, the bestower of fortune, heaven, and liberation upon the worlds;
I am that eight-syllabled mantra which begins with the natural *praṇava*.
O Great King, among all sciences as well, Nārāyaṇa is the bestower of all goals; therefore, I am his very self, consisting of the nature of consciousness.
I alone am without a second, consisting of the glorious eight-syllabled mantra;
it is this very eight-syllabled mantra that possesses glory throughout the three worlds.
The glory of all sciences and even of the Vedas does not exist [without it];
therefore, the method of the glorious eight-syllabled mantra has spread throughout the three worlds. 65.
Arising from the mouth of Brahmā, she is the cause of the stability of the worlds;
among the Vedas, this glorious eight-syllabled mantra is my very essence.
"The Ṛg-veda, the Yajus-formulas, and the Sāman-chants—this indeed is Śrī, whose seat is immortality"—thus was it proclaimed by the Vedas emerging from my own mouth. (67)
Śrī, whose splendor is the renowned immortal nectar, is my power whose nature is consciousness; Nārāyaṇa, endowed with Śrī, is my name, which is the Supreme Brahman.
Indeed, this glorious state is the very nature of my own eight-syllable mantra;
all other rites, however, are endowed with the glory of the *prakṣipta* [inserted] syllables.
The supreme Śrī, whose form is consciousness, who is hidden, whose essence is the seed-syllables of the three Vedas, consisting of supreme splendor,
and the sovereign leader of the great empire of pure awareness.
Bearing this secret [knowledge] without distinction, I am indeed Nārāyaṇa;
I bestow this Great Vidyā upon you for the attainment of spiritual luster.
The Gāyatrī is declared to be the best among all meters;
indeed, no other meter is said to arise that is not the Gāyatrī. (72)
Therefore, she who consists of twenty-four syllables, the mother of the three worlds,
should be known as consisting of eight syllables, endowed with a portion of my own splendor.
I am indeed the cause, the Virāj, whose nature is the Puruṣa;
endowed with half of my splendor, the woman is called Lakṣmī.
I am Nārāyaṇa, the eternal Puruṣa of manifold forms;
I am composed of Brahman, whose nature is the great mantra of twelve syllables.
That which they call the "Knowledge of Brahman" (brahmavidyā) is indeed my twelve-syllable mantra;
and because I consist of the universe, I am the Jāgata meter, the best among meters.
This *jagatī* meter, known as having twelve syllables, is the most excellent to be employed;
it is renowned as the "Knowledge of Brahman" (*brahmavidyā*) because of its bestowal upon you from this point forward. (77)
It is also recorded in the Smṛtis that through giving at the Brāhma-muhūrta, one attains the knowledge of Brahman;
so too is this Great Vidyā named Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa.
"O high-minded one, receive this portion of my splendor at the conclusion [of the rite], for I am that ancient Puruṣa who is manifest as Virāṭ. (79)
Consisting of all the Vedas, the eternal soul of all five elements, he alone is the Veda-Purusha; I am that very Narayana of the Vedas.
Furthermore, O Prajāpati, your rays, having constantly pervaded all the worlds,
will provide assistance to you in the work of creation.
O Brahmin, she who is manifest in my form as Gāyatrī, the mother of the Vedas—
her designator, the god Savitṛ, am I, Nārāyaṇa.
He is Time, the Soul of all beings, the Soul of the Vedas, and faces in every direction;
he is the destroyer of birth, death, old age, disease, and the fear of saṃsāra. || 83 ||
Consisting entirely of ignorance yet pure, having the form of the fifty letters,
she is known as Mātṛkā and is indeed proclaimed to have the nature of the Sāman.
Whatever form is entirely feminine and likewise whatever form is entirely masculine, and whatever form is that of Lakṣmī—that is my own form; it is the essence, without a doubt. (85)
This twelve-syllable Brahma-vidyā is therefore remembered as consisting of the entire universe;
I am its worshiper, assuming the form of the Virāṭ Puruṣa.
Therefore, the Great Vidyā, which consists of light, is my very self and is composed of my own imperishable syllables;
the man who worships her with the sense of "mine-ness" attains direct union with me.
One who is proficient in the Brahman of Sound attains the Supreme Brahman;
therefore, one should contemplate me as consisting of mantra, for I am identical with that. 88.
Having first meditated upon the knowledge of Brahman at the time sacred to Brahmā, one is born [into that state];
then, having meditated upon the Gāyatrī and offered oblations into the fire, Jātavedas.

Then, having worshipped the one named Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇī, who is the embodiment of the primordial Vidyā and other forms, as well as the illustrious eight-syllabled mantra (Aṣṭākṣarī), for as long as [necessary].
For the sake of establishing identity with me and for the attainment of the fruits of the four aims of life, become my attendant Kālāmuka and be the creator of the universe. 91.
"O Prajāpati, I am the son of Rudra;
this universe created by you, I withdraw at the time of its dissolution. (92)
Vārāha, Adādi, and others are living beings, and I am their refuge;
therefore, I am Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of the lords of all worlds.
(***? O Khyāṃ, take this illusion, the mother of the three worlds;
by means of you as her companion, she creates and sustains [the universe]. 94.
This alone is the Great Reality, consisting of the Supreme Brahman;
having understood this from the mouth of the Teacher, one should seek its meaning. 95.
Necessarily, in a single birth, one attains identity with Me:
non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, purity, and restraint of the senses. (96)
Service to the feet of the teacher and constant delight in all dharmas—these seven are the causes for my success at that time. (97)
Having taught this and more to Prajāpati, the Blessed One,
praised by those eternally liberated, quickly vanished from sight.
Brahmā also, having first created that supreme and great reality, spoke it to Sanaka and others, as well as to Vasiṣṭha and others. (99)
Having realized that supreme reality, the cause of oneness with Brahman, those who were devoted to austerity became one with Brahman and remain happy even today. (100)
All mantras consist of phonemes and are composed of sound; they are all eternal, O best of the twice-born. All mantras possess inconceivable power.
O you whose wealth is austerity, through the path of the authentic tradition and by the grace of a true teacher,
all perfections are attained through faith in the words of the teacher.
Death at one's own will, the recollection of past births, and the vision of Brahman—no other means for outwitting Time is recognized [as superior] to these. (3)
Having learned the glorious eight-syllabled lore (vidyā), along with its ancillaries and its secret teachings,
from the lotus-like mouth of the preceptor, he should serve the preceptor daily.
O you whose wealth is penance, by conquering the unassailable Time, one attains Brahman;
thus has been briefly described the true nature of the Supreme Brahman.
"O best of Brahmins, this is well-guarded; why then do you wish to hear more?
Thus ends the chapter spoken in this *Dāśarathīya-tantra*, a compendium of the meaning of the Vedas, which contains the secret of the unsurpassed reality of Brahman.
[Thus ends the second chapter of the *Śrīmadanuttarabrahmatattvarahasya*, the *Dāśarathīya Tantra*, which is a compendium of the meaning of the Vedas.]
The sages said:
O highly fortunate Ṛṣyaśṛṅga, storehouse of all knowledge and penance!
Even though it is well-guarded, [please explain] the truth regarding the Supreme Self, O Brāhmaṇa. || 1 ||
O Teacher, you have stated that service to the teacher must be performed;
O Sage, what kind of person is a teacher in this world, and what is a disciple like? (2)
How should service be performed by a disciple at the feet of the teacher? O Auspicious One, tell that to us, who are devoted to those lotus-feet of yours. (3)
Śrī Ṛṣyaśṛṅga said: Listen, O sages, you who are most excellent and though already omniscient,
[to this account] which is devoted to the method for drying up the lotus-feet of the Teacher.
He was one who had realized the true meaning of the essence of the Vedas and Vedānta, who had reached the further shore of the scriptures,
who was constantly devoted to Vedic conduct, and who had mastered all the sacred texts.
He was peaceful, self-controlled, and had conquered his enemies; he had mastered his senses and was constantly engaged in the study of the Vedas and the contemplation of their meaning.
Accompanied by affection for his own disciples and sons, that best of knowers of Brahman,
devoted to Vedic conduct, [taught] day and night the sister of the Śruti.

O twice-born ones, he was constantly devoted to non-violence, always contemplating the meaning of the reality of Brahman, and eternally engaged in the practice of viewing Śiva and Viṣṇu as non-different.
One born of a noble family is called a guru by the wise,
as is one who performs the recitation of the Gāyatrī mantra a thousand times every single day.
Free from envy, with anger subdued, and constantly engaged in the study of the Vedas— you who possess the secret of all the Agamas—
I grant this Great Knowledge (Mahāvidyā) for the attainment of spiritual luster for you.
The Gāyatrī is declared to be the best among all meters everywhere;
O Prajāpati, its meter is indeed the Gāyatrī, and no other has been spoken of.
Therefore, the twenty-four-syllable Gāyatrī, the Mother of the Vedas,
should be known as consisting of the syllables seen by me and endowed with a portion of my own splendor.
I am indeed Virāṭ, the cause who consists of both male and female;
endowed with half of my splendor, the woman is called Lakṣmī.
I am Nārāyaṇa, the eternal Puruṣa in the form of Virāṭ;
I am Brahman, whose nature is the great twelve-syllable Vidyā. || 75 ||
They call my twelve-syllable mantra "Brahmavidyā";
because I am identical with the universe, I am the preeminent Jāgata among the meters.
This supreme *jagatī* meter, known as "twelve-syllabled," has been worshipped by me;
it is renowned as the "Knowledge of Brahman" (*brahmavidyā*) because of its bestowal upon you from the very beginning. 77.
It is recorded that through giving at the Brāhma-muhūrta, one attains the knowledge of Brahman;
so too is this Great Vidyā named Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa [attained]. (78)
O great-minded one, take this portion of my splendor for the sake of your attainment;
I am that very ancient Person (Puruṣa) who is manifest as Virāṭ.

Consisting of all the Vedas, the eternal self of the entire phenomenal world, he alone is the Veda-Puruṣa; I am indeed that Nārāyaṇa of the Vedas. He is declared to be the Great Guru, the Knower. (10)
He who recites the Gāyatrī, the mother of the Vedas, many times,
should perform the ritual reception of the sciences on earth in her presence.
Indeed, greatness is not found merely through the thorough knowledge of mantras, nor for one who is ignorant of the ritual placements (nyāsa), as well as the worship, yantras, and so forth. (12)
O ascetics rich in penance, one who has not mastered even a little knowledge is not called an *ācārya* by the virtuous;
rather, it is he who has reached the further shore of the meaning of the secrets of all the scriptures and is devoted to the Vedas. (13)
Or, having traveled even a thousand yojanas, one should take refuge in that Guru;
for [otherwise], one is constantly joined with hypocrisy, greed, and the like. (14)
He was constantly slanderous, cruel, foolish, and a habitual liar;
he was dominated by the quality of darkness (tamas) and was always devoted to the wives of others.
Or else, having heard the censure of his guru from all sides, he becomes crooked, harsh in his disposition, and constantly intent on anger. (16)
Seized by envy and avarice, he reviles the conduct prescribed by the Vedas; he is a speaker of what is outside the Veda, a maker of harsh speech, and a perpetrator of evil deeds. (17)
One should always avoid these as disciples, even if they are of noble birth;
[one should instead accept] one who constantly studies the Vedas and is free from hypocrisy and greed.
Free from envy and anger, always devoid of greed, he was constantly devoted to Vedic conduct and had mastered the Vedas. (19)
Born of a noble lineage, he is free from desire for the fruits of his meritorious deeds; he is devoted to the service of his father and mother, and is devoid of [worldly] attachments. || 20 ||
O twice-born ones, he was a giver even of wealth, life, and body to his guru;
day by day he served the lotus feet of his guru, free from envy.
Having thus examined such individuals for their suitability as a basis for knowledge and compassion—
if, however, one's mind is once even slightly attached to censuring the guru— [then they are not fit].
To such a person, [this knowledge] should be given even if one's life-breaths have reached the throat;
even if he has been reviled, beaten, or struck with whips and kicks. (23)
To him who never transgresses the command "Great favor," the lore that bestows heaven and liberation must certainly be given.
The father, the mother, the brother, and the teacher who instructs one in the Vedas with their auxiliary branches—these four are declared to be gurus, who should be honored daily with reverence. (25)
Guruhood consists in being worthy of honor and being an object of daily salutation;
it consists in being served daily with devotion through such acts as attending upon his feet.
One who provides instruction in the scriptures is called an *upādhyāya*.
There is the scripture composed by Akṣapāda, as well as the two-fold Mīmāṃsā. (27)
Beyond this, the *Pāṇinīya-pañcayoga-śāstra* was composed;
these are declared as the six treatises (*śāstra-ṣaṭka*) which are the cause of liberation and other goals.
One who provides instruction in the Dharmaśāstras of Manu and others is called an Upādhyāya; he is to be honored daily like a Guru.
Having instructed [him] in the twelve-syllable Brahma-vidyā of the Lord of Śrī,
together with its ancillaries, nyāsas, and so forth, as well as the worship of the yantra and other rites.
Having imparted the glorious six-syllabled Vidyā as proclaimed by the Vedas, he should daily instruct him in right conduct while awakening him even to the secret [teachings]. (31)
In this world, the teacher is said to be the supreme guru among all gurus;
he should be known as Nārāyaṇa himself in person—salutations to that Puruṣa.
Having studied the science of mantras in one place, and having learned the ritual procedure from another, as well as the method of yantras, the rules of nyāsa, or even their secret essence; || 33 ||

He who imparts the secret knowledge (*vidyā*)— which is called "the secret" (*rahasyaka*)— along with the ritual procedures for the secret worship of the yantra and so forth, to a disciple who is fully prepared, he too shall possess greatness and even deserve honor. (36)
He who, without knowing the ritual procedure for the Great Vidyā along with its secret [teachings], takes it up and mutters it, should be known as a human donkey. || 37 ||
O twice-born ones, in the presence of one who knows the Kalāpa along with its secret (rahasya), we consider another who has studied the Āśrama [grammar] and knows the secret to be superior. (38)
Furthermore, O twice-born ones, one should choose as an ācārya a śrotriya who knows the reality of Brahman,
even if he must travel many thousands of yojanas to reach him.
For the purpose of receiving instruction in the sciences along with their ancillaries, one should rely upon another teacher;
[for] through a single birth, one may attain the bliss known as the direct experience of Brahman.
Desiring to attain the supreme and great welfare that crosses over saṃsāra, one should constantly take refuge in a teacher, even at the cost of one's life, wealth, and intelligence. (41)
He is proclaimed in the world as a great preceptor who bestows the knowledge of Brahman;
he [bestowed] the rays of the Lord along with the sciences, together with their secret doctrines. (42)
O best of the twice-born,
one should know that he who imparts the glorious eight-syllabled lore is the all-pervading Lord of Śrī himself in the form of the teacher.
In sacrifices, festivals, marriages, and all auspicious rites,
one should honor the preceptor at the forefront with garments, ornaments, and even abundant wealth.
Having worshipped the Preceptor, who stands before one like Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśa, and the other gods, one attains the eternal perfection of all dharmas. || 45 ||
O twice-born ones, one attains great perfection only by performing worship, and not otherwise;
even by giving away all one's possessions, or even one's life and body. (46)
If one desires supreme accomplishment, one should generate satisfaction in the teacher; otherwise, having treated the guru—who bestowed even a single syllable—with contempt, [one will fail]. (47)
Having performed the act of *huṃ-kāra* for sixty thousand years,
one attains birth as a dog and is subsequently born among the *caṇḍālas*.
An Ācārya who is afflicted by disease, impoverished, prone to anger, or has failed to conquer his senses must not be disregarded, even if one's own life-breaths have reached the throat.
He who even once hears disparagement of his teacher should be known as a great sinner; him alone one should avoid at all times.
If there is but one teacher for the injunctions of the knowledge of Brahman and so forth, then indeed no one more blessed or superior to him exists on earth. (51)
The worship of the glorious Guru alone bestows the realization of identity with Brahman;
likewise, the venerable eight-syllabled Vidyā and the [other] Vidyā do so as well. (52)
This pair of Vidyās is a compendium of all the Vedas and Vedāntas;
the third is the hymn named Raśmimālā, which is supremely purifying.
If this triad of sciences is obtained from a single preceptor, that fortunate person becomes endowed with the bliss of Brahman. (54)
And they fashion images made of stone, metal, or wood,
regarding them with the thought that they are the Blessed One, adorning the temples with excellent ornaments.
In this world, one should always be devoted to that which is beneficial for those bound by the fetters of existence—the root of all dharmas and the cause of both heaven and liberation. (56)
Those who are utterly deluded do not worship the Preceptor, who is Nārāyaṇa himself and the embodiment of Brahman, in the same manner as they worship images.
Therefore, O Ācārya, the true nature [of the teacher] is hidden even in all the Smṛtis;
the Ācārya alone is the Lord, the omnipresent Nārāyaṇa himself.
O you whose wealth is austerity, this Supreme Self is to be known;
truly, truly, he is the Lord, the husband of Indirā, manifest in human form. (59)
Having worshipped that Vidyā constantly, even once,
one crosses the ocean of saṃsāra and attains the great state of Brahman.
Without having first worshipped with reverence the true teacher who is identical with the Blessed One,
[one does not attain the goal] even by means of ten thousand great gifts or ten thousand horse sacrifices.
One does not attain the supreme state even by ten thousand pilgrimages,
nor by uttering "dhik," "huṃ," or by reviling others while residing there.
Having abandoned their sons, friends, wives, and other possessions, they fall away and, after leaving the body, sink into the foremost of hells. (63)
O you whose wealth is penance, even upon hearing the censure of the wives or sons of their preceptors, those who incur such sin sink down into the Raurava hell.
The teacher alone is to be honored daily with one's life and wealth according to the prescribed rule;
the teacher alone is to be praised in the assemblies of kings and the learned.
The teacher alone should be worshipped day after day at the three junctions of the day;
for he is indeed our wealth, clothing, food, and ornament. (66)
The teacher alone is to be constantly honored for the sake of all accomplishments;
the excellent qualities of the teacher should be heard daily by the wise. (67)
One should always behold only the two lotus feet of the teacher;
indeed, one's entire possessions should be offered with reverence to the teacher alone.
The wise should remain in the presence of the teacher every day;
thus, even while performing service to the teacher for one full year, || 69 ||
"He shall undoubtedly ascend to half the throne of Mahendra, having thus performed service to his preceptor on earth for three years. (70)
By performing service to the teacher with diligence throughout his entire life, he will certainly attain the world of Brahmā; of this there is no doubt.
In this very life he has become Brahman, a liberated one while living; of this there is no doubt.
Thus, O Teacher, one should perform service with daily devotion. (72)
Endowed with conduct prescribed by the Vedas, devoted to the study of the Vedas, a seeker of the knowledge of Brahman, and a meditator upon the garland of rays; || 73 ||
The ascetic who is devoted to the glorious eight-syllabled mantra (aṣṭākṣarī), accompanied by its ancillaries, ritual placements (nyāsa), and so forth,
certainly attains union with Śrī at the end of the body.
The eternal Śruti, emerging from the mouth of the Blessed One, together with its limbs and appendages,
consisting of injunctions, explanatory passages, and mantras, bestows all perfections.
Thereafter, the sages beginning with Svāyambhuva, whose impurities were destroyed and whose wealth was their austerity,
composed the divine treatises on Dharma.
The Brahmins Akṣapāda and the others possess a splendor equal to that of Maheśa; these six supreme sages have composed the systems of philosophical doctrines. (77)
The teacher who instructs these [students] is called a Mahāguru; likewise, that twice-born man who initiates a disciple and teaches him the Veda is [also so called]. (78)
The wise know that teacher to be one who possesses both the ritual manuals (kalpa) and the secret doctrines (rahasya);
he is declared to be a second Brahmā, the bestower of knowledge. (79)
The third teacher mentioned was the venerable Raśmi, the bestower of mantras [who taught] the secret of the Nyāsa-yantropaniṣad and other texts concerning the Lord of Liquor (Indirāpati).
That preeminent among brahmins who bestows the glorious eight-syllabled mantra—
him alone they call the supreme teacher, the very form of the Lord.
There is no other teacher like him on earth;
he is Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of the World, the Blessed One, the Consort of Indirā.
In the Tretā Yuga, the all-pervading Lord born from the womb of Kauśalyā from Daśaratha became renowned in this world as Śrī Rāma, the son of Daśaratha.
Having slain the wicked and invincible night-stalker Rāvaṇa, who was guarded by hosts of rākṣasīs and resembled a mass of crushed collyrium; (84)
Having been consecrated in the kingdom together with his brothers, Lakṣmaṇa and the others, he [performed] that which was commensurate with the great seers such as Vasiṣṭha... 85.
O best of sages, he spoke to Rudra as he was questioning him.
For the welfare of all the worlds and for the establishment of the Dharma, this true [teaching], which is the secret essence of the meaning of the Vedas and Vedāntas, has come forth. 88.
The Lord of Jānakī has proclaimed this great treatise, the Jewel of Liberation;
herein lies the secret essence of Brahman, a compendium of the Vedas.

The supreme and complete ritual procedure for the eight-syllable mantra and others of the Brahmavidyā is taught therein, along with its secret aspects, which bestows worldly enjoyment, heaven, and liberation.
Therefore, O best of the twice-born, this auspicious Tantra called the Dāśarathīya has emerged from the lotus-like face of the Blessed One.
O twice-born ones, this scripture, which is a compendium of the essential meaning of all the Vedas, is to be understood from the lotus-like face of the Teacher, and not otherwise.
One should offer even one's own life to the expounder of this Tantra;
moreover, by reciting even a single verse here, one who is living is liberated.
Having heard this unsurpassed scripture from the lotus-like face of Janakīśa,
the four-faced Brahmā subsequently recited it to Sanaka and the others.
Having previously heard this from the lotus-mouth of Brahmā, the Grandfather (Pitāmaha) then spoke these words to his son Vibhāṇuka.
O twice-born ones, he studied from the mouth of his father Vibhāṇḍaka this compendium of the essential meaning of all the Vedas.
Even a single verse here in this treatise is equal to the Vedas and Vedānta for the sake of accomplishing the vision of Brahman and for the abundant attainment of the fortune of liberation.
This scripture composed by the Lord of Janakī must be studied;
having seen this Tantra known as the Dāśarathīya, the great sages [declared it so]. 98.
The venerable Sanatkumāra, the son of Dattātreya and Lord of the World, composed the Saṃhitāpañcaka as a compendium of the Vedānta.
Vasiṣṭha, the husband of Arundhatī, was the foremost among the Brahman-sages;
so too was Bhārgava Jāmadagnya, who was devoted to the Blessed One.
The son of Dvaipāyana himself, a knower of Brahman and the best among yogis, composed these five Saṃhitās which are equal to the Ṛgveda and Vedānta. || 1 ||
Whatever was spoken by the Blessed One in this work concerning the son of Daśaratha, that supreme reality should be understood from the mouth of the Teacher. (2)
Therefore, for the sake of attaining the direct realization of the Blessed One, one should serve the two lotus feet of the Teacher day after day. (3)
The knot of the heart is rent asunder, all doubts are cut away,
and one's karmas are exhausted upon seeing that Supreme Self.
This earthly body is a mass of blood, flesh, and bones;
it is joined with old age and death, and filled with a flood of impurities and urine.
Having reflected constantly for the sake of attaining the vision of the reality of Brahman,
one should always serve the pair of lotus feet of a true teacher, which are the seeds of liberation.
Again birth and again death, and once more the physical body;
again old age and again childhood, and again ailments and diseases.
Therefore, O twice-born ones, for the sake of attaining identity with the Blessed One,
one must daily worship the two lotus-feet of the Guru alone.
O best of the twice-born, he is to be praised, worshipped, and served.
Thus ends the ninth chapter in this *Dāśarathīya Tantra*, the *Vedārthasaṃgraha*, which contains the secret of the unsurpassed reality of Brahman.
[Thus ends the third chapter in the *Śrīmadanuttarabrahmatattvarahasya*, the *Dāśarathīya Tantra*, the *Vedārthasaṃgraha*.]
The sages said:
O highly fortunate Ṛṣyaśṛṅga, O lord, son of Vibhāṇḍaka!
[We wish to hear of you] together with Rāma, the husband of Jānakī, the Supreme Soul.
How did this scripture come to me from the high-souled Lord of Gaurī?
For what purpose did he speak this tantra, which is a compendium of the meaning of the Vedas?
"O high-minded one, offer this to Rudra, the Lord of Gaurī, for our sake.
Śrī Ṛṣyaśṛṅga said: "Listen, all you sages; I shall speak even that which is a secret. (3)
That ancient reality of Brahman which was proclaimed even by Āśara,
[concerning] that one of great strength and evil soul born in the lineage of Pulastya— || 4 ||
Śrī Rāma, the Lord of the world, who is the manifest Supreme Brahman, [confronted] Rāvaṇa, the night-stalker and sovereign of all the hosts of Rākṣasas.
Having crossed the ocean by means of the bridge, surrounded by my sons and others,
I slew in battle that invincible hero Rāvaṇa, the terror of the three worlds.
Śrī Rāma, the all-pervading Lord Nārāyaṇa himself,
was consecrated in the kingdom along with his brothers by Vasiṣṭha and other great sages.
Having been consecrated, he sat upon a beautiful throne in the lovely city of Ayodhyā and protected the earth.
To behold him, the eight world-protectors, headed by Śakra, arrived,
accompanied by all the hosts of gods and joined by the Siddhas and Vidyādharas.
Having prostrated before Rāma, the Lord of the three worlds, with the eight limbs touching the ground like a staff,
they sat down upon very beautiful seats by his command.
He was attended by Sanaka and others who were personified embodiments of the four Vedas;
he was the unborn Hari, Nārāyaṇa himself, assuming a human form.
Even the four-faced Brahmā approached to behold the lord Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, who was born from the womb of Kauśalyā.
Jaigīṣavya, the great lord of yogis Śatānanda, Gautama,
the blessed Dattātreya, Agastya, and Kaṇva as well.
Medhātithi Bhāradvāja, Viśvāmitra of great asceticism, Ekata, Dvita, Yavakrīta, and Gālava. (14)
The great seer Kapilācārya, the very sharp Sūtikṣṇa, the best of sages, and then Jāmadagnya, the son of Rāma, possessed of great ascetic power; [these were] Devarāta. 15.
Nārada, Parvata, Uśanas, Mārkaṇḍeya of great austerity, the teacher of yoga Vālmīki, and Amamanyu, a treasure-house of penance; || 16 ||
These and many others [worshipped] Śrī Rāma, the Supreme Soul, the unborn and all-pervading Nārāyaṇa, who assumes a human form.
Sages of radiant splendor, devoted to her, approached her whose eyes were like the petals of a lotus and whose face was a serene lotus.
Mahādeva, the lord of the Daughter of the Mountain, arrived from Kailāsa, accompanied by Nandīśa, Bhṛṅgīśa, Vīrabhadra, and the lords of the Gaṇas.
Accompanied by the lords of the Pramathas and surrounded by crores of Mothers,
he went to behold the gracious Lord of Jānakī, who is dark as a blue lotus.
Raghunandana assigned half of those seats, as well as the first one,
to Śiva and Brahmā, and ordered the others for the rest.
The gods, beginning with Brahmā and Rudra, seated upon their thrones, spoke these extraordinary words to the lotus-eyed one: || 22 ||
O Lord of the World, what great fortune, what supreme fortune is ours, that we behold you, the imperishable and unmanifest, O Lord of the World! (23)
O Lord, our penance has borne fruit; it was earned over many lifetimes.
Our sacrifices have become fruitful, having been performed many times accompanied by liberal sacrificial fees.
We behold you, the god Nārāyaṇa himself, in human form;
even the Vedas and the Upaniṣads [behold] you alone as the embodiment of Brahman.
Just as bards constantly praise the Supreme Lord,
so too do they extol Him from whom words turn back, unable to reach Him along with the mind.
O Lord, O All-pervading One, you alone are the embodiment of truth, bliss, and consciousness;
[you have slain] that hero, the thorn of the three worlds, who was unassailable even by the immortals. 27.
Having slain the one who causes the three worlds to flee and having made the world free of thorns,
protect this [world] like an elephant and return again to that state.
Having thus offered praise, the gods remained silent upon their seats;
gazing at Rāma, whose eyes are like lotuses, they waited upon him in worship.
Having beheld the imperishable Śrī Rāma— who is the embodiment of truth, bliss, and consciousness, who is exceedingly gracious,
blissful, and tranquil— together with Gaurī, [he did so] with great reverence.
Seeing Rāma, whose eyes were like lotuses, the Lord was filled with joy;
looking upon him with palms joined in reverence, he spoke to the Supreme Soul, the delight of the Raghus, the Sovereign. The Lord said:
O Blessed One, Lord of the gods of gods, Nārāyaṇa, Lord of the universe, ocean of compassion for Rāmacandra, you who are affectionate toward those who have come for refuge! || 32 ||
Desiring to say something, I have come here out of a wish to see you;
these are the gods beginning with Brahmā, and the lords of the directions beginning with Śakra.
The Brahman-sages such as Vasiṣṭha and others, the yogins such as Sanaka and others, the great Siddhas such as Kapila and others, and also Dattātreya and others; 34.
"O Lord of the World, O Master, in the presence of these deities, I wish to petition something; please grant me your permission. (35)
Thus addressed, the Blessed One, the ocean of compassion, replied,
"So be it," and commanded the Lord of Girijā, saying, "Speak likewise."
Īśvara said:
"O Blessed One, Lord of the gods, Protector of the worlds, Master of the universe!
For the constant welfare of all the worlds and the great sages," || 37 ||
O Lord, whose very self is Nārāyaṇa and who consists of the Supreme Brahman, I now desire to behold the inquiry into the true nature of Brahman. (38)
How may the composed Brahmins realize that supreme reality? How, while submerged in the ocean of saṃsāra, may they perceive you who are the very form of Brahman? (39)
How may the twice-born attain Your vision after having crossed over [the world]?
You alone are the embodiment of Brahman, whose nature is truth, bliss, and consciousness.
But how, O Lord of the World, being pleased, do you bestow the supreme abode? 38.
I shall fully declare that secret to him, by which these people attain liberation—
whether through charity, or vows, or ritual procedures, or mantras, hymns, and recitations.
O Blessed One, tell that which is pleasing to you, for you are the threefold sacrifice;
even the Vedas and the Vedāntas are your own great form.
Indeed, they do not know the reality whose essence is Nārāyaṇa according to its true nature;
yet these [beings], beginning with Brahmā and including the supreme sages, impel me.
"O Lord of the World, [I wish] to inform you regarding the pair of your lotus feet.
Thus addressed, the Blessed One, the illustrious Rāma, the Lord of the World, [spoke] there. 42.
In the presence of the four-faced Brahmā and other gods, as well as the great sages, he,
with a gracious countenance, spoke to Śaṅkara, the benefactor of the world.
The Blessed Lord said: O Lord of Gaurī, I shall proclaim the truth—the secret even of me, the Blessed One—which is a compendium of the essential meaning of the Vedānta.
Truth, consciousness, and the nature of bliss— imperishable, infallible,
the light hidden within the cave of the heart, immovable, eternal, and constant.
That very form of mine is the Supreme Brahman, known by the name Nārāyaṇa.
I am the realization of Vedānta, and likewise, through my words, I am eternally one whose desires are perfectly fulfilled.
O Lord of Yoga, I am the object of meditation for the hosts of perfected beings (siddhas), and I am eternally worshipful by all throughout the worlds.
I alone am the form of the Vedas; I am the form of the sacrificial altar, and I am Time, whose self is the four-faced Brahmā.
I am Nārāyaṇa, assuming the form of a man; I am Rudra, the Lord of Time and Death, and Śakra.
That which is the abode consisting of Brahman, the supreme light, eternal, having the nature of truth, bliss, and consciousness, constant, everlasting, and undecaying. || 48 ||
It is imperishable, supreme, divine, pure, and the essence of both being and non-being;
it is directly named Nārāyaṇa, established beyond the darkness.
That alone is my supreme form, beyond the reach of mind and speech;
it is not attained through vows, nor by great gifts, nor by sacrifices accompanied by abundant fees.
O Lord, O Consort of Gaurī, that form of mine cannot be attained through pilgrimages, acts of daring, nor even by hundreds of sacrifices and works of public utility; it is impossible to reach.

By those devoted to the service of the sandals of the Teacher, whose conduct is praised, and who are intent upon the muttering of the mantra and the fire-oblation of the glorious eight-syllabled vidyā; || 52 ||
Indeed, that form can be attained by those devoted to the thorough study of the Vedas, by those who contemplate the knowledge of Brahman, and by those who recite the *Raśmimālā*.
This power of mine, Jānakī, is Śrī, whose essence is consciousness;
she appears as if divided in this world through my Māyā, which is difficult to overcome. (54)
By this very power, born from a portion of her, the universe is utterly deluded;
and the eternal Śruti, along with its auxiliary limbs (Aṅgas), has manifested from my mouth. 55.
"This right arm of mine is the Grandfather (Brahmā), the creator;
you, O lamp, are Viṣṇu, my left arm and likewise my heart. (56)
Here, in the midst of the city, is the lotus, free from impurity, which has become a sublime abode;
even there, one who is free from sorrow beholds the sky, and within that, the state of reality (tattva) should be meditated upon.

I, whose essence is truth, am designated by that sound which is proclaimed at the beginning of the Vedas and established at the end of the Vedas— the Supreme Brahman which possesses the nature of sound.
I am the leader of the three worlds, known by the name Śrī Nārāyaṇa;
that which is named Nārāyaṇa is the form of Brahman, whose nature is Being-Consciousness.
That alone is my supreme reality— beyond the three qualities (guṇas), imperishable,
eternally transcendent of the universe, and having Viśvanārāyaṇa as its very self.
He who has a thousand heads, the non-cause of the creation and maintenance of the universe,
imperishable, eternal, divine, and beyond even the reach of the Vedāntas.
That which is proclaimed as "Being" (Sat) occurring at the beginning, middle, and end—that alone is my great, secret form, the imperishable light. || 62 ||
This entire universe is indeed the Puruṣa; he lives upon this entire universe.
He is the Lord of the universe, the Master of the Self, eternal, auspicious, and immutable.
One should know that the auspicious [reality] which is the great universal self is named Nārāyaṇa;
the light and the principle named Nārāyaṇa is the auspicious one whose essence is Nārāyaṇa.
This great form of mine is eternal, named Nārāyaṇa;
Nārāyaṇa is the Supreme Brahman, the Reality, and Nārāyaṇa is the Ultimate.
Nārāyaṇa is the supreme light; Nārāyaṇa is the supreme Self.
Whatever is seen or even heard in this world, [it is all He]. (66)
Nārāyaṇa stands pervading all that is within and without;
this is what is propounded by the Nārāyaṇopaniṣad and other such texts.
That very form named Nārāyaṇa is my supreme self;
you too should constantly remember me by the name "Nārāyaṇa."
The attainment of the fruits of the four aims of life is their success at every step, O Prajāpati, if you have a desire to fully understand my true nature. (69)
Having worshipped the pair of the teacher’s sandals day after day,
one should become intent on service through one's life-breaths, wealth, and even one's intellect.
Day after day, having taken refuge at the lotus feet of the Teacher with devotion, I have performed the contemplation of the knowledge of Brahman. (71)
I [bestow] the glorious eight-syllabled lore, endowed with my secret splendor,
accompanied by my radiant rays of knowledge, and joined with all the Nyāsas.
Having obtained [this] through the grace of the teacher, being devoted to his service and constantly reciting [the mantra] with devotion, he attains union (sāyujya) with me.
My knowledge is not to be attained through vows, nor through austerities, nor even through the Vedas or the Āgamas,
without the grace of the teacher.
O Lord of Creatures, devotion to me arises from merits accumulated over many births;
the supreme practice is the performance of rituals such as the recitation of my mantras and fire offerings. (75)
The fruit is obtained through the heaps of merit accumulated over many births;
even therein, service to the lotus feet of the Ācārya is unsurpassed. (76)
O Lord of Gaurī, if this is obtained every day by the most excellent of Brahmins, he will certainly assume my own form within a single birth. (77)
Thus, O Śaṅkara, the omniscient one, I have said something to you;
what more do you wish to hear regarding the knowledge of my true nature? (78)
[Thus ends the fourth chapter in the venerable *Anuttarabrahmatattvarahasya*, the *Dāśarathīya Tantra*, which is a compendium of the meaning of the Vedas.]
Ṛṣyaśṛṅga said:
Having thus heard from the mouth of the Lord of Śrī, Śiva, the consort of Gaurī,
spoke once more these words for the welfare of the world to the Lord of Jānakī.
Īśvara said:
O Blessed One, Lord of Jānakī, ocean of Nārāyaṇa’s compassion!
These perfected brahmin-sages have attained their majesty through your grace.
"O Mā, impel me here to inquire about the secret of Brahman as proclaimed by Manu and other sages, as well as the conduct ordained by the Vedas. || 3 ||
Filled with curiosity to hear from your lotus-like mouth the discourse on the characteristics of one devoted to the Guru— the rays of light for the Lord of Śrī— they waited.
Filled with curiosity, they [desire] to hear specifically the greatness of the glorious eight-syllable mantra along with its secret, as well as the greatness of the Brahma-vidyā.
O Sage, tell me all this: how can the direct realization of Brahman come about for the twice-born in this world within a single lifetime? (6)
The Blessed Lord said: Listen, O highly fortunate Rudra, grandson of the four-faced one!
Even the Brahman-sages, as well as the Siddhas and those whose wealth is penance, listen in this manner.
In this regard, I shall relate an ancient legend,
hearing which from the mouth of the Teacher one may become Brahman even here in this world.
Having churned the great ocean of the Vedas and Agamas with the churning-stick of knowledge,
I— who am a knower of the essence— have extracted this secret vision of Brahman.
Our father-in-law, our father, was devoted to all dharmas;
intent upon the study of the Vedas, he protected the earth. || 10 ||
By means of sacrifices such as the Aśvamedha, in which abundant sacrificial fees were given,
he worshipped the Lord, the Consort of Śrī, with the Tulā, Hiraṇyagarbha, and other rites.
O Lord of Girijā, for the sake of attaining the realization of knowledge beyond the senses, Brahmā propitiated the sage Gautama, who was entirely devoted to Brahman.
The preceptor always places upon his ears a pair of earrings made of refined gold and set with rubies.
Having fashioned a pair of sandals made of gold, adorned with the nine gems and decorated with strings of pearls; || 14 ||
Pure every day, reciting the *pādukā-vidyā* while uttering the name of his preceptor, he should mount the pair of the guru’s lotus feet with that pair of sandals. 15.
Then, having performed service to the pair of sandals with perfumes, unbroken grains, flowers, umbrellas, fans, and chowries, [one should say] "Obeisance! (namaḥ).
Having fashioned a pair of sandals for the Preceptor out of gold weighing one karṣa each, he, being pure, should worship them daily.
Thus, for twelve years, he daily worshipped the pair of sandals with the two lotus-feet of his teacher.
Having performed the worship of the two sandals with the Vidyā, one attains the vision of Brahman;
for the sake of perfection, one first acquires the Brahma-vidyā conjoined with the rays of the Lord.
He received from his preceptor Gautama the venerable eight-syllabled mantra (vidyā), accompanied by the complete ritual placement (nyāsa) and preceded by the worship of the yantra.
Having offered his body, wealth, and life at the feet of the Guru,
he undertook a severe discipline for the sake of attaining the vision of Brahman.
Having worshipped the pair of the Guru’s sandals with thousands of golden flowers, from this point forward I shall eat [only] after doing so constantly.
Having thus made this vow, he would rise at dawn, worship the two sandals of his own guru with ritual offerings, and [proceed].
Having eaten together with Brahmins in this manner for twelve years,
he attained the power of recollecting his past births through the worship of the pair of sandals.
Once, while the king was reciting the mantra of the Preceptor’s sandals, his pair of wooden sandals vanished from his own palace; he remained there without eating.
Chanting the glorious eight-syllable mantra, which is a garland of rays consisting of the essence of Brahman,
he was entreated by his father and mother as well as by the foremost of the Brahmanical sages.
Even by his own teacher, Prārtigautama,
the high-minded King was instructed while remaining without food, with his heart fully surrendered to the Blessed One.
Gautama, being pleased with that high-souled Janaka,
bestowed upon him the eight-syllabled perfection (*aṣṭākṣarī siddhi*) which grants the perfection of vision.
Nevertheless, that king did not eat because of the absence of his sandals;
then, one wearing the guise of a madman arrived there to see Saṃbhūti.
Accompanied by a mass of matted locks, clothed in bark garments, with a black antelope skin as his upper garment, and joined by a single disciple; (30)
He who dwells in Sauvadarī, having become a supreme *paramahaṃsa* protected by the guardians of the three worlds, is indeed the all-pervading Lord Nārāyaṇa himself.
Having recognized that the supreme sage had arrived at his own abode, seated upon a pair of sandals and accompanied by a single disciple; || 32 ||
Then Janaka, the lord of Mithilā, having first saluted him with joined palms,
beheld the pair of sandals upon which that Great-Souled One had ascended.
Filled with the bliss of Brahman, having beheld that pair of sandals,
he bowed down again and again and worshipped them with golden flowers.
Seeing a golden web of flowers placed upon the pair of sandals on his head, he was filled with respectful wonder.
Then, seeing the teacher Gautama endowed with such conduct, he prostrated before me with his eight limbs touching the ground, repeatedly saying, "I am blessed! (36)
Beholding his splendor, which was like ten million suns and manifested in the form of the Teacher, he closed his eyes and struck him with both feet.
Having raised him up, the Lord of the World granted him divine vision;
then, within his stony body, he beheld this entire world of moving and unmoving beings.
Brahmā, the Sun, Śeṣa, and you accompanied by Gaurī;
Indra and the other desired guardians of the quarters, as well as the Sādhyas together with the hosts of Maruts. || 39 ||
Then, having seen Mitrā and the other twelve Ādityas, as well as the eleven Rudras, and this entire universe without exception, my father-in-law [said]: "O others! (40)
Then, seeing that the net of arrows given by the feet of the Teacher was inexhaustible, the sons were filled with wonder; they [then took] those two sandals.
Placing his two lotus-feet upon his own head,
he prostrated himself like a staff with all eight limbs, and offered many hymns from the Vedic scriptures.
Having offered praise with palms joined in reverence to the omnipresent Lord who was wearing the guise of a swan,
he beheld the Brahmin as before, endowed with matted hair and bark garments.
Having become one with his own gurus, he experienced yet another wonder through the worship of the pair of the preceptor’s sandals and through pleasing the guru.
My birth has become fruitful; I have attained the vision of Brahman.
This is the direct vision of Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Self.
Thinking that he had been born through the grace of Gautama,
that king prepared a seat for him who was wearing the garb of a yogin.
Accompanied by his disciple, the yogi sat down upon a seat,
[honored] with offerings of water for the hands and feet, divine perfumes, and auspicious flowers.
That high-minded one worshipped his feet with tears from his eyes;
O Śaṅkara, he worshipped the pair of the teacher’s sandals as if they were the teacher himself. 48.
Then the omnipresent Lord Nārāyaṇa, the one to be attained, being pleased with him,
spoke these words again to him as he stood with palms joined in reverence.
The Blessed Lord said:
"I am pleased with you, O Mahī; if there is anything most desired by you, I shall grant it to you, even a reward greater than what you have requested."
The king said:
"The sight of your feet has occurred, and your wonderful form has been beheld.
What other desired boon should I choose? Everything has been attained by me today. (51)
May there be firm and constant devotion toward the lotus feet of the Guru;
may the daily worship of the pair of the Guru’s sandals be mine. (52)
May my delight be in Vedic conduct, my devotion in the feet of the teacher,
and may my firm devotion always be toward the service of your knowledge.
Thus addressed there by the king, the lord of Mithilā,
the omnipresent Lord Nārāyaṇa, the yogi, spoke together with Nara.
"I am pleased, O Lord of Mithilā; whatever desired fruit you seek, may that be yours, O protector of the earth, through your constant service to the teacher. (55)
By constantly pleasing the teacher, I shall remain forever satisfied;
all other [gods] are surpassed by you in their fruits, being nothing but substitutes for you.
"All of them shall attain union with me here; of this there is no doubt.
I myself, having become the son of Daśaratha on earth, with Lakṣmaṇa as my follower," || 57 ||
"I shall become the son-in-law of Rāma, who is renowned by that name;
and Śrī, whose form is consciousness, is known in the Vedas as my power (śakti). (58)
"O Lord of the Earth, by my grace this daughter shall be yours;
having become one who has attained all fortune and is freed from sin, you shall possess her as a son. (59)
"After my departure, you shall attain the supreme abode together with your ancestors.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed One sat in silence upon his proper seat.
He became present in the house of Janaka, facing toward grace;
seeing Sanātana facing toward grace, [he... 61.
King Janaka, with palms joined in reverence, spoke these words to Nārāyaṇa, the friend of men, the all-pervading Lord and sovereign of great yogis: || 62 ||
The king said:
"O Blessed One, Lord of the gods of gods, Nārāyaṇa, Lord of Victory!
For the welfare of all the worlds, I am prepared to make a certain request."
How and by what birth may the direct realization of Brahman be attained?
How should service to the lotus feet of the Guru be performed with devotion? (64)
O Lord, how indeed should the conduct of the sacrificial altar be performed by those who have attained [this] knowledge?
By what rite should the worship of Your Vidya be performed? (65)
"O Blessed One, O All-pervading Lord, tell me this and other matters that bear fruit.
The Blessed One said:
"This which you have asked with devotion is beneficial to the three worlds."
O Janaka, I shall tell you, who are devoted to your guru and possessed of wisdom,
that which is the indivisible Brahman— truth, consciousness, and bliss, devoid of all qualities.
The supreme twofold form is both with attributes (saguṇa) and without attributes (nirguṇa)—eternal, divine, known through the Vedas, and higher than the highest. (68)
Indeed, that Brahman exists as a form of splendor, devoid of qualities (nirguṇa),
consisting of being, consciousness, and bliss (saccidānanda), non-dual, in the form of light, and higher than the highest.
That form of Brahman which is devoid of qualities (nirguṇa) is mine alone, transcending the universe;
while that which possesses qualities (saguṇa) is the wondrous cause of creation, destruction, and maintenance.
The cause of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa is endowed with the three guṇas; this is the intention of the Śruti regarding my manifestation from the mouth of the Saguna [Brahman].

For those who disregard the command of Nārāyaṇa, the eternal Veda itself is their enemy; such a person, a destroyer of ignorance yet a traitor to Me, shall find his abode in hell at the end of his body.
Constantly engaged in the study of the Vedas and endowed with Vedic conduct,
he enters the abode of Nārāyaṇa eternally at the end of his body.
A twice-born man who is devoted to his own duty for a hundred births attains thereafter the supreme Śiva;
by serving the lotus feet of the Teacher, he becomes a recipient of Nārāyaṇa’s grace.
The eternal Vedas, along with their auxiliary limbs, emerged from the mouth of Nārāyaṇa; one who is established in them, endowed with right conduct, and devoted to my worship [is truly wise]. (75)
Then, preceded by devoted service to the sandals of the teacher, he attains that supreme state known as Nārāyaṇa.
Constantly performing Vedic conduct and chanting the Brahma-vidyā,
he should chant the Śrīmad-aṣṭākṣarī accompanied by all the nyāsas.
A perpetual celibate student, a householder, and even a forest-dweller certainly attain liberation in this very birth; indeed, it is not otherwise. 78.
Having indeed completed the study of the Vedas, one certainly becomes a Brahmin;
for the deities exist in the form of mantras, and those mantras are established within the Vedas. (79)
Therefore, the Brahmins consist of the Vedas and are joined with the study of the Vedas;
the Brahmins consist of all the Vedas, and Hari consists of all the gods.
The god Nārāyaṇa is himself the eternal Supreme Self.
[Thus ends the fifth chapter of the Śrīmadanuttarabrahmatattvarahasya, the Dāśarathīya Tantra, which is a compendium of the meaning of the Vedas.]
Śrī Rāmacandra said:
Listen, O highly fortunate Rudra; when questioned by the high-souled Janaka, the all-pervading Lord Nārāyaṇa, who dwells in Badarikā, spoke as follows.
The Blessed Lord said: Listen, O King, protector of the earth, to that which has been proclaimed among the gods regarding right conduct,
which bestows the attainment of direct knowledge of the Supreme Brahman.
O Lord of the Earth, a twice-born man must cultivate the state of possessing proper conduct;
for through conduct one attains happiness, and through conduct one gains renown. (3)
Through right conduct one attains prosperity; through right conduct one attains the higher goal.
Having studied two Vedas, or one Veda, or even a single Veda according to his ability, the twice-born [should practice it].
One endowed with the conduct prescribed therein perceives that Supreme Brahman;
the first half of the final watch of the night is known as Brāhmī.

O Lord of the Earth, the wise declare that the period of *samaya*, which bestows the perfection of the vision of Brahman, consists of four *nāḍīs* occurring at the time following the evening twilight (*saṃdhyā*).
Having risen at the hour sacred to Brahmā, while still remaining on his bed,
he indeed remembered his mother’s feet, which are the most excellent of all holy places.
Having bowed thrice to the pair of feet of his father, O King,
and having remembered five times the feet of his preceptor, he then [remembered] Acyuta, the Lord of Śrī.
Having recited the Daśārṇa mantra twelve times with devotion,
he then meditated upon the elephant-faced Lord, the omnipresent Viśveśa, who is accompanied by Pārvatī.
[He bowed] to Vāṇīpati (Brahmā), the Creator, the lords of the directions such as Mahendra,
the virtuous women beginning with Arundhatī, and the celestial sages beginning with Nārada.
[He saw] the great siddhas such as Kapila, the yogins such as Dattātreya,
the poets headed by Vālmīki, and even the two types of ascetics beginning with you.
He [beheld] the hosts of jewels beginning with the Kaustubha, the trees such as the Kalpavṛkṣa,
and the great and firm sons of Āyus beginning with Karāñja.
Having paid homage to the Brahman-sages such as Vasiṣṭha and others, as well as to the Earth, he placed his right foot upon the surface of the ground.
Having placed the left foot forward, one should then place the right foot behind;
with palms joined in reverence, bowing to all one's gurus, one should contemplate Brahman. (14)
Having meditated upon the two lotus-feet of the Guru within the auspicious aperture of Brahman (brahmabila), [one is purified] by the drops of nectar flowing from those lotus-feet.
Then, having meditated upon himself as being completely bathed, he becomes pure;
[he perceives] the supreme consciousness blazing from the base (mūlādhāra) up to the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra). || 16 ||
Having meditated and put on two garments made of radiant light,
he sat properly upon his seat and restrained his vital breaths with the utterance of sacred syllables.
One should recite the mantra of the Guru’s sandals twenty-eight times;
having recited it twelve times, one should bow to the lotus feet of the Guru.
Alternatively, every day with devotion, having restrained one's speech at dawn,
[one should worship] the pair of Śrī-pādukās mounted upon the lotus-feet of the Guru.
It may be made of gold and jewels, or of silver, or even of iron,
or fashioned from wood, on an auspicious day and at a favorable moment.
Having placed [the mantra] upon the lotus-feet of the Teacher from the very beginning, one who desires unsurpassed welfare should rise every morning. (21)
Beholding the pair of sandals of his guru with undivided vision,
O King, he should prostrate while reciting the mantra of the sandals of the preceptor.
[He cursed] Tulasī, the Jāhnavī, and even the very great river Godāvarī;
[he cursed] King Pāpaka and that best of Brahmins who had reached the further shore of the Vedānta.
He who rises early in the morning and beholds [the sandals] is freed from sin;
he who, having risen early in the morning, daily [beholds] the pair of sandals of the Guru.
Having first seen with his two eyes, he beholds the Supreme Brahman;
[he beholds] the sacred fords such as the Jāhnavī and the seven Ṛṣis as well.
By that [vision], even deities such as Brahmā and others are seen;
for even in the absence of the guru’s sandals, the two feet of the guru are present.
Having meditated for a long time with undistracted mind upon the thousand-petaled lotus at the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra),
he worshipped [the deity] with auspicious offerings mentally conceived.
Afterwards, he should call to mind the Lord Nārāyaṇa, the husband of Umā;
the teacher who bestows the knowledge of Brahman is called the Smara-ācārya (the teacher of remembrance). || 28 ||
Accompanied by the complete ritual placement (nyāsa), preceded by worship, and endowed with the Bhagavadraśmi mantras and Vidyās, it bestows all spiritual accomplishments (siddhis). || 29 ||
He who bestows the glorious eight-syllabled Vidyā upon a disciple is called a great Ācārya, for he is the very form of the Lord himself. (30)
The wise know that very [reality] to be Brahman, the root cause of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa, as well as the foundation for the attainment of identity with it. || 31 ||
What is the use of saying more here? Hari, who is Nārāyaṇa himself, is eternally worshipped in the form of the Teacher; one should worship him day after day with great devotion.
Having recited the mantra of the Guru’s sandals and the Brahma-vidyā,
one should then recite the Krama-sūkta of the mantras of the Lord’s rays.
Having recollected the hymn to the Blessed One five times, or three times, or twice, or four times, or even just once, he should then recite the name of Nārāyaṇa once.
Afterwards, having gone seven steps outside, he should void urine, excrement, and so forth, covering his head with a cloth, while refraining from spitting and exhaling. || 35 ||
Having strewn the ground with grass, one should void excrement and urine;
during the daytime, one should discharge excrement and urine while facing north.
Facing south at night, one should void urine, excrement, and so forth;
having taken pure earth, one should apply earth to the penis once.
It is taught that one should apply three applications of clay with the left hand during the exhalation;
ten applications should be made with the left hand, and seven applications of clay for both hands.
Three applications of clay on the top of the feet and three on the soles of the feet constitute this purification for a householder; for a student (brahmacārin), it is double that.
For forest-dwellers, it is said that [the fruit] is threefold, while for those who have crossed [to the further shore], it is fourfold;
however, for one devoid of purity and right conduct, all ritual actions—whether performed or not—are fruitless.

Having thus performed purification, the twice-born should practice the cleaning of the teeth; however, one should avoid it on the first day of the lunar fortnight, the new moon, the sixth, the ninth, and on Sundays.
The use of a tooth-stick consumes one's lineage up to the seventh generation;
therefore, one should always perform the Ayācā observance with grass and leaves, except on Ekādaśī.
Having placed the two lotus-feet of the Ācārya in his mind,
he should perform his bath in a great river, or in a pond, or even in a lake.
Impurity always flows from the apertures of the body;
therefore, one should perform bathing, which destroys both external and internal impurities. (44)
