They say that the bath performed every morning when the beautiful dawn has appeared is equal to the Prājāpatya penance; it is a great destroyer of obstacles.
Having meditated upon the lotus feet of the teacher as the very sacred water of a river, one should perform ablution for the purification of all sins. (45)
Having performed the preliminary stretching exercises, one should daily perform the ritual bath of intention (saṃkalpa-snāna),
while mentally recollecting the twenty-four names beginning with Keśava.
O King, that brahmin who bathes day after day for twenty-four days, or even performs the bath with devotion on a single day, [attains the fruit]. (47)
One is instantly liberated from millions of mortal sins;
having bathed and put on two clean garments, one should remain composed in mind. (47)
Then one should perform the twilight rite (saṃdhyā-karma), facing either east or north;
they know the morning twilight to last for three ghaṭikās prior to sunrise.
For three ghaṭikās after the sun has set,
one who abandons the twilight rites is excluded from all ritual acts.
Whatever action one performs, one shall not partake in its fruit,
provided that one has abandoned the rite called *saṃdhyā* and instead performs it elsewhere.
That Śūdra must be excluded from all rites performed by Brahmins;
he shall perform the morning twilight devotion while the stars are still visible, according to the prescribed rule.
The western twilight, accompanied by the sun, occurs when the sun has half-set and the sky has become half-filled with stars. || 52 ||
O King, the time of twilight should be understood as the mouth of the day;
having restrained the breaths and made the formal resolve (saṃkalpa), one should commence the twilight ritual (saṃdhyā-karma).
Even if the twilight ritual (saṃdhyā) is performed according to rule, if it is performed after the proper time has passed, it is considered to yield no fruit;
this is indeed like the example of sexual union with a barren woman.
For the sake of removing the bodily hemorrhoids of the Maṇḍehas, he who offered three handfuls of water from the Gāyatrī mantra at the times of sunrise and sunset— [55]
What could not be accomplished by Savitṛ at that time? By him, with that adamantine water, the three worlds were swiftly delivered from the bodies of the Rākṣasas.
The sun and the planets dissolve like mountains struck by a thunderbolt;
one who abandons the twilight rituals becomes a Maṇḍehorā demon.
Then, with the mantra beginning with "asau," one should perform a circumambulation;
by that, the earth with its seven continents and forests has been circumambulated.
One should remain victorious in the morning until half-rising occurs;
seated upon one's seat and observing silence, one should perform japa until the stars in the west have risen. (59)
During the middle twilight, one should perform worship facing the sun;
for the Lord together with Lakṣmī is directly the form of Brahman, the Lord of Śrī.
Stationed within the solar orb and bearing the form of the threefold manifestation,
one should meditate upon the all-pervading Lord Nārāyaṇa as situated within that orb.
Just as one should daily recite the Gāyatrī, the mother of the Vedas, with devotion— one thousand times at most, one hundred times in the middle, or ten times at the minimum.
One should constantly recite the Gāyatrī; thus one is liberated from the multitude of sins.
The Brahman-sages say that he was born from a portion of Vasiṣṭha;
one should mutter this [mantra] either a hundred times or even four hundred times.
Reciting it three hundred times daily, a twice-born man is called "supreme";
by reciting it one hundred and eight times day after day, he becomes a true Brāhmaṇa.
A Brahmin who merely bears the name, having recited [the mantra] twenty-eight times,
is pure at every step when he recites the Gāyatrī a thousand times.
One should always honor such a person with services as one would Vasiṣṭha;
for Brahminhood does not arise from the recitation of the Vedas, nor even from the study of the Śāstras. (67)

Through occupying the three periods of the day with the Goddess, one's status as a Brahmin shall not be otherwise; even if incapable, one should constantly recite [the mantra] while standing or indeed while sitting. 68.
Purifying his soul at the three junctions of the day, he [should recite] the Sāvitrī, the mother of the Vedas;
and when the thousand-rayed sun has risen, he should meditate upon the All-pervading Lord situated within its orb.
Having meditated upon the god Nārāyaṇa, who is inseparable from Śrī, who is golden-hued, whose form is the triple Veda, and who is mounted upon a chariot drawn by the Vedas; 70.
Remaining seated with palms joined in reverence, one should daily offer salutations to the quarters of space with the Maitra Sūkta, and thereafter to the gods.
The wise man, having touched his own feet with his hands, should bow down to himself;
then, having become pure through the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), he [should meditate upon] Him who dwells in the center of the solar orb.
Having meditated upon the Lord Nārāyaṇa, the Sovereign accompanied by Śrī, and having performed the venerable eight-syllabled twilight prayer with devotion for the sake of attaining perfection; 73.
Then, having recited the Vaiṣṇava Gāyatrī according to one's capacity,
as well as the glorious eight-syllabled mantra (vidyā), even if it is devoid of the ritual placement (nyāsa) and other such rites.
Facing the sun, one should constantly recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times, or even twenty-eight times; otherwise, it will not be accomplished within half a day.
Then, having praised the omnipresent Lord Nārāyaṇa with the Puruṣasūkta,
one should, with palms joined in reverence, mutter the Nārāyaṇa-sūkta.
Having restrained the vital breaths and formed the mental resolve (saṃkalpa), one should commence the rite of oblation;
having invoked the pervasive Lord of Sacrifice, the Consort of Śrī, into its midst with the Gāyatrī mantra.
O Lord of the Earth, having worshipped with ritual services and performed twelve oblations with the glorious eight-syllable mantra, one should then [offer] cow-derived ghee.
Having offered oblations twenty-eight times with the Śrī-mantra thereafter,
one should then offer twelve oblations into the fire for the limbs of the Lord of Śrī.
And according to Manu, having offered oblations with cow-derived clarified butter according to one's capacity and with due respect,
one should perform the recitation of the Ṛg, Sāma, and Yajur Vedas for the purpose of the Brahma-yajña.
One should satisfy the gods, the ṛṣis, and the ancestors with auspicious waters on Sundays,
Fridays, the thirteenth lunar day, the seventh lunar day, at night, and during the two twilights.
One who seeks spiritual welfare should never perform sesame libations in one's own home;
during optional vows, one should offer oblations once with the Raśmividyā mantras.
One should perform the complete recitation of the Vedas day by day according to one's ability,
and feed two Brahmins at the auspicious opening of the Veda (brahmavila) before the feet of the teacher.
Having bowed with palms joined in reverence, he sat upon his seat;
having restrained his breath (prāṇāyāma) and made the formal resolve (saṃkalpa), he performed all the ritual placements (nyāsa).
Being pure, one should recite the glorious eight-syllable mantra a thousand times;
or one may recite it five hundred times, or even four hundred times.
One should daily recite three hundred or one hundred and eight times;
having praised the Lord, the husband of Śrī, with the Nārāyaṇa Sūkta.
Then, one should recollect even once the Great Vidyā of a thousand syllables;
thus one may approach the King of Atharvaṇa for the sake of attaining security, well-being, and the fulfillment of goals.
When midday has arrived, having bathed and sipped water thereafter,
one should perform the daily evening twilight rite (saṃdhyā), pure and facing the sun.
One who is unable or afflicted by disease should bathe with warm water;
even if unable to bathe regularly, one should do so at the times of morning and midday.
Having wiped his body with a moist cloth, he shall become pure;
and at midday as well, having worshipped the Gāyatrī according to his ability.
One should worship the Lord of Indra (Indira-pati) upon the disc-marked Śālagrāma stone if a pair of the preceptor’s sandals remains in the temple. (93)
Having worshipped with all ritual offerings, one should thereafter worship Śīpati.
One should always place a small sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) near the sandals.
Having given [the gift] or having formed a resolve in the mind, one should offer it month after month;
indeed, by the worship of the sandals (pādukā) with their qualities, one performs the satisfaction [of the ancestors] for three years.
He will certainly behold the Lord of Śrī directly with his own eyes;
he shall attain great accomplishment through the mantras—of this there is no doubt. (96)
One should worship Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa upon the discus-marked stone of Sālagrāma, or one should constantly worship Pārvatī and Parameśvara upon a liṅga. 97.
Then, having performed the Vaiśvadeva rite according to the ordinance of Manu,
he offered food soaked in cow's ghee into the fire in twelve portions.
After offering the *bhūtabali*, one should feed the preceptor (*ācārya*), as well as his wife and sons, with food accompanied by [offerings to] the Sun and other deities. 99.
Then he should offer to the preceptor raw rice, soup, and other such items;
or else, wealth equal to a year's worth of food at the feet of the preceptor.
If one desires one's own success, one should offer [gifts] on the auspicious festival days;
nevertheless, something should be given daily at the feet of the teacher.
Even if one intends it with a focused mind, whatever is offered month after month [to the deity] and then eaten by Rudra is called *nirmālya*, and is unfit to be consumed.
That which has been eaten by Viṣṇu should be offered; even that is recorded as unfit for consumption [for others].
That which remains after being eaten by the preceptor is nectar, the destroyer of sins.
The remains of an offering, the presented oblation, and that which is joined with the remnants of the sacrificial food are declared pure by the Veda;
otherwise, they are considered impure.
One who eats without bathing eats filth; one who eats without reciting prayers eats pus and blood;
one who eats without offering oblations eats worms; and one who eats without giving gifts becomes a consumer of poison.

One should recognize as a guest (atithi) a person who has traveled a long distance, who is weary from the road, and who arrives at the conclusion of the Vaiśvadeva rite; one should feed such a guest with great care.
The teacher, one's father, mother, wife, son, and likewise a guest—
these six should be fed here every day with various kinds of food.
He who eats without having first served his teacher with food, clothing, and other necessities— doing so constantly and inevitably— surely eats of hell.
If one eats vegetables, soup, or even ghee every day without first offering it to one's own teacher,
one certainly eats only sin.
One must certainly feed one's father, mother, wife, sons, and guests with various kinds of food, such as solid foods, as well as those to be sucked or licked.
One should eat the fivefold meal while mentally recollecting Śrīpāra;
having eaten as much as desired, one should wash the hands, the feet, and the mouth.

At the conclusion of the meal, one should, with a concentrated mind, perform the remembrance of the deities; thus the man shall reach the end of the acquisition and preservation of worldly existence. || 12 ||
Then, at the time of evening, he should commence the evening twilight ritual (saṃdhyā),
having performed the evening fire-oblation (homa) and half of the mantra of the Lord of Śrī.
The wise one should then recite one hundred and eight times the supreme Anuṣṭubh mantra consisting of eighteen syllables, which is the essence of the array of wheels.
Having performed the recitation according to his ability, he should then eat together with his kinsmen;
with his mouth fragrant from betel, he [should worship] the two lotus-feet of the Guru.
Having bowed with palms joined in reverence while mentally recollecting the Narmadā,
he then remembered the Lord who is the husband of Śrī, and thereafter Añjaneya.
Then he should sleep on a white bed; thereafter, performing the Vedic rites with devotion day and night, he should sleep on his left side. (117)
At the end of the body, one attains that supreme state of Brahman.
[Thus ends the sixth chapter in the Śrīmadanuttarabrahmatattvarahasya, the Dāśarathīya Tantra, known as the Vedārthasaṃgraha.]
The Blessed Lord said: Once again I shall fully declare the Vedic conduct that brings glory,
by performing which a person in this world may attain great spiritual welfare.
From the rite of impregnation until the cremation ground, such is the Vedic ritual for the twice-born;
he who is devoid of Vedic conduct is considered dead even while living.
At the beginning of the recitation for a son, a twice-born man should first perform a bath with his clothes on;
having sipped water (ācamana), he should diligently perform the Hiraṇyābhyudaya-śrāddha.
One who is firm in his vows should give gifts of cows, gold, and the fruits of sacrifice,
as well as betel, perfumes, garlands, and ornaments.
One would remain impure for ten days; yet one may perform Vedic rites, and even during birth or death impurity, one must not abandon the Sandhyā ritual.
A twice-born man should recite the mantras mentally, except during breath control (prāṇāyāma).
On the eleventh day, he should perform the naming ceremony (nāmakarma), and thereafter [the other rites].
Or, from the third year onwards, one should perform the tonsure ceremony (caula) and the feeding of Brahmins;
for a Brāhmaṇa, the initiation (upanayana) should take place in the eighth year from conception.
The initiation for Kṣatriyas should take place in the eleventh year, and for Vaiśyas in the twelfth;
from that point onward, he shall remain a celibate student for the sake of mastering the study of the Vedas.
Having gone to the teacher’s household, he should constantly engage in the study of the Vedas;
he must not transgress his command, nor fail to provide sacrificial fuel, flowers, kusha grass, and other such items.
The one of great intelligence should constantly collect alms and practice the mendicant's way of life;
having always prepared food from those alms, he should offer it to his guru.
By his command alone one should eat, remaining composed, the food left over by him;
one should always reside in his empty dwelling and constantly sweep his house. (11)
He should perform the washing of clothes, massaging the feet, and so forth;
having studied the Vedas—whether all four, two, or one—a twice-born man according to his ability.
One should marry a woman who is distinguished by her unviolated vow of celibacy, who has not belonged to another before, and who is sleeping, departing, or even weeping. (13)
Then he gave her to another man who was a speaker of truth— a shaven-headed woman born of a diseased family,
with red hair and beard, tawny eyes, and a deformed body.
O high-minded King, one should avoid a girl who has a protruding belly, a long neck, or is afflicted by many diseases during her selection for marriage. 15.
She should be healthy, have brothers, be beautiful, and endowed with auspicious marks;
she should be born into a family of Vedic scholars and always devoted to the worship of the household deities.

If she possesses the auspicious marks of a woman, she enjoys domestic happiness eternally; therefore, for the sake of the prosperity and happiness of the household, one should marry a woman endowed with such marks.
If one has a favorable wife, what happiness is there even in the third heaven, O King? If one has an unfavorable wife, what suffering could even hell itself provide? (18)

Submissive wives, sons of good conduct, a wife devoted to her husband like a consort of knowledge, faithful spouses, delight in righteousness, and association with the virtuous—these five are the uprooters of the root of suffering. (19)
The sixteen nights of women’s fertile period are those following menstruation; during that time, he should approach her on the even nights.
Four nights should be avoided, and he should not approach her on the odd nights. (20)
When the moon has entered the eleventh mansion and is endowed with the strength of the moon and the stars,
one may engage in union with women, except on the occasion of the Ekādaśī festival.
One should not engage in sexual intercourse during the day, nor should one gaze upon the female organ;
likewise, falsehood, the smell of liquor, and fifthly, sexual union by day [are forbidden].
The evening twilight, when performed outside, purifies the food of a Śūdra;
likewise, the gods, the ancestors, and the sages always [accept the offerings] of the householder.
Even worms, insects, and other such creatures come here to this hermitage for the sake of sacrificial offerings;
therefore, this householder’s stage of life (gṛhasthāśrama) is said to be the most excellent of all stages.

A householder who has acquired wealth through righteous means, is devoted to the knowledge of reality, is fond of the lunar days, performs ancestral rites, and speaks what is true, is said to be liberated while still living.
While performing the complete recitation of the Vedas, he should investigate the meaning of the Veda. || 15 ||
She should be healthy, have brothers, be beautiful, endowed with auspicious marks,
born into a family of Vedic scholars, and always devoted to the worship of the household deities.
If one possesses the wealth of the characteristics of women, one enjoys the happiness of domestic life constantly;
therefore, for the sake of the prosperity and happiness of the home, one should marry a woman endowed with auspicious marks.
If one has a compliant wife, what happiness could there be even in heaven?
If one has a hostile wife, what suffering could there be even in hell? (18)

A submissive wife, a son who fulfills one's desires, a wife devoted as a companion to learning, a chaste wife, delight in righteousness, and association with the virtuous—these five are the uprooters of suffering. (19)
The sixteen nights of women's fertile season are those; among them, he should approach her on the even nights.
Four nights are to be avoided; he should not approach her on the odd nights. (20)
When the moon has reached the eleventh mansion and is endowed with the strength of the moon and the stars,
one may engage in union with women, provided it is not on the occasion of the Ekādaśī festival.
One should not cross a river by swimming, nor should one gaze at the private parts of women;
one must avoid falsehood, the smell of liquor, sleeping during the day, and sexual intercourse with five types of women.
Excluded from the evening twilight devotion, she purifies the food of a Śūdra;
likewise, the gods, the ancestors, and even the sages always [purify] the householder.
Even worms, insects, and other such beings take refuge here for the sake of sacrificial offerings;
therefore, this householder’s stage of life is said to be the most excellent of all stages.

A householder who has acquired wealth through righteous means, is devoted to the knowledge of reality, is fond of guests, performs ancestral rites, and speaks what is true, is said to be liberated. (25)
By performing the complete study of the Vedas and reflecting upon the meaning of the Veda,
he is honored in the world of Brahmā for a hundred births as a Brahmin.
At the end of each birth and body, he enjoys the bliss of exhaustion in heaven;
and until the end of the eon, even in Satyaloka, he enjoys captivating pleasures.
Returning once more to the surface of the earth, he was born into a lineage of Vedic scholars (śrotriya),
constantly devoted to righteous conduct and dedicated to the recitation of the Vedas.
At the end of the body, having reached Kailāsa, one becomes equal to Rudra after having enjoyed great happiness for a thousand kalpas with devotion.
Returning again to the earth, born into a family of Veda-knowers,
he was pure and devoted to serving the lotus feet of his teacher.
And [he taught] the Brahma-vidyā, conjoined with the Bhagavad-raśmi-vidyā,
as well as the glorious eight-syllabled vidyā (Śrī-daṣṭākṣarī) together with all its ancillaries.
Upon the dissolution of that body, he worships the eternal state of the Blessed One;
he attains there a state free from rebirth—of this there is no doubt. || 32 ||
If the splendor whose nature is the Supreme Brahman does not abide within one's body,
then that auspicious and glorious eight-syllabled Vidyā cannot be attained by him.
Having performed sacrifices such as the Aśvamedha with complete sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā),
they enjoy divine pleasures in the world of Mahendra until the end of the kalpa.
Having returned once more to the surface of the earth and entered a human womb within a noble family, they perform virtuous deeds and are again endowed with the happiness of heaven. (35)
Furthermore, O Lord of the Earth, they attain a human womb once more;
there is rebirth again, death again, sorrow again, and happiness again. (36)
Indeed, in this body of mortals there is no happiness at all;
in sin there is suffering in hell, and in merit there is no happiness even in the third heaven.
When their merit is exhausted, even the gods cause them to fall from the heavenly world;
for even in heaven, happiness is comparable to suffering, like food mixed with poison. (38)
The sages who know the reality of Brahman declare that the bliss known as the bliss of Brahman is supreme, infinite, and indeed eternal. (39)

Day by day, through service to the pair of lotus feet of the true teacher, through the constant contemplation of the knowledge of Brahman, and through the recitation of the glorious eight-syllabled mantra; || 40 ||
Having attained the bliss of Brahmananda, he rejoices in the supreme state;
yet a day devoid of the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) for the lotus feet of the Guru is [as empty as] a void.
Those pure ones who know the reality of Brahman declare this to be "midday," if one desires the state of identity with Brahman in a single lifetime. (42)
Having performed service to the teacher with his life, his wealth, and even his intellect, he [attained] the knowledge of Brahman, which is joined with [the knowledge of] the rays. || 43 ||
One should perform the worship of the glorious eight-syllabled mantra along with its secret teachings;
for the householder alone is remembered as the best among all stages of life (āśramas). 44.

Having entered no other stage of life (āśrama), one may become happy through the bliss of Brahmanic joy, provided one enters the householder stage (gṛhasthāśrama) and is endowed with right conduct (sadācāra). || 45 ||
Bringing satisfaction to the gods, the sages, and the ancestors, he attained great majesty through their contentment and their grace. (46)
Through pleasing the teacher and through the direct grace of Nārāyaṇa, he rejoices in the immeasurable realm together with ten ancestors and ten descendants. (47)
One should place one's foot down purified by vision; one should drink water purified by a cloth;
one should speak words purified by truth; and one should accept wealth purified by justice. 48.
In times of distress, when alms from the four castes are unavailable,
the practitioner may even beg from those of the lowest birth and give the teacher’s fee.
By giving gold as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) amounting to hundreds of thousands of crores in sacrifices such as the Aśvamedha, one enjoys the fruit of those sacrifices. || 50 ||
A sacrifice with very meager sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) would destroy the sacrificer;
therefore, one should give abundant fees for the successful completion of the sacrifice. 51.
Or, having offered wealth equal to a year's worth of food at the feet of the Teacher, one obtains the fruit of the sacrificial fee for a thousand horse-sacrifices. (52)
By truth the wind blows; by truth the sun shines in the sky;
and the moon, Mars, and the other planets, as well as the days, abide in heaven through truth.
By truth alone even Mahendra attained sovereignty over the three worlds;
by truth one conquers the worlds, and liberation is established upon truth.
The truth of the Śruti and Smṛti has issued from the mouth of the Blessed Lord;
so too have the yogis beginning with Sanaka and the great sages beginning with Vasiṣṭha.
The celestial sages beginning with Nārada, the perfected ones (siddhas) such as Kapila, the guardians of the quarters beginning with Mahendra, and even the former lords of the elements; 56.
Those most righteous ones have attained supreme prosperity through truth;
the word of the Blessed One is true, and likewise, that which is proclaimed in the Vedas is true.
The word of the Brahman-sages is true, and the word of the gods is also true;
they are eternally knowers of the reality of Brahman and have reached the further shore of the Vedas and Vedāntas.
This which is called the Nārāyaṇīya is to be highly honored by householders for the sake of attaining the vision of Brahman; this very truth is spoken by me. 59.
Having become the son of Daśaratha, I [Rāma] expounded that compendium of the meaning of the Vedas, a system adorned with the Vedas and Vedānta, to Rudra who questioned me.
"I shall speak this great scripture in the presence of the Brahman-sages;
beginning from that point, O great seers, it is the treatise known as the Dāśarathīya."
O Lord of the Earth, they call this work by the name Vedārthasaṃgraha;
herein, whatever has been proclaimed in that Tantra known as the Dāśarathīya, [is contained].
All that should be accepted as if it were the Veda from the lotus-like mouth of the teacher;
therefore, a householder should constantly practice the gratification of the gods.
Devoted to the study of the Vedas along with Vedic conduct,
he was a seeker of Brahman-knowledge and a practitioner of the glorious eight-syllabled mantra.
Having perceived with his two eyes the direct realization of Brahman known as Nārāyaṇa,
he becomes one with Nārāyaṇa and rejoices in the supreme abode.

On the meritorious occasion of the sun's transit (saṃkrānti), during solar and lunar eclipses and the like, when rare astrological conjunctions (yogas) have occurred, and even during the nine nights of Navarātra; || 66 ||
Abundant wealth should be given to the pair of lotus-feet of the preceptor;
furthermore, the gift of land and the gift of cows must be offered without exception.
The gift of a Śālagrāma stone is for the sake of attaining the vision of Brahman;
and one must certainly offer a pair of earrings upon the ears of the preceptor.
Abandoning stinginess with wealth, this auspicious vow of the nine nights must certainly be performed on a Friday for the sake of attaining prosperity and fortune. (69)
One should constantly honor the wives of the three [officiants]—the preceptor and the others—with ornaments, clothing, food, and abundant offerings such as betel leaves and the like. (70)
She should be worshipped with special care by disciples in all religious observances as well, with the thought that she is Mahālakṣmī, for the sake of attaining the fruits of the four aims of life.
On auspicious festival days, wealth and other gifts should be given even to worthy recipients;
however, the preceptor alone is said to be the most excellent recipient among all worthy ones.
O Lord of the Earth, one who constantly studies the Vedas and is endowed with virtuous conduct is called a worthy recipient (pātra) in the Vedas and the scriptures. (73)
One who acts contrary to the Vedas is called an unworthy recipient, the lowest of the twice-born;
for the sake of purifying his body, he should wait either six months or a year.
O Lord of the Earth, one should eat the remnants of food left over from the preceptor’s house;
furthermore, one should not even ask for the preceptor’s fee or wealth within his family.
Having personally offered the sacrificial wealth into the two lotus-feet of the teacher, one directly perceives Brahman within six months.
By reciting the Dharmaśāstras and the Itihāsas and Purāṇas, one may deliver even a thousand families dwelling in hell.
Men should listen [to the teachings] every day at the mouth of the teacher;
a day devoid of the teacher’s fee is called barren.

Whatever may be given, even the slightest, should be offered daily at the feet of the teacher for the sake of accomplishing all branches of knowledge and for attaining the fruit of the realization of Brahman. (79)
One who gives a book of the Dharmaśāstras, a book of the Itihāsas, or even a Purāṇa, attains the fruit of liberation. (80)
Having diligently accomplished it, one must certainly give gifts;
thus, one will always possess the prosperity of never being separated from one's wife, sons, and others. 81.
On a Saturday, the vow that accomplishes the goal should be performed by the best of men;
the five great sacrifices must always be performed by Brahmins of celebrated vows.
The sacrifice to the gods, the sacrifice to the ancestors, and thereafter the sacrifice to the spirits;
then there should be the sacrifice to humans, and after that, the sacrifice to Brahman.
This oblation with fuel-sticks, performed every day at dawn and dusk, is called the sacrifice to the gods (devayajña); it is declared to be the means for attaining heaven.
He who daily gratifies the fathers and grandfathers with sesame seeds performs what is called the Pitṛyajña, which wards off the obstruction of time.
The offering of a portion to the spirits that is given is called the *bhūtayajña*; that which consists of the gift of food to the twice-born is called the *nṛyajña*. (86)
O King, he who studies even a single Ṛg verse, a Yajus formula, or a Sāman chant, this is declared by the most eminent knowers of Brahman to be the Brahma-sacrifice (brahmayajña). (87)

For the successful completion of the recitation and fire-offering (*japa-homa*) of the illustrious eight-syllable mantra (*vidyā*), one should offer some fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the preceptor (*ācārya*) according to one's ability. (88)
The sacrifice named Vaiṣṇava should be performed daily;
through the six sacrifices, the Lord, who possesses the perfection of true qualities and sovereignty, is manifested. (89)
One who constantly performs the six sacrifices shall attain absorption in the Blessed One.
The five sacrifices are proclaimed for the purpose of gratifying the gods, sages, and ancestors. (90)

When midday has arrived, having offered an oblation to the spirits upon the ground, the Vaiṣṇava sacrifice should indeed be performed for the sake of attaining the prosperity of the fortune of liberation.
Then, in the courtyard of the temple of Godāhemātra-vaikālantiṣṇedra,
one should honor the guest who has arrived there with a welcome and other such courtesies.
Likewise, by the gift of a seat, by washing [the guest's] feet, by the offering of food with faith, and by listening to what is pleasing; || 93 ||
A householder should inspire joy by following those who arrive from a distant land whose family name and lineage are unknown. (94)
A twice-born man who has arrived as a guest is to be recognized as such, even if he resides in the same village;
one should not inquire about his Vedic study, his lineage, his branch of the Vedas, nor likewise his family.
When a guest arrived at the end of the street of Hiraṇyagarbha,
thousands of guests used to eat in his palace.
One should certainly feed at least one teacher; one will surely obtain that fruit.
[One should also partake of] the water used for washing the two lotus-feet of the venerable teacher.
By drinking it, one attains internal purity; by holding it on the head externally, O Lord of the Earth, the fruit of bathing in all sacred fords is accomplished. (98)
I shall speak of the lotus feet of the Teacher; one should drink that water.
Both the ascetic and the student are the rightful owners of cooked food. (99)
Having eaten the food of those two and having discharged it, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance;
one should give water into the hand of an ascetic, and one should give both alms-food and water.
That alms-food is equal to Mount Meru, and that water is like the ocean;
yet the teacher, turning his face away, takes it and returns home. (1)
By that very [merit], they go to the deities together with the ancestors;
the wise must certainly provide sustenance for the wife and sons of their teacher.
Rising early every morning, the wise should reflect upon that which was promised by mind and speech to a poor family man.
That [debt] would become even greater than it was at the outset and cause fear regarding the next world;
therefore, that debt, which bestows the happiness of heaven, must be repaid immediately.
Even a promised fee for a preceptor of virtuous conduct, though smilingly offered as a mere niṣka coin,
becomes a great debt that must be repaid even from atop Mount Meru.
Starting from the day of the initial agreement, that object, together with its interest,
must be returned within one month or even within two months.
Whatever fruit one obtains by giving hundreds of millions of riches to thousands of Vedic scholars,
that same fruit one attains at the feet of a true teacher.
Even by giving a single gold coin (niṣka), one obtains a fruit greater than that;
for they say there are three supreme gifts: a daughter, land, and knowledge (Sarasvatī).
O Lord of the Earth, by giving a daughter adorned with ornaments to a poor man,
one goes to the world of Brahmā at the end, and one's ancestors become partakers of heaven.
The wealth of a maiden given to the twice-born leads to the state of hell in the next world;
[one should give] to a Brahmin who is the sole father of his marriage, who is poor, and who has mastered the Vedas.
Necessarily, at the end of this life, even those ancestors who reside in hell shall ascend the divine Puṣpaka chariot and, together with their ancestors, [attain liberation].
One certainly attains the state of a Lord here; of this there is no doubt.
The particles of dust of the earth may be counted, and the stars in the sky may be counted. (12)
O Lord of the Earth, even the Creator does not reckon the fruit of establishing a Brahmin firm in the Veda who is poor. (13)
Having given wealth for the sake of marriage, he attains imperishable increase of his lineage here,
and reaching the world of Brahmā, he dwells there as long as the moon and stars endure.
Then, giving to a learned but poor Brahmin a Mahīsā sacrifice well-prepared and accompanied by many sacrificial fees, together with four bulls; || 15 ||
In the presence of the Blessed One, he rejoices together with his ancestors;
[he beholds] the earth abounding in ripened crops and accompanied by four excellent bulls.
Having placed his two feet upon the teacher's feet along with a sacrificial fee, he caused even a thousand ancestors who were submerged in the ocean of hell to be uplifted. (17)
Having raised up the divine Puṣpaka chariot and ascended it together with his ancestors, he,
possessing a form identical to that of the Blessed One, rejoices in the abode of the Blessed One.
Having bestowed the Vedic knowledge along with its secret doctrines upon the Brahmins,
the Brahmin attains a state of worshipfulness and rejoices together with Brahmā.
By giving a manuscript of the Itihāsas, the Purāṇas, or the Rāmāyaṇa,
one shall become a master of all branches of knowledge.
At the end of the fall of this body, one shall attain Satyaloka;
there is no interval between the gift of a Śālagrāma stone and the destruction of the great sins of Māyā.
Even a single Śālagrāma stone, endowed with the pure circle, fashioned from the diamond-insect (vajrakīṭa), and accompanied by a gift for the officiant; 22.
O Blessed One, having adorned and given [this], one shall attain proximity [to You];
whatever fruit a man obtains by the gift of ten million cosmic eggs (brahmāṇḍas), [that he obtains here]. || 23 ||
One shall obtain that same fruit by the gift of a Śālagrāma stone;
food should be given daily, especially to Brāhmaṇas. (24)
One should consider the raw food to be double the amount of that used for the Vaiśvadeva and other rites;
[one should give] a milch cow with her calf, accompanied by a bell-metal vessel.
Having adorned her with golden hooves and the tips of horns, and with garlands and gold,
even the poor who give such a cow to a householder [attain great merit].
One attains Goloka, endowed with divine enjoyments,
where the rivers flow with leaves and milk, and where sins are like mere mud.
Wherever trees such as the *parijāta* and others grow, there he dwells;
[he gives] especially to the preceptor a milch cow with her calf.
Having offered [the gift] either once, twice, thrice, or accompanied by many sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) at the abode of the Blessed One, he rejoices together with his ancestors.
O Blessed Goddess, he who respectfully drinks the milk, curd, and ghee from her [cow] is equal to ten thousand ancestors, including his own father.
O Brahmins, O lord of the earth, one who sells cows—whether they have been captured or not—rejoices, possessing a form like that of the Blessed One and enriched with divine enjoyments. (31)
Together with his ancestors, he sinks into the hells until the end of the kalpa;
[this applies] to all three types of ornaments when they are provided with rubies.
A pair of auspicious earrings, radiant like refined gold and described as divine ornaments, should then be placed upon the ears of the preceptor.
One shall obtain the fruit of great gifts, such as the tulāpuruṣa-dāna;
indeed, one will certainly possess a form resembling that of the Blessed Lord in Vaikuṇṭha.
The giver of fine garments rejoices in the city of Śakra;
by the gift of a horse, one attains equality with Kuvera in his station. (35)
He who especially gives a palanquin to the preceptor will certainly become a partaker of divine enjoyments like an elephant on Mount Kailāsa.
Endowed with the wealth of that life, or having shaken off his sins through [the merit of] the field,
he ascends a celestial chariot bearing the Garuda-banner and is possessed of divine enjoyments.
In the presence of the Blessed One, he attains the foremost rank among servants;
together with his ancestors, he assumes the very form of Nārāyaṇa.
If the preceptor should bestow an auspicious small bell,
he who constantly worships it will certainly attain the state of Brahman.
Having offered pure gold, liquids, garments, ornaments, and so forth to the Brahmins, one should especially offer them to one's own preceptor.
At the end of the body, she shall dwell with her ancestors in Satyaloka;
therefore, one should daily offer vegetables, ghee, and other such things to the preceptor.
At the end of the body, the conscious soul attains the enjoyment of heaven;
[this is achieved by] food offered to Viṣṇu, combined with the remnants of the sacrificial oblation (havis). || 42 ||
Even one who eats only the remnants of the food consumed by the teacher is liberated from their committed sins at that very moment.
One should eat food silently, without disparaging it;
this "great silence" of five mouthfuls is for the purpose of nourishing the vital breaths (prāṇas) and the rest.
One should not look at the sun as it rises, nor when it is setting; nor when it is eclipsed, nor when it is reflected in water, nor a naked woman who is another's wife.
He should never sit on the same seat as the teacher;
he should not dwell on a higher seat, nor should he sleep within the range of the teacher's bedpost.
One should never, under any circumstances, step upon a pair of the Guru’s sandals; nor, having stepped upon a sandal during the day, should one enter the village by the middle [door].
Approaching women during their menstrual periods is extremely bitter and harmful to great men;
it bestows sin upon men by day, and one should not even look upon the womb of such a woman. 48.
O King Campaka, at the end of the day he should duly and properly perform the evening twilight worship with the sun, and the morning twilight worship accompanied by the stars.
A king is required to visit the pleasure garden at all times during the two twilights, except in cases of birth-impurity, death-impurity, confusion, illness, or fear. (50)
O King, that Brahmin who is abandoned by the sun at sunrise, or who does not sleep while the sun is shining, must perform penance upon the ground; such is the distress for him.
Therefore, O Lord of the Earth, having risen before the sun has appeared,
a man should himself perform the twilight worship (saṃdhyā) belonging to the beginning and end of the day.
Those evil-minded ones who do not perform the twilight devotions (saṃdhyā), neither the morning nor the evening,
certainly go to the Tāmisra hell.
Having thus lived as a householder for only a single birth,
one necessarily attains liberation along with ten ancestors and ten descendants.
By performing only the obligatory and occasional rites, one brings about the destruction of evil and purifies knowledge; through such practice, one should seek [liberation]. || 55 ||
A person whose realization has become true through practice attains liberation;
one who does not belong to any stage of life (āśrama) should not remain anywhere even for a single moment.
The student, the householder, the forest-dweller, and the mendicant—these, O lord of the earth, are the four stages of life for the twice-born. (57)
If the thought of the forest-dweller’s stage of life has arisen in a householder,
he should entrust his wife to his sons, or depart together with her.
There too, serving the teacher, with his senses restrained, having offered oblations in the evening as well as in the morning, and having performed the Cāndrāyaṇa and other penances; || 59 ||
Whether subsisting on withered leaves or even eating fruits and roots,
he should bring satisfaction to the deities, the sages, and the ancestors.
Performing the complete study of the Vedas, chanting the glorious eight-syllabled mantra,
and remembering the Lord Nārāyaṇa, one shall attain the station of Viṣṇu.
If detachment arises, then the wise man should go forth,
especially by constantly serving a true teacher.
While performing [this], he should not eat in one place; being intent on that, he should practice the *praṇava*.
When the pestle has been set aside and the food has been consumed, [he should remain] in the state of *vibhūti* (the ashes).
One should go for alms to five houses or even seven,
always keeping one's mind fixed on Nārāyaṇa and performing salutation to the teacher.
Day and night, the husband, being pure and constantly devoted to serving his teacher,
must certainly mutter the glorious eight-syllabled mantra.
Constantly practicing the three sixfold duties, free from desire, with senses conquered,
he possessed only a single garment, a staff, and a water-pot as his wealth.
He should not look at gold, silver, or even iron anywhere;
he should always keep his face turned away from women, remaining free from passion by taking refuge in the Vedānta.
By constantly practicing the secret doctrine (upaniṣad), one shall attain perfection;
the teacher alone is the refuge for all, and no other is ordained.
The Ordainer and the Non-Ordainer, Brahmā, and even the Blessed Lord Śaṅkara;
Ravi, Soma, Mahendra, the Grandfather, the Mother, the Preceptor, and the Friend. (69)
For those who desire to cross over the ocean of saṃsāra in this world, the teacher alone is the path;
for the virtuous, there is only one refuge in the lotus feet of the teacher. (170)
This auspicious rite prescribed by the Vedas has been explained by me.
O protector of the earth, what more do you wish to hear beyond this? (171)
[Thus ends the seventh chapter in the venerable *Anuttarabrahmatattvarahasya*, the *Dāśarathīya Tantra*, which is a compendium of the meaning of the Vedas.]
The King said:
"O Blessed One, Lord of the gods of gods, Nārāyaṇa, Master of the universe!
The conduct of the virtuous as ordained by the Vedas has been heard by me from your lotus-like mouth. (1)
For the sake of attaining the direct realization of Brahman, what should men constantly perform with devotion, beginning from the Brahma-vow? (2)
"O Blessed One, you have told me that by reciting the *Raśmimālā*, how can liberation be attained by men in this very life through a single birth? (3)
"O ocean of mercy, please speak to me the *Bhagavadraśmisūkta*.
The Blessed Lord said:
"Listen, O King, I shall explain that which you ask of me. (4)
By merely hearing it, even the most grievous sins are destroyed;
therefore, having risen at the hour of Brahmā, a twice-born man should listen with a focused mind. (5)
One should first recite the mantra of the Guru’s sandals day after day;
being composed, one should utter the Praṇava, the seed-syllable of the Citkalā, at the beginning.

Then [one should write] the seed-syllable of Śrī (ŚRĪM) devoid of the bindu, followed by the word "Bhagavat," then the title "Rūpācārya," and finally the name of the previous teacher preceded by "Śrī."
Beyond this is the eight-syllable mantra: "I worship the Śrīpādukā. Then follows the Ācāryapādukā-vidyā, which is most secret and auspicious.
She is the one who bestows the great sovereignty and the great siddhis upon the great kings; she is the destroyer of great sins and the bestower of perfection in the vidyās. || 9 ||
I am indeed the sandals of the Teacher, the knowledge, and the sage;
that which is called the *Chandoga* and the *Gāyatra* is the Teacher, who consists of the Blessed One.
The deity is the True Guru, the Lord, the Omniscient One, the embodiment of compassion;
this is declared to be the application [of the mantra] by the masters accomplished in compassion. || 11 ||
I worship the Swan (Haṃsa) upon my head— the source of the cool-rayed moon within the thousand-petaled lotus, the lotus-like hand of Śiva,
the embodiment of all deities,
the bestower of all mantras, and the abode of all splendors.
Having first addressed the Guru by name. || 12 ||
In the thousand-petaled lotus at the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra), she possesses the luster of the full moon;
her eyes are filled with compassion, and her lotus-face is serene.
His hands display the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness; he is adorned with white perfumes, garlands, and the like;
he wears white garments and is embellished with divine ornaments. || 14 ||
Accompanied by his own power, seated in the heroic posture (vīrāsana), a treasure-house of compassion, the giver of all sciences, and affectionate toward those who have come for refuge. || 15 ||
I worship the omniscient Ācārya, who possesses the form of the Blessed One;
having meditated thus at the time of Brahmā, one should recite the mantra of the Ācārya’s sandals. 16.
One should constantly recite it twenty-eight times or even twelve times;
by this, one becomes worthy of performing the recitation and fire-offerings (japa-homa) for all vidyās.
With this mantra, O Teacher, having reverently worshipped the two sandals with the five-fold offerings (pañcopacāra) and honoring them twelve times with flowers; || 18 ||
Then, having offered whatever fee as a gift upon the pair of the teacher’s sandals,
one should daily place it at the lotus feet of the teacher.
O King, whether giving month by month or even year by year,
one may offer even vegetables, ghee, and other such items daily upon the ground.
One who has known what is to be known and whose dispositions are constant shall be entitled to the recitation of mantras and other rites, even without formal instruction. (21)
Having worshipped the pair of the Guru’s sandals with golden flowers, he becomes a perfected one even without the preliminary rite (puraścaryā). || 22 ||
When an auspicious festival arrives, one should worship the pair of the teacher’s sandals with flowers and other offerings, and give wealth equal to a year's worth of food.
Having placed them upon the sandals and offered them at the feet of the preceptor,
or in his absence, one should entrust them to his son.
Or by offering Mount Meru, a million yojanas in extent, to his wife;
he shall obtain a fruit even greater than that which one receives from giving [the aforementioned gift]. || 25 ||
One attains great perfection in that [place] within a year—a perfection difficult even for the gods to obtain among all branches of knowledge; of this there is no doubt. (26)
O King, by reciting the mantra of the Guru’s sandals every morning, or even at other times,
one first attains great accomplishment among all mantras.
One who desires the complete perfection of all sciences, daily auspiciousness,
and great fortune must chant the sandals of the Guru.
O King, without having recited the mantra of the Guru’s sandals every day,
one does not attain the perfection of the mantra even after reciting it a thousand crores of times.
I shall describe the sequence of the garland of rays; listen, O high-minded King, by the mere recollection of which one is eternally liberated from sins. (31)
The Great Knowledge (Mahāvidyā) beginning with the Gāyatrī is the Mother of the Vedas and the bestower of fruits;
indeed, this eight-syllabled knowledge (Aṣṭākṣarī Vidya) destroys all mental and physical afflictions.
Then follow the two great twelve-syllable mantras of Dattātreya, and the fourteen-syllable mantra of the great sage Vaiśampāyana. (33)
The twelve-syllable mantra of Śrī Śiva is the embodiment of all knowledge;
it is the Brahma-vidyā of the three worlds, which should be remembered as the bestower of all perfections. 34.
Then follows the Mātṛkā consisting of fifty syllables;
thereafter, one should remember the glorious eight-syllabled Vidyā, which is supreme even beyond the fallen.
The eight-syllabled Mahālakṣmī-vidyā bestows all supernatural powers (siddhis).
Then there is the six-syllabled Śrī-mahāvidyā, and thereafter the twelve-syllabled [mantra] of Śrī,
the sovereign lady of the great lion-throne of all prosperity and imperial sovereignty.
Therefore, this twenty-seven-syllable mantra bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
hence, it is called Vasundharā, the Kalpalatā (Wish-fulfilling Creeper) of knowledge and liberation.
Then follows the eighteen-syllable mantra of the Lord of Lakṣmī (Pāśrīpati), half [of which];
then the twelve-syllable Great Vidyā, and thereafter the auspicious Nārāyaṇī.
Then follows the Brahmā-Nārāyaṇī mantra, preceded and followed by the Praṇava;
thereafter, the Haṃsa-Nārāyaṇī Vidyā is to be remembered. (39)
Furthermore, there is the Vidyā-Nārāyaṇī accompanied by Śrī and Padmā;
after that, there is also the Aṣṭākṣara-Mahālakṣmī.
O King, when properly combined, the auspicious Vidyā-Nārāyaṇī, the Vidyā known as Ānuṣṭubh, and Hayagrīva bring about these results.
Then [the worship] of the Blessed One in the form of the Fish, auspicious;
then that of the Great Knowledge of the Tortoise and the Boar; and after that— || 42 ||
And then, O King, [he heard] that which is called the Nṛsiṃha-anuṣṭubh of Yāmana,
then that of Bhārgava-rāma, and thereafter that of Daśarathi.
Then follows the Śrīkṛṣṇa-vidyā, then the Caturvidyā, and thereafter the vidyā of the Supreme Soul, the Lord of Śrī, in the form of Kalki.
Then follows the Great Vidyā of the Three Names, which bestows all fruits;
and the Great Vidyā of Sudarśana, which destroys all fears. (45)
Then follows the Garuḍa-vidyā, and after that the auspicious Hanumat[-vidyā]; the Bhagavad-raśmi-mālā-lepa is proclaimed as bestowing all perfections.
It is the destroyer of all mental anguish and physical disease, and the dispeller of sins and other afflictions;
it was first narrated by me to Brahmā, the supreme lord.
To Rudra, the Lord of Gauri, he shall speak once more in the form of Śrī Rāma,
in the presence of all the gods and the great sages.
O treasure of austerity, this sixteen-syllable mantra of the Lord of Śrī, which is recited by some, brings about that which is beyond the mind and constitutes half of the body of the Consort of Śrī.
Some mutter the names of Añjaneya and Garuḍa even without [the prescribed] recitation; others likewise mutter the Vasundharā-vidyā even without [the prescribed] recitation. (46)
O Lord of Speech, know this complete Vidyā, named Raśmimālikā, which is established with its own garland of rays. || 47 ||
Even each single Great Vidyā, abiding within the garland of rays, possesses a supreme fruit that cannot be fully described for each individual Vidyā. (48)
O King Raśmisraja, even Parameṣṭhin was not capable [of mastering] this knowledge,
Raśmisrajā, which bestows the accomplishment of all fruits.
Know that the Atharvaṇī [Vidyā], which directly bestows the accomplishment of the vision of Brahman, belongs to that brahmin in whom the compassion of the Teacher arises. (50)
Indeed, the garland of rays bestows great accomplishment upon that very person who serves his own teacher, a treasury of compassion, for even many years. (51)
The garland of rays is to be attained by serving with one's life and wealth;
the giver of the garland of rays is the Lord, the giver of the garland of rays is the Father.
The giver of the garland of rays is the Mother; the giver of the garland of rays is the Guru.
This very one is to be known as the true Ācārya by those most learned in the scriptures. (53)
O King,
the most excellent Manus are the very essence of the Ṛgveda, the Yajurveda, the Sāmaveda, and the great Atharvaveda.
Others, having been shielded by the garland of the Blessed One’s rays, [attained this]; and through him, they [attained] this Ātharvaṇa knowledge from a teacher who had practiced it for many years.
Having served him with all his wealth, even with his life and his intellect,
and having constantly attained [him] at the Brahma-hour, he whose vows were well-undertaken— || 56 ||
Having performed the preliminary rite (*puraścaryā*) for all the vidyās by reciting them once, twice, thrice, four times, or even five times, one shall obtain the fruit.
Desiring a mass of all auspicious things and every kind of prosperity, one should recite the *Raśmimālikā*, filled with the compassion of the Teacher. (58)
Consisting of all knowledge, possessing the nature of all deities, and the Lord of Śrī, he is composed of all the Vedas; therefore, [one should offer] a garland of rays of the Blessed One.
Having recited it daily, one whose self is purified becomes directly composed of Brahman;
by means of this *bhagavadraśmimālikā*, which is to be recited constantly.
By him, all the Ayurvedas along with their auxiliary branches shall be studied day after day;
all the deities will undoubtedly be granters of boons to him.
By one who desires to certainly attain the bliss known as Brahmananda at the end of the body,
the Raśmimālā mantra should be recited five times or even three times.

Without having given this garland of rays of the Blessed One, which bestows auspiciousness, nor even the glorious eight-syllable vidyā accompanied by its ritual placement (nyāsa), [how can one attain the goal]? 63.
Having bestowed this fivefold [knowledge] upon himself and his disciple, he becomes a guru;
for even a single science is worth the entire earth with its seven continents.
O King, why should the teacher’s fee be given in the form of rays of light or dust?
Therefore, one must certainly go to the teacher even if he is many yojanas away.
One who desires to cross the ocean of saṃsāra in a single birth should take refuge in the Omniscient One, pleasing him with all one's possessions.
One may obtain this garland of rays from the lotus-face of the Teacher at the conclusion of the recitation of the Brahma-vidyā, or before it, or indeed at any time.
Having established himself in the supreme secret of the Brahman-vow, and having recited the glorious eight-syllabled mantra, he shall become one who experiences the bliss of Brahman-joy. || 68 ||
O King Janaka, do not entertain doubt in this matter;
this tantra known as Dāsarathīya is equal in significance to the meaning of the Vedas.
He who is endowed with the teacher's grace understands the secret;
having traveled a great distance, he should take refuge in the teacher alone as his wind.
Those who worship the teacher day after day with the thought that he is the Blessed One attain great perfection both in this world and in the hereafter.
What is the use of much speaking in this matter? I shall tell you this one thing: day after day, [one should worship] the two lotus feet of the Guru alone.
Those who have taken refuge here at Vaitarāṇī and whose nature is absorbed in the Blessed One,
shall attain great perfection even in this world and obtain liberation.
Thus, O Great King, the majesty of the garland of rays has been briefly described to you; what more do you wish to hear beyond this?
[Thus ends the eighth chapter in the glorious *Anuttarabrahmatattvarahasya*, the *Daśarathīya Tantra*, which is a compendium of the meaning of the Vedas.]
The King said:
O Blessed One, you who have spoken all things without exception, O treasure-house of compassion!
This garland of rays from the Blessed One has issued forth from the lotus of your mouth.
This work is a compendium of the essential meanings found in all the Vedas and Shastras;
please describe, in due order, the majesty of each individual branch of knowledge.
The Blessed Lord said: Listen, O King, I shall declare that which you ask of me;
by the mere hearing of it, one attains great perfection.
Having risen at the hour sacred to Brahmā and having recollected the sandals of the Ācārya,
[one should meditate] thereafter upon the garland of rays belonging to the Blessed Lord, the Consort of Śrī.
She who is to be meditated upon, the eternal cause of all accomplishments—
therein, first of all, I shall fully proclaim the Gāyatrī, the mother of the Vedas.
By the mere knowledge of which one becomes directly composed of Brahman:
the Praṇava, followed by "bhūr bhuvaḥ" and the two syllables "suvar."
That foot of Savitṛ is beyond [the sun], the most excellent;
after that, the word "bhargo devasya," and after that, "dhīmahi. (7)
"May that [Brahman] who impels our intellects... and so forth; one should extract this path.
The Gāyatrī, joined with the three Vyāhṛtis, consists of thirty syllables. (8)
She is the mother of all the Vedas, the bestower of the realization of identity with Brahman,
the destroyer of the flood of great and minor sins, and the granter of spiritual perfections.
On one side were all the arts and the Vedas together with the Gāyatrī; on the other side was this supreme [Gāyatrī] alone. When weighed by Brahmā in the past, this latter proved to be superior.
O King, Brahminhood is not attained through the recitation of the Vedas, the Purāṇas, and the Smṛtis, without the study of the Sāvitrī. (11)
That is the supreme reality, the Brahman of Savitṛ,
the Supreme Self, the Blessed Lord, the husband of Śrī, the God who is the Lord of the worlds.
We meditate constantly upon that which is most excellent and supreme, the all-pervading Bharga, within the lotus of the heart, as "I am indeed He. (13)
May that Lord Savitṛ himself, the husband of Śrī and the Sovereign God, who dwells within our own selves, eternally inspire our intellects. (14)
"O Great-minded One, that which is declared in the Śruti as 'pracodayāt' is said to be the impeller of all dharmas, constantly urging them forward. (15)
He who dwells in the midst of the solar orb is Savitṛ himself;
he is Nārāyaṇa, composed of the Vedas, the Great Person, the Lord.
Thus, the Sāvitrī, the mother of the Vedas, who bestows fruits, is as it were her verbal manifestation;
there is no mantra equal to the Gāyatrī, nor is there a city like Ayodhyā. (17)
There is no sacred ford equal to the Jāhnavī; there is no deity equal to the Lord of Śrī;
and there is no goal equal to the pair of lotus feet of the Preceptor. (18)

There is no happiness greater than the attainment of the Self, nor is there any sacred learning equal to the Vedas; yet, having failed to attend upon the Sāvitrī, one directs one's mind elsewhere. (19)
O King, one should know him as an outcaste, excluded from all religious duties, who does not daily worship the Mother of the Vedas many times over. (20)
Even after reciting ten million *mantras*, one hears of no success whatsoever;
therefore, one must certainly recite the *Gāyatrī* many times every day. (21)
Or even by remembering it but once, one shall attain supreme accomplishment in the vidyā;
he who, being pure, recites the Sāvitrī mantra a thousand times every day.
Indeed, even after traveling many thousands of yojanas, one would encounter that twice-born man, who was a manifestation of the Lord himself and honored by the Brahmanical seers.
One should honor the teacher for the sake of attaining the realization of the glorious eight-syllable mantra;
all the Vedas, sacrifices, sacred fords, vows, and so forth, taken together, [are not equal to it]. (24)
If one should be thus smeared with excessive impurity on one side,
one must certainly recite the Gāyatrī mantra a thousand times every day.
One should recite either five hundred times, or four hundred,
or three hundred, or two hundred, or one hundred and eight times.
One who is afflicted by disease should mutter it twenty-eight times;
Gāyatrī alone is the Supreme Brahman, and Gāyatrī alone is the Supreme Hari.
Gāyatrī alone is the supreme Brahman; Gāyatrī alone is the supreme Śiva.
Gāyatrī herself is visibly the three Vedas, having the nature of the Word-Brahman (Śabdabrahman).
By the power of the Gāyatrī alone, the Kṣatriya Kauśika, observing his vows,
abandoned the status of a royal sage and attained the rank of a Brahman-sage.
Therefore, the sage Viśvāmitra is said to be the seer (ṛṣi) of the Gāyatrī;
its meter is Gāyatrī, and its deity is Savitṛ, the Supreme Lord.
The Lord of Śrī, the Great Yogin, the Divine Nārāyaṇa, is remembered [as the Self].
Agni is His mouth, Brahmā His head, and Rudra, the Lord of Umā, His tuft of hair (śikhā).
The heart-mantra is Viṣṇurekhā; she is called the womb of the earth.
Her application (viniyoga) is declared to be for the sake of attaining the fruits of the four aims of life. || 32 ||
Accompanied by ten *praṇavas* and preceded by the seven *vyāhṛtis*,
this should be recited three times daily during the *kumbhaka* phase of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*).
One should recite the Gāyatrī, which is said to consist of three feet and is endowed with the triad of the syllable Om; it is speech that is without beginning or end, the cause of all things.
Having meditated upon the eternal one, consisting of all splendor, named Brahman-Nārāyaṇa, the supreme mother of all the Vedas, one should worship her.
O King, the uninterrupted worship performed every day at the three junctions of the day is declared to be its *puraścaraṇa*, which bestows the perfection of the Lord’s own form.
He who recites the Sāvitrī mantra one thousand and eight times every day is liberated from even the most grievous sins and minor transgressions within a single month.
Having recited the Gāyatrī mantra a thousand times with devotion for three years, one becomes equal in intellect to the perfected ones (siddhas) who possess the form of the Blessed Lord.
Having recited the Mother of the Vedas twenty-four hundred thousand times,
even a killer of a Brahmin, a drinker of liquor, and a stealer of gold is liberated.
Whatever fruit is obtained by men through reciting the Gāyatrī ten million times,
that same fruit one enjoys by offering a thousand oblations of sesame seeds in the Saṅghana fire.
O King, by offering a thousand oblations of sesame seeds during the solar transits (saṃkrāntis),
one beholds the Blessed Lord situated in the center of the solar disc.
For the sake of attaining identity with Brahman and for constant purification,
one should daily recite the Mother of all the Vedas many times.
Having not recited the "Mother of all Vedas" many times every day, one does not attain mantra-perfection even through ten million preliminary rites (puraścaraṇa).
Having first offered ghee twenty-eight times and also twelve times, one attains the fruit of the oblation for all vidyās.
He who is the illuminator of the entire world by his splendor, the mass of all lights, the essence of all parts, and the leader of time. || 45 ||
The Lord Sūrya— the illustrious Śrīśa, Nārāyaṇa, the infallible Acyuta— is said to be his inner controller, who daily impels even him.
He alone is the supreme Viṣṇu; he alone is the supreme Śiva;
he alone is the supreme Rudra; this Acyuta is the embodiment of the three Vedas.
Know that all-pervading Lord Nārāyaṇa, who is mounted upon the chariot drawn by the Vedas, resides within the lotus of the heart of all embodied beings. 48.
In the forenoon, they constantly praise the omnipresent Lord Nārāyaṇa, the master of the world, who is the Supreme Self of all moving beings and whose form is Brahman.
At midday, the Yajus hymns praise him who is the Lord of Śrī in the form of Rudra—
the one worshipped by the three worlds, whose form is the universe, and who is higher than the highest.
In the evening, the Sāman hymns praise that all-pervading Lord, who is composed of Viṣṇu himself, the husband of Śrī, the supreme Sovereign.
The Lord Savitṛ, the husband of Indirā, is the destroyer of the mass of darkness within and without;
he is manifestly the Blessed One, the Lord of the three worlds who possesses the three qualities.
Therefore, by daily worshipping the Sāvitrī many times,
one shall obtain from its study the fruit of all three Vedas.
He who performs sacrifices such as the Aśvamedha and others will certainly become a master of all sciences and shall remain so eternally. (54)
Having gone to the world of Brahmā, he is honored within the assembly of Brahmā.
O King, listen attentively as I shall declare the eight-syllabled mantra of Sāvitrī.
Having known this, the wise practitioner attains imperishable perfection.
Having uttered "Praṇava" (Oṃ) and "Ghṛṇi," one says the two syllables "Sūrya. (56)
"Ādityoṃ"—thus the learned know this auspicious eight-syllabled Sāvitrī mantra;
it is the destroyer of all mental anguish and physical ailments, and the eradicator of all diseases. (57)
The auspicious Karīśubhā, who bestows splendor, power, fame, speech, and garments, is declared to be his divine portion; the sage Brahmavidāṃvara is [his] portion. (58)
The metre is said to be Gāyatrī, and the deity is proclaimed to be Savitṛ;
its application (viniyoga) for the propitiation of the Blessed Lord has been declared by the great seers. || 59 ||
From the words *satya*, *brahmā*, *viṣṇu*, *rudra*, *vahni*, and all the [directional] terms,
[one obtains] the word *tejojvālāmaṇi*, followed by *huṃ phaṭ* and then *vāhnipriyā*.
Having performed the placement of the six limbs (utkāṣaṣṭhāṅga), one should meditate upon Ravi, the Lord of the World,
who holds two lotuses and dwells in the center of a circle of splendor.
Having meditated thus— worshipping the body with its shadow as the pacifier of all diseases— the donor should mutter the auspicious eight-syllabled Sāvitrī mantra.
Free from all mental anguish and physical disease, the radiant one beholds Brahman in each and every ray during rites such as recitation and fire-offerings.
Having ascertained one's own inclination for each individual *māṣa* [unit of time], one should recite the mantras daily during the study of the garland of the Bhagavat’s rays and vidyās.
O King, having recollected the *chaṃda*, the *āryā*, and so forth, it should be recited daily;
O Lord of the Earth, [this is the procedure] for the entire collection of the Bhagavat’s rays and vidyās.
I alone am declared to be the sage, as well as the son of Dvaipāyana; the meters such as Gāyatrī and others, and the twice-born ones such as Viśvāmitra and the rest [are likewise my forms]. 66.
O King, the sages of the various branches of knowledge beginning with the Vedas have been described;
even therein, the all-pervading Lord consists of all splendors and possesses manifold meters.
The Lord of All, the Virāṭ, the Lord of Śrī, and the Lord of the worlds—Hari, Nārāyaṇa, the Master—is proclaimed as the Deity. (68)
The application (viniyoga) is declared to be for the pleasure of Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa; [he beheld] the mass of [light], countless and turning the quarters of the sky tawny. (69)
I salute the Blessed Lord, the husband of Śrī, who consists of a garland of rays.
Having thus recited the garland of rays, one should perform the placement (nyāsa) of the seers, meters, and other elements.
When the power for the recitation of each of the vidyās of the rays has been attained,
one should then perform the placement of the respective ṛṣi, the meter, and the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) for each.
The practitioner should recite all mantras and also perform oblations;
the eight-syllabled Sāvitrī lore bestows great supernatural powers.
It constantly removes disease and grief and bestows the bliss of Brahman-joy;
one should perform the preliminary rite (puraścaryā) by reciting it eight hundred thousand times and offer milk as a tenth part of that number.
One should offer clarified butter ten times the number [of recitations] as oblations, and the mantra will become perfected;
or else, on a Sunday coinciding with a solar parvan.
Beginning from the time of touching [the body] until the end of the time of liberation,
one should reverently offer oblations into the auspicious, consecrated fire using sesame seeds mixed with cow-ghee.
Having given a pair of auspicious earrings to the ears of the preceptor,
and having bestowed the earth abounding in abundant crops along with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
Having recited twelve hundred thousand times and having offered libations with cow's milk, one attains the unsurpassed perfection of the eight-syllabled Sāvitrī mantra.
Having offered twelve thousand oblations of sesame seeds soaked in cow's ghee, one is liberated from the many various types of leprosy. 78.

Having recited the mantra three hundred thousand times, and then having offered oblations of milk-rice soaked in the three sweets (honey, ghee, and sugar) according to one-tenth of that number, one is liberated from wind-related diseases.
One should daily offer a thousand oblations of clarified butter for one month;
thus, one is liberated from fistula, urinary diseases, and impaired digestion.

One should daily offer three hundred lotuses soaked in cow’s ghee; by performing a thousand oblations for one month, one will certainly and eternally attain great and unshakable prosperity from the Maṇḍala.
One should offer blue lotuses daily, saturated with the three kinds of honey;
thus one is liberated from the disease of indigestion and from terrible eye diseases.
By offering one hundred and eight oblations daily with Aśoka flowers,
one shall be liberated from headache as well as from unbearable diseases of the root [the feet].
One should constantly offer three hundred oblations of rice mixed with curd and saturated with the three sweets;
by means of this maṇḍala, one is liberated from various kinds of diseases of the limbs.
Having consecrated water with the mantra one hundred and eight times, the practitioner,
by rinsing his mouth, will certainly be liberated from diseases of the oral cavity.
Having recited the mantra sixteen hundred thousand times and having offered one hundred thousand oblations of cow-ghee,
he is liberated even from networks of incurable diseases that are most difficult to endure.
Free from disease, radiant, and long-lived, the practitioner here attains great fortune endowed with qualities such as the power of atomization (aṇimā) and the rest. (87)
He who, having bathed every morning, recites this one thousand and eight times day after day, goes without a doubt to that supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
His prosperity, sons, health, and splendor increase,
and at the end of his body, he attains that supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
The greatness of the Veda-mother and of the eight-syllabled Sāvitrī has thus been declared;
now that of Ātreya and Vyāsa shall also be told.
[Thus ends the ninth chapter of the *Śrīmadanuttarabrahmatattvarahasya*, the *Dāśarathīya Tantra*, which is a compendium of the meaning of the Vedas.]
The Blessed Lord said: I shall describe the greatness of Dattātreya, Manu, and Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana; by knowing which, one attains great perfection.

The Praṇava, the seed-syllable of the noose (Pāśa), Māyā, and the goad (Aṅkuśa), followed by the vowel of Indra (the letter 'I') and the seed-syllable of space (Ha) joined with the third vowel (Ī). || 2 ||
After "Dattātreyaparam," one should then recite "Vahnipatnīm.
Thus is declared the single great mantra (mahāvidyā) of the yogi Dattātreya.
First the Praṇava, then the word "hṛdayam," then the word "bhagavate," and after that the word "dattātreya" followed by the fourth case ending.
This second [mantra], which is praised by Atri and Nandana, has been proclaimed;
one should recite this vidyā either individually or recite both together.
My very own auspicious form is named Datā, which bestows the perfection of yoga;
it grants the attainment of the sovereignty of all vidyās and bestows liberation.
Those yogins and followers of Sāṃkhya-Kapila who desire the state of liberation—by them this great vidyā of Dattātreya should be chanted; by it they are exalted.
Immovable and great sovereignty, as well as imperishable mastery over speech;
yoga endowed with its eight limbs, and the eternal knowledge of Brahman.
One who desires to remember past births should recite the mantra of Dattātreya;
likewise, one desiring the eightfold supernatural powers (siddhis), such as the sandals, collyrium, and the sword, [should do the same].
O Lord of the Earth, the great vidyā of Dattātreya should be recited;
it wards off the great fear arising from thieves, enemies, and wicked conspiracies.
O Lord of the Earth, this vidyā, which brings about the protection of unlost property and the recovery of what has been lost, should be recited by one who desires these things. 11.
The seer is Atri of great splendor; the two branches of knowledge belong to Dattātreya;
the meter is said to be Jāgata; and its essence consists of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva. 12.
The Lord Dattātreya Harisvāmī is declared to be the Deity;
Māyā is the Śakti, the seed-syllable of the noose (pāśa), while the goad (aṅkuśa) is known as the kīlaka. || 13 ||
Furthermore, from Dattātreya, they say that for this knowledge, the *praṇava* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*) and *natti* is the power (*śakti*), for the sake of attaining identity with Brahman.
The application for the sake of pleasing Dattātreya has been declared:
the syllable *māyā* (hrīṃ) joined with the six long vowels, and the six limbs with the two syllables *kuśa* (kṣauṃ). || 15 ||
In the heart of the piṇḍa, one should directly meditate upon Hari as Attātreyi,
resembling a dark blue cloud and adorned with a circle of matted locks.
His entire body adorned with celestial ornaments, endowed with peerless heroism,
he was seated upon a divine lion-throne at the foot of the Pārijāta tree.
He is served by great yogis such as Sanaka and others, and is affectionate toward his devotees;
he holds the mudrā of the knowledge of reality in his right hand, and likewise the gesture of fearlessness in his left.
He is joined by the lotus-serpent, adorned with golden earrings,
with a gracious countenance, peaceful, and possessing a beautiful smile like a lotus.
Accompanied by Anasūyā and Atri, it was praised by the Brahman-sages,
and served by hosts of Siddhas and Vidyādharas as well as great ṛṣis.
Adorned with divine ornaments, accompanied by Śrī standing at his left side,
and served by Nārada and others— he is the Lord of the three worlds.
"I worship this Dattātreya, the Supreme Lord";
having thus meditated upon Dattātreya as the Great Vidyā, he, being pure, chanted [the mantra]. || 22 ||
O King, one who performs the preliminary rite (*puraścaryā*) three hundred thousand times for each individual mantra certainly becomes a knower of the reality of all sciences (*vidyā*).
The practitioner should offer ten parts of the oblation into the fire, soaked with the three sweets;
then, having given a sacrificial fee to the Guru, the adept may even give his entire possession.
O Lord of the Earth, by means of the great lore of Dattātreya, one attains unsurpassed perfection,
whether one is devoted to fasting or [performs it] during an *atyatīpāta* yoga.
Having recited [the mantra] nine thousand times, one should offer oblations of Kapila-ghee into the blazing fire;
then, as the tenth part [of the recitation], one should present two earrings to the preceptor.
Having given those two earrings made of gold set with gems to his pair of ears, and having given three sacred threads along with a pair of garments; || 27 ||
One attains eternal perfection in the great vidyās;
even a single great vidyā of the yogi Dattātreya [is sufficient]. (28)
By reciting [the mantra] three thousand one hundred times every day with devotion, one will,
within six months, become endowed with the eightfold supernatural powers, beginning with *aṇimā*.
Having recited the mantra one hundred thousand times at the seashore or in a cow-pen while observing a milk-vow,
and having offered oblations of milk-rice mixed with clarified butter, one becomes a treasury of knowledge.
Having risen at the time of Brahmā, and having meditated with care upon the three sons [of Brahmā],
one should recite the mantra one thousand times, or once, or even twice.
Or else, within six months, he beholds with his own eyes Dattātreya, the Lord of the Universe, who bestows all perfections. || 32 ||
If one should see one's own wealth, such as cattle and other property, carried off by thieves,
one should constantly recite [the mantra] three thousand times at night while facing the western direction.
Within seven nights, one obtains lost property without a doubt; having recited the mantra one hundred and eight times near a crop of grain, [the same result follows]. (34)
No fear of thieves and the like, nor any sorrow, shall ever exist on earth for that man who, having recited [the mantra] one hundred and eight times, travels upon the road. (35)
There shall be no fear from wicked thieves, tigers, or enemies who lie in wait;
and during afflictions such as all kinds of diseases, one should perform a thousand recitations of the mantra.
Even one who seeks the eightfold yoga, subsisting on fruit and observing fixed vows, shall be liberated from even incurable clusters of diseases within three days. (37)
Having recited [the mantra] three thousand times daily for a month without weariness, one who practices the eightfold yoga certainly becomes a sky-walker (khecara). || 38 ||
Seated at the foot of an aśvattha tree in the forest, subsisting on a diet of milk and firm in his vows,
he constantly recited the mantra three thousand times.
O son of Atri, being pure, one should daily recite this single Vidyā of mine; thereby one shall obtain from the circle of women prosperity abounding in wealth and grain.
Having conquered his senses and observed his vows with praise, he who has recited the mantra a thousand times for a full year, whether in the abode of Viṣṇu or in the house of Rudra; || 41 ||
Within a year, he obtains prosperity endowed with eightfold qualities,
as well as the auspicious and incomparable perfection of speech along with the yoga consisting of the eight limbs.
Having obtained prosperity consisting of sons and grandsons, unsurpassed long life,
and the eight kinds of enjoyments, one shall attain liberation at the end.
