This yantra of the son of Atri consists of a hexagon, an octagon, an eight-petaled lotus, and a square; it bestows the abundance of great fortune. (48)
Having worshipped Dattātreya, who is accompanied by Śrī, in the center of the hexagon,
one should worship the six limbs in the six corners and the Father (Pitṛ) with Anasūyā.
Sanatkumāra, Sanaka, Sananda, and after him Sanatsujāta; Prahlāda and after him Kārtavīrya. (46)
Having worshipped Indra and the other [deities] in the eight corners, and [the others] on the eight petals;
thus [one worships] the son of Atri, the Lord himself, endowed with Śrī.
By constantly worshipping with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, one attains eternal auspiciousness.
O King, hereafter I shall proclaim the mantra of Dvaipāyana.
This is the means of accomplishment for all devotees, bestowing the success sought by everyone;
it consists of the syllable *praṇava* joined with "namas," followed by "to the Blessed One" (*bhagavate*). (49)
Then, from the right nostril, one should draw forth the second sibilant (Ṣ) together with the thirty-first letter (KṢA), followed by the word "Dvaipāyana. (50)
This auspicious, syllable-by-syllable mantra of Parāśara’s son is proclaimed as this very Vidyā, joined with the dative case ending. (51)
I myself am that other form known as Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana, who brings forth glory and is the very essence of the truth of the Vedas and Vedāntas. 52.
Born of Parāśara from Satyavatī, she was the son of Śakti;
she was the divider of the Vedas and the benefactress of the worlds. (53)
The teacher of all the worlds, the omnipresent son of Parāśara, known by the name Dvaipāyana, is the Lord Hari himself, the infallible Acyuta. (54)
He became the instructor of all branches of knowledge to his disciples;
rising at the hour of Brahmā, he would remember the sandals of his teacher.
O Dvaipāyana, having first recited the great vidyā three hundred times, or even twenty-eight times, with a concentrated mind; || 56 ||
One should mutter the Brahmavidyā preceded by the garland of rays [of the syllable Om], and one should constantly contemplate the teacher as being identical in form with Vedavyāsa. (57)
Indeed, there is not even a trace of difference regarding the teacher Dvaipāyana;
he is the Supreme Self, the Teacher, manifest in the form of Dvaipāyana himself. (58)
By meditating upon him constantly and worshipping him well, one obtains the bliss of Brahmananda;
Vādarāyaṇi is declared to be his sage (ṛṣi), the best among those who know Brahman.
"Jagatī is said to be the meter; O Lord of the Earth, the great yogi Vedavyāsa is declared to be the very essence of Nārāyaṇa, a god. (60)
The application for the sake of propitiating Vedavyāsa has been declared:
[with] one syllable, two, four, or seven. (61)
Furthermore, the ritual placement of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa) is declared to be performed with three Rudra-mantras.
[One should meditate on the Lord] seated upon a divine lion-throne, possessing the luster of a dark blue cloud at the time of universal dissolution.
Wearing a tiger-skin garment, bearing a mass of matted locks,
displaying the mudrā of pure consciousness, and seated in the vīrāsana posture.
[He beheld] the Teacher of the World, whose every limb was adorned with ashes, whose lotus-face was serene, and whose lotus-face was made radiant by a pair of earrings. (64)
It was served by the personified four Vedas, by Śuka and other foremost among yogis,
and was surrounded by throngs of Siddhas who were knowers of Brahman.
I worship the sage Dvaipāyana, the speaker of all sciences, whose eyes are filled with compassion—the Lord himself in person. (66)
Having thus meditated upon his preceptor Dvaipāyana, who is identical with Nārāyaṇa,
one should worship him within a six-spoked yantra provided with five triangles.
Having worshipped Vedavyāsa, the teacher of the world, in the center of a six-cornered [diagram] adorned with a square and provided with eight petals, || 68 ||
One should worship Parāśara, Śuka, Paila, Vaiśampāyana, Jaimini, and Sumantu in the six corners.
The Ṛgveda, the Yajurveda, and beyond that the Sāmaveda;
then the Atharvaveda, and after that the Itihāsa (the Epics and Purāṇas). || 70 ||
Having worshipped [the deity] in the five-cornered [mandala], one should then worship the great sage Yājñavalkya, named Romaharṣaṇa, upon the eight-petaled lotus.
Likewise, one should worship the sages Kātyāyana, Udaka, and Audalaka,
as well as Baudhāyana and Āpastamba, and the lords of the directions in the four squares.
Thus, one should daily worship the preceptor Dvaipāyana, the source of all sciences and the refuge of all prosperity. (73)
O Vedavyāsa, one who is purified by reciting this great mantra three hundred thousand times quickly becomes a knower of Brahman and attains liberation while living. 74.
One should offer oblations amounting to one-tenth [of the total] using black sesame seeds soaked in cow’s ghee;
O King, having given twelve niṣkas to the feet of the preceptor.
O Vedavyāsa, one attains unsurpassed great accomplishment through this great rite;
or else, on a pure Ekādaśī in either the month of Kārttika or Māgha.
One who is firm in his vows should always recite the mantra while abstaining from food;
on the twelfth lunar day, he should offer a thousand oblations of Kapila cow’s ghee into the fire.
Having given a pair of auspicious earrings to the ears of the teacher,
[he gave] the book of the narrative called the Mahābhārata, complete with all its sections.
Or, O King, having offered to the preceptor a copy of the Dharmaśāstra with its commentary, or a Purāṇa, along with a sacrificial fee of three niṣkas, as prescribed; || 79 ||
Having fed the Brahmins, he then attains unsurpassed success;
he who, being pure and constant, resorts to the root of the Aśvattha tree according to the rule.
If one recites the Manu-mantra one thousand three hundred times, one will undoubtedly become a master of all branches of knowledge within three months. (81)
Always wearing white garments and seated upon a tiger skin,
Vedavyāsa, being restrained in his vows, chanted the great vidyā one hundred thousand times.
Having recited this Lākṣa-mantra and having diligently propitiated the Guru, || 84 ||
Through wealth, grain, and garments, one becomes a treasury of all knowledge;
one attains vast prosperity and certainly becomes a knower of Brahman. || 85 ||
This knowledge dispels the dullness of the intellect for one whose mind is inert;
even when recited by others for a mute person, it bestows the perfection of great speech. (86)
Having constantly recited the great mantra of Vedavyāsa a thousand times in the presence of his preceptor for one year, he became pure in soul with his senses subdued. (87)
Having attained long life, health, sovereignty, and the supreme perfection of speech,
he directly beholds the Supreme Brahman.
The wise man should constantly worship the teacher with all manner of offerings, regarding him as Dattātreya or even as Vedavyāsa.
Ambarīṣa and others, Kaca and other great sages (maharṣis),
Vṛṣaparvan and other Daityas, and Udaṅka and other best of the twice-born (dvijottamas).
And the brahmins headed by Gālava, observing the vow of silence, day after day considered the body to be perishable and worldly existence to be filled with suffering. (92)
O King, one should daily worship the feet of the preceptor with devotion, using wealth, grain, ornaments, and all other articles.
One should daily serve the peaceful teachers who are free from egoism;
by doing so, they attain in a single birth that perfection which is difficult to achieve.
Endowed with a portion of the Blessed One, you shall therefore become liberated while living;
thereafter, having attained a physical body crowded with suffering upon the earth... (94)
He who does not worship the teacher—who is himself subject to birth, death, and old age—and for whom there is no full grace of the teacher upon this earth, [is lost]. (95)
(*** ) He who is submerged in the ocean of saṃsāra is born again;
yet, he who desires to cross the ocean of saṃsāra in a single lifetime [should practice this]. 96.
Having constantly performed service to the teacher and being firm in his vows,
he [should receive] the garland of rays preceded by the knowledge of the teacher’s sandals.
Having obtained the knowledge of Brahman and the twelve-syllable mantra of Śrīśa,
one should mutter the glorious eight-syllable mantra accompanied by all the ritual placements (nyāsa).
Having attained the bliss of Brahmananda and being endowed with a portion of the Lord, he becomes one whose form resembles the Lord and who is a servant of the Lord. || 99 ||
O Great King, this knowledge belongs to Dattātreya and even to the sage Dvaipāyana; it has been told to you—what more do you wish to hear? 100.
Thus ends this tenth chapter, surrounded by those possessing knowledge of Brahman, in the *Dāśarathīya-tantra*, a compendium of the meaning of the Vedas. (101)
[Thus ends the tenth chapter in the venerable *Anuttarabrahmatattvarahasya*, the *Dāśarathīya Tantra*, which is a compendium of the meaning of the Vedas.]
The King said:
O Blessed One, Lord of the gods of gods, Nārāyaṇa, Master of the universe!
I have heard from the lotus of your mouth the garland of rays of the Blessed One.
I have also heard the majesty of Sāvitrī and the eight-syllabled Sāvitrī mantra,
as well as the majesty of Dattātreya and of Dvaipāyana.
"I now wish to hear the majesty of the knowledge of Brahman.
Thus questioned by Ṛṣyaśṛṅga, the venerable Lord, the husband of Jānakī, spoke. (3)
He related to Rudra that which was uttered by Nārāyaṇa in the past.
The Blessed Lord said: "Listen, O King, I shall proclaim [the glory] of the Supreme Self, the Lord of Śrī."
The majesty of the knowledge of Brahman, by hearing which one becomes a partaker of liberation,
is contained in this compendium of the essential meaning of all the Vedas and the Upanishads.
The greatness of the twelve-syllabled mantra of Śrī-Śrīśa destroys all fear;
it is the supreme Brahman, which is beyond the reach of mind and speech.
Devoid of beginning, middle, and end, the Puruṣa exists by his own will;
his power is named Citkalā, the auspicious Mother of the entire universe.
That Great Being is called by the name Nārāyaṇa;
he is the Supreme Person accompanied by that power whose nature is consciousness.
Thus, from the lotus of my own navel,
I created the Unborn, the Self-Existent Lord, the Ordainer, known by the name Viśvasṛṣṭividhāyaka (the Ordainer of the Creation of the Universe).
Seeing that the Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati) was incapable of creating the world, I,
the all-pervading Nārāyaṇa, who am the manifest Supreme Brahman, [spoke].
For the sake of attaining identity with Brahman, I have received from Dakṣa this Śrī-Śrīśa twelve-syllable mantra, by which I am endowed with its fruit.
At the time when he received the Great Vidyā, the twelve-syllabled mantra of Śrī-Śrīśa, from the instruction of the twelve syllables, Dhātṛ attained the status of Brahmā.
I, Mahākāla, have bestowed this which is known as Brāhmī;
because the Vidyā is of the nature of Brahman, they call it Brahmavidyā. || 13 ||
Because it was given by me to Brahmā at the time of Brahmā, it is designated as "Brahmavidyā" through its bestowal during that sacred hour. (14)
It should be recited at the time of Brahmā; therefore, it bestows the desired fruit.
Because it is the cause of identity with Brahman, this is proclaimed as the "Knowledge of Brahman" (Brahmavidyā). || 15 ||
O King, because it is the cause for the attainment of the state of Brahman and even for that of the Creator, they call this ten-syllable mantra, beginning with the word "Śrī," the "Brahmavidyā. (16)
By the mere non-grasping of this [intellect], the self-existent four-faced one,
having become composed of the Supreme Brahman, created the entire universe.
Through the constant recitation of the Brahmavidyā,
the indestructible power of the Lord entered the body of the supreme Brahman, Parameṣṭhin.
Enveloped by my luster, Brahmā is worthy of worship even throughout the three worlds;
he possesses the agency over all the worlds as well as the qualities such as *aṇimā* and the rest.
He attained the great perfection consisting of identity with Brahman;
therefore, this twelve-syllable mantra of Śrī-Śrīśa is known as the Brahmavidyā (the Knowledge of Brahman).
Having necessarily recited [the mantra] at the Brāhma hour, which bestows all auspiciousness,
one should rise during the Brāhma hour and call to mind the sandals of the Ācārya.
By constantly chanting the Brahmavidyā, the twelve-syllabled mantra of Śrī-Śrīśa,
one attains eternal auspiciousness as well as imperishable riches.
By this very authority, the glorious twelve-syllabled queen of mantras has become superior to all other vidyās, even among the Vedas.
That very Vidyā by which auspicious results are accomplished day after day through recitation, fire-offerings, and other rites, is remembered as the most eminent among all Vidyās. || 24 ||
O King, from whichever mouth one obtains this knowledge and on whichever auspicious day, starting from that very day, there shall be a constant succession of supreme welfare. (25)
He alone, who consists of the Blessed One, is to be known as the remover of all misfortunes and the supreme teacher; one should constantly [worship] that very omnipresent Lord.
One should honor [the teacher] with wealth, grain, and so forth, and by such acts as massaging his feet; one should never, even in thought, practice malice toward that guru.
One should not even mentally utter a word of censure toward anyone, anywhere;
nor should one ever go to a place where such censure might be heard. (28)
If there should arise agitation in the mind of the teacher who bestows the knowledge of Brahman, they fall away from their prosperity consisting of sons, friends, wives, and so forth. (29)
Having reviled even once the teacher who bestows the knowledge of Brahman,
one attains the state of a village pig and is subsequently born among the Caṇḍālas.
At auspicious places and times, having abandoned the Guru who bestows the knowledge of Brahman, one gives wealth, grain, ornaments, and other auspicious things to someone else. (31)
Even after giving to a knower of Brahman, one might become averse to the Blessed One;
having abandoned the prescribed action enjoined by the Vedas, the twice-born man becomes intent on something else. (32)
He is submerged in most terrible hells until the moon and sun cease to exist;
yet he constantly and with devotion nourishes the wife and children of his preceptor.
Since this has been enjoined by the Vedas, the Vedāntas, and those who know Brahman,
one must therefore certainly [take refuge in] the two lotus-feet of the Guru.
Having honored him with heaps of jewels, wealth, and garments with great respect, one may give these even to another who knows Brahman, or one may not give them at all. (35)
They know that the worship of the teacher is the direct worship of the Goddess;
they know that the worship of a virtuous wife is the direct adoration of Mahālakṣmī. (36)
In the absence of the preceptor, one should worship his son as if he were the preceptor;
and in the absence of the preceptor’s wife or sons, [one should worship] the Lord of Śrī.
One should offer every object in its entirety, at the proper place and time;
all that offered object [yields fruit] even if one has traveled many yojanas away. || 38 ||
One should bestow the teacher's property upon the teacher’s wife, or his son, or his grandson, or else one should hand it over to his brother. || 39 ||
By performing prohibited conduct and by avoiding that which is not prohibited,
one enters into blinding darkness until the dissolution of all beings.
Therefore, practitioners must daily support the wife and children of their preceptor and others, with constant and diligent effort. (41)
During auspicious places and times, after performing rites such as recitation (japa) and fire-oblations (homa),
one should thereafter provide sustenance for one's ancestors, followed by the support of one's wife, sons, and others.
One should recognize the teacher as one's father, and his wife as the goddess Śrī.
O high-minded one, know that Vidhātṛ was his son, Śakra was his grandson, and that those born in his lineage were the Sanakas and others.
By nourishing his father and mother, there is no exhaustion of his enjoyment in heaven;
by nourishing his wife and others, he enjoys inexhaustible happiness in this world. (47)
O King, by nourishing the wife and children of the preceptor and others day after day,
at the end of this life, I grant him my own form.
One should abandon one's own mother and father; one should abandon other elders as well;
one should abandon one's own wife, sons, and so forth, and one should abandon brothers and kinsmen. (49)
One should never abandon the preceptor who bestows the garland of rays (initiation), even at the time of universal dissolution;
nor should one abandon one's mother, father, brother, or kinsman.
One may kill or abandon one's son, kinsman, or even a teacher of sacred knowledge, as well as one who reviles the preceptor.
"Let all my kinsmen, including my wife, sons, and others, revile me;
let people laugh at me upon seeing me, or let kings punish me. (52)
"The pair of lotus feet of the Teacher's feet alone is my refuge; may such a thought remain firm even for me when I have fallen into calamity. (53)
He crosses over the cycle of worldly existence; people may praise him or revile him, and prosperity may stay or depart—yet he finds both enjoyment and liberation. (54)
One should not abandon one's teacher even at death, as if it were the end of the age;
he who bestows the knowledge of Brahman is a master, he who bestows the knowledge of Brahman is a father.
The giver of the mother is Brahmā-avidyā; the giver of Brahma-vidyā is the Guru;
the one who directly imparts Brahma-vidyā is called the Ācārya, and no other.
Having served for either ten years or even a hundred years the Teacher, who is the embodiment of the Blessed One and a treasure-house of compassion, || 57 ||
One should study the twelve-syllabled mantra of Śrī-Śrīśa, which is the essence of the knowledge of Brahman;
it consists of the Praṇava, the letter *ma*, and the letter *u* adorned with the left eye (the vowel *ī*).
One should extract the syllable mounted upon *jātavedas* (the letter *ra*) and joined with the bindu;
then that same [syllable] without the bindu, followed by the third sibilant (*śa*) and the fourth dental (*tha*). (59)
He [visualizes] the field-seer as the fourth, and likewise the contact that has ascended to the intellect;
then he [visualizes] the long vowel, the seed-syllable of the tip of the left foot, followed by fire.
Then follows the seed-syllable of Vāyu joined with the letter *m* (the "mouth"), which consists of thirty-one syllables and is subsequently adorned with the long vowels and so forth. || 61 ||
The forty-syllable mantra consists of the letter *ya* (the long form of Vāyu) adorned with the nasal bindu;
when joined with the heart-mantra (*hrīṃ*), it becomes the twelve-syllable mantra of Śrī-Śrīśa.
This [scripture], known as the Brahmavidyā, which is a compendium of the essential meaning of the Vedas, has been declared;
it consists of all yoga and embodies the nature of all sacrifices and sacred fords.
She consists of all knowledge, she bestows the fruits of all desired objects, she is the destroyer of all sins and the eradicator of all diseases. || 64 ||
She is the remover of all calamities and the creator of all prosperity;
she bestows the abundance of long life, health, sons, wealth, and royal fortune. (65)
This eternal twelve-syllable mantra, which is the cause for the perfect realization of identity with Brahman, cannot be fully described even by me. (66)
Whoever desires eternal auspiciousness, inexhaustible prosperity in all its forms, and ultimately the imperishable state of the Blessed One in this very life—[should perform this]. (67)
He must certainly mutter the twelve-syllabled mantra of the illustrious Lord of Śrī.
The Pārijāta and other trees, as well as the Prajāpatis who possess the knowledge of Brahman,
dwell indeed within that palace as long as the moon and stars exist.
Divinity, immortality, or even the imperishable state of a Brahmarṣi is attained right here through the power of the continuous contemplation of the knowledge of Brahman.
Sacrifices accompanied by complete sacrificial fees, performed throughout many thousands of births—
even by such means, the twelve-syllable mantra is not attained.
O Lord of the Earth, the pursuit of the knowledge of Brahman and the contemplation of the garland of rays cannot be attained in this world through small effort or through mere austerity.

O King, having daily recited this eternal Brahma-vidyā, the twelve-syllabled mantra of Śrī-Śrīśa, at the time prescribed for Brahmanical rites through the grace of the preceptor, [one attains the goal]. 74.
Whether a thousand, five hundred, four hundred, or even three hundred times, the pure and wise one, having recollected the sandals of the teacher, [should recite]. (75)
Having recollected the garland of rays either fivefold or even threefold,
by this one shall become like me in this very birth, endowed with my kalā.
Even today, Brahmā, Rudra, and others, as well as the yogis such as Sanaka and his brothers, perform on earth that which is impossible to achieve and difficult even for the gods to obtain. (77)
Merely by the recitation of the Brahmavidyā, they attained imperishable perfection, as well as long life, freedom from disease, sovereignty, cattle, and riches. (78)
Furthermore, for one who worships the pair of the Guru’s sandals day after day, these eight kinds of enjoyments are not difficult to obtain. 79.
For one who practices the contemplation of the knowledge of Brahman during the hour sacred to Brahmā,
after the contemplation of the knowledge of Brahman, there follows the recitation of the *raśmi* [mantra].
Like a maidservant, the fickle Goddess Lakṣmī remained constantly in his house;
it was filled with an abundance of wealth, grain, arts, horses, pearls, and heaps of jewels.
Moreover, O King, Vāgīśvarī herself appears in his mouth like a servant,
constantly overflowing with various forms of knowledge.
O Great-minded One, among all the gods together with their retinues, and even among seventy million humans, no one is seen who possesses the mantra-deity of this Great Vidyā. 83.
And among all the Vedas and all the sciences without exception,
there is indeed only one that is like a crest-jewel, namely the supreme knowledge of Brahman.
Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa, Vāṇī and Dhātṛ, Girijā and Śiva, Śacī and Indra, Rohiṇī and Candra, Svāhā and Vahni, Prabhā and Ravi. (85)
Know that Agni and Soma are the Bindu and Nāda, as well as Prakṛti and Puruṣa; all forms of female and male are born from portions of Śrī and Śrīpati.
Therefore, this twelve-syllabled mantra of Śrī-Śrīśa should be understood as consisting of everything;
therefore, one should [worship] the twelve-syllabled Śrī-Śrīśa, which consists of all vidyās.
Japan is truly Virārāmaya; he himself is Nārāyaṇa manifest.
Within it are the fourteen worlds, together with all things moving and unmoving. || 88 ||
He dwells eternally within the bodies of those who contemplate the knowledge of Brahman;
he is the manifest sustainer of the universe, the teacher of the way to Brahman. || 89 ||
O Lord of the Earth, that very Hari is Brahmā and that is Śaṅkara;
one should daily worship with reverence this pair of the Preceptor’s sandals.
For those who daily engage in the contemplation of the knowledge of Brahman,
the bliss of heaven shall be inexhaustible in their home day after day.
The proud bow down before them, and their enemies become like servants; even their foes turn into friends, and deceit behaves as if it were virtue.
Even Dharmarāja would become their physician for the sake of their enjoyment,
while the Lord of Wealth and the gods, headed by Śakra, would perform service for them daily.
Indeed, even Maheśa and the others act as friends,
as do the yogis such as Sanaka and the great sages such as Vasiṣṭha.
Even the Goddess Brahmavidyā honors him daily,
for he is devoted to worshipping the two lotus-feet of his teacher.
O Lord of the Earth, wherever one who pursues the knowledge of Brahman resides,
that very place is declared to be a field of perfection (siddhakṣetra), extending ten thousand yojanas in every direction.
In that very place, all sacred fords (tīrthas) reside at every step;
even that which is unattainable for the gods, though situated on another continent, is there.
For that progenitor, the knowledge of Brahman shall be constantly accomplished;
through the continuous contemplation of the knowledge of Brahman, his lineage shall also come into being. 98.
All those by whom the constant contemplation of the knowledge of Brahman is performed attain the perfect realization of identity with Brahman. (99)
By him the four Vedas, along with their secret portions (Upanishads), have been studied;
the supernatural powers, beginning with atomization (aṇimā), stand waiting at the door of his house. || 100 ||
Caṇḍikā and the other Mothers protect this person like their own son;
therefore, this is the Great Vidyā, the illustrious Śrī-Dvādaśākṣarī. 101.
Preceded by the propitiation of the two lotus-feet of the teacher, [the practice] should be diligently cultivated every day by those firm in their vows. (102)
Thus, in this *Daśarathīya Tantra*, which is a compendium of the meaning of the Vedas, [is contained] the unsurpassed secret of the reality of Brahman, the means for achieving liberation. || 103 ||

Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Means for Accomplishing the Purpose of the Knowledge of Brahman," in the *Śrīmanuttarabrahmatattvarahasya*, the *Dāsarathīya Tantra*, which is a compendium of the meaning of the Vedas.
The Blessed Lord said:
O King, listen as I shall proclaim the means for the knowledge of Brahman, by the mere understanding of which the knowledge of Brahman is swiftly accomplished. (1)
The eternal essence of the Vedas, Vedānta,
and all scriptures is the twelve-syllabled mantra of Śrī Śiva, which is the divine Brahma-vidyā.
This ignorance, which causes intoxication, has neither been bitten nor heard by you.
Listen, O King, as I shall speak of the means for the knowledge of Brahman.
Having arisen at the Brāhma-muhūrta, one should recite the mantra of the Guru’s sandals while placing the joined palms upon the head, repeating it ten, eight, or twelve times.
Having placed the two auspicious sandals upon the lotus-feet of the Preceptor,
and having beheld those two who possess unswerving vision, he also worshipped them according to his own ability.
Having always offered whatever sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) was possible, being firm in his vows,
they chanted the twelve-syllable mantra of the Lord of Śrī, which is the knowledge of Brahman.

Alternatively, having risen in the morning and meditated upon the sandals of the Ācārya— even in the absence of the specific mantra for the Ācārya’s sandals— one should place them upon one's own head.
Having meditated upon the lotus feet of the Teacher's feet, with a serene mind,
he worshipped them with mental offerings such as golden flowers and other ritual services.
One should constantly recite the Brahmavidyā, the twelve-syllabled mantra of Śrī-Śrīśa.
Its seer is the Great Yogin, its meter is the Mādhyandinī, and its pervasive deity is Nārāyaṇa. (90)
The seer is Brahmā, the meter is said to be Jagatī, and the deity is the all-pervading Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa, the parents of the entire world. 10.
When the king was told that the deity was of two kinds because of its dual divinity, he replied:
"The two who sleep [there], the all-pervading protectors of the worlds, are exceedingly beautiful. (11)
O King, Citkalā and Paramātman are declared to be the deity; Trayī is the seed-syllable (bīja), and Vidvāja is the seed-mantra (bījamantra) for the king.
Śakti is declared to be Nati; she is the Lakṣmī of Lakṣmīśa.
This application (viniyoga) is proclaimed here as one that bestows desired objects for the sake of affection. 13.

Having performed the sixfold ritual assignment (ṣaḍaṅga) with the seed-syllable of consciousness (cidbīja) beginning with the six long vowels and the sound 'praṇada', one should meditate upon the measure of the bow, endowed with the digit of consciousness (citkalā).
The city of Ayodhyā extended for infinite millions of yojanas,
endowed with groves of wish-fulfilling trees and beautified by the Saṃtāna garden.
It was beautified by thousands of groves of trees that offered salutations to Hari;
it was honored by the garden of Mandāra and brought forth from the forest of Pārijāta.
It was resplendent with a great rampart of jewels from the Puṣparāma mine,
and further beautified by a rampart of rubies known as Padmagaga.
It was beautified by walls of gomedha gems and walls of vajras,
and adorned with walls of vaiḍūrya gems, frequented by gods.
It was beautified by a wall of great sapphire jewels, or else encircled by a wall of great pearl jewels. || 19 ||
Likewise, it was enveloped by a jewel possessing the luster of an emerald, and encircled by a short, shimmering, and radiant halo.
There, in that most enchanting pavilion made of the nine gems,
within that water consisting of jewels, extending for thousands and tens of thousands of yojanas, [he performed his penance].

It possesses a divine luster like that of a thousand rising suns; and there, for the sake of support, it is held by the foundational power (Ādhāra-śakti) and others, being golden and adorned with jewels.
In that auspicious eight-petaled lotus, which consists of various jewels, is filled with various mantras, and is composed of the beautiful syllables of the mantra; || 23 ||
In the center of that most beautiful pericarp, upon the two syllables of the Lakṣmī-mantra,
there was a light equal to thousands of millions of rising suns.
The glorious Lord Nārāyaṇa sat upon a lotus seat together with the Sovereign Goddess Viśvā; he was Vāsudeva, whose face was as radiant as the moon.
Adorned with a garland of human heads,
ketaka flowers, and jasmine, his lips have the luster of smooth bimba fruits, and his lotus-face bears a gentle smile.
His teeth shone like priceless pearls;
he was adorned with wrinkles; his limbs were anointed with yellow sandalwood paste; and he was graced by a tilaka mark of musk.
He is graced by four long arms with well-rounded shoulders,
and he is adorned with sprout-like hands that resemble the color of the Japā flower.
Adorned with shimmering armlets, bracelets,
and earrings, and graced by the glorious Śrīvatsa mark and the Kaustubha gem, he is the vast earth itself.
Adorned with pearl necklaces of exquisite beauty and divine garlands,
he was clothed in excellent yellow garments that shone like the light of the rising sun.
He shone with a pair of arms adorned with jeweled bracelets,
and was beautified by rows of nails that resembled the stainless moon.
He possesses ten smooth and beautiful red lotuses and a cluster of priyaṅgu flowers;
his two hands shine with a fivefold [ornament] and a chariot wheel.
The Mother of the World, closely embraced by the two worlds,
shone like a dark sword-blade enveloped by a flickering creeper of lightning.
In the midst of the Gadā and Paramekri, who were of unceasing beauty like molten gold and smooth bell-metal,
the Lord of the Universe himself was born.
She was like gold, adorned with all ornaments,
possessing divine limbs, and decorated with golden garments and finery.
She is resplendent with a mass of very glossy, dark-blue, curly hair,
and is adorned with divine flower garlands such as those of the coral tree and the pārijāta.
Adorned with a parting-line of precious gems and a forehead mark of musk, she was graced by the beauty of jeweled earrings; her hair-ends appeared as if smeared with collyrium.
Delighting Hara with her full, curved breasts and deep navel, she was adorned by him with ornaments such as armlets, bracelets, and necklaces. || 38 ||
Constantly in the prime of youth, she is the sole protectress of all the worlds;
their arms and hearts are entwined with one another, and they are resplendent with divine ornaments.
Clad in divine garlands and garments, the two youths were exceedingly beautiful;
they were the refuge of all the worlds, yet they themselves sought no refuge.

The parents, who are praised by all the worlds, who are endowed with the three-fold sacrificial rites, who are the creators of all the worlds, and who are intent upon the protection of the Lord of the Universe. (41)
The givers of all perfections and lords of all vidyās,
they are beautified by Nīlādevī and Bhūrevī on their left and right sides.
They are surrounded by the powers (śaktis) beginning with Navanirvimalā,
and by the luster of the rubies situated in the directions of Brahmā, Rudra, Maheśvara, and the others.
Their pair of feet were resplendent, and they were intent on protecting those who sought refuge;
seated upon jeweled thrones, they shone with stainless ornaments.
The two Lords of the World, who are the fruit of the blessings of Parā and Parāparā, are to be worshipped within the lotus-heart of the yogi; they are eternally served by the gods. (45)

O Lord, I daily worship Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa, who are worthy of being meditated upon by Siddhas and Sādhakas, who are supreme objects of devotion, and who grant the fulfillment of the desires of their devotees.
Having thus meditated upon Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa situated within the center of the heart-lotus,
O Brahmā, one should recite the twelve-syllable mantra of Śrī and the Lord of Śrī at the proper time.
Or else, having meditated upon the preceptor who bestows the knowledge of Brahman as Nārāyaṇa himself within the lotus of the heart, adorned with all ornaments; 48.
Having meditated upon the splendor of his leaves, adorned with all ornaments, he [worshipped] the preceptor’s wife as Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa. 49.
Having meditated constantly upon this Vidyā as being non-different [from oneself], one should recite it; know that she is the consort of the Ācārya, and likewise [meditate upon] Śrī. (50)
There is indeed no difference at all, none whatsoever, from his own teacher, the Lord of Śrī;
or rather, he abides in the imperishable nature of being, consciousness, and bliss.
Resembling ten million suns and moons, beyond the reach of mind and speech,
stainless, incomparable, consisting of the nature of light, and higher than the highest.
Having meditated upon and recited this Brahma-vidyā, one becomes directly identical with Brahman.
This auspicious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇī is indeed one, though it has two deities.
There is no other knowledge superior to or even equal to this, by constantly reciting which one attains all auspiciousness in every existence. (54)
O King, even in the next world, inexhaustible merit arises for Jayāda on an auspicious month,
at an auspicious lunar mansion, and on an auspicious day.
O King, one should undertake the study of the Brahmavidyā and other sciences;
a true guru is declared to be a bestower of auspiciousness, and an auspicious month is remembered as a bestower of auspiciousness. (56)
That [lagna] should be known as auspicious and bestowing good fortune when it is free from malefic planets;
however, in the month of Madhu (Caitra), great suffering arises for the practitioner. || 57 ||
In the month of Mādhava, one who is free from laziness attains inexhaustible prosperity;
in Jyeṣṭha, one meets death along with kinsmen, as if drinking the poison of knowledge.
In Āṣāḍha, one shall experience separation from sons, friends, and others;
in Śrāvaṇa, one attains great fortune and likewise auspiciousness in the world. (59)
In the month of Bhādrapada, one undergoes terrible bodily suffering;
in Āśvina, one obtains this wealth filled with pearls and rubies.
In Kārttika, there shall be mastery over speech for one who possesses the compassion of a teacher;
in Mārgaśīrṣa, there will be prosperity, yet it will be beset by the loss of wealth and other such troubles.
O King, there is the destruction of births and deaths without the transition to another existence,
and even the direct manifestation of the Blessed One and Lakṣmī herself.
Furthermore, in the month of Māgha, [the practitioner] is born [into the state of grace], and the supernatural powers (siddhis) are accomplished;
in the month of Phālguna, there shall be a success that is difficult even for the gods to attain.
The second, third, fifth, and auspicious seventh;
the tenth, eleventh, twelfth, and thirteenth of the bright fortnight. (64)
The full moon day is also an auspicious lunar date that bestows success upon the sciences;
some, however, have declared the auspicious eighth day of the bright fortnight to be a giver of success.
The days of the Sun, the Moon, Jupiter, and likewise Venus are to be known as bestowing auspiciousness;
whereas Mars and Saturn bring about loss. (66)
Among the auspicious times of the day, the hour of Brahmā (brāhma-muhūrta) is the most excellent;
other moments that fall under the influence of auspicious planets also grant success.

Therefore, one must certainly choose as one's preceptor a lord who is omniscient, learned in the Vedas, a master of the scriptures, and most proficient in the secrets of all the traditional teachings. 68.
O Lord of the Earth, without disregarding place and time, and without understanding even the ritual diagrams, worship, and so forth, as well as the secret of the vidyās. (69)
He who bestows that which grants perfection and he who receives it upon this earth—
both of them are miserable, O Śrīpāla, being joined together even here in this world.
Even one who has gone to the blind darkness for as long as the moon and stars exist, shall surely become once again a master of the Vedas and the Dharmaśāstras. (71)
One who knows the secrets of all the Agamas and is devoted to Vedic conduct may travel even thousands of yojanas across the surface of the earth.

The wise one should take refuge in a teacher, offering even his life, wealth, and other possessions; for the secret of the sciences, along with their constituent limbs, resides only in the mouth of the teacher.
Then, having recognized and received the Great Vidyā from his mouth,
one should constantly please that very teacher, who is composed of the essence of existence.
O King, one should worship the gurus who previously instructed one when they arrive at one's own home at the proper time according to one's capacity; in this matter, there is no fixed rule.

[He meditated upon] the venerable eight-syllabled mantra (vidyā), which is accompanied by the rays of the Blessed One, which destroys the city of Smara through the knowledge of Brahman, and which is joined with all the ritual depositions (nyāsa).
That preceptor, who was a direct incarnation of Bṛhaspati,
gave him the entire earth, filled with wealth and grain, along with his two wives.
Even after offering himself to the teacher, he remains as if perpetually in debt;
therefore, [he should study] the yoga, the proper time, and the mantras along with their secret doctrines.
Having ascertained [the recipient], the sciences that grant all perfections should be bestowed;
one should receive all the remaining ones only in the presence of an omniscient being.
O King, having taken even the Mantras by force in the presence of the ignorant,
one must certainly take them again in the presence of the Omniscient One.

One should invariably offer a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) for the rites such as recitation and fire-offerings, along with their constituent parts, to the lotus feet of the preceptor who has previously removed all impurities. 81.

O King, by one who constantly desires the merit resulting from sacrifices such as the Aśvamedha, whatever [wealth] may be obtained should be given away after first covering it with the right hand. 82.
Whatever fruit is declared in the Dharmaśāstras and the Vedas for one who bestows wealth by the thousands in sacrifices such as the Aśvamedha; [that fruit is obtained here]. (83)
The gift of a fee to the preceptor is remembered as yielding that same fruit every day as giving it thousands of millions of times in sacrifices such as the horse-sacrifice (aśvamedha). || 84 ||
The best of the wise attain enjoyments in the world of Śakra;
when their merit is exhausted, they indeed return once more to the world of mortals.
By giving the teacher’s fee for rites such as recitation and fire-offerings,
one attains the eternal state from which there is no return.
They were always devoted to worshipping the two lotus-feet of their teacher,
intent on the victory of the knowledge of Brahman, and constant meditators upon the garland of rays.
Accompanied by their respective consorts, they were meditators upon the glorious eight-syllable mantra;
equal in form, they were adorned with the divine ornaments of Śrī Viṣṇu.
Clothed in divine garlands and garments, and anointed with divine sandalwood paste, they were present in person within that auspicious city of Ayodhyā belonging to the Blessed One. 89.
Having attained identity with Brahman, they rejoice in his presence;
having come here, they dwell together with Viṣṇu, free from all suffering.
For those wise ones, there is an auspicious and uninterrupted constant union with Viṣṇu; they eternally attain a bliss equal to His own.
Where the wise attain the world of Hari, they do not undergo rebirth again, unlike living beings who remain within the cycle of creation.
Just as Saumitri and Bharata, and as Saṃkarṣaṇa and the others were born,
so too are they born by that very same [Lord] in the world of mortals according to his will.
Furthermore, they did not go to that supreme, eternal, and ten-horsed [sun] state; for those whose souls delight in the knowledge of Brahman, there is no bondage of karma or rebirth.
The ancients have indeed declared that service to the Blessed One is liberation;
for servitude to another master is proclaimed to be bondage. (95)
The servants of Hari are liberated from all bonds and are free from disease;
whereas all worlds, up to the realm of Brahmā, are characterized by the necessity of return.
They produce fear through the bondage of karma, bestow a mixture of happiness and fear,
yield fruits of great exertion, and are the causes of birth, suffering, and physical defects.
Let the enjoyments of heaven for men be like food mixed with poison;
for the gods, upon seeing those men in heaven when their merit has been exhausted, [feel aversion]. (98)
When these two, karma and death, are joined together and provoked, they cause one to fall;
therefore, O King, the happiness of heaven has as its sole means of accomplishment great effort.
The yogin should abandon that which is impermanent, harmful, and mixed with suffering;
however, he should not abandon those actions enjoined in the Vedas that take the form of sacrifice or austerity.
Performing actions with the realization that they are an offering to Brahman, one is not bound by the fetters of karma;
thereafter, one should daily honor the wife and sons of the preceptor and others. || 1 ||
Constantly devoted to the path of the Vedas and engaged in the recitation of the Brahma-vidyā,
he would chant the glorious eight-syllabled mantra while holding onto the garland of rays.
Even here, having become one with Brahman, he shall attain the eternal state;
he should constantly remember only the two lotus feet of his teacher.
The twelve-syllable mantra of Śrī-Śrīśa should be recited by one who is pure;
having omitted the first two seed-syllables, it becomes the ten-syllable mantra of Śrī-Śrīpati.
The wise man should constantly exert himself if he desires his own welfare,
whether in the forest or not in the forest, at home or on the bank of a river.
Whether in a settlement of Caṇḍālas or in the assembly of kings and wise men, whether sitting, lying down, reclining, standing, or even while walking; (6)
Even though he was pure, he became impure upon touching this imperishable consort of Śrī and Śrīpati;
having obtained the grace of his preceptor, he bathed along with his wife while wearing sacred ash.
He is liberated even from great sins, minor sins, and the like, and is endowed with the fruits of ten million vows, ascetic penance, sacred fords, and great sacrifices. || 108 ||
At the end, he goes to the eternal and imperishable state of the Blessed One;
or else, through the mere knowledge of the Daśārṇa mantra, he does so by means of a virtuous teacher endowed with compassion.
By remembering [this] every day, one attains inexhaustible prosperity even from the earth, and achieves the sovereignty over all sciences, which is difficult to obtain. (110)
Having attained prosperity consisting of sons and grandsons and manifold enjoyments,
at the end of the body, he indeed goes to that supreme abode of the Lord of Śrī.
Having become constantly devoted to that which is prescribed in the Vedas— consisting of ritual action, sacrifice, charity, and the Soma-pressing— one should meditate upon the Blessed Lord.
The knowledge of the Śruti, Smṛti, and Itihāsas is for the benefit of the worlds;
O Lord of the Earth, one who transgresses the command of the Lord of Śrī is a bringer of harm to the entire universe.
The Vedas should always be studied; sacrifices accompanied by sacrificial fees should be performed;
and food should also be given, especially to worthy recipients.
Neither by knowledge alone nor even by austerity is one a worthy recipient; that person in whom both of these are established is declared to be a true recipient.
Having constantly studied the Vedas and reflecting upon the meaning of the Veda, and performing the Vedic conduct, a twice-born man becomes a worthy recipient [of gifts]. || 16 ||
One who is devoid of Vedic study and bereft of Vedic conduct is a Śūdra even while living; one should not look upon his face.
The speech of a Brahmin devoid of the Vedas should not be heard even by others.
From giving to an unworthy recipient one goes to hell; from giving to a worthy recipient one attains the supreme state. 18.
Whatever fruit is declared to result from giving wealth by the thousands of millions to thousands of worthy recipients, that same fruit resides at the feet of the Teacher. (19)
Or by giving even a single gold coin (niṣka), one attains that same fruit.
O King, lord of the earth, listen as I tell you another secret.
This Vidyā called Bhagavadraśmimālā, which has been proclaimed by me, must not be spoken of anywhere to anyone, even to one's own son or to one who has given up his life. 21.
Through the grace of his teacher, by means of this constant recollection, being pure day after day,
intent on the conduct prescribed in the Vedas, he became devoted to the conquest of the knowledge of Brahman.
Reciting the secret Great Vidyā, the glorious eight-syllabled mantra,
he is declared by the wise to be the most excellent of all worthy recipients.
Even if he is devoid of Vedic knowledge or even devoid of sacrifices, provided he is always devoted to the prescribed conduct and is a worshiper of the feet of his teacher. (24)
By the constant study of all four Vedas,
he obtains the fruit of all sacrifices daily, even though it was never heard before.
Having constantly performed the actions prescribed by the Vedas with the realization that they are for the sake of Brahman, one attains the primordial,
beginningless, and imperishable station of Brahman.
Worshiping the preceptor’s wife and the preceptor with the thought that they are Śrī and Śrīpati,
one who recites the twelve-syllabled mantra of Śrī-Śrīśa [attains] the knowledge of Brahman.
The goddess Mahālakṣmī protects him like her own son, and the Blessed Lord also certainly always looks after him like a father. (28)
The hand of one who worships with both hands the pair of Śrī-pādukās resting upon the lotus-feet of the Ācārya is like a conch and a discus.
He whose two eyes always behold the auspicious pair of sandals,
rising early every morning, gazes upon them with undivided attention.
One sees here the pair of sandals as the manifest Supreme Brahman; one should bow to the pair of feet of the Teacher, whose head—adorned with a crown set with jewels—is honored by hosts of kings.
One should wear the pair of earrings fashioned for the ears of the Teacher, which is like the face of the Blessed One.
Brought by a digit [of time]. || 32 ||
The highly fortunate ones, such as Vasiṣṭha and others, who were devoted to the practice of recitation and burnt offerings,
attained the status of Brahman-sages through their constant contemplation of the knowledge of Brahman.
In the past, the progenitor Dakṣa was consumed by the fire from the eye of Rudra;
having become Prācetasa once again through the contemplation of the Brahma-vidyā, [he regained his status]. || 36 ||
O lord of the earth, having attained the state of Brahmā, or even the status of being the creator of the entire universe,
the highly fortunate Pulaha and others were the sons of Brahmā.
Merely by the recitation of the Brahmavidyā, they attained the state of Brahman;
the contemplation of the Brahmavidyā and the worship of the feet of the Teacher [are the means]. || 36 ||
It is difficult to obtain even for sages and yogis within the three worlds; therefore, during the auspicious months and on very favorable days, || 37 ||
The Great Vidyā must be attained; otherwise, it is said that success will not occur. There would be the defect of the nine months, and there would be an eclipse of the moon and the sun for Brahmā.
O Lord of the Earth, whatever recitation (japa), fire-oblation (homa), and other rites are performed there by one's own self,
the fruit of that continuous recitation, oblation, and so forth shall be inexhaustible.
Whatever gold is given during the eclipse of a woman (the Moon) should be known as equal to Mount Meru; there is no doubt about this gold.
During an eclipse of the sun or moon,
one should give gifts with great effort, free from greed for wealth, even if they are of small measure.

Having performed the preliminary rite (puraścaryā) along with its auxiliary parts and sacrificial fees during the planetary conjunctions in the presence of the preceptor, together with Mahālakṣmī; 42.
He beholds Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of the World, directly; the previously taught mantras become effective for the auspicious grasping of the [divine] form. (43)
Furthermore, these [teachings] should be studied once again from the lotus-like mouth of one's own teacher;
for this is declared by the great seers to be a supreme and great festival time (parvakāla) in its truest sense.
Others maintain that times when [the planets] are invisible are also suitable;
for it is said that during the eclipses of the sun and moon, there is a continuous [opportunity] for the acquisition of all branches of knowledge.
If the month of Māgha is joined with the constellation Mādhya (Mṛgaśiras) and others, it is declared to be great; for from the mouth of the Teacher, all branches of knowledge arise.
Study is the task to be performed there, and the deity grants the vision [of the Lord].
O King, water for the feet and gifts of all kinds should always be offered during the month.
There is no doubt that these bestow the perfect realization of identity with Brahman;
or rather, it is for the sake of his initiation that you offer me wine today. (41)
He certainly attains the status of a Brahmanical sage (brahmarṣi) in another birth;
[he who gives] excellent wealth for a wedding to a poor man in the month of Māgha. || 42 ||
O Lord of the Earth, having given gifts and performed marriages for thousands of ancestors, he delivered those residing in hell and established them in the world of Brahmā.
Even if the dust particles on earth were to be exhausted by the water of the oceans,
there would still be no depletion of the merit of one who dwells in the supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
O Lord of the Earth, as far as the mandala of the moon, including its mountains, forests, and groves, so long shall there be the increase of your lineage in this world.
Each single day in the month of Māgha is remembered as being equal to a festival;
the full moon day (paurṇimā) occurring there in conjunction with the Padyāna constellation is considered especially sacred.
That full-moon day is called Mahāpuṣyā, and it bestows great fruit;
the months of Vaiśākha, Śrāvaṇa, and so forth, are indeed equal to the month of Māgha.
The months beginning with Caitra and Puṣpa, as previously mentioned, are remembered as inauspicious; O King, even during these inauspicious months, there may occur an eclipse of the sun or moon.
It should be known as bestowing all accomplishments and free from all defects;
even those yogas that are difficult to attain will come to pass, whether auspicious or inauspicious.
Therefore, having carefully examined both the place and the time with diligence, the teacher should impart the instruction of knowledge; otherwise, success is not said to occur.
O Lord of the Earth, without knowing the auspicious month and so forth, as well as the secret and the path, one should neither bestow nor receive the collection of vidyās here.
What is the use of saying much more here? Listen to the essential point:
one should worship the pair of feet of the teacher day after day.
Having first diligently undertaken the investigation of the knowledge of Brahman (brahmavidyā), preceded by the garland of rays (raśmimālā) and accompanied by all the ritual placements (nyāsa).
Having beheld the glorious Akṣarī-vidyā, one should recite it for the sake of attaining the state of Brahman;
this alone is the supreme reality in the Vedāntas and in the Śrutis as well.
"There is no other secret of the Vedas nor any sought-after reality beyond this," thus [it is stated] in this *Vedārthasaṃgraha* by the son of Daśaratha.
Thus ends this twelfth chapter, which establishes the meaning of the reality of Brahman.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter of the *Vedārthasaṃgraha*, the *Dāśarathīya Tantra*, which is the illustrious secret doctrine concerning the unsurpassed nature of Brahman.
Ṛṣyaśṛṅga said:
Once again, the Blessed Lord Hari, the delighter of Jānakī,
personally explained the means for the knowledge of Brahman to Śabara.
The great yogi Nārāyaṇa spoke that which is supreme to the high-souled Janaka, who was formerly a royal sage engaged in ascetic practice.
The Blessed Lord said: Listen, O King, descendant of the lineage of Mahīpāla; this means for attaining the knowledge of Brahman is not to be spoken of anywhere else.
For her, there is no other practice such as the forest-dweller’s conduct with its web of rules, nor is there fire-offerings or libations; she is a perfected lore that grants all desires.
More secret than the secret, the essence of essences, auspicious, it directly bestows the perfection of swift vision of the Supreme Brahman. (5)
It bestows the attainment of the essence of the bliss of Brahman and grants all fruits;
it must certainly be recited by one who desires the perfection of all goals through the power of Brahma.
Desiring a succession of higher welfare and auspiciousness day by day,
one who is pure should worship this Brahma-vidyā at the time of Brahmā.
One should recite it daily a thousand times, or perhaps five hundred;
or one should recite four hundred, or even three hundred or one hundred.
Having remembered the garland of rays of the Blessed One five times and then three times,
one attains the great and desired accomplishment of the mantra without a doubt.
When an eclipse of the sun occurs, or likewise an eclipse of the moon,
one should always subsist on food offered as an oblation for three days prior to that.
Then, at the auspicious edge of the sacred ford (tīrtha) reached by the time of contact,
he should perform the formal resolve (saṃkalpa), uttering the names of Keśava and the others as desired.
Having bathed twenty-four times while observing silence,
the practitioner is instantly liberated from tens of millions of great sins.
By drinking even a drop of water used for washing the pair of lotus-feet of the Guru’s feet,
one becomes pure within and immediately becomes free from all taint.

Having bathed and put on a pair of bright garments, and having sipped water three times according to the rules of good conduct, he, whose vow is well-proclaimed, remains in the presence of the preceptor.
One should mutter this Brahma-vidyā from the moment of touch until liberation;
having bathed the wife of the preceptor and the preceptor himself, who are the embodiments of Śrī and the Lord of Śrī.
At the conclusion of the recitation, being well-composed, he should adorn [the deity] with three types of ornaments:
one made of refined gold and set with rubies.
Having given a pair of auspicious earrings made of pearls and gems to the ears of the Teacher, Satyabhāmā also offered him her own jewelry.
Having offered land endowed with abundant crops as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) at the lotus feet of the preceptor,
he should present him with two cows.
Or else, O King, when the conjunction of the sun and the moon occurs at the time of the festival,
the omnipresent Lords Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa are joined with all their retinues.
With leaves of basil or *vātulasī*, or with lotuses grown in water,
one should [worship] with devotion from the time of touch until the time of release.
The wise man who worships with the Śrī-Śrīśa-Brahmavidyā according to this method obtains the fruit of ten million years of worship performed with a hundred thousand golden flowers.
Having attained the state of Lakṣmīśa, he beholds Him directly;
thereafter, he should give the fee for the teacher as previously described.
At that time, by giving even a single stone bearing the name [of the deity], accompanied by a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā),
to the preceptor, the practitioner [attains success] within three months.
Or else, one should offer ornaments made of natya-iron;
or twenty āḍhakas of mudrā, or twelve āḍhakas.
Or eight *āḍhakas* or half an *āḍhaka* of sugar, or jaggery; or a *prastha* or half a *prastha* of ghee produced from a cow.
Or else, one should offer five *āḍhakas* of rice or twelve *āḍhakas* of rice, together with the wife and son, to the preceptor. || 36 ||
Thereafter, O King, one should feed twelve well-perfumed Brahmins;
he who gives [the gift] consisting of twelve syllables goes to heaven and attains perfection.
O King, by the grace of Śrī and the Lord of Śrī, the yogas of the Blessed One are indeed accomplished instantly for one in that holy place.
He certainly attains great fortune that is unshakable and abounding in jewels, endowed with wealth and grain, and extending through his progeny. (39)
One attains great success in speech of incomparable splendor, as well as great health, strength, and unsurpassed, long-lasting life. (40)
Having enjoyed all worldly pleasures here, one is absorbed into Brahman at the end;
this occurs on the third lunar day of the bright fortnight in Vaiśākha, conjoined with a Saturday.
Accompanied by Rohiṇī, it is a continuous and imperishable success;
that lunar day, beginning with Tretā, is the birth-day of the Great Soul.
On this day, the wise declare the union of Śrī Gaurī and Yoganātha, the one known as Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa, and the union of Umā and Śaṅkara.
This is indeed the yoga of the crane, difficult to attain even for the gods;
that which is given or recited here yields imperishable fruit. (44)
On the third day, Akṣayākhyā, which increases inexhaustible sovereignty,
one who is pure in intellect, having obtained the command of the preceptor, should bathe in the morning.
Then, for the purpose of concluding the daily rites, [he should worship] with tender, cool *sītala* leaves mixed with jasmine flowers and combined with *bilva* leaves.
Having worshipped with flowers until the fruit reached the ground, || 45 ||
At that time, having obtained each individual tulasī leaf with the mantra, the practitioner, being pure in soul, attains immortality. || 46 ||
Then, taking a beautiful betel leaf along with areca nut and cloves, he prostrated himself like a staff before the pair of lotus feet of the Teacher.
One should give to the feet of the preceptor [an offering] made of gold weighing one *niṣka*, or half of that, or even half of that again, or perhaps two *niṣkas*.
One should offer a pair of beautiful earrings upon his two ears,
and one should give the preceptor many ornaments and other such gifts.
O Lord of the Earth, if one is poor, one should give even a single garment;
thereafter, one should offer a vessel of cow's products, or half an āḍhaka, or even half of that.
On the Akṣaya Tṛtīyā, having performed this rite, the best of the twice-born should offer many other fruits at the feet of Āvārya.

Having attained on this earth inexhaustible and very great merit, difficult even for the thirty gods to obtain, and the imperishable perfection of mantras that cannot be accomplished by others; || 55 ||
Within the middle of that year, even one of meager fortune beholds Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa in person and attains prosperity endowed with the eightfold qualities.
In prosperity he was like Kubera, in learning he was like Bṛhaspati, and like Kaśyapa himself, he was endowed with an abundance of sons and grandsons. (57)
Having enjoyed all pleasures difficult even for the gods to attain,
he reaches Vaikuṇṭha at the end, along with ten preceding and ten succeeding generations.
On the third Akṣaya day, whatever object a pure-souled person offers at the feet of the Teacher, even if it is merely the measure of a single atom; || 59 ||
Then, within that very year, there is no doubt that the Blessed Lord, the Consort of Indirā, will grant him the perfection of dexterity.
O Lord of the Earth, one who desires imperishable perfection and the vision of the imperishable Brahman should perform [this rite] in this manner on the third lunar day, which is itself imperishable.
O King, when the month of Āśvina has arrived in the midst of the year,
there occurs the jewel of festivals known as Navarātra, which bestows all perfections.
It brings victory to those who have been defeated, wealth to the poor,
good fortune to the unfortunate, and it is the direct cause for attaining the state of Brahman.
On that [day], every single day, there is the Mahānavamī, which is like an eclipse of the sun and bestows the attainment of all fruits.
No auspicious lunar day is said to be equal to Mahānavamī, which is renowned as being like a hundred solar eclipses and bestows the fruit of victory and prosperity.
Indeed, there is no festival on the surface of the earth equal to Mahānavamī;
whatever desired rite one performs on the day of Mahānavamī, that [is fulfilled].
One should know that the recitation, fire-oblation, worship, and so forth, are equal to Mount Meru itself when the constellation is Uttarāṣāḍhā and the day is that of Bhārgava (Venus).
That lunar day, which is difficult to obtain at all times, is indeed the Vaiṣṇava Tāraka;
that great lunar day is joined with the beginning of the Manvantara known as Svāyambhuva.
O King, this conjunction with the Goddess of Imperial Sovereignty on that lunar day is difficult to obtain;
indeed, this yoga is unattainable, being hard to find even for the gods.
Whether one is unfortunate or poor, or even if one possesses a wavering intellect regarding the greatness [of this rite],
one should certainly perform the Navarātra vow, which bestows all perfections.
The fruit that arises for men when the Navarātra vow is performed cannot be attained even by performing ten million other vows.
On this ninth lunar day, when the Goddess of Imperial Sovereignty (Sāmrājyalakṣmī) is present,
whatever is given, offered in sacrifice, poured into the fire, or chanted becomes a bestower of infinite fruit and accomplishment.
There is no other union equal to the union with the Fortune of Sovereignty;
whatever action is performed here yields the fruit of that very sovereignty. (73)
Then, beginning from every single image and with constant devotion, one should daily worship Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa with the Brahmavidyā.
Or, on a Śālagrāma stone, or upon a yantra consisting of eight syllables with the word "Śrī," the wise man, eating but one meal a day, should worship there a thousand times.
When the great existence has been attained with leaves mixed with flowers, [there are] one thousand three hundred and twenty. || 76 ||
One should worship with tulasī leaves mixed with bilva and flowers;
then, having respectfully prostrated before the lotus feet of the preceptor with the eight-limbed salutation (aṣṭāṅga).
Having given to the ears of the preceptor a beautiful pair of earrings made of refined gold and set with rubies. (78)
One should bestow the earth, endowed with abundant crops and accompanied by the gift of ornaments, at the lotus-feet of the preceptor.
One should also present to him a single Śālagrāma stone, one milch cow,
and many other ornaments.
One should give even very fine garments and ornaments, even if they are not costly; a pair of linen garments should be provided, and they should be made as delicate and fine as possible.
One should offer garments for the newly married women and others as well;
on the ninth day, one should present [the vessel] to the preceptor of the earth.
By giving away the earth consisting of seven islands, filled with wealth, grain, and other riches, one obtains merit by the thousands; of this there is no doubt.
By giving a pure Śālagrāma stone accompanied by a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), one attains the supreme fruit of the gift of ten million cosmic eggs (brahmāṇḍas). || 84 ||
Having given a pair of auspicious earrings to the ears of the preceptor,
he shall deliver even a thousand ancestors who remain [in the lower realms].
Furthermore, may all those born in his lineage be dear to Maṅgalā, endowed with divine enjoyments, and possessed of long life. (86)
Having enjoyed [the fruit of] that merit, one returns again to that village where there is at least one milch cow;
this is the result born from the gift of a thousand cows accompanied by all their limbs and ritual fees.
Having attained the fruit, the one whose self is purified perceives Brahman directly,
like a pair of auspicious golden earrings adorning the ears.
It should measure thirty *cihvuka* of gold, which is equivalent to one *karṣa* of gold;
or it may consist of a pair of *vālī* gems set within a lattice of pearls.
Or rather, the wearing of a nose-ornament by the wife of a guru is for the sake of equalizing [the merit];
there is no doubt that he is the very abode of Lakṣmī herself, a follower of the Blessed One.
Then, having given a pair of auspicious garments to the teacher and his wife,
he became a divine bearer of excellent forms, adorned with celestial jewel-ornaments.
He dwells upon a celestial chariot attended by ten million divine maidens;
this is declared to be the merit of the gift of land, which abides in all the worlds. 92.
A desirable object, such as a cow or the like, or else an excellent sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā);
or twenty-four niṣkas, or in its absence, half of that. || 93 ||
If that [gift] is not obtained, or for the sake of that purpose, one should avoid greed for life;
or else, one should provide a substitute for the land along with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
O beloved of the king, one who desires the fruit of the gift of land should give two oxen to the preceptor at his feet after having spoken [the request], as part of the gift of land. 95.
O King, the price for one bull should be one *niṣka* or half a *niṣka*;
for four bulls, it should be four *niṣkas*.
For a person who practices in this manner, even once, Lord Hari himself, accompanied by Mahālakṣmī, becomes truly pleased. (97)
What could be unattainable for one when the Lord of Kalās (the Moon) is pleased?
That Vaiśākha third lunar day of the bright fortnight which is known as Kṣayati has been proclaimed [as such]. || 98 ||
The two days of the ninth lunar day of the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvayuja are auspicious;
on these two days, everything performed regularly yields inexhaustible results. (99)
On this ninth day, the attainment of the fortune of universal sovereignty is extremely difficult to obtain;
it is gained only after many years, being hard to achieve even for the gods.
There is no yoga equal to this to be found in the three worlds;
it is rare, occurring on the tenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Vaiśākha, conjoined with the Śravaṇa nakṣatra.
There too, O King, the wise practitioner should worship the Lord of Śrī with flowers and leaves using the twelve-syllable mantra of the Lord of Śrī for one thousand times.
There too, one should offer a pair of cows along with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the lotus feet of the Teacher,
or two niṣkas of gold, or even a single niṣka.
O King Vijayaśrī, investigate with respect today that which was proclaimed in the presence of the King, even amidst tears,
regarding the great battle.
Whether in a forest or on an inaccessible mountain, one shall be ever victorious;
for a man who acts in this manner, heaps of fortune fall at every step.
There is no doubt regarding your leaf; I am telling you the truth.
I shall describe the fruit that arises from worshipping with leaves and flowers.
Having performed this in the world of men, one becomes manifestly composed of Brahman;
he who worships with a thousand bilva leaves [attains this].
One is liberated from millions of great sins within a month;
one shall possess stable and great fortune that extends through one's lineage.
Constantly worshipping Lakṣmī and Lakṣmīśa with Mallikā flowers produced over a hundred lifetimes, he [attains his goal] in just a single month for every thousand [flowers offered].
Freed from the multitude of sins and equal to Kubera in splendor, he indeed becomes a great poet and a master of speech through this prostration; of this there is no doubt. (10)
By constantly and with devotion worshipping [the deity] a thousand times with blue lotuses,
one is liberated from even the most grievous sins within a month.
Equal to Madana in splendor, he shall bring the three worlds under his control by constantly worshipping with *ketakī* flowers while possessing the knowledge of Brahman.
Within a mere month, he shall be liberated from all sins;
he shall obtain longevity, health, and unshakable sovereignty. (13)
Having worshipped with *naṃdyāvarta* flowers daily for a thousand times with devotion,
even one who has committed great sins (*mahāpātaka*) is liberated within just one month.
Having become like a living embodiment of knowledge and having attained unfailing prosperity,
he shall obtain great abundance of sons, grandsons, and other blessings.
Constantly worshipping with *namālī* flowers, the pure one conquers hosts of enemies and shall obtain unshakable prosperity. || 16 ||
By worshipping Lakṣmī and the Lord of Lakṣmī (Viṣṇu) with a thousand *caṃpaka*, *vakula*, or *punnāga* flowers for even a single month, one is freed from all sins.
The practitioner attains the yoga endowed with the eight limbs of liberation,
through the auspicious and tender sprouts arising from the laughter of the Jaks.
By means of the Brahma-vidyā, one hundred thousand repetitions of the *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa* mantra liberates one even from the sins accumulated over many millions of births. (19)
It is indeed the foundation of all states of existence, the support of all prosperity, and the abode of all enjoyments; of this there is no doubt. (20)
By worshipping [the deity] for just one month with a thousand tender tulasī leaves accompanied by the Brahmavidyā mantra, one is liberated from terrible and great sins.
O King, he who is thus liberated attains great health, longevity, unshakable prosperity, and even the abundance of sons, grandsons, and other blessings.
By constantly worshipping with a thousand blooming lotuses through the knowledge of Brahman for even a single month, one is liberated from heaps of sins.
Having become endowed with divine enjoyments, he shall behold all branches of knowledge, be the foremost among all prosperous ones, and possess the glory of sons and grandsons.
O King, having attained long life, great health, and imperishability,
there is no doubt that one goes to the presence of the Blessed One by means of this path.
O King, having offered a thousand *hauma* flowers, or a hundred flowers, or even a single golden flower to the Blessed One, [one attains the fruit]. (26)
Within three months, he regards even the splendor of Indra as a mere blade of grass;
or [he attains the fruit of] a single golden flower fashioned from ten cihukas.
By giving daily gifts to the needy and constantly bestowing them upon his preceptor,
he became like Mahendra in prosperity and like Bṛhaspati in the brilliance of his learning.
Having become the support of all fortunes, one shall attain liberation in the end;
[this applies even if offering] a single golden flower or any other fragrant flower. || 29 ||
Having offered even a single bilva leaf or likewise a single tulasī leaf to Lakṣmī and the Lord of Lakṣmī every day with the twelve-syllable mantra, [one attains the fruit].
One attains great perfection and is liberated from all sins by offering clarified butter, sacrificial oblation, fruit, or the three sweets. || 31 ||
Having offered oblations twelve times into the fire with the Śrī-Śrīśa-Brahmavidyā, one eternally obtains the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice; of this there is no doubt.
Rising at the hour sacred to Brahmā and recollecting the knowledge of Brahman,
and remembering the garland of rays [of the sun], one should perform auspicious acts day after day.
If they possess firm devotion to the younger brother of the venerable Ācārya,
by this very authority, they attain [liberation] even among the seven crores of Manus.
O Great Lord, there is no knowledge equal to the knowledge of Brahman;
by this very authority, the teacher of the knowledge of Brahman is the most excellent. (35)
O King, know that among all gurus, the teacher who bestows the knowledge of Brahman is superior; indeed, there is no one equal to him in the three worlds. (36)
If even those who possess the most profound knowledge do not find it within the scriptures, what need is there to mention others?
Therefore, one must with reverence [worship] the pair of sandals of the Teacher.
Having seen [the deity] with undivided vision and having risen at the Brahma-hour,
one who honors [the deity] even by bowing attains a mass of auspicious blessings.
In the absence of the teacher’s sandals, one may use either a *tulasī* leaf or a *bilva* leaf;
or else, a great river, a learned *śrotriya*, or even a precious gem. (39)
Having seen nothing else, one who has arisen at the time of Brahmā shall be liberated from all calamities and shall eternally attain the highest good. || 40 ||
Having daily completed the obligatory rites with diligence and remaining pure, one who knows Brahman should also begin the recitation of the glorious eight-syllable mantra and other practices. (41)
Thus, the greatness of the knowledge of Brahman, which destroys all sins, has been briefly told; O King, what more do you wish to hear?
[Thus ends the thirteenth chapter in the glorious *Anuttarabrahmatattvarahasya*, the *Dāśarathīya-tantra*, which is a compendium of the meaning of the Vedas. 13.
The sages said: O illustrious Ṛṣyaśṛṅga, best among those possessed of all knowledge,
we have listened with reverence to the majesty of the Brahma-vidyā.
"O Lord, please tell me the Great Vidyā known as Ajapā, which is the Mātṛkā.
Śrī Ṛṣyaśṛṅga said:
"In the presence of the great sages, such as Vasiṣṭha and others, the Lord of Jānakī [spoke]..."
Just as the son of Daśaratha formerly spoke to Rudra when he inquired,
and just as it was told with reverence by Nārāyaṇa to Janaka in the beginning.
Therefore, O best of sages, listen as I shall proclaim it:
[the mantra] is joined with the infinite *vindus*, and the *śakti* is endowed with two *vindus*.
Again, the thirteenth is the power joined with the sky and the nasal drop (bindu). || 5 ||
This is declared to be the Haṃsa-vidyā, consisting of four syllables and bestowing fruit.
The individual soul (jīvātman) dwelling within the body is born from a portion of the Supreme Brahman.
In the form of the rising of the breath, he recites the mantra daily.
The seer (ṛṣi) of this Brahma-mantra is said to be Brahmā; its meter (chandas) is Gāyatrī;
and the deity (devatā) is Hari himself in the form of a swan, who is indeed the Supreme Self (paramātman). || 7 ||
The first is declared to be the seed-syllable (bīja), and Śakti is proclaimed as the power (śakti);
its application (viniyoga) is stated to be in the contemplation of the Supreme Self (paramātman). || 8 ||
One should perform the hand-gesture (mudrā) while reciting "haṃsaḥ so'ham";
one should assign the six syllables of power, beginning with "haṃsaḥ," to the fingers.
Having uttered "I am that Haṃsa," being fully concentrated on the syllable *Ahaḥ* everywhere,
he should likewise place it in the heart as the essence of the Sun, starting with the long vowels beginning with *Ā*.
Having placed "Haṃsī" upon the head for the nature of Soma, one should then utter "Haṃsa."

One should likewise assign the fruitless self-mantra to the crest-lock, the stainless mantra to the mind, the armor mantra with the *haṃsa* syllable to the feet, and the Brahma-mantra to the intellect.

One should meditate upon the Self of Awakening, which is beyond the subtle body of the three worlds, consisting of fire and the two moons (the Guru and the disciple), the Praṇava, and the Bindu; blazing in the triangle of fire,
radiant with the face of the Rudras, auspicious, facing east,
with the moon and fire at its sides, resembling ten million flashes of lightning and suns, and pervading the universe as the Haṃsa.
One should meditate with a smile upon the one whose body is the Brahman of Sound, dwelling within the nest of the hut of the heart-lotus. || 13 ||
I remember in my heart with my mind the supreme abode of Maheśvara, known as Brahmā-Nārāyaṇa, which is endowed with a digit of Śrī. 14.
Having restrained the breaths with the Gāyatrī mantra on the preceding day,
one should daily offer the recitation of the Japā-vidyā to the deities.
She for whom there is no recitation (japa) is proclaimed as Japā;
by means of the seed-syllable of space, the individual soul (jīvātman), and the moon, she is the supreme preceptor.
The individual soul (jīva) constantly recites the mantra "I am Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Brahman" every day for the sake of attaining the Supreme Brahman. 17.
O best of the twice-born, every day, as the breath goes out from the tip of the nose, he recites "haṃsa, haṃsa, haṃsa."
He enters the body again through the womb; his very nature becomes the breath, and he incessantly mutters "I am He, I am He" in a continuous stream.
By the letter *ha*, the Supreme Person Nārāyaṇa, whose nature is the Supreme Brahman, is expressed;
because the letter *ha* is infinite, consciousness (*cit*) is denoted by the letter *sa*.

For this very reason, because she is the seed-syllable of power (śakti-bīja) whose form is the triple power (tri-śakti) of the Supreme Power, the great seers [proclaim] this Vidyā as Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇī. || 21 ||

O twice-born ones, I shall now declare the procedure for the recitation (japa) of this mantra, which is the essence of all Vedānta, bestows liberation, and consists of the realization of consciousness.
Having first uttered the seeds of nectar (*sudhā-bīja*) and the powder of the snake (*ahi-cūrṇa*),
[one should contemplate] in the pavilion of the *mūlādhāra* from the word "four-petalled" (*catur-dala*).
