One should utter the syllables beginning with *padme sthitā* and ending with *aparaktā*, followed by the word *gaṇeśāya* and then the word *mayā kṛtam*; this is the *ajapā* mantra.
Having recited six hundred and fifty [verses] of the Gāyatrī, and then the six seed-syllables ending with *vādila*, one should thereafter offer [the oblation]. || 25 ||
The word "svādiṣṭhān" [is for] the pedestal; the word "maṇḍape" [is for] the six-petaled lotus pedestal;
the word "brahmaṇe" [is for] the one seated upon the lotus, whose color is like gold and other [precious metals]. || 26 ||
Having recited "mayā" and so forth, one should offer six thousand [oblations];
having recited the letters from *ga* to *pha*, in the pavilion of the Maṇipūraka.
Then, one should offer six thousand oblations to Viṣṇu, who resides upon a ten-petaled lotus, while reciting the Śrīmahāpadastotra.
Then, the twelve syllables beginning with the letter *ka* and ending with the vowel *ā*, [are placed] in the twelve-petaled lotus at the site of the Unstruck (Anāhata) within the pavilion. || 29 ||
Then the word "śuddhātmane" [is used] for one seated upon a lotus; thereafter, the word "sphaṭikādipadaṃ," followed by the syllables, and after that, the word "sadāpūrvaśivāya."
Having recited "mayā" and so forth, one should offer six thousand [oblations];
having proclaimed the sixteen vowels in the maṇḍala named Viśuddha.
On the first petal from the sixteenth, one should place the word *indraparātparaṃ*;
then the word *gopakāya*, and after that the word for the individual self (*jīvātmane*).
Having said "May [it be so]," one should offer a thousand-fold recitation;
then, having uttered "haṃ kṣaṃ" at the center of the eyebrows, one says "in the pavilion of the command."
Then the word "established upon a two-petaled lotus," followed by the word "of manifold colors," and then the word "of the Supreme Self. (34)
Having carefully pronounced the letters from 'A' to 'Kṣa', he should offer to him a recitation (japa) of more than one thousand times, saying "May it be so. (35)
"I am that Haṃsa; I shall utter my station in the pavilion of the Brahma-randhra. Today, I shall not remain in the lotus known as the thousand-petaled one."
Then, with various colored flowers and the recitation of the word "Śrī-guru," he should offer the mantra one thousand times and present it to him as the water for washing the feet (pādya). || 37 ||
Having thus offered [the oblation] and again restrained the breath while maintaining silence,
one should perform the formal resolve (saṃkalpa) regarding the lunar day, the weekday, and so forth, and then begin the recitation of the *Arka-hṛdaya*.
Until sunrise tomorrow,
one should recite the mantra twenty-one times for each word, totaling six hundred and sixty words for both the day and the night.

Then the word *sahasram* (thousand), followed by the word *saṃkhyā* (number); then the word *nāsāpuṭa* (nostril) with the two [words] *ucchvāsa* (exhalation) and *niśvāsa* (inhalation); and then the word *jāgratsvapna* (waking and dreaming). (40)
Even in states of deep sleep, through the knowledge of that [Self] consisting of darkness,
one likewise [perceives] the Ajapā Gāyatrī and other mantra-sentences beyond that.
One should always utter the formal resolve (saṃkalpa), saying "I shall perform the recitation (japa)";
thus, with inhalation and exhalation, one offers the recitation to the venerable Supreme Self (Śrī Paramātman).
By offering [it], one becomes one who has fulfilled his duty; the practitioner becomes perfected.
For that lower self which is the knower of the mantra, there is no recitation [other than this].
This knowledge, which bestows immediate accomplishment, is proclaimed by Sāyaṇa;
yet the Brahmins of dull intellect have fallen under the sway of desire and delusion. (44)
Indeed, he spent his days with long inhalations and exhalations;
though knowing the essence of mantras, he did not recite even a single mantra with the Ajapa.
By reciting this day after day, one attains perfection; of this there is no doubt.
Without knowing the Haṃsa-vidyā, one cannot transcend the mantras.
For him, there is no accomplishment even in hundreds of millions of eons, despite his constant study of the Vedas, Purāṇas, and Dharmaśāstras. (47)
There is no doubt that through the thorough knowledge of the Haṃsa-vidyā, one attains these;
having recited this mantra of four syllables twelve thousand times. (48)
Within six months, one beholds that state of Brahman directly;
this rule is prescribed for women, not for others.
Reciting the mantra one hundred and eight times daily, or even twenty-eight times with *ajayā*, a householder shall become possessed of wealth.
Whether one is of improper conduct or even pure, by always forming a firm resolve with effort and constantly recollecting this four-syllabled mantra, one becomes eternally pure.
Within the interior of the body, he indeed beholds with his own eyes the Self, manifest in the form of Brahman, free from old age and death.
Henceforth, I shall proclaim the Mātṛkā, which bestows all accomplishments;
for when she is not perceived, all mantras are indeed devoid of power.
The seer of this mantra is Brahmā; its meter is declared to be Gāyatrī;
the deity is known as Śrīmātṛkā, the most excellent of teachers. (54)
Indeed, all [the syllables] beginning with 'a', 'k', 'l', 'ī', 'va', 'ha', 's', 'va', 'd', 'ī', 'r', 'gh', 'ā', and 'nt' are entirely in vain.
The seer (ṛṣi) of this mantra is Brahmā, and its meter (chandas) is declared to be Gāyatrī. (54)
The venerable Mātṛkā is declared to be the deity through the six groups [of consonants].
These six limbs are to be designated in sequence, continuously upon the fingers as well.
If one is capable, one should perform the tenfold nyāsa of the Mātṛkās;
or, having performed at least the six-limbed (ṣaḍaṅga) nyāsa, one should recite this [mantra] for the purpose of subjugation (vaśya). || 56 ||
Her face, arms, and the region between her breasts are adorned with the fifty letters of the alphabet;
she wears a radiant crown bound with a crescent moon, possesses long and lofty breasts,
and holds in her lotus-like hands the gesture of protection (*mudrā*), a rosary, a jar of nectar, and the *vidyā*.
I take refuge in the Goddess of Speech, who possesses three eyes and radiant, pure luster. || 57 ||

The vowels (svaras) were sixteen in the past, followed by the twenty-five consonants (sparśas); then the ten beginning with ya and ending with kṣa are declared as semivowels (caras); thus the alphabet consists of fifty letters.
The venerable Sarasvatī, the Mother of the Gods, is said to be joined with the *bindu*;
she should be recited either devoid of the *bindu*, or joined with the *bindu*, or with the *sa*. (59)
The Vedas, the Śāstras, specialized knowledge, as well as Sāṃkhya, Yoga, and so forth; likewise, the seventy million great mantras and the Dharmaśāstras. (60)
The eternal Vidyās have originated from the venerable Mātṛkā;
he who recites other mantras without first reciting the Mātṛkā-vidyā [incurs a fault]. (61)
Even ten million recitations, fire-offerings, and other rites for him would be in vain;
he should always utter the mantra "Haṃsa" as the yantra for recitation at the end of the syllable Kṣa.
Thus, with devotion, one should indeed utter the letters of the alphabet, saying "I am capable";
by reciting the mantras daily, one partakes in the merit of the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa).
One who, with one-pointed concentration, constantly joins the Mātṛkā beginning with the letter 'a' and ending with 'kṣa', together with the Bindu, is indeed the Supreme Lord himself.
Because she is the mother of all sciences, Mātṛkā is declared by Śrī Rudra to be the Mother;
Hari, in the form of the Swan, is the manifest Supreme Self, the Lord of Śrī.

Śrī, the Mother, who has arisen as the aggregate of consciousness and is the supreme deity—having first offered [the oblation] with Ajayā and having likewise performed the ritual resolve (saṃkalpa), thereafter... 65.
One should recite the Śrīmātṛkā Mahāvidyā one hundred and eight times;
as a result, one becomes a master of all sciences and lives like an immortal.
By merely hearing it once, one would grasp the four Vedas.
And from the exposition of the scriptures he has heard, within at most three years, he will certainly become one who knows the essence of the Itihāsas and Purāṇas. (69)
Even the seventy million great mantras, always assuming embodied forms,
become visible after a year and, being pleased, grant boons as well.
Unshakable and great fortune arises in his home;
indeed, even the god Mūka himself does not touch his hand for years.
One becomes a master of all sciences; of this there is no doubt. Drawn by that vision, one becomes a treasure-house of a thousandfold riches.
Having rescued his own lineage situated in hell,
he thereafter ascends a divine celestial chariot and dwells in Vaikuṇṭha.
One should constantly practice the fifty-lettered Mātṛkā three hundred times;
[this grants] omniscience, mental clarity, and the unsurpassed status of a Brahman-sage.

Whether it be the state of a Siddha, the state of a Marut, or the inexhaustible power to assume any form at will, one attains it within one year or even two years; there is no doubt in this matter. || 75 ||

By means of the garland of letters fashioned from the phonemes of the Mātṛkā, beginning with 'a' and ending with 'kṣa', accompanied by the nasal bindu, and arranged in both direct (anuloma) and reverse (viloma) order.
By reciting each pair of syllables, one obtains all perfections; even the mantras of enemies, let alone other mantras, become effective for men. (77)
Accompanied by the complete nyāsa,
the venerable eight-syllabled progenitor [of mantras] should be recited constantly twenty-eight times, or alternatively, ten or twelve times.
One should recite the Mātṛkā mantra five times or even three times every day;
one will certainly attain great accomplishment in this matter, of this there is no doubt. (79)
The repeated recitation of the Gāyatrī with its twelve syllables joined together,
accompanied by the entire network of ritual placements (nyāsa), and the contemplation of the glorious eight-syllable mantra.
And the daily service to the lotus feet of the teacher is the fruit of the penance performed by remaining intent on the contemplation of the venerable Mātṛkā. (81)
One may abandon all the Vedas, one may even abandon the great mantras, and one may abandon all dharmas; but one must never abandon the supreme Mātṛkā.
The contemplation known as Ajapā is the supreme Śrī Mātṛkā-vidyā;
one from whose lotus-like mouth this is obtained should never abandon it, even at the end of his life.
Mantras found within the Vedas, as well as those from the Purāṇas and the Tantras, are considered fruitful only when received from the lotus-like mouth of a teacher. (84)
The power of mantras in the three worlds is uncommon;
if the Guru is perfected, his disciple’s knowledge quickly becomes perfected.
Everyone on earth knows the mantra "Śrī Rāma,
Rāma," which they receive from the mouth of their guru or of the Lord himself at Kāśī upon the departure of the body.
Even for a mere insect, it bestows supreme liberation;
Vālmīki, though being only a brahmin, attained it through union with a female crane. (87)
Even those who have become outcasts on this earth due to such acts as stealing gold may,
through the grace of the great sages, become blessed by that name of Rāma.

After studying and reciting [the scriptures], he attained the status of being foremost among the Brahmanical sages and yogis, as well as the state of being worshiped even by Brahmā and the other gods.
Therefore, O twice-born ones, if the teacher becomes perfected through austerity, the disciple shall become perfected instantly; even Brahmā himself beholds this.
Therefore, one should always be ashamed of failing to study the Vedas;
hence, one should perform the recitation of the Gāyatrī mantra a thousand times every single day.
Even for those twice-born ones who possess such a true guru, constantly engaged in the recitation of the Great Vidyā which is the essence of the Vedas— (92)
Even a mantra composed in a vernacular language grants them success;
however, all kinsmen are to be censured, while wives, sons, and others are to be abandoned.
Whether I see you being harmed or see kings meting out punishment, my only refuge is the pair of lotus feet of the Teacher. 95.
I constantly go for refuge to the all-pervading Teacher alone;
O Nameless One, I have no other resort than the two lotus feet of the Teacher. 96.
Thus, he whose devotion to the lotus feet of the Teacher is perfectly steadfast crosses over saṃsāra and attains liberation and final release. 97.
"Let people praise or revile; let Lakṣmī stay or depart;
let death come today or at the end of the Yuga—one should abandon the teacher. (98)
One should always abandon one's father, or even a mother of virtuous vows; likewise, one should abandon sons, fruits, food, brothers, as well as the Vedāntas and the Śrutis.
Until the fall of this body, a wise person should not abandon the teacher;
he who does not receive the Mātṛkā, nor he who does not give the Mātṛkā. (100)
There is no doubt that both [the mother and the child] share in the portion of the deity for a man who is self-restrained and recites the Mātṛkā-mantra every day. || 1 ||
And clearly, even though they had not studied them, the four Vedas, complete with their secret doctrines (rahasyas), shone forth from his lotus-like mouth. || 2 ||
Even scriptures that have not been studied appear as if they were ancient;
therefore, having obtained the Mātṛkā through the compassion of the teacher, the practitioner [should proceed]. (3)
Having recited it ten times or even five times, one should mutter other mantras;
through uninterrupted practice, one attains great and supreme perfection.
The Ajapā Mātṛkā-vidyā is the destroyer of sins;
it was proclaimed by the Lord of Jānakī and has likewise been uttered by me. || 5 ||
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter in this Daśarathi-tantra, which is a compendium of the Vedas concerning the secret of the unsurpassed Brahman-reality.
[Thus ends the fourteenth chapter in the *Śrīmadanuttarabrahmatattvarahasya*, the *Dāśarathīya Tantra*, which is a compendium of the meaning of the Vedas.]
The sages said: O highly fortunate Ṛṣyaśṛṅga, best of all-knowing sages,
we have heard from your mouth the greatness of the knowledge of Brahman.
Furthermore, the greatness of the Sāvitrī, the eight-syllabled mantra, and others has been heard from this compendium of the essential meaning of the multitude of Vedas,
Vedāntas, and Śāstras.
The glorious eight-syllabled mantra is said to bestow the accomplishment of all fruits;
[I shall now describe] the majesty of the glorious eight-syllabled lore with great devotion. (3)
"O Blessed One, ocean of compassion, O Great-minded One, grant us [this] Brahman.
Śrī Ṛṣyaśṛṅga said:
"Listen, O best of Brāhmaṇas, you who are omniscient and far-sighted! (4)
When the son of Daśaratha had thus addressed him, the illustrious Maheśvara spoke to Rudra, who was questioning him:
"O Blessed One, Lord of the gods of gods, O Lord, beloved of Jānakī! (5)
It is declared that the venerable eight-syllabled lore (Śrī-aṣṭākṣarī-vidyā) is the root cause of all four Vedas as well as of the three worlds.
Moreover, in this very life, even for men of limited intellect, the knowledge of Brahman—which is otherwise difficult to attain—is the means for crossing the ocean of saṃsāra. (7)
"Liberation, known as the bliss of Brahman, would result from the vision of the Lord of Śrī.
O Radiant One, please tell me either the glorious eight-syllabled mantra or some other vidyā."
Thus questioned by Rudra, the Blessed Lord, the husband of Jānakī,
truly recounted the glorious eight-syllabled mantra.
Śrī Rāma said:
Listen, O Śaṅkara, I shall tell you that which you ask of me.
Formerly, in the city of Videha, [it was told] to the high-souled Janaka.
O Lord, listen to that which was spoken by me in my form as Nārāyaṇa for the benefit of the worlds—the greatness of the glorious Eight-Syllable [Mantra]. (11)
The Blessed Lord said:
"I shall proclaim the eternal and glorious majesty of the Eight-Syllable [Mantra], which is the essence of all the Vedas and Vedāntas, as you have requested."
Listen, O King, protector of the earth,
to the glorious eight-syllabled lore (vidyā), which bestows the abundance of all fortune and grants the realization of Brahman.
That which is unmanifest, devoid of beginning, the stainless Brahman,
free from qualities and changeless, established beyond even darkness.
That which consists of truth and bliss, pure, the one light, higher than the highest—
that very same [reality] became manifest in the form of a person, having Nārāyaṇa as its essence.
Having become the Great Being, the Lord known as Nārāyaṇa,
though united with non-conscious matter (acit), set his mind upon the creation of the world.
O Supreme Self, Lord of the World, having previously created this world filled with cities, how can You be seen by us two, O Lord of the Earth? (19)
How could this world not be composed of you, being of the nature of the essence of Brahman—this very Brahmā, the Lord and Master of speech, who is without end? (20)
Mahārudra questioned the Supreme Lord.

Then Brahmā and Rudra were unable to behold the Lord, the Master of the World, who was continuous with the radiance of infinite millions of suns; they both became powerless to see the All-pervading One.
O Maheśvara, you whose eyes are filled with the drops of the compassion of the Omniscient One, speak to us both. || 20 ||
The Blessed Lord said: "I am Nārāyaṇa by name, the Great Person (Mahāpuruṣa), the Sovereign (Īśvara),
the Supreme Self (Paramātman), the Supreme Brahman, characterized by Existence, Consciousness, and Bliss."
This web of the Vedas has issued forth from my mouth;
having grasped it, may you constantly bring about the highest creation.
I am the essence of the castes, the soul of the Vedas, the eternal embodiment of the mantras;
I am Acyuta, I am Ānanda, I am Śiva, and I am Śaṅkara.
Furthermore, what else shall I proclaim that is the very essence even within the Vedas—a supreme secret kept hidden, which has never been spoken of anywhere? (24)
Having performed the contemplation of that most well-guarded secret knowledge called the glorious Eight-Syllabled Name, one always [becomes] both the Self and Viṣṇu. (25)
Through this extraordinary power, you two— who are endowed with the eightfold fortune—
will certainly achieve freedom from old age and death.
Having taught all this and more, O King, Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of the World and great yogi, vanished from sight.
Therefore, I am this Lord Śrīpati, whose nature consists of eight syllables;
I am the eternal Supreme Self, dwelling within all beings.
Know me alone as the supreme Brahman, eternal and ancient;
O protector of men, I am subtler than the subtle and greater than the great.
I am the savior from saṃsāra, and I am the ancient teacher;
I am that light situated in the sun which illuminates all the worlds.
O Indra, that splendor of yours consists of the nature of consciousness;
indeed, having become Vaiśvānara, I abide within the bodies of living beings.
I am that which is eternally joined with prāṇa and apāna, and that which has consumed the fourfold food;
among the Prajāpatis I am Brahmā, and among the Rudras I am Śaṅkara.
Among the Ādityas I am Viṣṇu; among the Vasus I am Pāvaka;
among the immortals I am Mahendra; and among the Yakṣas and Rākṣasas I am the Lord of Wealth (Vaiśravaṇa).
I am the eternal self of time, the bestower of the fruits of merit and sin;
I create the entire universe and withdraw it again and again.
I protect the entire universe; I am the imperishable one whose self consists of eight syllables.
I am the Lord of Sacrifice, the enjoyer of sacrifice; I am indeed Nārāyaṇa, the Knower. || 35 ||
I am Sādhyanārāyaṇa, dwelling in the midst of the Badarī forest;
and I am Yajñanārāyaṇa, the bestower of the fruits of all sacrifices.
O King, know this eight-syllabled mantra to be the eternal essence of all four Vedas, accompanied by the complete Nyāsa.
The syllable Om (Praṇava) is the soul of the Vedas, the beginning of all, and the bestower of liberation upon ascetics;
among letters, its essence is the letter 'A', and Varuṇa is likewise the leader of the ascetics.
Among the Ādityas, I am Tvaṣṭṛ, the lord of the world;
I alone, O lord of the earth, am the individual soul of all beings. (39)
I am the self of the mind within the organs of knowledge, the self of the eye in actions;
I am the Lord of the Quarters, the self of the world-protectors—I am the glorious one of eight syllables.
I am the Lord of the three worlds, the mantra that is the essence of the meaning of the ten million Upanishads;
the glorious eight-syllabled mantra is remembered as the great mantra that is the essence of the Vedas.
Those who daily recite the auspicious and glorious eight-syllabled great mantra (mahāvidyā), which is the essence of the Vedas, having received it from the mouth of their preceptor; || 42 ||
They are blessed, they have accomplished their purpose, and for that very reason they are dear to the Blessed One;
know me to be the Ācārya, the all-pervading Lord who bears the form of the Mantra. (43)
Together with all the Nyāsas, he [taught] the auspicious and glorious eight-syllabled mantra (aṣṭākṣarī),
along with the Bhagavad-raśmi-vidyās and the secret teachings.
O King, know that he who bestows this is none other than myself;
O Lord of the Earth, it is indeed this triple great lore, the essence of the Vedas. (45)
The supreme eight-syllabled Śrīvidyā is the mother of the Vedas and the life-force of all;
other mantras, when encapsulated by it, bestow all fruits in this manner. (46)
Mantras that are encapsulated by seed-syllables or other mantras are said to bestow the desired accomplishment; others that are not so encapsulated do not. (47)
This single, great, eternal seed-syllable known as Praṇava,
when not enclosed by other syllables, bestows the perfection of liberation upon ascetics.
The auspicious Gāyatrī, consisting of twenty-four syllables and joined with the three Vyāhṛtis, is the mother of all the Vedas and the bestower of all perfections. (49)
The glorious eight-syllabled mantra, which is the essence of the Vedas and eternal,
is traditionally held to be the very nature of the Praṇava itself and the bestower of great spiritual attainments.
If the eight-syllable mantra is enclosed by seed-syllables at the beginning and end of the mantra,
it is able to grant only that much fruit, but not the great fruit.
Just as honey mixed [with other substances] does not yield its own natural flavor,
so too the eight-syllable Vidyā, when mixed [with others], does not manifest its own power.
One who desires the highest good should constantly recite the pure eight-syllabled mantra;
the pure eight-syllabled lore [should be received] from the lotus-like mouth of the preceptor.
For one desiring great accomplishment and the supreme, imperishable welfare,
[this is] composed of all the Vedas and is the very embodiment of the meaning of all the Upaniṣads.
She consists of all dharmas, she is the embodiment of all dharma-scriptures;
she consists of all yoga, she is the form of all Sāṃkhya and Vedānta.
O King, this glorious eight-syllabled Vidyā embodies all sacred fords, consists of all knowledge, and bestows fame; there is no other such ignorance as this.
She is the eternal cause of all prosperity and sovereignty,
the bestower of all enjoyments, and the granter of the attainment of all sciences.
She who brings about all prosperity, the Great Lakṣmī herself, the bestower of wealth, she who rains down a flood of all kinds of pearls and jewels into the home of her devotee. 58.
She is the cause of the empire of liberation, whose form is the essence of the bliss of Brahman;
she bestows upon those born [in this world] beauty, good fortune, and the accomplishment of all sovereign powers.
She is the destroyer of all sins, the bestower of the fruits of all holy places,
the eradicator of all diseases, and the dispeller of all miseries.
She is the remover of birth, death, old age, and disease; the destroyer of grief;
the eradicator of all calamities; and the great dispeller of the afflictions of primordial existence.
There exists no poison equal to this, nor even any superior to it;
it is the great, immovable Goddess Lakṣmī herself, a mass of all auspicious blessings.

All accomplishments (siddhis) are attained through the recitation of the glorious eight-syllabled mantra (aṣṭākṣarī), even for one who desires day after day the fruit of sacrifices such as the horse-sacrifice (aśvamedha). 63.
Desiring the fruit of gifts such as the *tulāpuruṣa* sacrifice day after day, one should mutter the glorious eight-syllabled mantra (*vidyā*) for the attainment of the perfection of sacrifice. (64)
One should offer a gift according to one's ability at the lotus-feet of the preceptor,
in order to obtain the fruit of reciting all four Vedas.
The glorious eight-syllabled vidyā, conjoined with the nyāsas, should be recited;
for the practitioner of the glorious eight-syllabled vidyā, day after day—66.

This entire universe, consisting of the moving and the unmoving, is seen as abiding within the body through the recitation of the venerable Eight-Syllabled Mantra accompanied by the complete ritual placement (*nyāsa*).
Śakra and the other guardians of the quarters stand as if they were his servants. || 67 ||
[Thus ends the fifteenth chapter in the venerable *Anuttarabrahmatattvarahasya*, the *Dāśarathīya Tantra*, which is a compendium of the meaning of the Vedas.]
The Blessed Lord said: Formerly, there was a great sage named Sāṅkhyāyana, a yogi and a treasury of asceticism,
who, resembling ten thousand suns, wandered through all the worlds.
Blazing with divine splendor, it was surrounded by Brahmanical sages and accompanied on its four sides by the four Vedas personified in bodily form.
Together with the personified utterances of Svāhā, Svadhā, and Vaṣaṭ.
He beheld the omnipresent Lord of Sacrifice, who bore the form of the mantra, blazing with his own splendor even as he was being invoked by the personified *praṇava*.
He is accompanied by the Goddess Śrī, whose nature is consciousness, seated upon his left lap;
he is established upon a great lion-throne in Satyaloka, that jewel among celestial realms.
Having seen this, he was struck with wonder and prostrated himself with all eight limbs;
having bowed down, he rose again and beheld his smiling face.
He beheld the glorious eight-syllabled lore (vidyā) upon his tongue.
Then, seeing even the fourteen nyāsas beginning with Keśavakīrti upon him from head to foot, he was filled with wonder.
He beheld the four Vedas, resplendent with their own brilliance, intent upon expounding the greatness of the glorious eight-syllabled mantra.
Suddenly closing his eyes and bowing again with palms joined in reverence,
he spoke to Nārāyaṇa, the flawless Lord of Sacrifice.
O Lord of the Universe, Blessed One, Supreme Lord, he spoke to Sāṃkhya about that which is higher than the highest:
"I recognize you as the creator and sustainer of all the worlds. (9)
Furthermore, at the time of the end, she constantly invokes that Lord who is the destroyer of the world,
as well as this Great Illusion (Mahāmāyā).
"Who are you, this person composed of splendor, a mantra-form consisting of light?
And who are these [beings] blazing with your radiance, indicating the greatness of your knowledge? (11)
O Lord, how shall I remain forever in your presence? By worshipping whom may I constantly behold you standing before me? (12)
"O Blessed Supreme Lord, tell me this very thing in its true essence.
Śrī Yajñapuruṣa said: "O highly fortunate one, because you have questioned me after having calculated [the matter]. (13)
Therefore, I shall fully declare it; be attentive in mind.
I am the Lord of the worlds, whose self is the glorious mantra of eight syllables.
O sage, I am the performer of all sacrifices and the master of the sacrifice;
I am Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Brahman, the Supreme Self, and the Lord.
These, beginning with Keśavakīrti, are the nyāsas that are my limbs; these Vedas, which are my own words, are the causes for the creation of the world and so forth. || 16 ||
These perfected Brahman-sages are meditators upon the glorious eight-syllable mantra,
and they are ever devoted to worshipping the pair of lotus feet of the Guru.
These divine mansions are filled with heaps of jewels and wealth,
and are accompanied by thousands of celestial maidens and wish-fulfilling cows.
O Sage, this divine abode, whose name consists of eight glorious syllables when chanted,
is the wish-fulfilling gem, the kalpa-tree, the cow of plenty, and the essence of nectar.
For those who recite the glorious eight-syllable mantra on this earth, nothing is difficult to attain;
they should perform the daily placement (nyāsa) of the glorious eight-syllable vidyā every single day.
Otherwise, it should be recited [with the ritual placement]; for if recited otherwise, it yields only a result corresponding to that [limited] amount.
He who, out of delusion, imparts this vidyā devoid of nyāsa [will suffer]. (21)
O high-minded one, even that dull-witted person who takes [the land]— whether having first deprived it of its deposits or not— these two are destined for the abode of hell.

For the sake of receiving further instruction along with the ritual placements (nyāsa), he should take refuge in another teacher who has reached the further shore of the Bhagavat’s radiant vidyās and is free from all taint.
Having gone even many thousands of yojanas, one should take refuge in a guru who knows the secret knowledge of the glorious eight-syllable vidyā and has conquered his senses.
Even if his life were at his throat, he would not transgress the command of kings—
not even his father, mother, brother, or one who has bestowed upon him the four Vedas.
He is equal to the instructor of the various rays of the Blessed One;
that which is the supreme light of Brahman, consisting of the glorious eight syllables. (26)
That which is unbroken bliss, beyond duality, and situated beyond primordial nature (prakṛti)—
that alone is indeed the subtle supreme, as well as the gross, and is truly the Existent (Sat).
Then I am the Yajñapuruṣa, whose self is that [sacrifice], the primordial Nārāyaṇa; I am the eternal seed consisting of the three Vedas, known as the Praṇava.
That very seed-syllable of liberation is called the Seed of Śrī;
for the Ṛg-verses, the Yajus-formulas, and the Sāman-chants are indeed the immortal Śrī of the virtuous.
Thus, even the Vedas, which have issued from my mouth, declare:
"Among all letters, this 'A' is proclaimed to be the first. (30)
O Sage, because you are the first of all letters, the essence of the letter *a*, and the Lord of Śrī, you are Nārāyaṇa himself, directly expressed by the syllable *a*.
Lakṣmī, whose form is the syllable *ukāra*, is the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*) proclaimed as Śrī;
she consists of the three Vedas, is eternal, and is seated upon my left lap.
By the letter *ma*, the wise declare that this living soul (*jīva*) is our servant;
therefore, that which is expressed by the *praṇava* (Om) is Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa.
Know this seed-syllable named Praṇava to be the bestower of my own nature upon the embodied soul here; it is called the Śrī-bīja.
The omnipresent Nārāyaṇa, whose form is the Supreme Brahman, is [present] with the Praṇava; however, mantras devoid of the Praṇava may be chanted even by those who are not Brahmins.
Mantras devoid of the *praṇava* yield only some fruit;
they must necessarily be recited by Brahmins even when the *praṇava* has been omitted.
Nowhere has a science beginning with the seed-syllable of the natural Veda been heard of;
this eight-syllabled science begins with the natural *praṇava*. (37)
Therefore, there exists both an ignorance equal to that and one even greater than it;
the former is the seed-form of the mark of liberation, while the latter yields the fruit of the mark of nescience.
The supreme eight-syllable mantra, which is the seed of all vidyās and possesses splendor, concludes with the word "Nārāyaṇa" joined with the dative case ending. (39)
The Supreme Brahman is of the nature of consciousness; that very same [Brahman] is of the nature of the Praṇava.
O great sage, it has been said that even the Śrī of the Supreme Brahman is expressed by the Praṇava.
Known by the name Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇī, she is the very essence even among the Vedas;
she is remembered as the supreme seed of all branches of knowledge. (41)
O Sage, when the reality of the individual soul (jīva) is established through salutation,
it is declared that the soul is non-different from Nārāyaṇa.
The Vedas proclaim Nārāyaṇa; those intent on Nārāyaṇa are supreme;
the gift of Nārāyaṇa is the highest gift; and penance dedicated to Nārāyaṇa is the greatest austerity. || 43 ||
Nārāyaṇa is the supreme Brahman-reality; Nārāyaṇa is the highest;
Nārāyaṇa is the supreme light; the Self is Nārāyaṇa, the highest. (44)
Or the daily recollection of the mantra "Nārāyaṇa" destroys the great sins, such as the killing of a Brahmin, for those who chant it day after day. (45)
How much more so for that eternal [truth] which is the essence of all Vedānta;
it cannot be described by means of rules, negations, letters, or non-letters. (46)
In a single birth, he shall attain the supreme recollection of former lives,
the sovereignty of powers such as atomization (aṇimā), and stainless knowledge of Brahman.
One who desires [success] should recite the auspicious and glorious eight-syllabled mantra;
by her, these [mantras] are mastered, and she becomes a perfected one who worships the feet of the Teacher.
Having chanted the glorious eight-syllabled mantra (vidyā), they took refuge in me;
these eternal Vedas, along with their auxiliary limbs, have issued from my mouth. 49.
"O Mahāmati, inquire about these four Vedas. Then those four Vedas, possessing embodied forms, [spoke] to the high-minded one.
The Vedas spoke to Sāṃkhyāyana, the son of Brahmā, who was free from envy:
"O Sāṃkhyāyana, please speak our words with respect, O highly fortunate one. (51)
Listen, O Blessed Lady, to this supreme secret: this is Nārāyaṇa, the Undecaying One, the primordial source of all the worlds.
O Sage, this world shines forth as the light of Him;
I am the Lord, subtler than the subtle and greater than the great.
He is both with attributes and without attributes, infinite, and the ender of the world;
he is the manifest embodiment of mantra, the eternal Supreme Self.
The Blessed One, whose self consists of eight syllables, is joined with the limbs of the nyāsa for the welfare of all the worlds and for the attainment of one's own true nature.
"O best of the twice-born, whatever we—who were created by this Lord at the beginning of creation with these bodies—declare, that must be carried out. (56)
Action is said to be of three kinds: obligatory, occasional, and optional.
O Sage, these three types of action must be performed daily by Brahmins. (57)
All sacrifices should be performed with complete and excellent sacrificial fees;
every gift should be bestowed here for the sake of attaining fruits both in this world and the next.
Those who desire the great accomplishment of all vidyās must recite them;
I shall now speak that which was kept secret even by us, for the sake of liberation.
O Sage, know that this eight-syllabled lore dedicated to the illustrious Nārāyaṇī, which consists of all knowledge, is indeed the supreme one.
The gods are the rays of the Supreme Lord, portions of His divine splendor;
that auspicious eight-syllabled mantra is joined with the knowledge of those rays. 61.
Obtained through the compassion of the teacher and recited, they grant all fruits;
yet they must not be spoken even with the breath of one's throat to a wicked person.
Day by day, the secret of the Vidyā should be understood from the lotus feet of the teacher as well as from the scriptures; the auspicious eight-syllabled mantra should be recited.
Day after day, living beings on this earth pass away from the world of mortals;
yet, having attained birth once again, they sink into the ocean of hell.
Nowhere at all is there an end to birth, death, old age, and disease;
yet, in order to cross the ocean of saṃsāra, one must [overcome] even birth, death, and old age. 65.
The auspicious and glorious eight-syllabled mantra should be recited along with its secret [teachings].
By whomsoever this glorious eight-syllabled vidyā is constantly recited, [he attains success]. (66)
Janaka has fulfilled his duty; his mother is endowed with good fortune, and there is no doubt that even his fathers and grandfathers have been liberated.
All his descendants shall likewise be endowed with great merit; O friend, his friends, kinsmen, and relatives shall also be purified. (68)
O high-minded one, no one other than the Blessed Lord himself truly knows the greatness of the illustrious Daśārṇa; no one else knows it in reality. (69)
Even here, the wish-fulfilling gem (cintāmaṇi) resides in the house of one who is more devoted than even the god of love;
Indra and the other eight guardians of the quarters even perform service for him.
O Sage, by means of the recitation and fire-offerings of the glorious eight-syllabled mantra (aṣṭākṣarī-vidyā), the abodes of all perfections remain in close proximity to that disciplined one.
One obtains even that which is unattainable for the gods, situated in another continent, desired, and difficult even for yogins to acquire.
The body is constantly accompanied by birth, old age, and death;
it consists of excrement, urine, and phlegm, and is joined with flesh, marrow, fat, and bone.
Indeed, from the eyes, the ears, the tongue, the teeth, and the nostrils,
foul-smelling impurity flows day and night.
The wind situated in the downward breath (apāna) is also joined with foul odors;
whatever object is associated with the tongue, all that is located within the body.
O wise one, that which is cooked by the fire of the matted locks is indeed impurity;
even a collection of objects just released from the mouth is vomited back out again. (75)
On this earth, there is nothing more to be shunned than impurity;
for from the organ of generation, urine flows forth like a garland day and night.
Even perspiration arising from the armpits is foul-smelling;
likewise, the seed, which is the cause of progeny, is constantly foul-smelling as well. (77)
This perishable, impure physical body made of earth is to be abandoned;
herein reside anger, desire, and qualities such as attachment and aversion. (78)
Though restrained by them, that wicked-souled one, though desirous of excellent wombs,
remained attached to the wombs of celestial women and was lustful even on sacred festival days.
Having experienced great suffering within the mother’s womb for three months, crowded with impurities such as feces and urine, he emerged from the mother’s birth canal.
O sage Hara, he is tormented by bedbugs, mosquitoes, and the like;
he is constantly afflicted by excrement, urine, and other impurities, and is beset by hunger.
Having been initiated by his guru and dwelling at home under his instruction, he remained constantly attached to sense-objects in his youth and devoted to the acquisition of wealth. (82)
Afflicted by phlegm, wind, and other humors in old age, and beset by hunger—thus does even a great king become, just like an ordinary man at all times. (83)
Some of one's life has passed in childhood, some has been spent on sensory objects, some has been taken by sleep, and likewise, some has been consumed by diseases. (84)
O Sage, some of my life has passed in eating and such, some in the acquisition of wealth and the like, and some in laziness during old age. (85)
Immediately thereafter, death arrives for him while he is still being anointed;
he is bound by the noose of Time by the servants of Dharmarāja. (86)
He experiences great suffering for a long time, submerged in the ocean of hell;
then, by the remainder of his sin, he returns once again to the state of a living being.
The birth of worms and other such creatures is attained among mosquitoes and the like;
and the birth of dogs and so forth is known to be attained among the womb-born outcastes (caṇḍālas). 88.

O Sage, having subsequently entered the womb of a Śūdra, and then through the sequence of births those of the Kṣatriya and Vaiśya castes, he shall be born into a family of Brāhmaṇas by virtue of the remainder of his merit.
If one performs there great merit as enjoined by the Vedas, then one enjoys the happiness of heaven and is born again upon earth. (90)
Due to the conjunction of birth and death, it is as painful as food mixed with poison; the happiness of heaven is mixed with suffering and is therefore declared to be nothing but suffering. (91)
Therefore, one must certainly [offer] wealth—even if it has been acquired by the teacher or inherited from the great-grandfathers—to one who is omniscient and has mastered the Vedas. 92.
Having offered all the wealth earned by his own hands at the feet of the Teacher,
and even giving up his own life, he remained devoted to serving him for a long time.
O Mahāmati, even after traveling many thousands of yojanas,
one should reach the pair of lotus-feet of the Teacher, which remove all impurities.
Having served for many years with body, life-force, and even wealth,
[one should worship] the glorious eight-syllabled mantra preceded by the rays of the Lord.
Having received [the teaching] together with the other [initiation], he shall have fulfilled his purpose on this earth, remaining ever devoted to serving the pair of feet of the preceptor. 96.
Having chanted the glorious eight-syllabled mantra in a single lifetime alone,
one will certainly attain the supreme abode from which there is no return.
Upon the fall of this body, he attains [the goal] without a doubt;
one who merely bestows knowledge is not called a great teacher. 98.

O high-minded one, by the mere granting of the ritual placement (nyāsa), by the offering of the fire (agnipūjā), and by the imparting of the mantra—even after having received the knowledge (vidyā), the ritual placements, and so forth elsewhere— [one attains the goal]. 99.
O Mahāmati, even if one were to travel many thousands of yojanas to find one who is omniscient, learned in the Vedas, and has mastered the meaning of the scriptures; || 100 ||

On an auspicious day, at an auspicious moment, and when the moon and stars are favorable, he should respectfully choose another teacher for the sake of learning the science along with its auxiliary branches.
In the months of Māgha, Phālguna, Vaiśākha, Śrāvaṇa, Āśvina,
Kārttika, or Mārgaśīrṣa, [one should strive] even at the cost of body, life, and wealth.
Having satisfied his wife and even his sons, grandsons, and others,
he should first receive from the mouth of the preceptor the garland of rays of the moon.

Then, having first performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*), he received from the lotus feet of the Guru the glorious eight-syllable mantra which bestows all accomplishments, as well as his entire possession.
O Great-minded One, having surrendered himself, he should remain dependent on the teacher for as long as he lives; rising every morning, he must constantly strive to please the teacher.
Having become necessarily diligent, one should mutter the glorious eight-syllabled mantra preceded by the rays of the Blessed One and accompanied by all the ritual depositions (nyāsa).
Thus, for one who is constantly devoted to Yādava, the teacher of the people,
there arises either the sovereignty of powers such as *aṇimā* and so forth, or incomparable and auspicious wisdom.
Prosperity accompanied by sons, grandsons, and others at every step;
omniscience, loveliness, and imperishable power to assume any form at will.
The power to enter the bodies of others and so forth is not difficult to attain;
even the state of Brahmā, Rudra, or Viṣṇu is not hard to reach.
Thus, for one devoted to the Teacher, through the contemplation of the venerable Dṛṣṭārṇa,
the supernatural powers of the sandals, collyrium, the sword, and the horse are also accomplished.
With this very body, the person, whose form consists of light,
attains yoga endowed with its eight limbs, as well as the state of moving through the sky.
Having attained the state free from old age and death, which is difficult even for the gods to obtain,
he now sports in the abodes of the Lord, such as Śvetadvīpa and others.
One must certainly possess firm devotion, thinking "The Teacher is indeed the Blessed One";
day by day, one should be firmly devoted to the lotus feet of the Teacher.
Devoted to the recitation, fire-offerings, and other rites of the glorious eight-syllabled mantra (aṣṭākṣarī-vidyā),
he attained the memory of his past births and realized the nature of Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa.
One necessarily beholds the Supreme Brahman with one's own eyes;
this alone is the highest good, and this alone is the supreme austerity. (15)
This alone is the supreme initiation; this alone is the great wealth.
This alone is the supreme yoga; this alone is the supreme fruit. || 16 ||
This alone is right conduct; this alone is the great sacrifice;
and this indeed is the triad of Vedas, along with the Shastras and the Agamas.
Thinking thus, one should daily recite the supreme, glorious eight-syllabled mantra:
"Father, mother, friend, supporter, life-breath, heaven, well-wisher, and companion. (18)
One should always mutter the venerable eight-syllabled mantra, thinking "the teacher alone [is the Lord]";
for the teacher alone is the Blessed One, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara. (19)
Thinking that the true master is Nārāyaṇa himself, who is the supreme Brahman and the absolute, one should always recite the eight-syllabled mantra from a virtuous teacher.
Desiring the fruit of a thousand horse-sacrifices day after day,
one should mutter the glorious eight-syllabled great mantra (mahāvidyā) together with its secret lore.
O Sage, we have been created by the Lord of Indirā to daily recite with devotion the greatness of the glorious eight-syllabled mantra (Aṣṭākṣarī-vidyā), along with its secret teachings.
The power of consciousness (cicchakti) is Śrī, the power of the Blessed One;
she who is the Mother of the World (Agaṃdambikā) bestows the greatness of the eight-syllabled Śrīmantra even as Sarasvatī herself.
Having become the son of Dharma and a great yogi on earth as Nārāyaṇa,
he imparts the majesty of the glorious Eight-Syllabled [Mantra] to the great sages.
Afterwards, he will speak to Janaka, the lord of Mithilā;
subsequently, having become the son of Daśaratha in the city of Ayodhyā. (25)
The highly illustrious husband of Jānakī became renowned in the world as Śrī Rāma in the presence of Vasiṣṭha and the other great sages.
He shall proclaim to Śaṅkara the glorious majesty of the Eight-Syllabled [Mantra],
the Tattva known as Dāśarathīya, which is the essence of the Vedas and of great exaltation.
Having performed that which brings about the highest good in the world, they shall proclaim it at the time of creation;
having heard this essence of all the Vedas, which bestows glory. (28)
The son of Brahmā, Sanatkumāra, who is of great and supreme intelligence, omniscient, and highly illustrious Vasiṣṭha, [expounded] that Tantra known as the Dāśarathīya. || 29 ||
Paraśurāma, the son of Jamadagni; Śuka, the son of Vyāsa; and the great yogi Dattātreya, who was born from a portion of the Blessed Lord. || 31 ||
And they shall compose this compendium, a summary of the essential meaning of the Vedas;
they too will respectfully recite the glorious *Daśārṇamāhātmya*.
Even those devoted to Āñjana, Pādayobhakta, Nārāyaṇa,
and Hari will speak of the essence at the end of the greatness of the glorious eight-syllable mantra.

O bull among gods, by the power of the glorious eight-syllable mantra, neither the Brahmanical sages such as Vasiṣṭha and others, nor the celestial sages such as Bhṛgu and others, could prevail [over him].
Śakra and the other guardians of the quarters, Sanaka and the other Yogins, the Vasus, Rudras, Arka, Candra, and others, as well as the Siddhas and Sādhyas, [worship him] constantly. (35)
Even today, these people continue to recite it, having attained great perfection, for he who knows the truth of the glorious eight-syllabled mantra remains here upon the surface of the earth. (38)
That place is designated as a divine field extending for a yojana in every direction,
where one who possesses firm devotion to the lotus feet of the Ācārya remains even in the midst of the sky.
One should install the glorious eight-syllabled vidyā while reciting it a hundred times,
and therein [one should visualize] Gaṅgā, Gayā, Kāśī, Kurukṣetra, and the ocean.
And she who dwells on the banks of the Yamunā will undoubtedly come here through the recitation, fire-offerings, worship, and other rites of the glorious eight-syllabled mantra. (41)
This Nārāyaṇa is the manifest Lord of Sacrifice and the Master of the worlds;
he becomes pleased with his devotee and remains ever gracious toward him.
When the Lord of Śrī is pleased, the three worlds become pleased;
the three mortal states, the triad of fires, and the three worlds [are all pleased]. || 43 ||
The three powers of the Lord are also his three feet;
they arise from the three feet of the glorious eight-syllable vidyā.
The eight Vasus, headed by Mahendra, are the guardians of the eight directions;
likewise, there are the eight Mothers, beginning with Brāhmī, and the Bhairavas, beginning with Asita.
Vaikuṇṭha and the other worlds, as well as the eight supernatural powers beginning with aṇimā,
arise from the eight syllables of the glorious eight-syllabled mantra.
Therefore, this auspicious eight-syllabled mantra embodies all the gods;
constantly reciting that glorious eight-syllabled lore with devotion, [one attains the goal]. 47.
"You shall become one endowed with a portion of Nārāyaṇa and liberated while living," [said he] to the lord Sāṃkhyāyana, the son of Brahmā and the best of yogis.
O King, at that time, in the presence of Bhava, the Vedas, longing for an incarnation along with him, became inward-looking. 49.
The Blessed Lord said: O King, from that time forth, the sage Sāṅkhyāyana, a yogi and king of Janaka,
constantly worshipped the pair [of deities] at the station of the True Teacher.
Having chanted the glorious eight-syllabled lore (vidyā), he attained supreme perfection.
Thus, the greatness of the glorious eight-syllabled mantra, which destroys all sins, has been briefly told; now the method of its practice (sādhana) shall be explained, O protector of the earth. 151.
[Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, the Summary of the Meaning of the Vedas, in the glorious *Anuttarabrahmatattvarahasya*, the *Dāśarathīya Tantra*.]
The Blessed Lord said:
Now, therefore, O King, I shall explain in brief the ritual placement (nyāsa), meditation (dhyāna), and other rites pertaining to the illustrious eight-syllabled mantra; be attentive in mind.
Having risen during the *brāhma-muhūrta* and bowed ten or twelve times even while remaining on his bed to the two feet of his own teacher, he should then [proceed].
Having remembered his other gurus as well, he then remembered the lords Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa, Gaurī and Maheśa, Vāṇī and Dhātṛ.
Having bowed to Śacī, Indra, and the other eight guardians of the directions, as well as to the Brahman-sages and yogis,
he placed his right foot upon the ground while facing eastward.
Having placed the left foot in front, one should then place the right;
[one should thus place] the pair of venerable sandals that have ascended the lotus-feet of the Guru.

Having seen a crafted image accompanied by [the deity], whether made of gold, silver, or even wood, and perceiving no other [object], he should bow with devotion, prostrating himself fully on the ground with his eight limbs.
In the absence of the guru’s sandals, one should look upon Tulasī, or a great river, or a cow,
or even its hindquarters, with undivided vision.
Having washed both his feet and both his hands,
and having put on clean garments, he [should wear] the sandals of the venerable Ācārya.
Having first recollected the Brahmavidyā in twelve ways, one should then recite it;
and one should likewise recite this Bhagavadraśmividya five times or three times.
Then, having praised [the deity] with Vaiṣṇava hymns or with Puranic praises,
one should mutter the Mahāvidyā either a thousand times or even a single recitation.
Then, having performed purification and other rites, and having cleansed his teeth, he should bathe in the morning; with a purified soul, he should wipe himself dry with a wet cloth.
Having performed the twilight worship according to the rules and having approached the Sun, he should daily recite the *Saura-sūkta* beginning with "He who shines, rejoices," and so forth. (12)
Then one should perform the mantra-sandhyā of the Lord Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa;
daily, one should recite the Sāvitrī hymn beginning with "yosau tapan mudeti" and so forth. (13)
Having obtained [this] from the mouth of the teacher, and having performed the meditation daily immediately after the twilight prayers (saṃdhyā),
one who has sown [the seed] before the face of the Sun attains long life and freedom from disease.
Having obtained a wife, sons, and physicians, he shall never suffer separation from them;
nor shall he ever be deprived of wealth or cattle. (15)
O King, at the end of the body, he attains the imperishable abode of the Lord;
having restrained his breath and made the formal resolve (saṃkalpa), he should commence the mantra-sandhyā.
Having performed the bath with water consecrated by the mantra and having completed the ritual bathing,
one should draw the yantra, complete with its limbs and endowed with the seed-syllables (bījas) and other elements, upon the water.
Having carefully drawn a six-cornered or an eight-cornered yantra,
one should then install the seer, the meter, the deity, the seed-syllable (bīja), and the power (śakti).
Having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the six limbs or merely the [principal] parts, and having meditated upon the Lord of Śrī,
one should thereafter worship Him with the mudrās of invocation and so forth with joy.
Having taken water in his right hand and having recited the glorious eight-syllable mantra twelve times,
he should pour it out into his left hand.
Having wiped the head three times with the twelve-syllable Vāsudeva-vidyā, one should drink water consecrated by the six-syllable Vaiṣṇava mantra.
Having taken water in his cupped palms and consecrated it with the Gāyatrī mantra,
he should offer the Arghya three times and then recite the Vaiṣṇava Gāyatrī.
Having extracted the seed-syllable of the three Vedas (Om) joined with the dative case-ending,
one should then utter the word "Nārāyaṇa," and thereafter the word "vidmahe."
Then one should utter the word "vāsudevāya," followed by the phrase "dhīmahi," and then the syllable "yat" from the mantra "dhiyo yo naḥ pracodayāt. (24)
This Gāyatrī is declared to belong to Viṣṇu; it destroys great sins, bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, and directly grants the perfection of the vision of Brahman.
In this Viṣṇu-gāyatrī, I am the sage Nārāyaṇa;
the meter is said to be Gāyatra, and the deity is the Supreme Self, the Lord of Śrī. (26)
Lord Nārāyaṇa himself, the infallible master of the worlds,
should constantly recite [the mantra] twenty-eight times, or even twelve times.
Having restrained the breaths, made the formal resolve (saṃkalpa), and performed the six-limbed assignment (nyāsa),
he meditated upon the all-pervading Lord Nārāyaṇa situated within the orb of the sun.
Facing the sun, always pure, one should perform one hundred and eight recitations of the glorious eight-syllabled mantra, which bestows all perfections, according to the prescribed method.
One should daily perform the praise of the Blessed One with the hymn known as the Nārāyaṇīya-sūkta and twelve libations (arghas), either five times, three times, or once.
Then, having returned to the temple, one should perform the daily fire-sacrifice (anityahoma),
after which one should satisfy the ancestors, the gods, and human beings.
One should recite the illustrious eight-syllabled mantra preceded by the ritual placement (nyāsa);
through a single birth, it bestows liberation and grants all perfections.
The glorious eight-syllabled lore (śrīmadaṣṭākṣarī-vidyā) is to be recited preceded by the ritual placements (nyāsa);
the recitation, fire-oblation, and other rites of the glorious eight-syllabled lore should always be performed. (33)
Desiring to achieve great perfection in a single lifetime,
one should perform the daily fire-oblation (nityahoma) and then bow at the lotus feet of the preceptor.
Whatever fee one may give, even if it be merely vegetables, ghee, and so forth;
or whatever fee, however small, one places at the lotus feet of the preceptor. (35)
They say that a day [spent thus] is barren, for it increases a great flood of sins;
however, by offering oblations every day and remembering the lotus-feet of the Preceptor, [one avoids this].
Gold or silver, grain, minerals, raw rice, thread, vegetables, or even ghee—whatever serves as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). || 37 ||
By necessarily giving [the merit] to the guru, one is eternally liberated from sins;
even by performing this for a single day, one obtains the fruit of sacrifice. (38)
Having mentally resolved upon some small gift for the lotus-feet of the Teacher, one should daily offer it to me, whether by means of this [mantra] or otherwise.
Or, even in their absence, one may give it to a learned Vedic scholar (śrotriya).
O King, a foremost among the twice-born who is endowed with both knowledge and austerity is called a worthy recipient;
wealth given to those who are unworthy recipients, even if equal to Mount Meru, [yields no fruit].
One who is the cause of a constant flood of sufferings in hell and brings about sin, yet is accompanied by Vedic conduct and knows the Vedas, is remembered as a Śrotriya. (43)

A twice-born man who is devoid of the Vedas is considered fallen by the wise; furthermore, whatever gift is given to one who does not know the Vedas— Please note: The provided text contains a typographical error ("avēdavidaṣēdānaṃ"). The corrected Sanskrit text has been used for the translation. The phrase "yatkiṃcidapyatha" (whatever little [is given] then) implies that no gift whatsoever given to such a person yields its intended fruit.
It is taught that an oblation poured into ashes leads to a certain residence in hell;
however, when offered into a fire kindled by the fuel of recitation and burnt offerings, it serves as an expiation for the sins of one learned in the Vedas.
O King, even if one gives only a single toothpick at the lotus-feet of the Preceptor, it shall deliver ten million ancestors, even those submerged in hell.
They say that this bestows union with Brahman and is honored even by the ancestors; for even a mere promise made to a Brāhmaṇa regarding wealth and other things is so regarded.
"It must be paid within six months; beyond that, O King, listen to the great [consequence]. And whatever has been promised by word of mouth must be fulfilled within six months, O King. (48)
O King, even vegetables, ghee, and other such items promised to the teachers, if not given, bestow much suffering in the foremost hells. (49)
Even if this debt, though small as a mustard seed, is as vast as Mount Meru,
one will incur the curse of the deities even here and go to hell at the end.
O Blessed One, ocean of compassion, by constantly offering even the slightest thing at the feet of the Guru, one attains success that is otherwise difficult to achieve. (53)
That which is given on the eleventh day, on the full moon, on my own birthday, on the twelfth day,
during a solar transit, or on a Friday, bestows the fruit of inexhaustible success.

On a Saturday, even if it is the day of the preceptor himself, one who desires his own welfare must not give away the preceptor’s wife in his absence, even if he were the Lord manifest before him. 55.
The third day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha—on that day, what is given becomes inexhaustible;
even when all [the women] are reciting prayers, whatever is given there bestows spiritual accomplishment (siddhi).
During the Navarātra vow, during lunar and solar eclipses,
and during rare astrological conjunctions (alabhyayoga), that which is given becomes inexhaustible and bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Constant giving brings happiness and bestows long life, heaven, and liberation;
on a Saturday, a gift grants inexhaustible prosperity and abundance. (58)
This [account] of the eclipse of the moon and sun destroys great sins, bestows infinite happiness, and grants the abundance of celestial enjoyments and liberation. (59)
Among all gifts, there are five great gifts;
the first is the very great gift [of land] abounding in a flood of many crops.
O Lord of the Earth, the gift of land consists of [a plot] joined with four bulls and accompanied by two cows, provided with the prescribed sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). 61.
There is no gift equal to this which bestows happiness both in this world and the next:
giving even a daughter without wealth for her marriage to a poor man learned in the Vedas.
It delivers the ancestors and grandfathers of the donor;
this second great gift is the cause of the increase of one's lineage.
The gift of a Śālagrāma stone, accompanied by five grains of rice, and provided with a pair of ruby earrings set in gold; || 64 ||
The third gift of flowers is the cause for union with Brahman;
it consists of a *sāla* tree that yields much milk, along with five milch cows together with their calves.
In that [rite], a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) of three niṣkas of wealth was given at each step to the lotus-feet of the preceptor, especially on the occasion of a festival.
This is the fourth gift; it shatters the multitude of sins, immediately removes all suffering and grief, and bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
The giving of wealth measured by a year's worth of food, along with a pair of garments and a new house,
results in the increase of all one's afflictions.

The removal of the flood of great sins, the granting of heaven and liberation along with its exhaustion, and even the very great gifts, of which the Tulāpuruṣa is the foremost—[all these are surpassed by this]. (69)
There is no doubt that those who provide a palanquin, a swing, or a litter on festival days instantly remove great sins. (70)
Accompanied by his father’s and mother’s lineages, he was instantly liberated from the great masses of evil associated with many sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇās).
Having ascended a divine celestial chariot, he enjoys inexhaustible pleasures in the abode of Brahmā, which are difficult to obtain even in Satyaloka and endure until the end of the kalpa.
O King, on an auspicious day, he constructed a beautiful temple for Tāvinī,
accompanied by a sacrificial fee of wealth amounting to a hundred years' worth [of his income].
Having given [these gifts], he is honored by Mahendra, Dharmarāja, and others,
and he enjoys rare pleasures at his ease in the Nandana and other celestial groves.
Having offered the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) for the sake of the sacrifice at the feet of the preceptor along with all its constituent parts,
he was immediately liberated from the multitudes of great sins (mahāpātaka).
Liberated along with his ancestors and being honored by the lords of the gods,
he rejoices for all eternity in Vaikuṇṭha, the supreme abode.
The constant giving of food destroys great misfortune;
the gift of clothing is of great merit and bestows the abundance of divine enjoyments. (77)
The constant gift of gold grants the attainment of proximity to Hari;
the gift of jewels is of great merit and bestows happiness upon the summit of Mount Meru. (78)
The gift of a ring adorned with divine red gems bestows desired objects;
the gift of pearl ornaments for the ears bestows the enjoyments of Indra.
Indeed, the gift of jeweled ornaments for the ears instantly destroys the great accumulation of sins and bestows both liberation and the means to liberation. (80)
The gift of the Purāṇas, the Dharmaśāstras, and likewise the Saṃhitās, which destroys heaps of sin, bestows happiness in the abode of Brahmā. (81)

If there is any other auspicious object that captivates the mind kept in one's own home, by offering each of those at the lotus feet of the venerable Master, one shall attain supreme accomplishment. 82.
The gift of sesame seeds is a great merit that wards off the afflictions of Yama;
the gift of grain bestows all desired fruits both in this world and the next. (83)
The presence of all sacred fords and the destruction of all sins reside solely in the two lotus feet of the Preceptor; of this there is no doubt. (84)
The life of humans is fleeting, and prosperity is as fragile as a moment; worldly pleasure is mixed with suffering; therefore, one should be devoted to Dharma. (85)
In this world, both dharma and adharma are declared by the Vedas; dharma bestows the bliss of liberation, while adharma brings about the attainment of hellish suffering within my abode.
Therefore, by performing with great devotion the dharma proclaimed in the Śrutis,
one will be honored by the great sages, the Siddhas, the Gandharvas, and even by the gods.

One who performs the recitation of the Mother of the Vedas many times, who is devoted to the Vedas, who is intent on Vedic conduct, and who is a learned scholar (śrotriya), is called a worthy recipient (pātra). || 88 ||
Material wealth and other gifts should be given to a Brahmin who is a worthy recipient;
one devoid of Vedic knowledge is an unworthy recipient, excluded from all sacred rites.
O King, even for one who does not know the Vedas, [the sin] is as small as an atom;
yet it leads to a terrible hell that bestows manifold suffering for an entire kalpa.
By giving even a single object, such as wealth or other goods, to one learned in the Vedas (śrotriya),
the donor causes ten generations of his lineage before him and ten generations after him to cross over [to liberation].
A single teacher is superior even to thousands of Vedic scholars;
by giving even a small measure to a teacher, one attains the supreme goal.
Whether he be a student, a householder, a forest-dweller, or a mendicant,
one should take refuge in the all-pervading Master, the Guru, for the sake of attaining success in the glorious eight-syllable mantra.
For those who are celibate students, householders, and forest-dwellers, there are three gurus:
the father, the mother, and likewise the preceptor; they are not abandoned here or in the hereafter.

Among the female ascetics (pattīs), there was a single teacher, a Brahmin who was a guru identical with the Blessed One and wearing the garb of a yogi; he was to be honored even by his own father. || 95 ||
One should provide nourishment for one's mother; in that act, neither unrighteousness nor lack of merit exists.
Because of her bearing and nourishing the fetus, the mother is more venerable than the father.
Even by an ascetic who is worthy of universal veneration, his mother must be diligently honored; for even in that case, the preceptor alone is indeed to be worshipped as a divine being.

O King, for one who has directly perceived Brahman, the guru who leads him to that realization is his father and mother; indeed, for such a person, the teacher alone is the deity to be worshipped every day.
Even for those who possess knowledge, when Brahman is directly perceived,
[the failure] to abandon the teacher leads to a continuous dwelling in the floods of hells.
No other state of existence is ordained that is so fraught with manifold suffering, even for those who possess the knowledge of the nature of Brahman realized through direct perception. (100)
O King, he who is worthy of honor and salutation three times every day is the teacher;
therefore, one must certainly [revere] the teacher, who is omniscient and identical with the Blessed One. || 1 ||
Having paid obeisance, one should worship with garments and auspicious ornaments, such as earrings, waistbands, and various kinds of finger-rings. || 2 ||
One should diligently nourish [them] every day with wealth, grain, and jewels;
this alone is said to be the great means for attaining the highest good, and nothing else.
There is no knowledge equal to the eight-syllable mantra, no merit equal to the worship of the Guru, no deity superior to the Lord of Śrī, and no fruit equal to liberation. || 4 ||
In the three worlds, there is nothing superior to the worship of the lotus feet of the Guru of Merit;
nor is there anything else that bestows a higher state both here and in the hereafter than the recitation, fire-offerings, and worship of the eight-syllable mantra.
For students and for householders as well as for ascetics, the pair of the Teacher’s lotus feet alone is their refuge;
there exists no other sacred ford more purifying than the sacred ford of the pair of the Teacher’s lotus feet.
Neither Lakṣmī, nor Umā, nor Sarasvatī is worthy of worship if they resemble the wife of a teacher;
rather, it is the wife of the teacher who is like Pārvatī, Vāṇī, Śacī, Bhūmi, and Arundhatī. (7)
Having thus meditated daily upon his teacher as Hari, the Lord, the most worshipful and most excellent,
and having honored and nourished him with manifold riches, he inevitably attained the form of Hari at the end.
Śrī Ṛṣyaśṛṅga said:
Thus was it sung of old by the Blessed One, the Lord of Janakī;
O twice-born ones, whatever was spoken by the Blessed One in the beginning to Nārada [is here recounted].
Therefore, having constantly and respectfully worshipped the omniscient teacher,
one should mutter the glorious eight-syllabled mantra preceded by the ritual placement (nyāsa).
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, which destroys the rising tide of sins, in this unsurpassed mantra concerning the son of Daśaratha.
[Thus ends the seventeenth chapter of the venerable *Anuttarabrahmatattvarahasya*, the *Dāśarathīya Tantra*, which is a compendium of the meaning of the Vedas.]

Śrī Ṛṣyaśṛṅga said: Now, therefore, O twice-born ones, I shall briefly describe the venerable placement (nyāsa) of the eight syllables, the primary [mantra], and so forth, as it was previously taught by the Blessed One.
The Lord Nārāyaṇa is the goal to be attained; he is called the Blessed One and the Sage.
The metre is said to be Gāyatrī, the Chāndoga, the most excellent among all metres. || 2 ||
The Supreme Lord, the eternal God Nārāyaṇa, the master of the three worlds, is accompanied by Lakṣmī, whose very form is splendor.
The letter *a* is said to be the seed-syllable (*bīja*), and the letter *kā* is called the power (*śakti*). This application (*viniyoga*) has been well-proclaimed for the sake of the Lord’s grace.
Gautama, Atri, Bharadvāja, the great sage Viśvāmitra, Jamadagni, Vasiṣṭha, Kaśyapa, and Agastya. || 5 ||
The seers of the eight-syllabled [feet] should be known in their respective order as Gāyatrī, Uṣṇih, Anuṣṭubh, Bṛhatī, and Paṅkti. (6)
The Triṣṭubh, the Jagatī, and the Virāṭ are indeed the meters in their respective order;
likewise, Dharā, Dhruva, Soma, Āpa, Agni, and Vāyu.
Pratyūṣa, Prabhāsa, and [the third] Prabhāsa are to be known as the deities in sequence;
they are dark-complexioned, like the fire born from a blazing meteor, and are as fierce as a wrathful bolt of lightning.
Then, with his head bowed, [he offered] to the one who has the color of gold from the smelting of fire like a great meteor;
at the end of the recitation of the "Fire of Compassion" mantra, the Hero added the word "piṅgalāya" (to the tawny one).
Then, at the location of the crest-lock (śikhā), [one worships] the beloved Agni of two meteors;
then the armor (kavaca) of golden color, from the word "sahasra" and "klāya."
Then one should assign the weapon-mantra (astra) ending with the word "vidyudvarṇāya," and thereafter,
one should likewise perform the assignment of the five fingers (aṅgulīnyāsa).

Having placed the syllables accompanied by the bindu and joined with "namaḥ" upon the fingers starting from the index finger (tarjanī) down to the little finger (kaniṣṭhā), one should then place them on the navel and the secret organ.
It is taught that the placement of the seed-syllable of Viṃduka should be performed upon the knees, the pair of feet, the head, the eyes, the nose, and the heart.

One should perform the eightfold ritual placement (nyāsa) by placing [the mantras] on the heart, the head, the tuft of hair, with the armor-mantra on the eyes, and likewise the weapon-mantra on the belly and the back.
Having thus performed the five-limbed or eight-limbed nyāsa with a concentrated mind, one whose intellect is focused should perform the nyāsa known as the Mātṛkā, both internally and externally. 15.
The seer is Brahmā; the meter is declared to be Gāyatrī;
the deity is Śrī-Sarasvatī, who is the manifest Mātṛkā and the very form of consciousness. || 16 ||
The seed-syllables (bījas) are said to be the ploughs, and the vowels are declared to be the powers (śaktis).
By means of the six groups of consonants, joined with their short, long, and initial-final forms, the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅgaka) is formed.
Having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa), one should then meditate upon the Supreme Goddess Mātṛkā,
who wears a row of letters from 'A' to 'Kṣa' like a garland of rubies.
We praise Mahālakṣmī, who is of the nature of consciousness, the goddess of speech, and the Mother (Mātṛkā).
Now follows the internal placement of the Mātṛkās (Antarmātṛkānyāsa) in the throat, heart, navel, and private parts.
In the path situated between the eyebrows, in the lotus of sixteen petals, twelve petals, ten petals, six petals, four petals, and two petals; || 20 ||
The arrangement of fifty syllables shall correspond to the number of petals in sequence;
O King, one should place each single syllable within each individual petal.
Having thus distributed [the syllables] within, one should then mentally assign them to the head,
the face, the two eyes, and the pair of ears.
One should place the sixteen vowels upon the nose, the pair of cheeks, likewise the pair of eyes, and upon the upper and lower rows of teeth.
One should place the two *ka*-groups on the five joints of the hands;
likewise, one should place the two *ṭa* and *ta* groups on the joints and tips of the feet. (24)
The labial consonants (pavarga) are on the two sides, and [the gutturals] are on the back, the navel, and the abdomen;
[the palatals] are on the heart, the base of the arms, the neck, the armpits, the chest, and so forth, as well as on the row of hands.
One should likewise apply it pervasively to the belly and the face;
thus is the placement of the fifty syllables prescribed in due order.

The seed-syllable beginning with *mā* (māṃ), ending with *na* (namo), or devoid of the nasal drop (*bindu*), preceded by the seeds of Māyā, Lakṣmī, and Kāma, is intended to be deposited [as a mantra]. (27)
One should assign "namas" for the sake of Keśava and Kīrti, as well as for Nārāyaṇa and Kānti, and likewise for Mādhava and Tuṣṭi. || 28 ||
Then [there are] Govinda for nourishment (puṣṭi) and Viṣṇu for fortitude (dhṛti);
likewise Madhusūdana for peace (śānti) and Trivikrama for action (kriyā). || 29 ||
Then [one should worship] Vāmanā and Padmāyā, Śrīdharāya and De, Medhā and Hṛṣīkeśa, and likewise Harṣā; obeisance to them. || 30 ||
To Payanābha and Śraddhā, as well as to Dāmodara;
to Lajjā and Vāsudeva, and to Lakṣmī and Saṃkarṣaṇa. || 31 ||
"Salutation to Sarasvatī and to Prīti, O Pradyumna," so it is desired; then one should utter "and to Aniruddha for prosperity" at the end of the vowels. (32)
Then one should assign [the mantras] to Cakrin, Vijayā, Gadī, Īśāṅgin, as well as to Durgā, Prabhā, and Khaḍgin.
Then one should utter "Salutation to Satyā, to Śaṅkhinī, and to Caṇḍā";
likewise, one should speak [the name] Halinī, as well as Āvāṇī and Amuśalinī.
Then one should address Vilāsinī and Śūlin, Virajā and Pāśin, and likewise Vijayā and Aṅkuśin.
Salutations to Satyā and Utsrā, to Sattvā and Amṛtā, and to Viśvā and Mukunda; then salutations to Vimadā, to Nandajā and Sunandā, to Nandin, and likewise to Smṛti.
One should likewise say "Nārāyaṇa" for the sake of prosperity; "Narakajit" (Conqueror of Naraka) for success; "Hari" for purity; and "Kṛṣṇa" for supreme purification. (37)
One should utter "Salutation to Satya, to Muktī, to Satva, and to Amyta," and likewise to Śauri, to Kṣamā, and to Śūra, who is supremely expanded. (36)
When one desires prosperity for Jarā, Īnārā, Bhūdharā, Kledinī, Eṣi, Mūrti, and Klinnā, then immediately [this mantra should be recited]. || 39 ||
Salutation to Vaikuṇṭha in the west, and after that to Vasudhā;
likewise, Puruṣottama and the supreme Vasudāvalī.
And to Valānujā and Parāyaṇā, after that;
then to Valā and Sūkṣmā, and after that to Vṛṣāghnā. || 41 ||
To Sandhyā and Vṛṣā, and then further to Prajñā;
to Haṃsa and Prabhā, and likewise to Varāha and Niśā.
To Vimala and Amodhya, and after that to Nṛsiṃha;
then to Vidyuta, Tvagātman, and after that indeed to Asṛgātman. || 43 ||

One should utter: "Salutation to the self consisting of flesh, likewise to the self consisting of fat, and also to the self consisting of bone; salutation to the individual self (jīvātman) and to the supreme self (paramātman). || 44 ||
Having thus performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the supreme Mātṛkā, who is composed of all the gods and is directly Vaiṣṇavī, the king undoubtedly becomes the Virāṭ form itself. 45.
Whether preceded by Māyā-Śrī-Kāma or preceded by Kāma alone,
this sequence of ritual placement (nyāsa) beginning with the head, face, and limbs is traditionally taught.
This ritual placement beginning with Keśava destroys great sins;
by the mere performance of this placement, it grants embodied beings the attainment of identity with Brahman. (47)
Having constantly performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) of this supreme Vaiṣṇavī Mātṛkā, which consists of all the gods, the wise man shall attain the state of being absorbed in the Blessed One.
Having daily performed this Vaiṣṇava Mātṛkā-nyāsa while remaining pure, and having recited the glorious eight-syllabled mantra, one becomes Nārāyaṇa in person. (49)
Or, having installed even a single Vaiṣṇava Mātṛkā,
one should daily recite the glorious eight-syllabled mantra according to one's capacity day after day.
The Lord of Śrī, who is manifestly composed of all the gods and whose form is Virāj,
attains great perfection by means of the grace of the preceptor.
He becomes worthy of worship by all the gods and sages;
this very arrangement beginning with Keśava, through its mere placement, [bestows grace] upon embodied beings.
"He indeed bestows immortality; I speak the truth, the absolute truth.
Now I shall explain the nyāsa of reality (tattva-nyāsa); listen attentively, O King. (53)
Having performed the placement of the principles (tattvas), one certainly becomes a knower of the principles.
The vowels beginning with 'mā' [ma], arranged in reverse order, are known as the sparśas.
Salutations to the Supreme; these are established at the beginning and at the end of the Praṇava:
the individual soul (jīva), vital breath (prāṇa), intellect (buddhi), ego (ahaṃkāra), and likewise the mind (manas).
Having placed [the mantras] on all the limbs and in the heart, one should then [place them] upon the objects of the senses such as sound;
