likewise in the head, the nose, the heart, the generative organ, and the feet.
Furthermore, one should again place the organs of knowledge— namely, hearing, touch, sight, taste, and smell— in their respective locations within embodied beings.
The organs of action— speech, hands, feet, the anus, and the genitals—
one should likewise install each one in its respective place.
In the head, face, heart, as well as in the secret parts and the feet,
[one should contemplate] ether, air, fire, water, and earth.
Those skilled in the ritual of placement (nyāsa) have declared that one should perform the placement as before;
likewise, the five [vowels] along with the *śa*, *ṣa*, and *la* sounds, as well as the *ya* and *va* sounds. (60)
The ten syllables beginning with "kṣauṃ" are as before at the end of the Praṇava;
[one should meditate on] the orb of the moon and sun in the heart-lotus, joined with its own digits.
Having thus placed the triad in the heart, one should likewise place Vāsudeva and the others—
Parameṣṭhin, Puruṣa, Viśvavyāpin, and Nivartaka.
Then Nārāyaṇa and Nṛsiṃha, along with Saka and Karauvākyapūraka, [are assigned] to the head, the face, the heart, the secret place, and the feet; thereafter follows the pervasive [assignment].
One should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) in those respective locations with the mantra "Salutation to that Self" (*tadātmane namaḥ*),
because even for one who has not yet realized that reality and is not yet worthy of worship, this serves as the cause for attaining it.
The wise who know reality have declared that there is no other ritual placement (nyāsa);
he who performs the placement of the principles (tattva-vinyāsa) certainly becomes [the Absolute] itself. 65.
Having entered into it as its very self, the Blessed One remains here;
therefore, He alone is the principles (tattvas), for everything is established within Him.
Even one who does not know all the principles, by the constant application of the principles, becomes directly possessed of all principles and becomes a knower of the principles. (67)
By the constant application of the *tattva-nyāsa*, one attains eternal worship;
having become the self that is the consciousness of the universal ocean, one becomes Nārāyaṇa in person. (68)

Having thus performed the deposition of the principles (*tattvanyāsa*) or having deposited [the mantras] daily with devotion, and having obtained the grace of the preceptor, one should mutter the glorious eight-syllabled mantra. (69)
The Sustainer of the Universe (Viśvaṃbhara) shall become worthy of worship even by all the gods,
through the placement of the cage of his forms for the sake of attaining perfection in those forms.
Listen to this essential point, for there is another fruit in this:
one should then say, "Obeisance to the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva. (71)
Oṃ! Having first uttered the syllable "mā" from this mantra, and then the eight-syllabled Śrī-vidyā, one should recite it at the very beginning. (72)
In the same way, one should utter the syllable *vā* from the word *vāta*, and then the glorious eight-syllabled mantra;
thereafter, pronouncing each individual syllable of the twelve-syllabled Vāsudeva mantra.
Taking each name one by one from among the twelve names of Viṣṇu, and likewise taking each name one by one from among the names of Sūrya. (74)

Ending in the dative case and ending with "namaḥ," it should be deposited according to the method of nyāsa upon the forehead, the navel, the heart, the throat, the sides, the shoulders, and the neck. (75)
On the sides, the shoulders, the back, the hump, and also on the head, Keśava should then say the pair: "Nārāyaṇa. (76)
Mādhava, Govinda, Viṣṇu, Madhusūdana, Trivikrama, Vāmana, and Śrīdhara is remembered as the ninth. (77)
Hṛṣīkeśa, Padmanābha, and likewise Dāmodara; these, O seventh among sages, are the twelve names of Viṣṇu in their proper order.
Dhātṛ, Aryaman, Aṃśa, Mitra, Varuṇa, Śukra, Indra, Citrāvasu, Pūṣan, and Parjanya is remembered as the tenth. (79)
Tvaṣṭṛ and Viṣṇu—these are the names of the twelvefold Self. O Lord, this placement of the cage of His forms has been described by me to you. (80)
Having performed the placement of the limbs upon that image (tanmūrtipaṃjaranyāsa), becoming one whose self is the Blessed One,
he should always mutter the glorious eight-syllabled mantra through the grace of his preceptor.
Having attained great perfection, one shall become the manifest Lord of Śrī;
therefore, having performed the *mūrti-pañjara-nyāsa* for the sake of attaining that form, [one should proceed]. 82.
Through the grace of the teacher, one attains the realization of identity with the auspicious Brahman;
hereafter, I shall proclaim the tenfold placement of the phonemes (varṇanyāsa).
Through the grace of the teacher and by means of his realization, one who partakes in the nature of Brahman should first,
with his intellect, contemplate his own body as consisting of the yogic posture.
One should visualize the pair of hands and feet as consisting of the legs of the throne, and the surface of the throne as facing toward the two sides and the navel. (85)

Then, having meditated upon one's own belly as being identical to that [of the deity], within the lotus of one's own heart, which is joined with the mantra of the great seat (mahāpīṭha) of the nine powers; thereafter—

Then, for the sake of favoring his devotees, having meditated upon his own self as the infallible Lord, who has assumed a form through divine play and is identical with the Supreme, [he should worship]. 87.

One should perform the tenfold deposition of the letters (*varṇanyāsa*), which bestows the attainment of oneness with Brahman, in the foundation (*ādhāra*), the heart, the face, the two arms, and likewise in the pair of the feet and the genitals. (88)
The placement (nyāsa) at the pair of feet and at the navel is declared to be one;
each [syllable] consists of a letter from the root mantra, preceded by the Praṇava and ending with "namaḥ. (89)
The wise one should place the *bindu* for the sake of attaining the state of the deity:
at the throat, the navel, the heart, the pair of breasts, and the two sides. (90)
This second method of placement (nyāsa) of the mantra is declared to be performed on the back;
then [it is placed] on the head, the mouth, the pair of eyes, and the pair of ears.
O King, the third placement is said to be on the two nostrils and the back;
[the fourth] is on the eight joints of the arms and the joints of the feet.
The fourth placement is the first [of this group], and the fifth follows after that;
the sixth placement is performed on the eight fingers, excluding the thumb.
The seventh [assignment] is the placement of the toes, excluding the big toe.
O King, [the elements] skin, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, and dried excrement [are assigned]. 94.
Then, having sequentially placed the seven syllables of the root mantra,
one should place those syllables in the form of the vital breath (prāṇa) within the lotus of one's own heart.
This eighth placement has been described: [it is performed] on the head, the pair of eyes, the mouth, the heart, the navel, and subsequently on the two thighs, the two shanks, and the two feet.
This ninth nyāsa is proclaimed as bestowing the accomplishment of the state of divinity; it is performed on the two cheeks, the pair of shoulders, the two thighs, and the two feet. (97)
This tenth nyāsa, consisting of the letters of the root mantra, is proclaimed to bestow success.
Having thus performed this tenfold letter-nyāsa day after day, [one attains the goal]. 98.
O King, having performed the placement of the syllables of the root mantra and having performed the tenfold placement, one attains the state of the deity, by which all perfections are achieved.
Endowed with a portion of the Blessed One, he attains unsurpassed perfection.
Some who are pure knowers of Brahman perform the ritual placement of the letters of the Mātṛkā.
They perform this for the sake of attaining the state of the Blessed One, which bestows all perfections;
this initial arrangement of the letters of the Mātṛkā is called "pure. || 1 ||
The first [nyāsa] begins with the Praṇava; the second begins with the Vāgbhava [bīja];
the third begins with the Māyā-bīja; and the fourth nyāsa is thus proclaimed.
The fifth nyāsa is proclaimed as beginning with the seed-syllable of Lakṣmī;
the sixth nyāsa is proclaimed as beginning with Vāk, Māyā, and Kamalā. || 3 ||
The seventh deposition (nyāsa) proclaimed consists of the seed-syllables of desire (kāmabīja) and so forth;
thereafter, the eighth deposition is proclaimed as beginning with the Haṃsa-mantra.
The ninth is declared to be the Śrīkaṇṭha-mātṛkā-nyāsa;
the Vaiṣṇava-mātṛkā-nyāsa is declared by Daurāma.
Some knowers of Brahman constantly perform the tenfold nyāsa of the Mātṛkās, which bestows the state of the Blessed One and grants all perfections.
The supreme Vaiṣṇavī, who bestows the fruits of the installation of the ten Mātṛkās,
has been proclaimed in the Vedas, Āgamas, and Purāṇas by those most excellent in the knowledge of Brahman.
O King, having performed either the *daśadhāmātṛkā-nyāsa* or another [prescribed] ritual placement (*nyāsa*),
one must certainly perform the Vaiṣṇava *nyāsa* beginning with Keśava-kīrti.
Having performed the placement (nyāsa) of the Mātṛkā internally and externally day after day, it will undoubtedly bestow the fruit of the tenfold Mātṛkā-nyāsa. (9)
Thereafter, having performed the nyāsa of the Vaiṣṇavī Mātṛkā which grants the accomplishment of all aims,
one should then perform the nyāsa of the Tattvas and the nyāsa of the Pañjara of His Form.
Then, one should perform the tenfold placement of the syllables of the root mantra.
Having thus performed the placement according to the rules, one becomes Nārāyaṇa himself.
In this matter, there is no doubt that the minister is capable of both suppressing and uplifting;
having performed the fourfold ritual placement (nyāsa), one should daily worship with devotion. (12)
The Guru, having first taught this entire system of nyāsa, beholds the Lord Indirānātha, the beginning of the year.
Then, O King, the preceptor should impart the auspicious and glorious eight-syllabled mantra to the resident disciple,
provided he has mastered the fourteen types of ritual placement (nyāsa).
On this earth, he bestows the glorious eight-syllabled lore (vidyā).
Both of them are declared to be non-deceivers of the self; of this there is no doubt. (15)
Therefore, one should constantly rely upon a teacher who is truly omniscient, who possesses perfected mantras, who is widely learned, and who is great-souled. (16)
O lord of the earth, this great science must be sought out;
one should go even a thousand yojanas to find a master who has reached the further shore of the meaning of the Vedas.
One should either bestow or receive the auspicious and glorious eight-syllabled mantra (Śrī-Ṣoḍaśākṣarī) accompanied by the fourteen-fold ritual placement (nyāsa) of the Supreme Self. 18.
Otherwise, even through ten million recitations, fire offerings, and so forth, one does not attain success;
nyāsa is the essence of mantra, for without nyāsa, it bestows no accomplishment. (19)
The auspicious placement (nyāsa) of Keśa, Kīrti, and so forth is of fourteen kinds;
having performed this fourteen-fold placement and having recited [the mantra] day after day, [one attains success]. || 20 ||
He attained unsurpassed worship among the fourteen auspicious worlds for the Lord of Indirā,
preceded by the fourteen-fold ritual placement (nyāsa).
Know that teacher on this earth who bestows the glorious eight-syllabled lore to be the all-pervading Lord himself in my own form. (22)
The status of a teacher for a twice-born person is not attained by the mere imparting of knowledge;
he who bestows the Mantra along with its secret (rahasya) is to be known as a teacher, a lord.
O Lord of the Earth, having grasped only the mere mantra without understanding the secret mysteries, one may travel even many thousands of yojanas. (24)
Having bestowed many years of service, or even his life and wealth,
[he should receive] the glorious eight-syllabled mantra (vidyā), preceded by all the ritual placements (nyāsa).
Or, O King, he may receive it from another supreme brahmin;
for that all-pervading Lord alone is the bestower of the entire ritual placement (nyāsa) and the primordial knowledge.
In this world, the teacher is said to be the very embodiment of Nārāyaṇa;
know that he alone is the deity, the true teacher, and a treasure-house of compassion. 27.
He alone is one's own father and mother, the true guru, the Creator, and the Lord;
He is the Supreme Self, the Supreme Brahman, and He alone is called Hari. (28)
Therefore, having served the preceptor as the Lord with diligent effort,
[one should receive] the glorious eight-syllabled mantra (vidyā), preceded by all the ritual placements (nyāsa).
Having performed the installation in its fourteenfold manner, one who regards his own teacher as the Lord daily attains a mass of all that is most auspicious. (30)
"Without bowing to another, even to one's own tree,
one should not worship a god who is not a god"— this is the eternal Vedic revelation.
Having become one whose form is that of the Blessed Lord through this ritual placement (nyāsa), one should therefore worship Hari;
having thus performed the nyāsa with devotion, one should do so constantly with the permission of the preceptor.
After one year, there is no doubt that he shall not be bound even by the gods;
O King, he becomes a great yogi perfected through the power of command, equal to Brahmā.
By means of that single birth alone, he crosses the ocean of existence which is so difficult to traverse, and attains perfection that is hard even for the gods to obtain. (34)

Having performed the daily recitation of the glorious eight-syllable mantra preceded by the ritual placement (nyāsa), one obtains the fruit of ten million recitations even from a single remembrance. || 35 ||

Without knowing the complete ritual placement (nyāsa), one cannot achieve success in the glorious eight-syllabled mantra even through hundreds of preparatory rites (puraścaryā), nor even in hundreds of millions of kalpas.
"O Lord of the Earth, one obtains nothing at all—this is the truth, the absolute truth—even that merit which is the essence of essences found in the Āgamas and the Śrutis. (37)
I shall now declare one even more secret placement (nyāsa), having first diligently uttered the glorious eight-syllabled mantra (vidyā). (38)
O King, one should arrange all the letters of the Mātṛkā as before; this is called the Vidrūpā Mātṛkā, which grants all desires. (39)
Even if one performs the fourteen-fold Nyāsa every day,
one must necessarily perform the *mātṛkā-nyāsa* of the nature of consciousness every single day.
Having performed the placement (nyāsa) of the auspicious Mātṛkā preceded by the illustrious eight-syllabled mantra,
one should recite it every day one hundred times, or eighty-four times.
One constantly attains the fruit of *puraścaryā* in this matter; of this there is no doubt.
Having performed the fourteen-fold ritual placement (*nyāsa*), one should place the insentient-form *mātṛkā*.
The auspicious and glorious eight-syllabled mantra, accompanied by all the ritual placements (nyāsa), is worshipped even by the deities beginning with Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa. 43.
Having performed it thus, it should be known as fruitful; otherwise, it is remembered as fruitless.
[It bestows] the attainment of identity with Brahman, the powers such as *aṇimā*, and prosperity.

Desiring [liberation], one should receive from the lotus-mouth of the teacher the venerable eight-syllabled vidyā preceded by its ritual placement (nyāsa); when recited, it bestows all accomplishments.
Having first recited the *raśmimālā* and performed the *nyāsa-jāla*, the true guru should thereafter bestow the venerable eight-syllabled mantra (*vidyā*) upon the disciple. (46)
Truly, truly I shall declare: furthermore, the illustrious eight-syllabled vidyā should be recited preceded by the ritual placement (nyāsa).
In this *Dāśarathīya Tantra*, which is a compendium of the Vedas concerning the supreme secret of the reality of Brahman, the eighteenth chapter is recorded.
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter of the *Vedārthasaṃgraha*, the *Dāśarathīya Tantra*, which is the illustrious and unsurpassed secret of the reality of Brahman.
The Blessed Lord said:
Thus, having eternally surrendered his body and being manifestly of the nature of the Blessed One, he should meditate upon the flawless Reality, the leader of the entire Brahmāṇḍa. || 1 ||
Beyond the range of words, the agent of creation, maintenance, and destruction, unsurpassed, invincible, difficult to comprehend, and incomparable. || 2 ||
Resembling ten million rising suns and possessing the splendor of ten million moons,
it is devoid of beginning, middle, or end— partless and stainless.
Nor can that wondrous, most imperishable light— from the base of the feet to the aperture of Brahma— be perceived by the gross, nor even by the subtle.
One should meditate upon the Imperishable Supreme Self within the lotus of one's own heart, His form made tawny by a mass of great splendor.
In the midst of the ocean of nectar, it was surrounded by groves of pārijāta trees,
filled with clusters of kalpa-trees, and adorned with divine ramparts.
Studded with various clusters of jewels and surrounded by diverse regions,
that supreme abode of Viṣṇu is renowned as Vaikuṇṭha.
Adorned with ramparts, celestial palaces, and mansions of jewels,
in its center stands that divine city known as Ayodhyā.
Ayodhyā, the eternal city established by the Vedas as the foremost among the gods,
is surrounded by many ramparts adorned with jewels, gold, and various ornaments.
It was completely adorned on all sides by divine groups of women and surrounded by arched gateways.
It is endowed with four gates, enclosed by jeweled gate-towers,
and well-guarded by the gatekeepers Caṇḍa and others, as well as Kumuda and his companions.
It was surrounded by rows of houses resembling millions of suns,
and it was constantly filled with divine men and women who had reached the prime of youth.
In the midst of that was the delightful inner apartment of Ayodhyā, which captivated the mind,
possessed walls of jewels, and was adorned with golden archways.
It was surrounded by many palaces, excellent houses, and ramparts,
and was adorned on all sides by hosts of divine Apsaras and women.
In its center was a divine royal assembly hall of great height,
auspicious and composed of jewels, adorned with a thousand pillars of rubies.
It was filled with eternal liberated souls and graced by the splendor of Vedic chants;
in its center was a beautiful, auspicious throne embodying all the gods.
The eternal deities, consisting of the four feet, are eternally composed of Dharma and the others;
they possess the forms of the four feet: Dharma, Knowledge, Sovereignty, and Dispassion.

It is eternally surrounded by the forms of the Ṛg, Sāman, Atharvan, and Yajus Vedas in their respective order, and encircled by the foundational power (Ādhāra-śakti), the power of consciousness (Cic-chukti), and the primary powers (Mukhya-śaktis). || 17 ||
Accompanied by fire, sun, and moon, surrounded by Vainateya and others,
consisting of the Vedas, composed of all mantras, and adorned with jewels.
The divine and unsurpassed seat of yoga consists of all syllables;
in its center is an eight-petaled lotus with the splendor of a hundred rising suns.
Within that single atom of the Sāvitrī, however, he beheld the Lord of the World,
the Supreme Self, seated together with Śrī, higher than the highest.
Dark as the petal of a blue lotus, more beautiful than ten million gods of love,
a youth possessing a splendor equal to ten million rising suns.
Endowed with delicate limbs, resembling the full moon at its peak,
the awakened lotus-eyed one with symmetrical eyebrows was [manifested] for Kāmadeva.
It was not a lotus that possessed such a beautiful nose, lovely cheeks, and fine ears; nor did it have teeth like pearls and coral-like lips accompanied by a gentle smile.
His lotus-like face was serene, resembling a hundred full moons, and he shone with two earrings having the hue of the rising sun. || 24 ||
Adorned with very glossy, dark-blue,
and curly locks of hair, her tresses were fashioned into a braid enriched with mandāra and pārijāta flowers.
Adorned with the Kaustubha gem, which shines like the sun rising at dawn,
his neck was resplendent, its throat graced by a necklace and a golden garland.
He was resplendent with high, thick shoulders resembling those of a lion,
and graced by four long, rounded, and stout arms.
Exceedingly adorned with finger-rings, bracelets, and armlets, they were further embellished with the Kaustubha jewel and other ornaments, resembling the brilliance of ten million rising suns.
His broad chest was resplendent, his entire body beautiful,
wearing divine garlands and garments, and adorned with a forest wreath.
Adorned with the navel-lotus, the place of origin for the Creator,
he was clothed in a pair of smooth yellow garments resembling the morning sun.
It was resplendent with two bracelets richly adorned with various jewels,
and beautified by rows of nails resembling the full moon and stars.
He is Acyuta, a treasure-house of the exquisite beauty and loveliness of ten million Cupids,
his limbs anointed with divine sandalwood paste and adorned with celestial flower garlands.
He is resplendent with two arms holding a conch and a discus,
and likewise with his other two hands, which display the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
The goddess Mahālakṣmī, the Great Sovereign, is seated upon his left lap;
she is golden-hued, tawny, and possesses offspring of gold and silver.
Endowed with all auspicious marks, her body at the onset of youth, adorned with jeweled earrings and beautified by a pair of locks of hair. || 35 ||
Her limbs were smeared with divine sandalwood paste, she was adorned with celestial flowers,
and her earrings were filled with mandāra, ketakī, and jasmine blossoms.
Adorned with a nose-ornament inlaid with pearls and rubies,
she shone with a pair of breasts resembling the splendor of the Blessed One.
Her eyes were like the petals of a lotus, adorned with collyrium,
and her face resembled a thousand autumn moons.
Her appearance was like a net of pearls, adorned with rows of teeth;
her lips shone like a single bimba fruit, graced by the two [teeth].
She was adorned with ear-ornaments resembling the rising sun,
and graced by beautiful, dark, and wavy locks of hair.
With a smiling face and wide eyes, her lotus-like countenance serene,
she was adorned with the primary ornaments, including necklaces, bracelets, and other finery.
Adorned with necklaces and golden garlands, resplendent with armlets,
possessing a luster like the color of molten gold, and wearing ornaments of refined gold.
She was endowed with four hands, adorned with garments and ornaments of gold,
and possessed a garland of golden lotuses variegated and enriched with various jewels.
She was adorned with necklaces, armlets, earrings, and finger-rings,
and she shone with a pair of uplifted lotuses held in her two arms.
I bow to the Mother of all the worlds, who is compassionate toward those who have come for refuge, and who holds in her hand a golden citron.
Her lotus feet are resplendent with a luster born from the rubies in the crowns of Brahmā, Rudra, Maheśvara, and the other gods; she is solely devoted to the protection of her devotees.
Thus, he was accompanied by Mahālakṣmī, who is ever-showering her grace;
he is the leader of ten million billion universes and is affectionate toward his devotees.
One should behold the Supreme Lord, Śrīpati, who is composed of light and worthy of being seen by the world,
accompanied on his two sides by the goddess Dharaṇī and by Nīlādevī.
It was attended in the eight directions by the eight powers (śaktis) beginning with Vimalā,
and by the lords of the gods beginning with Senānī, as well as by the lord of the infinite birds (Garuḍa).
It is crowded with those eternally liberated as well as other attendants;
it is to be worshipped by all the supreme gods and meditated upon by all yogis.
"I bow to Nārāyaṇa, who is devoted to the very life-breath of his devotees.
Having thus meditated upon the unborn and all-pervading Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of Lakṣmī, [he spoke]. (51)
Having bowed one's head to the teacher, one should mutter the glorious eight-syllable mantra;
from the mouth of the teacher, this auspicious hymn of meditation [is received]. (52)
Having grasped it, constantly meditated upon it, and recited it day after day, one swiftly attains the perfect realization of identity with Brahman; of this there is no doubt.
Or else, he is mounted upon a chariot drawn by four horses, possessing the luster of molten gold like the orb of the rising sun, and resplendent in yellow garments.
Wearing a crown and earrings, resplendent with a necklace of pearls,
and adorned with signet rings inlaid with gold and gems.
With eyes like the interior of a lotus, a serene lotus-face,
possessing the splendor of a thousand rising suns, and a radiance equal to ten million gods of love.
Resembling a thousand stainless autumnal full moons,
it was adorned with signets inlaid with gold and jewels.
Holding the conch, discus, mace, and lotus, with the Śrīvatsa mark upon his chest,
his breast illuminated by the Kaustubha gem, and adorned with a forest garland.
O Supreme Goddess, you are praised by the four Vedas personified,
as well as by the sages beginning with the Vālakhilyas, and by the deities beginning with Brahmā and Rudra.
He was praised day and night by yogis such as Sanaka and others,
seated in the heroic posture (vīrāsana), with a splendor equal to ten million flashes of lightning.
Endowed with Śrī, the goddess Mahālakṣmī, and the Fortune of Sovereignty;
the Lord of Śrī, the eternal cause of the three worlds.
I worship Hari, the Supreme Self, the Lord of Śrī, Bhū, and Nīlā;
these two meritorious hymns for meditation have been spoken by me to you.

Having received [the initiation] from the grace of the teacher alone on an auspicious day, having gratified him with excellent offerings, and having continuously recited the mantra and meditated upon it; |||
Having chanted the glorious eight-syllabled mantra one thousand times, or four hundred,
three hundred, or even one hundred times, one becomes Nārāyaṇa in person.
Or, having recited daily the two hymns on meditation— the "Marvelous" and the "Imperishable"— the wise man is liberated from all sins.
"At the end of this life, he falls into the supreme, eternal abode of Viṣṇu.
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Two Hymns on Meditation," in this compendium of the meaning of the Vedas concerning the son of Daśaratha.
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter in the *Śrīmadanuttarabrahmatattvarahasya*, the *Dāśarathīya Tantra*, which is a compendium of the meaning of the Vedas.
The Blessed Lord said: O King, listen attentively as I now describe the extraction of the yantra;
by worshipping the Lord of Lakṣmī therein, one may attain the bliss of Brahmananda. (1)
O Lord of the Earth, this network of nyāsas which was previously taught by me must necessarily be performed with the permission of the Guru. (2)

Having become one whose form is the Blessed Lord through the ritual placement (nyāsa), the person consisting of mantra should then meditate upon the all-pervading Nārāyaṇa within the lotus of the heart.
Or else, one should meditate on the Lord as Nārāyaṇa, one’s own preceptor;
and one should also meditate on Śrī, the mother of the three worlds, who is dissolved within Him. || 4 ||
For the sake of attaining the perfection of the Lord’s form for oneself, one should mentally offer a handful of flowers while reciting the Kirīṭa-vidyā. || 5 ||
Observing silence, one should offer [the seed-syllable] five times into the lotus of the heart;
then, one completes it with the words "trayībījaṃ kirīṭe."
Then he says, "Wear the crown," and "Wear the earrings";
after that, he recites the words "with conch, discus, mace, and lotus in hand."
"She who wears yellow garments" is stated; then, by the word "marked with Śrīvatsa," the term "chest" follows; and then, "accompanied by Śrī and Bhūmi. (8)
O King, it is declared that "the light of one's own self" (svātmajyotiḥ) leads to the state of imperishability;
from that comes the state of "the radiant one" (dīptikara), and then from the word "the infinite sun" (anantāditya).
"O King, the mantra for the crown of the Lord's form, which bestows the perfection of the deity's manifestation, is: *tejase hṛdayopeta vahnipatnīpadaṃ*. (10)
Whatever ornaments and so forth are mentioned for the mantra-deity within this mantra, that is declared to be divine ornamentation; anything else is human ornamentation.
If a disciple should worship the preceptor with divine ornaments,
he will certainly and surely himself become the very form of the Blessed One.
The divine ornament for the face, which was mentioned as the pair of earrings—that very ornament mentioned is also highly esteemed among these [other ornaments]. (13)
Therefore, it must necessarily be fashioned from refined gold,
adorned with a gem known as a pure ruby and embellished with a drop-like mark.
On an auspicious day and at an auspicious moment for rites such as the *puraścaryā*, having first prostrated, one should place [the mantra] into the ears of the preceptor.
Having honored the preceptor’s wife with a pair of golden earrings or with an ornament such as a *tāṭaṅka*, [he should give] six *māṣas* or more, up to a lord of two villages.
"O lord of the earth, you see with your own eyes that this is indeed the truth;
know me alone to be the Lord of the World appearing in the form of a teacher. (17)
Know that his wife, my beloved Śrī, the mother of the three worlds, is fashioned from refined gold in the form of a crocodile. || 18 ||
Having given a pair of beautiful earrings adorned with rubies to the ears of the preceptor on an auspicious day and at an auspicious moment, [he should perform the rite].
Having certainly rescued a thousand ancestors who were submerged in the ocean of hell,
he shall attain a divine, imperishable celestial chariot made of gold.
Having ascended, beautiful as Kandarpa at his peak, and partaking of divine enjoyments,
he pierces the entire cosmic egg and attains the eternal state.
Here too, one shall obtain supreme prosperity, abounding in wealth, grain, and so forth, as well as sons and grandsons, long life, and health. (22)
Whatever divine ornament one may offer to the preceptor, that will undoubtedly bring about the attainment of the bliss of Brahmananda. (23)
The pair of yellow garments that the Blessed One always wears, those very same ones are worn daily by the Goddess, who is adorned with supreme splendor.
Firm in his vows, he also gives fine silk garments to the teacher and his wife on auspicious occasions such as the commencement of Vedic study.
Wearing divine yellow garments and adorned with divine ornaments,
he shall certainly attain the perfect realization of identity with Brahman.
Therefore, ornaments, wealth, and so forth must certainly be given continuously to the preceptor, his wife, and also to his sons. (27)
I shall describe the nature of the yantra of the venerable Supreme Self, by worshipping the Lord of Lakṣmī within which one may obtain the bliss of Brahman-joy. (28)
Having first drawn a six-spoked wheel, then an eight-petalled lotus surrounded by a circle,
one should thereafter draw a square outside that circle.

Having written the name of the person to be accomplished (sādhya) and the ritual action (karma), interspersed between two *praṇavas* in the center of the hexagon, one should thereafter [place them] in the six corners.
One should write the six syllables of the manifestation of Nṛsiṃha;
one should write the eight glorious syllables of the Ṛṣṭākṣarī mantra upon the eight petals.
Having written one syllable each from the Śrīkara mantra at its tips,
[one should write] from the Vāsudeva mahāmantra upon the twelve spokes.
Having written one letter for each of the thirty-two spokes,
one should thereafter write one letter from the Nṛsiṃha-anuṣṭubh mantra upon each spoke.
Then, one should encircle it with ghee using the single-syllable mantra of Nṛsiṃha;
this is declared to be the yantra for the venerable eight-syllable vidyā.
Afterwards, one should cause a square of fifty syllables to be drawn;
without that square, the eight-syllable yantra is declared to be "light" (laghu).
The great yantra, joined with four corners, has been proclaimed;
having first drawn this yantra, made either of gold or silver, || 36 ||
Having established the vital breath (prāṇapratiṣṭhā) of the Lord of Śrī within a living image made of wood, copper, or stone, on an auspicious day and at a favorable moment; || 37 ||
Having fully honored the lotus feet of the preceptor with various offerings, as well as his wife with ornaments and garments; (38)
[He who recites] the glorious eight-syllabled lore, conjoined with the placement [of mantras] upon the body (*nyāsa*), for the sake of destroying the three peaks of evil. (37)
Having fully worshipped the lotus feet of the preceptor with offerings and ornaments,
and having recited the mantra more than a thousand times, he offered a hundred oblations of clarified butter.
O Leader, one should worship it daily with the Raśmi-mantras;
or else, one should diligently wear the yantra as a finger-ring.
If one has respectfully drawn two yantras for the purpose of preservation or for worship, and having first worn them, should worship them continuously; || 41 ||
Even one of little fortune may become comforted by all forms of prosperity; for the riches of another may shift from here to there, or from one house to another. (42)
It provides protection against mental and physical ailments, fear, and the terrors of Kūṣmāṇḍas and other demons;
it brings about auspiciousness and destroys all calamities and misfortunes.
Through its retention and worship, there is indeed no fear of death or the time of death;
through the grace of the Teacher, for him there is liberation and eternal, auspicious prosperity.
That indeed belongs to the lineage of Kamaleṣṭha; of this there is no doubt.
Now, I shall describe to you the procedure for worship in two ways.
By the mere realization of which one directly becomes composed of the elements (*maya*) among the worlds;
likewise, [the stages] Vimalā, Utkarṣiṇī, Jñānā, Kriyā, and Yogā. (46)
We whose powers are unimpaired by the Lord of Truth,
having first worshipped the sacrifice sustained by the nine powers, [we praise] the Lord of Śrī.
O Śaṅkha, [recite] "Oṃ namaḥ" and then that word which is the ineffable state belonging to the Blessed One. || 47 ||
Having uttered for Viṣṇu the word "to him who is the self of all beings," and then the word "Vāsudeva," and thereafter the word "to the self of all. (48)
Then, with this mantra— consisting of "to the self of the Yoga-pīṭha," "to the self of the West," and joined with the word "namas"— one should worship the Pīṭha for the Blessed Lady.
In the center of the hexagon, with the root mantra joined by the Lakṣmī-mantra, one should invoke the Lord of Śrī using the syllables "Śrī Śrī" and the six-eyed one (the six-syllabled mantra).
One should perform all the ritual services while reciting the root mantra of Śrī, the mantras of Śrī, and the Brahma-vidyā, as ordained by Śrī, Śrīśa, and Brahmā. (51)
Having thus worshipped the two lords, Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa, one should also worship the six limbs beginning with the heart using the six seed-syllables. || 52 ||
One should worship Vāsudeva, Saṃkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha in the cardinal directions, and Śrī, Vāṇī, Rati, and Prīti in the intermediate directions.
The second enclosure is said to consist of the discus, the conch, the mace,
the lotus, the Kaustubha gem, the pestle, the sword, and thereafter the forest garland.
The third enclosure is proclaimed; then the Banner (Dhvaja) and the Lotus-treasure (Padmanidhi), Garuḍa and the Conch-treasure (Śaṅkhanidhi) in the cardinal directions, and then Vidyeśvara.
Then one should worship Vaṭuka and Durgā, and Viṣṇu and Vāsudeva in the intermediate directions;
this is declared as the fourth enclosure (āvaraṇa), while the fifth is known to consist of the guardians of the quarters (dikpālas).
This bestower of desired fruits has been declared in the mantra for the procedure of worship today;
thus, having duly worshipped the Lord of the World, the Master of Ramā, according to the Tantra— || 57 ||
Liberated from all doubts, he shall possess the attainment of all fruits;
[I have told you] this ritual for the emission of the Vṛṣas, which is a perpetual secret.
I shall describe to you for your benefit that which is not found elsewhere:
Candra, Pracaṇḍa, Īśa, Bhadra, and Subhadraka at the eastern gate.
One should worship Jaya and Vijaya as the gatekeepers at the rear, and then one should worship Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ on the two sides of the door.
Kubhuḍa, Kumudākṣa, Puṇḍarīka, Vāmana, Ambukarṇa, Saṃvanetra, Susamukha, and Sujātiṣṭhita. || 61 ||

One who is devoted to meditation should worship the guardians of the directions outside the enclosure of the meditation-pavilion; in its center, one should worship the divine [deities] of the Lord, beginning with the inner sanctum and extending to the outer quarters.
When the Lord Ulkā is seized by the city of Meru, and the essence of the jewel-prakya is drawn into the tomara, that is the *āsara*. (63)
Thus, the descent of the divine chariot of the Blessed One from here [is described];
that chariot is to be worshipped there in its midst with divine sounds. (64)
It was said that those who are without protection are "women without protectors" (aśarastrī) by virtue of their very hearts;
since there is something unreal in the midst of that, the King therefore established this court of justice (rājāsthāna). 65.
One should utter the name "Mahoccayapada-maṇḍaya. Having thus worshipped Maṇḍaya, one should then place that which is within its center.

Furthermore, having worshipped the jewel-pavilion (ratnamaṇḍapa), which is endowed with a thousand pillars of rubies (māṇikya) and is worthy of salutation with the word "namaḥ" in the dative case, [one should proceed]. 67.
After worshipping the pavilion, he should subsequently offer the ground for fear;
in its center, having consecrated it with all mantras, he should place the supreme footstep.
Having worshipped the pavilion with the mantra "To the Jewel-Lion Throne," ending in the dative case and accompanied by the word "namaḥ. || 67 ||
After worshipping the pavilion, he then again addressed the Earth:
"In its center, O Sarvavedī, is the supreme, divine, and most beautiful lotus. (68)
Having recited "ratnasiṃham siṃhāsanāya" and so forth, one becomes [the lion-throne];
having thoroughly worshipped the lion-throne, thereafter [one worships] Dharma and Jñāna. (69)
Dispassion as well as sovereignty are superior to the nature of the individual soul;
likewise, ignorance, lack of dispassion, and lack of sovereignty are known by those who seek knowledge.
Having worshipped thoroughly, one should then recite the Ṛgveda,
the collection of hymns, the Sāmaveda, and thereafter the Atharvaveda.
Having worshipped Śakti, the Support-Power (Ādhāraśakti), the Consciousness-Power (Cicchakti), and Sadāśiva,
he should worship the mandala of Fire and the mandala of the Sun.
Having worshipped the lunar mandala, one should then worship the Tortoise, the Lord of Nagas, Garuda, and the King of the Three Vedas; after that, one should worship the Vedic meters.
Having worshipped all the mantras, [one should recite] "sarvamantrākṣara" (the syllable of all mantras),
and then "yā yad divyapadaṃ yogapīḍāya namaḥ" (to that which is the divine state, salutation to the one who causes the pressure of yoga).
Having worshipped the Yoga-pīṭha with the previously mentioned mantras as well, one should then utter that which is in its center: "O Child-Sun, [thousandfold]! (vālasūryaśata). 75.
One should utter "to the lotus resembling [the sun], from the eight petals";
having worshipped the lotus, one should utter "salutation to Sāvitrī" in its center. (76)
Having explained the meaning, meter, deity, and the hundred seed-syllables (bījas) of the glorious eight-syllabled mantra, he then [worshipped] the God of gods, the Lord of Śrī.
Having meditated upon you within his own lotus-like heart,
he should then recite the glorious eight-syllabled mantra of Vāsudeva Ananta.
Then one should recollect the six-syllabled Vaiṣṇavī mantra and the Śrī-mantra; having uttered the Brahmavidyā and invoked the supreme form of Śrī,
one should perform the ritual movements (savovacāra) with the Śrī-Brahmavidyā.

First the Praṇava, then the seed-syllables *cit* and *kāla*, followed by the venerable eight-syllabled mantra (*śrīśāṣṭākṣara*), and then the words "I fashion this jeweled lion-throne; obeisance. (80)
With the primary seats for the attendants and all the various types of servants,
one should offer the jeweled lion-throne, as well as the water for welcoming (arghya) and the water for sipping (ācamanīya).
Having performed the bath with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and then with pure water, one should then offer two garlands made of one's own leaves and flowers.
One should then prepare divine, auspicious sandalwood paste and unbroken grains of rice,
and likewise arrange various kinds of divine flowers.
Then, having arranged various kinds of divine ornaments,
one should prepare incense and lamps, and thereafter perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana).
One should also arrange a pair consisting of an umbrella and a fly-whisk, as well as a mirror;
furthermore, with great reverence, one should offer water for protection, water for sipping, and the food offering (naivedya).
After that, one should perform the washing of the hands and feet,
as well as the offering of black [incense], and thus arrange the twenty-four modes of service (upacāra).

Then, according to the previously mentioned procedure, one should meditate upon the all-pervading Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of Lakṣmī, as present within the Śālagrāma stone. Or else, [one may meditate] upon Him there.
Having recited the Brahmavidyā five times,
one should then worship Bhūdevī with offerings to the right and Nīlā to the left.
Thereafter, one should worship the six limbs in the directions of the East, Northeast, Southeast, Southwest, Northwest, and the Center; thus there is a triad of sequences for all directions.
Then, O King, one should worship Avimalā at the tips of the petals in the eight directions; thereafter, beginning from the front, one should worship Vimalā, and then Utkarṣiṇī.
Then, for the sake of the grace of the Lord, one should worship Jñānā, Kriyā, Tathā, Yogā, Prahvī, Satyā, and Mataḥparā, as well as Iṃśā; thereafter, one should worship Vasudhāyate.
Then, in the eastern and other directions, one should worship Vāsudeva and Śrī, Saṃkarṣaṇa and Vāṇī, and likewise Pradyumna and Rati.
The non-ceased suchness is peace; it is known as the second veil.
[It is also known as] Keśa, Nārāyaṇa, Mādhava, Govinda, and Viṣṇu. (93)
Having worshipped Madhusūdana, those two [then worshipped] Trivikrama and Vāmana,
Śrīdhara, Hṛṣīkeśa, and thereafter Yamunābha.
Dāmodara, Saṃkarṣaṇa, and Vāsudeva beyond that;
then Pradyumna, Aniruddha, and also Puruṣottama. (95)
One should worship Adhokṣaja, Nārasiṃha, Acyuta,
Vajranārdaṇa, Upendra, Hari, and thereafter Kṛṣṇa, O destroyer of sins.
Then follows the third incarnation: the Fish, the Tortoise, the Boar, the Man-lion, the Dwarf, and after that, the son of Jamadagni (Paraśurāma).
One should worship Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, followed by Balabhadra, and thereafter Buddha and Kalki; having worshipped these, one should then worship the other [deities] beginning with Ananta.
The fourth practice is declared to be truth and indeed the infallible;
having worshipped the infinite All, one should thereafter bow to Viṣṇu.
Then, one should worship Gajānana and Śaṅkhanidhi as the representative;
this is declared to be the fifth enclosure, consisting of the Ṛgveda and the collection of Yajurvedic texts.
The Sāmaveda, the Atharvaveda, Sāvitrī, Vihageśvara, Dharma, and Yajñapuruṣa are declared as the sixth enclosure. || 1 ||
The conch, the discus, the mace, the lotus, the sword, the Śārṅga bow,
and likewise the pestle with its companion are declared to be the auspicious enclosure of the Lord.
Śadhī, Mahendra, Svāhā, Agni, as well as Saṃhāriṇī and Yama;
then Tāmasī, Nisṛti, Bhārgavī, and Varuṇa. (3)
Then [he worships] Gati-vāyu and Pati-kuveṇa;
after that, Rudrāṇī and Śaṅkara; and finally, Vāk and Caturānana in the upper [direction].
And with Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa, the eighth enclosure is traditionally remembered;
[the deities of the weapons are] Vajrāyudha, Śakti, Daṇḍa, Khaḍga, Pāśa, Dhvaja, and Gadā.
The trident, the lotus, and the discus are known as the ninth enclosure;
beyond that are the Dhyānamārutas and the Viśvedevas.
[He saw] the yogis beginning with Sanaka, the divine sages beginning with Nārada,
the great perfected ones (mahāsiddhas) beginning with Kapila, and the yogis beginning with Atri and Nṛpa.
To the great devotees such as Prahlāda, to those who act as servants such as Hanumān, to the wise such as Janaka, and to kings such as Daśaratha; (8)
Having performed worship and reciting the Śrī-Brahmavidyā, the illustrious one,
having fully honored Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa with a hundred thousand repetitions, shone with splendor.
Offer the ritual services, such as incense, lamps, and food offerings;
then, O King, with the preceptor in mind, perform these in the presence of the Blessed One.
Whatever may be given— be it gold, gems,
or even copper, grain, or ghee— one who desires [to give] should offer it with joy.
Or else, one should make the day fruitful by reciting what has been resolved upon, as if with a sword; otherwise, one becomes a partaker of sin. (112)
This complete procedure for worship has been fully proclaimed;
it destroys the accumulation of great sins and bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
If one is unable to perform it by force, one should do so on the day of Bhārgava; or else, one may perform it month after month on the first day of the lunar fortnight dedicated to Bhārgava.
During the Navarātra vow, one must certainly perform the worship of Brahmā;
O King, worship should always be performed even when the planets are unfavorable.
Lakṣmīpati protects him with great joy, as if he were his own son; for a man who worships in this manner, a mass of spiritual welfare increases day by day. (16)
All prosperities, even those enjoyments that are very difficult to obtain, are accomplished;
thus is the worship of the illustrious Lord of Śrī declared to be the Great Sacrifice (Mahānyāga). || 17 ||
The Rājasūya sacrifice, or even a Soma-sacrifice, would not be equal to it;
[this is for] the perfection of what is deficient or excessive, and for the attainment of the fruitfulness of the sacrifice. (18)
One should give the teacher’s fee (dakṣiṇā), free from greed for wealth;
O Lord of the Earth, that day which is devoid of the teacher’s fee is [fruitless].
Even by Yama himself, who has been brought there by his messengers, he is seen;
for fear of Yama destroys the obstacles to the enjoyment of heaven and liberation for men.
O Lord of the Earth, as he thus worshipped Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa daily, O King, he made offerings to his preceptor every day.
All accomplishments (siddhis), even those difficult for the gods to attain, are achieved through this.
O Janaka, the procedure for worship has thus been declared to you.

For one who is constantly engaged in the study of the Vedas, who practices virtuous conduct day after day, and who is perpetually intent upon the victory of the glorious eight-syllabled mantra (Aṣṭākṣarī-vidyā), [there is no fear]. 23.
By this method, for one who performs worship daily with devotion, even that which is most difficult to attain shall be accomplished, along with all their desired objects. (24)
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "The Compendium of Śruti on the Secret Essence of the Unsurpassed Brahman," as proclaimed in the work of Daśarathi. 125.
[Thus ends the twentieth chapter in the glorious *Anuttarabrahmatattvarahasya*, the *Dāśarathīya-tantra*.]
Salutations to Śrī Rāma.
The sages said: "O highly fortunate Ṛṣyaśṛṅga, O Blessed One, best among yogis!"
The conduct of the virtuous proclaimed in the Vedas, as also that uttered by Manu and others.
Our supreme curiosity is that we wish to hear from your lotus-like mouth how the prosperity and well-being of your devotees may truly come to pass.
Just as there may be purity of consciousness, so that the body becomes pure,
[one should meditate on] the glorious eight-syllable mantra, endowed with a garland of rays of wisdom.
"O Sage, tell me how this may be accomplished without effort.
Śrī Krathaśṛṅga said:
"In former times, this was proclaimed by the Blessed One to Rudra when he questioned him. (4)
I shall describe the Vedic conduct of the Lord of Jānakī,
which was spoken by Nārada to the high-souled King Sādhyā.
Again, the son of Daśaratha, the husband of Jānakī, spoke to Śambhu:
"Celibacy, dwelling in the waters, residence in the forest, and extreme hunger."
O high-minded one, there are four stages of life for the twice-born;
yet the glorious eight-syllable mantra belongs to all those in every stage of life.
Having recited [the mantra], one attains the desired perfection and eternal liberation from the heart;
this [practice] is always accompanied by all the ritual depositions (nyāsa) for those who possess constant right conduct.
The glorious eight-syllabled mantra bestows even that success which is difficult to attain;
O high-minded one, first [practice] right conduct briefly as previously described.
Furthermore, I shall speak specifically; listen with focused attention, O sage.
The Blessed Lord said: Listen, O King of great intellect, I shall proclaim the conduct of the virtuous (sadācāra).
Having heard which, even a wise man shall not enter into the darkness of ignorance.
Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas—these three castes are known as the twice-born (dvijas). 11.
The first birth is from the mother, and the second is from the Veda;
for them, there is the worldly ritual beginning with the initiatory consecration (kriyā-abhiṣeka) and ending at the cremation ground.
A wise man should cause the embryo to be conceived; then, after the birth of the child, he should perform the *puṃsavana* rite, followed by the *sīmantonnayana*. Then, [the other rites]. 13.
The birth-rite (jātakarma) should be performed on the sixth, eighth, or even the tenth day after birth;
the naming ceremony (nāmakaraṇa) on the eleventh day; and he should be brought out of the house in the fourth month.
In the sixth month, the first feeding with solid food (annaprāśana) takes place according to family custom;
likewise, the tonsure (cūḍākarman) occurs, as well as the rites concerning the seed and the womb.
These rites for women are performed silently, while the grasping of the hand is accompanied by mantras; O gods, a Brāhmaṇa kills the Sāvitrī at the very same time as the eighth [year]. || 16 ||
A man may give [a cow] on the eleventh day after death, or on the twelfth day according to family custom;
a Brahmin deserves to receive it for the sake of increasing his spiritual luster (brahmatejas). || 17 ||
The Guru should cause the Kṣatriya to be initiated at the age of eleven, the Vaiśya at eight, and the Śūdra at sixteen;
for these, the sacred thread ceremony (mauñjī) is performed with the Mahāvyāhṛtis as the preliminary, and he should instruct them in the Veda.
Then, having initiated the disciple, he should instruct him in the rules of purification;
he should perform purification according to the previously stated method, continuing until the mind is fully purified.
Having purified his teeth and tongue with this purification formula, he should bathe and, having restrained his breath according to the rules, recite these mantras.
Having performed the ritual attendance toward the sun at both twilights,
and having then performed the fire-rite, he should be devoted to the glorious eight-syllabled mantra.
Having saluted the teacher, he should then salute the foremost of the Brahmins;
having approached the teacher, he should say, "I am so-and-so. || 23 ||
For one who is habituated to saluting others and who delights in serving the elders, strength, fame, and prosperity shall increase day and night. (24)
Having studied what was brought forth by the teacher, he should report his understanding to him;
he should always strive to perform for him whatever is beneficial through action, mind, and speech. (25)
They were learned in the Dharma and devoted to its practice; they were virtuous, possessed of right knowledge, capable, grateful, and free from envy. || 26 ||
By carrying out the commands of the virtuous king, they shall attain dharma;
and they shall constantly strive to understand the glorious eight-syllabled mantra along with its ancillaries.
A Brahmin, for the sake of attaining liberation, should also practice his daily conduct according to his station;
and for the sake of accomplishing the study of the Vedas, he should remain established in the eight syllables during times of distress.
The wise one should take refuge in either one or both of the two gurus;
he should wear a girdle, a staff, and likewise a deerskin.
One should practice alms-seeking among Brahmins who are not of low birth for the sake of maintaining one's livelihood;
[one should seek it] from Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas at the beginning, middle, and end [of their meal]. (30)
Following the sequence of wandering for alms, she should remain standing and observe silence; permitted by her guru, she should eat the food without disparaging it.
One should not eat more than one meal at a śrāddha, even if it is desirable;
for excessive eating leads to ill health, shortens life, and brings misfortune. (32)
That which is unwholesome and loathed by the world should therefore be completely avoided.
Furthermore, O best of the twice-born, one should never eat a second time on the same day, nor at any time during the day.
Twice daily, at dawn and dusk, he should perform the *dvijīṣṇīya* rite according to the rules for maintaining the sacred fire (*agnihotra*);
he should avoid honey, meat, injury to living beings, and the gaze of the sun; and he should not apply collyrium.
One should avoid a woman who has been enjoyed by another, as one would avoid the remnants of a sacrifice;
this is the rule for the initiation of the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas. || 35 ||
From sixteen up to twenty-two, and from twenty-four years onwards—
from this point upward, those who have been deprived of the sacraments but are not subject to the laws of outcasting (patita) are to be purified.
One should completely avoid associating with a Brāhmaṇa who has performed that sacrifice, as well as avoiding contact with those who have performed the Sāvitrī-vrata. || 37 ||
The skins of the bamboo-horned deer (vaiṇa), the ruru deer (raurava), and the black antelope (asta) are, in order, for the twice-born;
their sacred threads (upavīta) should likewise be made, respectively, of silk, hemp, and wool.

That vow is to be observed for three days and nights, and it serves to increase one's lifespan. [One should perform this] at the junction of the *vilva* and *bilva* trees, or at the abode of a Brahmin, or at a human habitation. (39)
Nyagrodha, vāladala, udumbara, and viśa [are the materials];
having bent them down to the forehead or to the tip of the nose according to the measurement.
Having heard [the account] from the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas, and being adorned by the fires of the sacred scriptures and the Vedas,
he circumambulated the fire and uttered words of consolation to her.

The body, the skin, the sacred thread, the tongue, the teeth, the mother, the mother’s mother, the father, the father’s mother, the sister, the brother, and the lover—these are as they are ordained. (42)
First, they should seek alms from their kinsmen; after that, from others;
then at the time of the *aupaniṣadika* [final] meal, they may go to the house of an eminent Brahmin.
O King, the wise man should practice the life of a mendicant until he has mastered the Veda; he should live as one who practices the Vedic way of life. (44)
One should remain a celibate student for a long time; thereafter, one should become a householder.
Alternatively, one may always serve the teacher as an attendant (upakurvan), or as a lifelong student (naiṣṭhika) following his specific instructions.
One should remain in the state of a householder for as long as life lasts;
yet, having relied upon the householder's stage of life, one may again partake in the practice of celibacy.
He should not remain without a stage of life; he should be free from all [other] stages of life. A twice-born man should not remain without a stage of life even for a single day. (47)
One who does not abide in the hermitage must perform penance;
for he destroys victory, this vow, charity, Vedic study, and offerings to the ancestors.
One who undertakes a stage of life (āśrama) without [proper initiation] does not enjoy its fruit.
The girdle, deerskin, staff, and [shaven] head are the insignia of the student (brahmacārin). (49)
For a householder, the absence of nails and body hair is prescribed because of his attachment to worldly objects;
here, the mention of the triple staff and so forth for the ascetic is merely an illustrative indication.
One who is devoid of these characteristics must perform penance day after day;
likewise, he must replace a worn-out water-pot, staff, girdle, and so forth.
Having discarded these tears, one should take up others according to the mantras;
one should undergo the tonsure ceremony at the sixteenth year, performing the rites in due order.
In the twenty-second or twenty-fourth year, for the sake of entering the householder stage, [he should renounce] all ascetic practices, observances, and auspicious deeds.
Sacred revelation (Śruti) is the sole cause for the glory of the highest beatitude for those who have transcended the pairs of opposites;
at the beginning of the Vedas, it should always be recited like a protective amulet during the act of creation.
For one who has cut down the fruitless [branches], even if he recites the Veda, it does not lead to success;
the recitation of the Veda is said to be subordinate to the Gāyatrī.

Those who always perform this triad—consisting of the three [mantras] preceded by the *praṇava*, the *mahīvyāhṛtis*, and the *sadas*—plus a little more than a thousand [repetitions], are victorious. (56)
One who remains outside for a month every day is released from the great earth;
likewise, one whose mind is focused on nothing else is freed from the sin of the Vedas by standing below the three stars [of the Pleiades] for three years.
The pure Self, whose form is the sky, ascends to the abode of Brahman,
[reaching] the three-syllabled Oṃkāra and the triad of Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, and Svaḥ.
One should recite the three feet of the Gāyatrī, which are more firmly established than the three Vedas;
these victories are preceded by the Vyāhṛtis. (59)
A knower of the Vedas who meditates is joined with the fruit of a sacrifice;
however, the sacrifice of recitation (japa) is declared to be ten times superior to a sacrifice involving ritual offerings.
Victory over one's own home is more glorious than victory over eight enemies;
two things are said to be superior even to sacrifices such as the horse-sacrifice (aśvamedha).
The giving of the teacher’s fee (ācāryadakṣiṇā) is declared by the teachers of the Vedas, Vedānta, and logic to be superior even to hundreds of great gifts (mahādāna).
Having studied the three Vedas, two Vedas, or even one Veda according to his ability, a twice-born man enjoys the fruit of a gift of a full earth filled with grain. (63)
The best of the twice-born, performing austerities, should always practice the study of the Vedas;
for the study of the Vedas is said to be the supreme austerity of a Brahmin. 64.
Having abandoned the study of the Veda, he who desires to master other [sciences] is like one who, having let go of a milch cow, wishes to milk a village dog. (65)
The twice-born who initiates a student and teaches him the Veda until he has mastered it, along with its kalpas and rahasyas, the wise know him as an *ācārya*. 66.
From whose lotus-like mouth is obtained the glorious eight-syllabled mantra (Aṣṭākṣarī), accompanied by its limbs, along with all the nyāsas joined with the rays of the Blessed One? (67)
This teacher is a hundred times more venerable than even one's previous guru, he who teaches a portion of the Veda or likewise the various branches of the Śruti. (68)
For the sake of livelihood, the Veda is studied thoroughly by the learned;
likewise, the twice-born performs rituals such as the Niṣeka and others according to the prescribed rules. (69)
In this context, the Guru is described as being honored by others;
furthermore, he is preeminent due to the rites of establishing the sacred fires (*ādhāna*), the *Atyagniṣṭoma* sacrifice, and the *Agrayaṇa* and other principal offerings.
A father and mother exceed a thousand [other elders] in respect;
even more so than a father, a mother, a teacher, and an ācārya. (71)
Bestowing the glorious eight-syllabled mantra accompanied by the rays of the Blessed One, this venerable teacher is declared to be superior to a thousand [others]. (72)
The marriage of Brahmā and Nārāyaṇī, together with the one named Bhārāyaṇī;
the sixteen-syllable and other vidyās; and the Nṛsiṃhānuṣṭubh and others—these were clearly [revealed]. (73)
He [knows] even a sixteenth part of the pure eight-syllable Vidyā, and he is likewise well-versed in many millions of scriptures.
It is said that among all the four Vedas and the Purāṇas, this pure and glorious eight-syllabled queen alone is superior to all others. 75.
That Brahmin who bestows the glorious eight-syllabled lore, together with its ancillaries and its rays of light, upon a practitioner, is highly honored.
O King, he is hundreds of times superior even to his father, mother, elders, bridegroom, and teacher, and even to Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa.
O good teacher, one should thus understand the reality as it is heard from the mouth of the guru;
such a devotee should always remain at the lotus feet of the teacher. (78)
The superiority of Brahmins is through knowledge, that of Kṣatriyas through valor,
that of Vaiśyas through grain and cattle, and that of the fourth [caste] through birth alone.
Just as a wooden elephant, and just as my own practice, so too are these Brahmins who do not study and who wear the marks of the three Vedas. (80)
And he saw daily those devoted to their own duties, performers of Vedic sacrifices and rituals,
and well-disciplined Vaiśyas who were like excellent celibate students.
One should not act according to one's own whims in his presence,
nor should one utter his name even in his absence, nor speak ill of him.
Wherever there is censure of the guru or wherever there is slander,
one should either stay with the ears covered or depart from that place in secret.
From reviling a donkey, one becomes a dog with eyes like those of a snake; from insulting a goat, one becomes a cricket; and from deriding a sheep, one becomes a worm. (84)
Even by hearing the name of the venerable teacher of the eight syllables just once,
one attains nourishment for eight thousand years and reaches the state of immortality.
One should not bow to the wife of a guru; if she is touched, she becomes a woman who has borne a son.
Through twenty years of cultivation, one gains knowledge of both virtues and faults.
The nature of men is known to be such that they are longed for by women;
therefore, wise men never exert their power over women.
Even those who are learned, though pierced by knowledge, women bring under their own control—just as a bird bound by a string—even if the man is otherwise fearless and dear to them. 88.
Even for those who possess the character of a mother, a daughter, a sister, or a devoted wife, the powerful senses delude even the wise. (89)
Through constant service to the guru with his very life and abundant wealth, his knowledge attained perfection;
thereafter, he beheld the Absolute Brahman alone.
The parents endure the suffering associated with the birth of a son;
even in a hundred years, they are unable to repay his debt to the best of their ability. (91)
Therefore, one should always do what is pleasing to those two and to the preceptor;
[one should be] endowed with the glorious eight-syllabled mantra along with its ancillaries, and enveloped by the rays of the Lord.
The full enjoyment of heaven and liberation, obtained from the lotus-like mouth of whom, cannot be described by anyone even in ten million eons. (93)
A wise person should certainly worship him constantly with the three qualities, just as one worships Nārāyaṇa at the beginning of the age, when his father and mother are well-pleased. 94.
Then, having transcended the three kalpas, one who is self-restrained indeed attains that which is called the supreme, which bestows the perfection of union with Brahman.
Having propitiated these three vital breaths here, the wise man should conquer the *ulphrūkā* [the internal obstacle];
thereafter, the mother Pītā is the bestower of knowledge and longevity. (96)
The giver of the glorious eight-syllabled mantra is called the fourth guru;
the fruit of the four aims of life is said to result from the worship of the four gurus. (97)
One may even abandon a father or a mother who is a teacher of the Vedas;
however, one should not abandon a preceptor who bestows the knowledge of Brahman, even at the cost of one's life.
Even a single Great Vidyā is obtained everywhere;
yet you remain in that most terrible hell until the moon and stars [have passed away].
O Ācārya Raśmimālāprada, it cannot be described;
for in this ocean abide all the sciences of the bees (insects), which bestow spiritual perfection. 100.
Therefore, the guru who bestows the knowledge of the rays of the Blessed One is great;
he alone is the Blessed One in person, the giver of enjoyment, heaven, and liberation. (1)
The noble one, who bestows the knowledge of rays, stood nearby as the supreme tutelary deity of the assembly of disciples at the end of his life.
If one were to honor him with wealth for as long as an aeon, one would dwell in hell; therefore, one should satisfy the teacher every day with various kinds of jewels and excellent fires.
Whether a knower of Brahman gives to another or does not give,
this practice of the wise is always directed toward the noble goal of Nirvana.
Just as there is virtuous conduct in the householder stage, so it is in the other stages of life;
having mastered the various branches of knowledge, one should then take recourse to the householder's life.
For one who has departed from the householder's stage of life, there is no such thing as submissiveness;
yet this very submissiveness is indeed required for the sake of attaining the fruits of the three aims of life.
If the wife is favorable and beautiful, what need is there for heaven?
If the wife is unfavorable and ugly, what need is there for hell? (7)
The householder stage of life is for the sake of happiness, for that happiness has its root in the wife;
indeed, when one's own wife is well-disciplined, the three aims of life certainly increase.
Those of dull intellect perceive this [woman] as a leech;
she is merely a leech, like a blood-sucking fly, taking away only the blood.
There is a vast difference between the reflections of those who have conquered their senses and those who have not;
for a woman takes away everything—mind, wealth, strength, and happiness. (10)

Dakṣī, Prajāvatī, Sākṣāt, Strī, Vākya-vaśaṃvada— endowed with these qualities, she is a woman who, through her discernment, does not yield to the great difference between the known and the unknown; she possesses a mind that is steady, auspicious, beautiful in form, and wise.
Having bathed with the permission of the guru and having completed his period of residence here,
he should then marry a wife of the same caste who possesses the auspicious marks.
Should a twice-born man marry a wife who is free from disease, who has not previously been married to another, who is more beautiful than himself, gentle in speech, and pleasant to behold? (13)
Having first examined the auspicious marks, one should then marry a maiden; for by marrying one with excellent marks and virtuous conduct, one increases one's own lifespan.
Even one with auspicious marks may be of bad character and the crest-jewel of those with ill-omened traits;
yet she who is virtuous, though possessing ill-omened traits, is the very essence of all auspicious marks. (15)
The deities who possess auspicious marks, move with grace, and are self-dependent will surely be found even in the home, solely through the favor of Lakṣmī and Īśāna. 16.
Those women who, in a previous birth, adorned themselves with various kinds of ornaments while remaining chaste, indeed become beautiful in this life. || 17 ||
Those who have been washed or caused to be discarded at excellent holy fords (tīrthas) by the wind, O Tālāvara, become indeed possessed of auspicious marks through their speech. || 18 ||
She is the one worshipped by the worlds, who removes their afflictions; she is the consort of Śiva here, or Śrī, the beloved of Nārāyaṇa, or Śacī, the beloved of Indra. 19.

Those women who possess virtuous conduct become ones whose husbands are under their own control; and for those deer-eyed women of good character whose ascetics are under their own control, [the same result follows]. || 20 ||
Indeed, the fruit of those auspicious marks is that one attains heaven and the group of Yavas right here;
yet, despite his auspicious marks and virtuous conduct, he was a husband of short life. || 21 ||
When women offer a lamp for longevity at the mouth [of the image],
they should honor the wife of the preceptor with garments, ornaments, and other such gifts.
Those who were worshipped by disciples or even by women in a previous birth,
they all possess every fortune and have a splendor like that of Kandarpa.
Together with his sons, grandsons, and others, the king, along with those who take refuge in kings,
[is established] in this compendium of the Vedas regarding the secret of the unsurpassed reality of Brahman.
This is the twenty-first chapter in the tantra proclaimed by the son of Daśaratha.
[Thus ends the twenty-first chapter in the *Vedārthasaṃgraha*, the *Dāśarathīya Tantra*, which is the illustrious secret essence of the supreme reality of Brahman.]
The Blessed Lord said:
O protector of the earth, I shall also describe the forms of marriage;
by the mere knowledge of which one is liberated from all sins. (1)
The Brāhma, Daiva, Ārṣa, Prājāpatya, Āsura, Gāndharva, Rākṣasa, and Paiśāca are said to be the eight forms of marriage. || 2 ||
That is the Brāhma marriage, the most excellent, wherein a well-adorned maiden is given;
the son born of it attains twenty-one generations of heaven.

The son born of a woman through a priest (ṛtvij) purifies fourteen generations; the son born of a woman through a divine (daiva) rite purifies thirteen; the son born of a woman through the ārṣa rite purifies six generations; and the son born of a woman through the prājāpatya rite purifies twelve.
It has been said that for those who practice dharma together with their wives, when one gives [a daughter] to a petitioner,
he purifies eight generations of his lineage by means of that marriage to a maiden.
These four are recorded as the marriages for Brahmins:
the Āsura, which is through the purchase with wealth; and the Gāndharva, which is by mutual consent. || 6 ||
The forcible abduction of a maiden is censured by the virtuous as being Rākṣasa;
the abduction of a maiden through deception is even more despised as being Āsura, the eighth [form].
The Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Muktas, Gandharvas, Asuras, and Rākṣasas have been mentioned;
the eighth among these is said to be the birthplace of the most sinful.
A goad is to be given by a woman of the same caste for the sake of mounting;
a whip by a Vaiśya woman; and likewise, a garment at the end [of the marriage] by a Śūdra woman.
This procedure for the *āsava* [liquor] is prescribed when the wages are high;
with all those of the same caste, the hand is to be taken—this is the specific rule for each.

From marriages that are righteous, only righteous sons with a hundredfold qualities are born; from those that are unrighteous, children devoid of dharma are born, possessing meager fortune, wealth, and lifespan.
Approaching one's wife during her fertile period is the supreme duty of a householder;
it should be done by recollecting the boon granted to women, or it may be done according to one's desire.

Approaching [a woman] during the day is considered by the wise to be the highest flower among men; likewise, all festivals, especially those associated with the Śrīdhā, should be observed with devotion by the intelligent.
Moving about there, he becomes possessed of splendor and arises from ten thousand-fold joy;
he who approaches his wife during her fertile season and is devoted solely to his own wife. (15)
He who practices celibacy along with virtuous men is to be known as one belonging to all stages of life (*sarvāśramī*).
The menstrual period consists of sixteen nights; among these, four are excluded. (16)
In the Prakrāstā asterisms, twins are born; in the Ayugmā asterisms, daughters are born.
Having joined with the Moon situated in the Dūstha asterisms, excluding the Madya and Mūla, [the results are as follows].
Being pure, he should approach his wife, especially under a male asterism;
thus he shall procreate a pure son who accomplishes the goals of human life.
The Ārṣa form of marriage, as well as the exchange of a pair of cows, which has been prescribed, is not praised;
even the giving of white garments for a girl is considered a sale of the daughter. (19)
One who sells his daughter for a future price shall live on excrement and worms;
likewise, one who subsists on the wealth of a maiden while she is still a child [shall suffer the same].
Those kinsmen here who, out of delusion, live off a woman’s property or other such means,
go solely to hell, as do their ancestors.
Where the wife is satisfied with her husband and the husband is satisfied with his wife,
there Mahālakṣmī dwells, never departing by means of the waters of the ocean.
Trade, service to the king, failure to study the Vedas,
improper marriage, and the omission of sacred rites— these are not the causes of one's downfall from the family.
On the wedding day, the householder should perform the domestic rites (gārhya-karma),
as well as the daily performance of the five great sacrifices (pañca-yajña) and the wife's own daily duties.
For a householder in the stage of life (gṛhasthāśramin), there are five acts of slaughter day after day:
the mortar, the winnowing basket, the grinding stone, the kitchen knife, and the broom.
And for those five slaughter-houses, the five seasons—which are free from enmity and increase the highest good—are the causes for their non-abandonment. (26)
Recitation is the sacrifice to Brahman (brahmayajña), libation is the sacrifice to the ancestors (pitṛkratu),
the burnt offering is the sacrifice to the gods (daivayajña), the bali offering is the sacrifice to beings (bhūtayajña), and hospitality is the sacrifice to guests (atithikratu), in that order.
Desiring to produce satisfaction for his ancestors, a householder should perform a śrāddha with whatever is appropriate, even if it consists merely of water, roots, or fruits. 28.
Whatever merit is obtained by the gift of a cow accompanied by the recitation of mantras, one may not attain even that much by giving alms to a mendicant after honoring him. || 29 ||
The threefold knowledge, when offered as fuel into the fire by the wise,
saves one from the multitude of obstacles and even from the most difficult-to-cross array of weapons.
If a guest departs from one's house unhonored, he takes away the merit accumulated by that person since birth;
thus, that person becomes excluded from the fruits of his religious merit.
Words that are soothing to the heart and pleasing to the ear should always be offered for the satisfaction of guests, even when one is cursing or dealing with beings who are difficult to subdue.

A householder who, having been nourished by the food of others, eats the remnants of the offerings made on the lunar days (tithis), shall attain great splendor after death; he should accept that which is given as food,
for it increases his lifespan.
One who drives away a guest, one who eats food alone, and one who is defiled by sin—these three bring misfortune to the home.
A guest who arrives after the Vaiśvadeva rite has been completed and when the sun has risen is not considered to have come at the proper time; therefore, he is never desired [as a guest]. (35)
If a guest arrives at the time of the *bali* offering while the Brahmin is engaged in that rite, one should not give him that *bali*;
rather, one should give him food according to one's ability.
Maidens, women whose husbands are living, pregnant women, those who have recently given birth, guests, and seekers—these should be fed; there is no doubt about this. (37)
Having given meat and fish to the ancestors, gods,
and guests, the householder who eats for his own sake alone is merely filling his own belly.
He who eats food, ghee, and so forth belonging to the wife or sons of his teacher without their permission, eats inexhaustible sin.
One should always perform the Vaiśvadeva rite at midday with diligent effort;
for those who are devoid of the Vaiśvadeva rite are likewise deprived of the hospitality due to guests.
All those twice-born men who eat without having first performed the Vaiśvadeva rite are to be known as outcastes (vṛṣala), even though they may be brahmins in this world. (41)
In this world they would be base, and then they go to the womb of a crow;
therefore, one should constantly perform one's own duty as ordained by the Vedas without sloth.
There they performed their supreme song according to their ability;
on the sixth and eighth days one should abandon fear, and oil and meat are not to be eaten during that month.
On the tenth lunar day of the dark fortnight, he should avoid sexual union with a woman;
he should not look at the sun when it is rising, nor when it is setting, nor when it is at the meridian.
One should not look at the sun when it is reflected in water, nor when it is eclipsed by Rāhu, nor when there are two suns; one should not look at one's own reflection, nor run while it is raining.
One should not step over a young heifer, nor enter water while naked; one should avoid a temple, a Brahmin, a cow, honey, clay, and ghee.
One should offer water and ghee to the preceptor, who is advanced in conduct, advanced in age, and perfected in knowledge, and who is like a sacred fig tree or a peepal tree. || 47 ||
Going toward the goal for the sake of attaining perfection, he should perform his circumambulation to the right;
he should not consort with a woman in her courses, nor should he eat together with his wife.
One should not eat wearing only a single garment, nor should one eat on a seat made of grass stalks (itkaṭa).
