O best of the twice-born, one who desires spiritual power should not look at a woman who is menstruating.
One should never eat new food without first satisfying the gods;
one should never wear a jewel without first having satisfied a virtuous teacher.
One who desires to live for a long time should avoid meat from a crippled animal,
nor should one void urine in a cow-pen, in a field, near an anthill, or in ashes.
He does not stand in pits, nor among living beings, nor in a village; he is not born from a womb, nor is he fire, wind, flame, moon, sun, or even the earth.
Facing north during the morning twilight, he should release his urine and feces while looking toward a place free of living beings, impurities, and water,
with his sacred thread over his right ear.
One should always void urine at night facing the south;
one should not blow on a fire with the mouth, nor should one look at a naked woman. (54)
One should heat the *naṃdhrī* over fire and place it in a clean spot;
one should not eat while causing injury to living beings, nor during the two twilights.

One who desires to live long should not go to sleep during the twilight hours, nor should one even point the feet toward the east; likewise, one desiring longevity should not discharge feces, urine, or saliva facing the sun.
One should not speak of a cow that is about to give birth, nor should one point out a rainbow.
One should not study the Vedas alone, and one should not wake a sleeping person with a snap of the fingers.

One should not drink water from a single vessel, nor should one drink from the hollowed palms of the hands; nor should one eat food from which the essence has been extracted, nor consume curd at night.

One should not greet a woman during her menses, nor eat food from her hand until she has bathed after her period; one should not be fond of mechanical devices, and one should not wear a garment that is too tight.
If one performs a *śrāddha* without faith, being devoid of the knowledge of the *uṣṇīṣa*, there is no fruit of the *śrāddha* for the donor; the eater, however, becomes a partaker of sin. (60)

One should not wear clothing or vehicles that have not been mentioned [as permissible], nor should one eat from broken vessels; one should not eat food that has been heated by fire or the like, nor food that is excessively hot.
One who desires to live a long life should avoid ascending a mountain peak, traveling behind a funeral procession,
gazing at the sun at dawn, and sleeping during the day.

One should not wipe one's feet here [in the temple], nor should one release the topknot on the path; one should not follow behind another with hands or head, nor should one pull up a seat when it is offered.
One should never clip the hair or nails with the teeth, nor should one cut the nails with the nails; one should avoid cutting grass or wood with the teeth.
One should abandon this [world] by means of the auspicious path; one must not go through a difficult way. One’s own home is the sky, while the house of another is the earth.
He may play with dice together with those who are not addicted to vice and are free from passion;
however, he should never sleep with his clothes on, nor should he ever eat while clothed.
One should eat food with wet hands; thus one lives for a long time.
One should not go anywhere with wet feet or with remnants of food on the head.
A twice-born man should not drink water while lying down, nor should he do so while wearing his upper garment;
he should eat while standing and maintain the *ārṣa* (sipping) practice.
One who desires well-being should not consume anything made of sesame at night; nor should he look at excrement or urine, nor touch the mouth while impure from food remnants.
One should not stand upon a heap of grain, a straw hut, ashes, a place where four roads meet, or a false balance;
nor should one associate with outcasts, for such acts lead only to rebirth in a body.
One should never teach a Vedic mantra to a Śūdra;
from a Brāhmaṇa woman it is lost, and from a Śūdra a Brāhmaṇa falls from his high status.
Instruction in the Dharma should be given to Śūdras so that they may attain their own welfare;
service to the twice-born is recorded as the supreme duty of Śūdras. (72)
Scratching the head with both hands is not considered auspicious,
nor is swinging the hair with the two hands or plucking out the hair.
A Brahmin who, having accepted a gift, lives by means other than weapons, goes along with his lineage to twenty-one hells.

During unseasonable lightning and thunder, during the showers of the Ṛṣis, during heavy rain, and during great winds or thunderstorms at night, these are proclaimed as times unfit for study (anadhyāya).
If there is a fall of meteors or a thunderclap here during the middle of the night, at the two twilights, at the end of a drought, or during a royal affliction or a famine; || 76 ||

Having accepted the Śrāddha offerings on the day of Harṣeṣṭakā, which has become auspicious, one should perform it even on the first lunar day (pratipad), or on the full moon (pūrṇā) or the new moon (amāvāsyā), for all purposes.
If there is the sound of a crow, a lizard, or a frog; if there is the sound of a dog, or even the sound of a camel;
during the Upākarma or the Utsarga rites; or when the sun is not visible on the northern side [of the horizon]. 78.
Even after studying the Āraṇyaka, a twice-born man should never recite it in the presence of a whetstone, a grindstone, or a loud noise,
nor during these times when study is prohibited.
A king should recite [this] at the intervals of the day; he should always remain celibate on the eighth and fourteenth lunar days, as well as on the fifteenth.
One who has not attained the supreme state here suffers the humiliation of others;
therefore, the service of merchants must be avoided from afar.
He should not lead himself away from those who have abandoned him,
for among you, the knowledge of the highest good is not difficult to find.
Even at the cost of one's life, one should speak the truth; even for the sake of a friend, one should not speak an untruth out of fear. One who speaks the truth is exalted by this dharma.
One should always speak only what is auspicious and contemplate only what is auspicious; one should never associate with the inauspicious, but only with the auspicious.
A wise person should not dwell among those who are devoid of stūpas and lineages;
for one who observes this, the truth, the brahmin-sages, the planets, and the stars do not shine.
One should avoid downward force, mental agitation, and the force of speech;
one should abandon from afar wealth obtained through bribes, gambling, or from those who are wretched or distressed.
One who has not yet consumed the remnants of food (ucchiṣṭa) should never touch a cow, a Brahmin, or a fire;
nor, unless one is ill, should one touch objects that have not been consecrated or those that have been buried.
Even the hairs born from the private parts become impure through contact with them;
likewise, water used for washing the feet, urine, and the remnants of food-water [are impure]. (88)
One should cast away spittle and phlegm into a pit;
by day and night, one should resort to food that is very hot or cold. (89)
With a mind free from malice, he remembers his various births;
he should diligently salute the elders and offer them his own seat.
With a humble mind, he followed as many of them as were there—
those who were learned in the Vedas, those who were brahmins, and those who were gods among men, kings endowed with the excellence of goodness.
One should never anywhere disparage women who are devoted to their husbands; one should not praise base men, nor should one hold oneself in high esteem. 92.
One should not fail to bow to one who has approached with an offering; one should act with such courtesy toward women of noble lineage.
One should practice righteousness while refraining from abandoning those previously encountered.
Even a man who is otherwise auspicious in every respect perishes along with his lineage if he draws [water] from a reservoir containing impure water after having lifted five lumps of clay.
And by not disturbing the doer of that act, one becomes free from sin;
whatever wealth is given to a worthy recipient with faith is [meritorious]. (95)
A thousand gifts given to ten million Brahmanas do not equal even a sixteenth part of the merit of a small gift given to a teacher.
He who accepts with faith and he who gives with faith—both of them shall go to heaven;
therefore, one should offer with faith.

A sacrifice perishes through falsehood; the merit of these two [sacrifice and study] flows away through pride. Fame flows away through boasting; the lifespan of a Brahmin flows away through being insulted.
Fragrances, flowers, kuśa grass, a bed, a jar, meat, curd, yogurt, jewels, garlands, a house, and grain— these may be accepted when they are offered.
Honey, water, fruit, roots, medicinal herbs, and a gift offered out of fear—
these, when presented spontaneously, may be accepted even from a person of low character.

Thus, having abandoned both the son of Devī and the son of Agni, one should resort to impartiality by means of the *aṇ* suffix derived from the root *ṛ*, which signifies the state of being a seer (*ṛṣi*) among the gods. 3.
In the home, one should practice the science of consciousness and conquer the eight-syllabled mantra of Śrī;
one must certainly perform the duties of a householder and the worship of the feet of the Guru.
Liberation in a single birth is attained by reciting the glorious eight-syllable mantra;
liberation in a single birth is attained at the hermitage of Nara-Nārāyaṇa.
Liberation in a single lifetime is highly esteemed in Vārāṇasī;
liberation after many lifetimes comes from worshipping the feet of the Teacher.
A wise person should never, even in thought, transgress pure conduct;
he should always be devoted to virtuous behavior and serve a teacher of good conduct.

Having recited the glorious eight-syllabled mantra (aṣṭākṣarī), accompanied by the rays of the Blessed One and joined with all the ritual placements (nyāsa), one becomes directly identical with Brahman.
The virtuous conduct of a householder is thus proclaimed;
by hearing it, a wise man is honored and casts off the darkness born of ignorance.
[Thus ends the twenty-second chapter in the *Śrīmad-Anuttara-Brahma-Tattva-Rahasya*, the *Dāśarathīya-Tantra*, which is a compendium of essential meanings.]
The Blessed Lord said: I shall again declare the specific details that adorn right conduct;
by hearing which, even a man is liberated from the multitudes of sins.
The complete accomplishment of one's well-purified purpose is obtained through the weight of merit;
therein, O Brahmin, merit arises from partaking [of the teachings] according to the path of the Smṛtis.
O Sage, just as a man’s well-composed praise is tormented by a touch,
so too is a constant flaw tormented even by the Kali age, which seeks to destroy the seeker.
By the performance of what is forbidden and the non-performance of what is prescribed,
even one who has been struck down by the Kali age [is ruined] through looking for faults in a Brāhmaṇa.
Therefore, having first spoken of what is forbidden, one should speak of conduct;
by abandoning that [forbidden conduct], a person shall not fall into hell.
Brahmins should avoid tree exudations, milk-rice, and *eyūlī* preparations;
one should first offer meat to the ancestors, and one should avoid that which has no calf.
One should avoid garlic, leeks, and onions; as well as the meat of goats, one-hoofed animals, birds, two-hoofed animals, kramelakas, and sheep.
Those who desire long life and those who desire heaven should not eat curd at night, nor indeed fresh butter; one should diligently renounce meat.

"Abandon all other branches of activity—such as the pursuit of sacrifice, wealth, fame, and the injury or exhaustion caused by worldly toil—which are devoid of [true] purpose; rather, abandon everything that has been accumulated through unbroken affection."
One who eats meat at dawn for the sake of sustaining life, during a Śrāddha rite, for medicine, or out of a desire to see a Brahmin, is not subject to fault. (10)
The gain of one who desires the livelihood of a hunter is not such as that which comes to one who, out of lack of greed, offers meat in a sacrifice to Ambhava. (11)
Created by Brahmā for the sake of sacrifice, those stainless sacrificial animals and herbs— by destroying them, a non-violent Brahmin attains an auspicious state.

When performed for the sake of the ancestors, the gods, or for the purpose of the madhuparka offering, there is indeed no violence here; elsewhere, however, such violence is very difficult to overcome.
For one who is weak in knowledge has no purpose for the sake of liberating living beings;
therefore, for one of evil conduct, there is never any happiness here, even in this world.
The consumer, the consenter, the preparer, the buyer, the seller, the killer, the benefactor, and the one who causes slaughter—these are remembered as the eight types of killers. (15)
He who might perform the horse sacrifice every year for a hundred years, and he who subsists on raw meat—of these two, the latter is distinguished as superior. (16)
Just as one who desires a friend should treat another as oneself, so too should one regard the joys and sorrows of others as equal to one's own. 17.
Whatever happiness or even suffering is performed by another, whatever has been done, all of that indeed becomes one's own. (18)
Without the hair of Nala, how can there be wealth for one devoid of means?
Without means, how can there be action? Without action, how can there be dharma? And without dharma, how can there be happiness? (19)
For that essence, the ocean of Dharma, is desired by all; therefore, the extraction of the essence of Dharma must be undertaken with effort for the sake of the four castes. (20)
Just as at the arrival of evening, one must perform whatever worldly duties are required;
likewise, a gift should be given according to the prescribed rule at the proper time. Thus it is said.
If one accepts a gift even from a person devoid of merit, yet lacking the prescribed ritual, he does not merely destroy his own merit; the remainder of that donor's merit is also lost.
That which is given for the sake of one in distress, for the sake of a kinsman, and for the sake of a guest becomes inexhaustible in this world and the next;
of this there is no doubt. (23)
One who is firm in his vows for the sake of supporting his parents, wife, sons, and others, and who has been supported by his wife and children during times such as eclipses, [is liberated].
I am not able to fully describe the fruit of his merit;
it is so great that the wealth [required for its measure] is said to be a hundred *niṣkas*, equal to a year's worth of food.

Half of that, or half of that again, or even less than that, is prescribed as the wealth to be offered at the lotus feet of the preceptor for the duration of a year's stay during the rainy season. (26)
O King, having given on a single day for an entire year,
he bestowed numerous great gifts, foremost among them the Tulāpuruṣa.
By performing this day after day, one shall obtain its fruit:
being joined with hundreds of subjugated ancestors and even hundreds of subjugated mothers.
In the presence of the Blessed One, they attain imperishable happiness, even for those deprived of mother and father through the rites of the sacred thread ceremony, marriage, and so forth. (29)
By performing these purificatory rites for them, their supreme merit is said to reach its fullness;
likewise, wealth sufficient for the marriage ceremony should be given to a poor Brāhmaṇa.
The righteous-souled one who bestows [this] grants him a city;
neither by Agnihotra rites, nor by hymns, nor by sacrifices such as the Agniṣṭoma and others is this attained.

Behold that which is the highest good attained by mortals alone when established in a Brahmin: even in the house of one afflicted by bile, see how this daughter is devoted to her husband and well-refined.

She who wears ornaments is to be known as one whose father has been slain; even a daughter [so described] is likewise [to be avoided]. He who, out of delusion, would marry her, would become the husband of a *vṛṣalī*.
He should engage in continuous conversation with him who is worthy of praise and beyond reproach, having informed both the bride and the groom of their respective faults and fears.
One should subsequently cause the marriage bond to be established; otherwise, the father incurs fault.
Women are eternally pure; they are never defiled by anything whatsoever. (35)
Soma gave to women the quality of being purified by fire, and the Gandharva gave them the quality of having auspicious speech; therefore, women are always pure.

If a maiden has been enjoyed during her menstrual period, or if fire, the moon, or a crow are seen [at the time], or if it occurs through hearing [the sound of thunder], or by Gandharvas, she is given away upon the abandonment of the [defiling] act. (37)
One should avoid a girl who has no body hair, who is a killer of her husband's family, who destroys her lineage, who is excessively young, who kills her father, or whose menses are abnormal. || 38 ||
Therefore, one who desires the fruit of giving should offer it to the worthy;
otherwise, the recipient would be inferior to the giver of that fruit. (39)
One who gives a maiden who has not been enjoyed by Soma and the other [gods] shall obtain fruit;
however, a giver who bestows one already enjoyed by the gods does not attain heaven.
The wise never find fault with gifts of beds and seats, straw mats, the face of a woman, a parrot, sacrifices, or pilgrimages. (41)
The calf is pure in the forest where it grazes; the bird is pure when seeking fruit; the woman is pure in the practice of sexual pleasure; and the hunter is pure in the act of capturing deer. 42.
Goats are pure in their mouths; cows are pure at their backs;
Brahmins are pure in their feet; and women are pure in every part.
A woman who has been enjoyed by a powerful man, or who has even fallen into the hands of a thief, is not considered defiled by that act; she is not to be excluded from the rites of the gods. (44)
Brass is purified by ash, and bronze by the water of a river;
a woman of low birth is purified by her menses, and a river is pure by its current.
Even in her mind, a woman should not think of another man;
she who observes this shall enjoy happiness with her husband and shall possess fame in this world. (46)
The father, grandfather, brother, a kinsman, and likewise the mother;
in the absence of each preceding one, the giver of the girl is the next, provided he is of sound mind. (47)
O King, by not asking [for her hand], one incurs the sin of killing a fetus; therefore, in the absence of eligible suitors, a maiden should herself choose a husband through a *svayaṃvara*.
One who lives by alms, having her authority destroyed and being defiled,
should cause the unchaste woman— who has been humiliated— to dwell upon a bed on the ground.
Purification occurs when one is struck by a transgression; likewise, there is purification upon the miscarriage of a fetus or the administration of poison.
Furthermore, purification occurs in cases such as the killing of a fetus or a husband, even if death results from eating [forbidden food] during a time of distress.
If a Brahmin places a Śūdra woman on the bier and follows her to the cemetery, he falls from his caste; by begetting a son upon a Śūdra woman, he is deprived of his Brahminhood. (51)
But he whose offerings to the gods and guests are consumed by his own body,
does not go to heaven even though he performs many sacrifices.
If he were to constantly worship those who are fit for sacrifice here, they would surely destroy you all with their magical powers (kṛtyās), as if you had been slain; of this there is no doubt.
Therefore, those desiring prosperity should always honor well-dressed women with ornaments, clothing, and food,
especially during times of great distress.
Where noble women, delighted by ornaments, clothing, and food,
sport with their husbands, there all religious rites shall bear fruit.
Desiring inexhaustible welfare, one should especially worship the preceptor’s wife with divine ornaments, garments, and food on the day of Bhārgava (Venus).
On the third [lunar day] called Akṣayā, and also during the vow of Gaurīrātri,
[one should worship] with ornaments such as earrings, golden cintāmaṇi-jewels, bracelets, and pairs of anklets.
O King, by approaching the teacher’s wife with the thought that she was Lakṣmī herself,
he was liberated even from the most difficult and all-encompassing crisis.
One who possesses wealth like that of Kubera shall attain liberation;
for where a woman is pleased with her husband, and the husband is pleased with her.

In that regard, one should perform auspicious rites for the household at every step; for if these are neglected, the *homa*, the *prahuta*, and the *bhautika-bali* offerings are as good as destroyed, destroyed, destroyed. (60)

Performing these five sacrifices— the offering to the ancestors (śrāddha), the pouring of oblations into the fire (homa), the honoring of Brahmins, the study of the Veda, and hospitality toward guests— a Brāhmaṇa does not fall into ruin.
By failing to perform this, one would fall into hell;
one should ask a Brāhmaṇa about his welfare and a Kṣatriya about his health.
Having attained happiness from the Vaiśya and contentment from the Śūdra, the child remains thus for eight years from birth; so it is traditionally taught.
One may incur fault regarding what is edible and what is inedible only as long as it has not been offered;
the maintenance of one's wife and family yields both visible and invisible fruits. (64)
One's own offspring should be supported with effort;
likewise, the teacher and those who have taken refuge in one’s own sacrificial fires [must be maintained]. (65)
A guest who has arrived unexpectedly is the foremost of guests; those who have gone abroad are not so.
One lives through them, and by them alone is one sustained with sacrificial fires.
One who merely fills his own belly should be known as one who is dead while living;
wealth should not be given to such people by those desiring prosperity, but rather it should be given to distinguished persons.

They were givers of gifts, performers of recitation, endowed with good fortune, and lived as sacrificers; they were possessed of the virtue of sharing, endowed with compassion, and filled with forgiveness. || 68 ||
A householder who is devoted to the deities and guests is considered righteous. [The offerings consist of] that which remains from the oblation during the two middle watches of the night. (69)
In this regard, neither one's own kin nor strangers, nor even a Brahmin, should be allowed to perish;
these nine, O Teacher, must be supported by the householder from his own body and wealth. (70)

Joyful expenditure, equanimity, the restraint of speech, eyes, and mind; rising to greet those who arrive, affection toward them, and being the first to speak—[these are the marks of a noble person]. (71)
Devotion, following [the teacher], and remaining in the household are the causes;
likewise, these duties should be performed even when joined with impermanence.
A seat, such purity as one possesses, the earth as a bed according to one's capacity, a grass mat for a bed, water, ointments, and the daytime—all these grant success to the householder. (73)
In the same way, a householder should avoid new undertakings, backbiting, the wives of others, malice, anger, falsehood, and what is unpleasant. (74)
Hatred, hypocrisy, and deceit are indeed bolts on the path to heaven;
therefore, the nine essential duties must be performed every day. (75)
Bathing, the twilight prayers, recitation, fire-offerings, self-study of scripture, worship of the deities, hospitality toward guests, and the ninth, the libation to the ancestors. (76)
Listen now to those nine things that must be concealed from others:
one's birth star, sexual intercourse, counsel, domestic secrets, and the forest [where one dwells]. (77)
One's age, one's debt, a gift, and a woman—these should never be made public;
likewise, these nine things should not be disclosed: a secret, a sin, and that which is blameless. (78)

The purification of the *prāyaścitta* rite, the auspiciousness of one's own lineage, buying and selling, and the giving away of a daughter in marriage—these should be performed by one who possesses good qualities; otherwise, none of these may be done by anyone anywhere. (79)

May there be inexhaustible freedom from distress toward those who are enemies, those who are disciplined, the poor and helpless, those who do good, and likewise toward one's mother, father, and teachers.
It is fruitless to give wealth to a rogue, a warder-off of elephants, a thief, a quack physician, a hypocrite, a swindler, a cheat, a wrestler, or to bards. (81)
One should never give away nine things, even in times of distress: water, a wife, one's own self, a son, one's entire property, and those who have sought refuge. (82)
The meaning of a trust, family property, a deposit, a woman’s dowry, or a son—
whosoever gives these away with a pure mind is purified by those who have sought refuge.
In the rite of *puraścaraṇa*, one’s entire possessions should be given to the preceptor alone; by one who has mastered all knowledge, nothing else should be given to anyone anywhere. (84)
Having understood this group of nine, one shall attain prosperity;
I shall now speak of another group of nine that grants the path to heaven for all.

Truthfulness, purity, non-violence, fortitude, self-control, compassion, and so forth, as well as non-stealing, restraint of the senses, and freedom from anger— these are the means for accomplishing dharma for all.
One who studies this ninety-verse work, which is a lamp for the path to heaven and is esteemed by the virtuous, does not come to grief while living as a householder.
He whose wife, son, brother, friend, servant, and dependents are rich in discipline possesses honor everywhere. (88)

Traveling by carriage, association with wicked people, separation from one's husband, wandering about, residing in the houses of others, and [excessive] intimacy with women—these are the six vices of women. (89)
He who gives grain at an equal price or at a high rate is called a usurer;
he is declared by the scriptures to be excluded from all ritual acts.
One who is bitten by a female buffalo that has become fearless due to intoxication and is afflicted by passion is known as an *āhīṣika*. (91)
Seeing the foremost buffalo-herders, then the masters of two women in the middle,
and finally seeing the usurers, the women became hopeless, pale, and afflicted by disease.
As long as the food remains warm, as long as it is eaten in silence, and as long as one eats without being satiated, so long does the quality of the sacrificial offering endure.
When one endowed with right conduct and discipline comes to the house of a learned Brahmin, all medicinal herbs rejoice, thinking: "We shall attain the supreme goal. (94)
"O Brahmin, fallen from purity, vows, and conduct, and devoid of the Vedas, you weep while being offered food; what evil have I done? (95)
He for whom this vessel of boiled rice is crossed over by means of the study of the Vedas causes the donor to cross over—ten ancestors and ten descendants. (96)
One should not engage in weaving for women, nor should one follow after new cows;
one should not dwell for nine nights with a widow, and one should perform the Vedic revelation.
Having removed all the hair, one should cut off two finger-breadths;
for women who have recently given birth, it should be thus, and there shall be no shaving of the head.
Whether he be a king, a prince, or a Brahmin of great learning,
for the sake of preserving his hair, he should give double the sacrificial fee.
If one takes hold of her who is called "the exiled woman" (vivāsinī), it shall be thus and not otherwise; there shall be a shaving of the head. || 98 ||
A king, or one associated with a king, or a Brāhmaṇa who has heard much, for the sake of protecting his hair, should give double the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). || 99 ||
One who, having taken [the image] from the temple, considers himself a householder—his food must not be eaten; for what is he remembered to be other than a thief? (100)

He who, while his elder brother is established [in the householder state], takes a wife, performs the fire-sacrifice (agnihotra), or undergoes initiation (dīkṣā), is to be known as a *parivettṛ*; and the elder brother is called a *parivitti*. (1)
All these—the giver, the priest, and the fifth, the solicitor—go to hell;
and when the seat is located in another region, it is declared that the fool has been initiated into the Sūkta.
By drawing out [the syllables] or shortening them, a fault occurs in the recitation;
therefore, one should employ as many Vedic syllables as necessary for the sake of the meaning.
One who, having taken a vow of celibacy, again engages in sexual intercourse with a woman, incurs as many sins as the murder of Brahmins incurred by one who sells his own daughter.
For sixty thousand years, O worm, you shall dwell in excrement;
[as a result of] contact with a Śūdra woman, eating the food of a Śūdra, association with a Śūra, and sitting together with a Śūdra. (5)
The acquisition of knowledge from a Śūdra might cause even a Jābāla to fall; those twice-born ones who, being ignorant, take up and practice [teachings] brought from a Śūdra [are likewise fallen].
Deprived of Brahmanic luster, they go to a terrible hell,
constantly [afflicted] by such things as hand-given salt and pungent condiments.
The giver incurs sin when he does not bestow it upon a worthy recipient;
for food that is offered by means of an unworthy vessel does not reach [the intended goal].
The one who eats [such food] would become impure, and the giver would go to hell;
this applies to that which is eaten with a finger, that which has been tasted by a poem, and that which has visible salt [in it].
Eating clay, eating together with those of equal status,
and dwelling happily before him— endowed with such virtues, he shall remain.
A gift should be given to one endowed with virtues; there is no transgression in this case regarding a fool. There is no offense in bypassing a Brāhmaṇa who is devoid of Vedic knowledge. (11)
Just as one does not scatter ashes after having cast away a blazing fire,
so too [the sin] accrues to him who passes by a Brāhmaṇa who is nearby and engaged in Vedic study.
He who eats and speaks without a teacher is indeed a sinner;
[he should avoid] cowherds, traders, and those who are lecherous. (13)
Having lived abroad, he should treat usurers and even Brahmins as if they were dogs;
by dividing the property of the gods, that teacher becomes a sinner, as do those who tend cattle, merchants, and those addicted to lustful practices.
One should act with haste toward messengers and usurers;
likewise, by the seizure of the property of the gods and the theft of a Brahmin’s wealth, one should proceed with urgency.
Families quickly perish through a dog, a thief, or a rogue bull; likewise, when the words "Come here" are spoken to Brahmins, cows, and others, if one dies within five months,
even if it be by a mere stumble, those who desire the highest welfare must give [the gift].
In the rite of *puraścaraṇa*, [one should worship] at the lotus-feet of the preceptor.
The auspicious sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) must necessarily be given immediately by the performer of the rite who is well-versed in the scriptures,
or at least within a month.
One desiring great accomplishment should present [the offerings] to the teacher;
they should be given with interest after two or three months. (20)
O King, after three months have passed, double [the amount] must be given;
if six months have passed, one falls into the Svarṇeyī hell.
Whatever has been promised by the teacher, let the father obtain it all within this month; he shall bestow a gift as white as nectar, resembling the moon.
Therefore, in the rites of *puraścaraṇa*, one must certainly offer wealth immediately at the pair of lotus-feet of the Guru. (23)
Thus, even if one has not begged for various things oneself, one should immediately provide them for the sake of the teacher; such a person is highly honored.
Or, having performed the propitiatory rite for the deity, one should immediately beg for alms-food at the feet of the teacher;
indeed, one should beg right there in the teacher's household.
In sacrifices such as the Agniṣṭoma, the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) is prescribed by the Śāstra;
it should be given either on the same day, or after three months.
O King, that sacrificer, though having a good son, perishes otherwise;
he should always be one who desires knowledge and one who eats first [of all]. (27)
The nectar of the sacrifice (amṛta) should be the remnant of what has been enjoyed by the learned;
having washed his hands, he should drink it from the hollow of his palms after the meal. 28.
He should offer three oblations to the gods, the ancestors, and himself;
[and likewise] to the Gaṇas, the Aṅganikas, and the Yākas. || 29 ||
If a twice-born man does not visit the house of one who has conceived her first pregnancy, whether it be after a fortnight or a month, he should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance for eating.
The wicked-souled one who steals the food of those performing sacrificial sessions,
of those initiated for sacrifice, of ascetics, or of those devoted to Brahman, must perform the Cāndrāyaṇa vow.

There is no impurity (sūtaka) for these [persons]: for those who have purchased [food], for those performing ritual acts, for one who has vomited due to indigestion, and after shaving or sexual intercourse.

In the case of bad dreams and the touch of the wicked, fasting is indeed prescribed; likewise for those who dwell under auspicious trees, fasting is ordained, as is the consumption of food offered to Śiva.
Having touched one who sells the Vedas, one should enter the water with one's clothes on;
likewise, one should do so in the presence of a Brahmin, in a cow-pen, or near cows that have just eaten the finest grass.

One should avoid food from one's own Vedic recitation, as well as that which has been brought from afar; likewise, grain found in threshing floors or fields, and water from wells—these should be shunned. (35)

That which is eaten from the tip or the edge, that which is held in the hollow of the hand, that which is eaten while standing in a cow-pen, that which is eaten with the head wrapped [in a cloth], and that which is eaten facing the south—[these are forbidden]. (36)
Those twice-born ones who have mounted the chariot of the Dharmaśāstras and wield the sword of the Vedas may drink this [liquor] and eat meat when they have overcome their aversion to them. (37)
Even for the sake of his own enjoyment, the Wind is remembered as being supremely devoted to dharma,
for he constantly provides perfumes, ornaments, and garments.
O Prajāpati, wherever that fragrant one is always seen, there the food of a Brāhmaṇa is considered nectar, and the food of a Kṣatriya is remembered as ambrosia. || 39 ||
The food of a Vaiśya is indeed considered [impure] food, while the food of a Śūdra is declared to be blood;
[one becomes pure] by means of the Vaiśvadeva oblation, fire-offerings, worship of the deities, and acts of victory.

Because he gave nectar (amṛta) to the Brahmins, it is remembered as the Ṛgveda and Sāmaveda; and because he protected the people with justice in accordance with legal proceedings, [it is known as the Yajurveda]. || 41 ||
By that [power], the Kṣatriya desires the protection of his subjects; he seeks to drive away the kodrava weed and to remove what is obstructive to the flow [of prosperity].
The food of a Vaiśya is traditionally prescribed for one who performs sacrifices according to the rules;
however, for one who is blinded by the darkness of ignorance and devoted to the drinking of liquor, it is not so. (43)
A wise man should not, even for a very small purpose, consume blood, the food of a Śūdra, or that which is devoid of divine mantras,
nor should he engage in useless expenditure.
For one who performs [these acts] in vain perishes both here and after death:
in matters of lustful women, in marriages, in providing fodder for cattle, and during a slaughter of people. (45)

For one who has transcended the states of being a Brahmin and so forth, there is no longer any "going" (yātaka); because he does not go to Yama, nor is he seized by Yama, he is indeed called "Yama" (the Self). 46.
What can Yama do to one who has restrained himself? For the patient, there is but one fault, and that is never a second. (47)
When people consider him to be powerless because he is endowed with patience. || 48 ||
Liberation is not for one who delights in treatises, nor for one who is fond of pleasant dwellings;
it is not for one who is more intent on food and clothing, nor for one who is eager to captivate the world.

For one who is devoted to solitude, whose deity is virtue, who has turned away from the gratification of all the senses, whose mind is intent on the yoga of sacred study, and who is eternally non-violent, liberation is certain. (49)
The Blessed Lord said:
"One who has acquired wealth by righteous means, who is devoted to the knowledge of reality, who is free from malice, who is prosperous, truthful, and constantly serves his teacher. (50)
Through the grace of the deities or the sages, [it arises] from the glorious eight-syllabled mantra accompanied by the rays of the Blessed One. || 51 ||
Through the grace of the teacher, even a householder attains liberation;
[this is stated] in the *Śrutisaṃgraha*, concerning the secret essence of the unsurpassed reality of Brahman.
This is the twenty-third chapter in the treatise spoken by the son of Daśaratha.
[Thus ends the twenty-third chapter in the glorious *Anuttarabrahmatattvarahasya*, the *Dāśarathīya Tantra*, which is a compendium of the meaning of the Vedas.]
The Blessed Lord said:

Having thus lived as a brahmin in the householder stage, which is the source of all other stages of life, and being endowed with strength and wealth, he should resort to the third stage of life (vānaprastha). || 1 ||
Having looked after his offspring, having released his evening meals, and having entrusted [his concerns] to his wife and sons, he enters that which is his own dwelling. || 2 ||
Wearing garments of skin or bark, subsisting on the food of sages, and even living on vegetables, roots, and fruits, he should perform the five great sacrifices along with the sacred fires.
Wearing matted hair, sleeping at night on a bed of darbha grass, and bearing a beard and long nails,
he should honor mendicants and guests with alms consisting of roots and fruits.
Otherwise, he was a giver of vegetables, self-restrained, devoted to the study of the Vedas,
and intent upon serving the lotus feet of his preceptor.
Accompanied by the rays of the Blessed One, one should offer the Vaitānika Agnihotra sacrifice from the milk of the venerable eight-syllabled cow (Marāṣṭākṣī) according to the prescribed rule.
One should offer sacrificial cakes (puroḍāśa) made from grains produced by oneself and grown on one's own land;
likewise, one who bestows honey and fruit should himself prepare the moving and stationary [offerings].
One should avoid bilva, śigru, cakataka, palana, honey, saline earth, and firewood that has been stored for more than a month. || 8 ||
One should not abandon wild fruits and roots nor the protection of living beings;
one who gathers fruits, roots, and other provisions for three, six, or twelve months [is a forest-dweller].
Or he may eat only at night, or eat every other day, or even for a fortnight or a month;
or he may observe the Cāndrāyaṇa vow, or eat only when food is left over, or eat only once a month.
Whether dwelling in a fire-sanctuary or subsisting on fruits and roots,
he should wither his body through austerity and satisfy the ancestors and the gods.
Having established the sacred fire within himself, he should then wander as one who has transcended the ritual fire;
for the sake of sustaining his life, he should beg from ascetics dwelling in the forest.
Or, having brought eight morsels from a village for the sake of one who dwells in the forest,
a Brahmin living in the forest stage of life is thus honored by the sons of Brahmā.
Having spent the third part of his life in the forest, and having abandoned attachments,
he should wander as a mendicant during the fourth quarter of his life.
Likewise, one who has not purified the three steps, as well as those sons beginning with the fourth, and those who have not performed sacrifices, go to the lower state even if they desire liberation.
Since not even the slightest fear is aroused by him toward living beings,
all beings here always grant him freedom from fear.

Wandering always alone, like a fire that has no fixed abode, he should remain without companions for the sake of spiritual perfection; he may resort to a village only for the purpose of obtaining food.
A renunciant should never desire either life or death;
he should always await his time, being constantly intent upon the state of Oṃkāra.
A practitioner must necessarily perform all the ritual placements (nyāsa) every day;
he must certainly be devoted to the glorious eight-syllable mantra.
Through sweeping the house and other such tasks, as well as by means of vehicles and the like, and through washing clothes and so forth, he constantly serves his master. (20)
One who is empty of the sense of "mine" everywhere, endowed with equanimity everywhere, and whose dwelling is at the foot of a tree—such a person is praised here as one seeking liberation. 21.
Bathing, purification, begging for alms, and constant practice of solitude—these are the four duties of an ascetic, which he does not abandon. (22)
During the four months of the rainy season, a leader should not wander anywhere, for therein occurs the injury of living beings such as insects and ants. (23)
One should go [to the water source] at dawn, midday, and sunset, and drink water purified by a lotus-strainer;
one should speak words without agitation, never repeatedly, and never anywhere [inappropriately].
Accompanied by Codānma, he dwells in hell without support;
he is utterly devoid of delight, possessing short hair and a belly like that of a human.
A vessel made of flowers, bamboo, *iḍā*, *chobhikṣāśīra*, or *ativajita*; or one made of gourd, wood, clay, or bamboo—such a vessel is praised for the practice of begging. || 26 ||
A mendicant should never accept a vessel made of metal; he should seek alms only once a day at the house of a single person, and there he should not engage in elaboration.
The ascetic should always wander for alms at a place where the pestle has been laid aside, where the coals have been extinguished, and where the bowls have been put away.
Eating little, remaining in solitude, free from hypocrisy and greed for gain, and liberated from passion and hatred—the mendicant who is thus becomes fit for liberation. (29)
O Lord of the Universe, if a yogi may rest even for a moment in these hermitages, what need has he for other systems? He has accomplished his purpose. (30)
Whatever has been accumulated in his house, including his wealth and ornaments,
the ascetic will empty it all in a single night.
Having seen the unbearable onset of old age, the torment of passion, the exhaustion of the body, and the terrible suffering within the womb; (29)
And [he perceives] thousands of various births, separation from those who are dear, union with those who are unpleasant, and the arising of suffering through the nature of conditioned phenomena. (30)
Furthermore, there are the various hells and the tortures of hell for those people who are densely packed with the defects of their karma, as well as their manifold births. (32)
Having perceived the impermanence of the body and the eternal nature of the supreme Self, one should strive for liberation regardless of which stage of life (āśrama) one is devoted to.
Whether he be a student, a householder, a forest-dweller, or even a mendicant,
he must necessarily be devoted to the service of his teacher and his elders.
Day by day, performing the rites whose essence is the Veda as released from its own source,
he was endowed with the entire network of ritual placements (nyāsa) joined with the knowledge of the rays.
By being born from the glorious eight-syllabled mantra (aṣṭākṣarī), one certainly becomes one with Brahman;
[this applies to those] associated with the Kṛta, Tretā, and Dvāpara ages, as well as the various stages of life (āśrama).
There are high-souled Brahmins capable of both restraint and favor;
for them, the life of celibacy and dwelling in the forest exist according to the Tiṣya Yuga.
Even the dress of ascetics leads to the downfall of Brahmins in the Kali age;
their minds are attached to women, such as sons, friends, wives, and the like. (37)
In this Kali age, Brahmins will appear wearing the garb of ascetics,
yet they will be possessed of hypocrisy, arrogance, and falsehood, and will be utterly devoid of purity and sacred study.
O King, daily devoted to eye-salve, food, ghee, and long life, he constantly and in vain abandons his meal for the sake of begging alms. (39)
They were devoted to women whose husbands had departed— women who signify the fourth stage of life— and they were intent on associating with them, longing for the sight of their sons.
He who will assume the garb of an ascetic in this Kali age,
even while remaining in the household state, is said to be the most excellent among all stages of life (āśramas).
Even after performing a terrible sacrifice, a wise householder remains liberated through expiatory rites, provided he is not attached elsewhere to the raw (unripe) state.
The householder stage is proclaimed to be the support for all [the other stages] during the night; yet in this terrible Kali age, even householders are constantly... (43)
They have fallen away from the conduct prescribed by the Vedas, yet they are joined with the immortality of the Akhaṇḍala [Vedic] rites;
they are devoted to the wives of others and are fond of deceit, greed, and falsehood.
Even if they have practiced the Great Vidyā, those who revile their preceptors and others shall all become guests of Yama and partakers of hell.
Therefore, performing daily the Vedic conduct appropriate to his stage of life (āśrama), and serving his teacher even at the cost of his life and wealth; || 46 ||
Having recited the glorious eight-syllabled mantra, which is endowed with all the deposits (nyāsa) and accompanied by the constant study of the Vedas, one attains pure liberation (kaivalya).
One who is incapable [of performing major rites] should be disciplined by the vows prescribed for the Soma sacrifice and other such rites;
being well-composed, he should observe the vow on the full moon, the new moon, or the final day of the month.
Having consecrated the fire according to the rules with mantras proclaimed by Āvaraṇaga,
one should offer oblations one by one, reciting the root mantra one hundred and eight times.
Having recited the *raśmi-mantras* once, O King, one should then offer a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) at the feet of the preceptor, consisting of a *niṣka*, a *tanka*, or half of one.
Whoever recites this every day shall obtain the fruit that is gained month after month if [the moon] should be joined with the sun on the new moon day. 51.
Having thus performed the fire-oblation according to the prescribed rite, one should diligently offer a *niṣka* of gold or even a portion of the remainder at the two feet of the preceptor.
In that month, one undoubtedly obtains at will the merit born of ten Agniṣṭoma sacrifices accompanied by complete sacrificial fees. || 53 ||
A twice-born man who has not studied the sciences, who does not perform sacrifices with abundant fees,
and who has no son, sinks into the hells.
Therefore, the wise must necessarily understand that the purpose of the Vedas is action;
sacrifices such as the Agniṣṭoma, accompanied by complete sacrificial fees, constitute that action.
Sons who bestow happiness both in this world and the next are to be produced;
or rather, one who desires the fruit of all sacrifices on the surface of the earth [should do so]. (56)
The glorious eight-syllabled Vidyā, conjoined with the rays of the Lord,
should always be recited when combined with the ritual placement (nyāsa), and offered as oblation with clarified butter.
For one desiring the fruit of sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) amounting to a hundred thousand,
during the auspicious Navarātra vow at times such as the lunar eclipses and others, [this should be performed].
On the third lunar day known as Akṣayā, during the half-moon and other such times,
the prescribed sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) along with its constituent parts must be given, for it yields great merit.
The *Lakṣmīnārāyaṇīvidyā*, consisting of a thousand syllables, brings forth glory;
it purifies even one named Nārāyaṇa and destroys all sins.
A wise person should daily conquer [the senses] with devotion for another day by serving the lotus feet of the teacher, desiring the fruit of the complete study of the Vedas.
One who delights in the glorious eight-syllable mantra, conjoined with the placement of the rays of light (raśmividyānyāsa),
and who dwells in Vārāṇasī for as long as life lasts, is highly exalted.
In the sacred field of Śrī Puruṣottama, there are four means for attaining the fortune of liberation within the cremation ground of the physical body. (63)
The fifth [perfection] consists of possessing wealth; it directly bestows the fruit of a physical form.
In that regard as well, there is service to the preceptor and delight in the glorious eight-syllabled mantra. (64)
Even here, she bestows all sovereignty and grants the perfection of liberation;
she belongs to the householders, and indeed to the householders among the gods, as well as to the gods and the yogins. (65)
He is the refuge of all beings; those who are without refuge—such as mendicants and others, as well as those who are deaf, mute, or blind—are incapable of performing Vedic rites. (66)
For indeed, by attaining the stage of the ascetic (yati-āśrama), one becomes a partaker of liberation;
the fourth stage is prescribed for those who are incapable of performing the rites mentioned in the Śruti.
A householder, while performing all his duties with diligence and from afar,
having rendered service to his teacher, should recite that glorious eight-syllabled mantra.
A king who is exalted by his paternal lineage and endowed with a hundred maternal lineages will certainly attain the state of Brahmānanda and the flow of creative power (māyā). 69.
With a mind constantly and respectfully intent on serving the pair of lotus feet of the Guru,
one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) along with the eight-spoked wheel, the subtle creation, and the worship of the couples consisting of the eight [deities] beginning with Īta.

In the hour of Brahmā, while reciting the mantra of the Lord of Kamalā (the Sun), on a day in the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha during the conjunction known as Kṣaya— a rare and auspicious yoga— on the seventh lunar day, when the Moon was in conjunction with the Sun.

And on the ninth day of autumn, O Lord of the Earth, having recited [the mantra] and offered oblations at the time when the sun is joined with the constellation Āditya and the moon is in the *suyava* asterism, one should offer abundant wealth at the feet of the Guru.
Having respectfully offered a pair of earrings to both ears and having adorned his wife with ornaments such as a necklace of pearls and a pair of bracelets, the Brahmins should then be fed.
He who, endowed with self-restraint, performs year after year the rites of recitation, mantra-chanting, and fire-offerings for this [deity],
shall obtain longevity, health, and the attainment of wealth, as well as jewels, pearls, horses, and herds of elephants.
Having obtained sons, grandsons, knowledge, prosperity, and inexhaustible fortune,
and having fulfilled hundreds of generations of his mother’s and father’s lineages, he ascends a divine celestial chariot yoked with jewels and gold.
Having ascended [the chariot], one who possesses the very form of the Lord reaches the beautiful city of Ayodhyā;
likewise, the daughter of Bhṛgu, through the abundance of her splendor day by day, [attains it] according to the rule for human beings.
By honoring even the teacher’s wife with garments, ornaments, and excellent offerings, one attains divine prosperity;
and having attained abundance accompanied by sons, grandsons, and great-grandsons, one then truly reaches Hari, who dwells in the heart.

Month after month, on a Saturday or on the day of Vyāsa, having honored the foremost of the twice-born—who are accompanied by the sons of a true guru—with various kinds of food, royal delicacies, garments, and auspicious ornaments; || 78 ||
Having obtained wealth consisting of all kinds of riches and gems, as well as prosperity and unsurpassed health,
and having attained the increase of his lineage, he goes to that supreme city, the abode of Viṣṇu.

Those who are devoted to the recitation and fire-offerings of the eight-syllable mantra, who serve at the feet of the preceptor, and who are intent on grain, attain their goal among men; having always obtained all desires, they then go to liberation.
[Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter in the venerable *Anuttarabrahmatattvarahasya*, the *Daśarathīya Tantra*, which is a compendium of the meaning of the Vedas.]
The king said:
"I am blessed and my purpose is fulfilled, O Nārāyaṇa, Lord of the Universe!
Please tell me the meter, the seer, and other details regarding the placement (nyāsa) of the glorious eight-syllabled mantra."
O son of Dharma, perform the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*), the practice for specific desires,
and the ritual of the six-faced image.
The Blessed Lord said: Now, therefore, I shall fully declare the entire system of meters beginning with Āṣā, which grants success to the web of nyāsa, by knowing which one becomes accomplished.
The seer of the *antarvahir-mātṛkā* is Brahmā Prajāpati;
the meter is declared to be Gāyatrī; and the presiding deities are Vidrī, Śrī, and Sarasvatī.
This yoga, spoken by the deity for the sake of pleasing the Lord of Śrī, is proclaimed;
with six syllables consisting of non-weak (vowels), long vowels, the letter *hrī*, and the guttural (*avarga*) class, it constitutes the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅgaka*).

Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*), the wise one should meditate upon the Supreme Goddess Umā, composed of the fifty letters of the Mātṛkā, whose face, arms, and middle of the chest are divided by those letters;
who has the crescent moon bound to her own crest; who is dark-blue like a fresh *nīla* lotus;
and who bestows boons with her four lotus-hands holding a mudrā, a rosary, a jar of nectar, and a golden vessel of knowledge, and who possesses a brilliant white radiance.
I take refuge in the three-eyed Goddess of Speech.

Without performing daily the ritual placement (nyāsa) known as the Mātṛkā both internally and externally, a practitioner of mantra does not attain success even through hundreds of preparatory rites (puraścaryā).
One should perform the placement of the Mātṛkā, beginning with the Praṇava, O Supreme Goddess,
after likewise having performed the previously mentioned ritual placement (nyāsa) of the Ṛṣi, meter, and so forth.

One should meditate upon the Goddess, who possesses the luster of vermilion, is adorned with immeasurable ornaments, has three eyes, and holds a book, a rosary, a deer, and a hunter by her side; likewise, one should meditate upon the Lord, along with the Ṛṣis, the meters, and so forth.

I meditate upon the Lord who possesses the luster of yellow orpiment, is adorned with immeasurable ornaments, has three eyes, and holds a book, a rosary, a deer, and a hunter; and I also meditate upon the Goddess standing at his side, who is golden-hued and holds a book and a rosary of letters in her hands.
By meditating upon this Mātṛkā, which has the Praṇava as its abode and bestows all perfections,
one indeed becomes the very form of Brahman, consisting of truth, bliss, and consciousness.
One should perform the nyāsa of the Mātṛkās beginning with Vāk, which bestows the fruits of all vidyās;
Prajāpati is the seer (ṛṣi), the Gāyatrī is the metre (chandas), and Aparā is indeed the deity.

One should bow to Vāgīśvarī, whose face is the Mātṛkā, who holds in her hands a rosary of beads, a deer, and a lofty axe— just as previously described; who possesses three eyes, whose crown is the non-dual [Śiva], whose complexion is like the rising sun and the lotus, who is the sovereign of letters, and who bends under the weight of her breasts.
Having performed this placement (nyāsa) of the Vāgbhava syllable using the Mātṛkā,
even a dull-witted person certainly becomes one who has reached the further shore of all ritual procedures.
Then, one should place the five Brahma-kalās, followed by the three Vedas beginning with their phonemes (varṇas); thereafter, the seer is declared to be Prajāpati and the metre Gāyatrī.
The goddess Śāradā is remembered as the deity who generates the letters of the alphabet from her own essence.
The six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga) is prescribed by means of the Praṇavas situated between the short and long vowels. || 15 ||
Carrying in her hands the discus, the conch, the deer, the book, the rosary of letters, the chisel,
the bright skull-bowl, the trident, and the golden jar overflowing with nectar;
she bends her chest under her own lion-like faces, which are beautiful with their five heads and shine like a fresh rain-cloud flashing with lightning amidst pearls.
I bow to those whose portions resemble the full autumnal moon. || 16 ||
Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, Vidhā, Śānti, as well as Rodhikā, Dīpikā, Recikā, and the supreme Mocikā. (17)
Sūkṣmā, Asūkṣmā, Amṛtāyā, Vījnānāmṛtā, as well as Āpyāyinī, Vyāpinī, Vyomanī, and Ka-sāddhamā. (18)
Arising from Sadāśiva, sixteen Mahas are declared.
Sṛṣṭi, Ṛddhi, Smṛti, Medhā, Kānti, Lakṣmī, Dyuti, Sthirā,
Sthiti, and Siddhi— these are the ten external kalās beginning with Prī.
Jarā, Pālinī, Śānti, Īśvarī, Ratikāmikā,
Varadā, Hrādinī, Prīti, Dīrghā, and Viṣṇu— these are the ten kalās.
Tīkṣṇā, Raudrī, Bhayā, Tritā, Tandrā, Śrutkardhinī, Kriyā, Utkārī, and Mṛtyu— these are said to be the ten kalās of Rudra.
Yellow, reddish-brown, white, and black—these are the four *kalās*.
These fifty *kalās* are said to have originated from the limbs of Īśvara. (23)
One who possesses this entire *kalpa* of Kalānyā, directly endowed with the portion (*kalā*) of Brahman,
attains the perfection of the Command (*ājñāsiddhi*) and becomes a body composed of radiant energy.
One should perform the Śrīkaṇṭha-mātṛkā-nyāsa, endowed with the Vyoma-śakti,
consisting of the fifty pairs beginning with Śrīkaṇṭha and Pūrṇā.
One should [place] that which has "taṃ" as its third prior [syllable], ending with "om," joined with Rudra,
and conjoined with the elements, the vital breaths, the powers, and the self, in due order.

The sage is Dakṣiṇāpūrti; Gāyatrī is declared to be the meter; and Arddhanārīśvara is proclaimed by those who know that [mantra] to be the deity. The preceptor should perform the nyāsa with the syllables *ha* and *ṣa*, joined with the six long vowels. || 27 ||

We take refuge in that Lord who possesses eyes as beautiful as the Bandhūka flower and gold, whose brow is adorned with a creeper, who holds a noose, a goad, and the gesture of granting boons in his own arms;
who wears ornaments shaped like fish, who has three eyes, half-mooned hair, and who is the sovereign of the goddess Umā.
Śrīkaṇṭha, Ananta, Sūkṣmeśa, Trimūrti, Amareśvara, Ajeśa, Śobhāveśa, Arbhakeśa, Tithīśa, Sthāṇu, and Hara; || 29 ||
Kaṇṭheśa, Bhautika, Sadyojāta, Anugraheśvara,
Akrūra, and Mahāsena— these are the sixteen forms of Śiva.
Then Ekānada, Rudra, Kṛmi, Mokana, Jñāna, and Caturānana [spoke]. || 31 ||
Ajeśa, Śarva, Someśa, Rājahiguladhāraka,
Ardhanārīśvara, Cīmākānta, Aṣāja, and Daṇḍin.
There may be those named Trimūrti and Meṣa, as well as Lohitākṣa and Śiva;
likewise Chagalaṇḍa, Dviraṇḍeśa, Mahīkāla, and Kapālī. (33)
Bhujageśa, Pināyīśa, Khaḍgīśa, Dravya, Vakas, Śvetabhṛṅgīśa, Lakūliśiva, and then Saṃvartaka. || 34 ||
These Rudras are white and red, holding tridents and skull-bowls;
[the goddesses] Pūrṇodarī and Sthādvirajā follow, and after that, Śālmalī.
Kolākṣī, Vartulākṣī, and Dīrghakarṇā are mentioned;
likewise Sadīrghamukhī, Gomukhī, and Dīrghajihvā. || 36 ||
Kuṇḍodarī, Ūrdhvakeśī, and likewise Vikṛtamukhī;
thereafter Jvālāmukhī is to be known, and after that Ulkāmukhī. (37)
Suśrīmukhī and Vidyāmukhī—these indeed are the powers of the vowels;
Mahākālī and Sarasvatī are endowed with all supernatural attainments (siddhis). || 38 ||
Gaurī is the Vidyā of the three worlds; beyond that is Maṃtraśakti. Then there is Ātmaśakti, who is considered to be the Mother, as well as Laṃbodara.
Śaviṇī, Nāginī, Māyākhecarī, Cāpimañjarī, Rūpiṇī, Vāriṇī, and then Kyakodatanā. (40)
There may be Bhadrakālī, Yoginī, Śaṅkhinī, and Garjinī; likewise Kālarātri, Kubjī, Kapardinī, and Vajrā. (41)
Jayā, Sumukhī, Icchā, Revatī, and likewise Varā;
Vāruṇī and Vāyavī are proclaimed, as well as she who wears the protective amulet (Rakṣopadhāriṇī). 42.
Then, Sahajālakṣmī, who is all-pervasive and endowed with Māyā, [is present];
these Rudrās, established in their seats, possess bodies as red as vermilion. (43)
With their lotus-like hands adorned by a red lotus and a skull-cup,
one should first install this Śrīkaṇṭhamātṛkā day after day.
The glorious eight-syllabled mantra, once born in the heart, becomes directly identical with Brahman;
it is undoubtedly Rudra himself, the manifest agent and destroyer. 54.

Preceded by the seed-syllables of the three Vedas, the goddess Ramā, and Kāma, this placement (nyāsa) should be performed constantly; it bestows desired objects and grants the realization of identity with Brahman. 46.
Or one should install these [deities] beginning with Smara, which grant the desired success through the Mātṛkās;
they are Sa, Dhātu, Prāk, Aṇa, Śakti, Ātman-yukta, Yādi, and Iṣu-Viṣṇus.
The seer is Prajāpati, the meter is said to be Gāyatrī, and the deity is declared to be Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of Lakṣmī, who is the essence of food. 48.
One should duly place the six limbs upon the long [form],
bearing in his hands the lotus, mace, conch, and discus.
By her, the golden pitcher [of the universe] was made to appear like the play of lightning amidst clouds;

and out of a longing for constant embrace, she merged her body with that of Lakṣmī—the lotus-eyed Viṣṇu—so that their left breast and his right breast became one, as if they were an unceasing ornament. 49.
Victory to Him who eternally holds the conch, discus, mace, and lotus in His thousand-petalled lotus-hands; who bears a mirror and a golden vessel, as well as the forms of the bow and arrow;
who wears a crown, armlets, bracelets, necklaces, and earrings, and whose face shines with the splendor of rubies; and who is accompanied by Lakṣmī.

Having performed the placement (nyāsa) even of a single Vaiṣṇavī Mātṛkā for six days, and having realized the glorious eight-syllabled mantra, one becomes Nārāyaṇa himself— Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of Śrī. 50–51.
And here, the minister should be beyond doubt, capable of both restraint and favor;
he should be truly one with Brahman, having applied the Vaiṣṇava Mātṛkā.
The knower of mantras should place the Mātṛkā-mantra preceded by Śakti;
Śakti is declared by the wise to be the Seer (Ṛṣi), Gāyatrī the Metre (Chandas), and [Śakti] the Deity.
She is proclaimed as the mother of the universe and the bestower of all prosperity;
the wise one should form the limbs of the long and even-numbered [feet] with the nature of Māyā.
Her thighs are filled with the brilliance of two rising suns; she possesses breasts that surpass the moon; she is resplendent with a crown, necklaces, rays of light, and anklets.
Bearing in his lotus-hands the mace, the noose, the goad, and the book, may the Three-eyed Lord of the universe grant happiness from his lotus-feet.
Having performed the placement (nyāsa) of the seed-syllables of the powers and the Mātṛkā which bestows all accomplishments, one becomes the locus of all fortunes; herein there is no doubt.
One should perform the placement (nyāsa) of the Mātṛkā, endowed with the seed-syllable *Śrī*, upon the body according to the prescribed rite;
Bhṛgu is remembered as the seer (ṛṣi), Gāyatrī as the metre (chaṃdas), and Śrī is considered the deity (devatā).
The wise should not perform the *saṃyama* of all [the limbs] starting with the head;
rather, the practitioner should first form the *aṅgas* (limbs) using this seed-syllable (*bīja*) as the primary subject.
I behold her who possesses a thousandfold radiance, being sprinkled with nectar lifted by the trunks of four elephants resembling Mount Kailāsa;
she holds in her lotus-like hands a rosary and two books, and is resplendent with shining jewels.
One should meditate upon the Mistress of the World, whose breasts are full.
Having placed the Mātṛkā preceded by the seed-syllable *śrī*, which bestows all perfections, one becomes directly endowed with the glorious *kalā* through the grace of the Ācārya. (59)
One should perform the placement (nyāsa) of the Mātṛkā, beginning with 'A', which bestows auspiciousness;
Saṃmohana is declared the seer (ṛṣi), and the Gāyatrī is said to be the meter (chandas). || 60 ||
The supreme Mother of all beings is proclaimed by the mantras of the deities;
one should perform the assignment of the limbs with the syllable *smara* joined with the long vowel [Ā]. (61)

One should meditate upon the Mother of all beings, who possesses three eyes, who holds in her lotus-like hands a rosary of crystal beads radiant as ten million rising suns, a bow made of sugarcane, and the arrows of the God of Love, and who shines like the new moon.

One who possesses a luster equal to that of the creator Brahmā, having performed the nyāsa of the letters of the Yātṛkā-mantra beginning with Smara (Ka), shall bring the three worlds under his control and moreover become identical with Brahman.
One should also perform the placement (nyāsa) of the Mātṛkā beginning with the Śrī, Śakti, and Kāma-bījas; for this mantra, the seer is Sammohana, the metre is Gāyatrī, and the deity is the Mother.
She is proclaimed as Trailokyamohinī, the subduer of all the worlds;
one should perform the ritual assignment of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) by means of the three seed-syllables rotated [in order]. || 65 ||
I meditate upon her who holds in her hands a rosary, sugarcane arrows together with a noose, two Yamas, a parrot, arrows, and a fresh book;
she who possesses compassion in her single eye, is distressed by her breasts, is enchanting, has three eyes, and wears the crescent moon as her crest-ornament.
Having performed the placement (nyāsa) of the Mātṛkā beginning with the three seed-syllables, which bestows the desired perfections,
one becomes endowed with all good fortune, self-restraint, splendor, and complete sovereignty.
Endowed with all branches of knowledge, he shall live for a hundred autumns;
one who bestows all desired things should install the Mātṛkā, beginning with the Haṃsa-vidyā and the rest.
The seer is Brahmā; its meter is declared to be Gāyatrī;
it is said to bring about the attainment of all things and to be auspicious through its splendor and power. (69)
O King, one should assign the five limbs to the deity known as Time, Brahmā, and the Supreme Self, starting with Svāhā and the sky, along with the five sages. (70)

In the directions of the weapons and so forth, the great-minded one [perceives] the power of the Vedas and the rest, along with Ajeśā and Paramātman, which depend upon the ninefold arising of the well-established root. || 71 ||
The five syllables ending with the wife of Vahni (svāhā), when recited, bring auspiciousness for the sake of attaining identity with Brahman;
then, one should place the mantra "sādyomāttakām," which consists of the Supreme Brahman and grants the attainment of all fruits.
Worship that supreme splendor— the single root of the universe,
the imperishable Lord of all worlds, whose essence is truth and consciousness, who is attained solely through the grace of the Guru, and who is the ocean of thick nectar—
while performing the placement (*nyāsa*) of the *mātṛkā* beginning with *haṃsa* and reciting the glorious eight-syllabled mantra.
This Blessed One is endowed with the sovereign powers (aiśvarya) of the qualities beginning with atomization (aṇimā).
Thus, having performed the eleven-fold Mātṛkā-nyāsa, I attained the victory of the glorious eight-syllabled mantra through the grace of my teacher. (75)
He should be known as Nārāyaṇa in person, capable of both restraint and grace;
he is the creator, destroyer, and protector of all the worlds along with their inhabitants.
O Lord of the Earth, he who is capable of the elevenfold nyāsa becomes one to whom the winds and the mountains must pay homage. (77)
Being pure day by day, one should also perform the nyāsa of the Vaiṣṇava syllables (KĪM);
thereafter, one should perform the nyāsa of the principles (tattva-nyāsa), by which the person becomes composed of those principles.
The Virāj is the seer, Hari is the witness; there is no doubt in this matter.
The Ṛṣi is Brahmā, the metre is Tātaśchanda-gāyatra, and it is remembered that the deity is Hari. || 79 ||
The Lord, the deity Hari, who is manifest and consists of all reality, should perform the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*) by means of the six long vowels preceded by the *praṇava*. (80)

I take refuge day and night in that Great Light named Nārāyaṇa, who consists of the entire universe composed of the five elements— earth, water, fire, air, and ether— who effects the maintenance, creation, and dissolution of the world, who is the true essence of the syllable Om, who possesses the forms of Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and Śiva, who is praised by gods and sages, and who dwells in the lotus of the heart, endowed with the power of consciousness.
Having learned the installation consisting of reality from the lotus-like mouth of the teacher, the wise one,
having performed the installation, should mutter the glorious eight-syllable mantra.
He becomes Nārāyaṇa himself, one whose command is spontaneously effective; therefore, the worshipper of the One without a second should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of His form. 83.

Furthermore, the Lord, the ancient seer Prajāpati, the soul of the sun situated within the solar orb, is known as the deity of the Gāyatrī; he is remembered as the divine leader of the world and the source of the Veda.
One should always meditate upon Nārāyaṇa, who dwells in the center of the solar disc, seated upon the lotus born from the waters;
he wears armlets, a crown, and earrings, possesses a golden body, and holds the conch and the discus.
Having first performed the installation of the jar-form (yaṃjaranyāsa) day after day,
that person shall become the Lord, the Form consisting of the Śabdabrahman.
One should perform the ten-fold placement of the syllables (varṇanyāsa), which bestows the perfection of the fire-ritual (vahnisiddhi).
O King, I myself am its seer (ṛṣi), and Nārāyaṇa is the one to be attained (sādhya). 87.
The Gāyatrī is the deity and the meter; the Lord who is directly the husband of Lakṣmī, Hari Nārāyaṇa, the Master, is declared to be the presiding deity. 88.
I bow to Him whose body is as tender as a blue lotus, who bears the conch, the discus, and the mace, who is beautified by the pair of Lakṣmī and Bhūmi resting upon His two lotuses,
who is eternally delightful with hundreds of divine ornaments, and who sits peacefully upon a jeweled throne.
O beautiful one, worshipped by the gods, the immortals, the sages, Brahmā, Īśa, and Śakra! 89.
Having thus constantly practiced the tenfold transposition of colors with devotion for a black [image],
one will subsequently, through the grace of the teacher, necessarily partake of the form of Hari.

One should certainly perform the placement of all [mantras] (sakalanyāsa), which brings about the attainment of all existing states through the placement of the Mother who is the very form of consciousness, and which grants the fruit born of its practice. 91.
I am declared to be the sage of this [mantra], the omnipresent Lord Nārāyaṇa who is to be realized;
the meter is the goddess Gāyatrī, and he is the supreme husband of Śrī.

Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of the World, is remembered by the wise as the presiding deity. For Him also, the root five-limbed nyāsa (mūla-pañcāṅga-nyāsa) has been proclaimed by the virtuous; or one should perform the six-limbed nyāsa (ṣaḍaṅga) using the six groups of consonants, which bestows the earth.

I perpetually salute Lord Nārāyaṇa, the forest of consciousness, the omnipresent one who is eternally gracious, the goal of the lords of sages and gods, who is seated upon a great lion-throne at the root of the wish-fulfilling tree, accompanied by the Goddess Śrī with her manifold digits, resplendent with hundreds of divine ornaments served by the blue earth, and who is exceedingly beautiful.
O King, although I was incapable of performing all the nyāsas, through the grace of my own teacher, I have completed this placement which bestows the attainment of all fruits. (95)
Having performed the ritual of invocation, one should daily mutter the glorious eight-syllabled mantra;
by performing the placement (nyāsa) of the Mātṛkā, whose nature is consciousness, one becomes Nārāyaṇa in person. || 96 ||

One shall become composed of all mantras and honored even by all the gods. Having gone even a thousand yojanas to honor an Ācārya who has reached the further shore of the Vedānta, who is learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*), and who is twice-born (*dvija*), one attains mastery and is glorified.
Seeking identity with Brahman, one attains liberation in a single birth. 98.
Having attained the previous [state], he also associated with those possessed of ignorance;
for many years he served them, even at the cost of half his life-force.
One should certainly take up the glorious eight-syllabled mantra (aṣṭākṣarī-vidyā), conjoined with the rays of the Lord and accompanied by all the secret depositions (nyāsa). 100.
One should always recognize that teacher as none other than myself;
for all the ritual placements (nyāsa) necessarily proceed from the lotus feet of the teacher.
The deities who bestow the accomplishment of the state of divinity must be installed and not withheld;
they must certainly be taught, whether [the disciple] performs [the rites] or not.
O Great Sage, the Teacher, having bestowed this auspicious collection of other [tantric] systems upon his own undisciplined disciple, has departed. (3)

Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) with the glorious eight-syllable mantra and having recited it one thousand one hundred times for three months, whoever does so shall surely behold the Lord of Śrī.

Filled with the power of the Blessed One, possessing a radiance equal to ten million desires, consisting of pure splendor, and liberated from the fourfold death and old age, he becomes such [a being]. || 5 ||
By practicing this auspicious net of offerings daily, making it a constant habit, this accomplishment arises. 6.
But if she disregards her teacher, or even her mother or father,
while being honored by one observing a vow, she will undoubtedly meet death within a month.
Within three months, even Śakra and the other gods become his servants;
on an auspicious day and at an auspicious lunar station, this pure network of deposits is established.
And having taken [the first], O King, one should take the third syllable with the suffix *śreyas*;
the earth will then possess cows and barley, and be filled with wealth, grain, and prosperity.
In the scripture concerning the prescribed sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā), one may give even one's entire property,
or a quantity of goods sufficient for a year's subsistence, or as much as the sun [shines upon].
Having performed this collection of ritual placements (nyāsa) daily with devotion, one attains immediate success even without the practice of asceticism, fasting, and the like. 111.
Or one should mutter the glorious eight-syllabled mantra one hundred and eight times on a Saturday, or on a Tuesday, or month after month.
This net of seed-syllables (bīja-sena) should be deposited for three months;
it should be deposited every day by the wise who desire great accomplishment.
This meritorious collection of Nyāsa-mantras, which constitutes the essence of the vast ocean of the Vedas, Vedānta, and the Śāstras, bestows the perfection of the Lord. 14.
On the third day of the Akṣaya festival, or on the day of a solar or lunar eclipse, or during the nine nights of Āśvina, one may conquer on the tenth day.
The auspicious and glorious eight-syllabled mantra, accompanied by the rays of Bhaga emerging from the lotus-like mouth of the Teacher, is endowed with all the ritual placements (nyāsa). 16.
Having given the teacher’s fee, it should be studied again and again;
thus one will certainly attain great accomplishment, endowed with qualities such as the power of atomization (aṇimā) and the rest.
In this [state], one attains the eternal cause for the realization of identity with Brahman; there is no doubt regarding this, as well as marriage, victory, and so forth. 18.

If one is capable of performing all the nyāsas, one should indeed perform the Vaiṣṇava Mātṛkā-nyāsa as well; then, O best of men, having performed the Tattva-nyāsa, one should perform the nyāsa of that particular form of the Lord.
Having performed the ten-fold deposition of the phonemes (varṇanyāsa) and the Mātṛkā of the triangle of consciousness,
one who daily recites the glorious eight-syllabled mantra is glorified.
If one is unable even for that, the wise one should perform the tenfold placement of the letters (varṇanyāsa) of the Vaiṣṇava Mātṛkā, which is the Mātṛkā whose nature is consciousness.
One should mutter the glorious eight-syllabled mantra, which bestows all perfections;
having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa), one must certainly perform all the placements for the sake of the grace of Śiva.
I shall speak [of this] every month, or every six months, for it brings great honor;
indeed, by the command of Hari, the complete ritual placement (nyāsa) must necessarily be performed.
Otherwise, great accomplishment will never be attained;
therefore, perform the recitation during all the auspicious times, or even on a day of Bhārgava (Venus).
This auspicious web of ritual deposits (nyāsajāla) should be performed on the eleventh lunar day, or on the new moon, or even during the transit of the sun, or during the vyatīpāta yoga.
Together with the ritual placements (nyāsas) and the eight-syllable mantra, he whose mind was intent on serving his preceptor day after day,
having divided the sacrificial offering into twelve parts according to the Vedic *yāvaka* rite...
Especially on a Saturday, having performed recitation (japa) and burnt offerings (homa), one should offer food dear to the Guru,
as well as eatables mixed with ghee and honey, and ornaments such as colored gems and pearls.
