Having given it, one obtains inexhaustible gain and prosperity, as well as the increase of glory;
one attains a radiance extending through the three times, fashioned from jewels and gold, and finally reaches the state of the Blessed One.

Necessarily, even during the month of Māgha or on a Tuesday, one who is composed in mind, having recited [the mantra], offered oblations according to the rules, and honored the preceptor with offerings such as jewels and gold; 28.
Having attained long life, health, inexhaustible wealth, and various kinds of pearls, fruits, and jewels,
as well as the prosperity of his lineage and enjoyments, he directly obtains bliss from the Blessed Lady.
The Great Soul (Brahmā) is the creator who, through ritual placements (*nyāsa*), is a reciter of the eight-syllable mantra;
Śiva likewise, through ritual placements, is a conqueror of the eight-syllable mantra and a reciter of the six-syllable mantra.

O Blessed One, by means of these nyāsas, this Great-Souled One (Viṣṇu) is the conqueror of the nine-syllable mantra; by means of these nyāsas, the Creator (Brahmā) is the conqueror of the eight-syllable mantra;
and Nārāyaṇa, the most venerable teacher of all that is moving and unmoving, is also worthy of universal worship through these nyāsas. || 31 ||
Truth, truth, and again truth—it is not spoken falsely by me.
Know this alone to be the supreme reality, O lord of the earth. (132)
[Thus ends the twentieth chapter in the venerable *Anuttarabrahmatattvarahasya*, the *Dāśarathīya Tantra*, which is a compendium of the meaning of the Vedas.]
The Blessed Lord said:
I shall describe the rite known as *puraścaryā* for the glorious eight-syllable mantra (*aṣṭārṇavidyā*), which bestows all perfections upon the practitioner; it is like nectar to the ears. 1.
Thus, having performed the fifteen nyāsas,
with his body adorned, he meditated upon the lotus feet of the Guru at the auspicious aperture of Brahma (brahmabila).
Having meditated upon the Lord of Śrī, born of the Yati meter, in the center of the pericarp of the heart-lotus,
one should then recite the glorious eight-syllable mantra daily according to one's capacity.
Having recited [the mantra] for more than six months or even a year, he may take another's life when the fire of his own knowledge has been kindled. || 4 ||
Having honored the wife and sons of the preceptor and others with heaps of wealth,
one attains for years a great accomplishment that is difficult even for the gods to obtain.
The emptiness of old age and death, the attainment of long life,
fortune equal to that of Kāmadeva, and the supreme perfection of speech.
He possesses the power to enter the bodies of others and other such feats;
he can even restore the dead to life merely by the touch of his thousand-rayed hand.
It restores life once more; there is no doubt about this.
Endowed with the eightfold powers (aṣṭaiśvarya) such as atomization (aṇimā) and the rest, one becomes a self-sovereign wanderer within a year.
O highly fortunate one, the accomplishment of the eight-syllable mantra is said to be achieved even without preliminary rites (puraścaryā),
provided that no obstacles arise.
It is said that [the duration] was four hundred thousand in the Kṛta age, eight hundred thousand in the Tretā,
one hundred and twenty thousand in the Dvāpara, and sixteen hundred thousand in the Kali age.
The banks of the Gaṅgā and Godāvarī, the excellent inner banks of the Madā, as well as the banks of the Sarasvatī and the shore of the Yamunā. (11)
The banks of the Kāverī, Kṛṣṇaveṇī, Catuṅgā, and Bhīmarathī; the seashore, Goṣṭha, and the course of the Suvarṇamukharī.
The interior of a Tulasī grove is highly praised for the performance of japa; they say that the presence of the Ācārya therein is especially distinguished and bestows desired fruits. (13)
Performing the prescribed duties every day with his senses subdued,
he may eat only at night, or eat on alternate days, or even subsist on fruits and roots.
Constantly eating only sacrificial food (haviṣya) for three hundred years,
he [recited] sixteen lakhs of the glorious eight-syllabled mantra.
Having kindled the fire according to the rules, one should offer sixteen thousand oblations of sacrificial cakes soaked in ghee; thereafter, for the preceptor and others... [16]
The wise man should offer his entire possessions, including the earth crowded with cattle,
along with twelve calves accompanied by abundant milk.
And having also given a pair of earrings, along with a necklace and a head-ornament, he satisfied the preceptor’s beloved wife and sons with various objects.
Afterwards, one should feed more than a hundred Brahmins along with married women;
having performed the *puraścaraṇa* in this manner according to the prescribed rule, one does not suffer from hunger.
One who practices the procedure of the glorious eight-syllabled mantra attains perfection immediately;
having mastered the glorious eight-syllabled mantra, one becomes established in the state of perfection.
At that very moment, he beheld the Blessed One directly with his own eyes—
He who is worshipped by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and the other gods, and who is the very essence of austerity.
One will certainly behold Nārāyaṇa, who is established in the method free from duality, endowed with the splendor of the Goddess of Fortune, and whose form is the Supreme Brahman. 22.
The complete fulfillment of one's heart's desires, which is difficult even for the gods to attain, certainly comes to pass;
of this there is no doubt—for one who is honored in this year.
Furthermore, he certainly becomes filled with a portion of the Blessed One;
O God, [this is achieved] through recitation, fire-offerings, gifts, vows, and the worship of the twice-born.
Without the performance of the *puraścaraṇa* rite, [the mantra] will not become fruitful;
therefore, the *puraścaraṇa* must necessarily be performed with devotion. (25)
Success is not achieved otherwise, even by hundreds of millions of *japa*s;
thus has the great *mahāpuracaryā* been fully described by me. (26)
If performed according to the prescribed ritual, the accomplishment of knowledge (vidyāsiddhi) will necessarily occur,
even if the rite is performed without exertion and with the utmost secrecy.
I shall proclaim [this], O protector of the earth; be attentive.
In the month of Vaiśākha, during the bright fortnight, there is the day known as Akṣaya.
Jupiter is conjoined with the constellation Bhṛguvāsa (Śravaṇā) and Mercury is conjoined with Prajāpatya (Rohiṇī);
Jupiter is situated in the sign of Leo while the Sun has entered the sign of Aries.
This union of Lakṣmī and Bhavānī is difficult for all embodied beings to attain;
O King, this yoga is obtained in six years and not otherwise.
Indeed, they say that this very half-day of the Tretā Yuga brings about inexhaustible joy for all the ancestors as well.
There, Gaurī was born from Himācala through Enakā;
on that very day, an auspicious Thursday, she was established by Bhṛguvāra.
Born from the wife of Bhṛgu when she was gratified by his ascetic penance,
on this very day, while Rohiṇī was in conjunction with the moon, the all-pervading Lord [appeared].
At the end of the Dvāpara age, the Lord of Śrī appeared as Balarāma and Kṛṣṇa; moreover, being satisfied by the power of Dharma, He became the protector of the earth.
Born from a portion of Dākṣāyaṇī, I am Nārāyaṇa by name;
[this occurred] when the moon was in conjunction with the lunar mansion of Prajāpati (Rohiṇī) and on the day of Bhṛgu (Saturday). || 35 ||

O King, on this day in the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha, while Jupiter was situated in the constellation Rohiṇī (Prājāpatya), and the Moon and Sun were in the sign of Aries, I ascended [the mountain]. || 36 ||
O King, for the welfare of the entire world and for the establishment of Dharma— not for the sake of personal success— I was born from Dharma through penance, in the womb of Dakṣāyaṇī.
On this very day, under the constellation Rohiṇī on a Friday, the soul of the universe appeared, a sage named Nārāyaṇa. (38)
On this very day, Hari himself, the Lord, will bestow the earth upon him;
moreover, on this same day, the Moon-crested Lord [Śiva] will be with Rohiṇī.
He married the daughter of Himavat according to the prescribed rites;
therefore, this third [tithi] named Akṣaya bestows all perfections.
The daily course of practice has been declared to bestow inexhaustible and desired success;
therefore, a yoga endowed with these qualities is called *alakṣya-yoga* (the unperceivable yoga). || 41 ||
This third lunar day, known as Akṣaya, is said to be most exalted;
it becomes even more so if it occurs here in conjunction with the Rohiṇī asterism and the movement of Venus.
This yoga, known by the name Śrīgaurīyoga, bestows all perfections;
it occurs when the Moon is situated in Rīhiṇī (Mṛgaśīrṣa) and the Sun has entered the sign of Leo.
The Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa sacrifice and the Bhavānī-Śaṅkara sacrifice—
this third great festival is called Akṣaya and is proclaimed by Agni.
Beginning from the bright fortnight of the full moon of Kārttika, the leaders of the immortals, the sages, and the hosts of Siddhas worship me every day. (45)
On this day, which lasts for two days,
the gods, having attained the state of immortality, go to the third heaven while dwelling upon the earth.
Whatever is offered in sacrifice or recited on this day bestows imperishable success;
by my grace, it indeed becomes eternal on that very day.
The Badarī is not situated in the middle; I am Nārāyaṇa in various forms.
The hermitage named Nārāyaṇa does not liberate one whose mind is not fixed upon Him.
On this day in this hermitage, [he saw] the powerful son of Dharma,
the son of Dakṣāyaṇī, the sage Nārāyaṇa, who is celebrated as Nārada.
Seeing me alone as the Lord of the World, accompanied by Nara,
[one is freed] even from the most terrible multitudes of sins accumulated over ten million births.
Liberated even from all mixtures of worldly existence, he shall manifest his own true nature at the end of the body;
therefore, on this inexhaustible day, let the aforementioned yoga be practiced.
"O King, this yoga is obtained only once in sixty years; it has now arrived on this day known as Kṣaya, a conjunction so difficult to attain. (52)
Having risen early in the morning and having respectfully saluted the teacher, he then performed his nocturnal duties with the teacher's permission.
Together with the fifteen nyāsas, one should conquer the glorious eight-syllabled mantra;
[one should likewise conquer] one hundred portions of any other glorious mantra, numbering one thousand three hundred.
Having performed the preliminary rites, he should offer oblations into the fire—
either with sacrificial twigs or with leaves smeared with ghee— while reciting the glorious eight-syllable mantra.
Or, O King, having offered three hundred oblations of clarified butter with any one of the Śrī-mantras, or even with a non-material substance, he should offer the ghee twelve times.
Having recited the Raśmi mantra once, and being free from the need for expiatory oblations (prāyaścitta),
[one should worship] with blue lotuses, bilva leaves, or karavīra flowers.

Having first performed the worship of the limbs and the surrounding deities (aṅgāvaraṇa), one who is firm in his vows should then worship three hundred [times] while reciting the hand-mantra (hastavidyā).
O Lord of Men, even though it has been previously taught by the Teacher, the *Raśmimālā* must be studied by the disciple who is self-restrained and has bathed. (59)
Furthermore, all the ritual placements (nyāsa) must be performed with great effort;
on this very day, the auspicious and glorious eight-syllabled mantra must certainly be recited.
Then, it was taught once more from the lotus-mouth of his own teacher:
"It should be studied with great effort, preceded by all the ritual depositions (nyāsa)."
O King, having again obtained a thousand gold coins from Nārāyaṇī,
he then, endowed with fortitude and gravity, approached the lotus feet of his preceptor.
One should give one's entire property as the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), or half of it, or even less than that; or at least enough for a year's sustenance, or whatever wealth one possesses. || 63 ||
A pair of beautiful earrings, made of gold and set with jewels, must certainly be given to the ears of the preceptor.
One should give a single Śālagrāma stone accompanied by a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), and one should also give a pair of yellow garments, or a conch, or a golden image.
Then, for those who are deluded regarding the loss of their prosperity, one should also perform the gift of modesty (hrī-dāna);
furthermore, five fruits along with a vehicle must necessarily be given to the preceptor.
Or else, for the sake of accomplishing the rite, one should bring three jackfruit trees;
provided that there are other lands rich in wealth where such fruit-bearing trees are seen. (66)
One should present heaps of pearls and gems,
heaps of wealth, heaps of grain, as well as horses, palanquins, and the like for those who have departed.
One who offers [the merit] for the sake of the Lord’s temple is greatly honored;
therefore, one should perform every day whatever was done on this very day.
O you of vast intellect, let the two earrings certainly remain with the god;
or else, let them surely bring about the fulfillment of the journey for him who is afflicted by the wheel.
Even a single Śālagrāma stone, accompanied by a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), must be offered;
the wise must necessarily give wealth equal to ten years' worth of food.
Then, for the Sun, the fee (dakṣiṇā) given by one who is poor and destitute of wealth should be twelve niṣkas, or six niṣkas, or three niṣkas.
Having adorned [the deity] with garments, perfumes, flowers, unbroken rice, and other offerings,
it must certainly be done by practitioners, even if they are enemies of their preceptor.
Seeking inexhaustible perfection, for the sake of wealth, the embodiment of prosperity, and inexhaustible abundance consisting of sons, grandsons, and so forth, [one should worship]. (73)

By performing it in this manner on the third lunar day known as Akṣayā, those who recite the venerable eight-syllabled mantra shall attain the accomplishment of the inexhaustible throughout their entire lives.
It is difficult even for the gods and others to attain; there is no doubt about this.
Having received the embrace of the teacher, he was honored by his blessings.
Having honored the teacher’s wife especially on the Akṣaya day,
one should feed excellent Brahmins, aged women, and eight well-dressed young women.
Having drunk the auspicious water used for washing the lotus-feet of the teacher’s feet,
and having attained the fulfillment of one's purpose, one should eat together with one's kinsmen.
On this auspicious Akṣayā-tṛtīyā,
having abandoned deceit and guile, one who is pure should perform this purificatory rite (puraścaryā) according to the prescribed injunctions.
The fruit that one obtains by performing more than a hundred such great *puraścaryā*s, which were previously consumed by me, [is attained here]. (79)
One necessarily attains that fruit with all its constituent parts; there is no doubt in this matter.
Thus has been declared the fruit resulting from the yoga of the true nature of Śrī and Cit.

We have come to Sarasvatī, the mother of the sacrifice, to the ancient Vaikuṇṭha abode, during the bright fortnight of the month of Vaiśākha; on the third day of the sun’s station in Aries, while the son of Bhṛgu was present, and while the God of gods remained with his attendants in the abode of Viriñci.
They describe the union of Gaurī and Ramā as the "excellent passion," and they call the conjunction of Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa "the yoga.
They declare the one named Umā-Maheśa to be the same; indeed, she who was born from Mātrā is present right there in the sphere of Gaurī.

The Lord of the World, Nārāyaṇa, endowed with the three strides (trivikrama), was born upon the earth as the husband of Dharma and son of the daughter of Dakṣaprajāpati; thus they call him Takṣīpati. || 83 ||
O lotus-eyed one, having performed the nyāsa of my eight-syllable mantra along with all the other nyāsas,
and having offered oblations into the fire consecrated according to the rules, you may then meditate upon the garland of rays as desired.
Having received the eight-syllable mantra together with the various nyāsas from the lotus-mouth of the teacher,
he again took [the teacher’s] pair of feet and gave all his wealth and jewels to that pair of feet.
Then, one should give a beautiful pair of garments for the two sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) and feed the Brāhmaṇas;
having offered the three fruits and five jackfruits at the lotus-feet of the noble Preceptor, [one should proceed].
Prosperity endowed with the abundance of creepers, imperishable jewels, horses, livestock, and grain;
the increase of sons, all enjoyments, long life, and moreover, great and inexhaustible fortune. || 87 ||
This [merit] proceeds inexhaustibly for ten million generations of the father's and mother's families. || 88 ||
Having performed this for Sarasvatī with the *purātyokta* [mantra] and with wealth and splendor, one attains great perfection (*siddhi*) within a single day. (89)
How much more so, then, can the fruit when combined with yoga not be described? Through this king of yogas, an equal [attainment] is obtained; it is not otherwise.
One who desires inexhaustible accomplishment should not spend his days in vain; O King, listen as I describe the supreme preliminary practice (puraścaryā) for you. 91.
By performing which one attains supreme perfection in the glorious eight-syllable mantra,
whether during a solar eclipse or on a lunar day.
Once, on the fifth day prior to that [eclipse],
Mitāhīra went with his retinue to the river Sāgaṇī at the time of the commencement of the eclipse.
Having bathed and formed a mental resolve while duly uttering the names beginning with Keśava,
he who has bathed becomes endowed with the merit of the auspicious *avabhṛtha* (concluding) bath.
One should drink the water used for washing the lotus-feet of the teacher;
indeed, one shall immediately become liberated from all internal wanderings.
Then, starting from the time of touching [the image], he should duly offer oblations into the fire consecrated according to the rules, using black sesame seeds mixed with clarified butter. || 96 ||
Even there, one should perform the vow without the day of Bhārgava (Venus);
having remembered [the deity], one should offer an oblation to Brahmā and Ārya for the duration of a single *dhanāḍikā*.
One should bestow upon a worthy recipient land abounding in many crops, provided with four bulls, and equipped with means of irrigation. || 98 ||
For one who has performed the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), this is indeed the prescribed wealth;
then he should offer twelve niṣkas or twenty-six.
One should offer a single Śālagrāma stone to the preceptor,
along with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) of one niṣka, or three niṣkas.
One who is poor and unfortunate, having thus begged for alms, should offer them;
he who gives when the Sun or even the Moon is eclipsed [attains great merit]. || 1 ||
Until the moon and sun cease to exist, there shall be no doubt regarding that inexhaustible state;
for by giving nectar during an eclipse, one attains the great earth consisting of the island of truth.

Whatever fruit one obtains by giving that [other gift], that same fruit is declared to be obtained by giving a single Śālagrāma stone along with the previously mentioned sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). || 3 ||
I have heard that the fruit of giving ten million cosmic eggs (Brahmāṇḍas) is unsurpassed;
as are wealth, grain, garments, ornaments, earrings, and so forth.
And by presenting jars of curd, honey, and ghee to those learned in the Vedas (śrotriya),
she shall obtain the ultimate and great accomplishment of all her desires.
O twice-born ones, they say that this [gift] is equal to the Jahnavī (Ganges),
and that the gift of gold as vast as Mount Meru is equal to both on the occasion of the solar and lunar eclipses.

Gold is the first thing to be given away; likewise cows, and the cows that are the daughters of the Sun (the rays). He who gives these becomes the possessor of all the worlds; he who would give gold and cows attains the highest state.
Through the grace of the teacher, the auspicious and glorious eight-syllabled mantra immediately bestows the great siddhi that is difficult even for the gods to attain.
The Lord, the Beloved of Indirā, becomes fully gratified with him.
When the One whose mind is fixed on the Lotus (Lakṣmī) is pleased, what could there be that is unattainable for him?
For the sake of success, one should always be diligent in the practice of mantras.
Whenever the accomplishment of this eight-syllabled great vidyā occurs for anyone, then indeed auspicious and excellent blessings come to pass for him.
Longevity, health, undecaying fortune, the increase of sons, inexhaustible happiness,
all branches of knowledge, and divine enjoyments— one attains these, as well as me, the Blessed Lady, at the end.

In ancient times, great-souled sages, devoted to the eight-syllable mantra, attained perfection along with their disciples; they reached the state of identity with Brahman and the supreme glory that possesses all auspicious qualities.
Having offered oblations with clarified butter during solar and lunar eclipses, and having given wealth along with a pair of sandals to a virtuous preceptor,
he beholds Nārāyaṇa with his own eyes, as well as divine garments and grain.
Having seen the green [field], he, accompanied by his kinsmen, purifies even those who are peaceful and well-settled;
having come from the families of his father and mother, he goes to the supreme state, not remaining here.
[Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, the Compendium of the Meaning of the Vedas, in the glorious *Anuttarabrahmatattvarahasya*, the *Dāśarathīya Tantra*.]
The Blessed Lord said:
Once again, I shall fully proclaim the means for the accomplishment of the eight-syllable mantra,
by hearing which the wise father shall not enter the ocean of ignorance.
The third lunar day of the month of Vaiśākha, known as Akṣaya,
when joined with the previously mentioned sacrifice, bestows all spiritual accomplishments.
Now, I shall describe another method that instantly bestows great intelligence;
it is most secret, so listen with an attentive mind. || 3 ||
Having risen early in the morning and bathed well, he should bow to his own preceptor as the Lord; then, while the five musical instruments resound, he should bow to Gaṇanāyaka at the beginning.
Having adorned the noble teacher with gold, jewels, garments,
and ornaments, one should bow to him again like a staff.
Having offered my pair of hands at the feet of the venerable teacher,
O illustrious Ācārya, O omniscient one, [I take refuge in you] for as long as I live, O Great One.
O treasury of the senses, with my life-breaths, wealth, intellect, and speech, I perform worship at your feet; O Lord, I do not commit any transgression against your command.
In this matter, the Lord of Lakṣmī is my witness; in that very place, O Omniscient One, Your two feet are my refuge; I have no other goal at any time.
May I take refuge again and again in your very pair of feet; both father and mother are fearful, for you alone are my deity.
"Make me eternally free from this ocean of worldly existence which is difficult to cross";
having thus entreated the Teacher, one who has made such a request is exalted.
If the practitioner has previously received all the nyāsas as desired from the mouth of a teacher, he should grasp them as if they were nectar. || 14 ||
Then, once again, he was instructed by the lotus-like mouth of his own preceptor in that queen of the seven sciences, which bestows all perfections.
O Lord of the Earth, [he] receives the glorious eight-syllabled lore (vidyā), as well as initiation consisting of mantra and comprising all ritual placements (nyāsa). || 16 ||
Having attained [this], one should contemplate oneself, thinking, "I have accomplished all that was to be done.
O Dhruva, one should meditate on Vidyā, who is self-luminous, as she is departing.
Once [the teacher] has arrived, the disciple, endowed with the thought "I am blessed," should meditate upon his own body,
wealth, and life-breaths at the two feet of his own teacher.
Having offered [the gift], he should reflect, "I have accomplished my purpose; I am established in righteousness.
On the Akṣayā Tṛtīyā, the initiate should perform two auspicious rites here.
Having taken it, he would remain with his purpose accomplished for as long as he lives; there is no doubt that the Blessed One will certainly not be distressed by him on account of that. (20)
Having received these two unsurpassed initiations through the grace of the teacher,
one should then establish the petitioner in the presence of the teacher.
One should diligently perform more than a hundred, up to a thousand, oblations with pieces of sugarcane smeared with cow's ghee, using the eight-syllable vidyā.
Alternatively, one should offer oblations with clarified butter using the Śuddha-gati mantra,
or one may recite any other mantra one hundred and eight times.
Then one should perform the *haumam* rite three times with the *Raśmimantra*s in sequence;
thereafter, having offered oblations with the *Jayā* and other mantras, one should offer the *Ājyāhuti*s according to the prescribed rule.
With blue lotuses, red lotuses, bilva leaves, or basil;
or even with jasmine flowers, or likewise with *nandyāvarta* flowers. (25)
Having first performed the worship of the limbs and the surrounding deities with self-restraint, one should indeed worship Śrī-Śrīyati while reciting the secret Brahma-vidyā. || 26 ||
Three hundred, two hundred, or even one hundred and eight [times], then,
having first prostrated before the teacher with folded palms— || 27 ||
Having first offered either a pair of fine *dukūla* cloths or a fine cotton garment, and having adorned the preceptor, [one should then adorn] those who follow.
Taking five fruits, or else three vehicles,
one should make a single hole in the middle fruit and insert a silver rod.
Or else, a bronze vessel weighing two palas,
or even one's entire wealth— including jewels, medicinal herbs, and riches— situated within the temple.
In the presence of the *saṃsthāpaka*, one should place a small amount of food there;
having placed a fruit upon it, one should also insert a hole into its center.

For the pleasure of Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa, for the attainment of fullness in existence, for the onset of compassion, for the perfection of the knowledge of your form, and for the accomplishment of the King of Mantras. (32)
Desiring to cross the ocean of existence, I offer these things;
may success be yours, O Master, through the outpouring of your non-dual compassion. (33)
Having recited these two mantras, one should offer all things— including wealth, grain, and livestock— into the lotus feet of one’s own preceptor.

One who desires the attainment of the imperishable in the third [chapter] on the imperishable should give away one's entire possessions as the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), or half of that, or even a quarter of that. || 35 ||
Alternatively, one should respectfully offer wealth equal to a year's worth of food,
or else a pair of earrings fashioned from that same gold.
O King, having bestowed upon the pair of the teacher’s ears the power of subjugation, [he gave] twenty-one gold coins, fine cloth accompanied by a pair [of garments]. (37)
Having deposited [the seed-syllables] joined with the five fruits in the center of this [mandala],
and having offered them into the great fire, he shall attain imperishable accomplishment.
If one is unfortunate and poor, even after begging for all [the required wealth],
one should diligently offer six niṣkas, or otherwise three niṣkas.
O King, on the third day of the bright fortnight, having given a pair of earrings to the preceptor and the two officiating priests, he became equal to Mahendra in splendor.
Having rescued his father, grandfather, and maternal grandfathers by the hundreds who were submerged in the floods of hell, he is glorified.
On the third lunar day of the month of Akṣaya, one who gives wealth equal to a year's worth of food attains the eternal state of Nārāyaṇa immediately. || 42 ||
By giving wealth measured by one hundred billion to the preceptor, and having given it, whatever fruit one obtains—that fruit is proclaimed [to be equal]. || 43 ||
Having given a pair of earrings and twelve gold coins (niṣkas) as wealth,
and having offered five fruits to the lotus feet of the Preceptor (Ācārya), [he should proceed].
The fruit of giving a hundred gold coins on the Akṣaya Tṛtīyā is said to be unsurpassed; likewise for the gift of excellent yellow sandalwood. 45.
Or by giving forty apalas, or even twenty fruits,
one shall dwell at the feet of the Blessed One in the corner of the Kalpadruma grove.
On the third day known as Akṣayā, having respectfully given to the Brahmins food such as vegetables, soup, and the like, or even rice accompanied by curd; || 47 ||
One who bestows even a small portion of this upon one who is liberated attains here a splendor that is desired yet difficult to obtain;
of this there is no doubt. This is the truth, the absolute truth, which I declare.
This great preliminary rite (puraścaryā), complete with its ancillaries (sāṅga) and preceded by the preparatory rites (apūrva), has been described by me;
performing it one hundred and more times at Akṣayā leads to imperishable results.
When this procedure has been performed in this manner, there is no doubt here;
[one receives] a full hundred plus one horse-sacrifices as a boon and sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
Therefore, there is no doubt that the merit of a thousand Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifices has been obtained here;
on this birthday, may you become one who desires to cross the ocean of worldly existence.
One certainly attains the great accomplishment of the glorious eight-syllable mantra;
here, there shall be imperishable success for all one's heart's desires. (52)
Therefore, this [work] has been respectfully proclaimed as "Manorathatṛtīya" (The Third Fulfiller of Desires).
Furthermore, the state of being Dakṣiṇāmūrti has been sung here by Āpastaṃba;
and it has also been sung again by Śeṣa—all of this shall be explained here.

The hosts of sages and Siddhas of great power, as well as the Brahmarṣis and Maharṣis, arrived at Vaiśākha with the desire to dwell there, by means of the sacrificial oblation accompanied by the mantra that invokes Nārāyaṇa.
Having stolen a thousand desired clusters of jewels and offered them at the pair of his guru’s feet,
he fashioned for the pair of his guru’s ears two earrings made of refined gold, joined with gems and pearls.
Having given [this], they have fulfilled their purpose and, together with hundreds of lineages of fathers and mothers, have gone to the divine realm;
moreover, having attained supreme perfection here, they shall obtain those portions that are otherwise difficult to attain.
Those who delight in serving the pair of lotus feet of the Guru and are devoted to the eight-syllable mantra,
should with reverence perform this vow spoken by Nārāyaṇa on the fourteenth day of the waning moon in the month of Vaiśākha.
Even those who are poor, having made Nārāyaṇa—the sovereign deity of all—into their refuge, behold him directly mounted upon Garuḍa;
they shall have their purpose accomplished and attain infinite enjoyments.

Having uprooted the thicket of evil from the hells of their father and mother, they attain the splendor of the jewel of wisdom; having ascended to the very summit of the lotus, they proceed to the state of perfection—of this there is no doubt.
Whatever was taken away by birth and whatever was given by the couple in this world shall come to an end on this day;
for on this day of destruction, the eight-syllable *homakala* is distinguished above all the Purāṇas.

The Lord of Lakṣmī, the sovereign of the gods, Nārāyaṇa, the abode of the omniscient ones—when the ritual of the eight-syllable oblation has been performed in this manner, the Lord of the three worlds becomes pleased with him. (61)
When the sole Lord of the universe is present in person, what desired object could there be that is not attainable for him?
For him, there is no exhaustion from the Rājasūya, nor the Vājapeya, nor even the Gosava sacrifice. || 62 ||
Neither the eight-syllable mantra nor the oblation is equal to [the merit of this], nor is the gift of a thousand cows;
for one who is devoted to the oblation of the eight-syllable mantra on this very day known as the Vaiśākha-secana, there is indeed no decay. (63)

The two Nārāyaṇas, the sovereign of the gods, the two Rudras, Brahmā, the lords of the faces of Dakṣa, Indra and the others together with the guardians of the quarters, all the Siddhas, the Sādhyas, and all the Maruts; 64.

The Brahman-sages, headed by Kauśika, Karṇa, and Ādya, as well as those endowed with yoga such as Datta and Kumāra, and Gaurī, Amāvāsya, Śakti, and Cañcat— these four, being pleased, become bestowers of boons.

In this [place], one should worship the teacher’s wife with most excellent ornaments and offerings, and likewise with perfumes, sandalwood, and various kinds of food—both solid and soft—as well as alms. (66)
When this has been done, that blessed one, through the grace of the Lord, becomes fulfilled and worthy of the praise of sages;
he shall certainly attain all his desires and behold Nārāyaṇa as if with his very eyes.
Thus, O former lord of the earth, even that which was sung by the three Śeṣas should be performed in this manner on the third day of the bright fortnight for the sake of attaining success. (68)

O King, for one who practices the glorious eight-syllable mantra, there will be imperishable success; of this there is no doubt. Furthermore, the grace of the Lord of Śrī shall also become inexhaustible.
That which is given even to the lotus-feet of the preceptor shall become inexhaustible;
and that which is given in the presence of the Blessed One at the end [of life] shall result in an inexhaustible birth as a charioteer (ratha).
I shall once again describe another method of practice, which is highly esteemed for the performance of the glorious eight-syllabled mantra; listen with a concentrated mind. (71)
When the eleventh day (Ekādaśī) of the bright fortnight occurs in the month of Bhādrapada,
it is joined with the Atigaṇḍa yoga, or otherwise with a [favorable] conjunction for the performance of rites.
When joined with a Vaiṣṇava asterism and combined with Monday, or with Wednesday, or even on the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī). || 73 ||
When the sun was situated in Leo, the king of yogins named Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa was born,
possessing the splendor of a hundred rising suns.
On the third lunar day known as Akṣayā, the union with Māhī is proclaimed;
that union with Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa is said to be equal to it indeed.
Whatever is chanted, offered in sacrifice, or given here bestows the fruit of inexhaustible success;
O Lord of the Earth, this [land] is obtained on earth after twelve years. 76.
Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa is directly present as the bestower of all perfections upon his devotees;
he grants inexhaustible satisfaction to those who perform recitation, fire-offerings, and other such rites.
Whether it be a thousand horse-sacrifices, or a hundred Rājasūya sacrifices,
or a thousand great gifts, or even tens of millions of sacrifices.
Through the Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa yoga, which is equal to the Aṇu-dāna, this unsurpassed Nāma-yoga—the best of all yogas—is attained. 79.
Having bathed according to the ninefold rite at the confluence known as Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa, which is difficult to attain, he [honored] the gods, sages, and even the ancestors.
Having offered libations, one should enter the delightful sacrificial hall;
thereafter, one should bow to the pair of lotus-feet of the preceptor.
Having worshipped the Lord, the Master of Brahmā, and performed the *puṇyāhavācana* rite,
[he recited] one thousand three hundred [verses] together with the *samasanyāsa*.
Having recited the glorious eight-syllabled mantra of Śrī, or then the twelve-syllabled one of Śrī, or the six-syllabled vidyā of Sāmrājyalakṣmī, or [the other] six-syllabled mantra of Śrī; || 83 ||
Or one should zealously recite the eight-syllable mantra there; according to one's inclination, one may conquer the Vidyā with tender sprouts of *sulasī*.
Or one should worship with bilva leaves accompanied by ketakī flowers;
thereafter, one should worship Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa three hundred times with the Brahmavidyā mantra.
Having first performed the worship of the deity along with the limbs and the protective enclosures, being firm in his vows,
he [should offer oblations] in the fire duly consecrated according to the rules, using sesame seeds soaked in cow's ghee.
One should offer three hundred oblations into the fire with the eight-syllable Vidyā,
and having respectfully offered one hundred and eight [oblations] of clarified butter with the Śrī-mantra.
Then, one should offer clarified butter three times with the *raśmimantra* mantras of the Blessed One;
having performed the expiatory oblations, one should then offer the *brahmārpaṇa* oblation.

Having respectfully placed a pair of earrings, fashioned by the divine craftsman Viśvakarman and wrought with the finest gold, upon the ears of the Teacher, which were themselves produced from the passion of Brahmā; (89)
Then, having performed the ritual duties and honored him with ornaments such as rings,
he offered a pair of fine garments and an auspicious Śālagrāma stone.
Then, having requested the Saṃhitā along with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) equal to a year’s worth of food,
one should also offer sesame seeds many times over.
A wise person should accept four dronas of the left-over [grain],
or half of that, and store it for a short time.
The gift of cows and the gift of sesame seeds, when performed continuously during auspicious rites, or even if accepted only once, shall never incur the fault of a sin. 93.

In the case of intense and unwholesome actions, such as accepting a heap of sesame seeds or even twelve great loads of salt, it is necessary to offer lotuses at the feet of the preceptor; the cessation of that [transgression] is now described.
By giving away half of the wealth one has acquired, along with one's sons and wife, and by bestowing it upon another, one may be liberated from sins. || 95 ||
In the absence of wealth sufficient for a year's sustenance, twelve niṣkas—or whatever wealth is necessary—must be given to the lotus-feet of the Preceptor. 96.
One should give a single cow along with its calf, accompanied by a fixed sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā); or one may give whatever substance serves as a substitute for the cow, together with a fee.
One should give the gift of the ground for the recollection of dissolution; then another gift, known by the name Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa, in this yoga which destroys all enemies. 98.
Whatever one performs, all that shall undoubtedly become infinite;
thereafter, one should feed the Brāhmaṇas and also feed the married women.
Thereafter, with the permission of his preceptor, he himself, restrained in speech, partook of food;
[he meditated upon] the glorious eight-syllabled mantra (aṣṭākṣara-manu) of Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of Yoga.
Having thus recited [the mantra], performed the fire-oblation, and given the fee to the preceptor,
one will certainly attain the accomplishment of the glorious eight-syllabled [mantra], even on this very earth.
By resorting to Dullemādevī, one attains an imperishable state that is brought under control;
there is no doubt about this—this is the truth, so do not hesitate.
The great *Tīrthacintāmaṇi* with its twelve auxiliary sections was previously described by me; it has been composed in that same manner, of this there is no doubt. (3)
In the Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa yoga, by performing a single Āpyāhuti with sesame seeds soaked in cow’s ghee,
one obtains the fruit of a Lakṣmī-homa.
In the Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa sacrifice, having given a single auspicious Sālagrāma stone as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā),
he obtained the merit of giving ten million cosmic eggs (brahmāṇḍas).
There is no doubt that in this yoga of Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa, there exists the fruit of many [merits], whether it be a pure silver coin or auspicious gold.
By giving a piece of land equal to Mount Meru, one enjoys the fruit of that gift;
likewise, by the gift of a pair of earrings upon the two ears of the preceptor.
He who performs even a thousand recitations of the *Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa* enjoys the fruit of giving divine ornaments to the insects.
Whatever fruit one obtains by chanting the glorious eight-syllabled mantra (aṣṭākṣarī-vidyā) a hundred thousand times, that very same fruit is said to be attained [by this]. || 9 ||
Having thus diligently performed the *puraścaraṇa* rite for the union of Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa, he praised the Blessed One without any doubt regarding His name. (111)

Alternatively, he shall praise that Lord who is established in speech yet transcends it, who is worshipped by Brahmā, Rudra, and others, who grants all desires, and who is affectionate toward his devotees.
Then, having begun that residence in the abode [of the Lord], possessing a complete body and freed from the lords of sin, one experiences auspicious things day by day.
Having attained the glory of an unshakable kingdom, which is filled with Dhanya and others,
one attains incomparable prosperity for the lineage, abounding in sons, grandsons, and descendants.
Having obtained all enjoyments, both divine and human,
and having ascended a celestial chariot together with twenty generations of his lineage, he [shall depart].
One attains the supreme, inexhaustible, and eternal state of the Blessed One.
This supreme practice for the sake of accomplishment through the glorious eight-syllable mantra has not been told again during the day; it shall be proclaimed once more. 16.
[Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter in the glorious *Anuttarabrahmatattvarahasya*, the *Daśarathīya Tantra*, which is an essential compendium of the essence of the Vedas.]
The Blessed Lord said: O Lord of the Earth, listen once more as I shall fully explain the glorious eight-syllabled great mantra, which bestows immediate spiritual accomplishment. || 1 ||
The eclipses of the Sun and the Moon are declared to be great destroyers of merit;
regarding those, the procedure for the preliminary rite (*puraścaryā*) of the glorious eight-syllable mantra has been described by me.
Speaking further of the specific details regarding the eclipses of the moon and the sun:
if there is an eclipse of the moon on the full-moon day of the month of Śrāvaṇa, || 3 ||
This great conjunction (yoga) is obtained when it is joined with Monday, associated with the lunar mansion of Viṣṇu (Śravaṇā),
and conjoined with the Vasu asterism (Dhaniṣṭhā).
This [mantra] named Candracūḍāmaṇi is difficult even for the gods to obtain;
it ensures the certain and supreme accomplishment of all secret sciences (vidyās).
Through recitation, fire-offerings, and other rites, it bestows inexhaustible fulfillment of one's desires;
yet, the perfection of the glorious Eight-Syllable Rite cannot be attained [by such means alone].
Taking food only once a day for those three days,
he should bathe in the morning on that day and [worship] the two feet of his own teacher.
Having prostrated before the glorious eight-syllabled mantra accompanied by all the ritual placements (nyāsa),
one who has restrained his senses should recite it one thousand three hundred times.
Having recited one of the Śrī-mantras three hundred times, or at least one hundred times,
one should then recite five times the Bhagavad-raśmi-vidyā-sūkta.
At the time of grasping [the water] and upon touching it, one should bathe and thereafter bow down,
mentally reciting the names beginning with Keśava in silence.
Thus freed from all sins in twenty-four ways,
he then put on two garments and, firm in his vows, performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) three times.
Having drunk the auspicious water produced from washing the lotus-feet of the Teacher, he was liberated even from the fetters of worldly existence, both internal and external.
Having restrained his breath and performed the ritual intention (saṃkalpa) according to rule in the consecrated fire,
he should thereafter offer oblations with black sesame seeds mixed with the appropriate substances.
Or one thousand plus a hundred, or five hundred daily, or even four hundred, by means of the glorious Aṣṭīrṇa-vidyā. (14)
Then, one hundred measures of ghee—the sacrificial substance—should be offered by any of the venerable [officiants] in one, two, or three portions, while reciting the Raśmi mantras. || 15 ||
Having offered the oblations for atonement and performed the oblation dedicated to Brahman,
he respectfully circumambulated and bowed down to Jātavedas (the Fire).
Having prostrated before the pair of lotus-feet of the teacher,
he offered his entire wealth, or whatever riches he possessed, such as food for a year.
Having given a pair of earrings, one should offer twelve niṣkas, or three niṣkas, or even three niṣkas; it should not be offered for less than that.
One who is possessed of deceit does not attain the perfection of knowledge;
therefore, one must certainly offer at least a single *sālagrāma* stone to the guru.
One should offer the Purāṇas, the Dharmaśāstras, and the Vāyustaka; and if one has the means, one should offer a gift of land and a pair of cows.
And one should offer various other gifts at the feet of the Teacher,
even for the sake of attaining the great perfection of the glorious eight-syllable mantra.
He attains it without a doubt; he is glorified immediately. He who possesses the crescent moon as his crest-jewel shall become a lord for thirty years.
By offering even a single oblation of sesame seeds during the yoga of Candrācūḍāmaṇi,
one obtains the unsurpassed fruit of ten million sesame seed oblations.
In the yoga of the Moon-Crested One (Śiva), by making an offering at the feet of the preceptor,
one certainly obtains the fruit of ten million Tulāpuruṣa gifts.
O King, by performing the *puraścaraṇa* rite in this manner for the Moon-crested Lord (Śiva),
one obtains the fruit of a hundred *puraścaraṇas* of the glorious eight-syllabled mantra (*aṣṭākṣarī-vidyā*).
One will certainly attain [the goal] immediately and behold Him who is beyond all measure,
either on that very day or within seven days, or else directly the Lord of Śrī.
Having seen him mounted upon the vehicle of Vinatā, praised by Brahmā and Rudra, and honored day after day in heaven, he would certainly become the recipient of all good fortunes. (27)
Through a portion of the Blessed One, one obtains longevity, prosperity endowed with the eight qualities, long life, health, and the attainment of speech which is otherwise difficult to achieve. (28)
Having attained all enjoyments, both divine and human, he is honored for the incomparable increase of his lineage as long as the moon and sun endure. (29)
Accompanied by a thousand members of his father’s and mother’s lineages,
he ascends an excellent celestial chariot and attains the abode of the Lord.
When the month of Āśvayuja arrives, beginning from the first day of the bright fortnight, it is called Navarātra; it is honored for nine days until its conclusion. || 31 ||
And there, each single day, it becomes equal in radiance to the sun,
and it is offered as an oblation day after day.
The day called Anantakalanda is declared to be the inexhaustible bestower of Brahman and bliss;
that which is called Mahānavamī is likewise [the bestower] of the nine nights for the sake of the Lord.
Stirred by the combined radiance of a thousand moons and suns,
even that which is performed there but once bestows infinite fruit.

If the ninth lunar day is joined with the asterism Bhṛguvāsa (Śravaṇa), the Rasa (Mūla) nakṣatra, and the Daiva muhūrta, and if it occurs on a Sunday, that Navamī is indeed the supreme Vaiṣṇavī Tārakā.
This attainment of imperial sovereignty is difficult to find upon the surface of the earth;
for this jewel among men, honored by the world, stands here in the midst of the year.
This Navarātra vow is highly esteemed by all;
if it is undertaken during the Navarātra preceded by the command of one's own preceptor, [it is most effective]. (37)
Having bathed in the morning, with a purified soul, and having completed his daily obligatory rites,
he should worship the Lord of the Gaṇas and then honor the Ācārya with devotion.
Adorned with ornaments, garments, perfumes, flowers,
and unbroken grains of rice, he whose vows are praiseworthy [should worship] in the presence of the lotus-like feet of his own preceptor.

Having performed prostrations and made the formal resolve (saṃkalpa), he recited the glorious eight-syllabled mantra (aṣṭākṣarī-vidyā) one thousand four hundred times, accompanied by all the ritual placements (nyāsa).
Day after day, remaining silent, one should recite the twelve-syllable Śrī-mantra,
or else the six-syllable mantra of Sāmrājya-lakṣmī.
One should recite the eight-syllabled mantra of Śrī one thousand times,
or four hundred times more than that, or one thousand times every four days.
Or else, one may recite the mantra of Śrī Rājyalakṣmī, or even the six-syllabled Śrī-mantra.
Or else, one should chant the eight-syllabled mantra of Śrī;
or even the procedure for the glorious eight-syllabled mantra, which possesses the splendor of a thousand suns;
or else, during the Navarātra, with Tulasī leaves offered to Kumāra.
Having first performed the worship of the limbs and the feet, one should worship Śrī and Śrīpati three hundred times with flowers and bilva leaves while reciting the Brahmavidyā mantra.
This supreme Ātharvaṇa Mahāsūkta, consisting of one hundred and eight verses and mantras, is named Lakṣmī-udaya.
O King, during the Navarātra, one who desires the increase of progeny should recite [the mantra] with an increment of one;
or else, one should recite forty-five times, or even forty times.
Having arrived on the Mahānavamī day, preceded by the ritual of the left-hand path (vāmācāra),
one should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma) and, having made the formal resolve (saṃkalpa), [offer oblations] into the kindled fire.
One should offer clarified butter one by one with the mantras of the limbs and the coverings;
then, with the glorious eight-syllabled mantra, one thousand three hundred [oblations].
Thereafter, one should offer cow-derived clarified butter with the Āgneya mantra;
then, one should perform the oblation for Śrī using the twelve-syllable mantra combined with the three sweets.

With the eight-syllable mantra of Vākṣmī, or with the six-syllable mantra of Śrī, one performs the oblation; then, for the sake of attaining imperial sovereignty (sāmrājya), one performs more than a thousand oblations for Lakṣmī.
Having offered ghee to the Lord's rays one by one with mantras, and thereafter with the Lakṣmī-hṛdaya mantras in the form of verses; || 51 ||
Having offered a sacrifice for each verse with clarified butter mixed with iron filings,
one should then perform the *jāyādi* oblation and subsequently offer the expiatory oblations (*prāyaścittāhuti*).
Having performed the oblation with the *brahmārpaṇa* mantra and having bowed to the fire,
she then worshipped Śrī Śrīyātī as before with the Brahma-vidyā.
Then the preceptor, having respectfully prostrated with eight limbs before the two Bhojas, should offer them a pair of auspicious, beautiful earrings.
Having adorned it even with ornaments such as beautiful rings and the like, with garments, perfumes, flowers, and so forth, and crowded with a great abundance of various grains; || 55 ||
Having given land the size of a cow's hide or even that which measures a nivartana,
in the presence of the Blessed One, to the high-souled Ācārya, || 56 ||
Indra rained down food, which is remembered as the highest sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā);
the middle dakṣiṇā was fashioned as twelve niṣkas.
Alternatively, it should be weighed daily; the lowest of the low is six niṣkas.
One should certainly offer it with devotion into the lotus-hand of the preceptor, accompanied by a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
A pure Śālagrāma stone endowed with a pure discus, a single bed complete with its furnishings, and accompanied by a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). || 59 ||
One should give to the preceptor at once a cow along with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā),
and the earth should always be given accompanied by four bulls.
Alternatively, one may offer a substance equivalent to the earth before the feet of the Preceptor,
weighing twenty-five niṣkas, or half of that, or even a quarter of that.
One should avoid greed for wealth by offering two niṣkas as a substance equivalent to a bull, or one niṣka of gold. 62.
A single *niṣka* is declared to be the substance that serves as a substitute for a cow;
alternatively, half a *niṣka* may be given, as this price for a cow is highly esteemed.

For the sake of attaining success in the glorious eight-syllable mantra, a wise person should necessarily perform the rites for the Śālagrāma stone and so forth, whether they have been specifically prescribed or not. 64.
By offering even a single oblation with the glorious eight-syllable vidyā on the occasion of Mahānavamī, one obtains the fruit of ten million homas.
Having given on the day of Mahānavamī land equal in extent to a bull’s hide, endowed with abundant crops, he [attains merit] through the gift of Satyadvīpa.
Whatever fruit one attains through other merits,
one experiences that multiplied ten millionfold by performing the auspicious Mahāvaṃśī-prātyāyana rite at Kuṇḍalaka.
Having given millions of divine ornaments, one enjoys the fruit thereof;
whereas what [fruit] would there be for one who casts his parents into tens of millions of hells? (68)
Adorned with divine ornaments, they indeed go to the abode of Viṣṇu on the Mahānavamī day, having honored the auspicious Śāligrāma stone of the Lord.
Having given gifts accompanied by ritual fees (dakṣiṇā) through the offering of the limbs of Brahmā,
the pure-souled one, having attained the fruit thereof, beholds the Blessed One.
When the Mahānavamī has arrived, by giving eight [offerings] and four sets of four,
one obtains the fruit of that garland, of a small amount of gold, or of the gift of a hundred thousand cows.
Having reached that [state], accompanied by a thousand lineages,
he attains the eternal, divine, and imperishable abode of the Blessed One.
On that day, O Lord of the Earth, a wealthy person should perform the Tulāpuruṣa and other principal gifts, as well as land-grants. || 73 ||

Having thus performed the vow with all its ancillaries on that day of Mahānavamī, he completed the preliminary recitation (puraścaraṇa) of one thousand repetitions of the glorious eight-syllabled mantra (aṣṭākṣarī-vidyā).
Having inevitably attained the fruit and being endowed with a portion of the Blessed One, he obtains great fortune, abounding in wealth, jewels, and prosperity. (75)
Bestow long life and health, an abundance of elephants, horses, and chariots, great success in the threefold way, and the power to both restrain and favor others.
Having obtained sons, grandsons, prosperity, and even enjoyments that are very difficult to attain,
one reaches the presence of Hari at the end of the body.
No other vow is known to be equal to the Navarātra vow;
on the tenth day of the Navarātra, there is the attainment of the glorious eight-syllabled mantra.
Such great perfection is not found among those who observe other vows as that which arises from the Navarātra vow through the grace of the Lord of Śrī. (79)
Indeed, such grace from the Blessed One is not obtained through other vows;
rather, it is attained by performing the Navarātra vow with all its ancillaries according to this rite and with devotion. (80)
Having attained the perfection of the glorious eight-syllabled mantra, which is difficult even for the gods to obtain,
you have become one who is worshipped by Brahmā, Rudra, Indra, and the others.
Accompanied by a hundred members of the venerable Vāma-kula, he attains great, eternal, and non-transient perfection. 82.
In the Navarātra vow, which grants the constant accomplishment of all auspicious goals,
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara are pleased by the satisfaction of the preceptor.
They declare that one attains great perfection, even from the foremost of the gods;
indeed, even the guardians of the quarters, beginning with Śakra, perform service for such a person.
The great Siddhas, beginning with Kapila, will undoubtedly become bestowers of boons;
one should observe this Navarātra vow for as long as one lives. (85)
Even when a crisis has arrived and even when one's assets have increased, the best of the twice-born who desires prosperity should perform the Navarātra vow. (86)
O King, for him whose vow is broken even once,
misfortune will undoubtedly arise within that very year.

Desiring the succession of supreme and unsurpassed prosperity, one who possesses a mass of all auspiciousness should perform the Navarātra vow for the sake of attaining the glorious eight-syllable mantra. 88.
For all vidyās indeed, during the auspicious nine-night vow, this great accomplishment has been proclaimed by the knowers of Brahman as the most desired. (89)
This vow of the nine nights is the essence of essences, a secret, most delightful, and auspicious; it is the destroyer of the entire mass of sins in this world. (90)
O Lord of the Earth, when the nine nights of the spring season have arrived,
one should bathe at dawn from the first day (pratipad) onwards, with the permission of the preceptor.
One should recite the auspicious and glorious eight-syllabled mantra, accompanied by all the ritual placements (nyāsa),
for thousands of suns of intentions during the nine nights.
Whoever should recite any one of the glorious mantras a thousand times in water, or should recite it eight thousand times, or indeed five thousand times; || 93 ||
Eating only at night, or eating every other day, or consuming sacrificial food (haviṣya) day after day on the ninth lunar day of the birth of Śrī Rāma, which bestows all perfections; 94.

Having bathed in the morning and become purified, one should [offer] sacrificial oblations in the presence of the preceptor into a fire consecrated according to rule with pieces of sugarcane soaked in ghee. (95)
One should perform a homa of one thousand one hundred oblations with the glorious eight-syllable mantra, using bilva leaves soaked in ghee and honey.
O King, one who is impure should offer oblations with clarified butter mixed with honey and curd,
or else with pure cow's milk alone.
Having offered three hundred oblations of pure ghee with the Śrī-mantra, one should then offer oblations in front with the mantras prescribed for the heart and the enclosure.
After the Śrīhoma, one should offer oblations three times with the Raśmimantra;
then, having performed the Jayāhomas and the Brahmarpaṇāhuti, [the rite is concluded].
Having circumambulated the fire and offered salutations thereafter,
he then respectfully touched the two lotus-feet of the preceptor.
Having paid homage to the noble ones and performed the fire-oblations,
one should place a pure Śālagrāma stone— measured by a year’s worth of food— upon some vessel on the ground.
Having fashioned it from bell-metal or lead with the Śrī-Śrīśa-Brahmavidyā mantra,
[one should worship] with twelve niṣkas of gold or even with wealth.
Having worshipped the glorious Lord of the World with five niṣkas of gold, may the Blessed One— the Lord of Śrī, whose self is Śrī Rāma— be truly pleased.
Born from the womb of Kauśalyā, he continuously attained even the great perfection of the glorious eight-syllable mantra through this very vow.
The venerable Lord Śrībhūtīnādyati, having given me this meat,
[spoke] thus with these two verses regarding the auspicious *sālagrāma* stone.
One should present to the preceptor the aforementioned sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā),
having given a pair of fine garments and the most excellent yellow cloth.
If wealth is available, one should take from one's heart golden ornaments,
such as earrings and other decorations for the Ācārya’s ear.

Having offered [the gift] with the consciousness of the deity, on the following day he should honor the Brahmins; those who have been fed and the women residing in the house should be honored with garments, sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā), and other gifts.
Having satisfied his kinsmen, he ate food with them with great respect;
thus, during the nine nights of Navarātra, he performed the vow with devotion.
On the birthday of Śrī Rāma, the glorious eight-syllable lore (vidyā) certainly bestows the assembly of perfections of the glorious eight-syllable mantra. 10.
Having performed the fire sacrifice according to the prescribed rite, one obtains the fruit of ten million sacrifices;
on the auspicious day of Śrī Rāma’s birth, [one should likewise honor] the Śālagrāma stone. 111.
Having given the aforementioned sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the preceptor along with the practitioner,
he obtains the fruit of giving ten million cosmic eggs (brahmāṇḍas), which is heard of as being absolutely unsurpassed.
By chanting the glorious eight-syllabled mantra even during the Navarātra in the spring, one obtains the fruit of a hundred *puraścaryās*; of this there is no doubt. (13)
Having attained great siddhi both in this world and hereafter, the practitioner will certainly obtain that which is difficult even for the gods to attain through the glorious eight-syllable vidyā.

Then, having obtained a great balance—filled with long-lasting flowers, health, wealth, jewels, and so forth, or else a beautiful balance made of words from Lakṣmī herself—(he weighed his merit). || 15 ||
Together with thousands of members of his lineage, he shall attain the state of the Blessed One, having cast off sons, grandsons, and other human enjoyments that cause delusion.
He rejoices there, of this there is no doubt, honored by hundreds of celestial maidens.
Now I shall describe another distinguished [rite] which bestows the perfection of the festival-parvan.
The glorious eight-syllable vidyā grants success within a single watch (yāma) [of time],
whether it is joined with the new moon day, Sunday, or even with Monday.
If a solar eclipse occurs there, it is known as the *Ravicūḍāmaṇi* conjunction. || 19 ||
This king of yoga is attained in twelve years;
indeed, it is as if it has been recited ten million times, even if done here only once or repeatedly.
In this matter, there is nothing equal to the *koṭi-homa* for one who has committed the sins of killing a cow or a Brahmin;
and having given a lotus made of gold weighing one *niṣka* to the preceptor, [one attains the same merit]. 21.
When the solar festival (raviparvan) has arrived, one obtains the eternal fruit of giving a hundred Merus; that [fruit] lasts for three days in the world of the ancestors.
Furthermore, even if one has recited [the mantra] once while eating sacrificial food (havirbhuj) with a focused mind,
thereafter, at the time of the first contact (sparśa) during a solar eclipse— || 23 ||
Having diligently uttered the twenty-four names beginning with Keśava and having praised him with words of praise and salutation, he was immediately liberated from fear.
Having drunk the water from the feet of the Guru three times, with a purified mind, and having established the fire according to the rules in the absence of the preceptor; || 25 ||
Then, having been uplifted by the mantras arising from the Jayā and Bṛhadāvaraṇa hymns,
he performed the *trimadhu-satīrti* oblations with goat's ghee.
Having performed the oblation with sesame seeds smeared with ghee at the time of liberation with due care,
one should offer one hundred and eight oblations with the Śrī-mantra.
Having offered clarified butter once with the Bhagavadraśmi mantras,
having performed the expiatory oblations, and having made the oblation of dedication to Brahman (brahmārpaṇa), || 28 ||
Having bowed with devotion to the pair of the Teacher’s feet with all eight limbs prostrate,
and having offered a thousand gold coins of fine gold and delicate workmanship for women, [he spoke].
He should give the *Sasyaudya-saṃhitā* along with a cow as the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*),
or else he may give it to the venerable Guru after providing him with ornaments according to his capacity.
The materials for the annual meal may consist of one *niṣka* of gold,
or even five *niṣkas* of gold, or three *niṣkas* of gold.
Free from stinginess regarding wealth, he must certainly offer it to his guru; thereafter, he should bestow these ten gifts upon those learned in the Vedas (śrotriya).
Being thus devoted, he should worship the two lotus-feet of the true guru with wealth such as three *niṣkas* or even as much as his own body can endure.
Those of the twice-born classes should be avoided, but even married women (suvāsinīs) may be fed in five ways;
having thus performed the rite with devotion and according to the rules during an eclipse, one attains the complete fruit.
O Sage, that which was previously described by me as the great *puraścaryā* for the venerable eight-syllabled Vidyā is even greater than that supreme one. (35)
One necessarily attains success that is difficult even for the gods to obtain;
endowed with long life and health, one becomes like Kubera in prosperity and wealth. (36)
O Lord of the Earth, having attained an increase of lineage that lasts for a kalpa, he shall be equal to Vācaspati and endowed with all branches of knowledge.
Having enjoyed delightful human and divine pleasures,
he shall lead a thousand generations of his lineage to the highest state and dwell happily with Viṣṇu.
Even upon the occurrence of a solar or lunar eclipse, there is no impurity (sūtaka) during the period from the first touch until the release; one should remain attentive and pure throughout.
Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter in the *Śrīmadanuttarabrahmātattvarahasya*, the *Dāśarathīya Tantra*, which is a compendium of the meaning of the Vedas.
The Blessed Lord further declared another [mantra], the most excellent among the glorious eight-syllabled lords:
"O moving beings, those whose minds are concentrated shall not [attain it] in a single day."
That which was previously mentioned as the third [state], known by the name Abhakṣya (the non-eating),
when combined with Yoga as described before, is difficult to attain even for the gods.
I shall again proclaim for you the supreme means for immediate accomplishment regarding the illustrious Aṣṭāṣṭākṣarī-vidyā, which is especially conducive to prosperity.
O King, it was on the third day of the waning moon when I was born;
there, the threefold Veda appeared from Bhrigu through Kāmalā, by means of his fame.
Where Girijā, the mother of the world and beloved of Śaṅkara, was born;
where this Blessed One, Cyuta, [met] his beloved Īśvarī.
Where even the non-intoxicating [liquor] is seized by Gaurī as something auspicious,
there one should take up the glorious eight-syllable mantra of the third vowel (Ī).

Having respectfully remembered the glorious eight-syllabled mantra along with all the ritual placements (nyāsa) three hundred times, the accomplishment of the mantra will certainly and surely come to pass.
The Mahāyoga is said to have passed away; it is remembered as the best of all yogas.
The new moon and the full moon are likewise remembered as twelvefold.
They know that transit of the sun [occurring] on a Sunday is equal to twelve [transits];
if the transit occurs on a Sunday, it is considered equal to twelve.
That day is declared equal to twelve [other days], and it is remembered as the day of Bhārgava;
its rising is known to bring the splendor of union, equal to that of the Moon-crested Lord (Śiva).
That conjunction known as Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa occurs twelve times;
it takes place on the third lunar day of the bright fortnight in the month of Vaiśākha, which is designated as "Akṣaya" (indestructible).
From that, the auspicious water of great siddhi is obtainable by the thousands;
on this third day, which leads to the imperishable, the three auspicious yogas have been released.
Otherwise, the earth is obtained [as a reward] after sixty years;
however, on the Akṣaya Tṛtīyā, it is attained immediately if the conjunction (yoga) occurs.
For indeed, the accomplishment of these rites is considered to depend on the deity of the [particular] lunar day;
even for those rituals prescribed by rule, they must be performed on that specific day.
If there is further study from the lotus-like mouth of the teacher, then great, immediate, and inexhaustible success will certainly arise. || 15 ||
Hunchbacks, the intoxicated, the elderly, children, the one-eyed, those with deformed limbs, eunuchs, those who have passed their prime, as well as women, ministers, and physicians; || 16 ||
Those [planets] which are free from the impurities of initial friendship, enmity, and so forth, and which are obtained in prohibited months and asterisms, bestow auspicious success. || 17 ||

Accompanied by the purificatory rite of initiation (dīkṣā), yet devoid of the recitation of the ajapa-mantra and fire-offerings (homa); constantly performing various preparatory rites (puraścaraṇa) as well as ritual placements (nyāsa) and oblations (homa).
Those who have received [the teachings] from the lotus-like mouth of the teacher, even if they are deficient in the teacher’s fee (dakṣiṇā),
must certainly be looked after with care by good disciples once again.
She becomes instantly perfected, bestowing the grace of Lakṣmī and Īśāna.
There, having approached early in the morning, he should honor the lotus feet of the preceptor.
At the beginning of the recitation of the Brahmavidyā, one should necessarily recite it three hundred or four hundred times and meditate upon the garland of rays of the Blessed One for five days.
Having bathed, one should recite the Gāyatrī mantra one thousand times, or a hundred, or three hundred; then, having offered oblations of sesame seeds, that person becomes a partaker of success.
Then, having completed the daily fire oblation, he should go into the presence of the teacher;
[the disciple], whose lineage is pure, should perceive him as the Lord himself, consisting of the Blessed One.
O illustrious Nācārya, omniscient true guru, ocean of compassion! Day by day, we are the servants of the pair of your lotus feet. 24.
O All-pervading Lord, with my body, mind, and speech, and with all other suitable objects, I perform this worship of Your feet; may I possess unwavering faith. (25)

Having thus been entreated by the three teachers with these verses, O King Vahniśāsana, he became once again composed for the purpose of acquiring all branches of knowledge. (27)
One should pray for the earth with all one's goals and even at the cost of one's life;

Having offered one hundred and eight oblations of clarified butter with the Śrīmad-aṣṭākṣarī mantra,

One should worship the pair of feet of the preceptor with many articles for the sake of receiving the injunctions and for the complete prosperity of all. (37)
Among the twelve months of the year, Vaiśākha bestows all accomplishments;

Therefore, may the Lord of Śrī be pleased with me through this [image] of the Blessed One from Śālagrāma, which possesses the splendor of the moon’s rays and embodies all the gods.
In this manner, one should offer the auspicious Śālagrāma stone, endowed with its fruit-bearing substances,

Having placed the vessel in the middle of the fruit, or having worshipped with flowers and other offerings the auspicious Śālagrāma stone of the Blessed One, which is situated within it, [one should proceed]. || 68 ||
Having given there boiled rice mixed with milk and fruits such as mangoes and others,
he should place a pair of earrings near the teacher's ears.
Having offered a pair of fine garments together with the five fruits,
one should offer with faith a purified Śālagrāma stone accompanied by a pilgrimage.
Then, having placed [the vessel] together with the two eyes into the hands of the teacher,

The wealth measured by a year’s worth of food is declared to be one hundred *niṣkas*;

All one’s possessions are said to be the sacrificial fee, or indeed a year’s worth of wealth; it should never be less than that.
If one is impoverished despite possessing golden coins and earrings,

Then, with the thought that his teacher is Mahālakṣmī herself, he should respectfully honor his beloved with divine garments, ornaments, food, and other offerings. (74)
Or, being of meager fortune, he should offer wealth according to his capacity,
along with curd, to twenty-five Brahmins.
Then, with devotion, one should offer food mixed with ghee and honey;
thereafter, one should honor women whose husbands are living with food, snacks, the six flavors, honey, clarified butter, and various edibles.
Having worshipped the twelve [deities] with the Śrī-budhya mantra, one should satisfy them with sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā).
One should then [drink] the auspicious water that has washed the lotus feet of the preceptor (ācārya). || 78 ||
Having drunk [the water], his self is immediately purified; the practitioner should then cause him to eat the remainder of that [food]. Sandals, umbrellas, and other such items are also mentioned.

then, having received an embrace from the preceptor, he should show his respect by accepting the preceptor’s blessings.
One shall likewise attain a great, inexhaustible, and rare accomplishment,
accompanied by a sacrificial fee of gold numbering one thousand million.
Whatever fruit a person enjoys after performing a hundred horse-sacrifices, one obtains that same fruit by thus performing this [rite] with its constituent parts. 81.

Then, month after month, she beheld in her dreams the Lord of Śrī, the bestower of all perfections, marked with the signs of the conch, discus, and other emblems.
Thus, when he beholds the granter of desires either in person or even in a dream, O Lord of Kamala, by the utterance of his name— || 85 ||

She shall be endowed with the eight auspicious qualities, filled with wealth, grain, and the like, possess mastery over all sciences, and attain the supreme recollection of past lives. (87)
O King, the perfection of knowledge of the three times, omniscience, mental charm, the power to enter another's body and so forth, and inexhaustible speech—[these are the qualities]. 88.
Indeed, for him, the practice of the vow of Śiva, endowed with its eight limbs, quickly brings about union [with the goal]:
the Lord who is the leader of the three worlds, the Blessed One, the husband of Indirā. (89)
It bestows upon this [devotee] its own likeness and even those desires that are difficult to attain;

And [he gave] Yāryatī, Nandi, Caṇḍīśa, and Gaṇeśa to the Great-Souled One.
In the month of Vaiśākha, on a day at the beginning of the waning moon, during the conjunction of the yoga-karman,

By the grace of the Guru, all knowledge was attained by him while he dwelt in this forest that destroys all suffering;

If, on the third day of the month of Vaiśākha, these three yogas are present there at the outset,

Then, having traveled the path and offered oblations with wealth consisting of sacrificial food, he worshipped the lotus feet of his own teacher;

Specifically, one should offer oblations with the eight-syllable vidyā using clarified butter mixed with substances and bilva leaves, along with the three sweets; and furthermore, one should honor one's own preceptor with garments and ornaments.

Having attained perfection, he beholds with his own two eyes the sole Lord of the World,

This is a compendium of the essential meaning of all the Vedas,
