He who is like the ocean, from whom all things emerge, who is constant both here and in the hereafter, is the Lord of Sacrifice, the Sacrifice itself, the enjoyer, the manifest Person of Sacrifice, the all-pervading one. (28)
He is worshipped through all sacrifices, he is eternally praised by the Vedas;
the Supreme Self, the Lord of Śrī, is clearly perceived within the eye situated in the heart. || 29 ||
He is the embodiment of all sacrifices consisting of all the gods;
he is to be worshipped with supreme honors through great sacrifices accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees.
By means of which sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) is given in great gifts when they are complete, one who is helpless and whose form is dedicated [to the goal] attains the [desired] state. || 31 ||

O Sage, for human beings, a birth devoid of giving is a vessel for the impurities and sufferings of hell; therefore, even by one who is destitute, it is not improper to give away vegetables and such things.
One who lives as a mendicant must constantly give, even if he is poor; especially in the Kali age, which has arrived, it is a path that leads to hell for those who do not give.
Among sacrifices, this great sacrifice (mahāyāga) is proclaimed as the "sacrifice of victory";
having performed daily with devotion the rites such as recitation (japa) and burnt offerings (homa), [one attains it].
Furthermore, whatever may be given to the lotus-feet of the preceptor, whether at the time of conception or during the month [of pregnancy], should be offered if one desires prosperity. (35)
These sciences, which bestow the fourfold aims of life, are known as the Great Sciences (Mahāvidyās).
For those who perform their recitation, fire-oblations, and other rites, [the results] are inexhaustible. (36)
That birth should be known as fruitful; he who does not partake in happiness [is not so].
Even there, that man [who recites] the glorious eight-syllabled mantra [attains it]. (37)
At that time, the Supreme Brahman, the Unborn Nārāyaṇa, is indeed the Self;
his very rays go forth and return to create all things.
He is composed of all vidyās, the Lord of Śrī whose form consists of all nyāsas,
the soul of the glorious eight-syllable vidyā, the Lord of Hari, the all-pervading one.
The Lord of the Universe should be worshipped with sacrifices such as the *puraścaryā*;
the auspicious recitation (*japa*), oblation (*homa*), and other rites of the venerable *Arṇavī* [Tantra] should be performed. (40)
One obtains a fruit even greater than that of sacrifices such as the Aśvamedha;
it cannot be attained by means of the Aśvamedha, nor by gifts of fine garments, nor by tens of millions of gifts of food.

In this Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa yoga, there is no need for pilgrimages, vows, or purificatory rites; by him, the inexhaustible merit of a gift has been accomplished—of this there is no doubt. Behold the Lord of Pārvatī! 44.
When this Lord, who is like Indirā’s lover (Viṣṇu) in person, is seen even for a moment,
he is worshipped again and again even by the gods, such as Brahmā and Rudra.
Having performed the preparatory rite (puraścaraṇa) and having failed to give the complete sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) at the feet of the preceptor, one shall conquer great sin and attain success.

When all the wealth that has been acquired is given away at a single occasion, thinking "this is my entire possession," that is called the gift of one's whole being; it is declared to be the complete sacrificial fee (*pūrṇadakṣiṇā*).
Even wives and so forth, as well as ornaments, clothing, and all other possessions—everything belonging to those who have no sons—is declared to belong to him. (48)
They say the highest sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) is the daughter; it bestows the attainment of oneness with Brahman.
Furthermore, the wealth of a year's worth of grain and fish is also called the highest sacrificial fee.

O high-minded one, there is nothing equal to the worship of the eight-syllable mantra, whether it be performed ten million times with the glorious eight-syllable "Bestower of Boons" (Śrīmad-aṣṭārṇa-varada) or even with all one's possessions offered as a sacrificial fee.
The Vedas, as well as the Upanishads, the Dharmaśāstras, the entire collection of Purāṇas, and whatever exists such as the Kalpasūtras and so forth— 65.
O one of great mind, may there be an increase in the commentary on the glorious eight-syllable mantra,
which is accompanied by the vision of the Blessed One and endowed with all the ritual placements (nyāsa).
The glorious eight-syllabled mantra (Aṣṭākṣarī-vidyā), along with its limbs and secret portions, was requested by him;
for whom the imperishable one, whose form is Brahman, grants success, prosperity, and growth.

Therefore, one must certainly exert effort with devotion for the sake of attaining success in the glorious eight-syllable vidyā; for when it is mastered, one becomes like a god, both in heaven and on earth.
O son of Brahmā, there is nothing unattainable even in the netherworld (rasātala);
his fame is imperishable and filled with the sovereign powers of the *aṇimā* and other qualities.
It is unwavering, of great fortune, and brings freedom from old age and death;
furthermore, it is a sacrifice endowed with eight limbs that causes the forgetting of birth after birth.

There is no doubt that through this alone, in a single birth, his lack of firm conviction will cease; know this very thing to be the bestower of success for one who follows the conduct of the Teacher, and the sole means of attaining the Supreme Brahman. 73.
The eight-syllable vidyā is said to be a rare remedy;
one should recite it as the cause for praising the vision of Brahman. (74)

The auspicious recitation, fire-oblation, and other rites of the glorious eight-syllable Vidyā are declared to be the primary cause for the attainment of dharma, worldly prosperity, and liberation. (75)
Because fear from Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the others was dispelled by him, he is called Nārāyaṇa;
he is constantly spoken of, heard of, worshipped, and likewise meditated upon. (76)
In the Nārāyaṇa [Tantra], the method for realizing consciousness is taught;
by means of it, the practitioner can attain the imperishable, mind-born state.
Again and again I speak this for those who have attained the auspicious path:
the glorious eight-syllable [mantra], which bestows fortune, should be practiced with diligent effort and respect. (78)
O delighter of the Brahmins, I shall speak again and again, even repeatedly,
having received the eight-syllable mantra from the lotus-like face of my preceptor.
Having performed the *puraścaraṇa* rite for the sake of both worldly and spiritual success,
it is known as the day of the birth of the sage Nārāyaṇa, occurring on the eighth lunar day (*aṣṭamī*) of the waning moon.
One should diligently and with reverence make an effort for the accomplishment of the glorious eight-syllable mantra;
the mastery of the eight syllables is equivalent to great gifts and great austerities.
"The Dharma is great; this great queen is even greater than that.
[Thus ends the thirty-third chapter in the Śrīmadanuttara-Brahma-Rahasya, the Daśarathi Tantra, the Compendium of the Meaning of the Vedas.]
Śrī Rāja said: O Blessed One, ocean of exceptional compassion, you have spoken everything without exception; now please describe the nyāsa, dhyāna, and other rites for all the *lakṣmīs* and *vidyās*.
The Blessed Lord said:
Listen, O King, protector of the earth, to the procedure for the illustrious mantras which was respectfully requested by the Blessed One; I shall now declare it in brief.
The seed-syllable of the Triple Veda (trayī), adorned by the left eye (vāmanetra) and joined with fire (agni) and the moon (indu)—this second seed-syllable has been held [by me]. || 3 ||
The seed-syllable of space (haṃ) ending with the anusvāra (ṃ), adorned by the face and the veil (the letter u);
the seed-syllable of earth (laṃ) joined with the mouth (u), the wound (the letter ṛ), and the wind (ya) and the sun (ra). || 4 ||
Joined with the twelve vowels and endowed with the heart-mantra,
this eight-syllabled great vidyā was proclaimed by Mahālakṣmī.
She is the sovereign queen upon the imperial throne of all self-restraint;
she is the destroyer of the suffering of poverty and the bestower of all perfections.
O high-minded one, Bhṛgu, the son of Brahmā, is her husband; she is the sage Ṛgvedin, and it is said that the Gāyatrī of the Sāmaveda is her beloved; Mahālakṣmī consists of the three Vedas.
The goddess who was spoken by the deity, the mother of all the world, beloved of Hari;
she is joined with the seed-syllable of Śrī and the seed-syllable of Śakti, as uttered by Rudra.
Thereafter, one should perform the six-limbed placement (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa) with the syllable Śrī joined with the six long vowels.
[She who is] like the entire [mass] of the copper-colored sun, a treasure-trove of beauty,
slightly resembling a lotus-mirror, holding a golden jar, as well as knowledge and likewise fearlessness.
At its base, upon a divine seat made of great jewels and fashioned from the finest wood,
she sat— possessing a beautiful countenance, radiant with divine splendor, and endowed with stainless intelligence.
Having meditated upon Mahālakṣmī as yellow, excellent, and adorned, one should daily recite this mantra.
May there be an abundance of all prosperity at every step;
[this is achieved] by reciting the supreme mantra eight hundred thousand times with *utpalas* or lotuses.

Then, having offered oblations mixed with honey and the three sweets (madhutṛtaya) using the prescribed leaves, and having bestowed many lakhs [of coins] upon the lotus feet of the preceptor; || 12 ||
One obtains knowledge and attains spiritual success; there is no need for hesitation in this matter.
One should cause [the image] to drink [water] in the month of Vaiśākha, Phālguna, Āṣāḍha, or Śrāvaṇa.
In the month of Kārttika or Mārgaśīrṣa, on the first Friday,
having made a formal resolve (saṃkalpa) for twenty-five thousand [recitations] ending on the full moon day (paurṇamāsī), || 14 ||
Having performed the ritual assignment (prajapti), one should offer oblations of clarified butter three times with the mantras;
then one should offer a tenth part of the total as oblations of bilva leaves, or even more.
Then, having respectfully offered a pair of cows along with a sacrificial fee at the lotus feet of the Noble One, he fashioned a pair of screens out of gold.
Having given three sacred threads and garments for the necks [of the images], and having adorned twelve women who are well-dressed, one should live [long]. (17)
By immediately honoring the teacher’s wife with garments, ornaments, and heaps of wealth, one attains success in knowledge; of this there is no doubt.
In this very way, this Great Vidyā is the destroyer of suffering and poverty; it pacifies mental anguish and physical disease, and leads to the complete fulfillment of all prosperity. (19)
One should recite the eight-syllabled mantra of Mahālakṣmī for the sake of the increase of fortune;
otherwise, misfortune and strife would prevail in that person's house.
For the sake of long life and health, for the prosperity of sons and youth, and for the increase of fortune, one should recite the eight-syllabled mantra of Mahālakṣmī. (21)
On the ninth day of the dark fortnight, or on the night of the new moon, or when the full moon has arrived,
one should respectfully perform the rites from the first day up to the ninth.
With the permission of the preceptor, one should there recite the glorious eight-syllable mantra;
having performed twelve thousand repetitions with devotion, the rite is accomplished.
One should recite the eight-syllable mantra of Śrī twenty-five thousand times;
on the ninth lunar day, one should reverently offer pure clarified butter from a cow into a blazing fire.
With the eight-syllable mantra *hūṃ*, he performed more than a thousand [recitations];
with the eight-syllable Vidyā of Lakṣmī, he was honored by the Lord as one who had attained splendor.
One should offer into the fire one thousand three hundred oblations of clarified butter mixed with milk,
combined with the leaves of the Viṣṇu-tree and accompanied by sesame seeds.
Then Acarma, having offered salutations and given the auspicious gift of two ear-rings,
subsequently gave him many earrings and a multitude of golden ornaments.

The wise man should offer the earth; he should offer inexhaustible [gifts] and [the earth] free from debt. He who has performed his penance should give that which is truly inexhaustible; indeed, he should give both [the earth and the gift], well-adorned.
Even a prince, though rich in wealth, would give thousands of gifts,
including ornaments, garments, and sacrificial fees, at the meal.
Thereafter, one should worship the beloved of the Teacher (the Goddess Sarasvatī) with the thought that she is Mahālakṣmī;
a man should certainly worship unmarried maidens as well.
Likewise, girls who are six, seven, or eight years of age, or those who have not yet reached puberty, are suitable;
or else, where the wind is endowed with the qualities of *vātyā* (favorable breezes), [the marriage should take place]. || 31 ||
O King, having honored them with food and other offerings, one should provide nine garments for each; and if one has the means, one should cause ornaments to be offered to them as well.
Having fed twenty-five Brahmins who have mastered the Vedas with delicious food, one should satisfy them with sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā).
Then, having received the blessings of the preceptor, one should eat with one's kinsmen;
when this ritual procedure has been performed during the observances of Navarātra, [the goal is attained]. || 34 ||
The omnipresent Lord,
whose mind is filled with compassion for the world, bestows upon the daughter of Diti a son who shall be the protector of the three worlds.
Then, having fed twenty-five Brahmins who had reached the further shore [of learning] with his desired food, the Blessed One attained great, noble, and illustrious prosperity.
The Blessed One bestows upon him human and divine enjoyments, as well as sons and grandsons; there is no doubt to be found here.

Having recited this mantra one hundred thousand times, one should perform the libation (tarpaṇa) ten thousand times with water from the Śruti, or with water from the seat of the Lord of Sacrifice, or with water from the seat of Umā. || 38 ||
One should offer oblations ten times that amount with lotuses mixed with honey and ghee;
thus, O Goddess, this [practitioner] becomes equal to Dhanasena and attains life.
In the temple of Śrī Viṣṇu, the knower of mantras, unwearied, having chanted the eight-syllable mantra of Mahālakṣmī one hundred thousand times at the root of a bilva tree; 40.
Having prepared [the mixture] with bilva, agaru, ghee, and honey—these three combined—he should effect the increase of his lineage and the removal of obstacles.

The one who constantly performs the recitation of the glorious eight-syllabled mantra, having conquered his own mind through constant practice, becomes a seat for the destruction of misfortune day after day. 42.
"The eight-syllabled mantra of Mahālakṣmī should be recited with devotion, O child.
Thus, in this *Dāśarathīya-tantra*, the compendium of the meaning of the Vedas, the thirty-fourth chapter has been spoken by the Supreme Lord. 43.
Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter in the *Śrīmadanuttarabrahmatattvarahasya*, within the *Dāśarathīya-tantra*, known as the *Vidārthasaṃgraha*.
The Blessed Lord said:
Now I shall declare the glorious six-syllabled mantra, the essence of the three Vedas, which brings great prosperity;
by the recitation of which even the powers of Brahmā, Indra, and the other gods are subdued.
Having first diligently uttered the supreme abode, which is the seed of the Triple Veda,
one should then [visualize] her mounted upon a white horse, adorned with beautiful eyes.
Then, the seed-syllable of twilight (sandhyābīja) joined with the bindu; then the syllable da joined with kṣī;
then [the syllable] devoid of the bindu and joined with fire (va); after this is the first part of the mantra.

Joined with the twelve vowels and accompanied by the words of salutation, it is to be placed within the venerable six-syllabled mantra; it is the destroyer of the distinctions between the pearls and the water-born [lotuses].
Bestowing the fruit of all sacrifices and sacred fords, granting prosperity and fortune,
she showers wealth, grain, elephants, horses, pearls, and gems.
Bestowing long life and granting all great fortune, this mantra,
when joined with the seed-syllable of Śrī, [brings these benefits] even to a high-souled person who is otherwise an enemy.
Having recited this, which grants all fruits to the practitioner, there is no doubt;
indeed, everything endowed with prosperity is honored upon the surface of the earth.
O Lord of the Earth, even one who is devoid of fortune, though possessing knowledge and having a mind liberated through the realization of Brahman,
is not honored on this earth like a low-born man, O Lakṣmī.
Even a sovereign king, a lord of the entire earth, if devoid of fortune, would not be worthy of worship even by the three worlds, and would be censured even by Śiva.
Trees that are devoid of the splendor of relying upon *śālagrāma* stones, *śīla*, and other virtues, even if endowed with flowers and fruits, cannot even be looked upon. || 9 ||
O Lord of the Earth, even a blade of grass in a cremation ground is endowed with glory;
O Lord of the World, it is indeed worthy of worship. (10)
Endowed with glory, or perhaps born of the earth, he who possesses the beauty of a young woman’s hips was worshipped by all people as their own beloved deity. (11)
Whether one delights in unrighteousness or delights in evil conduct, O protector of the earth, such a person is honored and endowed with prosperity throughout the world. (12)
He who is endowed with prosperity, born of noble lineage, and possessed of kinship—
that very person is a knower of Brahman, that very person is a noble one, day after day.
Where there is prosperity, there is pure substance; where there is pure substance, there is also great dharma.
O King, the Blessed One himself has said that one devoid of prosperity is truly destitute. (14)
One who bestows what has been purchased by another would not be worthy of worship in the three worlds;
therefore, this six-petaled lotus grants the fruit of the Goddess's grace. 15.
One must certainly recite the six-syllabled vidyā of Śrī, which brings about prosperity and abundance and puts an end to the cycle of rebirth. || 16 ||
She is the bestower of all prosperity and desired objects, the sovereign of the lords of all worlds; Bhṛgu is said to be her sage, and the Gāyatrī is declared to be her meter. || 17 ||
The Mother of the World, consisting of the three Vedas, the deity beloved by Śrī Hari, has been stated;
the seed-syllable is "dviti," and the power (śakti) is declared to be "nati. (18)
Thereafter, one should perform the placement of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa) upon the body with a long-drawn breath;
[one should meditate on] Hari, who resembles gold in luster and is borne by four elephants resembling mountains.
I bow to her who holds in her hands a vessel of nectar from which the illusion of worldly existence has been cast away, a rosary, a lotus,

and the two supreme gestures of granting boons and fearlessness; she who is radiant with a crown, adorned with silken garments, and possesses a form that is playful, beautiful, and free from all distress.
The initiated practitioner, having conquered his senses, should recite the mantra six hundred thousand times while worshipping Śrī with fragrant flowers and other offerings. (21)
The practitioner of mantra should offer six thousand oblations with lotuses drenched in the three sweets;
at the conclusion of the recitation, he should offer oblations of sesame seeds drenched in the three sweets.
The best of practitioners should offer oblations with bilva leaves;
or else, [he should recite] twenty-four thousand times the glorious eight-syllable mantra.
One should burn away the accumulation of sins by reciting the glorious six-syllable mantra a thousand times, and afterwards, the eight-syllable vidyā of Śrīmat. (24)
The pure-souled one, with devotion, should offer three thousand oblations of auspicious clarified butter with the mantra until [the desired result] is attained. || 25 ||
Having given a pair of auspicious earrings to the ears of the preceptor,
the wise man should then offer his entire possession at the lotus feet of the preceptor.
Or one should offer as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) enough wealth for a year’s sustenance;
and the beloved wife of the Ārya should honor him with ornaments and garments.
One should feed twenty-four lords of the Mīnas;
[this is] for the sake of the illustrious six-syllable vidyā and its syllables. (28)
Having attained supreme sovereignty, he was difficult even for the gods to overcome;
his majesty, splendor, nourishment, and fame were ever-present and unsurpassed.
The attainment of excellence and success is proclaimed as the ninefold state;
here, one should invoke the Goddess accompanied by the [six] flavors.
Having offered the seat beginning with the seed-syllable (bīja), one should fashion the form [of the deity] by means of the root-mantra (mūla).
Then, one should perform the worship of the limbs (aṅga-pūjana) in the directions of Agni, Īśa, Asura, Vāyu, and the center.
Vāsudeva, Saṃkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha—
these four are like the moon in its phases of Hīna, Mita, Amā, and Pūrṇa, and they are clothed in garments as dark as a blue lotus.
One should worship those four-armed deities holding the discus, conch, mace,
and lotus in the vessels located at the intermediate points of the body, beginning with Damaka and the others.
Both [trees] had faces resembling pearls, gems, and crystals, as well as *aśoka* and *kiñcī* flowers;
they were further graced with lovely, resounding *guggulu* incense and *arkaṭaṅka* resin.
Whatever was desired from the goddess of the treasure-conch, she bestowed it upon her beloved husband.
Intent on embracing one another, they hold a conch and a lotus.
One should worship him together with Prīti, marked on his head by two conchs raining down jewels, holding a lotus and a water-pot, and possessing a waist that causes the earth to bow down. 38.

One should worship the two lords of Sīndhu with white lotuses, and the two lords of Śīṣṭa with red lotuses, blue lotuses, and water-lilies; and the two lords of Mūhūrta with two lotuses accompanied by fresh buds and pollen.
One should worship Tuṇḍila, Paṅkajanidhi, Tanvin, Vasumatī, and also the deities beginning with Dalāgra and Yajñadevatā on the level surface. || 40 ||
Valākīvimālā, Kamalānavamālikā, Vibhīṣīṇīmālikā, Śāṅkārī, and Vasumālikā. || 41 ||
One should worship the Lokīśas, who hold two lotuses and possess a luster equal to strings of pearls; outside of them, one should worship the weapons beginning with Ativajra.
In this manner, the practitioner who worships the goddess Yamatodevi with devotion attains wealth, grain, prosperity, and fame that are beyond reproach. (43)

The practitioner of mantra, endowed with [discipline], should recite the mantra three hundred thousand times while focusing on the measure of the chest; he should meditate upon the Goddess within the solar orb.
In that state, O House of Viṣṇu, the knower of mantras attains great and inexhaustible sovereignty; he abides in the middle of the root of that very root of his own sport.

One should recite the mantra three hundred thousand times; then, one should offer oblations into the fire with bilva leaves mixed with the three sweets in an amount equal to one-tenth of the recitation. (46)
He attains the inexhaustible realm of the Dharma; of this there is no doubt.
O Aśoka, one should offer many oblations with those flowers from the silver and golden trees. 47.
The master of mantras shall subjugate even the three worlds in no time;
he should offer ten thousand oblations of pure sesame seeds soaked in the three sweets.
Even one who has fallen from royal glory is honored;
he should offer oblations in the Vedic fire with the marrow of a bull's fat. (49)

Having become a unique treasury of good fortune, one attains prosperity, glory, and vigor; therefore, dwell in the shade of a bilva tree, which is the ground for offerings to Viṣṇu, and having performed oblations for two years with its fruits or lotuses, you shall attain that fruit.
[Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter in the Veda-artha-saṃgraha, the illustrious Anuttara-brahma-tarahṣya-dāśarathīya Tantra.]
The Blessed Lord said:
Beyond the twelve-syllable mantra of Mahālakṣmī, I shall now explain a certain great king of mantras that bestows all desired objects. || 1 ||
O Great-Souled One, by the mere knowledge of this twelve-syllable *idirā* mantra, great calamities flee from the chest of the king. (2)
First, having extracted the seed-syllable of the Triple Veda (Om), one should perform the piercing of the initial [letter];
it is mounted upon fire (R) and adorned with the left eye (I). (3)

The letter *vi* conjoined with the time of dissolution (*kālā*), that same [letter] devoid of *vī*, then the syllable of the Earth (*vasuṃdharā*) joined with the Wind (*vāyu*) and Vaikuṇṭha (*va*). || 4 ||
Then follows the syllable of the Kṣetrapāla conjoined with the twelfth vowel;
thereafter, the syllable of Vaikuṇṭha, which is the letter 'va' without the bindu and joined with the earth-syllable (the letter 'la').
The group of seed-syllables consisting of Vyoman (ha), Dharitrī (la), Trī (e), and Vāyu (ya), joined with Mukhavṛtti (a);
then Vāṇī (a), Taṃdra (u), and Vāyu (ya), followed by the final letter of the Mātṛkā (kṣa)—this is the painless [mantra]. (6)
One should know that the venerable twelve-syllable [mantra] is remembered as the dispeller of fear for the heart;
it is the eternal essence of the multitude of Vedas, Vedāntas, and scriptures.
She who distinguishes the thousands of great protectors, the lords of wealth, and others;
she who pierces through all vidyās and bestows the abundance of great fortune.
This is the mother of all auspiciousness, the bestower of all arts and waters;
in former times, the sages who discourse on Brahman attained this perfected lore.
Even though the glorious eight-syllable mantra was recited, he became the lord of hundreds of millions;
yet the twelve-syllable Mahālakṣmī-mantra was forgotten, being neither practiced nor remembered. 10.
The Brahman-sages as well as the celestial sages are always there, along with the highly fortunate yogis who are liberated while living and have conquered their senses. (11)

Indeed, those who perform the recitation of the twelve-syllable mantra for the sake of removing all impurities, misfortune, and minor portions of fortune, and for the attainment of great fortune and all prosperity, [attain their goals]. (12)
This great mantra of twelve syllables should be recited; it bestows all accomplishments, generates long life and health, and destroys the afflictions of Māra. (13)
For the sake of averting all calamities and for the attainment of all prosperity,
even Brahmā, Rudra, and the other gods worship the twelve-syllable vidyā.
She has attained great and unshakable sovereignty that is difficult to obtain;
the seer of this mantra is said to be Bhṛgu, the foremost of sages.
The deity who has arrived, endowed with desire (*chanda*), is the one associated with the *anuṣṭubh* meter;

she is the bestower of all prosperity, the great sovereign (*mahāsāmrājñī*), and the peerless one. She is Mahālakṣmī, the daughter of Bhṛgu, proclaimed as the beloved of Nārāyaṇa, and her seed-syllable (*bīja*) is *Śrī*.
The seed-syllable (bīja) is proclaimed as "Pī" and the power (śakti) as "Nati.

The threefold seed is "Śrī," the seed-mantra is "Samī," and the power is declared to be "Nati. Following that, one should perform the placement of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) by joining them with the six long vowels, preceded by the Praṇava (Oṃ). || 16 ||
Or else, one should perform the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) on the four feet [of the diagram] or two.
One should meditate upon her who possesses the splendor of a thousand suns, who is ruddy-hued like the dawn, who is adorned with ornaments,

whose beauty is radiant like the goddess Lakṣmī, who rests upon the lotus-throne of the Sun, and who holds in her hands the gestures of fearlessness (*abhaya*) and granting boons (*iṣṭa*), as well as a beautiful jar of nectar and a lotus.
She possessed a splendor created by her excellent ornaments, a beauty equal to that of Lakṣmī; she was the dwelling place of wisdom-lotuses, with a complexion like refined gold,
shining with a radiant luster, adorned with divine ornaments, her limbs anointed with celestial sandalwood paste, draped with garlands of divine flowers, and her face was dark-hued.
She was as beautiful as the very essence of the goddess Viśālākṣī; she wore a red bodice and was adorned with a parasol that showered down a multitude of pearls from her own head. || 22 ||
Fanned by two chowries, surrounded by her female companions,
she was clothed in a pair of yellow garments resembling molten gold.
At the base of the Kalpa tree, upon an auspicious divine lion-throne made of jewels, sits the Lord of the World, whose abode is the radiant Goddess Vāmā.
Having meditated with devotion upon the Blessed Mahālakṣmī, the Mother of the Three Worlds, the mantra of the triple Mahālakṣmī, we pay homage. 25.
Devoted to the recitation and fire-offerings of the glorious eight-syllabled mantra,
one should recite the twelve-syllabled mantra of Mahālakṣmī one hundred and eight times.
The king should apply himself to the worship of the Lord’s abode according to the seasonal rites, and then he should worship Lakṣmī individually for each month.
Then a triangle and an octagon; beyond that, a circle;
and beyond that, a square provided with four gates.
Having invited Śrīyaṃtra there, one should worship it with ritual offerings;
the worship of the limbs (aṅgapūjana) is performed in the directions of Agni, Īśa, Śūra, Vāyu, and the center.
One should worship Gāyatrī, Īsā, Sāvitrī, and also Sāvitrī;
and Sarasvatī, Brāhmī, and the others, adorned with long vowels, in the eight corners.
In eight vessels, one should place the eight guardians of the directions headed by Mahendra;
and in the eight directions of the square [mandala], the weapons such as the vajra and others.
Thus, for the sake of pleasing Hari, one should worship Mahālakṣmī with the highest services,
beginning with the sixteen-fold offerings (ṣoḍaśopacāra).
For the successful accomplishment of this mantra, one should first recite it one hundred thousand times;
then, one should perform the libation (tarpaṇa) ten thousand times with sugarcane juice or milk.
One should recite the mantra twelve thousand times over a lotus flower for women, and eleven thousand times for men; having thus consecrated them, one should offer them to the deity. 34.
With devotion, one should respectfully offer a thousand lotuses at the feet of the Teacher,
or a hundred lotuses brought in golden vessels.
Alternatively, she should be constantly devoted to serving her teacher;
she should remain in the presence of the teacher, with her senses subdued and her mind focused on what is to be done. (36)
Having been initiated, he attains great success, which was difficult even for the ancients to obtain. || 38 ||
For the sake of success, one should perform the *puraścaraṇa* rite of the twelve-syllable mantra;
there is no festival greater than this, known as the Navarātra, which occurs once every year.
He who had mastered the scriptures proclaimed [himself] as the master of all the sciences that grant success;
therein, through the power of the mastery of the *alakṣmī* sciences, [he attained] success.
One is not able to describe the success attained through twelve hundred thousand recitations;
they know that each single day is equal to a crore of sacred festival days.
There, on the great ninth day, from each of the hundreds of Ḍāmarīs, there was a radiance. || 43 ||
O Great-minded One, beginning from the first lunar day (pratipad) of the month of Tulā, one should practice until the full moon; this bestows the fruit of the gift of a "Superior Man" (supuruṣadāna).
Therein, the Hṛdaya-mantra of the Goddess Kamalā, proclaimed by the Atharvaṇas, consists of twelve thousand syllables, while the Mahāla-mantra consists of twelve syllables.
One should likewise recite [the mantra] with devotion on the eighth day. || 44 ||
One should mutter the glorious Akṣarī-vidyā, which bestows the fruit of having the sun as one's mother.
One should recite this [mantra] involuntarily forty times,
and one should constantly worship the Brahmavidyā one hundred and eight times.
The ritual of *puraścaraṇa* extends until the completion of the recitation (*japa*). After the recitation has been performed, one should offer a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the preceptor.
One who possesses great discernment, such as a prince or even a wealthy man, should request a thousand [recitations] for each [verse]. (69)

One should give a milch cow that is well-nourished, healthy, and accompanied by a gift; and if one possesses pearls, gems, and jewels, one should offer them as the teacher’s fee (guru-dakṣiṇā), as well as land-grants and gifts of Sālagrāma stones and the like.
The gift of a cow and the offering of a bed are also traditionally remembered as being mandatory.
O Lord of the Earth, if a man who is extremely poor and wretched should give three cows to his preceptor and his son-in-law— therein, he should give the daughter of an incapable man,
one endowed with auspicious marks, a daughter of a grandson, and a woman who has drunk liquor, provided she possesses excellent characteristics.
In the absence of those two, he should be intent on serving the pair of preceptors— the father and the mother— along with his wife and children.
The teacher’s wife should be especially honored today on this auspicious day; she should be adorned with garments, garlands, ornaments, and fragrant perfumes.
O Bhoja, there the well-dressed women of firm vows must certainly be served;
or else, those well-dressed women of firm vows should not even be seen.
Or else, having worshipped me with garments, he thought, "I shall be a capable donor because I am free from debt";
thus, firm in his vow, he performed the preparatory rite (puraścaryā) during the Navarātra.
One attains the perfection of both vidyās arising from a hundred-fold preliminary practice (puraścaryā);
there is no doubt in this matter. 85.
He performed the Neneṣṭa sacrifice, accompanied by a thousand horse-sacrifices as the sacrificial fee;
for him, Mahālakṣmī was indeed the threefold Veda personified.
She becomes gracious, free from doubt, and endowed with all perfections; in that year, her house will be filled with a rising of jewels.
Endowed with wealth, grain, and so forth, she dwells indeed as long as life lasts;
her purity consists of qualities and sovereignty. || 88 ||
One whose lifespan is exhausted, one who has met death, and even one struck by a great disease, becomes free from illness, gains long life, and prospers in happiness. (89)
One is never separated from wealth, nor from one's wife, nor from sons;
such a person attains ever-increasing prosperity and receives blessings of constant well-being day after day.
Through death during the Navarātra, one shall obtain pearls, gems both released and unreleased, inexhaustible wealth and grain, as well as the abundance of elephants and horses.
O auspicious one, you who are devoted to the Navarātra vow performed by Puraṇa, know me alone as your protector; I am the mantra of prosperity for those who have conquered their senses. 92.
Here, one enjoys all pleasures that are difficult even for the gods to obtain, abounding in hundreds of divine maidens and enriched with every kind of enjoyment. (94)
At the end, having ascended a celestial chariot accompanied by thousands of his kin,
he shall abide in the presence of the Blessed One as the Blessed One himself.
The prosperity shall be such a flourishing prosperity. || 95 ||

Having performed even a single purificatory rite (puraścaryā) during the Navarātra vow with self-restraint, the lord of the earth, having declared the ritual fee along with its ancillaries, [should proceed]. || 96 ||
O King, he attains great knowledge and a perfection that is very difficult to obtain;
indeed, there is no other ground for perfection equal to the vow of Navarātra.
Or else, one should give increasing wealth at the feet of the preceptor;
during the nine nights, with devotion, one should offer nine niṣkas on the ninth day.
Having performed the auspicious Navarātra vow according to the desired rites, one should give [the gift] accompanied by a gift of land and endowed with a pair of earrings. 99.
Accompanied by the increase of his lineage, he remains as long as the moon and sun; having attained death at his own will, he possesses the eightfold glory of Śrī Yama.
Having eaten, one should laugh for a portion of the time; at the end of the meal, one attains the supreme goal.
During the spring Navarātra as well, one should perform this auspicious vow in this manner.
And having offered to the pair of the preceptor’s feet a gift for the preceptor consisting of a cow with thick limbs and a large udder, or else a gold coin (niṣka). || 2 ||
One gains knowledge through learning and attains prosperity; no doubt exists for such a person.
One should perform the Navarātra vow with all its constituent parts during the month of Āśvina.
A woman who performs the Navarātra vow during her menstrual period shall not perform the Navarātra vow with all its constituent parts (sāṅga) unless [the rite] is performed by her husband.
One should perform the Navarātra vow in the month of Caitra with all its constituent parts according to the prescribed rules;
even during a period of ritual impurity (sūtaka), the auspicious Navarātra vow must not be abandoned.
Having requested one's own preceptor, or otherwise having the son of a preceptor perform it according to the rules, one should observe the vow for nine nights during the Ārdrā constellation.
O Lord of the Earth, for that man whose observance of the Navarātra falls away, there will be a loss of prosperity within the year.
If there should be an obstacle on the day of Āśvini,
he should perform the Navarātra vow with its constituent parts and ritual fees, even if it begins on the following day.
In all cases, those desiring their own welfare should perform the gift of land accompanied by four bulls, provided it is endowed with its ancillaries and a complete sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
On the tenth day, under the Viṣṇu asterism, one should present a pair of golden [ornaments] to Skanda. (**********) Or [one may offer] gold. || 111 ||
The grace of the Guru should be enjoyed even in one's own home; or else, on a single day, one may attain success by means of the Goddess of Fortune. (12)
I shall also respectfully declare the secret preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) in the month of Vaiśākha,
Śrāvaṇa, Kārttika, or Āśvina.
If the full moon (Paurṇamāsī) should coincide with the Puṣya or Phālguna month,
and be joined with the asterism Pūrvaphalgunī, and further associated with its respective day, [it is auspicious].
An eclipse of the moon occurring there is said to bestow great fruit,
especially if the lunar festival (parvan) coincides with a Monday.
This yoga is said to be unattainable even by Śiva, whose crest-jewel is the moon;
when the new moon (Amāvāsyā) coincides with Monday, it is called the Padmaka yoga.
If the full moon day of the month of Śrāvaṇa occurs on a Sunday during the Mahāpadmaka yoga, it is endowed with the merit of a Vaiṣṇava sacrifice.
If the day of the moon (Monday) should coincide with a lunar festival (Somaparva),
this conjunction for the worship of the Moon-crested Lord (Śiva) is obtained on earth, though it is difficult to find even in an aeon.
In the same manner, one should likewise perform the daily recitation of the twelve-syllable mantra of Lakṣmī.
When the time of a festival has arrived, whether it be the sun or the moon [in eclipse], one should perform a bath at the moment of contact; even if there is no water, one may bathe within the heart.
Uttering the twenty-four names beginning with Keśava,
he bathed twenty-four times and was liberated from the heaps of his sins.
Having placed the preceptor nearby and having consecrated Nala according to the rules,
one should offer three hundred oblations of sesame seeds with the glorious eight-syllabled mantra.
With ghee from a cow mixed with honey and the three sweets (madhuparka),
and purified by the twelve-syllable mantra of Mahālakṣmī, one should respectfully offer the ghee from a cow.
The donor should perform the fire-oblation (homa) up until the completion of the channel for the liberated;
he should offer each individual portion of the knowledge-mantra of the Lord’s rays.
Then, having circumambulated the blazing fire,
he performed a prostration with eight limbs before the pair of feet of the preceptor.
A wise person, for the sake of attaining the form of the Blessed One, should offer his entire property;
or else, twelve *niṣkas* of gold, or even a single *niṣka*.
One should offer three *niṣkas* of gold, or a single *niṣka*, or even more than that. || 29 ||
One should feed a couple with delicious food containing all desirable flavors; one should offer a palatial residence free from fear of death, a single *śālagrāma* stone, and a book.
One should also present a single ornament to the preceptor’s wife, along with a *niṣka* of gold and other refined offerings accompanied by ritual fees (*dakṣiṇā*).
Having received the *āśīkha* from the teacher, he should remain silent, self-controlled, and with his head bowed.
Through the glorious eight-syllable vidyā and also through the twelve-syllable Śrī-vidyā,
one attains great siddhi, which is difficult even for the gods to obtain.
By performing this auspicious preparatory rite (purascaryā) for even as little as two parvas, one attains eternal success; of this there is no doubt. || 33 ||
Whether on a Monday, the day of the Moon-crest (Śiva),
or on a Sunday, the day of the Sun-crest (Viṣṇu), it is impossible to describe the success of the practitioner who performs the *puraścaraṇa* in this manner.
O King, if the conjunction of the Cūṇāmaṇi [asterism] is obtained on earth, it is impossible to describe the success one attains by performing the *puraścaraṇa* rite there. (34)
O King, if the Cūḍāmaṇi mantra is obtained in its true form,
then for the practitioner there, the fruit of a hundred *puraścaryās* arises from a single *puraścaryā*.
Today, by the grace of the illustrious Lord of Śrī, this great perfection—difficult even for the gods to attain—is born; through his favor, the jewel of the lineage is now seen. 36.
O Rāma, Mahālakṣmī, wealth, grain, and other such riches are indeed accomplished [through this], just as a flower is the cause for the longevity of the Cīrañjīva tree. || 37 ||

Prosperity consisting of excellent sons and so forth, which was previously difficult to obtain, as well as the perfection of speech—there is no doubt that the attainment of poetic skill and other such gifts has come about through this very [practice]. (38)
"May you become a mass of supreme bliss"—with these words, he should offer it continuously and inexhaustibly to the Blessed One, with ten predecessors and ten followers. (39)
When the day of Bhārgava (Śukravāra) arrives, one who is constantly observant of the vow of silence,
having bathed in the morning with a purified soul, should mutter the Gāyatrī mantra thirty times.
One should worship with leaves and flowers using the Śrī-Śrīśa-Brahmavidyā mantra;
furthermore, a couple or a second couple should be fed.
On a Saturday, the practitioner observing the vow should feed one virtuous Brahmin with delicious foods accompanied by ritual gifts, and [honour] the preceptor’s wife with meat and other offerings.
O King, having worshipped her according to the prescribed rites with fragrant flowers and other offerings,
one should present to her a niṣka, half a niṣka, or even a single gold coin.
O King, one should also offer well-prepared food along with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) in your presence, O monarch, in the absence of the preceptor’s wife.
In the presence [of the deity], one should offer gold with the mind into the hand of the preceptor,
or give it to his son, or else bestow it upon his grandson.
Necessarily, on the ninth lunar day of the month of Āgha,
falling on a Saturday, having performed all the rites on that auspicious day, he then worshipped the sacred images.
One should perform the divine rite for five years, or with increasing intensity, or even for as long as one lives, after having been bitten by a serpent that is capable of causing death.
Having observed the Bhṛguvāravrata on a day other than one’s own wealth [or specific time], and having performed it,
one shall not be separated from his wife, nor from his sons, nor from his kinsmen, even at the death of Rāmā or Brahmā.
Then there was that assembly, crowded with your own sovereign power, wealth, grain, and so forth; strewn with clusters of pearls and gems, and thronged with elephants, horses, and chariots.
Having attained a long life, O Venerable One, and great, inexhaustible health, one obtains those eternal enjoyments belonging both to humans and to the gods. (53)

O Lord of the World, even though I am of little fortune, by this [offering] of a garment, may there be eternal auspiciousness for the world; O Master of Policy, may there be the highest and most supreme welfare.
With the two [mantras] consisting of eight and twelve syllables, which are composed of eternal bliss, [he attains] Keśava and his consort Śrī. (56)

One should reverently offer clarified butter from a cow (gavya) three hundred times for each individual mantra. Having offered one oblation after another, the rays of the Lord, which grant the boon of knowledge, eventually dissolve into Brahman. || 57 ||
One should conquer five hundred obstacles with each leaf of the *brahmavidyā*;
or, with white water-lilies, one should feed five pairs at the pond.
Having given three niṣkas, two niṣkas, one niṣka, or even half a niṣka to the wife of the preceptor, one then attains success.
This great and supreme vow observed on a Friday is exceedingly powerful;
desiring my own welfare, I shall perform it, for it grants the attainment of union with Brahman.
Among yogas, Vyatipāta is supreme; among days, Friday is supreme.
These two alone are the most excellent in the world of mortals, being more constant than all other waters.
When [the time] has arrived, preceded by the command of one's own teacher and the knowledge of Puruṣa,
[one should recite] more than a hundred [verses], up to a thousand, accompanied by all the nyāsas.

Having recited the glorious eight-syllable mantra of Lakṣmī, and having performed one thousand one hundred recitations of the twelve-syllable mantra of the Mother Śrī, [he should do so] over the consecrated fire.
One should offer three hundred oblations of clarified butter with the eight-syllable Śrī-vidyā;
[alternatively], one should offer one hundred and eight [oblations] with the Śrī-vidyā. (64)
O Ācārya, one should likewise offer the price of a single cow, or perhaps a niṣka, or even a kṛtārpa, at the feet of the Ācārya.
Having offered this three-fold food— consisting of milk-rice (pāyasa) with ghee—
to Yamī on the day of Vyatīpāta, one should observe this single-day vow.
One attains great prosperity from Śrī, Śrīśa, and Vidyā,
and is liberated even from terrible, great sins.
Longevity, wealth abundant with gold, grain, and other riches, great power, and the eightfold yoga—these he shall obtain. (68)
He becomes honored for his mastery of sciences not previously heard,
and having attained imperishable happiness, he reaches this state of the Blessed One at the end of the body.
He attains ten thousand lineages, of this there is no doubt;
one should offer oblations with red lotuses using the ten-syllable mantra of Śrī-Hrī.
O King, within two months he obtains a supreme rain of wealth;
he who, being pure, offers three thousand oblations of bilva fruits attains this.
Having become a master of the sciences,
he attains imperishable prosperity on the third [lunar day] that is imperishable, preceded by the command of his teacher.
Furthermore, with grains and fruits devoid of seeds, mixed with the three sweets,
large and anointed with cow's ghee, he kindled the sacrificial fires.

Having offered one thousand three hundred oblations of clarified butter with the eight-syllable vidyā of Śīma, one should offer three hundred oblations of clarified butter with the illustrious twelve-syllable [mantra].
One should perform the invocation by means of the rays of light produced from each individual limb;
having offered oblations with the Brahmavidyā mantra, one should worship with three hundred flowers and leaves.
Having given twelve niṣkas of wealth to the feet of the teacher, or else three niṣkas, thereafter [one should give] to the teacher’s wife.
The ornament of the ear-lobes (tāṭaṅka) is for the pair of armlets (vāpī), while the half of that is for the purpose of the neck-ornament (niṣkaṃva).
The ornament of the forehead (ciṃtāka) is for the pair of bracelets (vāpī), and its half is likewise. || 77 ||
Having given [the gifts], he should feed five *brāhmaṇas* and the women whose husbands are living.
Having obtained from the Preceptor the union with the Goddess of Fortune (*lakṣmī*) through the yoga of the eight-limbed *siddhi*, he attains the fortune of the Lord of Wealth (*āṣīśa*).
In this matter, there is no doubt that one attains great and inexhaustible success, as well as great and inexhaustible sovereignty, abounding in floods of wealth and jewels. (79)
May there be good fortune, liberation, long life, health, and prosperity,
as well as the eightfold yoga together with sons and grandsons.
Having attained together with his kin inexhaustible prosperity, desired enjoyments, and difficult-to-attain [virtues],
and having remembered his past births for a long time, he goes to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
Having offered three hundred oblations with ripe mango fruits, which possess the luster of the three kinds of honey, with devotion using the glorious eight-syllable mantra; 82.
Having offered one hundred and eight oblations with the twelve-syllable mantra of Śrī, and having made each individual offering of clarified butter with the rays of the Lord of Śrī; 83.
Having performed this vow on the eleventh day of the dark fortnight in the month of Vaiśākha, one should give two niṣkas as a sacrificial fee to the preceptor.
Having offered one thousand, two hundred, or even two hundred jars that have been prepared,
he should then feed couples who are devoted to the Supreme.
Having acted thus, his state of existence, which had arisen from the exhaustion of great fortune,
was brought to an end in the presence of all the kings who were highly honored in the assembly.
At the end of the mantra for the Brahmin who is worthy of the highest honor, one becomes a partaker of liberation, possessing sons and grandsons;
[thereafter follows] the glorious twelve-syllable Vidyā of Śrī, which is the eight-syllable Vidyā.
This very [offering], which has become the primary limb of the *utkara*, is to be consumed by the Ṛṣis,
the deities, and the ancestors during the *ṣaḍi* and *āvāna* rites.
The sound of the ocean of the nectar of the goal is to be enjoyed like ambrosia;
come, for I shall speak of that which is not easily attained, by which one is exalted. (89)
One who constantly performs the recitation of the Gāyatrī a thousand times on this earth purifies even a thousand lineages of twice-born men, even those who are sinful.
O King, he who is constantly devoted to the Rudrajāpya is liberated from all sins; he purifies even those hundreds of sinful souls who have fallen into hell.
Chanting it five times every day, one purifies even more than a hundred rows [of ancestors]. || 194 ||
One who is constantly devoted to the Vīraja mantra and remains pure in twelve ways becomes one with Brahman; such a person eternally purifies even a hundred rows [of diners].
He who is daily devoted with reverence to the four great questions purifies even more than a hundred rows of people. 196.
Chanting daily with humility according to the rules, he becomes one with Brahman; even if he were the lowest of his lineage, he becomes the foremost of a hundred assemblies.
Reciting the Yavamāninī mantra five times every day with devotion, one constantly purifies even a thousand members of a row; of this there is no doubt. (198)
A man who constantly recites the Śuddhavatī verses one hundred and eight times purifies a thousand rows of people, even those who have fallen from their vows.
The ritual consecration of women through mantras does not occur because of causes such as their inferiority;
rather, having established this very point, [one should recognize] the cause of women's purity and so forth. (200)
To those who are declared purifiers of the row— pure and free from blemishes—
it is always to be given in rites for the gods and the ancestors.
If one gives inexhaustible wealth and grain to Brahmins who are not learned in the Vedas, it becomes as useless as an oblation poured into ashes; of this there is no doubt. (202)
One who has not accumulated a store of Vedic knowledge is an unworthy recipient; he has no entitlement to receive gifts, nor does he have the right to give.
All the giving that one makes to those who are not learned in the Vedas becomes entirely fruitless for him.
Furthermore, what suffering does the foremost son of the Sun (Saturn) not bring upon a city today?
Even after bestowing a birth upon a learned Brahmin, he attains at the end a terrible leprosy in hell.
"Since this Brahmin, though observing the conduct of the eightfold purity, is devoid of Vedic knowledge, what evil have I done by taking the meat of the Rohita fish and the lamp-offering? (205)
Therefore, O foremost of Brahmins, those who constantly purify the assembly must certainly be honored with clothing, food, and other offerings for the sake of prosperity. (206)
He who is considered more venerable than even a thousand preceptors is purified; for both the preceptor and the [other] teacher, one should offer gold weighing at least three *huṃkas*.
In the end, it becomes equal to Mount Meru, bestowing the attainment of union with Brahman;
it is the auspicious and glorious eight-syllabled mantra conjoined with the glorious twelve-syllabled mantra. (208)
One should recite [the mantra] daily with one-pointed concentration, purifying a thousand rows [of ancestors],
having offered one's entire wealth as a sacrificial fee at the feet of the two lotus-like feet of Ālārpa.
It is taught that even for one who has measured out [the offering] for the Lord of the Sixth (Śiva), there is an abundance of wealth;
likewise, in the venerable eight-syllable vidyā and in the twelve-syllable [vidyā] of Śrī, [there is abundance]. 210.
Devoted to recitation, fire-offerings, and other rites, he is the purifier of those who purify the assembly;
he alone is capable of bestowing grace upon or withdrawing it from those who receive the transmission of the knowledge of Brahman.
I am indeed that Lord whose self is Nārāyaṇa; of this there is no doubt.
One should worship him constantly with jewels and various kinds of riches.
There is no brahmin equal to him in heaven, on earth, or in the netherworld;
nor shall there be another such as he in his final birth, born from my own lineage.
O Prajāpati, he did not possess firm devotion to the lotus feet of the Guru;
whereas those who possess constant and firm devotion to the pair of the Guru’s feet [attain the goal]. 214.
He has constant delight in the auspicious eight-syllable mantra daily, and perpetual devotion to the twelve-syllable mantra of Mahālakṣmī. || 215 ||
The blissful delight in the knowledge of the rays of the Blessed One, practiced daily with devotion, is remembered as the final birth accompanied by pure liberation. || 216 ||
The greatness of the twelve-syllable Mahālakṣmī mantra, which destroys poverty, has thus been told to you;
now the [greatness] of the Lakṣmī-hṛdaya is being told.
[Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter in the glorious *Anuttarabrahmatattvarahasya*, the *Dāśarathīya*, which is a compendium of the meaning of the Vedas.]
Salutations to Śrī Śiva. The Blessed One spoke regarding the majesty of the Sovereign Fortune of Knowledge (Sāmrājyalakṣmī-vidyā) as it pertains to the earth.
Henceforth, O Śūṇḍa, listen with an attentive mind.
One should utter the seed-syllable of the Trayī (the three Vedas), followed by Śrī Rudrāṃ, Bhuvaneśvarī,
Vyajanādi, and then the syllable Advratyavaikuṇṭha.
Then follows the seed-syllable of Rudra together with the letter Śū, and beyond that, the seed-syllable of Brahmā;
the seed-syllable of Brahmā is adorned by the earth-seed-syllable and the covering of the mouth.
The Vāghama mantra consists of eleven syllables; the Marud mantra is superior to that;
the Prasīda pair follows, and then the Vāṅmantra accompanied by Vahni (the fire-syllable). || 4 ||
The left eye (va) joined with the bindu (ṃ), followed by the sky (a) conjoined with fire (ra);
then the fourth vowel (ī) with the bindu (ṃ), and thereafter the fifth semi-vowel (pa).
Then, having mounted Jātavedas [Ra] and joined it with Vi [Ū], one should utter the first of the antasthas [Ya] and Śiva [Ha] adorned with the long vowel [Ā]. (6)
One should extract that group of five syllables consisting of *vasudhā*, *kṣetrapāla*, adorned by *vāyu* and *vaikuṇṭha*, and joined with the essence of *savitṛ*.
This [Goddess] is the sovereign Fortune who grants all desires;
she is the destroyer of every calamity and the dispeller of all mental anxieties and physical diseases.
This Vidyā, which bestows all perfections, is the beloved of Lakṣmī’s heart; it shatters the multitude of miseries beginning with passion and delusion.
Just as the affection born in the hearts of masters results in happiness day after day, so too shall the affection born in the hearts of the wealthy result in constant happiness.
Knowing this to be the bestower of desired fruits—the sovereign glory of the Protector of the Three Worlds—he, free from doubt regarding this matter, shall always partake in auspiciousness. (11)
This knowledge is the sovereign lady upon the great lion-throne of universal empire;
it generates long life and health, and destroys all calamities.
This Mahālakṣmī, who brings about all prosperity, who destroys all suffering and poverty, and who bestows fruits, is always well-pleased.
Hrīḥ and Śrīḥ are the two wives; Vitipaṃsūkra is proclaimed [as the husband].
Therefore, the seed-syllable (bīja) of the Mistress of the Three Worlds and the seed-syllable of Śrī are likewise [to be known]. 14.
Since the two words "be gracious" (prasīda) are explicitly included within the Vidyā-mantra,
a Vidyā equal to this has never been seen anywhere at any time.
She is the producer of good fortune in the world, the sovereign mistress of all lordly powers,
the bestower of the sovereignty of qualities such as *aṇimā*, and the giver of the perfection of absolute liberation (*kaivalya*).
In ancient times, the lord of all the immortals, having been struck by the curse of Durvāsas, attained this unshakable fortune through the mastery of this Vidyā. || 17 ||
Kuvera also, through the instruction of Pulastya whom he had propitiated in the past, became the leader, lord, and sovereign of all the Vidyādharas. (18)
She who is the illusory power (māyā) of the worlds, manifesting through bodies for the creation, maintenance, and dissolution [of the universe],
is worshipped everywhere even by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśa, and others.
In ancient times, Indra attained lordship over the gods through his conquest;
Agni obtained the power of burning, and Yama the status of being the Lord of Progenitors.
This station was previously attained by great souls through the worship of this very [goddess], who is the Varuṇa of the waters and sovereignty, and who is the wind surrounding [all]. || 21 ||
If Nārāyaṇa himself does not grant one his final birth,
then even the great ordinance that bestows Lakṣmī and the two [other] eyes cannot be obtained.
By one desiring prosperity that pervades his own lineage and lasts as long as the moon and sun, this great vidyā, the *Lakṣmīhṛdaya*, must be resorted to; it cannot be obtained otherwise.
By one desiring prosperity that pervades all faults and lasts as long as the moon and sun,
this *Lakṣmī* mantra should be recited daily for the sake of subjugation.
The pair of feet of the teacher must be served even at the cost of one's body, life, and wealth;
O Bhaja, worship them daily, for thereafter the knowledge called compassion will arise.
O Brahmins, those who desire prosperity should never recite this [mantra] with scant regard; it bestows even small blessings only when constantly recited with devotion, and thus it is highly honored.
One who desires the imperial sovereignty of Mahendra’s city and is firm in his vows should recite this Great Vidyā, the Mistress of the Great Lion Throne.
Those who desire the imperial sovereignty of the city of Alakā should daily, with devotion, abandon this ignorance that is the enemy of Lakṣmī. (27)
What is the use of speaking much more on this matter? By one desiring universal sovereignty, this knowledge—which bestows all perfections—should be studied constantly and repeatedly. (28)
And by one who desires sovereignty over the Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Siddhas, Piśācas, Uragas, and Rākṣasas, as well as over the gods, with a self-restrained mind— 29.
This vidyā of imperial sovereignty should be recited day by day; by whomsoever this vidyā of imperial sovereignty is constantly recited, [for him... (30).
Misfortune and the source of strife shall not dwell even in his village;
on earth, he shall attain honor in the presence of all kings. (31)
Desiring [to attain] the imperishable, the seeker who has not yet mastered himself should travel a thousand *yojanas* to the feet of the Teacher.
O King, having given even her entire fortune or even her own body, and having served for many years according to this ritual, a maiden [attains] prosperity.
One should accept [the gift] from the two venerable ones who are rich in prosperity;
for the father alone is great, being the bestower of royal fortune and the great vidyā. || 34 ||
One's mother, brother, teacher, master, one's own preceptor, and even the Blessed One— among these,
at the end of one's life, one should not abandon the preceptor.
The power of the Lakṣmīhṛdaya-vidhā cannot be described even by me, though my mouths are as vast as the great earth and flow with nectar. 36.
Know me alone to be the all-pervading Guru, the bestower of the Lakṣmīhṛdayavidyā, who is characterized by omniscience and other such qualities. (37)
Having renounced even his parents, wife, children, food, and so forth,
he should constantly worship the preceptor alone with all his possessions.
Constantly pleasing the teacher so that I may be satisfied—no such merit arises even from a thousand purifying acts. (39)
The preceptor alone is the Blessed One—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara;
by his satisfaction, the three worlds, including all things mobile and immobile, are satisfied.
The constant propitiation of the teacher bestows enjoyments, heaven, and liberation;
yet, having failed to propitiate him through the actions of mind, speech, and body, one remains bound. (41)
If this Lakṣmī-hṛdaya-vidyā is recited on this earth, Lakṣmī’s grace will never cease; she remains eternally propitious toward him.
The accomplishments of the magical sandals, the vetāla, the pill, and the collyrium are swiftly attained on this earth through her propitiation. (43)
The supernatural powers beginning with *aṇimā*, as well as the treasures such as the *śaṅkha* and others,
stand constantly at the door of that house, ever ready to do his bidding.
Formerly, the lord Dakṣa Prajāpati, the son of Brahmā,
was consumed by the fire of Rudra’s wrath and subsequently became the son of the Pracetasas.
Having propitiated the teacher and obtained this knowledge, as well as the power to create the three worlds and heaven, and supreme prosperity; || 46 ||
Having attained this most great fortune through the power of this mantra,
she became the all-pervading mother of the three worlds.
She is the sovereign empress of all sciences, the bestower of prosperity in every assembly;
even great serpents who are yogins and sages of restrained vows [bow before her]. 48.
Chanting this great Vidyā for the sake of attaining the eightfold sovereign powers,
one finds a sacrifice equal to the Aśvamedha even within the three worlds.
There could be no other mantra equal to the *Kṣmī-hṛdaya* mantra;
there might exist a tree equal to the *pārijāta* if one were found. (50)
O King, a mantra equal to the Lakṣmīhṛdaya-mantra is the equivalent of thousands of baths in the Gaṅgā and hundreds of horse-sacrifices.
Neither the sovereignty over all the worlds nor the splendor of the city of Ayodhyā would be able to grant me the fruit of her innate recitation.
There is no doubt that this knowledge is capable of bestowing upon these [practitioners] a house made of wish-fulfilling gems (cintāmaṇi), even if it be crowded with enemies.
O King, even the goddess Śrī is unable to bestow upon you wealth, nor can the trees of the Kalpavṛkṣa grove, nor even the forests of Pārijāta trees. (54)

O Lord of the Earth, he who possesses the power to grant all desires shall obtain a thousandfold sacrificial rewards for his teacher, provided he serves him with forced devotion as long as he lives. (55)

The fortune of a hundred Kamadepas, as well as freedom from old age and death, will be swiftly attained through the propitiation of this [goddess] by one who possesses even a little [merit]; of this there is no doubt. (56)
Having obtained the grace of the preeminent teacher, he constantly possessed the splendor of sovereignty that captivates the hearts of all subjects,
as well as a fame and majesty equal to a thousand Kamadevas and a constant devotion to righteousness.
Having obtained longevity, health, splendor, fuel, grain, and elephants and horses,
as well as both divine and human enjoyments, one shall at the end become identical with the Blessed One.

He shall possess the memory of his past births, be free from old age and death, and have death at his own will; becoming possessed of great beauty upon the earth and attaining a splendor equal to that of Mahendra, he shall certainly become liberated.
By the constant worship of the lotus feet of the Guru, may the venerable *Hṛdaya* be born [within him];
for he, being honored even by all the Siddhas, attains every single desired object.

The Vidyā known as Sāmrājyalakṣmīhṛdaya is the cause of liberation from all arising suffering and the cause for the attainment of all prosperity; it is found nowhere else among the Vedas or the collection of Purāṇas.
The eminent great sages, headed by Vasiṣṭha and Bhārgava, and the gods, headed by Sureśa and Viśveśa,
having meditated upon the heart of the Fortune of Sovereignty, attained their purpose and reached the highest satisfaction.
He whose intellect is perfected by the grace of Brahmā, who has attained the heart of the Fortune of Sovereignty, and who possesses the wisdom of all the gods—
he alone is the manifest creator of the worlds, that blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa, whose very self is Śiva.
The gods, led by Indra, Viṣṇu, and Brahmā, who know the heart of the Fortune of Sovereignty, worship him as their preceptor, having granted all desired objects. (64)

Having attained sovereign power—possessing the heart of the goddess of empire, accompanied by a multitude of elephants, horses, and jewels, and endowed with equality and prosperity—he subsequently realized that the Blessed One is the very self of Nārāyaṇa. || 65 ||
The majesty of the knowledge of the Fortune of Sovereignty is also proclaimed in the Dakṣiṇāmūrtistotra, sung in the presence of the sages.
One who desires to cross the difficult-to-restrain ocean on the surface of the earth should mutter the great mantra known as Sāmrājyā Kamalāhṛdayā.
Like the flow of the Gaṅgā, there shall be an unceasing stream of sovereignty, poetic skill, and other such qualities;
along with sons, grandsons, and others, there shall be abundant prosperity and a wealth of riches. (68)
It is crowded with many millions of great chariots and elephants;
it possesses the absence of old age and death, and is a state of great, inexhaustible health.
The Lakṣmīhṛdaya-vidyā does not succeed quickly through mere recitation;
it is mastered by those whose very selves consist of the recitation and fire-offerings of the Lakṣmīhṛdaya-vidyā.
O King, the teacher’s wife should be honored on special days,
on Fridays, and on festival occasions such as the conjunction of Puṣya and the Sun, during eclipses, and so forth.
During the Vyatīpāta yoga, on Sundays, during the Navarātra vows and other observances,
by honoring the wife of one's guru with garments and ornaments, [one attains great merit].
This is the supreme, unsurpassed *vidyā* of the Heart of Lakṣmī;
it is also [found] in the union of the Moon-crested Lord (Śiva) and the Sun-crested Lord (Viṣṇu). 73.
In the Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Yoga, in the Puṣkara Yoga, and in the Yoga known as Ardhodaya, recitation, fire-offerings, and other such rites are auspicious. (74)
Having performed the specific vow for the Prasannalakṣmī-vidyā, and having honored the preceptor with beloved offerings and adorned him with ornaments, || 75 ||
One attains great accomplishment, difficult even for the gods to obtain, [by serving] a king who bestows a kingdom, or a kinsman who gives one's life. || 76 ||
This *lakṣmīhṛdayavidyā* should not be given to one who is like the earth;
when the *lakṣmīhṛdayavidyā* is mastered, one becomes like the earth. (77)
Even the glory of the eight directions, beginning with Mahendra, shall dwell in his house,
if he desires the attainment of his own supreme and rare welfare.
Nor to an atheist, a fool, a greedy person, or a slanderer; nor to one who commits treachery against father, mother, or teacher, or to one who acts with malice.
This knowledge of the propitious Lakṣmī must not be imparted to one who is devoid of Vedic conduct, nor to one who has not mastered the eightfold bonds of his own self.
If he should offer or bestow knowledge upon such a person who does not worship [the Lord],
the Blessed One, accompanied by Mahālakṣmī, will turn his face away from him.
The Vedas and all the mantras shall turn their faces away from him;
the Lord of the World will bestow upon him an exceedingly cruel curse. (82)

Therefore, having examined [the recipient], this jewel of ignorance (avidyāratna) should be bestowed by the teacher upon a disciple who is auspicious, on an auspicious day, for the sake of attaining prosperity.
Devoted to the wives of others, wicked, a thief of another's property, intent on false speech, and constantly meditating upon his preceptor with a perverted mind; || 84 ||

One who is constantly intent on censuring the Vedas, likewise one intent on censuring sacrifices, one constantly intent on censuring the gods, and a fool who reviles his teacher—[these are the four types of fools]. 85.
One who is greedy for wealth, prone to anger, lustful, and devoid of learning— such a person should abandon these disciples, even if they have surrendered all their possessions.
After examining his character and all his virtues for a long period of time, this auspicious and radiant knowledge should then be bestowed. 87.
[He saw] one who daily performed the recitation of the mantra of the Goddess Prasannalakṣmī, whose splendor was doubled by the crest-jewel divided into nine parts. 88.
Even while bestowing their entire possessions, lords of men serve him;
likewise, the royal fortune of the Asuras and the sovereignty of the wicked belong to Śakra.
One who knows the truth of the Vedas and Vedāṅgas and is firmly established in the treatises on Dharma attains success without effort through the grace of Prasannalakṣmī. || 90 ||
O you who possess a well of tranquil splendor, there is no doubt in my mind:
she is the sovereign empress of all sciences and the bestower of all perfections. 91.
"Truly, I have spoken this to you; place your trust in me.
Thus [ends] this summary of the meaning of the Vedas by the son of Daśaratha.

Thus has been told this thirty-seventh chapter, which bestows prosperity and abundance, in the glorious *Anugraha-brahma-tattva-rahasya*, the *Dāśarathīya Tantra*, which is a compendium of the meaning of the Vedas.
The Blessed One said:
O King, protector of the earth, listen to the ritual procedure for the Prasannalakṣmī-vidyā, which bestows all perfections; having heard it, O monarch, you shall be liberated. 1.
Having risen during the *brāhma-muhūrta*, having recollected his bow and sandals,
and having performed the twilight prayers (*saṃdhyā*), he then completed the daily fire-oblation (*nityahoma*).
Having prostrated deeply before his own teacher, the all-pervading Lord in embodied form,
O King, he performed breath control (prāṇāyāma) three times at the root of the tree of the Lord of Mountains.
Then, having performed the *ku-vīta* recitation along with the *saṃkulya*,
the sage of this mantra, which is the very mouth of Brahmā, is the all-pervading Lord whose intellect presides over the three worlds.
Dakṣa Prajāpati is called a Ṛṣi by some great sages; the Gāyatra of the Chāndogas is said to be Mahāsiṃhāsaneśvarī.
She is the sovereign mistress of the entire universe, the beloved of the Blessed Lord,
declared as the deity, the mother of the world, Mahālakṣmī, who consists of the three Vedas.
O King, according to the sequence of the second, third, and fifth seed-syllables and their powers,
they say one should place the *praṇava* as the *kīlaka*, and then one should duly assign the limbs (*aṅgas*).
The heart is declared to be "kamale hṛdayam," and then the head with the five-syllabled [mantras].
One should assign "prasīda" to the crest-lock (śikhā) and the armor (kavaca) with three [syllables].
Afterwards, the practitioner, who is a protector of the earth, should perform the placement of the Netra-weapon mantra together with its seed-syllables,
and then perform the individual placement upon the fingers.
In the midst of the ocean of nectar, on a charming island adorned with jewels, crowded with wish-fulfilling trees and surrounded by groves of Pārijāta flowers.
In the midst of that, within an auspicious pavilion made of divine gold and jewels,
at the foot of a Pārijāta tree constructed for the Navarātra festival— (11)
The Lord of the World was seated upon a beautiful divine throne,
resembling a dark rain cloud and adorned with hundreds of celestial ornaments.
The omnipresent Lord, whose four arms shine with the conch, discus, mace, and lotus,
bears the Śrīvatsa mark upon His chest and wears divine yellow garments.
He has a serene countenance and eyes that pierce through like lotus petals;
seated upon his lap is she whose luster slightly surpasses that of the *vūna* flower.
Resembling ten thousand rising suns and resembling the hibiscus flower, it shines,
fashioned from divine jewels such as emeralds and rubies.
She wears a crown upon her head that resembles a hundred rising suns;
moreover, she possesses a parting marked with vermilion and is adorned with flickering bees.
Her face is serene, and she is adorned with earrings that serve as ornaments for her ears;
she is beautified by a pair of armlets joined with pearls and gems. || 17 ||
Her large eyes were like lotus petals, her gaze was darkened as if with collyrium,
and she shone with two eyebrows that resembled the bow of Kāma.
Adorned with a tilaka mark shining upon her broad forehead,
she was beautified by a nose-ornament studded with clusters of pearls and gems.
Her face resembled the autumn moon, her lips were like the fruit of the *yakṛvī* tree,
and she was adorned with a row of teeth as white as jasmine buds.
With a smiling face and large eyes, her countenance like a blossoming lotus; adorned with beautiful earrings and decorated with pearl necklaces.
Adorned with a single-string necklace and embellished with the letter 'ya' and other ornaments,
she shone with a bodice studded with clusters of pearls and gems.
She was resplendent in divine garments with a luster like the dawn-red hair of a horse,
and was adorned with the blossoms and fruits produced by the wish-fulfilling trees of paradise.
Her body was anointed with divine sandalwood paste, and she was worshipped by hosts of gods and sages;
her hips were shaped like golden pillars, and her breasts were full and firm.
She was adorned with a girdle of gold shimmering with pearls and rubies;
she possessed broad hips and a deep, beautiful navel.
She was endowed with a pair of thighs resembling the graceful trunk of a plantain tree,
adorned with a pair of ornaments that resembled its fruit.
With feet whose soles were marked by the signs of the hidden cave, the lotus, the wheel, and the mountain; and with finger-rings on her toes set with gold and jewels. || 27 ||
Her sprout-like hands shone with tinkling bracelets and armlets;
she held a vessel of wealth filled with pearls, gold, and various jewels.
Holding two lotuses that are as beautiful as mirrors,
she has four arms and is radiant with ornaments such as shimmering jeweled anklets.
Her pair of feet is resplendent with the rays emerging from the crowns of Brahmā, Īśa, Śakra,
and Viteśa, and she is solely devoted to the protection of her devotees.
He was honored by sages and hosts of deities with garlands of flowers,
while a wise being held a parasol over his head as showers of jewels rained down.
She was joined by Varuṇa and surrounded by the eight guardians of the directions,
as well as by the excellent son named Dhṛtarāṣṭra and by Kāma.
She who is eternally fanned by both the noble ones, who consists of the three Vedas, and who is worshipped by Sarasvatī, Girijā, Śacī, and the foremost goddesses.
She was worshipped by the wives of sages such as Arundhatī and Anasūyā,
and was surrounded in front by celestial maidens who were dancing.
She who consists of all sciences, the sovereign leader of all assemblies,
the mother of all auspiciousness, and who is surrounded by the [eight] supernatural powers beginning with Aṇimā.
Her lotus feet are worshipped by the treasures such as Śaṅkha and Padma;
she is the support of all prosperity and the sovereign mistress of all sciences.
To the Mother of the Vedas, who showers down a rain of all kinds of pearls and gems;
to the Supreme Goddess, whose eyes are filled with the essence of compassion.
She who brings about all prosperity, she who causes all delight, she who effects the enchantment of all, and she who performs the summoning of all. || 38 ||
She is the bestower of all perfections, the one who brings all worlds under her control,
the eternal cause of the attainment of all sovereign powers.
She who brings about the glory of victory, who bestows the fortune of eternal sovereignty,
who consists of all principles (tattvas), and who grants worldly enjoyments, heaven, and liberation.
She who consists of all yoga, whose very nature is the essence of all dharma and scriptures, who is composed of all dharma, and who is the embodiment of all sacred fords and deities. (41)
