We worship Mahālakṣmī, who possesses all-knowing wisdom, who is intent on protecting the entire world, and whose abode is Nārāyaṇa.
Thus, one should meditate upon the Goddess who is dear to the necklace of Mahālakṣmī on the lotus of the heart,
or else as the Sovereign who assumes the form of the Lord, bearing the discus and other emblems, extending from the heart to the aperture of Brahmā (the crown of the head).
She appeared as if blazing like hundreds of thousands of rising suns;
composed of pure light, she was difficult to behold from close range, yet supreme and pervading the entire universe.

One should meditate upon her as consisting of pure knowledge, the destroyer of all delusion, and the threefold Veda; or else, one should contemplate her as the wisdom that reveals the nature of the Lord.
One who possesses supreme wisdom should daily regard the wife of the Ācārya as Śrī Rūpādhayā herself, or else as the wife of the Ācārya directly, with the thought that she is Mahālakṣmī. (46)
O King, having worshipped him, one should cause the *Vidyāratnaśrīhṛdaya* to be recited;
by this very measure, one should regard the preceptor as the Lord himself.
Know him to be my very form, and his wife to be Śrī herself;
therefore, one must certainly honor the preceptor when he is accompanied by his wife, sons, and others. (48)
If, through all these various means, the success of my grace should not be achieved,
then even if one abandons one's father, mother, wife, sons, brothers, and so forth— || 49 ||

One who desires the multitude of his own welfare should honor the teacher with wealth; likewise, one desiring prosperity should honor him with men, jewels, gold, horses, and other excellent things. (50)
Having thus meditated daily upon the jewel of knowledge—which grants all desires—the Brahmin should respectfully request permission from his teacher to obtain that jewel of knowledge. (51)
Having recited the *Lakṣmī-hṛdaya* one hundred and eight times with devotion, one attains supreme gentleness and obtains whatever wealth is desired. (52)
By constantly reciting two hundred [times], one obtains the heart-essence that grants all desires;
one quickly attains immovable wealth and freedom from fear amidst the turmoil of worldly existence.
He who should devoutly recite the *Lakṣmīhṛdaya* three hundred times, having offered oblations of clarified butter twenty-eight times or even twelve times; || 54 ||
He attains great sovereignty, filled with wealth, grain, and other riches;
freed from misfortune, he becomes as fortunate as Kāma himself.
Whoever recites the *Lakṣmīhṛdaya* four hundred times with devotion shall become filled with wealth, grain, and other riches, and crowded with pearls and gems. (56)
One obtains unshakable fortune and imperishable longevity and health;
one becomes equal to Kandarpa in splendor—of this there is no doubt. (57)
He who daily recites the *Lakṣmī-hṛdaya* mantra five hundred times,
having offered cow’s clarified butter into the fire constantly, or even twelve times [per day], [attains success].
Strewed with clusters of pearls and gems, filled with wealth, grain, and other riches,
and accompanied by a thousand horses— such great sovereignty was bestowed upon Aṣṭaka.
Having attained a lifespan of fifty years, as fortunate as Kāma, and having obtained prosperity consisting of sons and grandsons, as well as inexhaustible health; || 60 ||
She brings kings under her control, as well as the wives of kings;
she is constantly honored in assemblies and shall obtain incomparable perfection of speech.
O King, he who constantly recites [the mantra] five hundred times according to the rule, having offered cow-ghee twenty-eight times into the blazing fire; 62.
Having attained long life, vigor, and health, he became like Kandarpa himself and was the beloved of thousands of royal women.
He quickly attains great and unshakable fortune, abounding with gold, jewels, swift horses, and excellent elephants, and crowded with chariots.
In his lineage, no one of meager fortune or even a pauper shall be born;
rather, the power of his speech shall expand like the flow of the Gaṅgā.
Fortune does not abandon his lineage until the dissolution of all beings;
he dwells in Vaikuṇṭha accompanied by hundreds of divine maidens.
He who, with a serene mind, recites the great mantra a thousand times,
attains the state of stainless lotuses and great, inexhaustible health.
Without becoming free from old age and death, and without attaining the glory endowed with the eight supernatural powers (aṣṭaguṇa), one cannot become the lord of Śaṅkha, Yamunā, and the ocean.
Possessing glory like that of Mahendra, he becomes a sovereign ruler of the whole earth;
even until the end of the kalpa, the splendor of sovereignty does not abandon him.
This auspicious jewel of knowledge, Prasannalakṣmī, is difficult for mortals to obtain on this earth; it bestows the accomplishment of all that is beneficial.
This *vidyāralla* is being recited by one who is devoted to the teacher Caṇḍaṃdvaṃdvaṭha, who is self-restrained, and who is intent upon the foundation of the Vedas. 71.
One should constantly exercise restraint over the desire that has arisen within one's heart, treating women as if they were one's mother or sister. (72)
Day after day, he should adorn himself with perfumes, flowers, and other ornaments;
he should sleep upon a pure bed together with his youthful wife.
Facing westward, he should always eat his food with reverence; he should worship the wife of the teacher with devotion, regarding her as Śrī, through the observances of his vow.
On occasions such as the Navarātra and the Bhṛguvāra-vrata,
one should feed couples alone, regarding them with the thought that they are Śrī and Śrīpati.
Indeed, a sprout of the Jambū tree, a coconut, a lotus, a bilva leaf, and a tulasī leaf should be worn upon the head even when they have been bitten [by insects]. || 76 ||
A wise and excellent twice-born man desiring his own welfare should not place [the sacred thread] upon his head;
he must certainly perform the daily obligatory rites every day at home.
The wise man, for the sake of constant prosperity in battle, should offer ornaments such as earrings, which are as beautiful as pearls, to the preceptor.
Having honored the married women with garments, ornaments, and food, one should then worship Śrīvidyā, Lakṣmī, and thereafter Mahālakṣmī. (79)
The fifteen-syllable Vidyā, endowed with the three powers, the Fortune of universal sovereignty, and the bestower of the five desired perfections, is composed of three sections.
United with the three Māyās, she is proclaimed as Śrīvidyā;
she is the single-syllabled one, the eternal Lakṣmī, the bestower of great sovereignty. (81)
This auspicious twenty-seven-syllable vidyā is the Heart of Lakṣmī;
she is renowned as Mahālakṣmī, the sovereign mistress of all empires. (82)
The three-syllabled mantra known as Triśatmā is Lakṣmī herself, bestowing the attainment of sovereign empire.
When joined with the seed-syllable of Śrī at the beginning and the end, it becomes the auspicious eight-syllabled mantra.
She is the renowned Goddess of Imperial Sovereignty (Sāmrājyalakṣmī), who bestows the accomplishment of great imperial rule;
[she is to be worshipped] by one desiring the Goddess of Universal Sovereignty that is difficult to attain even in the three worlds. (84)

In the Cakrarāja, which is the city of Ayodhyā belonging to the Mother of the World, the piercing (bhidhā) should be performed according to the prescribed rite during the Navarātra vow and other such observances. 85.
One should not engage in the censure of women, nor speak familiarly with the wives of others; one should not abandon betel-leaf, nor wear a contemptible garment. (86)
One should eat curd at night, but likewise not the wood-apple fruit;
one should practice honoring even the teacher’s son with the same regard as for the teacher himself.
O King, having transgressed the command of the preceptor, one may even become a dog anywhere; yet, one should never neglect the Tulasī and Bilva trees.
Having gone through a hundred births as a dog or a pig, he is born as a Caṇḍāla. || 88 ||
Hearing the causes of obstacles, eating food at improper times, and associating with the wives of others are the causes for falling from one's family. 89.
That which is spoken by the teacher must always be performed; even that which is not [ordinarily] to be done should be undertaken.
Upon seeing a Tulasī or a Bilva tree, one should perform a prostration.
O Lord of the Earth, one should not eat the bilva fruit even at the cost of one's life;
thus devoted to his teacher and intent upon the worship of Viṣṇu, [he should remain]. (91)
One obtains great prosperity, difficult even for the gods to attain;
while reciting [the mantra], one should also mutter the Śrīsūkta, or else the eight verses to Mahālakṣmī of Kollāpura. 92.
One should also recite the *Ātharvaṇa-lakṣmīhṛdaya*, which bestows desired objects;
it was seen in former times by Bhārgava in the form of verses and brings about fame. (93)
One should daily recite the *Sahasranāma* known as the *Lakṣmīsahasranāma*,
or one must certainly recite daily the glorious eight-syllabled mantra (*aṣṭākṣarī-vidyā*),
or else one should recite daily the eighteen-syllabled mantra (*aṣṭādaśākṣarī-vidyā*). || 95 ||
A twice-born man should perform the daily fire-oblation every day, both evening and morning;
thus, the *siddhi* of the *Lakṣmīhṛdaya-vidyā* shall accrue to him day after day.
Having performed this, one attains great accomplishment here; of this there is no doubt.
[Thus ends the thirty-eighth chapter in the venerable *Anuttara-Brahma-Tattva-Rahasya*, the *Dāśārathīya-Tantra*, which is a compendium of the meaning of the Vedas.]
The Blessed One said:
I shall describe the procedure for worship preceded by the construction of the yantra,
hearing which even a person of dull intellect is liberated from all calamities.

The mantras of the deities situated at the beginning of the Vedas, conjoined with the pair of Śrī, Śakti, and Māyā, are placed upon the filaments; outside of that, the syllables of the mantra shine upon the petals of the sun.
One should draw a lotus with eight pairs of petals, shimmering with stamens and filaments;
it is surrounded by the syllables *vaṣaṭ* and *hūrtaya*, and the *tvaritā* mantra should be written there, facing outward.
The letters *ha* and *kṣa* should be written repeatedly within the squares of two earths;
this Mahālakṣmī yantra bestows the fruit of all sovereignty.
It pacifies all suffering and wards off all calamities; what more need be said here? There exists nothing superior to this. (4)

In this yantra, one should invoke the goddess Mahālakṣmī within the fire; first, having worshipped the deities of the directions starting from the southeast (Agni), northeast (Īśa), southwest (Nairṛta), and northwest (Vāyu).
And Śrīdhara, Hṛṣīkeśa, Vaikuṇṭha, Viśvarūpaka,
Vāsudeva, Saṃkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha.
Having worshipped at the bases of the petals, one should thereafter worship Gāyatrī, Pārvatī, Cāndrī, and Śavī in the intermediate directions within the middle of the petals.
One should worship Śrīdhara, Hṛṣīkeśa, Vaikuṇṭha, and Viśvarūpa in the intermediate directions for the sake of accomplishing all desires and goals.
In front of that, one should worship these [deities] of Mahālakṣmī in sequence:
Anurāga, Visamvīha, Vijaya, Vallabha, and Mada.
Beginning from the city, one who is joyful, strong, learned, and radiant should worship the eight guardians of the directions, including Indra, in the eight directions of the square [mandala].
Then one should worship his weapons and his attendants in due order;
O King, listen now as I shall describe another sequence of worship. || 11 ||
Having offered a seat with the seed-syllable of Śrī, one should fashion the form with the root-mantra;
one should worship the son of Śaṅkara, who is worthy of veneration, as the deity of the right side.
(*****) Otherwise, one should worship with a handful of flowers;
one should worship the limbs according to the rule in the previously mentioned locations. || 13 ||
One should worship the eight Śaktis situated in the middle of the petals in sequence:
Umā, Bhūḥ, Śrī, Sarasvatī, Durgā, Devī, and Rati. (14)
The goddess Gāyatrī and Uṣā, lotus-handed and beautifully adorned,
approached the son of the Sun and performed the washing of his feet.
Then, on the two sides, one should visualize Śaṅkha and Padma, who are worthy of worship and hold chowries; thereafter, in the west, one should visualize Varuṇa holding a noose.
Then one should worship the zodiac signs beginning with Aries, as well as the nine planets;
one should honor these [deities] adorned with four tusks in the various directions.
Aiśāvana, Puṇḍarīka, Vāmana, Kumuda, Añjana, Puṣpadanta, Sārvabhauma, and Supratīka— these are [the elephants] in order.
Thereafter, one should destroy Śakra and the others, as well as the vajras and so forth outside of them,
according to the procedure taught in the Āgamas, using lofty and most enchanting fragrances.
One should daily offer worship with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings to the Goddess with devotion.
Having thus worshipped according to the rules, one should pray to the delighted Kamalālayā.
Liberated from all calamities and having attained great glory,
he obtains long life and, through great prosperity, attains absolute liberation (kaivalya).
Even though it is easily understood within the Vedantas, the Vedas, and all the Puranas,
I shall describe this most venerable King of Yantras.
First, one should draw the circle of the bindu, and then draw a triangle;
thereafter, an eight-petaled lotus should be drawn, followed by two sets of ten spokes.
Thereafter, one should draw the Mantra-weapon (mantra-astra), followed by a circle provided with eight petals;
then a sixteen-spoked [wheel] should be drawn, again accompanied by a surrounding circle.
This city named Ayodhyā, adorned with four gates and possessing four corners, is known as Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa.
This Śrīcakra, which consists of Śiva and Śakti, should first be drawn according to the prescribed rule; here, the method for its inscription by means of the Mātṛkā is described.
This wheel is most secret even in the Āgamas and the Vedas;
it is the city of Ayodhyā by name, which bestows the attainment of great sovereignty.
That which consists of Śiva and the Ātman is proclaimed as the one named Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa;
the wheel consisting of the nine triangles is called the Śrīcakra. || 28 ||
The illustrious Goddess, the Mother of the World, who is called Citkalā and Annapūrṇā, is also designated as Mahālakṣmī under the names Tripurā and Lalitā. (29)
O King, that Blessed Lady, together with the Blessed One, was worshipped;
she who consists of the nine wheels [bestows] all this auspiciousness for the year.
Having worshipped Śrī and Śrīpati, as well as Umā and Śaṅkara,
the Trailokyamohana cakra is known to consist of three squares.
The wheel that fulfills all desires is known as the sixteen-spoked;
they know the wheel that agitates all as the eight-triangular one.
The fourteen-spoked [cakra] is renowned as the bestower of all good fortune; the outer ten-spoked [cakra] is likewise declared to be the bestower of all good fortune. || 33 ||
The inner ten-spoked wheel described here is supreme for providing all protection;
the eight-spoked wheel is said to be the remover of all diseases. (34)
The wheel that bestows all accomplishments is a triangle, most enchanting;
the wheel consisting of universal bliss is indeed the supreme sovereignty of the gods.
O protector of the earth, this auspicious wheel consists of nine wheels; it is the means for attracting the three worlds and the cause of the creation of the universe. || 36 ||
It is a swift protection against the fear of slander from others and against untimely death;
it bestows all good fortune and grants the attainment of every sovereignty. (37)
It bestows all branches of knowledge, grants the accomplishment of all great auspiciousness, secures victory in every battle, and crushes all enemies. || 38 ||
It pacifies all misfortunes, destroys great calamities and the like, dispels all suffering, and eradicates all mental anguish and physical diseases. (39)
Bestowing the attainment of universal sovereignty over all sacrifices and granting the perfection of liberation,
it is here that Lalitā herself, whose abode is the lotus, is directly worshipped.
The eternal Great Seat (Mahānyāsanātanī), accompanied by the Blessed One, is here worshipped in three ways by those who know the Vedas, the Āgamas, and the Vedānta. (41)

The worship of the *pīṭha* and so forth has been declared first; after that comes what is called the *aṅga* [worship]; the third is called the *bhogāṅga*. Thus, worship is considered to be threefold. (42)
On every day of the lunar fortnight, the worship of the limbs of the deity must certainly be performed; during the Navarātra and similar observances, it must be performed three times a day.

Beginning from the ocean of Amṛtā, this worship of the seats (pīṭha-pūjā), which is said to be the most excellent for special offerings (arghya) every day, bestows the accomplishment of eternal good fortune.
Having worshipped the beloved of the Blessed One with the sixty-four services,
one should also perform the daily worship of the six limbs.
Following that, the worship of the Guru's feet is proclaimed as the "Layāṅga" (the limb of dissolution);
beginning from the supernatural power of atomization (*aṇimā-siddhi*), this concludes with the worship of the Śrī Devī. (46)
The worship of the limbs and parts (bhāgāṅga-pūjana) is declared to bestow the attainment of a great empire;
O King, it should be performed in three ways for one month.
The doubt regarding the Śrī-devīs will certainly vanish before one's very eyes;
then, beginning from the start with twenty-four types of offerings (upacāras), [the worship should be performed]. 48.
Having worshipped the couple Lakṣmī and Lakṣmīśa with the Ākṛti-vidyā,
they are accompanied by the entire retinue of couples beginning with Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa.
I offer this worship with devotion in this tantra proclaimed by me, which is a compendium of the essential meaning of the Vedas, for the protection of all beings. || 50 ||
The accomplishment of all five sciences, including the Fortune of Sovereignty,
as well as the extensive worship of the Cakra, will be explained in the second chapter.
This [mantra] consisting of twenty-seven syllables is the bestower of sovereignty, prosperity, and desired objects;
herein is described that Vidyā which grants the fruits of the four aims of human life.
Constantly recollecting the Sovereign Glory of Mahāvidyā tenfold in the presence of the Cakrarāja, one shall attain perfection. (53)
This wheel, consisting of the arts (kalās), is said to be the nature of manifestation;
it is proclaimed in all the Vedas and is established in all the Tantras.
He who constantly worships the city of Ayodhyā together with the Ṛśyaśṛṅga stone is indeed identical with the Blessed Lord. 55.
The Jāhnavī is the best among rivers, as are the Yamunā,
the Sarasvatī, the Godāvarī, the Bhīmarathī, the Kāverī, and the Kṛṣṇaveṇikā.
The Śatadru, the Narmadā, the Sindhu, the Vipāśā, and the Payoṣṇī—
there is no doubt that they all dwell in the presence of the Cakrarāja.
Devoted to Vedic conduct and intent upon the study of the Vedas,
he was firm in his vows and possessed steadfast devotion to the pair of feet of his preceptor.
The wise one should worship the Cakra, which bestows the accomplishment of universal sovereignty;
whether it be the small Cakra, the large Cakra, or the city of Ayodhyā itself.
Having first received the command of one's own teacher,
the leaf of Ramā (the Goddess Lakṣmī) should be written upon gold, silver, copper, or a birch-bark leaf.
Having worshipped, one should recite this vidyā which bestows the accomplishment of universal sovereignty;
such a great vidyā grants the accomplishment of all sovereign powers.
Even though it has been heard or seen in the Vedas and Vedāntas, nowhere is there ever any wealth equal to that of one whose soul is devoted to yoga, even among all the gods.
Even while protecting the wealth of the Yakṣas and Gandharvas, it also belongs to the Kinnaras, Siddhas, and Asuras. (63)
For one who chants with a serene countenance, all supernatural powers (siddhis) are accomplished;
indeed, you yourself might even offer the seven continents, teeming with elephants, horses, and gold.
Or rather, he transcends all speech; enjoyments difficult even for the gods to obtain are attained by him without a doubt, through the grace of the propitious Śrī-Asāda.
[Thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter in the *Śrīmadanuttarabrahmatattvarahasya*, the *Dāśarathīya Tantra*, known as the *Vedārthasaṃgraha*.]
The Blessed Lord said:
O King, listen with a concentrated mind as I shall proclaim the practice of the Śrīprasannalakṣmī-vidyā, which bestows all perfections. Listen! (1)
O King, it is said in this world that for all branches of knowledge, there is no accomplishment without prior practice; therefore, a person should bring about such accomplishment.
O bull among men, it is declared that without *puraścaryā*, there is no accomplishment of any mantra, even through hundreds of crores of oblations and recitations.
He who has performed the preliminary rites (puraścaraṇa) together with the complete homa and japa,
and is endowed with full sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā), attains immediate and unsurpassed success.
The worship of the deity bestows the desired fruit that cannot be obtained even by a thousand acts of giving.
Nārāyaṇa is the leader of this entire phenomenal world;
he alone is called the Soul of the Universe and the Person of Sacrifice (Yajñapuruṣa). || 6 ||
Mahālakṣmī, who consists of the three Vedas, is the one and only mother of the worlds; she is the consort of the Lord and the cause of creation, preservation, and destruction.
Therefore, by worshipping the Blessed One, the Lord of the World, who is joined with Gama, one indeed attains the form of the Blessed One; it cannot be otherwise.
Then, even by means of all those various external disciplines, internal yogas, or sacrifices,
the realization of identity with Brahman cannot be accomplished without the worship of the illustrious Lord of Lords.
Therefore, one must certainly [worship] Nārāyaṇa, the eternal, the Lord of the three worlds, the infallible Sovereign, who is distinct from the eight-syllable vidyā. || 10 ||
Having first worshipped the consort of the Lord of the Universe, who possesses the three forms,
and then having worshipped Mahālakṣmī, one becomes a partaker in the attainment of identity with Brahman.
Even more powerful than a father is a mother in the protection of her own children;
therefore, sons should be known as devoted to their prosperity, which is as expansive as a lotus. 12.
Wealth is devoted to protection; therefore, O Blessed One, Mahālakṣmī, the beloved of Hari and the mother of all worlds, is superior to her. (13)
Those who worship Him have achieved their purpose and bear the very form of the Blessed Lord;
they alone are the sons of the Blessed One and also the sons of Mahālakṣmī.
Therefore, one must certainly strive for the accomplishment of knowledge;
for on this earth, he alone attains the perfection of the mantra of Prāsannakamalā whose success in knowledge is certain.
The Goddess Lakṣmī, accompanied by the Blessed One, protects him like a son;
one whose vows are unfailing attains success in the vidyā of the gracious Lakṣmī.
Having performed the preliminary rites (puraścaraṇa) without armlets or sacrificial fees, a man attains great success immediately; there is no doubt in this matter. || 17 ||
O King, it is accompanied by complete sacrificial fees, endowed with the excellence of the subsidiary fire-oblations,
and performed as a preliminary rite (puraścaryā) according to the prescribed rules.
Having attained the perfection of knowledge, he indeed becomes Hari himself in that place where the preceptor is worshipped during the rite of *puraścaraṇa*.

In that case, with garments and wealth accompanied by a full sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), that preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) shall become complete in all its parts and grant immediate success. || 20 ||
If one possesses even a small amount of wealth here while free from deceit, yet performs millions of *viprūcaryā* rites, that is proclaimed to be fruitless. (21)
In the absence of the teacher, one should worship the teacher’s son with that same intention;
or else, one should worship the teacher’s wife or his grandson.
In the absence of a grandson, O Lord of the Earth, one should honor the daughter or the daughter's son;
in the absence of a grandson, one should worship his brother.
In his absence, one should offer it to a sister’s son; if no such person exists, one should offer it to the Lord of Śrī.
Then, having placed it in [his] presence, one should finally entrust it to a worthy recipient.
O King, one should indeed construct a temple as a teacher’s fee (guru-dakṣiṇā);
for here, many great [temples] have been built in abundance according to the prescribed rites. (25)
It destroys even a sixteenth part of the fee due to the preceptor;
thus it is said, "one should perform the *puraścaraṇa* in the land of the Yavanas, for they are pure. (26)
My abode, the Badarī forest, is called Vaikuṇṭha;
there the Sālaka-nandā river emerged from the Himavat mountain.
Then there is the meritorious Vārāṇasī, which bestows great siddhis;
and Prayāga, the king of tīrthas, is remembered as the possessor of the three great siddhis. || 28 ||
The holy field of Śrī Puruṣottama, the abode of Jagannātha;
and the cities of Ayodhyā, Mathurā, Māyā (Vārāṇasī), Kāñcī, and Avantikā.
This city of liberation on the surface of the earth bestows the perfection of Dvārakā;
Gokarṇa is meritorious, and Kurukṣetra is even more so than that.
The confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean, the meritorious Rāmagiri,
Prabhāsa, the shore of the Sindhu, and beyond that, Padmanābha.
The confluence of the Vaśiṣṭhā and Sindhu, the mountain Tryaṃvaka, Satyāvaloman, Mahendra, Malaya, and likewise Śrīgiri; || 32 ||
The Śeṣācala mountain, the sacred site of Oraṅga, and the extremely purifying Kubhakoṇa; to the south of Setubaṃdha is the city of Mathurā.
Pāṇḍuraṅga, the great Siddhavaṭa praised by the sages,
and then Siṃhācala and other sacred fields (kṣetra) upon the earth.
The banks of the Gaṅgā, the Sarasvatī, and the Yamunā are supreme, bringing peace to many mortals and granting immediate success. (35)
Then [he went] to the bank of the Godāvarī, and also to the bank of the Narmadā, and to the bank of the Suvarṇamukharī, and to the bank of the Godāvarī. (36)
Then [he went to] the auspicious bank of the Mīmarathī, the beautiful bank of the Tunga-Bhadrā,
and the pure bank of the Kṛṣṇaveṇī, which bestows immediate spiritual perfection.
For all vidyās, success is achieved through the preliminary practice (puraścaraṇa). It is said that these [mantras] bring about immediate accomplishment in this world. 38.
The presence of the Ācārya everywhere is distinguished and bestows auspiciousness;
even when one possesses intelligence, there can be no accomplishment without the presence of the Ācārya. (39)
Whether it be the region of Trikalinga or wherever the Teacher is present,
that alone is declared to be the bestower of success for all branches of knowledge.
In the presence of the teacher, in a meritorious field that bestows success,
one who possesses the knowledge of the gracious Lakṣmī should perform the preliminary rites (puraścaraṇa).
Speaking untruths, lustfulness, sexual union with another's wife, malice toward Brahmins, envy, and eating forbidden food; (42)
One should always avoid those who speak unrefined words;
one should abandon the region of one who is censured for reviling his teacher. (43)
One who engages in the censure of an ācārya, or of one's father or mother, or even of a brother, a son, a wife, or a daughter; || 44 ||
One must certainly punish him; there is no fault in that, O Great Lord. If one who is capable does not punish the one who reviles the teacher, [he incurs sin]. (45)
He shall sink into the most terrible hells for as long as the moon and sun endure;
furthermore, what has been gained by him performing a hundred sacrifices with complete sacrificial fees? (46)
The fruits of the avaśati have been proclaimed by the great ancient teachers, as well as the [fruits] for sins such as the killing of a Brahmin, by Manu and other supreme sages. (47)

The scripture declares that there is no atonement for one who betrays the guru, for an enemy, or for one who has committed slander against the teacher; one should abandon such a person just as one would an outcaste.
Or else, those devoid of strength must go elsewhere while covering their ears;
[for they cannot endure] the earth consisting of seven continents and mountains, teeming with wealth, grain, and prosperity. (49)
O King, even though he had promised to give a single gold coin every day to his own teacher, he remained as if in debt to him day after day.

There is no doubt that by giving even a little food with devotion to those who are worthy recipients for the gift of millions of cosmic eggs, one discharges a debt equal to millions of cosmic eggs within a single month.
Even by the gift of all one's possessions, that [sin] is not pacified and perishes only after one month,
two months, or even three months.
Or [the word] *vām* [is used] together with the increase of the vowel and the consonant. || 54 ||
There is no one equal to one who possesses firm devotion to the pair of teachers;
nor is there anyone other than one who has firm devotion to the lotus-feet of the teacher and is steadfast in their vows. (55)
One who desires the highest good should always recite the Vidyā known as Prasannalakṣmī;
for the sake of its accomplishment, one should perform the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) beginning with the Brahmavārāha [mantra]. 56.

A twice-born man who performs the *puraścaraṇa* rite accompanied by its ancillaries and sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) shall be worthy of worship even by the gods; having attained mastery over the sciences (*vidyāsiddha*), he becomes honored upon the earth.
Or, eating fruits that are free from pungent, salty,
and sour flavors, he may subsist on sacrificial food (vāha-viṣyānna) or even eat only a single meal a day.
He may observe the vow of Prajāpati, or the vow of the Cāndrāyaṇa as prescribed by Vasiṣṭha;
or he may subsist on the five products of the cow, bathing daily and having his senses subdued.
Accompanied by Vedic conduct, avoiding the company of the wicked,
sleeping on the ground, observing celibacy, and always intent upon the practice of *sahoṣṭhī*.
Whether in the midst of a Tulasī grove, by a well, at the root of a Bilva tree,
or in the presence of the Ācārya, one should practice to achieve that which is dear to the Lord.
In the Kṛta Yuga, the preliminary rite (puraścaryā) consists of one hundred thousand recitations;
in the Tretā Yuga, it shall be two hundred thousand, and in the Dvāpara Yuga, three hundred thousand.
The great sages have declared that in the Kali age, four hundred thousand recitations are required;
whereas in the Kṛta age, O Brahmins, people were always devoted to the study of the Vedas.
Even in times of adversity, they always speak words that are like fresh sprouts; O King, they constantly acquire wealth solely for the sake of their preceptor. (64)
O noble teacher, he was constantly devoted to serving [his preceptor] day and night;
he was eternally intent on the *agnihotra* sacrifice, a performer of rituals, and one who gave liberal sacrificial fees.
Having traveled even a thousand yojanas, they should offer a lotus;
those intent on honoring their own teacher do so even at the cost of their lives and wealth.
O Lord of the Earth, in the Tretā age, one quarter of Dharma is lost;
therefore, two hundred thousand [recitations] are prescribed for the attainment of prosperity in the Tretā age.
In the Dvāpara age, the aforementioned dharma shall be deficient by one quarter;
therefore, it is said that in the age named Dvāpara, [the lifespan] is three hundred thousand years.
Devoted to the practice of arts and unrighteousness, devoid of Vedic study, lacking in the conduct prescribed by the Vedas, they were speakers of falsehood and takers of what was not given. (69)
They are those who have heard the censure of the teacher. || 71 ||
Composing false scriptures on this earth through their own intellects,
these deceivers— themselves ruined— silently cause others to perish as well.
The Yavanas, who possess vast stores of grain and jewels, rejoice when they have been bitten by a serpent;
yet there is no mantra that lacks a presiding deity.

Those of dull intellect and meager fortune, who long for sexual pleasure with the wives of others, [disregard] the preceptor who is identical with the Blessed One and who bestows enjoyment, heaven, and liberation. (74)
In the Kali age, those who are intent on the constant pursuit of women—such as daughters, daughters-in-law, and so forth—even abandon their own father, who is like a god. 75.
False speech, quarreling, malice, envy, and intoxication—these are the dharma that flourishes when the Kali Yuga has arrived. (76)
Even after receiving the supreme Mantras from the lotus-like mouth of their teacher,
those seized by envy abandon them and act as enemies to their teacher.
Those who are devoted to Vedic conduct and Tantric practices abandon their personal names, as well as their family name and lineage, and adopt the name of the preceptor alone.
In the Kali age, there will be performers of rituals who offer only meager sacrificial fees;
likewise, teachers who have not reached the further shore of the scriptures will act for the sake of their own worship. (79)

They will impart the mantras alone to their disciples, devoid of the essential [instructions], even without [the disciples] knowing the great mantras, the ritual placements (nyāsa), the diagrams (yantra), the meditations (dhyāna), or the hymns (sūkta).
In this terrible Kali age, crowded with great sinners, those greedy for their own livelihoods will bestow instruction upon unworthy disciples. (81)
Among the thousands of men who were devotees of the couple formed by the feet of the Teacher,
there was one who had conquered his senses and whose mind was fixed on the Blessed One.
Having obtained the vidyās from that teacher, which bestow all perfections, their impurities were destroyed through service at the pair of the teacher’s feet. (83)
Success for those who are pure is desired through the grace of their teacher, due to the poet’s relative paucity of sin and the favor of the illustrious and high-minded Śrī Mahāmanu.
The recitation of four hundred thousand [mantras] is prescribed with care for the purpose of the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa);
having performed this fourfold hundred-thousand recitation according to the stated rule, one becomes pure.
The wise one should offer libations ten times [the number of mantras recited] with clarified butter or sugarcane juice;
then he should perform oblations one-tenth that amount with clarified butter mixed with the three sweets.
O Lord of the Earth, one should worship with lotuses or bilva leaves, or with offerings of food;
likewise, one should honor a hundred married women and also a hundred Brahmins.
Having first offered a pair of earrings to the ears of the preceptor, he should then place his two feet upon a heap of jewels belonging to the preceptor.
O King, by performing the preliminary rites (*puraścaryā*) in this manner, one becomes worthy of worship even by the immortals when Śrī is propitiated; he beholds Śrī with his own eyes. (89)
When she is pleased, what is there in the three worlds that cannot be accomplished by this protectress of the universe?
It is heard even from afar, reaching as far as a hundred yojanas.
Even with his own two eyes, he sees for a hundred thousand yojanas;
even the great Indra and the gods perform service for him.
And the entire web of knowledge, such as the Vedas and other sciences, though never studied, will undoubtedly emerge of its own accord from the lotus of his mouth. 92.
Day after day, Kuvera himself personally bestows upon him inexhaustible wealth, according to his desire and as much as he wishes.
In this world, the eight-syllable mantra itself becomes his physician for the limbs of Dharma; there is no other knowledge equal to it, which is free from disease and decay.
O Lord of the Earth, there is no truth in what is unspoken or even in that which is spoken;
the great power of these [truths] is fulfilled through the completion of the limbs and the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). 95.
There is no doubt that he is blessed by that *kṛtāya* alone;
for among men, flowers are few and the mind is also fickle. (96)
I shall proclaim another concise *puraścaryā* suitable for the Kali age;
it occurs when the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*) falls on a Monday. (97)
If the new moon day (amāvāsyā) should coincide with a Monday, or if it is joined with a Sunday,
this conjunction is known as Padmaka.
On the full moon day of the month of Soma, or on the solar festival (Raviparva),
he is proclaimed as the crest-jewel of the Moon (Candracūḍamaṇi) and likewise as the crest-jewel of the Sun (Ravicūḍāmaṇi).
Having made the teacher his refuge, for those three preceding days he should eat only one meal a day, constantly sleep on the ground, and keep his senses subdued.
Accompanied by all the ritual placements (nyāsa) of the glorious eight-syllabled mantra,
or even joined with the placement of each individual letter, [one should recite it] more than a hundred thousand times.
Having first recited the Mahālakṣmī-vidyā, which bestows desired fruits,
three thousand three hundred times, one should then recite the Śrī-hṛdaya-stava.

Then, when the fire has blazed up, the wise man should offer oblations twenty-eight times, having first performed the preliminary rites three times. Then, having gone forth, he should sacrifice with the *ida* and other portions.
Thereafter, he should shake [the vessel] twenty-eight times with the eight-syllable vidyā,
and another hundred times with the vidyā of the gracious consort of the Blessed One.
One who serves the teacher should always offer cow-derived ghee into the fire;
furthermore, upon the arrival of the new moon or a festival day, one should likewise offer it.

Then, having bathed at the time of the [solar] conjunction, he respectfully bowed to the Lord; having praised Him according to the rules, he remained restrained, offering great reverence and the like.
Having performed the rite twenty-eight times with the glorious eight-syllable vidyā,
one should offer one hundred and eight bilva leaves smeared with ghee.
Or else, with black sesame seeds mixed with the three kinds of honey,
one should perform more than a thousand repetitions using the Lakṣmīhṛdaya mantra.
Or one should offer oblations into the fire with clarified butter alone;
having performed the ancillary rites of expiation, one should then bow down to the fire with devotion.
Having bowed with devotion using the eight limbs of the body to the pair of feet of the teacher,
one should offer all one's wealth, even that which is situated within one's own home.
Or he should offer to the preceptor the materials required for a year’s subsistence,
or else a pair of earrings together with twelve *niṣkas*.
Then, O King, he should offer it at the two feet of the preceptor, having offered whatever else is possible, such as an ear-ornament or another gift. (112)
Having given a pair of fine garments, one should give wealth measured by three *niṣkas*—either six *niṣkas*, or three *niṣkas* starting from that. || 113 ||
Having offered her at the lotus feet of the preceptor, he should then worship the preceptor’s beloved wife with garments, ornaments, and other such gifts according to his ability.
One should feed the most excellent brahmins and twelve married women;
immediately thereafter, one should perform the worship of the preceptor with gold and land.
Having given a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) according to one's ability to the Brahmins who have arrived as guests,
one should present the Dāsanī once the Brahmins have finished eating.
After the meal, he gratified the auspicious women with gifts;
through the grace of the preceptor, they immediately attained unsurpassed perfection.
If the king or the prince has been separated from many [possessions],
he should give this earth, endowed with much wealth, to the teacher.
Or else, O King, for the sake of attaining mastery in the *Vidyā* of Prasannalakṣmī, [one should perform the rite] accompanied by many sacrificial fees and joined with four bulls. (119)
Having given a Śālagrāma stone along with a gift according to one's means,
one should give the aforementioned fee (dakṣiṇā) together with clothing and ornaments.
Whatever object is offered in the Cūḍāmaṇimahāyoga at the feet of the Ācārya, that shall proceed to the Dakṣapāta [state]. || 121 ||
Having performed this preliminary rite (puraścaryā) according to the instructions of King Yugacūḍāmaṇi, he attains supreme perfection in the Cūḍāmaṇi-prasannalakṣmī-vidyā. || 122 ||
In that [state], one who has performed the sacrifice for a year necessarily attains an eternal, unshakable, and sinless prosperity, crowded with floods of jewels and wealth.
Having become one whose mind acts according to its own will, having attained unsurpassed long life and great good fortune, he shall be endowed with equal prosperity through his sons and grandsons.
Having thus performed the *puraścaryā* during an eclipse of the sun or the moon, one attains eternal liberation at the end of the body, even though it is difficult to obtain. (125)
Whether threefold, fivefold, or even twelve-hundredfold,
having long possessed the memory of past births, she shall be filled with an abundance of wealth, grain, and livestock.
Having obtained unshakable wealth consisting of an abundance of jewels, horses, and chariots, as well as a vast lineage of sons and grandsons; (127)
Having attained the limbs of yoga and enjoyed pleasures that are difficult to obtain,
he likewise dwells in Vaikuṇṭha accompanied by thousands of his kinsmen.
Or rather, when the nine-night period dedicated to the Aśvins has been completed,
each single day therein possesses a splendor equal to that of a crest-jewel (cūḍāmaṇi).
This was declared by all the exponents of Brahman at the great sacrifice of Arvavasu:
"This is the Vidya of the Gracious Lakshmi; it necessarily bestows its fruit therein. (130)
Day by day, the fruit there increases a hundredfold;
that [day] is declared by the supreme seers as the great Navamī.
The day of the hundred-thousandth lunar day is known as Ravicūḍāmaṇi;
it is conjoined with a Saturday and associated with the Vaiśvadeva constellation.
This path to the glory of universal sovereignty was taught there by the supreme sages;
having received the command of the Teacher on the very first day, [one should proceed].
Having bathed in the morning, with a purified soul, he should duly recite the Mother of the Vedas (the Gāyatrī) one thousand times,
or even three hundred times, while the fire is blazing.
Having offered oblations twenty-eight times with the Gāyatrī mantra using clarified butter and cow's milk,
one should offer twenty-eight oblations to the illustrious Aṣṭāparṇa using horse-flesh.
Having completed the fire-oblation rite day after day, one should offer one hundred and eight oblations with the Lakṣmī-hṛdaya-vidyā.

Having first performed the preliminary rites according to one's ability, one should recite the glorious eight-syllabled mantra and this Great Knowledge of Sovereignty (Sāmrājya-Śrī-Mahāvidyā) more than five hundred times.
One who is pure and attentive in mind should recite it a thousand times daily;
or else, having made a formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*), one may recite twelve thousand times during a nine-day sacrificial session (*navasatra*).
A wise person should constantly recite this auspicious Mahāvidyā, which is the Ātharvaṇa Mahālakṣmī Hṛdaya, the bestower of desires. 139.
The pure one should recite the mantra forty-five times; well-dressed women should be fed with the thought that they are the Great Lakṣmī herself. 140.
On the Mahānavamī day, having performed the ritual purification according to the rules,
he offered twenty-eight oblations of clarified butter preceded by the Vedic meters.
Having offered one hundred and eight oblations with the glorious eight-syllable vidyā, and having invoked the Fortune of Sovereignty (Sāmrājya-lakṣmī) and worshipped her with ritual offerings; 142.
One should offer one thousand three hundred oblations with *kuśeśaya* flowers, combined with curd, honey, and ghee, for the attainment of prosperity.
Alternatively, offer clarified butter mixed with honey—the three sweets—along with bilva leaves and black sesame seeds. (144)
One should offer one thousand three hundred oblations with the *Śrīsūkta* mantra;
thereafter, one should proceed with the *Lakṣmīhṛdaya* mantras in their worldly forms.
One should reverently offer oblations five times or three times into the fire with the *Ravi-mantra*;
or, according to one's capacity, one should offer oblations with the *Śrī-mantroddhāra* mantra.
Then, after that, [one should recite] the mantras of the heart of Lakṣmī, which take the form of moving worlds. || 146 ||
One should offer one hundred and eight oblations of auspicious cow-dung;
having performed the recitation and other rites, as well as the fire-offering, one should then perform the oblation for atonement.
Having offered the oblation as an offering to Brahman and bowed to the fire thereafter,
he prostrated with all eight limbs before the pair of feet of the preceptor.
One should offer perfumes, unbroken rice grains, ornaments, and garments;
and having offered two cows along with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) at the feet of the preceptor.
One should offer abundant wealth at the pair of feet of the preceptor—either a thousand niṣkas, or a hundred, or half of that, or half of that again. || 150 ||
Or twelve *niṣkas*, or even six *niṣkas*, or five *niṣkas* of gold, or three *niṣkas*, O excellent gurus. (151)
Having abandoned all attachment to the pair of his lotus-like feet,
he offered a collection of garments and ornaments to the preceptor’s wife.
One should respectfully offer [the gift] according to one's ability, honoring it with the thought that it is Śrī herself,
in the presence of the Ācārya, provided his wife, sons, and others are not present.
In the presence of the Blessed One, she offered all her wealth as a sacrificial gift; the teacher’s wife and sons took that wealth. || 153 ||
When wealth exists, there should be a gift of land accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees, joined with four bulls, and provided with a pair of earrings. || 155 ||

A wise person desiring supreme welfare must certainly offer [the oblation] to the highest [deity]; furthermore, twelve Brahmins should be fed, including those who have recently married and young women. 156.
Having received the embrace of the teacher and being honored by his blessings, he attains great success in the science of prognostication through clear conversation. || 157 ||
The attainment of imperial sovereignty is achieved in ten years, even after performing a hundred deeds or acquiring wealth with great effort. (158)
Having adorned his own preceptor with ornaments, one who desires success should offer him along with a full sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). || 159 ||
Having performed the Navarātra vow, which is exceedingly purifying,
one certainly attains the fruit of a hundred puraścaryās along with its ancillaries.
There exists no other vow equal to the Navarātra vow;
such is the auspicious accomplishment that arises from the Navarātra vow.
O Prajāpati, for a man who has observed the vow of Navarātra, such perfection as that which is attained through thousands of *puraścaraṇa* rites shall come to pass.
Having performed the Navarātra vow with devotion according to the prescribed rules along with its auxiliary rites, one should recite the mantra for that year; of this there is no doubt. (163)
Having attained great success, they shall reach the end of long life;
having attained great health, they shall be filled with an abundance of wealth, grain, and prosperity.

One who is devoted to virtue and whose cause is merit obtains unshakable prosperity, filled with elephants, horses, and chariots—a wealth that is very difficult to attain even in the three worlds. (165)
The goddess Ramā, who extends her lineage as far as the moon and sun, shall indeed dwell there, abounding in grain and other riches;
of this there is no doubt. (166)
Having thus performed the preliminary rites and having recited the *prasanna-śrī-mahā-mantra* five hundred times, he offered twenty-eight oblations of clarified butter as prescribed. (167)
Having offered oblations in the evening, one should again recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times;
for a man who practices in this manner, a mass of good fortune increases.
For one who protects Jayaśrī, great and supreme good fortune arises, and [the house] becomes filled with wealth, grain, horses, elephants, and cattle. (169)
Prosperity pervading his lineage and abounding with sons, grandsons, and others shall attend him;
even all the foremost of kings shall perform service for him.
Thus, having performed the *puraścaryā* daily with devotion every morning, he is honored day by day in the presence of kings, scholars, and the assembly. (171)
Having recited [the mantra] five hundred times, one indeed goes to the abode of Lakṣmī;
there, one shall possess unshakable, victorious fortune, as well as honor, manliness, and fame. (172)
In this temple, Mahālakṣmī increases day by day;
for him, there shall be the growth of his lineage as long as the moon and sun endure. 173.
Day by day, his welfare certainly increases at every step;
even that which is incurable for the gods, or situated on another continent, [is overcome]. 174.
Everything desired is indeed accomplished; there is no doubt in this matter.
One uplifts a thousand members of one's lineage from the foremost ocean of hell. 175.
At the end of the body, one attains the supreme abode of Viṣṇu; of this there is no doubt.
During the spring Navarātra, one should perform the *puraścaraṇa* with devotion. (176)
Having performed this very [rite], one attains great, unsurpassed accomplishment.
Now, O King, I shall explain another method of sādhana. || 177 ||
The vow known as Bhṛguvāra-vrata is a means for accomplishing the heart's desire for Lakṣmī;
it may be observed in the months of Śrāvaṇa, Kārttika, Mārgaśīrṣa, or Āśvina.
In the month of Māgha, Phālguna, or Vaiśākha, on an auspicious day of Śiva, during the first fortnight of the waxing moon, preceded by the command of one's own teacher; || 179 ||
Having bathed in the morning, with a purified soul, he should offer a thousand oblations of the Mother of the Vedas,
or even three hundred, into the blazing fire.
Having divided the clarified butter from cows, which consists of the measures of the Vedas, into twenty-eight parts,
one should likewise divide it twenty-eight times with the eight-syllable Śrīmantra.
Then, having offered one hundred and eight oblations of pure cow’s ghee with the Lakṣmī-hṛdaya mantra, one should worship Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa.
With fragrant flowers or bilva leaves, one should recite the Indirā-hṛdaya mantra one thousand three hundred times while employing the Brahmavidyā.
With the thought that they are Śrī and Śrīpati, one should reverently worship a pair of couples, or two pairs, or even a single couple. (184)
Whether having not eaten or having already eaten, one should again recite the Prasanna-Śrī-Mahāvidyā one hundred and eight times with devotion in the evening.
Then, desiring welfare, one who is pure should recite the *Śrīhṛdaya*, which begins with the syllable *ĀṬHA*, five times on every Friday.
Having performed the recitation (japa) in this manner, he began the fire-oblation (homa) starting from the first day of the month of Bhādrapada,
until the full moon of Śrāvaṇa on an auspicious day of the week presided over by Venus (Bhārgava).
On the day of Varalakṣmī, having offered three hundred oblations of clarified butter with the Lakṣmīhṛdaya-vidyā according to its name, one should then perform the recitation as before. || 188 ||
On that day,
[one should give] three niṣkas, two niṣkas, or even one niṣka to the teacher’s wife or to the teacher’s lotus-feet.
Having offered [the oblation] on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika when the sun has risen,
he should likewise offer three hundred oblations there with the Lakṣmī-hṛdaya-vidyā.
There too, as before, having given the teacher a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), on the full moon day of Mārgaśīrṣa, [one should worship] with the Lakṣmīhṛdaya-vidyā. || 190 ||
There too, having offered three hundred oblations with clarified butter from a cow,
the practitioner should give a sacrificial fee, as before, at the two feet of his own teacher.
In the absence of the guru, his wife or his son may perform this;
having thus performed the vow on a Saturday, O most purifying one! (192)
Within a year, one attains the accomplishment of the *vidyā* of Prasannalakṣmī;
one also obtains long life, flowers, and all forms of prosperity. (193)
Having attained great health, and having obtained vast prosperity extending through his lineage, [he was surrounded] by a multitude of elephants, horses, and chariots. (194)
One obtains even the sovereign power of qualities such as atomization (aṇimā), which is difficult to attain in the three worlds,
as well as divine collyrium that serves as the cause for the manifestation of supernatural powers.
From the curved horse of the wind, all eternal sciences emerge;
one shall not be separated from wealth, nor from wife, nor from sons.
One should not be separated from jewels, cattle, or even kinsmen;
for one attains the eight kinds of enjoyments that are otherwise difficult to obtain.
Accompanied by a thousand members of his lineage, he shall sport in Vaikuṇṭha;
this is for one of restrained self who desires perfection both here and in the hereafter. (198)
One should constantly perform this rite for the sake of a multitude of kings and Brāhmaṇas, for the attainment of unsurpassed fame, and for unshakable prosperity. (199)
O King, one who desires the state of the Blessed One and wishes to know Bharga must especially perform this vow, which brings about the increase of prosperity.
One who is the best of practitioners seeking success through the *lakṣmīhṛdayavidyā* and is capable should perform all the vows, such as the *navarātra*. (201)
O Blessed One, Mahālakṣmī herself, who consists of the three Vedas, is pleased with those endowed with poetic art;
of this there is no doubt. I speak the truth, the absolute truth. (202)
This great preliminary rite (puraścaryā), complete with its ancillaries and full sacrificial fees, has been described by me at length; it bestows success upon those who desire it. (203)
Through that goddess, the direct vision of Mahālakṣmī arises;
from that, even the most desired success of those things difficult to achieve will surely come to pass.
O King, it equalizes even the conduct of Indra and Yama;
there is no time for merit in the three worlds equal to the moment of the eclipse.
The sages who discourse upon Brahman have declared that all practices such as recitation (japa) and fire-offerings (homa), even during periods of impurity caused by childbirth, must not be abandoned.
As long as there is grasping and liberation, for that long my impurity (sūtaka) remains;
indeed, that very state is the Great Time (Mahākāla) consisting of the giving of everything to the Saṅghas.
If the crest-jewel (cūḍāmaṇi) is obtained there on the ground, then all [acts] such as recitation and fire-offerings yield inexhaustible fruit. || 208 ||

Those desiring the accomplishment of all vidyās should, with devotion, perform the preliminary rite (puraścaryā) during the months of Graiṣma, accompanied by the giving of sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā). || 209 ||
The Navarātra vow destroys all great sins and pacifies every misfortune; this occurs year after year, without a doubt. (210)
For all vidyās as well, there is a great and inexhaustible accomplishment;
during the vow of the nine nights, it becomes subject to one's will—of this there is no doubt. (211)
The Bhṛguvāra-vrata, which brings about all auspiciousness both here and in the hereafter, is declared to be unsurpassed and necessarily bestows all perfections.
In this compendium of the Vedas, titled *Anuttarabrahmatattvārtha*,
the forty-first chapter, which bestows all glory, has been declared.
[Thus ends the fortieth chapter in the venerable *Anuttarabrahmatattvarahasya*, the *Daśarathīya Tantra*, which is a compendium of the meaning of the Vedas. 40.
The Blessed One said:
Through this propitious Lakṣmī, who is both ignorance and supernatural power (siddhi),
one may accomplish all rites performed for specific desires and is thereby glorified.
Observing celibacy and eating sacrificial food,
one should recite this mantra— which bestows all accomplishments— one hundred thousand times at the base of a bilva tree.
By offering oblations there with bilva leaves smeared with ghee and honey, one obtains inexhaustible wealth, jewels, and grain.
Having offered one hundred and eight oblations daily with pure mango fruits soaked in the three sweets, cow products, and clarified butter, [he should worship] the two mandalas.
Within two months from that day, she, who is dear to the Blessed One,
will appear to you either in person or even in a dream, manifesting her embodied form.
In that person's house, there immediately arises great and inexhaustible prosperity, abounding in elephants, camels, horses, and so forth, as well as great and difficult-to-obtain wealth.
One joined with a portion of the Blessed One will certainly obtain a son;
one should daily recite [the mantra] three hundred and eight times while gazing at the rising sun.
If one performs oblations with offerings saturated with the three sweets, cow products, and clarified butter,
one shall attain imperishable, auspicious good fortune.
One certainly becomes equal to Kubera in wealth through the *amulā* [mantra];
one should daily offer oblations with *caṃpaka* flowers three hundred and eight times.
Purified as before by offerings drenched in the three sweets, cow-products, and clarified butter,
he became free from doubt regarding the mandala and possessed a splendor equal to that of Kāmadeva.
O King,
one who subjugates even rulers upon the surface of the earth attains royal fortune that never diminishes for his own lineage.
Having offered oblations with flowers from the *kiṃśuka* tree, drenched in the three kinds of honey,
into a blazing fire for one hundred times with devotion, [one should perform the rite].
He shall become the presiding deity over all branches of knowledge;
and all sciences, together with their auxiliary limbs, shall issue forth from his lotus-like mouth.
Having offered one hundred thousand oblations of dūrvā grass sprinkled with clarified butter, he becomes free from disease and lives for a long time; of this there is no doubt.
Having offered blue lotuses mixed with the three sweets, one brings kings under control, and even their servants thereafter. || 15 ||
Having reverently offered ten thousand oblations of milk-rice mixed with honey, the three sweets,
cow-products, and clarified butter, the Brahmin beholds the beloved of Hari.
Having obtained the Mahādāpuṣpa flower, one shall obtain a rain of wealth;
one should offer oblations of guḍūcī sprinkled with ghee for seven days.
By offering one hundred and eight oblations of sesame seeds smeared with ghee, performed one thousand and eight times, one shall obtain long life.
The mantra-knower who constantly offers oblations of three hundred and eight *śāli* rice grains attains health, as well as all his desired objects.
From the maṇḍala itself, great prosperity certainly arises;
the practitioner of mantras should offer oblations with flowers produced from the Lakṣmī-vallī creeper.
One who is born under the Nandyāvarta configuration attains great prosperity through the fulfillment of all desires and is honored by all living beings.

With apūpas mixed with black pepper and cumin, combined with the dust from the temples of female elephants, enriched with ghee and royal curd, and prepared according to the prescribed measurements, he performed the sacrifice.

One who has conquered the senses should daily offer oblations of milk-rice (pāyasa) accompanied by mantras one hundred and eight times; from the mandala, he shall become a forest-fire (consuming all obstacles).
One should offer oblations with clarified butter mixed with jaggery, and one will become possessed of food;
one should offer japā flowers one thousand and eight times.
Having taken [the ash] mixed with the juice of betel leaf, one should mutter the mantra while applying it as a tilaka upon the body; this is the supreme means for bringing all under one's control.
The self-controlled one should satisfy the Brahmins with fuel-sticks, flowers, and water from the *brahmavṛkṣa*;
the Kṣatriyas with *jātī* flowers; and the Vaiśyas with auspicious red lotuses.

The best of those who know mantras, having offered oblations of blue lotuses with *śūdrānnī* (rice cooked in the milk of a Śūdra woman), brings [the target] under control; likewise, by offering oblations with *manohā* flowers, he brings women under his power.
Having offered oblations and having fashioned the mandala consisting of nine parts, adorned with yantras,
one should perform the ritual according to the prescribed rule for the sake of attaining all siddhis.

The best of those who know mantras should place the jars upon those auspicious spots with flowers— jars whose entire bodies are smeared with sandalwood paste and which are provided with *kūrca* grass and syllables.
Then, having wrapped [the image] in fine silk (dukūla) and covered it with pure garments,
one should fill [the vessel] with excellent waters from sacred bathing places (tīrtha) that are fragrant.
The most excellent preceptor, having filled the central pitcher— which is fashioned from gold increased by nine gems— with water, should cause it to flow forth.
Having ground together one part each of candana, śīra, karpūra, jāti, bīja, kīla, kuṅkuma, kuṣṭha, agaru, tamāla, and elā, according to their respective portions; || 32 ||
One should also cast into all the jars the best gems,
as well as *lakṣmī*, *harivāsa*, *dābhadrā*, *sahadevī*, and *madhuvratā*.
Muśalī, cakravallī, cakra, kāntā, apāmārga, padmaja, priyaṅgu, mudga, godhūma, vrīhi, tila, and upava.
Having washed rice, beans, and lentils, one should place them into these [liquids]:
the juice of dhātrī, kucaka, bilva, āmra, kadalī, and coconut.
Having also scattered these various parts, one should strew these flowers:
the lotus, the saugandhika, the jasmine, the mallikā, and likewise the vakula. (36)
[He offered] leaves produced from the Campaka, Aśoka, Aśoka, Punnāga, Tulasī, and Ketaka, as well as from the Śveta, Bakula, Udumbara, and Śākhila trees. (37)
Having cast the *brahmakūrca* [mixture] and covered it with unripe fruits and unbroken grains (*akṣata*),
one should then cover the openings of the jars with cloths.
One should worship Mahālakṣmī in the central kalaśa within the āvartī;
one should worship Umā and the others in the remaining eight kalaśas, starting from the northeast and proceeding in a clockwise direction.
Having touched them with charming perfumes, flowers, along with incense and lamps, and with various offerings of food, both solid and soft, one should recite the mantra.
Desiring victory over the three thousand worlds, one should touch the middle jar with the *kalaśa-śaṃsī* mantra;
at the conclusion of the three-thousand-fold recitation, the preceptor should bring the object of attainment (*sādhya*) near.
Having established a pedestal upon the sacrificial ground, he should place the image upon it,
having adorned it with beautiful ornaments and garments with great care.
Accompanied by auspicious women scattering flowers and unbroken grains of rice, he was honored by the twice-born with blessings preceded by benedictions. (43)
While the five drums resound at the beginning,
the wise man should lift up the pitcher situated in the center, while recollecting Mahālakṣmī.
The preceptor should also consecrate [the disciple] in sequence with other jars, using the Puṃsūkta, or with various beautiful hymns (sūktas) headed by the Puruṣasūkta. || 45 ||
Having thus consecrated him with such hymns as the Ānādi-sūkta, the preceptor, the teacher,
should then apply the remaining water to the head of the disciple.
May there be auspiciousness and well-being; may Mahālakṣmī be gracious toward you.
May the Goddess protect you always, and may prosperity be yours at all times. 48.
Thereafter, he should also be sprinkled with drops of clarified butter named Śāṭī;
then, having risen after being consecrated, he should put on an upper garment.
Having performed the ritual ablution according to the prescribed rule, the practitioner should then prostrate before the Guru like a staff;
thereafter, he should adorn himself with perfumes and other offerings.

One should satisfy [the deity] according to the prescribed rite with garments, ornaments, grain, wealth, cows, horses, and so forth, as well as female and male servants, while regarding them with the thought that they are Indirā herself.
He should feed the Brahmins along with the poor, the elderly, and the wretched;
then, through the grace of his guru, he should contemplate himself as having attained his purpose.
An anointed king conquers his enemies after a long time;
one who desires a position attains that position, O son of Rīja, without a doubt. (52)
Having been consecrated, she who was barren gave birth to a son of great intelligence;
and when great diseases arose, the preceptor [performed rites] against the bodies possessed by malevolent spirits (kṛtyā).
In the event of portents of spirits, evil omens, and the like, one should perform an ablution;
it bestows all prosperity upon men and grants the attainment of all good fortune.
Those who are well-versed in the meaning of the scriptures call this consecration the pacifier of all diseases and the destroyer of all calamities. (55)
He who is consecrated according to the prescribed rite shall obtain undecaying royal splendor, great wealth,
flowers, health, elephants, jewels, and horses.
Even though great wealth, prosperity, and riches are easily obtained, hereafter follows the practice of this *Hṛdaya* of the Great Mahālakṣmī. (57)
I shall speak of that which bestows the great siddhis; listen with a concentrated mind.
When the month of Vaiśākha has arrived, it is the bestower of the *amiṇupha* siddhi.
On the third lunar day known as Akṣayā, or on the full moon day,
having bathed in the morning by the command of the teacher, one should perform the twilight prayer (saṃdhyā) and the life-essence rite (prāṇāyāma).
Having completed the daily obligatory rites according to the rules,
he should offer twenty-eight oblations of clarified butter from the cow into the consecrated fire.
Then, with the glorious eight-syllable mantra, one hundred and eight oblations of clarified butter should be offered,
along with the auspicious fruits of the crops of the pleased royal fortune.
Then, one who is firm in his vows should offer a thousand three hundred oblations of clarified butter mixed with honey and sesame seeds, free from any impurities.
Thereafter, having offered one hundred and eight oblations for each of the four forms of the Goddess of Universal Sovereignty (Sāmrājya-lakṣmī) with fruits soaked in wine; || 63 ||
Then, having offered oblations one by one with the great mantras of the Ātharvaṇa, which reside in the heart of Lakṣmī, he subsequently performed the expiatory oblations.
Having performed the oblation with the "brahmārpaṇa" mantra and having bowed down before the foremost [deity],
he then prostrated himself with all eight limbs at the pair of feet of the preceptor.
Having given a pair of beautiful earrings made of refined gold and set with rubies to the ears of the preceptor, [he should proceed]. (66)
Alternatively, one should offer [the image] made of copper weighing two karṣas;
or else, one made of heated gold weighing one karṣa.
O Lord of the Earth, one should also give a pair of earrings from Tāṭakā’s ornaments, or even a pair from Vālī’s,
to the two ears of the preceptor’s beloved wife.

Having adorned his own preceptor, who is identical with the Blessed One, with fragrant powders, incense, and flowers, and having offered him auspicious sandalwood paste along with a pair of fine garments; || 69 ||
One should give a large panasa fruit, endowed with many fruits,
along with abundant sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) in the presence of the preceptor.
One should give three fruits along with a large betel nut, accompanied by a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā),
consisting of either twenty-five hundred niṣkas, or twelve niṣkas.
If incapable, he should offer five niṣkas or three niṣkas;
thereafter, he should feed five Brāhmaṇas or five married women.
One who desires the earth should gratify the Brahmins with curd-rice, seasonal fruits, vehicles, banners, and other such gifts, as well as with sacrificial fees.
Having first observed his vows himself, he should eat together with his kinsmen;
then, having received the embrace of his preceptor and being honored by that teacher’s blessings, [he should proceed]. (74)
He beholds the Goddess Śrī herself, accompanied by Nārāyaṇa;
do not go below her—of this there is no doubt—for she is saluted even by Brahmā and Rudra. (75)
Even one of very little fortune obtains from the heart-mantra and others the great imperishable flower,
as well as the sovereignty of powers such as *aṇimā* and the excellence of recollecting past births.
Having attained and enjoyed great prosperity, filled with an abundance of elephants, horses, chariots, wealth, and jewels, as well as pleasures that are difficult to obtain; || 77 ||
He remains right here in the presence of the Blessed One; of this there is no doubt.
Furthermore, I shall describe the means of accomplishment which bestows great siddhi.
Having heard which, even a wise man is liberated from the multitudes of calamities;
formerly, all the gods and asuras, having come together with one another—
Beginning from the first lunar day (pratipad), those endowed with the power of Nārāyaṇa were deprived of their fortune and stripped of their prosperity due to a curse from Urvāsī. || 79 ||
O King, at the command of Mukunda, they churned the ocean for the sake of beholding Mahālakṣmī, who is the mistress of the churning for the nectar of immortality.
From the seventh day after their birth, all [signs] such as the casting of dice appeared at the proper time; yet, even when they were playing anywhere, no sweat appeared upon them. (81)
On the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika, there, the gods and demons, abstaining from food, [recited] the one named Lakṣmīhṛdaya.
Chanting the auspicious and glorious eight-syllabled mantra with one-pointed minds,
those monkeys of great splendor performed the churning of the ocean for Hari.
On the twelfth day at sunrise, the divine Mahālakṣmī, the Mother of the Universe, adorned with celestial ornaments, appeared from the midst of the ocean.
Adorned with a crown, necklaces, earrings, bracelets, and other ornaments,
she is graced with a garland of thousand-petaled lotuses and even possesses the three Vedas.
Having seen Nārāyaṇa, Brahmā, Īśa, and even those headed by Śakra, they fell prostrate before the chest of the Blessed One.
Beholding Tāpa, Śakra and the other gods, together with the hosts of Maruts, became the support of all prosperity for the sake of the earth. || 87 ||
Then the Blessed Lakṣmī spoke to all the gods as well:
"Listen, O Brahmā, Rudra, and others, along with Indra and the rest, together with the sages! (88)
For the welfare of all the worlds, I shall proclaim this glory-bringing [rite] in this month of Kārtika by name, [worshipping the goddess] Umā together with her husband.
All those men who perform sacrifices on this day of my birth become partakers of good fortune, provided they are observers of noble vows and worship me with devotion.
I dwell in the house of that person who, out of love for me, gives this golden necklace; it shall be filled with a flood of wealth and jewels.
I shall declare this supreme secret, which is the eternal essence of all the Vedas and Vedāntas, and which bestows all spiritual accomplishments.
When the first lunar day (pratipad) of the month of Kārttika has arrived,
one should begin by prostrating before the two lotus-feet of the preceptor.
Having bathed in the morning with the permission of his teacher, being pure every day,
he should mutter the Mother of the Vedas (the Gāyatrī) either one thousand or three hundred times.
Having completed the daily fire-oblation (nityahoma) in the Jātavedas fire blazing with straight flames,
he should offer clarified butter twenty-eight times, measured by the Vedic meters (vedamātra).
Having offered oblations twenty-eight times with the glorious eight-syllable vidyā,
one should offer clarified butter one hundred and eight times from the vessel of the gracious-faced one.

Having made a formal resolve (saṃkalpa) with devotion for one thousand recitations of the glorious eight-syllabled mantra, one should chant it day by day until the tenth day, with a mind focused on a single desire.
Thereafter, having made a formal resolve (saṃkalpa) regarding the great mantra known as the Heart of Mahīlakṣmī, Śibi should recite it ten thousand times a day until the tenth day.
Or he should eat sacrificial food (haviṣya) devoid of salt, fat, and sour substances;
[reciting] either the twelve-syllable Lakṣmī-mantra or the six-syllable Śrī-mantra. 99.
Endowed with devotion, the wise man should recite [the mantra] one thousand times;
and on the eleventh day, he should receive [the initiation] preceded by the teacher's command.

Having bathed in the morning according to the prescribed rules and having completed the daily obligatory rites, he should prostrate before the feet of the teacher, who is the witness and the limb [of the ritual]. || 101 ||
Having first offered one hundred and eight oblations of clarified butter with the Vedic meters into the fire consecrated according to rule, using the glorious eight-syllable mantra; 102.
One should offer clarified butter from a cow fifteen hundred times,
or one thousand three hundred times with lotuses or water-lilies.
The best of practitioners should offer oblations with the Lakṣmī-hṛdaya mantra, using cow’s ghee mixed with the three kinds of honey.
One should perform the oblation either with the twelve-syllable Lakṣmī mantra or with the six-syllable mantra,
using bilva leaves mixed with cow's ghee and honey in the absence of lotuses.
Being pure, one should offer oblations according to the prescribed rite into the blazing fire, using bilva leaves mixed with tulasī and auspicious flowers. 106.
O gods, these two, Vṛhadāraṇya and I, worship the illustrious Śrīśa;
Brahmā has bestowed upon us this thousand and three hundred-fold [mantra] through the Brahmavidyā.
Having worshipped at night, one should then perform the lustration ceremony with ghee;
then, having risen during the Brāhma-muhūrta on the twelfth day, one should bathe.
Having recited the Sāvitrī three hundred times, and having offered one hundred and eight oblations of clarified butter with devotion into the blazing fire while chanting the Gāyatrī; 109.
One should offer one hundred and eight oblations with the glorious eight-syllable mantra;
thereafter, one should offer one hundred and eight oblations with lotuses using my vidyā.
In the absence of a lotus, one should offer cow's ghee with my mantra;
or one who desires water alone should offer oblations with the rays of the Blessed One.

Having offered oblations on the previous day as well, and then [having been purified] in three ways by the rays of the Lord, he prostrated himself before the pair of preceptors with full-body obeisance (sāṣṭāṅga). || 112 ||
Having adorned it with perfumes and flowers, one should offer a pair of golden earrings, sixty *civukas* in weight, set with rubies.
Having offered gold as a token of trust at the lotus-feet of the preceptor,
he should then present a pair of garments made of linen or even cotton.
A pure Śālagrāma stone fashioned from cloth and insects,
along with two cows accompanied by their calves, should be offered together with abundant sacrificial fees.
The preceptor, the most excellent of teachers, should offer it into the lotus-hand of the disciple;
a wealthy man or a prince should give a thousand-fold sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
It may be one hundred [palas], or half of that, or even half of that again;
or it may measure five niṣkas, four niṣkas, or three niṣkas. || 117 ||
Free from greed for wealth, one should give riches to the teacher;
and having honored the teacher’s wife with garments, ornaments, and other such gifts. (118)
On that day, twelve unmarried girls and Brahmins should be fed;
one should honor them with gifts and with the banks [of the river], regarding them with the thought that they are deities.
Having received blessings from the teacher, he should eat together with his kinsmen;
thus, having performed the vow in Kārtika, he should go to the forest of extreme austerity.
One who possesses this supreme, eternal knowledge of the glorious eight-syllable mantra attains great siddhi immediately; of this there is no doubt.
I always protect those with many sons like my own children; of this there is no doubt.
Yet, for one of such ill fortune, it must constantly remain near him.
Having remained [in this state], I bestow upon you complete sovereignty endowed with the eight qualities,
as well as eternal lordship over the treasures beginning with Śaṅkha.
An inexhaustible heap of wealth and jewels, crowded with elephants and horses;
an inexhaustible great mountain of gold, and likewise an inexhaustible abundance of flowers. (123)
I grant him all inexhaustible enjoyments, both divine and human, as well as eternal good fortune; of this there is no doubt. (124)
This is the complete fee for my knowledge, which has now been brought to fruition, including all its ancillaries.
This great preliminary practice bestows great accomplishment;
for him, the fruit of that [practice] becomes tenfold—of this there is no doubt. (126)
Having thus performed the preliminary rite (puraścaryā) which grants success in the month of Kārttika,
one surely accomplishes even that which is unattainable for the gods, fulfilling every desire.
I bestow great prosperity upon those belonging to the lineage of Ācārya Anugraṭasva, as well as the eternal, supreme state even at the end.
Having daily acquired wealth for the sake of supporting the preceptor’s wife, sons, and others, he should constantly place that at the lotus feet of the preceptor. (129)
One certainly attains the fruit arising from a hundred horse-sacrifices performed with all their limbs and sacrificial fees; there is no doubt in this matter. (130)
The great divine sages have declared that the daily acquisition of wealth for the sake of one’s teacher, for marriage, and for sacrifice is a source of great merit. (131)
