By performing the act of honoring the sandals at the feet of the Teacher and giving the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) consisting of a Brahman, one attains eternal Brahman. || 132 ||
Having requested and given even a limited amount of wealth for the sake of marriage to a learned Brahmin who is poor, one attains eternal Brahman. (133)
Then, for the sake of performing sacrifices on the surface of the earth for either the preceptor or oneself, one should constantly acquire wealth, even if submerged by [the loss of] millions. (134)

Together with his ancestors, sons, grandsons, and others, he shall attain that supreme state; may he obtain that auspicious [state] from the lotus feet of the Blessed One’s Teacher on this day of my birth.
135. On this day of my birth, [may he attain it] at the lotus feet of the Teacher.
Even by giving whatever small fee one can, one shall attain supreme accomplishment. || 136 ||
From that time forward, having recited this mantra of twenty-seven syllables every day five hundred times in the morning and one hundred and eight times in the evening, [he attained his goal]. (137)
They shall attain supreme and long-lasting good fortune and the highest health; having quickly acquired true strength, their intellects shall become exalted. (138)
Through the excellence of his kingdom, like that of Bhagīratha, Aṃbarīṣa, and others,
he goes at the end of his body to the abode of the Blessed One, accompanied by his lineage.
O immortals, if one were to perform here the gift of land along with its constituent parts and the prescribed sacrificial fees, I would not be capable of describing the fruit of that merit.
The third lunar day of the bright fortnight in Vaiśākha bestows great siddhi,
and the full moon day of Vaiśākha is considered to grant great siddhi.
The Utthāna-dvādaśī in the month of Kārttika bestows all perfections;
the Ekādaśī in that same month is likewise remembered as granting great perfection.
One who is diligent for the sake of success, self-controlled, and devoted to me, should perform this vow without sloth on my birthday according to the prescribed rules. || 143 ||
Starting from the first day of the month until the twelfth day,
she performed that auspicious vow every year during the month of Kārtika.
Here too, endowed with a portion of the Blessed One’s own splendor, he is the mantra-form whose self is purified; he perceives his own self as being of the nature of Brahman. (145)
Even with his own eyes, he hears that which consists of the essence of consciousness and bliss; though dwelling at a distance, he beholds even the sky-dwellers.
Whether fortnightly or monthly,
he indeed beholds with his own eyes a woman made of meat alone, yet endowed with human features.
By reciting this vidyā that bestows my grace five hundred times,
one also makes others prosperous with wealth through the glance of one's own side-long look.
My devotee, by his own splendor, treats even the sovereignty of Mahendra and the wealth of the Asuras as mere blades of grass; of this there is no doubt. (149)
Having spoken thus, Mahālakṣmī, accompanied by Nārāyaṇa, said: "May she be well-disposed even as all the gods look on. (50)
Furthermore, I shall fully describe the vow to be observed on a Saturday, by performing which a practitioner attains great perfection in this world. (151)
In the month of Kārttika, or Mārgaśīrṣa, or Māgha, or even Phālguna;
or in Vaiśākha, or Śrāvaṇa, or even Āśvina—one may begin [the practice]. || 152 ||
A twice-born man, having commenced it on a Saturday, should perform this vow;
it is the cause of all prosperity, the source of clarified butter, and the bestower of both worldly enjoyment and liberation. (153)
The meritorious Bhārgavāravratam, which bestows fruit without effort, should be observed on the first Thursday of the auspicious months previously mentioned. (154)
One should undertake the vow that bestows the attainment of all fruits, reciting [the mantra] five hundred times daily, preceded by the command of one's own preceptor. (155)
Having likewise recited [the mantra] five hundred times on a Monday dedicated to Bhārgava (Śukra),
and having offered cow's ghee twenty-eight times into the fire beginning with the Gāyatrī, one attains prosperity.
Then, one should offer oblations one hundred and eight times with the Śrīmad-aṣṭākṣara mantra;
thereafter, one should perform three hundred oblations with the Prasannalakṣmī mantra.
One should feed three married women and also three virgins;
having honored the teacher’s wife, one should perform the rite of *ārātrika* on the day of Venus.
On the first day of the month of Bhādrapada, having worshipped the preceptor— who is like a father— or the son of Bhṛgu (Śukra),
one should offer garments and ornaments along with *jaṅghāpuṣpa* and other offerings.
O King, having offered a *karṣa* of gold, or half of that, or a *niṣka*, or half of that, to your own guru’s wife with the thought that she is Mahālakṣmī herself, [you shall attain success]. (160)
Or one should worship a single couple with the thought that they are the Lord of Lakṣmī;
in the presence of the teacher's wife and the rosary, one should offer [the oblation] at the feet of the Ācārya.
Or one may give it to the teacher’s son, or entrust it to his grandson;
O King, if none of these are present, one should do so in the presence of the Blessed One.
Having resolved upon the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), he should then send it;
or else, [he should offer it] to the pair of Śrī-pādukās resting upon the lotus-feet of the Ācārya.
After having offered [the vessel] and sent it forth, the practitioner,
observing the vow, should then perform the remaining part of this most excellent vow on a Saturday, the day of Bhārgava.
Having chanted this daily five hundred times, and one hundred and eight times in the evening, even one of meager fortune shall obtain wealth abounding in gold and jewels. (165)
Great fortune, consisting of elephants, horses, and chariots, is unstable;
it is not secured by sons, nor by a wife, nor even by jewels or wealth.
One shall never be separated from cattle, nor shall one ever become a consumer of grass;
furthermore, there shall be a constant increase in lifespan, as well as perpetual health and prosperity. (167)
He should have mastered the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas,
and he should also have reached the further shore of the two Mīmāṃsās, logic (tarka), and the various other sciences.
Having become endowed with all virtues and having obtained unsurpassed sons,
he enjoyed celestial pleasures after attaining the eightfold yoga.
At its end, one goes to the state of the family of the abode of the Blessed One along with a hundred [others].
There are other [powers] of this [river] which bestow great siddhis, as found in the Śruti and Smṛti. (170)
One who desires success must certainly accomplish these [perfections], remaining free from pride;
for this is difficult to attain even for humans, and it is even more difficult to attain for the immortals.
Through this, the accomplishment of all supreme welfare is attained;
one should be exalted, constantly pure and endowed with initiation, and should worship the glory of the sacrificial clarified butter with the Vidyā. 172.

Having chanted the glorious eight-syllabled mantra, one obtains the lineage [of teachers] and the majesty of the science of imperial sovereignty (sāmrājyalakṣmī), which destroys all sins. I have told you just a little; what more do you wish to hear? 173.
[Thus ends the forty-first chapter in the venerable and unsurpassed *Dāśarathīya Tantra*, the *Vedārthasaṃgraha*, which is the secret essence of the reality of Brahman. 41.
The king said:
O Lord Nārāyaṇa, you have spoken of initiation and consecration as being practiced by all; therefore, tell me today the procedure for them.
The Blessed One said:
Now I shall describe the consecration (abhiṣeka), the unsurpassed ritual of initiation (dīkṣā);
without this, one does not achieve success even through hundreds of practices.
Having eaten, the pure-souled disciple, exerting himself, should daily satisfy his own teacher with various offerings, endowed with devotion and faith. || 3 ||
When he, being satisfied and pleased, bestows the mantra as a boon, one should personally perform the sequence of duties exactly as instructed. || 4 ||
In pure places and at pure times, I am constantly served with devotion and respect by my disciple, whose soul is purified and who is ever-disciplined.
O King, having made the formal resolve (saṃkalpa), one should perform the sowing of the sprouts;
first, one should perform the Nāndīmukha Śrāddha and the recitation for well-being (svastivācana).
One should perform this very rite according to the procedure prescribed for one's own house;
if it occurs in the month of Madhu (Caitra), there will be suffering, and in Mādhava (Vaiśākha), a loss of jewels.
In the month of Jyeṣṭha, it is inauspicious; in Āṣāḍha, there is the loss of kinsmen. In Śrāvaṇa, there is prosperity and the joy of strength and vigor.
In Bhādrapada there will be suffering; in Āśvina, all prosperity;
in Kārttika, there will be knowledge; and in Mārgaśīrṣa, happiness shall also arise.
In the month of Māgha, there shall be the exhaustion of former ignorance and the vision of me;
in the month of Phālguna, there shall be the constant attainment of all desired goals.
It should be performed on a Sunday when Mercury and Venus are present, and under the asterisms of Aśvinī, Rohiṇī, Svātī, Viśākhā, and Hastā. (11)
One should perform the consecration with mantras specifically during the three constellations beginning with Jyeṣṭhā;
likewise on the full moon day, the fifth, the third, and the seventh lunar days.
The thirteenth and tenth lunar days are highly praised;
they grant all desires when occurring on a day auspicious in five respects (pañcāṅga-śuddha), or even when [the moon] is strong.
When Jupiter and Venus are rising, when the ascendant is purified, when it is strengthened by the twelfth house, and when the moon and the stars are favorable, it is recommended for all undertakings.
The defect of the nine months does not apply during an eclipse of the moon or the sun;
whatever is performed therein yields infinite fruit.
If one does not seek anything else, it becomes a vast and excellent forest;
the drinking of the Soma juice is superior even to the drinking of the sun. 16.
If the jewel of the *iḍā* were to be grasped at the tip of the nose, it would be impossible to describe the fruit of the multitude of actions performed. (17)
Whatever mantra is received here becomes immediately effective;
even though the Vidyā has been received, it must be preceded by initiation (dīkṣā) in that case.
Obtained from the mouth of the Teacher, she bestows great accomplishment;
furthermore, it pertains to the mastery of all sciences during the eclipses of the moon and the sun.
If attainment preceded by initiation comes from the mouth of the preceptor, then success will be achieved without effort and will grant its fruit immediately. (20)
All these sciences must be mastered there by all ascetics and disciples through ritual bathing at the sacred ford, for the sake of attaining their goals.
Having fashioned a beautiful mandala with four powders—perfectly red, yellow, white, and black—and having placed two handfuls of grain there; || 22 ||
There, he should place a water-pot filled with water from sacred fords,
encircled by a pair of garments and endowed with the five jewels.
It was adorned with branches bearing mango and aśvattha blossoms,
provided with coconut fruits, and glowing on all sides with auspicious objects.
Having performed there a sacrifice endowed with every festival,
one who is joined with a portion of Śrī shall attain the perfection of the eight syllables within the yantras.
One should praise the Lord with hymns from the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas, with praises from the Purāṇas, and also with mantras from the Āgamas and those composed by the Ṛṣis.
He should indeed invite Brahmins who are well-versed in the Vedas and adorned with excellent ornaments;
and through them, he should have the Suktas and Mantras recited during that festival of Viṣṇu.
The preceptor should perform the subsequent nyāsa according to the previous procedure; or else, he should perform the pure Mātṛkā-nyāsa and also the Vaihṛvī-Mātṛkā-nyāsa. (28)
Then follows the placement (nyāsa) of the cage of its forms, the placement of the principles (tattvas),
the placement of the phonemes (varṇas), and also the tenfold Mātṛkā consisting of consciousness.
Having respectfully performed the placement (nyāsa) of the five limbs in front,
and having applied the entire network of placements (nyāsajāla), one should worship there as before.
And one should worship the all-pervading Lord of Śrī with the previously mentioned means of accomplishment,
using excellent and captivating dances, songs, and instrumental music.
One should give to virtuous women and householders a very extensive gift consisting of fragrances, flowers, water-pots, fine garments, ornaments, and so forth.
O ascetic, having likewise provided food, drink, and other necessities to others there as well, one should perform worship there at the three times of day.
Having subdued his senses, he worshipped even his enemy three times a day;
for three thousand years, he remained without food, subsisting only on fruits.
Having recited the glorious eight-syllabled mantra more than a thousand times, or else the Heart-Vidyā of Lakṣmī, or even the twelve-syllabled one; || 35 ||
One should conquer the six-syllable mantra of Mahālakṣmī by means of the eight-syllable one;
likewise, on the following day at dawn, one should perform everything as before.
Having worshipped him in person according to the rules as the Lord Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa himself,
he constructed a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) according to the rules and prepared a mandala there as well.
There, having established the fire according to the procedure taught for domestic rites, the sage invoked the Lord of Śrī along with his limbs and retinue, and worshipped him there.
Then, by means of the glorious eight-syllable jewel-mantra, one should perform a thousand oblations with sesame seeds accompanied by curd, milk, and clarified butter. (39)
One should offer one hundred and eight oblations with any one of the glorious mantras;
having performed the final full oblation there, one should then worship that [deity] in the water-pot.
Then, having offered oblations to the attendants in all directions with a concentrated mind,
he addressed his excellent disciple, who was devoted to him and free from sin.
One should perform the consecration of the vital breaths according to the prescribed rite, with the Pāvamāna hymns and the mantras beginning with "surāstvām abhi. (42)
One should sprinkle that water from the pitcher upon the disciple who is thus deluded;
indeed, Nārāyaṇa Viṣṇu himself bestows it upon the disciple.
"O All-pervading One, you are present everywhere; you are the inexhaustible treasure-house of compassion.
Recalling this again and again, one should perform the consecration with those waters.
And having caused him to be clothed in garments, having anointed him with sandalwood paste, and having him wear finger-rings and all other ornaments in every way; 45.
Having performed the Nyāsa of the Vaiṣṇavī Mātṛkā, and thereafter the Nyāsa of the Tattvas,
one should perform the Nyāsa of the Pañjara of the [divine] forms, preceded by the Nyāsa of the Ṛṣis and other [limbs].
One should thus install [the deity] within the body of the disciple according to the rules as if it were one's own self;
then, having placed that [deity] within him, one should place one's own right hand [upon the disciple].
One should recite the glorious eight-syllabled mantra one hundred and eight times;
thereafter, one should recite any other glorious mantra one hundred and eight times.
Having recollected the *Raśmimālā* mantra once for the supreme deities, the preceptor, being well-pleased, then [bestows it] upon the disciple preceded by the offering of water. (49)
O Lord of the Earth, one should then give that king of mantras along with the dakṣiṇā, conjoined with either the Śrī-mantra or one's own chosen mantra. (50)
The Guru should contemplate that the knowledge, consisting of light by its own nature, is departing;
the disciple, for his part, should repeatedly contemplate it as it arrives, thinking, "I am fortunate. (51)
Into the right ear of the disciple, he should [recite] the twelve-syllable mantra of Śrī-Śrīśa,
and then he should present the King of Yantras consisting of the eight syllables of Śrīmat.
Then, one should impart the Mahālakṣmī mantra into these [vessels],
and subsequently, the desired mantras into the right ear of the disciple.
O King, having smelled his head, he should then perform an embrace;
then the disciple, having accomplished his purpose, should report everything to him.
Whatever and however much that was desired by his mind, O King—such as cows, land, gold, ornaments, houses, fields, and so forth—he gave to his preceptor. (55)
A walnut, half a walnut, or even a fourth part thereof—
one should give clothing and other gifts here, beginning from the Aśleṣā [nakṣatra], according to one's means.
Or the king, with a serene mind, should bestow upon the preceptor a hundred villages along with a treasury, as prescribed, accompanied by a sacrificial fee of a thousand [gold pieces].
Having first performed the initiation rite for seven nights, five nights, three nights, or a single night, the Guru should then bestow the Vidyā.
When the time for the eclipse has arrived, having performed the initiation for one day and having carried out the rites for the jar, the solstice, and so forth, as previously described; 59.
Having recited the glorious eight-syllabled mantra one thousand times with a concentrated mind,
one should then recite another of the glorious mantras three thousand three hundred times.
At the time of the eclipse and the touch [of the moon], the Guru himself should bathe in a river and recite the glorious eight-syllabled mantra one thousand three hundred times.
Having offered auspicious black sesame seeds together with honey, clarified butter, and mudrās,
one should then perform one hundred and eight oblations with any one of the glorious mantras.
Having performed the oblation with the *brahmārpaṇa* mantra,
one should worship both Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa in the water-filled pitcher as before.
Having consecrated with water the disciple who is endowed with desire and devotion, having clothed him, and having then adorned him with the sixteen ornaments; || 64 ||
Having touched the head of that [image] with the glorious eight-syllabled mantra, one should recite it a hundred times;
then, having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) upon the body, one should likewise perform the Vaiṣṇava Mātṛkā-nyāsa.
Or, by performing merely the five-fold placement (pañcāṅganyāsa), one is glorified;
[one should practice] the glorious eight-syllabled lore (aṣṭākṣarī-vidyā) preceded by the knowledge of Brahman.
Having given [the gift], one should impart the desired mantra into his right ear;
afterwards, having bestowed the desired mantras, one should then cause the benedictions to be recited.
Even one who has fulfilled his purpose should offer his entire wealth, or half of it, or even a quarter of that, at the two feet of his own teacher.
Just as [one might give] two cows, or land endowed with ripened crops, or twenty-five *nikas*, or half of that, or a piece of gold; || 69 ||
Having given a pair of earrings, one should present a new house;
and having given garments for dwelling by the fire, one should then give an inexhaustible heap of grain.
For the sake of attaining the state of Manu, one must certainly satisfy with many riches another teacher who possesses the same nature as myself and who is not bound by worldly ties. (71)
Then he should satisfy the teacher’s sons, wife, and others as well,
with various offerings such as dwellings, garments, ornaments, and food.

Having abandoned deceit, one who is devoted to this [practice] and respectful toward the guru shall immediately become one who has fulfilled his duty; there is no doubt that the mantra is mastered. || 73 ||
Furthermore, through the ritual of initiation and consecration,
he was again instructed by the lotus-mouth of the Ācārya in the unsurpassed mantras that bestow the power of yoga.
One will certainly attain great accomplishment immediately;
indeed, the fruit of the recitation and other rites performed during that time shall be inexhaustible.
It enters the body of this disciple; of this there is no doubt.
Therefore, a full sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) should be given at the lotus-feet of the teacher.
If the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) is not complete, everything becomes fruitless,
even after bestowing all the sciences and repeatedly imparting the secret.
After examining his disciples for a long time, the teacher further instructed them in this auspicious jewel of a mantra.

One should bestow that which has been perfected through recitation, fire-oblations, and other means, preceded by initiation; this is especially meritorious when the initiation is performed during an eclipse of the sun or moon. || 76 ||
Through the presence of the Ācārya, the mantra becomes instantly perfected;
at the end of this Kali age, he shall indeed reside in Vaikuṇṭha, in the abode of the Lord.
Without knowing the power arising from the month, the day of the week, the lunar mansion, the moon, and so forth, he would certainly have been consecrated with the royal fortune of the gods.
One who possesses knowledge should give the mere mantra to his own disciple;
therefore, one should take refuge in an omniscient teacher with the thought that he is the Blessed One.
At the conclusion of the instruction on the eight-syllable mantra, he [taught] all the venerable mantras,
beginning with Vāsudeva and others, as well as those consisting of single measures (mātrā), beginning with Vahni-Nārāyaṇa and others.
One should place the garland of rays into the right ear of the disciple;
this twofold initiation, pertaining to the Bhagavatī and to Nārāyaṇī, is declared to be auspicious.
It should never be given to one who is an atheist, nor to a non-disciple,
nor to one who is doubtful, nor to a fool, nor to one who is hostile to the Veda.

Furthermore, he who imparts the Great Vidyā without knowing the procedure for initiation (dīkṣā), despite possessing strength from the practice of mantras and so forth, [ruins] both the disciple and himself. (83)
One who does not learn the *amāsavāra* from the mouth of the preceptor for even a single day will surely reach the most dreadful hell in the world of Yama. (84)
He who grasps this great vidyā does not fail to attain a good rebirth;
moreover, being free from dispute, he experiences total fearlessness here day by day.
And having been instructed by him, they once again approached the destroyer of Subhū;
from the mouth of that all-knowing true guru, they received the unattained perfection.
This is the Narayana initiation, belonging to Vishnu, which bestows perfection;
among all those who have been initiated, the Vaishnava is indeed superior.
He is greater even than those initiated into sacrifices such as the Aśvamedha;
he is declared to be liberated in a single lifetime. (88)
Having received initiation and consecration, by the power of constant recitation, one is liberated even by remembering the venerable eight-syllabled mantra just once. (89)
One who is endowed with initiation and consecration should mutter the illustrious eight-syllabled mantra, or even the eighteen-syllabled one, preceded by the Brahma-vidyā. (90)
Whether it be the sovereign glory of Mahāvidyā, the Śrīmantras, or the Vaiṣṇava mantras— by means of these,
one who has attained perfection in knowledge is liberated even here from the ocean of saṃsāra.
Having become one who has entered the heart of the Blessed One, he shall become filled with the bliss of Brahman;
it instantly destroys heaps of sins and greatly increases abundant fame. (92)
The rite known as initiation and consecration (dīkṣābhiṣecana) belongs to Viṣṇu and bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
it may be the initiation and consecration of Viṣṇu, or even yoga endowed with its eight limbs.
O wise one, beholding the Blessed One is the means for attaining liberation; for those who contemplate this, there is no other cause for the attainment of Brahman.
Ṛṣyaśṛṅga said:
Thus was the consecration for initiation proclaimed by Rāma, the husband of Jānakī, as that which bestows the attainment of supreme welfare in this world and the next. (95)
Having certainly been initiated into the Viṣṇu-initiation and being bound by its restrictive vows,
worship Rāma-Cyuta with the glorious eight-syllabled mantra.
"Then you have accomplished what was to be done and attained the eternal Brahman; this indeed is the supreme austerity. (97)
This is another merit, this is likewise a great vow;
this indeed is the supreme yoga, and this is the auspicious Vaiṣṇava initiation.

Even one who has been initiated into the Aśvamedha and other sacrifices and is firm in his vows, if he is initiated into the initiation of Viṣṇu while muttering the glorious eight-syllabled mantra, [is truly consecrated]. (99)
The infinite, immeasurable, supreme Brahman was directly revealed;
having received initiation and consecration, he became fivefold and then unified as one.
Having attained great perfection, one becomes a possessor of the realization of identity with Brahman;
this is not achieved through the practice of the eightfold yoga nor by sacrifices accompanied by full sacrificial fees.
I shall declare again and again that such a state of attainment as is not found through the initiation of Viṣṇu belongs to those who are endowed with the initiation of the Blessed Lord.

"Having chanted the glorious eight-syllabled mantra and attained eternal perfection, the initiation and consecration have thus been declared to you with reverence. O best of the twice-born, what more do you wish to hear from me hereafter? (103)
[Thus ends the forty-second chapter in the *Śrīmadanuttarabrahmatattvarahasya*, the *Dāśarathīya Tantra*, which is a compendium of the meaning of the Vedas. || 42 ||
The sages said:
O highly fortunate Ṛṣyaśṛṅga,
from the lotus of your mouth I have heard this secret, which is exceedingly profound and bestows spiritual perfection.
O Teacher, you who have accomplished all that was to be done, we are exceedingly fortunate;
for we have heard this scripture of the Blessed One from the lotus of your mouth.
Furthermore, O Lord, we ask you to explain that nature of Yoga which sustains the world and which was heard by us from your own mouth as you spoke of Śrī Tākāmāja. (3)
What is the nature of this yoga? What is its supreme form?
It has been declared that it consists of eight limbs; know all of that from him.
Thus spoke the venerable Ṛṣyaśṛṅga.
Listen, O best of Brahmins, to how in former times the Lord of Janaka, the son of Daśaratha,
[spoke] in the presence of Vasiṣṭha and other great sages.
The omnipresent Lord explained the true nature of yoga to Śambhu, just as he had previously explained it to the great-souled Janaka, the yogi Nārāyaṇa.
He narrated the nature of yoga and the means for attaining Brahman.
The Blessed Lord said: "Listen, O King, I shall explain yoga endowed with its eight limbs. (7)
That through the practice of which one attains the supreme, eternal Brahman—
by performing only the obligatory and occasional rites, one effects the destruction of evil.
Now, that means for becoming devoted to the practice of yoga is being stated:
association with the virtuous, which is the seed for the destruction of the creation of foolish and wicked people. (9)
O Viṣṇu, I shall describe the eight limbs of yoga which extend over the eternal day and night of the city of the Kurus (the body). || 10 ||
One shall be liberated from sins even by merely hearing of those [practices]:
first, *yama* and *niyama*, and thirdly, *āsana*. (11)
Prāṇāyāma is the fourth, while pratyāhāra is the fifth;
likewise, dhāraṇā, dhyāna, and samādhi constitute the eighth. (12)
I shall describe the characteristics of each of these individually:
first, yama and niyama; then, the third is āsana. (13)
Next, I shall explain the characteristics of breath control (prāṇāyāma), its observances, and its divisions. || 13 ||
Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, straightforwardness, forbearance, fortitude, moderation in diet, and purity—these are the restraints (yamas). || 14 ||
Indeed, for all living beings, that which is truly the source of the Great Lord is called non-violence through speech, mind, and action. (15)

Furthermore, the description of the nature of objects exactly as they have been seen and heard is called "one's own" (svātmya) by the wise; that is the firm conviction regarding the attainment of Brahman.
O Lord of the Earth, not taking even a blade of grass belonging to others—this too, my dear, is the eternal limb of non-stealing for the attainment of Brahman. || 17 ||
In all circumstances whatsoever, the renunciation of association with women through deed, mind, and speech shall be declared as celibacy (brahmacarya). 18.

The wise declare that *karuṇā* (compassion) consists of the destruction [of suffering] and the restoration [of happiness] for others, whether perceived through direct observation or reported by others. (19)
In all worldly dealings, through the actions of mind, speech, and body, freedom from crookedness toward everyone constitutes straightforwardness (ārjava). || 20 ||
O best of the knowers of Brahman, you should practice forgiveness toward those who cause harm in every way, at all times, and in all places, just as one behaves toward one's own kinsmen.
O best of sages, those of wise intellect declare that freedom from desire even toward objects already known is true contentment, just as they do regarding greed.
One whose mind is composed should eat a fourth part of his meal, avoiding food that is excessively strong, pungent, bitter, or stale, and so forth. (23)
They declare that food which is beneficial and pure for a protector of the earth should be moderate;
it should be free from the nine apertures and even from the pores of the skin.
They say that dirt is what is washed away by that [water], and it is called purification (śauca);
likewise, the thorough removal of impurities from the body by means of earth and water is also [purification]. (25)
Stability of mind, external purity, and internal purity—the wise know these ten qualities to be the means for attaining the state of Brahman. (26)
The fourfold austerity, devotion to the Lord, as well as the contemplation of the Siddhānta, modesty, and the giving of one's mind [to Him]. (27)
O Sutīkṣṇa, these ten are known as the Jayovratas;
I shall now describe their characteristics one by one. || 29 ||
Austerity consisting of fasting is intended to be performed according to the prescribed rules;
it is not a life sustained by thirst for the sake of mere physical existence when it can be maintained without such exertion.
This contentment is the Self; one must cross over by means of it, for its attainment does not occur without it.
Indeed, they call that which consists of faith toward what is taught in the Vedas and other scriptures "āstikya" (the state of being a believer).
The proper worship of one's chosen deity every day, according to the prescribed rules—
whether performed at the three junctions of the day or at a single junction— is indeed the worship of the Lord.
There was the hearing and reflecting upon the established doctrines of the Vaiṣṇava scriptures,
as well as the discernment of the meanings spoken by the middle and final [ages] from the Vedas, Smṛtis, Purāṇas, and so forth.
This is proclaimed by the seers of reality upon hearing the established doctrine:
whatever is utterly condemned by the Vedas and other scriptures, as well as by worldly people. (33)
In that regard, there is also the non-engagement of the body, speech, and mind;
for even [actions] performed after meditating upon the chosen deity and with the intention of offering them to it [are included]. (34)
That which is accompanied by a lamp and so forth is called "giving" (dāna);
likewise, even the investigation through reasoning regarding what exists and what does not exist is "right" (samyak).
This is the opinion of the two treatises as declared by those who know the truth:
for it is the constant repetition of the mantra received from the guru. (36)
The placement (nyāsa) of the waveless syllables results in primordial victory;
a vow (vrata) is the undertaking of the rules for everything that is to be performed. (37)
Without the observance of the restraints (niyamas), everything becomes fruitless; whatever is performed through both the restraints (yamas) and the observances (niyamas) shall become fruitful. (38)
It is called one-pointedness of mind. || 40 ||
I shall describe the two breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) which are beneficial for one seeking liberation;
through their performance, O kings, one gives today and again today [the fruit of] dry wood as if by fire. (41)
The state of being firmly established through the previously mentioned restraints, together with that which has been entrusted to the teacher, is called this posture (āsana). || 39 ||
Even for one who possesses many sciences, there is concentration on a single science;
other sciences serve as its auxiliary limbs, and the recitation [of mantras] is its essence.
These defects, moreover, arise from wind, bile, and phlegm within the sense organs,
as well as from the skin, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, semen, and so forth.
All these are accomplished by the internal restraint of the vital breath (prāṇa);
this is indeed the primary atonement for those who consume intoxicants. || 43 ||
O virtuous one, those who desire the eternal Brahman, which is free from rebirth,
should constantly perform breath control (prāṇāyāma) according to the prescribed rules.
Having completely restrained the instruments of the vital breaths within the self,
he alone remains as the residue and becomes fit for union with Brahman.
Quickly touching the knee-circle three times with the tips of the fingers, one should snap the fingers once; this is the shortest measure (mātrā). || 46 ||
One who has mastered the breath should recite the Gāyatrī together with its head and joined with ten *praṇavas* three times; thus one is liberated by means of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*).
Breath control (prāṇāyāma) is indeed of three kinds: inferior, middling, and superior.
O King, the inferior [type] consists of inhalation (pūraka), exhalation (recaka), and retention (kuṃbhaka), as previously described.
Having uttered the *triśa* [mantra] while performing *recaka*, this is called *prāṇāyāma*.
O King, by constantly performing sixteen such *prāṇāyāmas* at all times, [one attains purification].
One is instantly liberated from the sins committed over a year by reciting this [mantra], as well as from the injury caused to others and the theft of another's property. (52)

One hundred breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) burn away the sin arising from sexual intercourse with another's wife; one hundred repetitions [of the practice] burn away minor sins (*upapātaka*), such as eating forbidden food or killing a cow. (53)
O King, all other minor offenses, even those repeated a hundred times,
are entirely expiated by four hundred prostrations.
One should diligently perform breath-control (prāṇāyāma) at the beginning and at the end of all actions, whether they be auspicious or inauspicious. (55)
Without breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma), even a performed rite becomes fruitless;
therefore, one should diligently perform breath-restraints on an auspicious lunar day.
Restraining his vital breaths as much as possible, he should mutter the mantra with his mind alone;
then, with one-pointed concentration, he should meditate upon Nārāyaṇa again and again.
Or, having fixed one's gaze slightly downward within the space between the eyebrows, one should follow that supreme light while meditating upon the Supreme. 58.
The witness of all actions, Prāṇayāmin, is magnified;
joined with ten *praṇavas*, he is present through the *Gāyatrī* in all rites.
At the beginning and at the end, one should perform [the rite], while constantly remembering Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of the three worlds, whether in the form of Prāṇava or in the form of Śaṅkara.
Purifying the mind by meditating upon the glorious eight-syllabled mantra (Aṣṭākṣarī-vidyā) and restraining the vital breath, one should perform *prāṇāyāma*, which destroys all rising sins.
Without breath control (prāṇāyāma), all acts of recitation, fire-offerings, and worship do not bear fruit at all, even if they are performed repeatedly with great effort.
The withdrawal of the senses from their objects by means of the heart is *pratyāhāra*; this is the perfect restraint of the senses. (65)

The determination of the individual soul as being of the nature of Brahman is established here through reasoning and the previously mentioned supreme mantras arising from three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas).

The stabilization of consciousness within the self is indeed *dhāraṇā* (concentration); *dhyāna* (meditation) is the perfect contemplation [of it], having placed the all-pervading Lord within the heart. (67)
Together with his limbs, ornaments, vehicles, and attendants,
he attained the state of a perfected adept (sādhaka) in that realm which consists primarily of truth, knowledge, bliss, and unity.
The nature of concentration remains unchanged even throughout hundreds of other births;
or rather, concentration is the mind of the individual soul absorbed in Brahman.
Having become Brahman, with his own life-force ceased and his breath dissolved into the heart,
he remains as himself alone, because no other existence exists apart from him.
Even if he remains for only a moment, he is impelled toward meditative absorption;
thus, being well-restrained, he is endowed with the yoga of the perfection of the eight limbs.
Having pierced the orb of the sun, he goes to the eternal Brahman—he who practices thus constantly, being disciplined and tranquil in mind. (72)
One who has brought the collection of the senses under control is fit for immortality;
he who has cast aside the sixteen [qualities], and is free from desire, anger, and the like. (73)
Thus, through the practice of yoga—whether by the yoga of action, the yoga of knowledge, or both—he attains the supreme goal. (74)
He who performs this daily, free from sloth, attains the eternal Brahman from which there is no return; such is the fruit thereof.
The sage attained that state which is the essence of recitation, the fruit of action—
the unborn, all-pervading Nārāyaṇa, who is both possessed of attributes and devoid of them.
Having meditated upon Lakṣmīpati, Raghupati, Kṛṣṇa, Viṣṇu, Hari, and Śiva, and having disregarded all ritual action, he then goes to the supreme state.
One should practice yoga daily through meditation and ritual action;
by doing so, one falls into the highest state from which there is no return.
Therefore, enter either the yoga of action, which is the means of generating [the goal], or the yoga of knowledge,
by performing the prescribed duties throughout your life.
When one desires to reach the further shore of this ocean of worldly existence, which is difficult to cross, through various sacrifices and perfect devotion to Nārāyaṇa; || 80 ||
Whether through the yoga of action or the yoga of knowledge, [I am] the refuge for all beings who are afflicted by suffering, exhausted, and whose minds are despondent. 81.
In this world, he alone is the protector of those who have no other refuge; he himself, the Lord of the Universe in the form of Brahman, is indeed that husband of Jānakī.
No other is said to be the savior from the foremost flood of saṃsāra;
for those whose remaining defilements are exhausted, the yoga of knowledge is praised. (83)
Indeed, for all people, the yoga of action (karmayoga) shall be the means to liberation;
through knowledge, one attains the Lord, the pervasive Nārāyaṇa, who is the master of action. 84.
Those who practice yoga are highly praised here for properly worshipping Rāma at the beginning, middle, and end.
The yoga of action, however, shall be the means of liberation for all; through knowledge or even through ritual action, one reaches the Lord, the omnipresent Nārāyaṇa.
For what is this body? It is subject to decay, prone to hunger, thirst, and exhaustion. || 85 ||
O King, this body composed of skin, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, and semen has been thoroughly described in the scriptures; practice it correctly, for it is the destroyer of suffering.
"O best among those who know yoga, someone might think, 'I shall perform the yoga of action or the yoga of knowledge; it is my duty to do so. (87)
One who is struck down by fate should cast away the dust of his own mouth;
one should perform tomorrow's task today, and the afternoon's task at midday.
O King, because of the abundance of obstacles, one should perform the evening rite at midday;
this is for one who possesses perfect dispassion and whose mind is fixed upon the supreme reality.
All sense-objects appear like vomited food to one who sees them as such;
indeed, O lady, embodied existence shines forth only for one who is truly dispassionate.
For one who is dispassionate, even that [body] must be abandoned with all one's being, having heard [the truth];
it is more impure than any other bodily excrement, even than feces.
One who is firmly established in reality perceives a living being as particularly struck down;
for in this body of living beings, there is indeed such impurity.
When each [element] beginning with the skin is touched, knowledge alone is the purification;
for even by jackals and vultures, if such is the destiny, they are carried away. (93)

Then, as he proceeded step by step, purified and correctly [proceeding], he brought about the loosening of the skin from the bodies of embodied beings; such was the state of calamities at every step. 94.
He whose mind is utterly deluded remains indifferent to this body of the universe;
yet, by what law has this been created for the sake of experiencing nothing but suffering? || 95 ||
Even one who knows the ultimate truth perceives this when observing it;
he is deluded by the power of the Supreme Self, the Lord of the World. 96.
Even one who knows the true nature of Viṣṇu enters into a state of impurity on the day of the new moon;
though he has transcended suffering, he experiences false misery even while remaining in happiness.
Having fallen into a state of possessing nothing, one becomes afflicted as if by a family calamity;
having become so, one is again shrouded in suffering. (98)
O Great Lord, even one who knows that it is suffering does not truly understand suffering;
therefore, it must be abandoned by everyone with all one's being, as it brings suffering to all. (99)
One may enter [the state] through fear or even through intoxication;
O Sage, no action whatsoever performed here is found to be fruitless. (100)
If, however, that [desire] were to exist for the sake of re-entry, even one who is liberated would be bound;
therefore, the wise do not act out of a desire for the fruits of karma.

If they were to produce such a fruit, then [the world] would not be seen as consisting of suffering, old age, death, and so forth; nor would one be deluded by existence within this vast cycle of saṃsāra. || 102 ||
Even a lord [is not able to prevent it] otherwise, unless he possesses the power to overturn [it], or is devoted to the practice of yoga, or intent upon service to his guru. (103)
By the glorious eight-syllabled mantra alone, one attains eternal Brahman.
(103) [Thus ends the forty-third chapter of the Śrīmadanuttarabrahmatattvarahasya, the Dāśarathīya Tantra, which is a compendium of the meaning of the Vedas.]
The king said:
O Father, you who possess the light of certain knowledge regarding the merit of the Śruti and Smṛti, please cut through my doubt;
I ask you this—grant me your grace.
Through the direct realization in the form of self-experience alone, one attains the eternal Brahman, which is free from rebirth and beyond all attachment. || 2 ||
Thus do the wise, who know the truth of the scriptures and are devoted to the practice of the knowledge of Brahman, proclaim that which has been declared by the Illustrious One.

They attain both worldly enjoyment (bhukti) and liberation (mukti); understand how this is so: cessation from activity (nivṛtti) is called liberation, while engagement in activity (pravṛtti) is called enjoyment.
Tell me, how can there be only one path for both?
The Blessed One said:
"O Noble One, what was said by you this evening is true, O best among those who know the truth. (5)
The eradication of all that is born of suffering, and the eradication of suffering itself by its very nature—because these are characterized by cessation, they are designated as "liberation. (6)
The contact of the sense organs with other objects, along with the heart, shall be described as "enjoyment" (bhukti) in this world; indeed, there is a disparity between both of these.
Nevertheless, the contemplation of the Self is observed in both cases;
for liberation is indeed the abiding in the Self through the contemplation of the Self.
Precisely because of this, those who know all realities everywhere, and who always experience the Self in both worldly engagement and renunciation, [are the foremost]. (9)
O King, those who constantly meditate, "I am indeed Brahman," and furthermore, "I am Rāma," are not subject to the cycle of worldly existence.
They alone on the surface of the earth are the very self of the Lord in person;
here, the Lord alone is the enjoyer, while the object of enjoyment is through the ritual of offering to the Lord.
But when only one [moment] remains, what purpose would there be for existence?
Therefore, enjoyment is not considered an obstacle to the path of liberation.
By this method, one should constantly worship the all-pervading Lord Nārāyaṇa,
Śrī Rāma, the husband of Indirā, with single-minded devotion.
He attains both worldly enjoyment and liberation; there is no doubt in this matter.
Just as injunctions and prohibitions do not depart from that which has been spoken, so it is here.
Likewise, one should not move about as a seeker of Brahman according to the prescribed rules;
for Brahman alone is the truth—I am that, I am the Blessed One, I am the Lord.
"I am Nārāyaṇa, I am Rāma, I am Vāsudeva, I am Hari"—those who thus remember me here, contemplating this day after day; || 16 ||
For them, nothing is prescribed in the world, nor is anything prohibited;
just as "ghaṭa" and "kalaśa," though denoting the same object, are distinct designations. || 17 ||
Likewise, Brahman and Rāma are certainly one in reality;
therefore, "I am Rāma," or else, "I am indeed Brahman. (18)
Those who constantly remember [this], or even just grasp the mantra in the Anuṣṭubh meter, speak according to reality; they are all directly of the nature of Brahman.
For this [reality] is not found anywhere as something enjoined or prohibited,
nor as a mantra, a meter, or even the meditation of a sage.

The Brahmatādātmya mantra is not at all [taught here], for it is remembered as bestowing supernatural powers (siddhi). Instead, from among these, one should employ a mantra that grants the realization of oneness with Brahman. || 21 ||
Having obtained an auspicious moment and an auspicious month, he should necessarily go every day—whether walking, sitting, eating, sleeping, or even laughing. (22)
Whether sitting or lying down, by recollecting the mantra with devotion,
he then perceives his own self as having become Brahman.
Neither bathing, nor recitation, nor worship, and so forth, are required;
one attains perfection through the mere remembrance of the knowledge of identity with Brahman.
A wise person should offer even his body, his life, and all that he holds most dear to the teacher who bestows knowledge upon him.
O King, one should honor such eminent Brahmins who have become one with Brahman,
by giving them even a small amount of water, food, clothing, and so forth, every day.
Those who constantly offer with the realization that the instrument of offering is Brahman reach the state of being Brahman;
therefore, for one who knows Brahman, this [offering] leads to infinity.
Those who hate and even revile [this] shall become vessels for the fruits of that sin;
they will undoubtedly be miserable, impoverished, and wretched. (28)
Having procreated sons by himself, he may even give them away;
yet he himself imprisons them all within dungeons. (29)
"May this misfortune of mine last until its exhaustion;
therefore, those who desire their own welfare should not harbor hatred toward the knowers of Brahman. (30)
One should not even cause [such] to be done; rather, one should practice only what is beneficial—those who praise it, those who rejoice in it, and even those wise ones who speak of it. (31)
Having understood that the Lord of the Universe is that very one, may you obtain all that merit— even including the fruits of vows and oblations— and perform your duty continuously.
By this alone, your desired goal will be attained; of this there is no doubt—provided you perform the recitation of the Gāyatrī a thousand times every day with devotion.
Then, for those who were intent on serving the pair of feet of the Teacher,
there was the victory of the glorious eight-syllabled mantra (Aṣṭākṣarī-vidyā) along with its secret teachings.
This triad bestows the direct attainment of Brahman in a single lifetime;
he should always contemplate the oneness of the Guru, the Deity, and the Mantra.
Indeed, upon the vision of Brahman, karmas are destroyed instantly;
the knot of the heart is rent asunder and doubts also perish. (36)
O King, there are exactly five causes for direct realization regarding Brahman:
daily and auspicious service to the lotus feet of the teacher. (37)
Then, he performed the recitation of the Gāyatrī mantra one thousand times every day;
furthermore, he daily observed at the proper time the conduct prescribed by the Vedas with great self-restraint.

Even the recitation of the glorious eight-syllable vidyā, performed daily and in secret, [yields results] when it is done continuously during the prescribed times, even apart from the specific restrictive observances (niyamas). (39)
And the recollection of the ignorance regarding identity with Brahman; thus it is fivefold.
There exists nothing superior to this set of five which brings about the attainment of Brahman. (40)
This secret, which is the compendium of all Vedāntas, has been declared by me;
it must not be spoken to atheists, to the ungrateful, or to the evil-minded.
Having recited the Gāyatrī three hundred times, one should offer clarified butter twelve times;
having chanted the glorious eight-syllabled mantra, this is the recitation of the Brahma-vidyā.
Or, by the very grace of five hundred teachers, one attains the two deities;
one should constantly perceive the teacher as Nārāyaṇa himself, which bestows the realization of oneness with Brahman.
Delighting the Gāyatrī, who is devoted to Vedic conduct, he chanted the venerable eight-syllabled mantra preceded by the Brahma-vidyā. (44)
Having constantly conquered the formidable Mahākāla, who is difficult to overcome, together with the Śrī-mantra and endowed with the Raśmi-vidyā. || 45 ||
Having attained the eight great siddhis and being freed from old age and death, he becomes one with Nārāyaṇa and reaches that eternal Brahman.
Having meditated upon the Self as having the form of Brahman,
one should daily recite the mantra and perform worship until the vision of Brahman is attained.
By means of complete worship with perfumes, flowers, unbroken grains of rice, and other offerings,
[one should worship] the Śālagrāma stone marked with the discus, which is endowed with the king of discs (cakrarāja).
Having propitiated the Lord of the worlds, the all-pervading one accompanied by Śrī Devī, one attains the most supreme and great accomplishment both in this world and the next. (49)
A householder does not attain auspiciousness in this world or the next merely through knowledge, without [performing] gifts of land, burnt offerings, and other such rites. (50)
If a householder does not give sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) and does not offer oblations,
nor worships the Lord of the Waters (Varuṇa) according to the prescribed rule, he goes to a terrible state.
There is no greater gift than that given to celibate students;
apart from those teachers, one does not attain the supreme state by giving elsewhere. || 52 ||
In the Kali age, there is no power for those dwelling in the city of men;
a wandering mendicant [attains his goal] through mere knowledge alone, without the performance of gifts, fire-offerings, and the like. (53)
One becomes liberated from all bodily impurities; it is not otherwise.
This applies whether one is a wandering mendicant who is not yet dispassionate, or one who is dispassionate, or likewise a householder. (54)
Both the one who performs the *kuṃbhīyāka* sacrifice and the householder who enjoys the wives of others are submerged in hell; yet those seeking auspiciousness honor them with auspicious rites. (55)
They should perform worship with the necessary implements and offer gifts daily,
using sandalwood, agallochum, musk, camphor, saffron, and water mixed with honey.
With ablutions of the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), with flowers, divine juices, and even water;
with many garlands of flowers, with dūrvā grass, bilva leaves, and unbroken grains of rice (akṣata). || 57 ||
With blue lotuses, jasmine, oleanders, and campaka flowers; with jasmine blossoms, bilva fruits, punnāgas, and bakula flowers as well. (59)
With kadamba and ketakī flowers, with red aśoka and kiṃśuka, and with the fragrant and captivating flowers of the nāga, vāṇa, and other trees; || 59 ||
One should diligently worship with fresh and tender fruits and many leaves produced in the water-lily pond.
In this manner, with these and many other flowers,
I have properly and with great effort worshipped the Lord of Śrī, who is the Self of all selves.
One should worship [the deity] three times a day or once a day, throughout the day and night,
with various types of fried offerings and flour-based sweets for the attainment of one's desired goals.
And with milk, water, ghee, and cooked offerings such as fruits, cakes, and *vaṭa*-cakes; with curd-rice, various foods and drinks, divine substances, perfumes, and so forth. || 63 ||
For a long time, he performed worship with many materials such as staffs,
water-pots, and other articles, using incense and lamps arranged for the ritual circumambulation.
One should worship day and night with rows of lamps blazing like fire, fashioned in the forms of the conch, discus, mace, lotus, and Garuḍa.
With flowers blooming at that very time, as well as nutmegs, camphor powder, and highly fragrant betel leaves; || 66 ||
Desiring their own welfare, they should daily perform a great offering of honor, diligently accomplishing everything according to their respective means. (67)
For those householders who seek auspicious results, they should never scatter [their wealth] in this manner;
rather, seeking welfare, they should give gifts and offer oblations into the consecrated fire.
And thus, with a noble mind, one should daily observe these excellent rules for householders as well as for those practicing celibacy. (69)
If they should perform worship here with effort using the means for that [worship], according to their capacity and without transgressing the prescribed rule; 70.
O protector of the earth, even for all those endowed with prosperity, such a deity is difficult to obtain;
by this very fact, there shall always be well-being for you.
Virtuous women, householders, and likewise celibate students, having propitiated the qualified Viṣṇu here with the aforementioned means of practice, [attain their goal]. (72)
One should worship day and night with whatever offerings one is capable of providing;
for them, both worldly enjoyment and liberation will surely come to pass, and not otherwise.
If forest-dwellers were to act in this manner every day,
they would not turn back from saṃsāra due to the fault of violating the prescribed order.
Those who have fallen after having ascended [to high status] would experience miserable food;
O Great Lord, for them alone is non-violence the supreme dharma. (75)
For indeed, flowers are not obtained without effort;
the worship of the lords [of the mantras] is prescribed to be performed with substances fashioned through meditative visualization (bhāvanā). (76)
The worship of the Lord through ritual service is praised specifically at dawn and dusk;
for the relationship between the one served and the server exists between the householder and this Lord. (77)

The worship consisting solely of reflection upon the reality of the Self is declared to be the great worship; however, the contemplation of the oneness of the individual soul and Brahman is free from rebirth. (78)
Constantly regarding themselves as Brahman, they maintain themselves; by this, no evil deed whatsoever nor any calamity arising from evil deeds shall arise for them. (79)
I shall also speak of the secret; listen, O you who discourse with the knowers of Brahman!
Having understood this, a living being is liberated from the bondage of birth and saṃsāra. (80)
Though devoid of eyes, he perceives;
though earless, he hears—this form of sound is the supreme light.
He who knows the knowable is himself unknowable even by the omniscient;
he is the Lord, the Great Puruṣa, distinct from both the manifest and the unmanifest. || 82 ||
Devoid of the forms of female, male, or neuter, he is that supreme Brahman;
Hari is the Lord of all, the form of all, and composed of all the gods.
By him, who consists of truth and knowledge, the beginningless ocean [of existence] is dried up;
he is unborn, yet by mere remembrance, he is the destroyer of the afflictions of birth and so forth. (84)
The notion of "self" regarding him brings about rebirth for all;
yet he is the Lord who, by his very nature, governs all according to the rules prescribed for their respective stages of life (āśrama).
He, who exists without distinction, should be meditated upon for the destruction of saṃsāra;
yet, having abandoned what is prescribed for their own stage of life (āśrama), they worship the Self [in a different manner]. 86.
Those who do not bow to him in that form are said to be liberated from the bondage of worldly existence; whoever knows him through the Śruti, Smṛti, and Purāṇas [is likewise freed]. || 87 ||

Whatever effort is to be prescribed by those seeking liberation for the removal of their respective fatigue, therefore one should practice meditation with undistracted mind, observing the rules with diligence. 88.

O King, the wise one [should know] that all this, consisting of the moving and the unmoving, is false and non-different from the Self, because it is an object of perception, just like the objects in a dream. 89.
With his own self in the form of consciousness, he himself, being alone with a restrained mind and single-minded devotion, should contemplate the Self which consists of truth and bliss.
The ignorance of "I am this" is imagined by one's own ignorance; whatever is imagined as distinct from oneself is imagined by oneself alone. (91)
One should not imagine that which is ultimately real as being like a mirage;
nor can the distinction between the horns of a rabbit be perceived by the eye through the command of a child.
This ancient Yavyā is followed by the ancients;
it is known as all-pervading, having been made known by those who possess knowledge of the supreme self. || 93 ||
From the lineage of pure descent extending back to Brahmā, on both the mother’s and father’s side,
there shall be no women who stray from their husbands, and the men shall likewise be righteous.
Sacrifices and the study of the Vedas flourish there for every individual;
there, the lunar days (tithis) are honored, as are the successive lineages of teachers and disciples.
Even in dreams, there is no slipping away from chastity for those who observe the vow of celibacy;
their disciplined stage of life never deviates at any time.
At those various times, gifts are bestowed upon those who seek them;
in whatever lineages they occur, it is only in those that this [merit] shines forth for all.
Through the instruction spoken by the king’s guru to the disciples who know Brahman, the supreme Brahman arose of its own accord; therefore, nothing else exists apart from that.
All this, the truth of Brahman, shines forth as the absolute truth for those whose evil deeds have been exhausted over thousands of millions of births. (99)
By some, this very state of Yamyā is not perceived as something beyond the senses;
it is the nature of the singular knowledge of truth, which delights in the tasting of the nectar of bliss. 100.
One experiences this for oneself through one's own wise fortune; oh, what great merit, what great dharma! There is nothing dearer than this. 101.
Even for all improper acts, this other expiation is prescribed:
the contemplation of the eight-syllabled mantra and the worship of the Guru and the deities. 102.
This is remembered as the fruit of penance accumulated over many births:
our daily and devoted service to the pair of feet of the Guru. (103)
This pair is the fruit of the great austerity of those who mutter the eight-syllable mantra;
you are fortunate, O Great King, for you alone are Brahmā and Viṣṇu.
O Teacher, you alone are the foremost among devotees on this earth;
it is solely by your good fortune that Hari, whose nature is the supreme Brahman, has been revealed.
Having become the son of Daśaratha, this Lord, known by the name Rāma—the Lord of Śrī who delights in the Self—became the sovereign of his own senses. || 106 ||
He will certainly become a son-in-law and shall be highly honored;
for she who is Cihnapiṇī is Mahālakṣmī herself in bodily form. || 107 ||
Rising directly from the earth, she will become the daughter of the King;
known as Jānakī, she will possess divine luster and be honored by the assembly of gods.
Oh, what great fortune for this vast and noble city of Mithilā, that it pays homage to the two lotus feet of the Blessed One! 109.
This secret, the essence of yoga that grants liberation, has been taken from the Great Scripture; though it is not to be requested even from Śanaiścara anywhere, it was obtained here in Mithilā.
O great king, this ancient scripture, which is a compendium of the essential meaning of the Vedas, has been spoken by me to you; it is not to be disclosed to others. || 111 ||
O observer of noble vows, if you desire this boat for crossing the ocean of saṃsāra,
you shall become liberated after chanting the glorious eight-syllabled mantra along with its ancillaries.
Constant service to the teacher and devotion to the glorious eight-syllable mantra are not easily attainable;
indeed, truth is what is truly honored. 113.

Thus ends the forty-fifth chapter, titled "The Means of Knowledge," in this *Daśarathīya-tantra*, a compendium of the meaning of the Vedas; now, the dispeller of doubts shall further explain the subject. 114.
[Thus ends the forty-fourth chapter in the glorious *Anuttarabrahmatattvarahasya*, the *Dāśarathīya Tantra*, which is a compendium of the meaning of the Vedas.]
The king said:
O Lord Nārāyaṇa, Master of the World, Treasure of the Dawn!
Once again, [I shall describe] the practice of the glorious eight-syllable mantra, which bestows all spiritual accomplishments.
O Lord of All, I desire to hear that which delivers one from the ocean of worldly existence.
The Blessed Lord said: O Lord of Mithilā, I shall again fully explain the practice of the glorious eight-syllabled mantra; listen with a concentrated mind.
The supreme and glorious eight-syllabled mantra is the sovereign queen of all vidyās.
For one for whom this is accomplished, even divine wealth is not difficult to obtain;
that third lunar day which is released in the month of Vaiśākha is known as Akṣaya-tṛtīyā.
Because she bestows inexhaustible desired objects, she is by her very nature inexhaustible;
having become pure in the morning and performed the twilight devotions (saṃdhyā), [one should worship her]. || 5 ||
Then, having received the preceptor’s command, when Nala had been duly consecrated,
[he was fed] with jackfruit seeds devoid of their kernels and mixed with the three kinds of honey.
Having offered oblations accompanied by cow-ghee with the glorious eight-syllable vidyā one thousand three hundred times, and with whichever other glorious mantra [is preferred], || 7 ||
One should offer three hundred oblations of clarified butter raised by the rays of the Blessed One;
having performed the fire sacrifice (homa) with cow’s ghee in three ways, one should perform it along with recitations (japa) and other rites.
Having performed the expiatory oblations and having offered the *brahmāyāṇa* oblation,
he circumambulated [the fire], paid obeisance, and spoke with great respect as if to his own son.
Then, having prostrated before the pair of lotus-feet of the teacher and having further adorned him with garments and ornaments, [he should proceed].
One should offer wealth measured by a year’s worth of food at the feet of the venerable Āvārya;
or else, one may offer two niṣkas, ten niṣkas, or even five niṣkas.
Having offered [the image] to the preceptor's wife and given her desired ornaments,
he should afterwards feed twelve Brahmins and twelve married women.
Having received blessings from the teacher and having given the prescribed sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā),
one should offer fruits such as pānasa and others to the guru.
On the Akṣaya Tṛtīyā of every year, one is greatly honored;
having performed this rite, one attains great success that is difficult even for the gods to obtain.
Just as the *saṃdyada* [sacrificial fires] are inexhaustible, so too is the ignorance (*avidyā*) that is attained;
and just as that is inexhaustible, so too is the supreme, eternal happiness that is to be established, which is likewise inexhaustible. || 15 ||
Having attained inexhaustible prosperity consisting of sons, grandsons, and so forth, as well as imperishable enjoyments, he rejoices in the state of the Blessed One.
I shall proclaim another great and supreme vow that leads to the highest austerity;
by performing this, all success arises for a man. (17)
The vow known as Navarātra, dedicated to the month of Āśvina, is a most great rite;
it is performed on earth for the sake of attaining mastery over all branches of knowledge. (18)
Where the gods, the foremost of sages, yogis, and exponents of Brahman perform the auspicious Navarātra vow for the sake of attaining perfection.
Every year, the vow known as Cūḍāmaṇi is constantly performed by the Siddhas for the sake of attaining all fruits of perfection.
Each single day is said to bestow the attainment of infinite fruit;
yet, compared to each preceding day, the merit of the subsequent day undergoes decay.
It bestows long life and health, causes the increase of sons and grandsons,
and grants the supreme prosperity of wealth, grain, elephants, horses, and great assemblies.
It removes all obstacles, produces supreme wisdom, grants desired objects, brings about welfare, and instantly destroys misfortune. (23)
Bestowing the fruit of all sacred fords and being the cause of union with Brahman,
one must here perform the *puraścaraṇa* rite with devotion and diligence.
He who performs the Navarātra vow every year becomes eternally victorious and is liberated from the miseries of existence. || 25 ||
One who is joined with even a fraction of you certainly becomes [liberated], there is no doubt;
this applies likewise to the vow of the month of Caitra and that known as Navarātra. (26)
It brings about all that is most auspicious immediately and destroys even the great sins;
if one is capable, one should perform both, or else the nine-night rite alone. || 27 ||
I shall proclaim its ritual procedure; listen with a concentrated mind, observing it with reverence from the first day until the conclusion. (28)
O King, the Navarātra vow has been proclaimed as a bestower of great success. On that occasion, having risen early on the first day (pratipad), one should remain restrained in speech.
Having recited the twelve-syllable Brahma-vidyā during the Brāhma-muhūrta, and having then meditated upon the Raśmimālā-mantra, one should thereafter divide the water into three parts.
Having bathed and performed the twilight devotions (saṃdhyā), he then recited the Gāyatrī along with its six ancillaries (ṣaḍaṅga) and the auspicious,
glorious eight-syllabled mantra (aṣṭākṣarī) accompanied by all the ritual placements (nyāsa).
Or else, the wise practitioner, observing the vow, should daily recite the auspicious eight-syllable mantra joined with the *śanmanyāsa*, as many times as there are thousands of suns of his resolve.
Or, having mentally conceived the twelve-syllable Vidyā of Śrī, or the six-syllable Śrī-mantra, or the Prasannalakṣmī mantra, one should [recite it] a thousand times for each solar day.
O King, having recited the Śrī-hṛdaya, one should sprinkle [the deity];
one should practice forty-one repetitions, or else forty-five.
One should always feed a couple, or otherwise, one member of the pair; or else, having fed a hundred couples with the thought that they are the Blessed One himself.
One should perform this great protective rite and worship the Lord of Śrī;
thereafter, one should worship with leaves and flowers for a hundred nights with the Brahmavidyā mantra.
Whether eating fruit, eating sacrificial food (vighasa), eating only what is offered in sacrifice, or even eating only once a day,
one should adorn oneself with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings day after day.
One should chew betel leaf during this [period] for the sake of attaining prosperity;
one should perform the Mahotsava festival day after day with diligence.
Then, at the evening hour, the auspicious and sacred *maṅgalārātrika* (evening lamp-offering) should be presented with streams of water from the *sruva* ladles; it is highly honored. || 39 ||
One should daily offer one hundred and eight oblations of cow-ghee into the fire with the glorious eight-syllable vidyā, and twenty-eight oblations with the [mantra] of Śrī.
This great ninth lunar day is like a hundredfold stream of excellent mechanical devices;
it is auspicious, immediately destroying all calamities and bestowing self-restraint.
When that ninth day has arrived, having risen in the morning, restrained in speech, and having bathed with the permission of the preceptor, he should complete his daily obligatory rites.
In a fire consecrated according to the rules, [he offered] honey and molasses accompanied by each individual bilva leaf, using the glorious eight-syllable vidyā.
Having offered one thousand three hundred oblations mixed with cow-products, clarified butter, and sesame seeds,
he should subsequently offer one thousand one hundred oblations with the Śrī-mantra.
In the same manner, having gathered the evil [spirits], one should offer oblations three times with lotuses soaked in ghee, using the *Lakṣmī-hṛdaya* mantras, and with cow-derived ghee.

Having offered oblations with the five-rayed [mantra], having performed [the rites] with the Hīmañjaya and others, having made the expiatory oblations, and having made the Brahmārpaṇa oblation; || 46 ||
Having circumambulated the fire one thousand times with the Brahma-vidyā,
one should worship it with bilva fruits accompanied by flowers and tulasī leaves.
Having worshipped five hundred [times] with the Brahma-vidyā, and having prostrated with eight limbs before the pair of the teacher's feet; || 48 ||
A pair of auspicious earrings, fashioned from two karṣas of gold and adorned with most beautiful gems known as padmarāgas. (49)
Then, desiring success, one should give two earrings made of gold, which are free from wear and imperfections, to the ears of the preceptor.
Free from greed and delusion, one should give a pair of jeweled earrings fashioned from gold weighing one karṣa.
One should offer a pair of garments, either fine silk (dukūla) or cotton (kāpīna);
in the absence of a pair of earrings, one should offer gold of that same weight.
Then, having further adorned it with seals, waist-bands, and so forth,
[he should offer] the earth accompanied by abundant grain and provided with sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā).
Having given a Śālagrāma stone joined with four bull-shaped marks,
one should subsequently give two cows along with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
In the absence of land, one should give this as a substitute; or, in the gift of land, [one may give] a field measuring eight hundred *āḍhakas*.
Half of that ground is [the area] from which it has been removed; in its absence, it is honored as the earth.
The substance deposited upon the earth is the supreme fifty-three-fold [measure]. (56)
Half of that is declared to be mediocre; half of that is remembered as inferior;
what is remembered as unrighteous is said to be the lowest of the low, yet even there, half is honored.
Whatever and however much constitutes one's entire property is the most excellent sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) for a gift of land;
alternatively, a quantity of goods sufficient for a year's subsistence is also considered the best fee.
One should abandon greed and choose instead a gift of wealth measured for a year's sustenance, such as one hundred *niṣkas*, or half of that, or even half of that. (59)
Thereafter, the preceptor’s wife, Śrībuddhi, should perform worship with beautiful ornaments such as golden necklaces, bracelets, and earrings.
Or else, one should offer a very fine silk garment (dukūla) or cotton cloth;
then, one should feed twenty-five couples, no more than that.
The observer of the vow should feed fifteen or nineteen couples;
he should honor them with garments, sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā), and various fruits.
Then, embraced by his gurus and honored with their blessings, he immediately attains even great success that is otherwise difficult to obtain. (63)
Alternatively, on the first day of the bright fortnight, on an auspicious occasion,
one gold *niṣka* should be given to the preceptor.
On the second day, two niṣkas; on the third day, three niṣkas;
on the fourth day, four niṣkas; and on the fifth day, one niṣka. || 65 ||
Then, on the sixth [day], six niṣkas; on the seventh, seven niṣkas;
on the eighth, eight niṣkas; and on the ninth, nine niṣkas.
Then, having given that, the donor of wealth should give a *sālagrāma* stone;
and having given a pair of earrings, he should give a cow along with a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
Having given a bed with its frame and legs, or a fine and auspicious pair of garments, and having received blessings from the preceptor, one attains success and unsurpassed joy. (68)
Then, young married women (suvāsinyaḥ) should be fed— either fifteen,
or thirty-five in number, or a thousand, provided there is the means.
A king, a prince, or even a wealthy man who is firm in his vows,
should bestow eight villages upon those who have performed sacrifices accompanied by a thousand-fold sacrificial fees.
A hundred cows, accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā), should be given;
as much as this [is required], so much dakṣiṇā should one give to the two feet of one's own teacher.
Success shall be attained to that same extent;
the wise man who is free from deceit should give a complete sacrificial fee according to his capacity.
If one is unable to give even half [of that], it is not accepted as a valid alternative;
for even a great pauper, when in distress, might give his own auspicious daughter. (73)
Having given [the gift], accompanied by his wife, sons, and others, he remains firm in his vows and constantly devoted to the service of the preceptor’s wife and sons. (74)
Or, even without performing the preliminary rites (puraścaryā), success is attained day by day for husbands through constant service to the guru and devotion to the deity. (75)
Even once, he whose intellect is deluded by violating the command of his own teacher sinks into a most terrible hell that lasts as long as the moon and sun.
Even after committing a thousand improper acts or begging from Śūdras as well,
the teacher’s fee (dakṣiṇā) must be given in rites such as the puraścaraṇa.
Where the teacher is not honored by those who seek to accomplish auspicious deeds, that place brings about the failure of their undertakings and bestows the suffering of a wretched existence.
Where the teacher is honored with ornaments, sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā), and so forth, that rite is declared to be fruitful, bestowing the attainment of all auspiciousness. (79)
In this terrible ocean of saṃsāra, which is crowded with manifold sufferings, the recitation of the glorious eight-syllabled mantra is said to be its raft. (80)
The pair of the teacher’s feet is the auspicious ornament [to be worn] day and night;
it is the bestower of the attainment of the glorious eight-syllabled mantra and the giver of liberation itself. (81)
Nothing else is considered equal to the Navarātra vow in bestowing spiritual perfection;
this great purificatory rite (puraścaryā) has been described by me previously. (82)
By giving a complete sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) at the feet of the preceptor,
one obtains the fruit arising from a hundred such preliminary rites (puraścaryās) performed during the Navarātra vow.
One certainly attains the fruit; this is the truth, the truth that I declare, having performed this auspicious preliminary rite (*puraścaryā*) during the vow of the nine nights (*navarātra*).
Even by means of a hundred improper acts, one obtains [the fruit] accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā),
free from disease, possessing long-lasting flowers, and endowed with the eight qualities.
One attains inexhaustible prosperity, abounding in wealth, grain, and the like, as well as a lineage filled with elephants, horses, and jewels, extending far and wide. (86)
Having attained all auspicious branches of knowledge, which are like the waves of the ocean, and having acquired great good fortune that brings all the worlds under one's influence; || 87 ||
Having enjoyed all pleasures, including the attainment of death at will and the great prosperity of sons and so forth, the great yogi Mahīmati— || 88 ||
He who possesses supreme wisdom regarding that [deity] rejoices for ten previous and ten future generations, accompanied by hundreds of divine maidens; of this there is no doubt. (89)
If he remains unmarried, he should constantly perform service to his guru along with his own wife until the end of his life.
Now I shall describe another yoga that bestows great accomplishment;
by hearing it, even the great calamities of brahmins flee away. (91)
If the full moon day in the month of Puṣya is joined with the constellation Puṣya and occurs on a lunar festival (parvan) of the moon, [that is a most auspicious occasion].
The one named Mahācūḍāmaṇi is declared to be attainable through yoga; it occurs when the Vyatīpāta yoga is conjoined with a Sunday. (93)
When the new moon occurs conjoined with a Vaiṣṇava asterism, that great conjunction known as Urdhvodaya arises; it is said to be difficult to obtain.
If the conjunction of the Sun occurs at that very time, it is meritorious;
this yoga, known as Trailokyacintāmaṇi, has been declared to bestow all knowledge. (95)
