O Lord of the World, even in ten thousand years, this king of yogas that bestows the attainment of the fruit is not found upon this earth.
Furthermore, when the month of Śrāvaṇa is joined with the asterism Śravaṇā and conjoined with a Sunday,
this yoga is known as Padmaka.
If the drawing of the Soma cup occurs there, provided it is performed, that great and unattainable yoga is remembered as the "Crest-jewel of the Moon" (Candracūḍāmaṇi). || 97 ||
In that month, there was also a new moon day (amāvāsyā) conjoined with Monday, or else conjoined with Sunday and the lunar mansion of the ancestors (Maghā). || 98 ||
This yoga named Mahāpadmaka bestows the fruit of exhaustion; it is obtained if one remains during the eclipse of the sun. 99.
The jewel that is the crest-ornament of the Sun is compared to a mass of heated iron;
yet, on these four festival days, even a single one of them may be obtained.
In this matter, that which is offered with devotion grants the attainment of infinite fruit;
in this rite of *puraścaraṇa*, there is only one single procedure.
It is said: O Lord of Mithilā, listen with a concentrated mind; if, among these four yogas, the previously mentioned one should occur, [then it is so]. (102)
For three days prior to that, one should consume food measured for a single meal;
[one should recite] the thousand and three hundred [verses] together with all the ritual depositions (nyāsa). 103.
Having recited the auspicious eight-syllable mantra of Śakrāṇī, or the twelve-syllable mantra of Śrī which bestows imperial sovereignty, one attains [the desired fruit]. (104)
Or, having become composed, one should constantly recite either the ritual of the glorious six-syllable mantra or the Vasu-varṇa mantra one thousand one hundred times.

One should daily offer one hundred and eight oblations of cow-ghee into the fire with the venerable eight-syllable mantra, and likewise offer one hundred and eight [oblations] for the sake of purification.
Then, one should offer clarified butter with each of the solar mantras one hundred and eight times daily, and worship with the Brahmavidyā mantra.

When that festival had arrived at the time of contact, he, being composed and having purified his soul by bathing in the river while reciting the names beginning with Keśava, [performed his rites]. || 108 ||
Having been purified in twenty-four ways and liberated from the heaps of sin,
he thereafter drank the water from the pair of feet of his preceptor.
Pure within and externally pure, he prostrated with eight limbs before the two feet of his own teacher, and then bore that command upon his head.
With one thousand three hundred oblations, consecrated with the milk of a tawny cow and clarified butter,
and combined with the three mantras, [one should perform the rite] by means of the glorious eight-syllable vidyā.
Or one may perform a sacrifice in the consecrated fire with a thousand plus a hundred oblations of sesame seeds, or with the juice of *prasannā* and molasses, using the twelve-syllable mantra of Śrī.
Having offered one hundred and eight oblations with either the six-syllable mantra, the Śrīsūkta, the Āyuṣyasūkta, the Svarṇaretasūkta, or with the Vāsudeva mantra, then—
One should offer oblations twenty-eight times with the six-syllable Vaiṣṇava mantra;
according to the vow, one should offer for each individual ray of the Blessed One.
Having performed the recitation (japa) and other rites, as well as the fire-oblation (homa), he should then offer the final oblations with lotuses;
having offered with the Mahāvyāhṛtis, he should perform the oblation of dedication to Brahman (brahmārpaṇa).
Then, having prostrated with all eight limbs before the blazing fire, and having likewise prostrated with all eight limbs before the pair of feet of the preceptor; 116.
Having given a pair of fine garments and a pair of auspicious earrings,
one should give to the lord of the earth a well-proportioned [gift] accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees.
Having given two cows along with their calves and accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā), one attains success that is difficult even for the gods to obtain. 118.
Even if a king is wealthy and performs great acts of charity,
he must present an auspicious Śālagrāma stone to the preceptor.
O Brahmin, on the occasions of an eclipse of the moon or the sun occurring in conjunction with the southern solstice (dakṣiṇāyana), other gifts also must certainly be bestowed. || 120 ||
O King, one should give excellent golden ornaments to the preceptor;
having given them in the presence of the Blessed One, one should then present them in the presence of one's own preceptor.
The wise man should send that substance to his guru or to his son;
whatever object is offered to the Sun, Mars, Jupiter, or the Moon, [that he should give]. (121)
Even at the dissolution of the universe, this bestows the perfection of imperishable bliss;
it shall become the wealth for one who has given it away during the Cūḍāmara and other such yogas. || 123 ||
The fruit of a single oblation performed during a solar or lunar eclipse cannot be described by me, nor by the Creator, nor by Śiva. (124)
Brahmā and the other gods, together with the Maruts, have declared that the fruit of a crore of fire-oblations is obtained;
especially so from the performance of the Śrīmaṣṭorṇa-homa and others. 125.

It is impossible to describe it; it is experienced during the conjunctions of the sun and moon at the time of the lunar festivals, or during the Cūḍāmaṇi and other yogas—who indeed is capable of describing its color? || 126 ||

In this regard, those who have reached the further shore of the Āgamas declare that the fruit born from the gift of a sacrificial fee at the lotus feet of the Teacher is equal to ten Himālayas and Merus.
Having given a pair of earrings to his own preceptor on an Upavasa-parvan or a Ravi-parvan,
he obtains the merit arising from the gift of ten million ornaments.
Having attained the fruit [of his actions], the pure-souled one [delivers] those born of his father's lineage and those born of his mother's lineage, by the hundreds and even by the thousands.
Having cast down the foremost of those in hell, he bows toward the world of Brahmā;
he then gives the earth, endowed with many ripened crops.
Whatever fruit is declared for one who gives the earth with its seven continents at the feet of the Teacher’s lotus-like feet, may that fruit be fulfilled by Rēvarvaṇi.
Having given a Sālagrāma stone along with abundant sacrificial fees to the preceptor,
the wise observer of the vow obtains the merit arising from the gift of ten million cosmic eggs.
One certainly attains the fruit and achieves unsurpassed perfection by thus offering abundant sacrificial fees at the lotus feet of the preceptor. (133)
One should give the dakṣiṇā with one's full capacity to those who attend the sacrifice, to those who are afraid, and to a śrotriya who is not poor and is devoted to the study of the Vedas.
He who gives wealth for the purpose of a marriage on the festival of the sun and moon—his sins are destroyed like waters in a desert, like the motes of dust in a beam of light. || 135 ||
Even in the world of Brahmā, at the end of a kalpa, there is indeed no exhaustion of the fruit thereof;

it is possible to count the particles of dust of the earth, the rain for the sake of a wedding, the wealth on the occasion of the solar and lunar eclipses, the waters of the ocean, and the motes of light in a sunbeam. (135)
Even in the world of Brahmā, at the end of the kalpa, there is indeed no exhaustion of the fruit of that [merit];
it is possible to count the particles of the earth, or the drops of rain. || 136 ||
Even Brahmā is unable to describe the merit of establishing a Brahman, nor that of giving wealth for the sake of a marriage during an eclipse of the moon or the sun. (137)
The fruit that one obtains by giving as much wealth as required for a lifetime to thousands of Vedic scholars is obtained by performing a single marriage.

The practitioner, firm in his vows, having performed the preliminary rite (puraścaryā) during the lunar eclipses before the pair of feet of the teacher, and having provided the complete sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), [should proceed].
Having given a thousand cows and having performed a sacrifice with complete sacrificial fees,
one obtains even greater merit than the fruit that results from those acts.
Whatever fruit one obtains by performing seven hundred million offerings with truthful words, that same fruit one attains through the glorious eight-syllable vidyā. (141)
By offering a thousand oblations during an eclipse of either the sun or the moon,
one attains that same fruit, according to the word of the Blessed One.
By offering the Avicchinnāvasordhārā oblation, one obtains that same fruit which is acquired by performing the twelve-year sacrifice during the eclipses of the moon and the sun.
O King, by offering oblations into the illustrious and glorious Aṣṭānaya fire, one obtains that very same fruit as if accompanied by a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) numbering a thousand crores.
Having performed a thousand horse sacrifices over the course of a thousand years,
accompanied by the gift of a chariot, he seized the moon and the sun.
Having performed this preliminary practice (pūrvacaryā) for the glorious eight-syllable mantra of Saptanṛsiṃha,
one obtains its fruit, which is equal to that born of a thousand Vājapeya sacrifices.
Having performed a thousand-fold *puraścaraṇa* along with its complete sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), one obtains that fruit which is known as the *cūḍāmārā* vow. || 147 ||
Having performed even a single *puraścaraṇa* with complete sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), one will certainly obtain that fruit again; there is no doubt in this matter. || 148 ||
Even one who is incapable, unfortunate, poor, or miserly,
by giving a Śālagrāma stone, obtains the merit of five gold niṣkas.
Or, having given three gold *niṣkas* as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the preceptor,
one attains the unsurpassed accomplishment (*siddhi*) of the glorious eight-syllable mantra.

He who performs the preliminary rite (puraścaryā) during the planetary periods (grahaṇa) will undoubtedly find that the Lord of Lakṣmī becomes manifestly pleased with him; of this there is no doubt. || 151 ||
One may hear news from afar, see many people, and possess powers such as entering another's body and the supernatural faculties beginning with *aṇimā*. (152)
That is obtained by the practitioner quickly through the performance of the preparatory rite (puraścaraṇa);
now the specific procedure for Bhargava will be fully explained. || 153 ||
Having heard which, the wise practitioner is liberated from all [obstacles] when the day of Bhārgava (Venus) has arrived, preceded by the command of his own teacher. || 154 ||
Having bathed in the morning and purified his self, and having completed his daily obligatory rites,
he [should perform the oblation] according to rule in the consecrated fire with the glorious eight-syllable mantra.
Having first offered five hundred oblations with cow's ghee while composed in meditation,
[he should do so] either with the mantra of Prasannalakṣmī or with the twelve-syllable Śrī-mantra.
One should offer one hundred and eight oblations of clarified butter with the six-syllabled Śrī-mantra,
and likewise with the six-syllabled Vaiṣṇava mantra of Vāsudeva.
Having offered twenty-eight oblations of clarified butter with the rays of the Lord,
one should then offer them individually three hundred times with the Brahmavidyā mantra.
Then, having honored them with food, one should respectfully feed three couples;
one couple should be fed with delicious food and monetary gifts (dakṣiṇā).
Having satisfied the lotus-feet of the preceptor with a mental offering of gold,
one should give a single *niṣka* of gold as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the preceptor.
Then, with the thought that she is Mahālakṣmī, he should eat together with his wife, who is like a vessel of prosperity; or else, having offered it into the fire, he himself should consume it.
Constantly performing the vow on Fridays for five years, he dwells together with his kinsmen.
For three years, one year, six months, or three months, being composed in mind,
he shall attain the unsurpassed perfection of the glorious eight-syllable mantra.

O King, one perceives the lord of the month and so forth through the application of the eyes, whether it be on the first day of the month or on the day of the preceptor of the Daityas (Venus). || 164 ||
Having thus performed the rite of oblation at the beginning, [one should offer] either one karṣa-measure of gold, or one suvarṇa, or even a single niṣka, at the two feet of one's own preceptor.
O King, by placing her right foot upon the lotus-feet of the preceptor’s wife,
she attains unsurpassed perfection within six months or even a year.
[He bestows] health, immovable sovereignty such as the powers of *aṇimā* and so forth, the capacity for grace through his glance, and prosperity joined with sons and other blessings. (167)
Having attained the power to assume any form at will, inexhaustible speed of mind, and great prosperity consisting of an abundance of wealth, grain, and horses; || 168 ||
Today,
may he attain the eightfold enjoyments consisting of horses, elephants, cattle, and jewels, as well as the supreme eightfold body.
Accompanied by a thousand members of their lineage, at the end of the body they reach the state of the Blessed One;
there is no doubt in this matter, for he shall be attended by hundreds of divine maidens.
He is never separated from sons, grandsons, cattle, or vehicles;
nor does he ever suffer separation from wealth or jewels. (171)
On the day of Bhārgava (Śukravāra), having observed this vow with fixed discipline anywhere at all, being pure and endowed with devotion to the Lord, [one should perform the rite]. || 172 ||
Having attained the eightfold sovereignty endowed with the eight limbs of yoga, he was one whose death was at his own will, whose soul was pure, and who resembled a hundred Kamadevas. || 173 ||
O Lord of the Earth, he attains union with Brahman, which is difficult even for yogis to obtain; furthermore, there are other goals to be accomplished by him.
Having been thus addressed by the great seers, one should become intent upon the attainment of supernatural powers (siddhi).
This glorious eight-syllabled lore (vidyā) has been declared as the means for such accomplishment.
Hereafter, I shall proclaim the method for attaining the status of a Brahman-seer and other such states. 175.
[Thus ends the forty-fifth chapter in the glorious Anuttara-Brahma-Tattva-Rahasya, the Daśarathi Tantra, known as the Vedārthasaṃgraha.]
The Blessed One said:
Listen, O King, protector of the earth, to the means for attaining the status of a brahmin-sage and other such states;
thereafter, I shall proclaim the glorious eight-syllable vidyā.

In this world of humans, which is further agitated by birth, death, and old age, the means to attain the status of a Brahman-sage and other such goals—which bestow glory—is accomplished by this very body. (2)
Without the accomplishment of the glorious eight-syllable vidyā and so forth, it is difficult to attain [this state],
even through the complete recitation of the Vedas or by means of a hundred horse sacrifices.
"O Lord of the Earth, it is possible for you to attain immortality and other such states through thousands of great gifts or by means of a hundred vessels at sacred fords."

Through the performance of rites such as the recitation and fire-offerings of the glorious eight-syllable mantra, through constant service to the preceptor, and by avoiding the loss of sacrificial fees and ritual materials; || 5 ||
By this very body, he becomes possessed of a divine form;
therefore, without the knowledge of the eight-syllable mantra, there is no such transformation in the physical frame.
O King, it is not possible to attain desired goals such as immortality, nor auspicious states such as that of a Brahman-sage, with this very body alone. (7)
I shall now proclaim how that is attained in this world:
first is Setubandha, a great sacred field (mahākṣetra), and after that, Raṅgadhāma. 8.
Śrīparvata, Piśeṣādri, Pāṇḍuraṅga,
Mahatara, Kīllāpurī, Mahāpuṇya, Dakṣiṇa, and Madhurāpurī.
Or is the great field Āhovala, or the confluence of the Vāsiṣṭha and Sindhu?
To the west is Sītārāmagiri, and [further] west is Prayāga, the leader of holy sites. || 18 ||
Avantī (19), Dvārakāpura (20), the supreme abode of Jagannātha (21);
the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean (22), the banks of the seven Godāvarīs (23), Gokarṇa (24), Naimiṣāraṇya (25), and likewise Northern Gokarṇa (26); and the meritorious city of Ayodhyā (27).

Madhurāpura, the most excellent (28); Gaṅgādvāra, of great merit (29); and the beautiful Kurukṣetra (30). Also the holy hermitage of Sītārāma (31) and the hermitage of Bharata (32); Kedāra, Mānasa, and the unsurpassed Rāmahṛda (35). And Padmanābha, the great holy city (36).
Prabhāsa, which is most excellent (37); Vṛndāvana (38); and the cowherd settlement (naṅgokula) (39), as well as the bank of the Jāhnavī (40);
the meritorious bank of the Sarasvatī (41); and also the bank of the Yamunā (42); the bank of the Godāvarī (43);
and the auspicious bank of the Kṛṣṇaveṇī (44); the seashore (45); Siṃhādri (46); and the supreme bank of the Kāverī.

47. Indeed, these are fields of merit that bring about the accomplishment of knowledge and other powers. 48. Vārāṇasī is the queen of all sacred fords and holy places; it is auspicious and bestows the great accomplishment of all sciences.
49. Even more than that, the Badarikāvana forest is declared to be the city of the sons of Mṛtyu.
They say it bestows immediate success and grants the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
even other divine sacred fields exist upon the earth, where a human being is liberated from the weight of sins and transgressions. 21.
Listen, O Vahīnaroja, to this means for attaining the status of a Brahmarṣi and other such goals;
by hearing which, even one who is not self-restrained is liberated from heaps of sins. (22)
Having taken refuge at the bridge of Setu, [he beheld] the two feet of his own teacher.
Having bathed at Dhanuṣkoṭi and prostrated with all eight limbs,
one should practice the Gāyatrī mantra a thousand times, or at least thirty times.

Being pure, one should recite the glorious eight-syllabled mantra (aṣṭākṣarī), conjoined with all the ritual placements (nyāsa), or else conjoined with the Vidyā of the Mother in the form of the Vidyārāja. 24.
One who has conquered the senses, for the sake of purification, should daily offer three hundred oblations of barley-meal and likewise recite the Śrī-mantra one hundred thousand times.
Day by day, he should offer flowers with the Triśānta-Brahmavidyā mantra;
at the conclusion of that, he should perform oblations in the fire with sesame seeds soaked in the three sweets (honey, ghee, and sugar).
One who is pure [should offer] ten thousand [flowers], one thousand with the Śrī-mantra, a thousand, or a hundred niṣkas, or half of that, or half of that again. || 27 ||
Having offered the pair of earrings to the lotus-like feet of the preceptor,
one should subsequently feed more than a hundred Brahmins and married women.
Accompanied by Lakṣmaṇa and Śatrughna, together with his sons,
and surrounded by Sugrīva, the son of the Wind-god, and the other leaders of the monkeys.
He beholds Rāma together with Jānakī with his own eyes;
by his grace, he immediately becomes free from old age and death.
Constantly honored by Śakra and the other gods,
Vibhīṣaṇa, by the command of Śrī Rāma, certainly attained the status of the king of kings.
Whatever one desires, that entire wish he grants:
wealth, divine garments, and celestial ornaments.
It constantly bestows inexhaustible grain and effort upon the practitioner;
by this very means, one becomes a sky-walker possessing the impetus of tranquility within this very body.
Having taken refuge in the presence of Raṅganātha, he constantly observes his vows and wanders through the worlds of the eight guardians of the directions, beginning with Śakra. (34)
Keeping his teacher close at hand and intent upon serving him,
he performed his ritual baths three times a day on the banks of the Kuveratanayā.

Having diligently recited the glorious eight-syllabled mantra one thousand times, one should afterwards offer oblations of clarified butter five times with the Śrī-mantra; then, one should practice [the recitation] for one hundred thousand times.
Having recited the Vāsudeva mantra ten thousand times, being self-controlled and pure, || 37 ||
One should recite the Bhagavadraśmisūkta one hundred and eight times,
using oblations soaked in cow's ghee and mixed with the three sweets.
Then, O King, having offered ten thousand oblations of sesame seeds with the eight-syllable vidyā,
one should thereafter offer three thousand oblations of sesame seeds with the Śrī-mantra.
One should offer one thousand oblations with sesame seeds soaked in ghee, using the mantra of Vāsudeva or the Vaiṣṇava mantra, along with woolen thread.
Then, one should offer clarified butter five times with the mantras of the Bhagavadraśmis,
after having given a Śāligrāma stone along with a cow accompanied by a hundred-fold sacrificial fee.
Having given twenty-five thousand *vipkas* or even ten thousand to the pair of feet of the preceptor, he should then [give] a hundred Brahmins.
One should feed a hundred married women and also give them sacrificial fees;
on that very day, one beholds Raṅganātha in person.
By my grace, immediately freed from old age and disease,
his body became composed of splendor, and he was honored by Vasiṣṭha and the others.
One attains the status of a Brahmarṣi at the end of the Kalpa; of this there is no doubt—on the peak of Śeṣācala, on the bank of the Suvarṇamukharī.
Performing the ritual bath with *śrīkhaṇḍa* (sandalwood paste), devoted to the service of the Guru, and having recited the *Gāyatrī* mantra a thousand times or three hundred times; || 46 ||

Then, having completed the daily fire-oblation (nityahoma) and having diligently recited the venerable six-syllabled vidyā, conjoined with all the ritual placements (nyāsa), one hundred thousand times; 47.
One should recite one's own chosen Śrī-mantra one hundred thousand times;
likewise, the great Vaiṣṇava Vidyā of Vāsudeva, the six-syllabled mantra. 48.
Having recited the ten-thousand-fold [mantra] for each [deity] while remaining firm in his vows,
he should then recite one hundred and eight times the *Bhagavad-raśmimālikā*.
One should offer ten thousand oblations of sesame seeds mixed with clarified butter while reciting the glorious eight-syllable vidyā; by doing so, one attains success even in that regard.
Having offered three thousand oblations of ghee-soaked lotuses with the Śrī-mantra,
one should then perform the rite with the six-syllabled Vaiṣṇava mantra of Vāsudeva.
One should perform the vow by offering one thousand three hundred oblations;
having offered them with the rays of the Blessed One, using cow's ghee alone in five ways.
A woman whose husband is living should feed one hundred Brahmins with delicious food at night;
she should offer a hundred cows along with sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) at the pair of feet of the preceptor.
Or half of that, or half of that again; having given gold as a substitute for that on that very day, [one should worship] the Lord Śeṣa, the Lord of the Serpents, in person.
He will behold the Blessed One accompanied by Śrī, Bhūmi, and Nīlā;
by His grace, he shall immediately become the sovereign of all the Vidyādharas. || 55 ||
He becomes truly liberated from old age and death; of this there is no doubt. || 56 ||
From his lotus-like mouth, all the auspicious Vedas, including the Vedāngas,
as well as the Purāṇas and Smṛtis, issued forth spontaneously.
With a body eternally composed of splendor, appearing as a youth of twenty-five years,
he attained the eightfold yoga and the prosperity endowed with the eight qualities.
With this very body, he ascends a celestial chariot and enjoys all imperishable pleasures until the end of the kalpa.
Or else, having resorted to a secluded place, being intent on constant ritual ablutions,
one should [meditate upon] the glorious eight-syllabled lore (vidyā) accompanied by all the ritual depositions (nyāsa).
One should then recite one hundred thousand times the Śrī-vidyā,
as well as the great Vaiṣṇava six-syllabled mantra of Vāsudeva.
Having recited [the mantra] one thousand times for each [deity], the wise practitioner, firm in his vows,
should repeat it a hundred times, like a lotus-stalk drawing up rays of light.
Having offered ten thousand oblations of milk-rice mixed with sesame seeds and blended with ghee and honey, one should offer three thousand oblations for the sake of prosperity.
Afterwards, one should offer oblations twelve times with the rays of the Blessed One;
two hundred Brahmins and two hundred women should be fed.
The earth, filled with crops, must necessarily be given with devotion, accompanied by a complete sacrificial fee, to the pair of feet of the preceptor.
O descendant of Arjuna, having given its price or even a small amount of wealth,
the omnipresent Lord, together with Idirā, beholds [the donor] directly with his own eyes.
By his grace, having attained mastery over the sciences and assuming a divine form,
he was released by Rāmaṇa and [obtained] a celestial chariot that grants all desires.
Then the Gandharva king, having ascended [his vehicle], certainly dwelt in Saumavati;
having reached the city of Kāñcī, he was constantly devoted to the three daily ablutions.
Having brought the preceptor into his presence, he should perform service for him;
[he should receive] the glorious eight-syllabled vidyā together with all the nyāsas.
Having recited the vidyā of Alarkaśrī one hundred thousand times, one should then perform the sacrifice;
or else, one should recite the great mantra of Vāsudeva twelve thousand times.
One should likewise recite the six-syllable mantra consisting of the *dyuvī* vidyā;
thereafter, one should repeat the *Bhagavadraśmimālikā* one hundred times.
Having offered twelve thousand oblations with bilva leaves that have been smeared with clarified butter and mixed with the three sweets (honey, sugar, and ghee), and three thousand for Śrī; || 72 ||
Having offered a thousand oblations each with clarified butter alone, using both the mantra of Vāstudeva and the six-syllabled Vaiṣṇava mantra, one attains greatness.
Then, having offered ghee twelve times with the rays of the Blessed One,
and having performed the oblation of "Brahmārpaṇa," [he should feed] one hundred and eight twice-born men.
He should also feed a hundred married women with pure foods; then, having offered two earrings to his own preceptor and his father, he should drink [the remainder].
Having given a pair of *dukūla* garments, one should give a thousand *niṣkas*,
or a hundred *niṣkas* of gold, or less than that, or half of that.
Free from desire and devoid of worldly attachment, he should offer [worship] at the lotus-feet of the preceptor on that very day, directly to the Lord who is the leader of Kāñcīpura.
With his own eyes, he beholds the Lord Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa, who has descended from the back of Garuḍa, and who is worshipped by Brahmā, Śiva, and the other gods.
By his grace, one immediately becomes free from old age and death,
free from disease, long-lived, and endowed with prosperity consisting of the eight qualities.
Having obtained a vast abundance of wealth and grain, filled with pearls and red gems,
he attained the seat of Indra and was honored even by the gods.
With this very body, assuming forms at will and moving with the speed of thought,
he attains the power of traveling through the sky and proceeds to the realm of the gods.
Then, in that highly meritorious field at the confluence of the Sindhu,
in the presence of Narasiṃha, preceded by the command of his own preceptor— || 82 ||
In the month of Māgha, or in Vaiśākha, Kārtika, Śrāvaṇa, or Mārgaśīrṣa, one whose soul is purified should perform this during the festival of the Sun.

Having fasted for three nights and bathed, one should offer a hundred oblations with clarified butter into the fire while reciting the *Yaśas* mantras; then, one should offer the clarified butter in three ways while reciting the mantras of the rays of the Blessed One.
Having prostrated with the eight limbs according to the prescribed rite before the Jātavadana-siṃha,
he then offered a pair of garments to the preceptor.
Having respectfully given a pair of earrings worth a thousand niṣkas, or gold worth a hundred niṣkas, or half of that, or half of that again; || 88 ||
Free from deceit and guile, he should offer [the gift] at the lotus feet of the preceptor;
on the following day, he should feed a hundred Brahmins and married women.
Having honored the teacher’s wife, sons, and others with collections of ritual manuals,
[one should worship] the pair of sandals when the teacher is in a distant land.
In the absence of that [recipient], one should offer it in the presence of the Blessed One;
otherwise, one devoted to that [practice] should send the object to the wife or the sons of the teacher.
During the planetary eclipses, one should perform the preliminary rite (puraścaryā) at the confluence of the Vāsiṣṭhā and Sindhu rivers,
having duly performed the worship of Ambā with all its ancillaries and complete sacrificial fees.
Through the grace of Nṛsiṃha, having immediately conquered even difficult death,
he quickly beheld Brahmāda, the leader of the empire of the Daityas.
For a long time he was the lord and sovereign of the Daityas;
however, through the grace of Prahlāda, he immediately became unswerving in his devotion to Hari.
Having constantly beheld with his eyes Narasiṃha, the Lord of the World, accompanied by Mahālakṣmī and surrounded by the deities, he gazes upon him. || 95 ||
Day after day, Prahlāda offered him jewels, sandals,
garments of great value, and even the eightfold prosperity.
O King, by the grace of Narahari, a great sage is born who possesses the splendor pervaded by a continuous succession of moving flowers. 97.
Having reached Kollāpura, she bowed with devotion before the pair of feet of the Teacher in the presence of Kamalā, performing a prostration with eight limbs (aṣṭāṅga-praṇāma).
By reciting the eight-syllable mantra there, one obtains imperishable fruit;
that very [mantra] is auspicious, bestows great fortune, and brings fame. (99)
On the surface of the earth, all [these] are located within the sacred seats (pīṭhas), for there is nothing superior to them;
they grant great accomplishments immediately and destroy even the most heinous sins.
There is no seat on earth equal to that [Pīṭha], which bestows immediate accomplishment for those seeking the fruits of the four aims—dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa. (101)
For the complete accomplishment of all desired goals, the wise man should worship Mahālakṣmī at the seat of Śrī, Kollāpura, by means of the Lakṣmī-hṛdaya-vidyā.
In this regard, O protector of the earth, listen with a concentrated mind; I shall speak concerning the great field of Kollāpura, preceded by the command of one's own teacher. (103)
Constantly performing the three daily ablutions and endowed with all the ritual placements (nyāsa),
he respectfully recited the venerable eight-syllabled mantra one hundred thousand times.
Thereafter, one should mutter the Lakṣmī-hṛdaya-vidyā one hundred thousand times, or else the twelve-syllable Lakṣmī-mantra, or even the six-syllable Śrī-mantra. (105)
O Sudeva, having recited twelve thousand times the great Vaiṣṇavī vidyā consisting of six syllables, which is garlanded with the rays of the Blessed One; || 106 ||
Having recited [the mantra] one hundred and eight times according to the rules over fire consecrated by ritual,
[he should offer oblations] with sesame seeds mixed with ghee and honey, together with bilva leaves.
Having slain [the obstacles] with the glorious twelve-thousand-verse *Aṣṭākṣarī* Vidyā, one should then offer three thousand oblations of clarified butter with the *Prasannalakṣmī* mantra. (108)
Having offered a thousand oblations of clarified butter into the blazing fire, one should perform the offering for Vāsudeva with the six-syllable Vaiṣṇava mantra.
Having performed the fire sacrifice (*homa*) with sesame seeds twelve times using the *bhagavadraśmi* mantras,
and having then performed the *japa* and other rites, one should then offer the *brahmārpaṇa* oblation.
Having circumambulated the fire and prostrated with eight limbs before the two feet of his own preceptor, he [offered] a golden vessel marked with sixty signs.
Having given a pair of earrings, as well as rings for the fingers,
one should also offer ornaments such as the waist-belt and so forth.
One should bestow upon this teacher a thousand gold niṣkas, or half of that, or half of that again,
or even fifty or twenty-five.
Having abandoned deceit, one should especially honor the preceptor with gold, ornaments, and garments, even if they are already dear to him. 114.
And on that day, one should feed more than a hundred Brāhmaṇas and women in their period of purification (suvāsinīs),
together with Mahālakṣmī, before one's own eyes.
He beholds the omnipresent Lord Hari mounted upon the son of Vinatā,
as well as the immovable Śrī, who is filled with the wealth of the world’s jewels, horses, and other riches.
By his grace, he attains long life, freedom from disease, and supreme sovereignty over all the Siddhas, and beholds Kapila. (117)

And having attained the prosperity consisting of the powers of the perfected ones, such as the power of the jewels and so forth, as well as the yoga endowed with eight limbs which bestows all perfections; || 118 ||
Having attained the power of moving through the sky, as well as the speed of thought and imperishability, he shall be free from old age and death with this very body.
In worlds such as Śvetadvīpa and those beginning with Satyaloka,
he dwells eternally in blissful sport through the grace of Kapila.
Day by day he beholds a hundred tawny-eyed women;
moreover, he attains such powers as the ability to enter the bodies of others.
Having approached Puruṣottama in the presence of the Lord of the World,
he bathed in the Mārkaṇḍeya lake, and after that, he bathed in the ocean.
Having prostrated at the lotus feet of the Teacher,
he chanted the glorious eight-syllabled mantra accompanied by all the ritual placements (nyāsa), while observing the vow of the white sun.
One should recite the six-syllabled Vaiṣṇava mantra of Vāsudeva, the great spell, ten thousand times for the sake of attaining prosperity.
Having duly consecrated Nala with the glorious eight-syllable mantra, one should offer ten thousand oblations of sesame seeds mixed with the three sweets, cow products, and clarified butter.
Having performed the oblation known as the *brahmārpaṇa*.
Having paid homage to the feet of the Teacher, he then prostrated himself like a staff at his two feet; [he also offered] a pair of earrings to his ears. (128)
Having offered a vessel marked with six lines, fashioned from refined gold, set with rubies, and accompanied by fine garments; || 129 ||
One should give a Śālagrāma stone along with a pair of cows;
one should give a great gift (mahādakṣiṇā), or half of that, or half of that again.
Or one should offer twenty-five niṣkas according to one's capacity;
and one should feed a hundred women of the guilds along with their leaders and married women.
Then, having given garments, ornaments, and so forth to the preceptor’s wife,
[he should immediately worship] the omnipresent Lord of the World together with Subhadrā.
Worshipped by Brahmā, Rudra, and others, he beholds with his own eyes the subtle one fallen from Garuḍa, situated in the midst of a circle of light.
By his grace, he immediately beholds Mārkaṇḍeya;
the sage, the son of Mṛkaṇḍu, becomes his eternal friend.
When the Lord of the worlds, accompanied by Mahālakṣmī, is pleased,
[one attains] either the great city of universal sovereignty or the realm of Brahmā.
Nothing is impossible for one who has attained the grace of Śrī;
having reached the city of Ayodhyā, he then bathed in the waters of the Śarayū. (136)
Then, having prostrated like a staff before the pair of feet of the teacher,
and having worshipped the illustrious Lord Śiva together with his attendants and the great circle of deities, [he spoke].
Having recited the glorious eight-syllabled mantra, conjoined with all the ritual placements (nyāsas), one hundred thousand times, and then offering one hundred thousand lotuses to Śrī; 138.
Having recited the Vāstudeva Mahāvidyā and the six-syllabled Vaiṣṇavī mantra ten thousand times each, one should then recite the garland-mantra of the Lord of Śrī.

He performed the fire-oblation for King Rāma, who had been consecrated to the kingdom, with a thousand oblations of clarified butter according to the rules, using the venerable eight-syllable mantra in a consecrated fire.
One should respectfully offer ten thousand oblations with the clarified butter of Kapila;
for the glorious eight-syllable mantra, one should offer ten thousand oblations with the secret goat's ghee.
One thousand oblations should be offered with the Śrī-mantra and the Vidyā of Vāsudeva,
using Vaiṣṇava-kapila ghee, cow’s urine, and cow’s clarified butter, performed with devotion.
One should offer oblations accompanied by the glorious eight-syllabled mantra.
Having offered three thousand oblations with the Śrī-mantra, a thousand with the Vidyā of Vāsudeva, and a hundred with the Vaiṣṇavī mantra, he should then offer oblations with the Śrīrāma-mantra.
One should offer one thousand three hundred oblations of cow’s ghee with the *Agra* mantra;
having offered it five times with cow’s ghee, one should offer it with the rays of Bhava.
Having performed the recitation, the fire-oblation, and then the oblation of dedication to Brahman,
one should circumambulate the fire and then the two feet of one's own preceptor.
Then, having prostrated with the eight limbs, [he offered] two auspicious sacrificial pits fashioned from refined gold and joined with rubies.
Having given two cows along with their calves, yielding much milk, to the younger brother of the preceptor, he then respectfully offered a thousand gold coins (niṣkas).
Having given even a hundred *niṣkas*, or half of that, or half of that again;
and having given ornaments and such to the preceptor’s beloved wife.
On that day, one should feed twenty-five pairs of couples, including the great king honored by Bharata and the others.
He beholds with his own eyes the Lord of Śrī Rāma and Jānakī, who is praised by Sugrīva and the other monkeys, and who is surrounded by Brahmā, Rudra, and the other gods.

Having bestowed his desired wealth along with his army—even that which was impossible for the gods to achieve and situated beyond the range of lamps—the illustrious Lord of the World [granted it]. 150.
The friend Añjanāsūnu will surely act; of this there is no doubt.
By the power of Hanumān, the Siddhas, Yakṣas, and others [will be subdued]. (151)
The foremost among those who wear sandals also attain swift accomplishments for him, as well as freedom from old age and death, and the inexhaustibility of his long life. (152)
Having reached Vārāṇasī in the presence of Viśvanātha, the son of this woman constantly grants her desired objects that are otherwise difficult to attain. (153)

Having performed his ablutions at Maṇikarṇikā, having bowed to the all-pervading Lord Viśveśvara, having worshipped and prostrated before Vindumādhava, and having bowed to the sandals of his own preceptor; 154.

Then, being pure, having recited one hundred thousand times the auspicious and glorious eight-syllabled mantra accompanied by all the ritual placements (nyāsa) in the presence of the Blessed One, || 155 ||
One who has conquered the senses and subsists on sacrificial food (haviṣya) should mutter the *Śrīsūkta* one hundred thousand times;
thereafter, one should mutter the six-syllabled Vaiṣṇava mantra dedicated to Vāsudeva.
Having recited the glorious eighteen-syllable mantra ten thousand times individually, and having recited the Brahmavidyā twelve thousand times and ten thousand times; 157.
Then, having worshipped the Lord Viṣṇu with flowers,
one should thereafter offer oblations into the fire with the Śrī-aṣṭākṣarī mantra.
With betel leaves mixed with sesame seeds and unbroken rice grains, and saturated with clarified butter. || 159 ||
Having offered ten thousand oblations,
one should offer three thousand with the mantra of Vāsudeva and with the six-syllabled Vaiṣṇava mantra.
Having offered thirty oblations for each [mantra], he should thereafter offer one thousand three hundred oblations into the fire with the *udhvaṅgira* mantra.
Having offered oblations into the petals of the Lord’s rays, having performed the fivefold offering,
and having performed the recitation and the fire-sacrifice (homa), one should then bow to the fire thereafter.
Having prostrated before the pair of feet of the Teacher and circumambulated them,
[he offered] an image fashioned from gold refined sixty-four times.
Having given a pair of excellent earrings to the ears of Caryapa, and having honored him with respect through ornaments such as pearls and the like; 164.
Having given a pair of linen garments, one should present a thousand niṣkas, or three hundred niṣkas, or one hundred niṣkas, or half of that, or even half of that again. || 65 ||
Then, with the thought that he was Mahālakṣmī, she adorned her preceptor— who was modest, free from deceit, and possessed of wisdom— as well as his wife.
One should offer earrings adorned with gems, as well as a ring;
or else, one should offer a silk garment, a complete set of clothes, and a bodice. (167)
Then, having given food to twenty-five couples and having satisfied them with sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) and other gifts according to his means, he proceeded on his way.
On that day, having remained without food in the presence of Vidumādhava,
one should eat at the [concluded] stages together with Brāhmaṇas and kinsmen.
Nāthī, who had certainly not gone [to him], beheld with her own eyes Acyuta, accompanied by Viśveśvara, as he was traveling toward Vidarbha. || 170 ||
Through his grace, even though he was mute, he became a master who had reached the further shore of all sciences;
endowed with great splendor, he attained the eighth stage, which is possessed of eight qualities.
Having attained health through each flower and honey, he becomes the lord of your servants;
and at the end, having become so, he goes into your presence accompanied by ten million members of his lineage.

At Prayāga, the foremost of sacred sites, at the beginning of the month of Makara-sthira-vau (Makara-saṃkrānti), having bathed every morning and completed his daily obligatory rites, he [should proceed]. || 173 ||
Having affectionately and respectfully saluted the pair of feet of his own teacher,
[he offers] the glorious eight-syllabled lore (aṣṭākṣarī-vidyā) together with all the ritual placements (nyāsa).
Then, having performed one hundred thousand recitations, and twenty-five thousand recitations of the Mahālakṣmī mantra and the Vāsudeva-ādyātman mantra; 175.
One should recite the six-syllabled Vaiṣṇava mantra ten thousand times for each,
according to the rules, in a consecrated fire with the glorious eight-syllabled vidyā.
Having offered twelve thousand oblations of sesame seeds soaked in cow’s ghee,
one should offer three thousand oblations with sesame seeds mixed with clarified butter for the sake of prosperity.
Thereafter, having offered one thousand oblations each to the Vāsudeva-dvādaśārṇava and the Vaiṣṇava mantras, he should perform the rite thrice with the Bhagavad-raśmi mantras.
Having performed twelve thousand oblations, one should worship with the Brahmavidyā;
then, one should honor the preceptor with ornaments such as earrings and the like.
Having given a pair of fine garments, one may give even a thousand *niṣkas*, or three hundred, or a hundred *niṣkas*, or half of that, or half of that again. || 180 ||
Having abandoned Vitalībha, satisfy the venerable Ācārya Vallabhā with wealth, intelligence, ornaments, and garments; thereafter, [proceed] further.

One should also feed twenty-five pairs [of guests], regarding them with the thought that they are Śrī and Śrīpati, and subsequently honor them with water, sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā), and other offerings.
On the final day of the month of Māgha, the wise man should increase the number of the venerable Lord Śrīśa by three hundred and one thousand repetitions of the Brahmavidyā mantra.
Having fasted on that day, he beholds the Lord of the Universe— the God who is the consort of Śrī— in a dream at night, as if seeing Him face to face.
By his command, the eight guardians of the directions,
headed by Śakra, the protectors of the worlds, appeared in person at the order of that Lord of Śrī.
Day after day, she performed service for him without a doubt—
[a service] like that of the Kalpa-tree, the wish-fulfilling cow, or a most wonderful jewel.
Having given it, they then bestowed the divine nectar (amṛta) without a doubt;
having drunk that divine nectar, he became free from old age and immortal.
Having become capable of assuming forms at will, possessing the speed of thought, and moving through the sky, he wanders through all the worlds, attended by Siddhas and Gandharvas. || 188 ||
Having reached the Badarī forest together with Nara,
and having bathed in the Cālaka river, they completed their prescribed rites.
Having first received the command of one's own preceptor, one should then recite the glorious eight-syllabled vidyā, conjoined with all the nyāsas, one hundred thousand times.
Having recited twenty-five thousand times the twenty-seven-syllable mantra of Śrī, as well as the Vaiṣṇava six-syllable mantra known as Vāsudeva, [one attains success].
Having recited the *Raśmimālī* mantra one thousand times for each individual,
and having recited it one hundred and eight times according to the rules over fire consecrated by ritual, [one should proceed].
With the venerable eight-syllable mantra, one should reverently offer milk-rice soaked in the three sweets,
or else clarified butter from a cow, a thousand times for each solar deity.
One should perform the vow by offering oblations three thousand times with the *prasannalakṣmī* mantra,
and likewise with the mantra of Vāsudeva and the Vaiṣṇava mantra.

Having offered three hundred oblations for each [deity] by means of the threefold rays of the Blessed One, and having performed the fire sacrifice (homa) in the blazing fire with recitations (japa) and other rites; || 195 ||
Having made the fire manifest and bowed to the feet of one's own teacher, one should recite the Nara-Nārāyaṇa Vidyā one thousand times. 196.
With that very [mantra], one should offer clarified butter into the fire one thousand three hundred times;
having again performed the recitation and the homa, one should offer the oblation of dedication to Brahman (brahmārpaṇa).
Having prostrated with all eight limbs before the pair of feet of the teacher,
he placed a beautiful pair of earrings upon the ears of the teacher.
Having given the finest ring and other ornaments, and having offered a pair of yellow garments at the two feet of his own preceptor; 199.
One should give a thousand gold niṣkas, or five hundred, or two hundred, or one hundred niṣkas, or half of that, or even half of that again. || 200 ||
Having abandoned greed for wealth, and having given to the two [the preceptor and his wife], one should give to the preceptor’s wife ornaments and other such items according to one's means. || 201 ||
One should also feed twenty-five pairs [of Brahmins],
and on that day, being pure, one should recite the *Naranārāyaṇī* mantra.
Firm in his vows and fasting, the omnipresent Lord,
who is to be known by Brahmā, Rudra, and the others, will join with Nara at night.
By my grace, he shall be directly endowed with a splendor equal to that of the sun;
free from old age and death, he shall be eternal and twenty-five years of age.
Whether it be the state of a perfected being (siddha), immortality, or the status of a Brahman-sage; or else the state of a great yogin, or even the state of Brahmā or Maheśvara.
Or else, having attained his desired goal— whether it be the state of Viṣṇuhood or something else— the practitioner,
becoming emaciated for a moment and then stout for a moment, shall again obtain the eightfold prosperity.
Having attained the eightfold yoga, he enters the bodies of others;
he understands the speech of animals and possesses continuous omniscience.
Having attained death at will— which is difficult even for the gods to obtain— at the end of the body, that wise one, together with ten million members of his lineage, enters indeed into my state.
Dvārakā, Mathurā, Avantī, Kurukṣetra, and Naimiṣa—
these sacred fields exist upon the surface of the earth as those which grant immediate spiritual perfection.
Having performed the fire-oblation, recitation, and other rites according to the procedure prescribed in the *Vadaryukta*,
and having acted with the permission of the preceptor, one indeed attains the desired accomplishment.
O King, it is said that in this world, the absence of these [deities] everywhere grants success; or rather, the presence of their wives, sons, and grandsons does so as well.
Or, the recitation of mantras and other rites should be performed in the presence of the sandals of the teacher;
the offering of a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) should be made to that pair of sandals.
Then one should entrust that forest to the wife or the sons of the teacher;
by this procedure as well, one attains the desired accomplishment. || 213 ||
The fruit arising from the recitation, fire-offerings, and other rites of the glorious eight-syllabled vidyā cannot be described even by the Creator, the Lord of Māyā, nor by Śambhu.
One should know that there is no deity higher than the teacher, nor any knowledge superior to the eight-syllable mantra;
having fully understood this and being constantly devoted to it, one rejoices, partaking in the nature of Brahman.
This indeed is another means for attaining Brahman that brings about the highest good; there is nothing superior to this. This is the truth, the truth; it is most exalted. || 216 ||
This greatness of the eight [mātṛkās] has been briefly proclaimed here;
thereafter, the means of accomplishment for the vidyās beginning with Vasudharā will be declared.
[Thus ends the forty-sixth chapter in the venerable *Anuttarabrahmatattvarahasya*, the *Dāśarathīya Tantra*, which is a compendium of the meaning of the Vedas.]
The Blessed Lord said:
Now I shall declare the supreme procedure for the practice of the Bhū-vidyā, as well as the ritual for the Nīlādhividyā; listen with faith. (1)
Having uttered the seed-syllable of the Three Vedas (Om), followed by the fourteenth [letter] (Ū) together with Gaṇapa (La), Bindu (M), and Nada (H). || 2 ||
Then, they know the fourth vowel as the one situated within; beyond that is the supreme *ut* (u).
That same [vowel] is also without the bindu (*ū*), joined with the fifth *bhṛgu* (m).
The fire [letter] joined with the bindu, not preceded by a consonant; the wind [letter] conjoined with the long [vowel], and accompanied by the heart [syllable] joined with twelve.
This Vidyā, consisting of ten syllables, is proclaimed as the Earth itself;
it embodies all sacred fords and bestows the supernatural powers of all holy sites, jewels, and other attainments.
It pacifies all present-day misfortunes and destroys great poverty;
the sage is said to be Varāha, and Vairāja is declared to be the meter.
The deity of all beings is considered to be Prakṛti, the Earth;
she is called the second seed-syllable and is declared to be the power of the heart (Hṛcchakti).
In the second [circle], which is six finger-breadths long, one should perform the nyāsa of the Vaṣaṭ-aṅgas;
[therein is] Śyāmā, who is multicolored, seated upon a lotus throne.
We worship the Earth, who is bent by her heavy breasts, who holds a cluster of rice stalks like a pair of excellent lotus stalks, and who bears a parrot.
The practitioner of mantra should devoutly recite the mantra of Dharā one hundred thousand times;
he should then perform oblations with ghee and milk-rice (pāyasa) in a portion equal to one-tenth of that number.
One should worship that [image] of Viṣṇu according to the procedure to be described;
first, one should worship the elements: earth, fire, water, and air.
Having worshipped [the deities] on the petals of the directions, one should worship the *natkalās* (nine digits) on the petals of the corners;
those digits are Jvalinī, Jvālinī, and Dhūmrārcis.
Then the guardians of the quarters (Āśāpālas), endowed with the vajra and other weapons, should be worshipped;
the practitioner of all perfected mantras and spells shall accomplish his desires.
Twenty-four thousand [years] constitute a day and night for Bhagīratha;
thus, it continues incessantly for one day and likewise for another.
One should offer three thousand oblations into the fire with clarified butter, honey-triad, and milk-rice;
[one then obtains] land equal in size to a cow-hide, provided it is cultivated and well-plowed.
One should present [the gift] accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to the preceptor;
or else, one should offer land or a substitute object to the teacher.
One attains the accomplishment of knowledge, which is difficult to find in these worlds;
one should perform oblations with red lotuses combined with the three sweets.
Having offered five thousand oblations of *priyaṅgu* flowers, smeared with honey, which are beautiful even when not yet fully blossomed, one attains a thousandfold increase in prosperity on earth.
The practitioner of mantra obtains inexhaustible wealth, grain, land, and the splendor of ripened crops; he also beholds hidden treasures. || 18 ||
Having constantly offered oblations twelve times from a vessel made of rice with flowering ears, weighed against three measures of honey, one shall become a husband of excellent women.
Having taken the earth from the root of the plant to be cultivated at the beginning of the day on a Friday,
and having cast it into water, one should cook the sacrificial oblation (caru) with the Śoṣiṇī mantra.
One should offer oblations into the fire with milk and ghee on Saturdays for six months; by so offering, one shall obtain excellent wealth.
In eight hundred years, he shall become the lord of a village;
having recited the *Dharādhidyā* one hundred thousand times, he should worship according to the prescribed rite.

One who has purified their soul should offer oblations into the fire with lotuses mixed with ghee and the three sweets; such a person becomes surrounded by a multitude of wealth and jewels, equal to a thousand suns.
He rules the earth bounded by the four oceans; of this there is no doubt.
Thus, the practitioner who worships Varāhī is like a beast, lacking wealth, grain, and other such things. (24)
The beloved of the Earth [is the king]; there is no need for deliberation regarding the crops and food here.
Thus, a certain portion of the greatness of the mantra upon the Earth has been described by me. (25)
Therefore, I shall hereafter proclaim the greatness of Nīlā on this earth:
the seed-syllable *trapī* (trp) joined with a bindu, followed by the fourth vowel (*ū*). (26)
Having uttered the twenty touches (sparśas) joined with Vāmalocanā,
followed by Mukhavṛtā, Utā, Bhūmi, Dhyānti, and Rudra.
Furthermore, the nectar (Amṛta) joined with Vāyu and mounted upon the Vāgbhava [seed-syllable], when conjoined with the Heart [mantra], is declared to be Nīlāvidyā. (28)
She bestows the perfection of all great assemblies;
she consists of all sacred fields and brings the three worlds under her control. (29)
The seer of this [mantra] is Brahmā; it is said that its meter is the Gāyatrī of the Chāndogas;
the goddess Nīlā is its deity; and its seed-syllable is Vāmalocana.
The Heart-power (Hṛcchakti) is said to consist of the long vowels; one should perform the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅgaka).
She has the appearance of a dark cloud and is marked with a tilaka of saffron.
She was endowed with divine ornaments, possessed of divine garments,
her body anointed with divine sandalwood paste, and adorned with divine garlands of flowers.
On the left side of the Blessed One is [a goddess] fanning him with a chowrie in one hand,
holding a lotus in her other hand, and possessing a face like the autumnal moon.
Having meditated upon Nīlādevī—the beloved of Hari, who has a smiling face, large eyes, and is blue in complexion—one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times with a focused mind. (34)

Having offered this [oblation] for the removal of the ten types of hemorrhoids, mixed with ghee and the three sweets, and having given the teacher’s fee, one shall attain the perfection of knowledge. || 35 ||
Alternatively, having performed twenty-five thousand recitations accompanied by sacrificial fees,
one should offer three thousand oblations with white lotuses on the following day.
Having given wealth measured by a *vaṣāśana* mixed with ghee, honey, and sugar to the preceptor, one attains success in the pair of *advandva*, just like my younger brother.
By this [practice], the minister shall accomplish all that is desired;
her worship is like that of the Earth, and she is also called Nīlā. (38)
Having recited this Nīlā-vidyā, which bestows fruits, one hundred thousand times,
one should offer oblations consisting of ghee mixed with the three sweets (trimadhu) in a quantity equal to one-tenth [of the recitation].
Even one of dull intellect or mute shall become a master of all sciences by respectfully offering five thousand *huṅkārāḥ* with *palāśa* flowers. (40)
By offering six thousand oblations of red lotuses mixed with honey, one who has conquered the senses shall become a treasury of all knowledge.
Having recited this vidyā one hundred thousand times within a grove of tulasī trees, one obtains great and immovable sovereignty abounding in jewels.
Having offered oblations with Tulasī leaves mixed with ghee and honey,
one obtains universal sovereignty and unshakable prosperity.
Having offered a thousand oblations with devotion using parched grains soaked in ghee,
one obtains a desired daughter endowed with beauty, good character, and virtues.
By reciting the great vidyā of Anilā every day while remaining pure,
one shall obtain wealth, grain, precious gems, and great knowledge.
A certain ritual procedure for the Nīladivya-bhūti,
as well as another for the Vāsudeva and other vidyās, and furthermore, their majesty shall now be described.
[Thus ends the forty-seventh chapter in the venerable *Anuttarabrahmatattvarahasya*, the *Dāśarathīya Tantra*, which is a compendium of the meaning of the Vedas.]
The Blessed Lord spoke the twelve-syllable mantra of Vāsudeva: "Listen, O King, protector of the earth, to the mantra of Vāsudeva, the wielder of the discus."
[She is] the primordial ignorance whose nature is the Supreme Brahman, which bestows all accomplishments.

Then, having uttered the Praṇava joined with "namaḥ," followed by the syllable "ma" and "ga," one should utter "vateyada" and "amaya," along with the nectar (sudhā) accompanied by the covering of the mouth.
Then [the syllable] *bha*, followed by *muṃ* and *sa-vā-ma-ka-ṇaṃ*; then *rudra-yukta-a-tri-m* as well;
then *varuṇa* conjoined with a long vowel, and also the syllable of the Wind (*māruta*). || 3 ||
This [work] is subject to Vāsudeva, the Brahman, the Supreme Soul;
it is a compendium of the essential meaning of all the Vedas and Vedāntas.
The great mantra of Vāsudeva, which destroys all heinous sins and dispels every suffering, was [revealed] in the past by Svāyambhuva and others.
Having chanted this twelve-syllable mantra of the Lord of Śrī, even Dhruva attained imperishable perfection at the command of Nārada.
Having merely recited it, he attained a perfection exceedingly difficult to find even in the three worlds:
long life, health, sovereignty, fame, wealth, and the fulfillment of all desires.
From this twelve-syllable mantra, there arises freedom from fever, hunger, and thirst, the auspicious recollection of former births, and all spiritual accomplishments (siddhis) are attained.
The Brahman named Vāsudeva, who is the essence of the universal womb,
shines eternally for him through the recitation of the twelve-syllable mantra.
For one desiring the attainment of identity with Brahman in a single lifetime,
there is the twelve-syllable mantra born from the great lore of Vāsudeva.
The seer of this mantra from the mouth of Brahmā is said to be Ājagarta;
its meter is called Jagatī, and it is declared by the wise that its deity is the one named Vāsudeva.

The seed-syllable is said to be the intellect (dhī), and the bow (namaḥ) is declared to be power (śakti). Having performed the placement on the heart with the Praṇava, one should perform the placement on the head with "namaḥ."
O Lord of the Earth, one should assign the word "Bhagavate" to the crest-lock;
with five syllables, one should perform the assignment of the armor for the whole body, and one should employ the weapon-mantra for the entire [body].
I always bow to Hari, who is resplendent with a brilliant discus, a mace, and a club, seated upon a lotus,
wearing bracelets, a breast-ornament, a necklace, and a crown, and shining like a fresh jasmine flower.
Having thus meditated upon Vāsudeva, the Lord of the universe, directly within one's heart,
one should worship him on the seat of water, joined with the Arghya vessel.
The first enclosure consists of five deities in the five directions in sequence:
Vāsudeva on the eight-petaled [lotus], then Śrī, and then Saṃkarṣaṇa.
And Sarasvatī, Prachumna, Rati, and Aniruddha;
in the twelve-petaled lotus, one should worship Keśava first, followed by Prīti.
Then, having worshipped Nārāyaṇa, Mādhava, Govinda, Viṣṇu, and Madhusūdana in succession, he attained the supreme state.
Afterwards, one should worship Vāmana, Śrīdhara, and thereafter Ṛṣīkeśa; then Padmanābha, and after that Dāmodara.

Then, having thus worshipped Vāsudeva, the Lord of the Universe and Master of the World, by Śakra and the others, the eight [directional] guardians beginning with Aṣṭha, and by those beginning with Vajra; || 20 ||
The practitioner of mantra should recite the Arkatākṣa mantra according to the rules over consecrated fire,
having offered oblations of white sesame seeds mixed with cow’s ghee, honey, and molasses.
Having offered a fee of a thousand gold coins to the preceptor, one attains the eternal accomplishment of the great vidyā of Vāsudeva. || 22 ||
Then, for twenty-one thousand [breaths], or even eleven thousand, one should practice during the twelfth [day] day and night with undistracted mind. (23)
On the thirteenth day, one should offer twelve hundred oblations of ghee mixed with the three sweets and auspicious sesame seeds, along with wealth equal to a year's worth of food.
Having bestowed the perfection of knowledge upon him at the lotus-feet of the preceptor,
[he did so] when the fire was kindled with milk-soaked *akṣīra* fuel-sticks.

Having offered twelve thousand oblations, one attains the threefold purity; likewise, by reciting the mantra a hundred thousand times while subsisting on a milk diet in a cow-pen or in Vṛndāvana, one attains the same.
Having offered ten thousand oblations of *palāśa* flowers soaked in ghee and the three sweets (*trimadhu*), one becomes a master of all sciences; O Blessed One, there is no doubt about this. (27)
On the bank of a river, one should mutter [the mantra] for one hundred and twenty thousand times,
having offered twelve thousand oblations of sacrificial food soaked in ghee and honey.
Presided over by Lakṣmī and Vidyā as his wealth-giver, possessing a splendor like that of Kubera,
and resembling Kāmadeva in beauty, he shall live for a hundred autumns.
Having offered ten thousand oblations of dūrvā grass and cow’s ghee, one obtains long life and cattle; of this there is no doubt. (30)
Having offered three odd-numbered oblations of *naṃdyāvarta* flowers smeared with cow’s ghee and mixed with the three sweets (*madhutritaya*), he becomes endowed with a portion of the Blessed One.
May there be mastery over the qualities such as *aṇimā* and the rest, perfection of speech, long life, incomparable health, and union with sons and other blessings. (32)
There is no doubt that one attains this through the grace of the Lord of Śrī;
[he who is] lying on the ground during the month of Māgha, eating sacrificial food (haviṣya), and having his senses conquered. || 33 ||
Having recited the twelve-syllable mantra of the Lord of Śrī one hundred and twenty thousand times,
what is there that the knower of mantras cannot quickly accomplish through this recitation?
Omniscience, mental charm, the sense of "mine," and the state of a great seer—whether you have achieved these, or even the power of moving through the sky; || 35 ||
Even that which is unattainable for the gods, he accomplishes as his desired goal, whether by means of the ten-syllable vidyā or by the recitation of the *krakucchanda* mantra. (36)
Having enjoyed all the pleasures here that are difficult for humans to obtain,
he uplifts a hundred lineages and rejoices in the supreme state.
I shall proclaim the six-syllabled mantra of Viṣṇu, which bestows all perfections; by the mere knowledge of which great calamities flee away. (38)
A Vaiṣṇava should utter the syllable Om for Viṣṇu, accompanied by the word "namas";
this is declared to be the six-syllabled Vaiṣṇava vidyā.
She is the eternal cause of the empire of all prosperity, the destroyer of great sins, and the bestower of the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation. (40)
The seer is Prajāpati Brahmā; the meter is said to be Gāyatrī;
the deity is the supreme self, Śrī Mahāviṣṇu, the Lord of Śrī. || 41 ||
The seed-syllable of the Triple Veda is said to be the seed, and *nati* is declared to be the power (*śakti*).
By means of one, three, and two [syllables], repeated twice, the six-limbed [mantra] is formed.
Having performed the ritual placement (vinyāsa) at the heart, one should meditate upon the Lord of Śrī, the Master of the worlds,
seated auspiciously upon a divine jeweled lion-throne at the root of the kalpa-tree.
He beheld the Lord of Indirā seated, possessing the luster of a fresh blue cloud,
bearing the conch, discus, mace, and lotus, with the Śrīvatsa mark upon his chest.
Wearing yellow garments, adorned with necklaces, earrings, and other ornaments, with large eyes like lotus petals, and possessing a splendor equal to ten million Cupids. || 45 ||
On his right side, he is accompanied by the goddess Kāmākasthitā, who is adorned with golden ornaments and holds a chowrie in her hand.
On the left side of Dhruvadevī, she is accompanied by Nīlādevī and surrounded by the eight śaktis, beginning with Vimalā, Utkarṣiṇī, and Jñānā.
I bow to Viṣṇu, the sustainer of the universe, who is praised by Ananta, Viśvaksena, Garuḍa, and others, and who is the supreme refuge for the protection of the world.
Having thus meditated upon Mahāviṣṇu, the sole witness of all the worlds,
one should conquer the six-syllabled Vaiṣṇava mantra which bestows all spiritual perfections.
First, one should conquer [the obstacles] by reciting six hundred thousand [times] in a cow-pen or in Vṛndāvana;
having brought the preceptor into proximity, one should satisfy him with a tenth part [of the recitation].
Then, having offered oblations with Tulasī leaves mixed with ghee ten times [the number of recitations],
one should present abundant sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) at the pair of feet of the preceptor.
One attains the perfection of knowledge and pleases the All-pervading Lord;
this is the Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Yoga, consisting of twenty-five thousand [verses].
Having recited [the mantra] on one day, on the following day,
being composed in mind, he should offer three thousand oblations of sesame seeds smeared with ghee into the consecrated fire.
By offering wealth equal to a year's worth of food at the lotus feet of the preceptor,
one attains the perfection of knowledge immediately, O great sage.
Having fasted throughout the entire month of Kārttika, with his senses subdued,
he recited this vidyā one hundred thousand times according to the rules in the consecrated fire.
Having offered oblations with lotus petals or bilva leaves soaked in the three sweets,
one attains the powers such as atomization (aṇimā) and certainly becomes omniscient.
Having become pure, one should daily offer one hundred and eight oblations into the fire according to the rules, using Tulasī leaves mixed with honey, sugar, cow-products, and clarified butter.
Within six months, having attained great fortune abounding in wealth, one becomes a master of all sciences; of this there is no doubt.
By means of this rite, one attains for a year all things that are difficult to obtain and even those beyond one's wildest desires;
thereafter, one eternally beholds Mahendra and the other gods.
Having become a Siddha in Amarāvatī, accompanied by a thousand members of his lineage,
he fell with great force in a body of radiant light in this very same physical form.
The wise man, honored by Mahendra, rejoices until the end of the kalpa, having daily recited this great six-syllable vidyā.
In the presence of the Lord of Śrī, or at the end [of the name], it becomes inexhaustible until the end of the aeon;
[one should utter] the Praṇava joined with the name, or likewise the words "Viṣṇave" and "Iśa."
Then the letter *va*, the letter *na*, the letter *ca*, the letter *sū*, the letter *kḍa*, the letter *pār*, the letter *śva*, and thereafter the seed-syllable of the navel (*nābhivīja*);
then the letter *va* (of Varuṇa), the letter *ru*, the letter *ṇa*, the letter *da*, the letter *kṣa*, the letter *ne*, the letter *trā*, the letter *rghā*, and then the second sibilant (*ūṣman*).
The water conjoined with the touch of the Yakṣa and accompanied by Rudra—
this is declared to be the Vaiṣṇavī Ekādaśākṣarī-vidyā.
It removes the fear of recollection, destroys all afflictions, brings about longevity, health, and prosperity, and bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation. 65.
There is no other rite on earth like this which bestows such accomplishment;
it is the destroyer of great sins and the slayer of great enemies. (66)
It should always be offered as oblation by Śūdras and women without the Praṇava;
it should be constantly recited by the twice-born together with the Praṇava and Māyā.
One who desires liberation in a single birth and supreme glory even in this world should constantly recite the eleven-syllable mantra of Viṣṇu. 68.
The seer of this [hymn] is Brahmā, or Bhīṣma the son of Śāntanu;
its metre is Triṣṭubh, and it is said to belong to Mahāviṣṇu, the Lord of Glory. (69)
The deity is the Lord of the World; the Praṇava is said to be the seed-syllable.
The heart-mantra is declared to be employed for the propitiation of Lakṣmīśa. (70)
The assignment of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa) is said to be performed with two syllables, three syllables, five syllables, and again with three syllables and five syllables. || 71 ||
Meditation has been described as before; now the means of accomplishment shall be fully explained.
Five hundred thousand [recitations] are to be performed with diligence by that silent sage for the purpose of the preparatory rite (purascarya).
The wise practitioner should perform the libation (tarpaṇa) ten times that amount with milk or sugarcane juice;
then he should offer oblations into the fire ten times that amount with sesame seeds soaked in clarified butter and honey.
Having offered abundant sacrificial fees at the feet of the teacher,
the wise man shall immediately attain even the greatest of accomplishments.
O King, beginning on the eleventh day of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, or otherwise,
until the full moon, [one should recite] twenty-five thousand [verses].

Having fasted for three nights on the full moon day and observed a strict vow, one should perform three thousand oblations with guggulu resin and sesame seeds, smeared with clarified butter and mixed with the three sweets (honey, sugar, and ghee).
By offering wealth sufficient for a year's sustenance at the lotus feet of the Teacher, one attains here the great accomplishment of knowledge; of this there is no doubt. (77)
Having reverently offered five thousand parched grains soaked in ghee,
one shall obtain a beautiful maiden endowed with beauty, character, and virtue.
Having offered ten thousand oblations of pieces of *guḍūcī* soaked in clarified butter and mixed with the three sweets (*trimadhu*),
one attains great health and shall live for a thousand years.
Having offered a thousand oblations of *ketakī* flowers mixed with ghee and the three sweets (*trimadhu*),
one becomes manifest as the very embodiment of a hundred billion Kamadevas.
One attains great and unshakable sovereignty, abounding in wealth,
by offering milk-rice mixed with ghee and honey into a blazing fire.
Having offered ten thousand oblations, he shall become a master of all sciences,
provided he performs them with devotion from the moment of the planet's appearance until the time of its disappearance.
Having touched [the water] and having recited the Brahmī mantra a thousand times with devotion, one should either drink it or cause another to drink it; it reveals all branches of knowledge.
There is no doubt that he will attain the great state of Sarasvatī; his speech shall become clear and free from stammering or hesitation, even by hearing this but once.
One should certainly maintain the complete ritual procedure with devotion to Viṣṇu,
offering either five niṣkas or even one niṣka of gold.
For the attainment of Mahāsārasvata, one should give the teacher’s fee;
for the sake of accomplishing the eight-limbed yoga, one should remain in the midst of a Tulasī grove.
Having recited this vidyā one hundred thousand times, and then having offered ten thousand oblations of tulasī leaves mixed with ghee and the three sweets (trimadhu) into a blazing fire; 87.
Having attained the eightfold yoga, one indeed becomes free from old age and death;
likewise, by constantly and respectfully reciting the eleven-syllable mantra of Viṣṇu. (88)
Having attained the memory of past births, he perceives Brahman with his eye;
all [the rites] such as the worship of the yantra for these two are like those for Vāsudeva. (89)
By daily practicing the eleven-syllable vidyā through constant application,
one obtains a virtuous son endowed with prosperity and long life.
Calamities go to destruction and prosperity attends him at every step;
having become a knower of wisdom, he attains liberation along with a hundred generations of his lineage.
O you who are free from the threefold duality,
I have thus fully related to you this greatness of Vāsudeva, which bestows all that is desired.
[Thus ends the forty-eighth chapter in the venerable *Anuttarabrahmatattvarahasya*, the *Dāśarathīya Tantra*, which is a compendium of the meaning of the Vedas. 48.
The Blessed One said:
Henceforth I shall proclaim the greatness of the Yajñeśa-vidyā, which is a secret even among secrets and a compendium of all the Vedas.
Listen, I shall speak of the greatness of the knowledge of Yajñeśa, which is the essence of the flood of Vedas, Vedāntas, and Śāstras, and which bestows all that is desired. (2)
The seed-syllable of the Triple Veda is the seed-syllable of Śrī; thereafter, the seed-syllable of the Triple Veda joined with the Heart-mantra is the imperishable syllable of Śrī.
The syllable of the belly (ja) is to be uttered, joined with the syllable of the mouth (va) and the letter ca;
following the syllable of the earth (la), it is conjoined with the wind (ya). || 4 ||
Having uttered the seed-syllable joined with the twelve vowels and accompanied by the *jaṭaroṇa*, one should then recite the glorious eight-syllabled mantra along with the *kṣetra* syllables.
This eighteen-syllable Vidyā of Hari, the Lord of Lakṣmī who occupies half His body, is proclaimed as belonging to Yajñadatta; it bestows all knowledge and grants the supreme state.
It is the destroyer of all sins, the dispeller of great suffering,
the remover of mental and physical ailments for men, and the bestower of universal sovereignty and prosperity.
The ancient sages, whose girdles were the winds, had conquered their senses;
they were ever intent on the welfare of all the worlds and were constantly honored even by the gods.
Having seen the divine and ancient sages named Kūṣmīḍa-Brahmas, she prostrated before them with all eight limbs and, her distress brought forth, questioned them thus: (9)
O ancient ones, we great sages pay homage to the lotus-feet of you, the Blessed Lords, the masters of the three worlds. 10.
"O King, we are pure and stainless; how shall we become superior men in this world of mortals, or even take on the form of Brahmins? (11)
Thus questioned, the far-sighted Brāhmaṇas, the Kūṣmāṇḍas,
then reflected upon the sages who were clad only in air and long practiced in austerity.
The Kūṣmāṇḍas said: We shall proclaim to you this purifying [text], which is for the welfare of the world, the eternal essence found within the Vedāntas and the six Vedāṅgas. (13)
Upon being born from Brahmā, he became indebted on earth to three groups:
the gods, the ṛṣis, and the high-souled ancestors. || 14 ||

Through the celibate life of the sages, through progeny for the ancestors, and likewise through sacrifices for all the gods, one shall become like Brahmā upon being liberated from the three debts. (15)
The fruit of the seasons, which is difficult to attain and destroys even the greatest sins, is proclaimed in all the Vedas and likewise in the Upanishads. (16)
And by these abundant sacrificial fees, there shall be liberation from the three debts toward the ancestors, the great seers, and the deities. || 17 ||

Having studied the Vedas in their entirety, or two Vedas, or one Veda, or even a single portion according to his ability, a twice-born man, having performed a sacrifice on earth with complete sacrificial fees— or even just one— [should proceed].
Having performed the Agnihotra sacrifice every single day, both evening and morning,
as well as the Full Moon and New Moon sacrifices which destroy sin, [he attains the highest state].
O King, having performed the Yaśodā-labha sacrifice year after year,
that sacrificer became thus purified— a noble Brahmin who was the lord of the earth.
This [deity] is worshipped in the world of truth by sages and even by the gods;
it destroys the excessive pride of those who are overly arrogant, provided there is no concealment. || 21 ||
Sacrifices with very meager sacrificial fees are like those devoid of fees;
they are fruitless, there is no doubt about this, and they bestow some measure of the suffering of hell. (22)
Even a single sacrifice performed on this earth with complete sacrificial fees,
when done with the realization that it is an offering to Brahman, bestows upon that person the attainment of residence in the same world as Brahman.
A Śrāddha performed without mantras is in vain; a sacrifice with meager sacrificial fees is in vain;
a Brahmin devoid of the Vedas is in vain; and even knowledge that is not Vedic is in vain.
