Therefore, a sacrifice accompanied by sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) must necessarily be performed by a Brahmin; one who does not give such fees is declared to be a non-sacrificer (ayājya).
Having performed even a single great sacrifice with complete sacrificial fees,
he purifies his entire lineage— ten ancestors and ten descendants— and brings them under his control.
Or during an eclipse, at the sun's passage into a new sign (saṃkrānti), or even during the Navarātra vow;
or on the full moon day, or on the tenth day, in the months of Vaiśākha or Kārtika.
One should offer abundant material for the sake of sacrifice to those who have become worthy vessels;
I am not able to describe the fruit of that merit, for it is immeasurable. (28)
Indeed, it is possible to describe the fruit of a thousand great gifts, or even the fruit of giving materials for the sake of a sacrifice, such as a grain-oblation. (29)
O King, even Rudra would not be able to describe its greatness;
it is as if a hundred great gifts were bestowed at Kurukṣetra during a solar eclipse.
The gift of wealth for the sake of a sacrifice does not equal even a sixteenth part [of the merit] of one who gives property for a wedding to a learned Brahmin who is poor. (31)
The great sages have declared that the gift of a cow is equal to a verse;
yet, for the sake of marriage, one may give wealth even if it be as small as a single grain of rice.

Having rescued by the thousands those belonging to his mother’s lineage and father’s lineage who were submerged in the ocean of hell, together with his fathers and grandfathers, [he attained liberation].
Having ascended to a celestial chariot at the end of his life, he remains in the state of Brahmā alone;
yet, because he has not offered oblations into the fire nor performed sacrifices, he is remembered as a "wicked Brāhmaṇa."
One who maintains the perpetual *agnihotra* sacrifice is called the best of Brahmins;
therefore, that sacrifice must necessarily be performed with complete sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*).
"He is eternally the purifier of Brāhmaṇas," so says the Śruti;
O Teacher, when he is present in his lotus-like heart, even those who are ineligible for sacrifices [attain purity]. (37)
O Lord of the Earth, for the sake of the sacrifice, you should bestow abundant wealth—gold by the hundreds of millions—upon those who know the Vedas and are learned in the scriptures. (37)
Having given [this], he obtains a fruit that is even greater and more excellent than that;
having attained that fruit, the radiant one, accompanied by a thousand kinsmen, [attains liberation]. || 38 ||
Honored by Brahmā and remaining thereafter in the world of Satyaloka,
he attained immediate union with Brahmā, the Lord of Śrī.
This alone is declared to be the purifying rite for the twice-born;
we shall now fully explain the Vedic ritual concerning flowers, even though it is well-guarded secrecy.
The supreme eighteen-syllable Śrīvidyā, known by the name Yajñavāhinī, is the most essential essence and has not been revealed to just anyone. (41)
Known as Vidyā, she is the glorious mistress of half his body; she is proclaimed in all the Vedas, obtained through the grace of the Teacher, and bestows the fruits of all sacrifices.
Day after day, at evening and at dawn, one shall obtain the fruit of the Agnihotra sacrifice by reciting the Yajñanārāyaṇī-vidyā with a well-concentrated mind. || 43 ||
Having offered one hundred and eight oblations of ghee with the *pūrṇāhuti* mantra, he should give a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) according to his capacity at the lotus-feet of the preceptor.
One obtains the eternal fruit of ten Iṣṭis and Pūrṇamāsa sacrifices by performing even a small, excellent preparatory rite (puraścaryā) accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees. || 45 ||
By performing this year after year, one obtains the fruit of the horse sacrifice;
she is the sovereign queen of all sciences and mantras, the glorious eighteen-syllable [mantra]. (46)
Like a supreme cow of plenty that grants all desires,
there is no other knowledge in this world equal to this, by which the earth has been pervaded.
O best of the twice-born, there exists no eternal Vedic revelation superior to this; nor are there sacrifices accompanied by sacrificial fees of gold amounting to hundreds of millions.
O King, having performed the Rājasūya, Aśvamedha, and other sacrifices, one attains that fruit which is obtained by a king who has mastered the eighteenfold Vidyāpuracaraṇa.
Having attained that very fruit year after year, the one of great intelligence [delivers] his fathers, grandfathers, and even those further ancestors who were bound by the debts of others.
Accompanied by them, he rejoices in the world of Brahmā, resembling Brahmā himself;
he is the sage of the eighteen-syllable vidyā, who is Brahmā, the Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati). || 51 ||
The meter is the divine Gāyatrī, and the deity is Nārāyaṇa Hari himself;
the Lord who is joined with Śrī as his half-body is called the Lord of the Universe.

The seed-syllable is said to be the giver of seeds, and Śakti is proclaimed as the bestower of what has been requested. One should then perform the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga) by means of the previously mentioned [mantras] beginning with Trapā and Śrī.

Having performed the placement (nyāsa) of the Śaiva Mātṛkā, the Vaiṣṇava Mātṛkā, or the primordial Mātṛkā— either by means of these or by another method— the wise man should meditate upon them within the lotus of his own heart.
Seated upon a beautiful jeweled lion-throne beneath a *pārijāta* tree, he was the manifestation of the universe, possessing a splendor like that of a lion.
With eyes as broad as lotus petals, with a face slightly bent down, with a row of teeth resembling jasmine flowers and pearls, and with lips like coral, she smiled.
Holding a conch, a discus, a mirror, a golden pitcher, and two lotuses,
and bearing a formidable mace on his left side, he is enveloped by lightning.
He is facing upward, accompanied by Lakṣmī, resplendent in yellow garments,
and adorned with a crown, necklaces, armlets, earrings, and other ornaments.
On the left and right sides [are] the goddesses Nīlā and Mahī;
he is accompanied by and joined with the eight queens beginning with Vimalā.
He was surrounded by Anantavighneśa, Viṣvaksena, and others,
and graced by his attendants headed by Sunandana and Nandana.

I bow to Hari, the remover of the suffering of those who have come to him for refuge, whose pair of feet has been illuminated by the splendor of the crests and crowns of Brahmā, Rudra, Mahendra, and the other gods.

One should constantly worship Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of the World, who possesses the splendor of Yama, whose intellect governs the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the universe, and who is the Supreme Self, the infallible Acyuta.
Having thus meditated constantly upon Yajñanārāyaṇa, the Lord of the World,
and having recited the eighteen-syllable mantra, one obtains the fruit of a sacrificial rite.
There is nothing else on the surface of the earth so pure as that, which is sanctifying in this world and free from all faults today. (64)
He alone is the Blessed One, manifest as the Supreme Lord;
even those joined with great sins are eternally purified by the eight-syllable mantra. 65.
For by reciting this eighteen-syllable vidyā, one indeed makes the impure become pure and renders them eternally liberated, just as if drinking it directly.
Indeed, even those joined with great sins [attain] liberation while living;
for this worship and so forth has been proclaimed in the venerable *Aṣṭārṇava*. 67.

For the sake of all the Brahmins, those who have mastered their senses—whether subsisting on sacrificial offerings (haviṣya), milk, or fruits—should perform the preliminary rites (puraścaryā) and so forth with full devotion. || 68 ||
Having recited this *Nārāyaṇīya* [section] three hundred thousand times,
one should perform the fire sacrifice with ten types of weapons, offering lotuses soaked in ghee along with the *patya* mantras.
Having offered either sesame seeds or bilva leaves soaked in honey and ghee into the two feet of the preceptor, one should give a complete sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
One who is not inferior attains perfection in the eight-syllable vidyā either in the month of Āṣāḍha,
or in Kārttika, Vaiśākha, or Śrāvaṇa.
In the month of Āśvina, or in the month of Māgha, or even in Phālguna, having recited eighteen thousand times the eighteen-syllable mantra. (72)
One should offer oblations of ghee mixed with honey and clarified butter into the portion of the eye,
[reciting the mantra] one hundred niṣkas, or half of that, or even as much as one's strength permits.
Having given [the gifts] to the preceptor and his wife, one should also feed fifty-three couples who are endowed with all their ornaments.
One attains great accomplishment in knowledge; there is no doubt about this.
Now, O twice-born ones, one should accomplish the rites for specific desires according to the prescribed method.
Having recited this vidyā one hundred thousand times, one should offer it with a rosary;
then, having performed a fire sacrifice (homa) with ten thousand lotus flowers mixed with ghee and the three sweets (trimadhu).
There, at the western Hāraliṅga, in the abode of Vṛṣabhuṇya, resides great good fortune, which brings immense joy and resembles hundreds of gods of love.
For one month, eating only sacrificial food (haviṣya), one should mutter the mantra one hundred thousand times;
there, one should offer oblations with bilva leaves mixed with cow's ghee and honey.
[He saw] a city endowed with wealth, grain, and vehicles, crowded with women, horses, and chariots,
strewn with pearls and gems, and possessing supreme, unshakable prosperity.
Having reached the giver of wealth, he becomes equal to Śrī;
standing in water reaching the navel, [he recites] three hundred and more maṇḍalas. 80.
Having recited [the mantra] and emerged facing the east, one who offers ghee one hundred and eight times becomes like Kubera in wealth and like Yama in wisdom through this vidyā.
Resorting to the root of the Aścantha tree for one month continuously, having recited [the mantra] one thousand three hundred times and having prepared a hundred oblations of ghee; || 82 ||
One who performs the recitation here at the proper time and season undoubtedly attains this;
having attained voluntary death, one is not overcome by diseases.
Having divided a coconut into four pieces and soaked them in clarified butter and the three sweets (trimadhu),
one should daily offer one hundred and eight oblations into the blazing fire.
By constantly offering one hundred and eight small plantain fruits from the grove, he attained even those goals that are difficult to achieve and impossible to reach. (85)
Having offered oblations into the blazing sky with clarified butter mixed with the three sweets,
he [attains] the Lord of the seven continents by means of two mandalas.
Having meditated upon the Lord of Śrī, who is the destroyer of Madhu and Kaiṭabha, the great wise one attains that unsurpassed state which is free from old age and death. 87.
Having recited this mantra one hundred thousand times and then offered oblations with arka flowers,
one swiftly subdues even wicked, ignorant, fearful, and passionate kings.
Having offered twelve thousand oblations into the fire with betel leaves mixed with ghee and the three sweets, one attains great prosperity.
He is honored by all the lords of the earth and by the gods along with the sages;
on the new moon and the full moon days, one hundred and eight oblations of ghee [should be offered].
Having offered it at the two feet of the preceptor, one should give gold as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā)— either a niṣka or half a niṣka— to him, or to his wife, or to his son.
Having attained the eternal fruit of the Darśeṣṭi and Pūrṇamāseṣṭi sacrifices, he is honored even by the great gods; how much more so, then, by mortals on the surface of the earth?
He obtains wealth, grain, and so forth, as well as unshakable prosperity and a noble lineage;
indeed, he becomes like Bṛhaspati himself, a true adept in the sciences. || 93 ||
He attains great supernatural power, endowed with sons, grandsons, and so forth; at the end, he dwells in Satyaloka together with a hundred generations of his lineage.
In the month of Māgha, Phālguna, Caitra, or Vaiśākha,
having recited the Yajñanārāyaṇī mantra twenty-five thousand times, || 95 ||

Having respectfully offered three thousand oblations of sacrificial material consisting of the three sweets, the three products of the cow, and clarified butter, [he should give] wealth equal to a year's worth of food.
Having bestowed upon the pair of feet of the Lord a gift accompanied by ten million fees,
one certainly attains the unsurpassed fruit of a horse sacrifice.
He is instantly liberated even from floods of great sins and minor sins;
he becomes like Mahendra in prosperity, and possesses the splendor of the presiding intellect through knowledge.
Having established his lineage on earth, endowed with splendor as enduring as the moon and sun,
he shall enjoy vast divine and human pleasures.
Accompanied by thousands of families, he rejoices in the abode of the Blessed One, constantly [rejoicing] even during all his own transits and eclipses. 100.
During the Vyatīpāta and other such yogas, having recited the glorious eighteen-syllable mantra according to the rules, one should offer oblations with sesame seeds mixed with clarified butter.
Even if all the other hundred [beings] were situated in the heart-hell,
he does not lead even a hundred of them out to the Satyaloka after having extracted them.
Having performed the daily fire-oblation (nityahoma) in the evening and morning, he worshipped Hari with sacrifices,
meditating upon Nārāyaṇa, Lord Hari, the Consort of Śrī, who occupies half the body [of his consort] within the fire.
One should recite the glorious eight-syllabled mantra (aṣṭākṣarī-vidyā) one thousand and one hundred times, or five hundred times, or even four hundred times. (104)
Having recited the three hundred [syllables] of the Vāta-mantra,
one should recite the glorious eighteen-syllable and ten-syllable mantras one hundred and eight times in the presence of the fire at evening.
Or, by reciting it twenty-eight times daily while restrained in his vows,
one obtains the fruit arising from the complete study of even the four Vedas.

Every day he attains this; he shall be liberated from even the most grievous sins, and likewise obtain the fruit of a horse sacrifice performed with all its constituent parts and the prescribed sacrificial fees.
Even now, having obtained all desired objects, one attains liberation at the end;
[this was proclaimed] by the Kūṣmāṇḍa sages formerly regarding the Lord Yajñanārāyaṇa.
That which was called the majesty of the mantra, that majesty of the mantra has been declared by me to you. || 108 ||
[Thus ends the forty-ninth chapter in the venerable Anuttara-Brahma-tattva-hṛdaya, the Tantra of Daśaratha, which is a compendium of the meaning of the Vedas.]
The Blessed One said:
The ritual procedure for Brahmā, Nārāyaṇa, and others will also be described;
by the mere knowledge of which, multitudes of calamities flee away.
Ending with the Praṇava, this auspicious and glorious eight-syllabled Vidyā of Brahmanārāyaṇī has been proclaimed by the supreme ṛṣis.
One should first form the *saṃhitā* [of the two words], and thereafter not [form] the *saṃhitā* [of the whole mantra];
this auspicious nine-syllabled mantra is proclaimed as Brahmanārāyaṇī. (3)
This [practice], by means of a single birth alone, bestows the attainment of identity with Brahman;
it is the path for the realization of Brahman, leading to the swift attainment of perfect knowledge.
One should perform the Brahmā-Nārāyaṇī-vidyā with the permission of the preceptor;
its ṛṣi, chandas, and so forth are all like those of the eight-syllabled mantra.
The Praṇava, the word "Haṃsa," and thereafter the word "So'haṃ," as well as this glorious eight-syllabled mantra— this is declared to be Nārāyaṇī.
For those desiring liberation in a single birth, this Haṃsanārāyaṇī-vidyā should be recited with devotion for the attainment of liberation.
This auspicious pair of vidyās should be recited by those desiring forest-dwelling;
however, this pair of vidyās should not be recited primarily within the home.
Because it brings about dispassion, it should be practiced by householders desiring spiritual perfection,
as well as by those in the forest stage, by widows, and by celibate students.
This glorious eight-syllable vidyā should be recited for the sake of attaining all siddhis;
for this [vidyā] as well, everything is declared to be like that of the glorious eight-syllable mantra.
The word "namo" followed by "bhagavate" ending in the dative case, and then the word "nārāyaṇa"—this is the twelve-syllable vidyā. (11)
She brings about great accomplishment and instantly tears asunder all primordial ignorance;
even that which begins with "Ārṣa" is declared for her, just like the eight-syllable mantra.

Then follows the glorious eight-syllabled mantra, which contains the seed of the three Vedas and the seed of Śrī, is endowed with the dative case ending, has "Śrī" as its prefix, and is joined with "Namaḥ. (13)
The fourteen-syllable Vidyā is called Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇī; it consists of the seed-syllables *praṇava* (oṃ) and *kamala*, joined with the dative case-ending. (14)
This sixteen-syllable vidyā consists of the word "mahālakṣmī," followed by "namaḥ," and then the glorious eight-syllable mantra. || 15 ||
This other auspicious Vidyā of Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa has also been declared;
because it consists of eighteen syllables, the number of years for its practice and other details are remembered as being the same as those for the two [previous] Vidyās.

Now I shall describe the preliminary rites (puraścaryā) and so forth, as well as the worship of the yantra and other matters; furthermore, I shall speak of the auspicious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇī mantra belonging to the Yajurveda.
Having first expanded the word "āvahatī," and then saying "kurvāṇa vīram" from the beginning, one should utter the word for oneself. 18.
Having said, "Come to the dwelling of Vāsava," he then uttered the word "Cows!
and likewise always the sound of food in a vessel and the word "Pad. (19)
Then, from that, the thread of glory brought forth the supreme state;
thereafter, through sacrificial animals, he reached the station of the thousandfold sacrifice. 20.
O Jātavedas, one should recite this mantra of Nārāyaṇa which subdues pride; it is said to be the Yajurvedic mantra for the attainment of Lakṣmī.

This great lore (mahāvidyā) belonging to the Yajurveda, known as Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇī, is remembered as the destroyer of the suffering of poverty and the bestower of all sovereign powers and accomplishments.
The seer of this [hymn] is Kahola, and its meter is remembered as Ānuṣṭubha;
the Lord is declared by the great sages to be Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa.
May she protect us—she who holds in her hands a lotus, mace, conch, and discus; who possesses knowledge and a lotus-like face;

who bears a water-pot as radiant as lightning amidst clouds; and who, with her breasts high and firm, incessantly attains the embrace of him whose body has become one with hers, like the flash of lightning upon a towering mountain.
Of Puṇḍarīkākṣa and Lakṣmī. || 24 ||

O King, her ritual worship involving yantras and so forth, as well as the preliminary rites (puraścaryā), shall be described by me in their entirety, like an ocean of merit that expands upon the earth. || 25 ||
One should recite the mantra of the preceptor one hundred thousand times in his very presence;
then, one should perform an oblation with clarified butter mixed with the three sweets (trimadhu).
Having offered abundant sacrificial fees at the pair of feet of the teacher, one attains the eternal perfection of knowledge; of this there is no doubt.
Having recited [the mantra] twelve thousand times in the presence of the preceptor,
one should offer a thousand oblations of clarified butter mixed with honey.
By giving wealth equal to the annual food-supply to the lotus feet of the Preceptor, one attains great accomplishment; there is no doubt that he shall bestow it. (29)
Having constantly offered the oblation twelvefold with fire twelvefold, one obtains pure food and *arāśis* even in the forest; of this there is no doubt. (30)
Rising daily at dawn and having offered oblations into the fire,
one should mutter this mantra of the Lord of Śrī one hundred and eight times.
Having placed the Ācārya nearby and standing in the midst of a grove of Tulasī, one shall daily obtain the unsurpassed great gain.
Having recited this mantra one hundred thousand times, one shall obtain all heart's desires;
it is the auspicious, glorious eight-syllabled Vedic knowledge by its very nature. (33)
She is proclaimed as the sovereign empress of all sciences;
the great vidyās such as Gāyatrī and others are said to be her rays.
O you who grant success even by a single remembrance, come quickly now to those who are constantly intent on the recitation of the glorious eight-syllabled mantra! 35.
Furthermore, there should be daily devotion to the recitation of the glorious eight-syllabled mantra (aṣṭākṣarī-vidyā),
and every day, with reverence, service to the pair of the preceptor’s feet.
Perfection in conduct as prescribed by the Vedas and a steady mind—
these indeed cause one to attain the presence of the Blessed One, even if they are offered with wavering hands.
The ritual procedure for Brahmā, Nārāyaṇa, and others has been briefly described;
now the majesty of the Hayagrīva and other vidyās will be set forth.
[Thus ends the fiftieth chapter in the venerable *Anuttarabrahmatattvarahasya*, the *Dāśarathīya Tantra*, which is a compendium of the meaning of the Vedas.]
The Blessed One said:
Now I shall proclaim the Vidyā of Aśvaśiras, by which one is greatly honored;
merely through the knowledge of which, supreme mastery over speech is attained. (1)
Having addressed [the disciple] with "Oḍgīśaya-dama," the word "udgītha" is uttered;
at the end, one should then say "sarva-vāgīśvara" followed by "īśvara. || 2 ||
This mantra, beginning with *Tārā*, is said to consist of all the Vedas, to be inconceivable, to bestow everything, to utter everything, and to awaken the non-dual reality. || 3 ||
The seer of this [mantra] is declared to be Brahmā; the meter is said to be Anuṣṭubh;
its deity is the all-pervading Lord Hayagrīva, the bestower of sovereignty.
One should duly assign the five limbs of the mantra to the Tādeṇaya trees.

We bow to him whose horse-face has the luster of the autumnal moon, who is adorned with ornaments made of pearls, whose pair of arms is encircled by conch-shell bracelets, and who rests his hands upon his two knees. 5.
One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times with kunda flowers sweetened with honey;
having offered a tenth part as oblation into the Vaiṣṇava fire, [one should worship] at the lotus feet of the preceptor.
Having offered abundant wealth together with this image of the Veda,
one attains the perfection of knowledge, or else [the merit of] a thousand recitations of the syllables.
Having made the ritual preparations in the month of Kārttika, one should reverently offer three thousand and thirty oblations into the fire, soaked in clarified butter, honey, and milk.
Or, having offered the Rāmāyaṇa or the Mahābhārata, together with a year’s worth of food,
into the lotus-like hands of one’s own teacher, one should bow down.
One attains great siddhi through this vidyā; of this there is no doubt.
One should worship Hayagrīva in the yantra described for the eight-syllable mantra.
Just as a seed is conceived as a form and the seed-syllable is uttered, so too is the coral-seed-syllable (va) situated in the region of the hips declared.
One should worship the four Vedas upon the filaments in the four cardinal directions;
in the intermediate directions, one should worship the Aṅgas, Smṛti, Nyāya, and all the Śāstras.
One should worship the deities of the limbs (aṅgadevatās) according to the ritual procedure within the central petals;
one should blow [the conch] for those Lords of the World (lokeśvaras), and one should worship their weapons, such as the vajra and others.
Thus, he who worships the God in this manner shall become Vāgīśvara himself;
it is proclaimed that an oblation performed with bilva fruits brings about prosperity.
One who desires inexhaustible prosperity should offer *kunda* flowers, combined with this mantra, along with clarified butter mixed with the juice of *brāhmī*. (15)
Having consecrated with this mantra speech that brings forth poetry and expands unrestrainedly among men, one should consume it every day at dawn.
After a long time, he becomes a renowned expounder of all the Vedas, Āgamas, and other scriptures;
there is no one equal to Manoratha in bestowing knowledge and sovereignty. (17)
Then [he uttered] the word "prāṇavam" joined with "namasā," followed by "bhagavate," and the word "vedāharaṇa," surrounded by the syllable "hetubhūtāya. || 18 ||
And let there be a sound accompanied by salutation for the Great Fish (Mahāmatsya), the Supreme Self, the Lord of Śrī, whose form is the Fish and who is the destroyer of ignorance. || 19 ||
Ending with "mahāmatsyāya" and "viṣṇave namaḥ," Aṅgiras and others employed this great mantra.
This knowledge (vidyā) brings success to speech, destroys great poverty,
and bestows the fruits of the four aims of human life known as dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa.
The seer of this [hymn] is remembered as the great king Manu Vaivasvata;
the meter is said to be Gāyatrī, and the deity is Hari in the form of the Great Fish.

The Lord of the worlds of the deities, the Supreme Self, the Lord of Śrī, is declared to be the seed-syllable *na* (Narayana), and the power of the heart (*hṛcchakti*) is proclaimed [to be the syllable *mā*]. || 23 ||
Having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the six limbs with six words, one should meditate upon the Lord of Śrī, who resembles the full moon of autumn and is like pure crystal. (24)
Wearing white garments and adorned with white garlands and ornaments,
his lotus-face was beautified by a pair of earrings, as he took the form of a fish.
Adorned with a crown, necklaces, armlets, finger-rings, and other ornaments, he holds a conch and a discus; his right hand displays the mudrā consisting of light.
Embraced by her with his left arm, the Lord of the World sat upon a divine lion-throne made of lotuses and other precious materials,
bestowing all the Vedas upon the Creator.
Worship the blessed Lord Viṣṇu, the omnipresent master of all gods, who grants the fulfillment of desires to Manu, the son of Vivasvat.
Having meditated thus upon Hari, the Lord of Indirā, who has assumed the form of a fish, and having daily recited [the mantra] one hundred and eight times, one obtains one's desired object. (29)

One who subsists on the food of a brahmin or sacrificial offerings should perform four hundred thousand recitations as the preliminary rite (puraścaryā). At the conclusion of that, one should offer oblations with milk or sugarcane juice while reciting the mantra of the Lord of the Mountain (Śiva).
One should offer plantain fruits into the fire; by performing this ten times the number of oblations, there shall be no obstacle.
Having given abundant sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) at the pair of feet of the preceptor, [one attains success].
Having offered eight thousand blue lotuses drenched in ghee, one attains eternal mantra-siddhi, which bestows all accomplishments.
One becomes a master of all sciences; of this there is no doubt.
Having recited this vidyā one hundred thousand times, one should then offer oblations with red lotuses.
Having obtained his desired wealth, he becomes like the Giver of Wealth (Kubera);
even if submerged in the great ocean, he is saved by recollecting this mantra with devotion.
When this [mantra] is recited one hundred thousand times, it bestows tenfold wealth, immediate youth, and even immortality; it cures even the mute or the dull-witted.
Having offered one thousand oblations of bilva leaves smeared with ghee, one becomes a lord of all speech, equal in splendor to Bṛhaspati and the sun. (38)
He beholds Manu Vaiveśvata directly with his own eyes;
by his grace, he obtains everything desired, which becomes inexhaustible. || 39 ||
Standing on the tip of his nose in the morning at every dawn,
let him daily recite the mantra one thousand three hundred times, always subsisting on sacrificial food (haviṣya).
Through this mandala, he attains his desires which are otherwise difficult to achieve; it is the cause for the attainment of all desired objects, being born from Manu. 41.
There is nothing equal to this, neither in the Vedas nor even in the Purāṇas:
first uttering the word "Oṃ," then "Namaḥ," and thereafter the word "Bhagavate. (42)
One should utter the sound "kūrmarūpāśabda" and then "viṣṇave namaḥ";
this is the seventeen-syllable mantra of the Lord of Śrī in his tortoise form. 43.
This [place] was established by King Indradyumna and bestows all perfections;
it grants the attainment of union with Brahman for the Lord of Śrī in his form as the Tortoise.
The sage is said to be Indradyumna; the meter is declared to be Paṅkti;
and the deity is Mahāviṣṇu in the form of the Tortoise, the Lord of the worlds. 45.
One should perform the obeisance ending with the seed-syllable and place the six limbs using six-word mantras.
[One should meditate on] Acyuta, who is dark-complexioned, four-armed, and has the form of a wandering ascetic (kaṭamaṭha).
On the tip of his nail, he saw the bearer of Mount Mandara, the wielder of the conch, discus, and mace, seated upon a divine, auspicious throne made of gold and jewels.
On his left lap [he bears] Śrīdevī, the mother of the worlds, who consists of the essence of the Vedas,
adorned with divine ornaments, and wearing celestial garlands and garments.
The all-pervading Lord Kṛṣṇa stood there embracing her, praised by the great sages,
worshipped by Indra and the other gods, and possessing a serene countenance.
I worship the Supreme Self, who desires the welfare of all worlds;
and also the ritual worship of the yantra-pīṭha and other elements of this Matsya-vidyā.
The application (viniyoga) for all eight [mantras] has been declared; it shall now be explained.
Having first recited [the mantra] one hundred thousand times, one should [offer oblations] ten thousand times with karavīra flowers.
Having offered abundant sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) after reciting [the mantra] over his lotus-feet combined with the three kinds of honey, one shall attain the perfection of the mantra.
Having offered ten thousand oblations of Madhūka flowers soaked in honey and ghee, one attains the power to favor dogs; of this there is no doubt. || 53 ||
Having offered ten thousand oblations of *vakula* flowers together with clarified butter, one obtains great fortune, abounding in wealth, grain, and other riches. (54)
By offering ten thousand betel leaves to Ādamaresvara,
one obtains all desired objects and attains unsurpassed liberation.
Or by reciting the great mantra of Kūrma one hundred and eight times every day, one may attain even that which is difficult to obtain: union with Brahman (brahmasāyujya).
Thus, I have briefly described the greatness of the Hiraṇyagarbha, Śivā, and other vidyās, as well as their power to destroy intoxication; now, the [greatness] of Varāha shall be told.
Having further performed the worship of the yantra of this pair of Fish and Tortoise, which is entirely like the eight-syllable mantra, one shall become a possessor of siddhi. || 57 ||
[Thus ends the fifty-first chapter in the venerable *Anuttarabrahmatattvarahasya*, the *Dāśarathīya Tantra*, which is a compendium of the meaning of the Vedas.]
The Blessed One said:
Now, a portion of the majesty of the Varāha-vidyā shall be proclaimed;
by hearing which even those who are not self-restrained are liberated from the bonds of their sins.
Then, "Tātāraṃ," "namo bhagavate varāhapadam," and "rūpāya bhūrbhuvaḥ svaḥ" should follow, and immediately after that, "pataye. (2)
"Grant me the status of a king at your feet;
let the mantra, ending with 'vahni-jāyā' (svāhā), consist of thirty-four syllables. || 3 ||
He is the great wind that scatters the clouds of all sins and misfortunes;
he bestows the perfect attainment of sovereignty and other blessings by means of dispelling the onset of suffering.
The sage is declared to be Bhārgava; the meter is Anuṣṭubh;
the deity is the Lord who is the soul of the Boar (Divārāha), the lord of the senses. || 5 ||
The heart is known as *ekadaṃṣṭrāpahṛdayam*, the head as *vyomolkāya*,
the crest-mantra (*śikhā*) as *tejodhipataye*, and the armor (*varma*) as *viśvarūpa*.
Furthermore, one should fashion five limbs for Mahādaṃṣṭrā, who possesses five weapons.

From the ankles to the knees, he resembles excellent gold; from the navel downwards, he has the luster of pearls; from the neck upwards, he resembles the rising sun; and from the head, he has a blue radiance.
With his jewel-adorned hands, he holds a discus, a sword, a shield, a mace, a spear, and the gestures of generosity and fearlessness.
The primordial Boar, with his gleaming tusks supporting the earth.
One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times and perform oblations with water mixed with honey in the tenth part of that number, offering them at the feet of one's own preceptor.
Having given land measured by a cow-hide, endowed with abundant crops,
accompanied by many sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā), and provided with water, one shall attain perfection.
Or, having recited the supreme mantra twenty-four thousand times,
[one should worship] with the lotuses of the month known as Mārgaśīrṣa, dripping with the three sweets.
Having offered oblations three thousand times at the two feet of the image,
and having bestowed land with a sacrificial fee, O Prajāpati, he became one whose mantra was perfected.
One should worship the Sacrificial Puruṣa on the eight-syllabled seat,
having conceived his form by means of the root-mantra according to the procedure to be described.
One should worship the heart and other limbs in the four directions starting from the east;
the weapon-mantra at the corners, below and above, and outside of that, the discus and other weapons.

Having worshipped the discus, conch, sword, shield, mace, and spear, as well as the gestures of granting boons and protection, one should blow [the conch]; then, outside, one should worship the world-protectors and the weapons.
Through meditation alone one may bestow wealth; the goddess Jayā grants the earth, and through worship and other rites, she surely bestows riches, grain, land, and prosperity. (15)
When the sun has entered Leo during the bright fortnight of the month of Āṣāḍha,
one should place a white stone in the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and, having touched it, recite [the mantra] ten thousand times.
Facing north, one should bury that stone;
it will destroy the afflictions caused by enemies, thieves, and great elemental spirits. || 17 ||
On Sunday at sunrise, one should collect earth from a Sādhya field;
having recited the mantra over it, one should divide it again into nine portions.
Having stirred even a single portion of milk from a cow for a full year,
one should then add rice that has been thoroughly purified by being washed in that milk.
One should cook the sacrificial oblation (caru) properly on the consecrated fire while reciting the mantra;
then, having removed the oblation from the fire, one should worship the deity according to the prescribed rite.
Having worshipped with incense, lamps, and other offerings, one should again offer oblations of caru mixed with clarified butter into the kindled fire, one hundred and eight times.
Thus, for the sake of attaining the field (*kṣetra-siddhi*), one should offer oblations during the Saturdays;
at dawn, [one should take] earth from the ground of the area to be mastered on a Thursday.
Having taken the oblation and prepared it as before, the wise one should offer it;
thus, opposition within the field perishes along with other calamities such as those caused by wandering spirits.
With fuel-sticks produced from the *rājavṛkṣa* tree, one should offer oblations three thousand times with the *vidyāpānayā* mantra; for him, all prosperities shall arise.
The mantra-practitioner should daily offer oblations with rice grains one hundred and eight times;
his residence shines with abundant heaps of grain.
One should offer oblations with clarified butter; from that maṇḍala, one obtains gold.
With those [oblations] smeared with honey, one obtains a maiden according to one's own desire.
One should offer oblations with nine palas of fresh [materials] sprinkled with the three sweets;
by means of this maṇḍala, according to the previously stated number, one attains great prosperity.
Now I shall describe the yantra of Yajñavarāha, which bestows fruit.

Having written in the six corners [of the hexagon] the syllables of the *dahana-pura-yuga-cakra* (the fire-city pair-wheel) in the middle, and having drawn a lotus with petals equal in number to the [remaining] constituent elements (*tattva*),

one should then write the eight-syllable mantra upon the filaments; there, one should write the mantra-syllables measured by the cloth [in total], with the remainder on the petals in the fourth [layer].
Beyond that, [is] the vowel 'Sva' situated upon the filaments of the lotus of the syllable *vasuhalaka*. 38.

One should draw the petals numbering the syllables of the mantra, writing the final syllable on the final [petal] and the first syllable on the first; likewise, one should properly place the sixteen-spoked lotus shining with the letters beginning with *ka* upon the filaments, and the mantra-syllables in order, ending with the last petal.

Having written the syllables of the remaining [mantra], it should then be surrounded by the seeds of *ātara*, *kṣmāka*, and *kola*, with the letters of the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) placed in the middle; this is further encircled on the outside by the letters of the mantra interspersed with the letters of the name of the person to be accomplished.
With the earth-element diagram (*bhūvinda*), the seed-syllable of the earth (*bhūvīja*) joined with the name of the person to be accomplished should be placed in its corners. (40)
One should write the syllable "Haṃ" together with the seed-syllable of the Earth (Laṃ);
this seed-syllable, preceded by Sa, Ī, Śa, Ri, Vi, Du, Ga, and Na, is declared to be that of Varāha. (41)
On an auspicious day, one should draw the yantra using a paste made of yellow orpiment, agallochum, camphor, lac, saffron, and sandalwood, ground together with cow-dung water.
One should write the mantra with a golden stylus for the accomplishment of all desires and goals;
one who writes the yantra on a golden pedestal shall attain royal prosperity.

One should write for the attainment of a village on birch bark; for the acquisition of wealth, on a copper plate; for one's own desired success, on a leaf of the *īkṣu* plant; and for the attainment of land, on linen cloth.

Having perfected the yantra through recitation, worship, and other rites, one should employ it for one's own desired ends; such is the majesty of the Vidyā, which is worthy of being established in villages and regions—a portion of this has been declared by me.
Hereafter, I shall proclaim the majesty of the Nārasiṃha [Vidyā], when this yantra is well-accomplished within kingdoms.
One should dig [the pit] starting from Sunday and worship one's own quarter in the cardinal directions;
[this protects] from minor dangers, death, thieves, and other such beings, as well as from great fears caused by wild beasts.
O excellent one, by the power of the deity, it is not possible to reach the further shore of that region.
[Thus ends the fifty-second chapter in the *Śrīmadanuttarabrahmatattvarahasya*, the *Dāśarathīya Tantra*, which is a compendium of the meaning of the Vedas.]
The Blessed One said:
Now, the ritual procedure for the Nṛsiṃha-Anuṣṭubh will be fully explained;
by the mere hearing of which, multitudes of calamities go to their dissolution.
The first step is called Ugra, the second step is said to be Vīra,
the third is Mahāviṣṇu, and then the fourth step is Jvalanta.
Then, having uttered the word "Nṛsiṃha" which faces all directions,
and having spoken "Bhīṣaṇa" and "Bhadra," one should then utter "Mṛtyu."
I bow to that state which is proclaimed as this fourfold science; at the beginning of a mantra, one should utter the Praṇava, or else the syllable "Vāmalocana-kha."
Even at the end, one should recite these seed-syllables in reverse order;
some indeed say that one should chant the great vidyā eight times for the sake of this purpose.
Some, having first placed the mantra accompanied by only the *hṛllekhā* [syllable], recite the pure *anuṣṭubh* mantra; others recite it with the word "Bhū" [added].
O King, even among the Vedas, Purāṇas, and Dharmaśāstras,
there is no knowledge equal to this, which bestows all perfections.
The sage is Prajāpati Brahmā, the Lord of the universe;
the meter is declared to be Anuṣṭubh, and the eternal seat is the Supreme Self.
The Lord of the gods and the worlds, the glorious Nṛsiṃha, the Great Lord (Maheśvara), is said to be the seed-syllable of Ananta; his power (Śakti) is proclaimed as Śaktirū.
With two, two, then one, two, and two;
thereafter, one should again perform the placement of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) with two words each.
One should assign the six limbs, endowed with the power of the Śadrīrya mantra,
to the head, forehead, pair of eyes, mouth, and the joints of the hands.
One should place the syllables of the mantra in sequence upon the joints of the feet, the tips [of the fingers], the belly, the heart, the hands, the throat, the sides, and the shoulder-blade.
One should meditate upon Him who possesses a peaceful form despite His fierce appearance,

whose hair is touched by His arms— arms that are brilliant with the luster of sharp, resonant claws and which rest upon His knees; He who, with two arms, holds a conch and a discus, and is ablaze with fire.

With his splendor equal to the sun, having shattered the Daityas, the Man-Lion, whose face has hair like that of a beast and is surrounded by garlands of flames, with three eyes consisting of the sun, moon, and fire, and fierce with a blazing tongue and fangs, shall devour him.
Or else, one should meditate upon Nārasiṃha, the Lord of the Universe, who possesses a peaceful form.
I bow to Him whose nature is truth, knowledge, and bliss, who is stainless, situated in the midst of milk and non-milk (the manifest and unmanifest),

whose mind is established in yoga, whose face is serene, who blazes with thousands of ornaments, who is three-eyed, who bestows the discus, the Pināka bow, the gesture of fearlessness, and the boon, whose splendor is radiant, and who has the hoods of serpents as His parasol.
I worship Nṛsiṃha, who possesses the splendor of lightning. || 15 ||
One should worship Nṛsiṃha accompanied by Kamalā upon a Vaiṣṇava pedestal;
having conceived the form with the root mantra, one should worship it with the various ritual services (upacāras).
The first enclosure should consist of the limbs; now the second will be described.
One should worship Brahmā in the directions starting with the southeast, northeast, north, and east, along with the lords of the quarters, Śaṅkara, and Ananta.
Śrī, Indrī, Catuṣṭi, and Puṣṭidevī are in the intermediate directions;
likewise are Bhāskarī, Vaśyakārī, and Māṇākārī. (18)
O Lord of the Earth, in the third enclosure, one should worship Dveṣakāryā, Karṣakarī, Yuṣṭhi, and Pramathanī.
One should worship the Discus, the Conch, the Great Lotus, and the Mace on the right side of the God;
thereafter, one should worship the Conch, the Shield, the Mace, and the Noose.
One should worship Lakṣmī on the right, Tuṣṭi on the left, and in that very place, the Kaustubha;
one should worship the Śrīvatsa on the right, and the forest garland (vanamālā) in the middle.
One should worship the yellow garment, the sacred thread, the navel-lotus, the crown,
and all the ornaments on the eastern side.
One should worship Śraddhā, Medhā, as well as Kāmā, Bhīmā, Māyā, and Bhayānakā, who possesses a moist radiance, in the eight directions starting from the east in successive order.
One should worship the eight guardians of the directions, beginning with Indra, along with their weapons such as the thunderbolt;
or else, having meditated upon the enclosure of Śiva, one should mutter the mantra of Nṛsiṃha.
Five-faced and most terrifying, with a luster like the fire of cosmic destruction, wearing a garland of intestines, and adorned with a fierce necklace and armlets. || 25 ||
[He holds] a rosary, armlets, a lotus, a conch, and [an object] resembling cow’s milk;
likewise, a bow, a club, and a broken discus.
He holds a sword, a trident, and an arrow; he is the embodiment of Nṛhari and Rudra, possessing the dark-blue luster of an indragopa insect and a complexion resembling molten gold. || 27 ||
One should meditate upon the Great Lord (Mahādeva) as having his face turned toward the east, north, and upward, with a complexion like the color of gold, for the sake of removing all diseases. 28.
I bow to the divine one who removes all death and grants all perfections upon being remembered;
who possesses sixteen arms, each holding various great weapons and vessels.
Nṛsiṃha, the Lord of all worlds, adorned with all ornaments, rich in the two acts of slaying and tearing out the entrails, is appropriate for both [the rites]. || 30 ||
Two held conchs and discs, two held moons and arrows,
two held swords and shields, and two bore maces and lotuses.
And two [hands] holding a noose and a goad, and two [hands] with the enemy's crown placed upon them; thus [he meditates on] the all-pervading Nṛhari, adorned with sixteen arms.
One whose mind is focused solely on the fierce act of slaying should meditate upon him who has the luster of a dark rain cloud;
he is the one to be meditated upon for the great purpose, possessing sixteen arms.
Nṛhari, the lord of all worlds, who bestows the fruit of all spiritual perfections,
holds in his right hands a discus, an axe, and a noose.
They brandished halas and musalas, as well as goads and discuses; likewise, they repeatedly hurled iron clubs and tomara-spears.
In his left hands, he holds a conch,
a sword, a spear, a trident, fire, a boon-granting gesture, a javelin, and thereafter a water-pot.
With his two hands, he holds a bow, the tarjanī mudrā, a ḍamaru, and a serpent, and he performs the crushing of the enemy's knees and head.
Likewise, Hari holds a garland with His two upper hands,
and with His two lower arms, He is depicted tearing apart Hiraṇyaka.
One should thus meditate upon Nṛsiṃha, who brings joy to his devotees and destruction to the Daityas, for the sake of overcoming the great fear of death. (39)

One should draw the yantra together with the *sādhya* (the object of the rite) in the center; then, having divided the mantras of the four directions among the eight petals, one should inscribe them, surround [the center] with the outer enclosure,
and recite [the mantra].

This yantra, surrounded by two houses— a triangle, a square, a seed-syllable, the earth, and a serpent— is the destroyer of minor poisons, planetary afflictions, and diseases, and it brings about prosperity.
Upon this yantra, one should place ten beautiful water-pots (kumbhas) filled with water from excellent holy fords (tīrthas), and endowed with weapons, gems, and medicinal herbs.
Having meditated upon the Lord Nṛsiṃha of peaceful form in the center,
one should worship Nṛsiṃha in the eight directions, starting from the east, in due order.
One should sprinkle a beloved person with a thousand drops of water consecrated by mantras;
thus, possession by spirits and madness perish along with their hosts.
Having been consecrated, one should feed the Brahmins with a focused mind;
one should duly worship the two feet of the preceptor with devotion according to one's ability. (44)
By this ritual, a king attains victory in battles;
the preliminary practice (puraścaryā) consists of one hundred thousand [recitations] followed by twenty thousand more.
The wise one should satisfy the ten spokes with milk, sugarcane juice, or honey;
he should offer three thousand lotuses mixed with ghee into the fire.
By offering a pair of earrings accompanied by a large sacrificial fee to two preceptors, one shall attain the perfection of knowledge.
Or, having recited the great Anuṣṭubh mantra two thousand times,
one should offer three thousand lotuses mixed with ghee into the fire.

Having given a pair of auspicious earrings to the ears of the preceptor, and having given the preceptor a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) measured by a year's income, he should give it with devotion. || 49 ||

Through knowledge, one attains success, fearlessness, and eternal, desired perfection; having propitiated the Mantra with three thousand oblations, the practitioner should then offer oblations into water for peace, for thus there shall be the Vedic revelation: "In this way, calamities are indeed pacified."
Or whatever other desire is wished for by one's own mind, may that be attained; and may he become beloved by all people. (51)
O Lord, for one who remains awake during the night amidst the sight of suffering and the conduct of the undisciplined,
there occurs at that moment a dream of bliss through the power of the mantra alone.
O Lord of Mithilā, for one who recites my mantra while wandering in a forest infested with wild beasts, snakes, thieves, and predators,
that which was unaccomplished shall certainly become accomplished.
One should consecrate eight thousand jars with water for the purpose of neutralizing snake venom;
even one who has consumed *ativiṣa* or *vatsanābha* poison will certainly be liberated and become happy, O Lord of Mithilā. (54)
One should pacify the poison arising from scorpions, spiders, centipedes,
and many-legged insects by applying ashes and other substances consecrated with one hundred and eight recitations over the head.

This mantra shall pacify ailments such as those of the ears, heart, throat, belly, and head, as well as fever, dysentery, hiccups, and other disorders caused by spells, medicinal poisons, or malevolent incantations. || 56 ||
Having recited the *brāhmī* mantra eight hundred times at dawn, and having meditated upon the Lord who is the source of all cattle,
one attains intelligence through the study of the Dharmaśāstras and achieves the fulfillment of desired goals within a year.
What is the use of many other names here? By this very one, whatever is prayed for is obtained in its entirety.
Therefore, those who know the ritual procedure and who desire to cross over the ocean of saṃsāra should worship him with minds fixed upon that goal.
One who desires prosperity and is skilled in mantras should offer ten thousand oblations with syamantaka flowers smeared with honey;
thus, he shall not become poor within his family.
O Prajāpati, through the oblation of fuel-sticks of *audumbara* wood, one attains the perfection of the *vājapeya*;
by an oblation of eight hundred thousand, one becomes equal to Indra. (60)
In the presence of the King of Herbs (Hudvalya), one should conquer [the senses] by reciting [the mantra] one hundred and eight times;
thereby one attains purity and gains his grace. || 61 ||
By offering oblations of *kudustuna*, one enjoys all auspiciousness;
by offering oblations of *madhūka* flowers, one shall obtain all desired objects.
O Lord of Creatures, by the offering of oblations with *tulasī* leaves, fame is attained without a doubt;
and by the offering of parched grain (*saktu*) into the domestic fire (*śālāgni*), the entire world is brought under one's control.
By offering oblations of pieces of turmeric, one may paralyze the continuity of the Vajra lineage;
by offering oblations of plantain fruit, one shall be liberated from all obstacles.
He who offers ten thousand oblations of *gulūcī* and *caturaṅgula* plants, sprinkled with curd, honey, and ghee, shall live for a hundred years, having conquered his enemies.
Having recited one hundred and eight times while stationed on the day of Saturn, that person’s tongue becomes such that he lives for a full hundred years, free from the fear of death.
One who desires prosperity should constantly meditate upon the previously described white Nṛhari,
embraced by Lakṣmī, who rests on his lap and holds a lotus in her hand.
Having chanted and offered oblations day after day to the lion-faced [deity] in the Ānuṣṭubh meter, one becomes perfected;
laughing at that [state], one shall become manifestly composed of Brahman.
Hereafter, I shall describe the King of Yantras as taught in the Tāpanīya;
having first drawn an eight-petaled lotus, one should remain composed.

Having drawn that [form] which consists of the essence of Brahman, one should then draw a very beautiful hexagon; therein, one should write the *praṇava* (om) containing the eleven syllables of the Nṛsiṃha mantra.
Then, one should write the six syllables of Sudarśana within the six corners;
having surrounded it with the measure [of the mantra], one should then write it upon a beautiful eight-petaled lotus.
One should also enclose it with the glorious eight-syllable mantra;
then, one should surround that with a great lotus of thirty-two petals.
One should write each individual syllable of the Nārasiṃha mantra there;
one should also surround it with thirty-two lotus petals.
Outside of that, one should draw a circle and write the eight letters beginning with *ka*;
then, in the eastern part of that, one should write the eleven letters beginning with *ha*.
Then, having drawn it to the right, and thereafter on the rear portion,
one should likewise draw the eight subsequent letters there.
Then, on the subsequent part, two syllables should be written; subsequently, two letters should be written on both sides of the circle, starting from the tip.
This Narasiṃha yantra, when perfected through recitation (japa), fire-oblations (homa), and other rites—
whether one worships it or wears it— one shall be liberated from all sins.
Having attained vast prosperity abounding in wealth and grain,
and having acquired great intelligence, one shall at the end become identical with Brahman.
This Nārasiṃha leaf bestows the fruits of worldly enjoyment and liberation;
it is the cause of longevity, health, and prosperity, and it increases one's progeny. (79)
Thus, O destroyer of sins, I have briefly proclaimed this greatness of the Nṛsiṃha-anuṣṭubh;
hereafter, its ritual procedure shall be told.
[Thus ends the fifty-third chapter of the *Śrīmadanuttarabrahmatattvarahasya*, the *Dāśarathīya Tantra*, which is a compendium of the meaning of the Vedas.]
The Blessed One said:
Now, I shall describe the vidyā that bestows all perfections, which was taught on the way to the Supreme Self, the Lord of Śrī, who assumed the form of a dwarf.
The Praṇava (Om) not joined with the letter Na, then the word "Viṣṇave," then the fifth vowel (Ū) joined with the right ear (Ra), then the second vowel (Ā) of that same [letter], and then Ma. (2)

Then there is the sixth [syllable], beginning with *va*, which consists of five letters starting with a vowel; following that is the first of the semivowels (*antaḥstha*), conjoined with Vāyu and Rudra. (3)
The face-portion combined with the sky-portion (0) and the back-portion (1) forms the syllable *ma*, which is the destroyer of the body.
The seer of this [mantra] is said to be Nalakūbara, the son of Dhanada. || 5 ||

The wise one should perform the deposition of the syllables (*varṇanyāsa*): he should deposit *chaṃ* in the head, which is declared to be the *jāgata* meter; *da* in the left arm, which has the form of *dadhi*; and *vāṃ* in the right arm. Then, he should deposit [the remaining syllables] on the crown of the head.
The pair of eyes and ears, the nose and face, the neck, the two arms, the navel, the back, and the private parts; || 7 ||
One should place the [remaining] letters upon the pair of knees, according to the sequence.
Shining with one or two lights, seated beneath a parasol of jewels dripping with nectar from the Sītā river,
his sides embraced by Śrī and Bhūmi, resembling a crystal gem, his body adorned with the serpent Śeṣa as a garland.
May the one named Śrī Vāmana— who is the bestower of wealth, who holds a vessel full of curd-rice and sugar-candies, a lotus, and a golden water-pot— protect us constantly from all misfortune.
One should meditate upon Vāmana, whose limbs are exceedingly graceful, who stands upon a silver lotus, who holds with his right hand a jar full of nectar adorned with beautiful and lovely jewels,
and who, with his thousand left hands, dispels all suffering.
Having thus meditated upon Viṣṇu as Vāmana within his own heart with a focused mind, and having mentally conceived the form of Hari by means of the root mantra, one should worship Viṣṇu as Vāmana.
Afterwards, at dawn, one should mentally worship the six limbs with that [mantra]:
Prīti, Tuṣṭi, Puṣṭi, Vṛddhi, and Ṛddhi, and after that [the others].
After Saumyā and Amaracinī, there are the goddesses Śūmālinī, Śaśinī, Durmātā, Lakṣmī, and likewise Chāyā. || 14 ||
And within the full mandala is the immortal sixteenth digit;
by these powers (śaktis), the auspicious second enclosure is described. || 15 ||
The third enclosure consists of the twenty-four deities beginning with Keśava, joined with their Śaktis; [the gatekeepers are] Kumuda and Kumudekṣaṇa as previously described.
Puṇḍarīka, Vāmana, Śaṅkakarṇa after that, Sarpanetra, Sumukha, and Supratiṣṭhita as well. (17)
The fourth enclosure is said to consist of the conch, the discus, and the mace;
then the staff, the sword, the pestle, the Śārṅga bow, and the arrows. Furthermore—
The fifth enclosure is said to be [occupied] by Indra and the others, and the sixth is described [likewise].
Having thus constantly worshipped Vāmana, Viṣṇu, the Infallible One, [one attains the goal]. (19)
Endowed with all perfections and powers, he shall become a servant of the Blessed One;
first, one should mutter [the mantra] two hundred thousand times, and then perform the libation ten times that amount.
One should offer oblations with churned curd and food; that portion of the Darśa sacrifice shall be magnified.
One should give a hundred cows as the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) at the footprint of the Ārya. || 21 ||
Or half of that, or half of that again, joined with two earrings;
or one consisting of twenty-five thousand [recitations] should be chanted during the invocation.
Then, having performed three thousand oblations with curd-rice while observing his vows,
he should offer [the gift] together with a calf and materials equal to a year's worth of food.
O Prajāpati, having given two cows as a sacrificial fee, the mantra becomes perfected;
one should then constantly offer oblations of curd-rice into the fire twelve times with devotion.
He attains abundance of food and liberation; of this there is no doubt.
One who is pure, by constantly and regularly offering a thousand [oblations], shall conquer [all obstacles].
One attains abundant gain, freedom from disease, and liberation;
here, one should always offer twenty-eight oblations for the fulfillment of desires.
One shall obtain inexhaustible food mixed with white rice and ghee;
one shall obtain a thousand desired meals, free from putridity and endowed with the six flavors.
Having offered ten thousand oblations of curd-rice mixed with sugar, one would obtain great prosperity, becoming like the Giver of Wealth (Kubera).
Wherever he may go, he indeed attains a mountain of food;
being pure, he should offer ten thousand lotus seeds while standing near a *vilva* tree. (39)
For there indeed Lakṣmī, who is fond of the flow of wealth, rains down riches;
one seeking knowledge should recite [the mantra] a hundred thousand times while meditating upon the god Janārdana. (40)
Having offered ten thousand oblations of milk-rice (pāyasa), one becomes Vāgīśvara in person;
one desiring a son should offer a hundred thousand oblations, and one seeking the life of a son should offer oblations with fruits.
Having meditated upon the Lord Trivikrama as having a reddish luster, one shall obtain sons along with one's wife by offering *karavīra* flowers into a fire kindled with that wood.
Having offered ten thousand oblations, one shall become victorious everywhere;
one desiring a kingdom, having offered ten thousand oblations with lotuses.
One attains sovereignty over a kingdom that is free from all thorns, by offering oblations with the petals of the Apāmārga flower mixed with honey and clarified butter. || 44 ||
One who desires to bring the world under control shall obtain it by offering oblations ending with the name of the twilight [deity] preceded by *ayuta*.
One who desires health should offer a thousand oblations with the *ayāmāga* mantras. (45)
Within seven days one shall be freed from diseases; therefore, one should wear this ash.
One who desires long life [should perform the rite] with sesame, dūrvā grass, kuśa grass, and kṣata, mixed with the three sweets (trimadhu).
One should offer ten thousand oblations until one conquers [the obstacle] and attains supreme longevity;
having meditated upon the god Trivikrama and recited [the mantra] ten thousand times.
There is no doubt that for him, liberation from slaughter occurs immediately. || 47 ||
He [should meditate on] the lotus whose pericarp is the *praṇava* of the goddess to be accomplished (*sādhyālakṣmī*), which has eight petals formed by pairs of mantra-syllables;
the remaining petals are radiant with the [remaining] syllables, while the final petal serves the purpose of a flaming leaf for the heart-mantra.

This is the diagram (yantra) consisting of the twelve-syllable mantra surrounded [by it], then encircled by the Mātṛkā alphabet, and further outside by the unbroken circle of letters; it is glorious and bestows all desires.
Having thus worshipped Acyuta Dadhivāmana, who is desired throughout the three worlds,
one enjoys all pleasures here on earth by subduing the forces of one's enemies, and in the end, shall go to the station of Viṣṇu.
Now I shall describe the lore of the best of the Bhṛgus, which bestows success;
by the mere knowledge of which, multitudes of calamities are destroyed. (51)
First the *praṇava* joined with *namaḥ*, then the word *bhagavate*;
then the words *jāmadagnyāya* and *aduṣṭe*, and after that the word *kṣāntiye*.
Accompanied by the dative ending in "kulakālāntakāya," and joined with the word "reṇukāputra" together with the heart-mantra (hṛdaya). || 53 ||
This is the lore of the best of the Bhṛgus, which bestows all fruits;
it pacifies all suffering and rends asunder the host of enemies. (54)
The Lord of Śrī, the master of the worlds, is free from enmity; he is declared to be the seed-syllable (bīja), and the power of the heart (hṛcchakti) is proclaimed as the seed of the three Vedas.
With three syllables, with eight, with five, and likewise with six, two, and six [syllables], one who is composed should perform the placement of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa). || 57 ||
Resembling molten gold, wearing a rosary and a sacred circle of ashes,
he was the heroic son of Jamadagni, bearing a splendid battle-axe.
I bow to Rāma, the descendant of Bhṛgu, the wielder of the bow with large eyes, the crusher of the king of kings, the lord who is the disciple of the consort of Gaurī. 59.
Having thus meditated upon Bhārgava, the subduer of wicked Kṣatriyas,
and having recited [the mantra] one hundred and eight times, one attains eternal perfection.
The practitioner, with a steady mind, should perform one hundred thousand recitations as the preliminary rite (puraścaryā),
having offered milk-rice mixed with ghee and the three sweets as a tenth-part oblation.
Having offered the sacrificial fee at the pair of lotus-feet of the preceptor, one obtains great accomplishment; for the offering of the fee is the means to accomplish all fruits.
Alternatively, having recited twelve thousand times while remaining pure and self-controlled,
one should offer oblations with devotion three thousand and one hundred times.
Having offered wealth measured by a year's worth of food at the lotus feet of the Ācārya, one attains great accomplishment through the Vidyā; of this there is no doubt. (64)
It is effective when both enemies and thieves arise, when there is fear of lions, tigers, and the like, and when there is danger from Rākṣasas, Kūṣmāṇḍas, serpents, and elephants. (65)
Having recited the mantra of the high-souled Bhārgava three thousand times,
he becomes instantly liberated from all calamities.
Constantly serving the teacher in his presence and free from the impulse to find fault,
one should daily recite this vidyā three thousand times with devotion.
Even one who is dull-witted may become a master of all sciences by means of the maṇḍala, on the bank of the Gīṣṭhī or Samudga rivers, or in the presence of the Guru’s feet. 68.
Having recited this vidyā one hundred thousand times, and having offered ten thousand oblations of palāśa flowers mixed with ghee, one should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the preceptor.
"O Lord, there is no doubt that he has mastered all four Vedas and reached the further shore of the science of logic; he is truly like Bṛhaspati himself. (70)
Seeking great fortune, one who offers fresh red lotuses without killing them,
having propitiated ten thousand suns, attains vast and inexhaustible prosperity.
If one recites [the mantra] one hundred thousand times on a mountain peak, subsisting on fruits or sacrificial food (haviṣya),
one will directly behold with one's own eyes the imperishable Rāma of Bhṛgu’s lineage.
When Bhārgava is pleased, no desired object shall remain unattainable:
longevity, health, sovereignty, wealth, and even cattle. (73)
The eight kinds of enjoyments are accomplished for him here; of this there is no doubt.
Without even conceiving of a physical form, one should worship the all-pervading Bhārgava.
In the six corners [of the hexagon], one should worship the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga), Jamadagni, Cāreṇukā,
Atri, Anasūyā, Dattātreya, and likewise Śrī.
One should worship Kumāra and Devasenā upon the lotus petals,
and Indra and the others, along with the eight deities of time, within the eight directions of the square [mandala].
Having thus constantly worshipped Bhargava, the Lord of the World,
one becomes eternally victorious and rejoices in the abode of Brahmā.
A certain means for the Dadhivāmana-vidyā, as well as for Bhārgava and Manu, has been told to you;
now the [means] of Śrī Rāma will be described.
[Thus ends the fifty-fourth chapter in the Śrīmad-Anuttara-Brahma-Tattva-Rahasya, the Dāsarathīya Tantra, which is a compendium of the meaning of the Vedas.]
The Blessed One said:
I shall proclaim the Great Knowledge (Mahāvidyā), which is the compendium of all Vedānta, belonging to Śrī Rāma, the Lord of the Universe, whose form is the Tāraka Brahman.
First the Praṇava, then the word "hṛdayāyartapada," followed by the word "bhagavate," and then the word "raghunandana" joined with the dative case ending. || 2 ||
Then the words "rakṣoghna-liśadāya," "madhura," and "prasannavadanāya" were uttered; thereafter, "amite-tajesa" was proclaimed. (3)
Having uttered *valāpāyadda*, one should then pronounce *pāvaka* joined with a long vowel;
thereafter, one should [utter] the first [syllable] joined with *mukhavṛta*. 4.
One should utter the word "Viṣṇu" accompanied by the dative case-ending and joined with "namaḥ";
this is declared to be the Vidyā of the Lord of Jānakī.
She is the shatterer of the multitude of diseases born of memory and of the arising of suffering;
she is the pacifier of great poverty and the bestower of the wealth of sovereignty.
She is the essence of all sacred fords, the bestower of the entire mass of all vidyās, the cause of universal imperial sovereignty, and the bringer of auspiciousness.
She who causes the enchantment of the three worlds, she who brings all people under her control, she who bestows the fruit of all sovereignty, and she who grants all vidyās. || 8 ||
[She] bestows the realization of identity with Brahman, whose form is truth, bliss, and consciousness;
[she is worshipped by] the ancient poets headed by Vālmīki, as well as Nārada and others.
Having first worshipped this knowledge, they attained their desired perfection;
this is the Tāraka-Brahma-vidyā, which bestows the perfection of all-bliss.
The sage of this Brahma-mantra is said to be Gāyatra-chaṃdas;
Śrī Rāma, the consecrated king, is the Supreme Self and Lord of the Universe. || 11 ||
The deity remembered by the wise is Viṣṇu, named Jānakī;
the great seed-syllable is said to be that called Praṇava, and the power (śakti) is declared to be obeisance (nati).
The application [of this mantra] has been declared solely for the sake of pleasing Janakī’s Lord;
therefore, it consists of seven syllables, and by means of these six [syllables], that [deity] is fully attained. 13.
The ritual placement of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa) is said to consist of nine parts, numbering eight;
[this occurs] within a forest of wish-fulfilling trees in the beautiful city of Ayodhyā.
Seated upon a beautiful lion-throne of lotus fibers at the foot of a coral tree,
he possessed the luster of a yellowish-blue cloud for the three worlds.
My Lord wears yellow garments, is resplendent with divine ornaments of jewels, and possesses a face like the stainless autumn moon. || 16 ||
The Lord possesses the loveliness of ten million Cupids, holds the mudrā of consciousness, and has his arms resting upon his knees, bestowing the fruits of all desired objects.
He whose face bears a most serene smile and eyes like lotuses, the source of all branches of knowledge and the bestower of all prosperity. (18)
And [he saw her] attended by Lakṣmaṇa, Śatrughna, and Bharata, with the daughter of Janaka, adorned with divine ornaments, resting upon his left lap.
Embraced by the great sages such as Vāmadeva and others, praised by them,
and constantly worshipped by Vibhīṣaṇa, Jānakī, and their attendants.
He was surrounded by Vasiṣṭha and others whose essence is compassion as they offered hymns of praise,
and he was encircled by Sugrīva and others, together with his eight ministers headed by Sumantra.
Whose lotus feet are eternally worshipped by all kings,
who is the refuge of all worlds, and who is compassionate toward those who seek his protection.
I bow to Viṣṇu, whose body consists of the three times, who delights in the heart;
[one should draw] a six-petaled lotus, an eight-spoked [wheel], and a symmetrical square.

This yantra belongs to the ascetic Sītā and bestows the accomplishment of all desired objects; in its center, one should write the seed-syllable (bīja) of the target (sādhya), conjoined with the Kāma-mantra. || 24 ||
O Lord of the Earth, one should encircle this [deity] with the five seed-syllables;
furthermore, O King, one should satisfy him with the ten-syllable mantra.
One should write the six limbs in these corners, beginning with the southeast, in their proper order;
the seed-syllable *huṃ* at the tip of each corner, and the vowels upon the tips of the filaments.
Having been consecrated in the kingdom, one should write the six syllables of this Śrī Rāma mantra on each petal,
and write the five syllables in the final triangle.
One should write the seed-syllables (bījas) of Narasiṃha and Varāha in the cardinal and intermediate directions;
this is declared to be the yantra of the Lord of Ramā (Viṣṇu) within a square.
Having invoked the Lord of the World (Viṣṇu) upon this yantra with the root mantra and having worshipped Him thoroughly with ritual offerings, [he should worship] the Daughter of Janaka to His left.
One should place the six limbs in the six corners starting from the front corner in sequence;
after that, one should place the Ātman, Antarātman, Paramātman, and Jñānātman.
Vāsudeva, as well as Lakṣmī, then Saṃkarṣaṇa; Pradyumna, then Rati, and after that Aniruddha. (31)
This shall be the second; now the third will be told:
Āgrahāyaṇa, Hanumān, Sugrīva, Bharata, and Vibhīṣaṇa.
Lakṣmaṇa, the son of Govāyu, also obtained Śatrughna;
[the others were] Dhṛṣṭi, Japanta, Vijaya, Siddhārtha, and Arthasādhana.
Aśoka, Dharmāla, and Sumantra— these eight ministers were first honored,
followed by Vasiṣṭha and then Vāmadeva.
Jāvāli was of the Gautama lineage, after him Bharadvāja,
then Viśvāmitra, Vālmīki, and the great sage Nīdada.
Nala, Nīla, Suṣeṇa, Gavākṣa, Gandhamādana, Śarabha, Tāra, Mainda, Dvivida, and after him Vitata. (36)
Having worshipped Viṣvaksena— who possesses a conch, a discus, a mace, a lotus, the Śārṅga bow, and arrows, and who is mounted upon Garuḍa— one should then worship him thoroughly.

Having thus worshipped Maheśvara and the other guardians of the eight directions, as well as the weapons such as the vajra and others, one should further gratify them with incense, lamps, and other offerings.
Thus worshipping the all-pervading Lord, the leader of Janakī, the minister becomes a treasury of knowledge and sovereignty and rejoices in the abode of the Blessed One.
First, for the sake of the preliminary rite (puraścaryā), one should diligently recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times;
having brought the preceptor into close proximity, [one should offer oblations] mixed with ghee and the three sweets (trimadhu).
Having first offered milk-rice (pāyasa) into the fire, and afterwards having presented abundant wealth at the feet of the preceptor,
one shall attain the perfection of mantras.
On the occasion of the sun’s eclipse or the moon’s eclipse,
being composed and eating but one meal a day, they remained thus for three days.
Then, beginning from the time of the ritual touch and continuing with devotion until the end of the purification,
he should offer oblations of black sesame seeds mixed with ghee, honey, and sugar.
Having offered a pair of earrings to the preceptor and having given wealth for a hundred years, one shall attain the perfection of knowledge (vidyāsiddhi).
Drink this water consecrated with the mantra twenty-five times;
you shall attain great health and become a treasury of all knowledge.
O King, by offering ten thousand oblations of bilva leaves soaked in cow's ghee and the three sweets (trimadhu) into the fire, one attains the fortune of sovereignty.
Having recited the mantra one hundred thousand times on a beach by the ocean or in a cow-pen while observing a milk-vow,
and having offered oblations of milk-rice mixed with clarified butter, one becomes a treasury of all things.
In the month of Vaiśākha, a pure-souled person, standing amidst five fires, should reverently offer three hundred thousand lotuses mixed with honey.
Having offered twenty thousand oblations, one becomes a sovereign ruler of the earth;
having offered ten thousand oblations of dūrvā grass sprinkled with clarified butter, [the same result is attained].
One shall be free from disease and long-lived; truth, when spoken, is honored.
Having properly offered ten thousand blue lotuses (*nīlotpala*), the most excellent practitioner [attains these fruits]. (50)
Having offered ten thousand oblations of red lotuses mixed with ghee, one brings the three worlds under one's control for as long as one lives; of this there is no doubt. (51)
Even one who possesses hundreds of thousands obtains his desired wealth,
provided he, restrained in his vows, offers six thousand oblations mixed with ghee.
One obtains an increase in livestock, as well as wealth and grain with certainty;
one should offer oblations made from bilva fruits mixed with lotuses and the three sweets (trimadhu).
By offering one hundred thousand *karavīra* flowers mixed with honey, one attains unsurpassed royal splendor for ten thousand years. (54)
One attains for a long time the unshakable prosperity equal to that of Mahendra;
one should constantly practice this for more than two hundred and eight years.
Having obtained all that he desires, he is glorified in the world of Brahmā;
this [mantra], which bestows sovereignty, consecration, fortune, and knowledge, has thus been proclaimed. 56.
Now I shall further declare the majesty of the Śrī Kṛṣṇa mantra.
[Thus ends the fifty-fourth chapter in the venerable Anuttara-Brahmatattva-Rahasya, the Dāśarathīya Tantra, which is a compendium of the meaning of the Vedas. 54.
The Blessed One said:
I shall proclaim the Śrīkṛṣṇa-vidyā, which bestows the accomplishment of all good fortune;
by the mere performance of which one becomes a possessor of the accomplishment of all good fortune. (1)
Having first uttered Kāmarāja, then "to Kṛṣṇa," then "to Govinda," and thereafter the word "Uteyī," || 2 ||
Afterwards, this [mantra] accompanied by the consort of Agni is for one's beloved;
it is declared as the Kṛṣṇa-vidyā, which bestows the attainment of great good fortune.
This knowledge, which pacifies all mental afflictions and physical diseases and bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation,
was formerly meditated upon by the venerable Nārada.
He attained the knowledge of the three times and the sovereignty consisting of the powers such as *aṇimā* and others;
[she is] the eternal cause of the imperial dominion over the three worlds. (5)
This Śrīkṛṣṇa-vidyā, which brings all the worlds under one's control, has been proclaimed;
its seer is Brahmā, its ritual procedure is that of Vidhi, and its meter is said to be Gāyatrī.
The Lord of the Fortune of Kṛṣṇa is proclaimed as the Master and the Deity;
the seed-syllable is said to be Kāmarāja, and the Power is the beloved of Agni (the syllable Raṃ).
The six-limbed ritual placement (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa) is declared to be performed with one [syllable], three, four, four syllables, and again with four and two [syllables].
With his left shoulder draped and wearing a beautiful earring, his brow slightly raised and his soft lower lip parted in a faint smile, casting sidelong glances;
he fills the flute with his tremulous, sprout-like fingers at the very source of joy.
One should meditate upon the world-enchanting Lord, who is more beautiful than the three-eyed Śiva and who is graceful.
Having thus meditated upon Kṛṣṇa, the son of Sudeva and Lord of the Universe,
the practitioner of pure mind should perform four hundred thousand repetitions of the purificatory rite (puraścaryā).
One should satisfy [the deities] with a tenth part [of the total] using water, clarified butter, or sugarcane juice;
then, one should offer oblations into the fire with lotuses mixed with honey, constituting a tenth part of that.
One should feed the most excellent Brāhmaṇas; one is honored by [giving] a tenth part of that. For the pair of the Ācārya and the Caru, a tenth part in gold [should be given].
Having given [this], one attains great accomplishment in knowledge (vidyāsiddhi), there is no doubt;
or rather, being pure, one should recite it eighteen thousand times during the month of Nabhas.
Having offered one thousand three hundred oblations of ghee mixed with honey and curd,
he presented a pair of earrings fashioned by the foremost of artisans.
Having given the teacher the wealth measured by a year's worth of food, and having given to the preceptor a pair of cows along with a calf in that region, [he attained his goal]. || 15 ||
