Having first drawn a six-spoked [wheel] and thereafter eight-petaled ones, one attains the eternal and great perfection of the Kṛṣṇa-vidyā. || 16 ||
Outside of that, having drawn sixteen petals, then eighteen petals,
and twenty-four petals, one is thereafter honored.
Within the thirty-two spokes of the wheel, one should draw a threefold square;
in its center, one should write the seed-syllable of desire (Kāma-bīja), accompanied by the name of the person to be acted upon (sādhya) and the ritual purpose (karma). || 18 ||
Then, one should write the six syllables beginning with *cakrāya* within the six corners; thereafter, one should write the eight black syllables upon the eight petals.
One should write the sixteen syllables of the sage among those with sixteen spokes;
likewise, one should write the syllables of the king of mantras upon the eighteen well-restrained [spokes].
One should write the Gāyatrī of Śrīpati upon the twenty-four petals; thereafter, one should encircle that with the Kāmarāja mantra.
One should write the Gopālānuṣṭubh mantra within thirty-two lotuses;
one should surround it with the mantra of Piṇḍagopāla.
Second, having encircled it with the letters of the Mātṛkā,
one should thereafter encircle it for the third time with the noose, using the Kuśa seed-syllable.
The Śrīkṛṣṇapatramocana has been told; it bestows all perfections, removes all suffering, and shatters the affliction of all poverty. || 24 ||
There is no other yantra on earth more excellent than this for producing supernatural powers;
having invoked Kṛṣṇa, the soul of the universe, with the root mantra, one should worship him. 25.
One should worship the six limbs in sequence within the six corners of the fire-pit;
the second [set] with Vāsudeva and the others, each accompanied by their respective Śaktis.
Then [he married] Rukmiṇī along with Sabhāmā, as well as Nāgrajā;
then Sutanu, Kālindī, and also Jāmbavatī.
One should worship Mitravindā and Suśīlā in the third enclosure;
then Valabhadra and Revatī, as well as Sudevakī.
Having worshipped Nanda the cowherd, Yaśodā, Subhadrā, and likewise Arjuna with the four viriṇas, one should then worship Śakra and the other deities.
Having thus constantly worshipped the omnipresent son of Devakī and having obtained all desired objects, we rejoice like gods.
Having climbed a kadamba tree at midnight and meditated upon the one who steals the garments of the gopīs,
he chanted [the mantra] three thousand times for seven days.
Even the wife of a king,
though firm in her vows, he shall attract by offering three thousand oblations of cow's milk in a cow-pen while remaining pure.
He obtains an increase in cattle for as long as he lives, without a doubt;
so too for one who daily offers curd-rice one hundred and eight times.
Having meditated upon Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of the Universe, at the foot of a Kadamba tree, he obtained within a month an abundance of food that pervaded his entire lineage.
Having respectfully recited this [mantra] two hundred thousand times for Śrī Kṛṣṇa, one attains the sovereign powers such as *aṇimā*; of this there is no doubt. (35)
Whether going to a village or even to a city, a person reciting mantras should constantly offer oblations of pure water— perceived as milk— from a vessel made of *kṛṣṇa* wood, while facing the deity.
He should always provide abundant food accompanied by many sweets, and he shall possess an abundance of wealth, grain, parrots, and other such things.
The giver of a wall. || 36 ||
The practitioner who meditates and constantly recites the mantra is liberated from sin and attains the state of the mantra.
In each respective state, he was exceedingly well-pleased and constantly played at will, like a god among humans. (*********) || 39 ||

A twice-born man desiring intelligence, having become pure in body for seven nights, should conquer [his mind] by reciting ten thousand times this mantra dedicated to the God of Memory, encased within the Praṇava.
One who expounds the meaning of all the Vedas and Shastras may become equal to Brahma;
subsisting on alms, he should recite the mantra for a year without weariness.
One attains abundant prosperity and certainly becomes omniscient;
one desiring a daughter should offer oblations of khadira wood ten thousand times with devotion.
Having meditated upon the beloved of Rukmiṇī, the wise one should offer ten thousand oblations into the fire with curd, wine, and *kulāja* mixed with clarified butter and the three sweets.
By meditating on Kṛṣṇa while eating fresh butter and using a mortar as one's wealth, one shall obtain a beloved daughter endowed with a beautiful form.

Having offered ten thousand oblations of fresh butter, one shall obtain a son; likewise, having recited [the mantra] one hundred and eight times while nursing at the breast, one shall obtain a son who drinks from that breast.
One should meditate upon Kṛṣṇa; then the seizing spirits flee from those who are possessed by them.
For the sake of destroying all poisons, one should meditate on Kṛṣṇa, the crusher of Kālīya.
Then, having offered a hundred oblations with the recitation [of the mantra], one destroys all poison,
even that which has ascended to the head and is taking away the *pārijātaka* flower.
Having recited the mantra twelve thousand times and then performed oblations with *karavīra* flowers,
one becomes eternally victorious and rejoices upon the earth like a god.
On a Saturday, one should recite over an *aśvattha* tree with the hand of a dog;
having purified it one hundred and eight times, this person is not overcome by enemies. (49)
By daily consuming food consecrated with this mantra, the wise man attains a lifespan comparable to that of Āyu, as well as strength and splendor.
Having recited this vidyā twelve hundred thousand times, one who has conquered his senses becomes like Kandarpa in splendor and like Adhishana in wisdom through the power of the vidyā.
Possessing a lifespan like that of Jāmbavat, resembling the sun in splendor,
he shall exist here and enjoy all manner of delightful pleasures.
Dwelling in the world of Brahmā, together with ten ancestors and ten descendants,
you have attained this greatness of the Kṛṣṇa-vidyā, which destroys all sins.
To him who has performed some mass of austerities, it grants the accomplishment of all smiles.
[Thus ends the fifty-fifth chapter in the *Śrīmadanuttarabrahmatattvarahasya*, the *Dāśarathīya Tantra*, which is a compendium of the meaning of the Vedas.
The Blessed Lord said:
Now, a certain method for the accomplishment of the vidyās of the Buddhas and others is described: even a mass of sins, including ignorance and the individual soul, is destroyed. (1)
The seed-syllable of the Triple Veda joined with the heart-mantra, followed by the word "to the Blessed One," and then the word "to the establisher of the foundation of the Vedic path. || 2 ||
One should utter the sound "Namaḥ" for Viṣṇu, who is the form of the Buddha;
this is the vidyā of Viṣṇu, the Lord of the three worlds, who possesses the form of the Buddha. (3)
Having bound those two with all-encompassing prosperity, the sage was impelled;
Brahmā was invoked, and the Gāyatra of the Chāndogas was proclaimed.
Mahāviṣṇu, whose form is the Buddha, is proclaimed by the virtuous as the deity [consisting] of three syllables, four syllables, or eleven syllables. || 5 ||
The placement of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa) is said to be performed with five, three, or two [syllables].
[He is] dark-complexioned, with a serene face, four arms, and wearing a crown.
One should worship Viṣṇu in the form of the Buddha, who is praised by gods and sages;
having meditated upon Mahāviṣṇu as being in the form of the Buddha, one should recite the mantra. (7)

One hundred thousand recitations for this mantra have been prescribed as the preliminary rite (puraścaryā) by the supreme sages; having offered one-tenth of that number of lotuses accompanied by ghee, honey, and milk, as traditionally taught.
By offering abundant sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to the pair of feet of the teacher,
one attains mastery of knowledge and is liberated even from sins.
Having resorted to a sacred field of accomplishment (siddhakṣetra) and recited this mantra one hundred thousand times,
one is immediately liberated from even the most heinous sins.
One should worship the Lord who has the form of a Buddha upon the seat described as having eight syllables—
the all-pervading Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of the World, the bestower of all accomplishments.
Now I shall proclaim the Great Vidyā of the Supreme Self, the Lord of Śrī, who has taken the form of Kalki, which bestows great supernatural powers.
First, the Praṇava (Om) joined with a salutation; then the word "Bhagavate";
and after that, the word "Kalkirūpa" followed by the dative case ending.
Having addressed "Viṣṇave pada," one should then utter the word "namaḥ."
This Vidyā of the one whose nature is Kalki is dearer than life to her beloved husband;
it is the supreme bestower of the fruits of all desires and the destroyer of the multitude of obstacles.
The great lustered sage Yājñavalkya is declared to be its seer;
Paṅkti is its meter, and Lord Viṣṇu in the form of Kalki is said to be its deity. 15.
The seed-syllable of the Triple Veda is said to be the seed, and its power (śakti) is declared to be the prostration (nati);
[this occurs] with a pair of syllables, or likewise with four or five.
The practitioner should perform the placement of the six limbs with three and two [syllables] respectively;
[he visualizes the deity] resembling a dark blue cloud, seated upon a divine jeweled lion-throne, according to the sacred tradition.

[He beheld] the Lord of the World seated there, dark as the color of time (the clouds), with the luster of a blue sapphire, the remover of all evils, served by yogins, sages, and perfected beings. || 18 ||
[He saw] Viṣṇu bearing a bow and arrows, accompanied by the goddess Śrīpā, the Lord in the form of Kalki, who is devoted to the welfare of all the worlds. || 19 ||
Having meditated upon Vāsudeva, the Lord of the world, in the form of Kalki,
and having recited the Great Vidyā one hundred thousand times, [one should perform] the tenth part [of that number] with Tulasī leaves.

Having offered the southern region of the earth, which was abounding in many crops and grains, together with the three kinds of honey poured over the lotus-feet of the Preceptor, he [attained his goal]. || 21 ||
One attains the perfection of knowledge and becomes liberated from heaps of sins;
one should worship Kalki, the Infallible One, on the seat (pīṭha) described for the eight-syllable mantra.
Having recited [the mantra] sixty thousand times in the presence of the preceptor,
and having offered oblations of lotuses ten thousand times, he [bestowed] a white horse along with its retinue.

Having given that which is endowed with many sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇās) to the venerable Guru, one becomes a sovereign of the entire earth in this world and shall attain liberation at the end of the body. || 14 ||

Having meditated upon the high-souled Kalki, the speaker of all sciences, who [appeared] to the sages on the bank of the Yamunā, and having thereafter recited [the mantra] one hundred thousand times; || 25 ||
Having offered oblations with *palāśa* flowers, one shall become a master of the sciences;
desiring a son, one should reverently offer ten thousand oblations with *putrajīva* fruits.

One who desires prosperity should worship with bilva leaves; one who desires sovereignty with ripe fruits; one who desires knowledge with clarified butter (havis); and likewise, one who desires enjoyment with blue lotuses.
One who desires long life, being pure, should offer oblations with the Ṛgvedic verses ten thousand times; or having recited them three hundred thousand times, or even a hundred times every day.
He indeed becomes liberated from the three worlds; there is no doubt in this matter.
Or rather, I shall further declare the Mahāvidyā of the Three Names. || 29 ||
Through the practice of which one becomes liberated from the ocean of saṃsāra—[the names] Acyuta, Ananta, Govinda, accompanied by salutation on the fourth [syllable]. (30)
This supreme Vidyā of the Great Lord, preceded by the syllable Śrī, is called Nāmātraya; it has been declared as that which shatters the rising tide of sins. (31)
She is the destroyer of incurable diseases and the bestower of the fruits of liberation and worldly enjoyment.
Vasiṣṭha, the yogi Nārada, and Kaśyapa are remembered as sages [who have attained her grace]. (32)
The meters are Gāyatrī and the others; the Boar (Varāha) and Hari are likewise [the deities];
Vāmana is declared to be the deity, and the application (viniyoga) is for the sake of accomplishment.
Having meditated upon the previously mentioned Yajñavārāha, Nṛsiṃha, and the all-pervading Vāmana,
and having constantly recited these three names, one shall attain perfection.
Those who have reached the further shore of the Vedas and Vedānta declare this to be a perfected vidyā;
the very fee given to the preceptor is said to constitute its purascaryā.
If a person is afflicted by a powerful disease of the wind (vāta),
he should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times while sleeping on the ground and with his senses subdued.
Then, by performing the Mṛgadābha rite with all its constituent parts, one is liberated from that [fever],
even if afflicted by a chronic intermittent fever, by reciting it a hundred thousand times with devotion.
Having caused the recitation to be performed by Brahmins, one should offer oblations with mango sprouts;
or, having likewise caused the fire-oblation to be performed, one may do so with amṛtā plants.
One is released immediately even from an incurable fever.
Seeking long life, O Long-lived One, one who is pure should [worship] ten thousand blades of ūrdhvā grass. || 39 ||
Having offered [the oblation], one becomes free from disease and certainly attains long life;
for the pacification of urinary disorders, one should offer sesame seeds mixed with the three sweets.
For the sake of pacifying the disease of leprosy, one who is pure, having recited [the mantra] three hundred thousand times,
should give a decorated bull along with the prescribed ancillary fees (dakṣiṇā).
One will certainly be liberated even from severe and variegated leprosy;
and by reciting it one hundred thousand times, there shall be the pacification of the disease of indigestion.
Having offered ten thousand oblations of clarified butter into the fire and then established the sacred fire,
one is liberated from that [sin] by giving a golden gift accompanied by a sacrificial fee.
Having conquered his senses and subsisting on sacrificial food (haviṣya), the wise man, after reciting the mantra three hundred thousand times,
should offer oblations of cow’s ghee ten times that amount, using the essence of the mantra-herbs.
One shall be liberated from all incurable diseases; of this there is no doubt, provided one recites the great mantra of the three names with devotion every day. (45)
Until the end of his life, he shall obtain great health, immense and inexhaustible prosperity, the increase of sons and grandsons, and even enjoyments that are very difficult to attain. (46)
Having attained the abode of the Blessed One, he dwells there eternally without doubt;
thereafter, he reaches the state that is joined with prostration and obeisance.
After the word "sarvādiguṇa," one should utter the number for the sake of counting, followed by the word "anaṃtāya" and then the word "avyaktāya namaḥ. (48)
This great vidyā of Ananta, who is himself Saṃkarṣaṇa, has been declared; when recited by Śaṅkara, it bestows the abundance of great fortune.
Maheśvara, the Lord of the Universe, is declared to be the sage (ṛṣi) of this mantra;
Gāyatrī alone is its meter (chandas), and the all-pervading Saṃkarṣaṇa himself is its deity.
This Patañjali is called Ananta by the wise;
he is the refuge [consisting] of four, eight, and four syllables respectively.
With two [mantras], the best of practitioners should constantly accomplish the six limbs:
the Lord with a thousand heads, adorned with a thousand ears. (52)
Bearing the earth upon his head, holding a plow, a pestle, and a share,
he was surrounded on all sides by great serpents such as Vāsuki and others.
I worship the infinite Supreme Self, the storehouse of all knowledge, who is saluted by the hosts of all gods and sages, and who transcends the world.
Having meditated constantly, he should recite the mantra of that Lord of the World;
having become one who has reached the further shore of all sciences, he shall attain supreme liberation.
On the Vaiṣuva day, one should worship the Lord of the World, the King of Serpents, on the pedestal;
having conceived his form through the root mantra, one should worship him with the various ritual offerings (upacāras).
Having worshipped the six-limbed [mantra] in the directions of Agni, Īśa, Sukha (Nairṛta), and Vāyu, as well as in the middle direction, one should then worship Vasuki, Takṣaka, and Karkoṭaka.
Then [he saw] Padma, Mahāpadma, Śaṅkha, and likewise Gulika; then Kumuda, Citraketu, Nārada, and Parvata. (58)
Having thus worshipped Saṃkarṣaṇa, who is beyond even Indra and the other gods along with their weapons, within the three worlds; || 59 ||
Having recited the Great Vidyā one hundred thousand times, and then having offered oblations ten thousand times with white sesame seeds soaked in ghee, honey, and sugar, one is glorified.
Having offered abundant sacrificial fees at the lotus feet of the teacher,
he shall attain mastery of the vidyā and become a treasury of all knowledge.
By reciting the great vidyā of Ananta every day with devotion,
one incurs neither fear of serpents nor fear arising from poison.
Having become one who has reached the further shore of the sciences and being endowed with a portion of the Blessed One’s power,
he attained great prosperity, abounding in wealth, grain, and other riches.
O King, at the end, those pierced by this great and infinite Vidyā go to the abode of Hari, assuming divine forms; thus has a small portion been described.
The power of the Nara-Nārāyaṇī-vidyā shall now be described.
[Thus ends the fifty-sixth chapter in the Śrīmadanuttarabrahmatattvarahasya, the Dāśarathīya Tantra, known as the Vedārthasaṃgraha.]
The Blessed One said:
Listen, O highly fortunate King, for I shall proclaim my vidyā, which dwells within the forest of speech and bestows all perfections immediately. (1)
Having first uttered the Praṇava, joined with the heart-mantra (hṛdaya), one should address the word "Bhagavat," endowed with the dative case ending. || 2 ||
The phrase "upādyaśamaśīlāyoya" is the word for *rata* (delight);
the word for *nātmya* (non-self) is *aviṃcana*, and then the word for *tāya* (protection) is also [the same]. (3)
After that, the word "Ṛṣabhāya," then "Naranārāyaṇābhyām," then the word "Parama" followed by "Haṃsāya," and after that the word "Parama. || 4 ||
Then, for the Guru, the mantra *padam ātmārāmādhīpataye*;
thereafter, the two heart-mantras (*hṛdayadvitaya*). This is declared to be the Vidyā.
Known by the name Naranārāyaṇī, she bestows the fruit of my knowledge;
she is the piercer of all sins and the remover of the continuous stream of suffering.
It directly bestows the attainment of knowledge and grants me the perfection of union;
it was formerly proclaimed by me, full of compassion, to Nārada.
I am celebrated as the preceptor named Samastalodha, who bestows all perfections and is the destroyer of the wealth of serpents. || 8 ||
To those who are devoted to me, this very [mantra] is proclaimed as the manifest Goddess Aparṇā;
I alone am glorified as the bestower of the illustrious eight-syllabled mantra.
To those who meditate day and night upon the true teacher, who is my very form, I shall grant worldly enjoyment; of this there is no doubt.
"For the welfare of all the worlds, I dwell eternally on the surface of the earth at Badarīkānta, accompanied by Nara. (11)
I alone am the Lord, the Supreme Lord, of these three worlds;
I am Acyuta, appearing in the forms of the deities Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśa, and Indra.
"I am the Lord Nārāyaṇa, omniscient and the sustainer of all;
by means of dharma, I have become the son of one who requested me. (13)
Having established myself in the Badarī forest as the protector of all, I shall grant the supreme state to all my devotees. || 14 ||
This ancient and exceedingly pure Vadarīkā forest, having become my possession, bestows the attainment of liberation through its repeated sight. || 15 ||
Wherever this Alakanandā has emerged by my command,
having bathed even once in the Alakanandā, one shall behold me, the All-pervading Lord.
At the end, they attain the mountain Maṣada, protected by the bliss of Brahmanic joy;
[this is] this six-syllabled knowledge of mine, Naranārāyaṇī. 17.
Wherever they may be, those who, firm in their vows, constantly perform this recitation shall attain great perfection and reach my own state.
This eternal [tradition], which bestows the fruit of all merit upon those who wear the *saṃhanīya* garment and perform the *saṃdhyā*, grants the attainment of the fourfold great liberation. 19.
To those of firm vows who daily worship me, the conqueror of sacrifice, and destroy ignorance,
I shall always grant every desire, just as a father would.
I always remain in his presence together with all the immortals; yogis call me Siddhavidyāmōmā, the seed-syllable Kaṣma.
The constant recollection of my vidyā instantly destroys misfortune;
indeed, the accomplishment of my vidyā is attained only through the payment of a guru’s fee.
If anyone here should have a direct desire for the vision of the Blessed One,
they should recite this auspicious Vidyā of Nara-Nārāyaṇī.
The sovereignty over all branches of knowledge existing here is constant,
whereas the sovereignty over the eight supernatural powers, beginning with *aṇiman*, is fickle.
He possesses constant sovereignty over the treasures such as the Śaṅkha and others, as well as lordship over the great seers, the brahmin seers, and the yogins. (25)
For those desiring this, this Vidyā grants all perfections;
one who is pure, constantly reciting my Nara-Nārāyaṇī Vidyā, [attains these]. || 26 ||
Then, by daily honoring with devotion the preceptor who has assumed that form,
one shall attain supreme perfection in the rites of the eight-syllable mantra and others within me.
Without the fire-sacrifice, the preliminary rite, or daily libations, this eight-syllabled mantra has been mastered by me, who am like you, through victory alone. (28)
Even ten million great mantras will be accomplished and become effective;
by reciting even a single great vidyā of mine daily while remaining pure, [the goal is attained]. (29)
He becomes perfected everywhere, endowed with the eightfold accomplishments, possessed of the eight-limbed yoga, and free from old age and death. || 30 ||
Having attained qualities such as *aṇimā* and others, he wanders through the worlds; the venerable Nārada is called his sage (*muni*) by the great seers (*maharṣi*).
The Lord Parameśvara, the presiding deity of the Badarī forest, is declared by the wise to be the master and the deity of Nara and Nārāyaṇa. (32)

O King, the application (viniyoga) has been proclaimed for the sake of pleasing the Blessed One; there is no placement on the limbs (aṅganyāsa), no placement on the hands (karanyāsa), nor any other placement.
O King, from the Siddhavidyā of Viṣvatiṣṭha, O monarch,
[it was obtained] at the very beautiful Badarikāśrama on the bank of the Irāvatī.
It was adorned by deities such as Brahmā, Rudra, and Mahendra,
and praised by great sages such as Vasiṣṭha and Vedavyāsa.
He who visibly wears the yoga-mudrā, the infallible creator of the universe,
possessing the luster of a fresh blue cloud and bearing a mass of matted locks.
[He saw] a ruby gem, adorned with a pair of golden earrings, holding a bow and arrows, and resplendent in divine yellow garments. || 37 ||
His chest was illuminated by the Kaustubha gem, adorned with pearl necklaces, and his head was covered by a crown set with divine jewels. (38)
Adorned with jeweled rings and a golden girdle,
with a smiling face and large eyes, he was as beautiful as ten million gods of love.
To him who is dedicated to the welfare of the entire world, the sole witness of all the world, the teacher of all worlds, and the supreme guru among gurus; (40)
We worship the Lord Nārāyaṇa, who delights in the Self, who is worshipped by the world, who is accompanied by Nara, and who is the omnipresent one revered by the universe. 41.
Having thus meditated upon the Lord of the worlds,
the husband of Lakṣmī, the wise man should constantly recite the mantra of Nara-Nārāyaṇī.
Without constantly worshipping my teacher Sadācārya, who is none other than me, one shall never attain perfection in the eight-syllabled and other vidyās. (43)
For one whose worship has been uninterrupted, the preliminary rites (puraścaryā) for the mantra are prescribed; having mastered the Nara-Nārāyaṇī Vidyā, which is dear to my school of thought. 44.
"Even with hundreds of preparatory rites (puraścaryā) for the eight-syllable and other mantras, one does not attain supreme perfection; such is the instruction of the Vedas. (45)
Constant service to the teacher and the recitation of the Nara-Nārāyaṇī mantra—these two alone are renowned in the world as bestowing great accomplishment. (46)

Even after studying the four Vedas along with their auxiliary branches, even after performing [mantras] ten million times, even after making great gifts, or even after performing a hundred *puraścaryās*; (47)
Having attained the perfection of manhood by following the Naranārāyaṇī-vidyā,
I shall thereafter proclaim the Sudarśana-mahāvidyā.
By constantly worshipping her, a man shall be endowed with victory and prosperity.
[The mantra consists of] the lunar seed-syllable (saṃ), the letter of the sky (ha), the moon (u), and the long [vowel] joined with fire (ra). (49)
Then follows Vaiśvānara, the armor, and the seed-syllable of the weapon;
this six-syllabled Mahāvidyā of Sudarśana has thus been proclaimed. (50)
Having first placed the Praṇava and the Nārasiṃha [mantra] at the beginning day by day,
this Great Vidyā, which wards off the multitude of obstacles, should be recited.
She is the warder-off of the great fears caused by spirits, ghosts, and piśācas;
she is the destroyer of all enemies and the eradicator of poison and poverty. || 52 ||
The sage of this mantra is declared to be Ahivṛdhyu,
and its deity is said to be the Lord Viṣṇu, whose nature is the Sudarśana discus and who possesses great intelligence.
The armor (kavaca) is said to be the seed-syllable (bīja), and the weapon (astra) is declared to be the power (śakti);
these are employed for the sake of pleasing Hari with the Sudarśana [mantra]. (54)
Holding a conch, a discus, a bow, an auspicious axe and sword, as well as a trident, a noose, a goad, a spear, and a mace; || 55 ||

One should meditate upon him who holds the sword, mace, club, and spear; who has fierce fangs and flaming hair; who is three-eyed and resembles a blazing fire; who is adorned with necklaces and earrings;
and who stands within a hexagon as the wheel that destroys the life-force of all hosts of enemies. (56)
Thus, having meditated upon Hari, the Lord of the World, as being of the nature of Sudarśana,
and having recited [the mantra] according to one's capacity, one becomes free from obstacles and immediately purified.
Having conquered all enemies and being liberated from all sins,
he is freed from all calamities and attains the four aims of human existence.
The practitioner who is constantly devoted to the teacher will certainly obtain [the results];
hereafter, I shall proclaim the great mantra of the Son of the Wind (Hanuman).
Worshipping this constantly, a person attains great victory and success; it consists of the *praṇava* joined with "namaḥ," followed by the word "bhagavate. (60)
First the word *tryambaka-janeya*, then the word accompanied by the dative case-ending,
then the word *mahābalāya*, and after that the word *hanumate*.
Consisting of twenty-three syllables and ending with the wife of Vahni (Svāhā),
this is known as the King of Mantras (Mantrarāja) belonging to Āñjaneya, the son of the Wind-god.
It destroys the sins of the great transgressions, bestows the fruits of all desires,
constantly grants the glory of victory, and brings the three worlds under one's control.
The venerable Agastya is called his sage by the wise;
the meter is said to be Gāyatra, and the presiding deity is Mañjanānanda.
Hanumān, the leader of the monkeys and son of the Wind-god, is declared to be the seed-syllable (bīja) consisting of the three Vedas; and "Obeisance" is said to be his power (śakti). 65.
The application for the sake of pleasing the delighter of the unborn (Viṣṇu) has been declared with three, four, five, and six syllables, as well as with five and four syllables.
Having performed the six-limbed ritual with these two [mantras], one should meditate upon the son of the Wind-god.
I bow to the one who resembles ten thousand suns at the end of an aeon, who destroys the pride of the enemies of the gods,
who bears the hymns of praise from the immortals headed by Indra, and who is the powerful destroyer of Sītā’s sorrow.

Having thus meditated upon the powerful and all-pervading messenger of Śrī Rāma— the best of monkeys, whose limbs are as firm as a thunderbolt, who possesses great strength, and who wears a loincloth and a black antelope skin shimmering with variegated earrings—
one should constantly recite this mantra, which is equal to Añjanā and bestows victory and success; thereby, one attains victory even in battle with the gods.
One should serve the pair of feet of the teacher day after day;
this is declared by the great sages to be that which brings about the perfection of the *puraścaraṇa*.
This [rite] daily brings about the destruction of enemies for those seeking victory;
it bestows the fortune of victory upon men and grants the eight supernatural powers (aṇimā and the rest).
Worship is prescribed for the Vaiṣṇava, Śaiva, and Dhāyisa seats;
and the mantra of Añjanā’s son (Hanumān) is the principal mantra to be recited daily. (72)
Whether three hundred, one hundred, or even thirty-eight times, the wise man who performs this blazing *vijaya* [mantra] shall become endowed with all accomplishments (*siddhi*).
Whoever worships the Lord of the Abode of Heaven with this king of mantras shall attain the supernatural powers beginning with *aṇimā*, and his fortune shall become unshakable. (74)
At the most terrifying royal gate, at an inaccessible cave entrance, or amidst the great terrors of yakṣas, rākṣasas, vetālas, īśas, and the like.
Remembering this great mantra, one shall be instantly liberated from distress;
by reciting this mantra three hundred and twenty-eight times every day. (76)
Having offered twelve oblations of clarified butter and having worshipped Hari, the Lord,
one obtains strength and good fortune, provided that one performs the recitation daily.
One attains unshakable prosperity, abundant with wealth, grain, and the like;
kings become submissive, and likewise enemies attain the state of friends.
Purified from all base arts, having attained great prosperity crowded with sons, grandsons, and other kin, he reaches eternal liberation. || 78 ||
Thereafter, I shall proclaim the great vidyā of Garuḍa, by worshipping which one may be liberated even from the fear of the Kālakūṭa poison. (79)
First, the Praṇava joined with "namaḥ," then the word "bhagavate," and the word "mahāgaruḍa" endowed with the dative case-ending. || 80 ||
Having uttered the words "padaṃ vajranarave," [one recites] the long-footed mantra "vajratuḍāyatapadī," and then the mantra for the body made from the emblem of Vajrayakṣa. || 81 ||
One should utter the great sound "etyethi," the word "garuḍa," and the words "duṣṭān nāgān chidhi" (destroy the wicked serpents), and one should not utter anything else that is wicked.
One should utter the three words "rākṣasān chiṃchiṃchiṃchīti" for the purpose of possession; then one should subsequently utter the word "vadohu phaṭ. This is the desired [mantra]. (83)
The great vidyā of Garuḍa is the destroyer of all poisons.
Brahmā is said to be the seer (ṛṣi) of this mantra, and its meter (chandas) is declared to be Gāyatrī. 84.
Garuḍa is the deity proclaimed as the destroyer of all poisons;
his form is like the peak of the golden mountain, and his face resembles the full moon. 85.
Nandīvardhana is on the right arm, Vṛṣaka is on the left; he is adorned with the ornaments of forest serpents. Ananta is on the left wrist, while Vāsuki serves as the sacred thread.
Takṣaka is the waist-thread, while Karkoṭaka is the necklace;
Padma is on the right ear, and Mahāpadma is on the left. (85)

Having meditated upon the Lord at the three junctions of the day and other times as being Garuda himself— with Śaṅkhapāla at the region of his head and Gulika between his arms— one should contemplate oneself as having become Garuḍa.
It quickly destroys poison, just as the wind swiftly disperses a cloud;
it is golden-colored down to the knees, while from the navel upward it has the luster of snow.
He who possesses the luster of fine white silk, who resembles the world of the upper realms, who is the life-breath of the universe,
and who is the very abode of Hari— merely by contemplating him, the wombs of the serpent-damsels themselves instantly fall away.

I bow to that Lord of the Vedas, who is composed of the Vedic meters, who is stainless, golden-hued, and the supreme Garuda, whose face is matured and whose broad wings have been clipped by the bite of his own thighs. 88.
Having thus meditated upon Garuḍa, the lord of birds who has no other vehicle,
one should daily recite the Great Vidyā of Garuḍa, which bestows its fruit.
Poison destroys all things, both moving and unmoving, instantly;
therefore, I bow to the Gāyatrī of Garuḍa, the bestower of all desired objects. (90)

Having worshipped whom, one becomes eternally stainless with the nature of Suparṇa; we know that state as "Puruṣāya," and then we meditate upon the state associated with the word "Suvarṇapakṣa" in the dative case, and then the word "Uragaruḍa" therein. || 91 ||
This knowledge, which brings about awakening, has been proclaimed;
it begins with the *praṇava*, it is non-different from all that exists at the beginning, and it is the destroyer of ignorance.
The Grandfather (Brahmā), the protector of the multitude of worlds, is declared its sage;
the Gāyatrī of the Sāma Veda is said to be its meter, and Garuḍa is remembered as its deity. || 92 ||
The meditation on this [Garuḍagāyatrī], which was previously described and praised by the best of sages, should be recited;
it shall remove all poison.
One who is well-disposed toward me should daily recite my *nityā* mantra one hundred and eight times, or twenty-eight times,
on the full moon day or on my own festival day.
One should offer three hundred oblations of clarified butter into the blazing fire;
by that, even those who have been struck down by the foot [of a king] shall have their lineage of sons, grandsons, and so forth restored. 95.

Even if a cruel serpent bites him, or even if he possesses a hundred mouths, after six months his [poison] is destroyed instantly by the mere touch of his two hands. Even the most terrible *hālāhala* poison perishes immediately. For eight days, one should vigilantly gaze into the eyes of a dog; for a thousand months, one should [consume] cow-ghee.
One should offer one hundred and eight oblations; or else, by having another do so, one is liberated from eye diseases. (96)
By reciting [this] three hundred times in solitude every day, the best of practitioners attains long life, health, immovable sovereignty, and the powers such as *aṇimā*. (97)
Having obtained the increase of sons and grandsons as well as imperishable honors, one goes at the end to that supreme abode of Viṣṇu; of this there is no doubt.
Jaya states that twelve thousand repetitions are prescribed for this preliminary rite (puraścaryā);
three cows are declared as the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), or its equivalent value along with the fee.
One should offer a thousand oblations of clarified butter into the blazing fire,
and twelve Brahmins should be diligently fed.

Having done this, there is no doubt that you shall become the very self of Garuḍa; O Lord, one who desires the perfection of this glorious eight-syllable vidyā is exalted by recollecting this garland of rays.
One attains eternal perfection even through every possible effort.
For one who possesses the auspiciousness of the glorious eight-syllabled mantra, there exists nothing on earth that cannot be accomplished.
There is yet another vidyā that bestows the accomplishment of the glorious eight-syllable mantra;
if it is performed, great siddhi will surely arise—of this there is no doubt. (102)
[Thus ends the fifty-seventh chapter in the glorious *Anuttarabrahmatattvarahasya*, the compendium of the meaning of the three Vedas, belonging to the *Daśarathīya-tantra*.]
The king said:
O Blessed One, Lord of the gods of gods, Nārāyaṇa, ocean of compassion!
Once again, [please grant] the practice of the glorious eight-syllable mantra, which bestows all perfections.
"O Lord of the Earth, speak for the benefit of the entire world!
The Blessed One said:
"Listen, O King, I shall describe another means that grants one's desired goals."
The auspicious Śrīmadaṣṭākṣarī, the Great Queen of all mantras, is the benefactor of all the worlds for the sake of the glorious eight-syllable vidyā.
For whomsoever this is accomplished, for them all supernatural powers (siddhis) are attained.
Listen, O King, for I shall speak while you are pure and with a restrained mind.
An excellent alternative method for the practice of the glorious eight-syllable vidyā is now being described; it is performed on a Sunday and is said to be without limit.
That lunar day (tithi) bestows the fruit of all merit and removes all sins; O observer of noble vows, if the sun's transit (saṃkramaṇa) occurs therein, [it is even more auspicious].
This yoga, known by the name Cūḍāmaṇi, is considered difficult to attain by the wise;
when the transit [of the sun] occurs there, it bestows the fruit of a hundred sacrifices.
The wise say that at night it yields half of that fruit;
however, if it occurs during the Brahma-hour (the final watch of the night), it bestows the fruit of ten million sacrifices.
This channel (nāḍī) shines like pure nectar even before sunrise;
the transit of the sun through it bestows the fruit of ten million horse sacrifices.
If, immediately after the day of Udayana, the day of the Sun (Sunday) or the day of the Moon (Monday) should occur here,
O King, the fruit of that merit shall be inexhaustible.
It cannot be described by me, much less by other great sages;
even there, it was eclipsed by the transition of the sun and the host of stars.
In that case, during the Brahma-time, it is impossible to describe the fruit;
indeed, it is possible to describe the fruit of a thousand horse-sacrifices. || 12 ||
I am unable to describe its inexhaustible fruit,
which exceeds that of a thousand great gifts and ten thousand Rājasūya sacrifices.
It can be said that this is well-done, yet it cannot be described as such,
provided there is auspicious non-transgression during the Brāhma-muhūrta.
Joined with the moon and the sun, it possesses the splendor of a hundred suns;
it is the supreme one known by the name Mahācūḍāmaṇi, which can be attained through yoga.
If on the seventh lunar day at midday there should be a solar transit (saṃkrānti), joined with the moon, the sun, or also with the asterism Hasta; || 16 ||

That which they call the *cintāmaṇi* (wish-fulfilling gem), the sole cause of the happiness of universal sovereignty, the cause of the destruction of all sins and calamities, and the cause of the side-glances of Lakṣmī for the sake of complete prosperity—[that is this]. (17)
Even by the Creator, nor indeed by Giriśa, can the beginning of that [age] be determined;
yet even there, it is said on earth that he is the supreme sovereign of yoga through his transition into the rays of the sun in every direction.
If the transit of the sun occurs on the seventh lunar day conjoined with the asterism Hasta, and it is joined by the moon at midday during the Vasu-muhūrta; || 19 ||
The great seers have declared that the great yoga called Vijaya occurs when the sun does not enter Sagittarius during the Brāhma-muhūrta.
They know that month as victorious (vijaya) when the sun enters [a new sign] at midday;
whatever recitation, fire-offerings, and other rites are performed there on each single day, [yield great fruit]. || 21 ||
Those proficient in the meaning of the scriptures declare that the fruit of *puraścaryā* can indeed be described as being equal to the fruit of a thousand great gifts (*mahādāna*). (22)
The merit arising from the worship of the venerable Lord here in each single day cannot be described even by the gift of an entire world to the preceptor. (23)
The hosts of deities, beginning with Brahmā, have declared that the fruit of a hundred sacrifices is obtained there by offering even a single oblation at each of those [sites]. (24)
One who performs the preliminary ritual (puraścaraṇa) of the glorious eight-syllable mantra for three months quickly attains the fruit of a thousand Rājasūya and Aśvamedha sacrifices.
Having performed ten million recitations, one shall undoubtedly obtain the fruit of the *puraścaryā* ritual;
this applies to the venerable eight-syllabled vidyā, which is as vast as the earth itself. (26)
I shall now proclaim the *puraścaryā*; listen with a concentrated mind. Having risen during the night of the sun’s transit into Sagittarius (*dhanuḥ-saṃkramaṇa*), [one should begin]. (27)
Having accepted his command out of devotion to the teacher as if he were a staff, and having adorned the teacher with garments, ornaments, and sandalwood paste; || 28 ||
Having bathed there, with a purified soul, and having performed the daily twilight devotions (saṃdhyā) at the mouth of the Śālagrāma stone of the Lord of the Earth, one shall attain glory.
Having reverently worshipped [the deity] together with the wheels, along with the limbs and the surrounding retinue,
while reciting [the mantra] that bestows the fruit of the Brahmavidyā of Indirānātha.
Or else with *komāra* tulasī leaves, or even with bilva leaves,
or with *āmalaka* fruits, or with the tips of dūrvā grass, accompanied by flowers.
O King, one should offer five hundred oblations daily with *śamī* leaves,
along with green gram porridge mixed with cumin, ginger, and ghee.
Having offered it together with jaggery and having given the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) along with honey and clarified butter,
one should daily recite the glorious eight-syllabled mantra (aṣṭākṣarī-vidyā) a thousand times.
Having recited the Vidyā named Śrīhṛdaya five hundred times,
one should likewise recite the twelve-syllable mantra of Śrī five hundred times.
Every day, into the blazing fire, one should offer a mudrā of food together with a finger-measure [of each],
combined with cumin and fresh ginger, and accompanied by cow’s ghee.
One should offer one hundred and eight oblations with the glorious eight-syllable vidyā, and likewise one hundred and eight oblations with the heart-mantra beginning with "Śrī Hṛd."
Then, with devotion, one should offer twelve oblations of clarified butter from a cow’s milk using ladles made of *ārṣa* wood, each oblation accompanied by the mantras of the Bhagavadraśmi-vidyās.
Having performed the transference of the *uṣas* in this manner day after day,
when the time for the transference of *uṣas* arrives, one should perform worship and other rites there as before.
There too, having recited as before, [one should offer] the mudrā-food combined with jaggery, joined with bilva leaves, and mixed with sesame, cow-products, and clarified butter. || 39 ||
Having first offered five hundred oblations with the glorious Aṣṭāraṇa-vidyā,
one should perform the rite for Śrī with the twelve-syllable Prasannalakṣmī mantra.
Having respectfully offered one thousand one hundred and thirty-eight oblations, he should then offer ghee three times with the *Aghora-vidyā* mantras.
Having performed the oblations with recitations and other rites, and having subsequently offered the *brahmārpaṇa* oblation,
one should circumambulate the fire and the Blessed Lord, the Consort of Śrī.
Having recited the Pañcaśatabrahmavidyā, one should then perform worship;
one should prostrate like a staff before the pair of feet of the preceptor, with all eight limbs touching the ground.
Having offered a nose-ornament (nāsa) that is yoked, new, subtle, most excellent, joined with rubies (padmarāga), and endowed with diamond-drops (vajrabiṇdu); || 44 ||
A pair of earrings fashioned from gold refined sixty times shall certainly be placed upon his ears. (45)
The wise man should offer to the preceptor a vast expanse of fertile land, endowed with abundant crops and accompanied by many sacrificial fees.
One should give a milch cow along with a sacrificial fee; five *āḍhaka* measures of mung beans and so forth should be given at the teacher's residence.
A wealthy prince, however, should bestow a single village;
the sacrificial fee for a village is said to be one thousand and eight measures of gold.
Or, according to one's capacity, one should give wealth while abandoning greed;
a field that yields little grain should not be given, for it causes distress and does not bestow happiness.
A cow that yields little milk and gives little fruit should not be given away;
rather, the king or the prince should perform great acts of charity.
For the sake of the increase of sons and grandsons, one should give a pumpkin accompanied by a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to a learned Brahmin who is poor, as a gift for his sustenance.

On that auspicious occasion of the sun's entry into Aries, which is like a single sacrificial fire, practitioners who possess the wealth of the ten gifts and other objects of charity [should perform worship].

The supreme ṛṣis residing in the city of Purāra have declared that the fruit of a hundred thousand oblations (lakṣahoma) is obtained there by giving to the preceptor land abounding in crops along with a lotus.
Whatever fruit one obtains by giving away the earth, girdled by the seven islands and the oceans of jewels, that one shall certainly attain here.
By giving a pair of earrings there to the preceptor of the two castes,
one obtains the inexhaustible fruit of giving for ten million kalpas.
Possessing the beauty of divine ornaments, anointed with divine sandalwood paste,
wearing divine garments and garlands, he was free from old age and death.
Whatever [debt] one owes to one's father and mother, even if submerged in the ocean of existence, that is uplifted by the gift of a hundred cows adorned with golden banners. || 57 ||
Ascending a celestial chariot accompanied by hundreds of divine maidens,
he, possessing a form like that of the Blessed Lord, rejoices in the supreme abode.
By giving a milch cow with its calf at the transit of the sun into Capricorn,
one obtains the inexhaustible fruit of a thousand great gifts, free from hunger.
Having thus performed the preliminary rite (puraścaryā) for one month during the transit of the sun into Capricorn,
and having performed a special fire-sacrifice (viśeṣahoma) here, one should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the preceptor.
Having obtained the imperishable fruit of a thousand *puraścaryās* of the *Sīṅga*,
one beholds the Lord of Śrī directly, as if in a dream.
Endowed with wealth and grain, adorned with pearls and gems,
the great Lakṣmī dwells unswervingly in his family and his home.
Then, having attained sovereign and inexhaustible mastery over all branches of knowledge,
he shall experience great prosperity through sons, grandsons, and other descendants.
Having obtained and enjoyed all the enjoyments here, which are very difficult to attain,
he shall certainly obtain liberation along with a thousand of his kinsmen.
Land measuring one hundred *āṭhaka*s, endowed with abundant crops and provided with many sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), is highly praised for the purpose of giving. (65)
By giving fifty hāṭakas, one obtains the fruit of giving a hundred cows; and by the gift of a thousand cows, as well as the gift of a thousand horses, one attains the state of Vasundharā. || 66 ||
The gift of earth excels the gift of a thousand elephants;
the gift of earth is a great gift that bestows success even more than a thousand [other gifts]. (67)
The great seers, as well as Brahmā and others who possess divine knowledge, have said:
"We are unable to initiate even Śūdras, for they are unfortunate and devoid of the power of hearing. (68)
Having given a pair of fine garments or ornaments and so forth,
and having honored the preceptor’s wife, one should give wealth amounting to five niṣkas.
One should offer it at the lotus-feet of the preceptor; even if one is unable to do so, one may instead give a milch cow or wealth measuring four *viṣka* coins.
Having given even five *āḍhaka* measures of mung beans, one shall likewise attain success;
even a poor person certainly attains accomplishment, there is no doubt. (71)
Whether it be a woman or a man, when an auspicious time has arrived,
one should give a pumpkin fruit along with its seeds to a learned Brahmin who maintains a family.
One is liberated from great sins and attains good fortune, sons, and the increase of one's power, becoming a partaker of the glory of Mahendra. (73)
On the full moon day of Kārttika and during the auspicious transit of the sun into Libra, one should offer a pumpkin;
it is heard that this bestows very great and auspicious fruit.
The full moon day of Kārtika joined with a Saturday and conjoined with Vyatīpāta is called the Mahatī Tithi.
They say that the conjunction with the Lord of Prasannalakṣmī on this day brings glory in every respect;
having bathed, offered oblations, and given gifts at the lotus-feet of the Guru, a mortal attains supreme perfection.
Among the days of the week, Saturday; among the lunar dates, the full moon day;
and among the yogas, Vyatīpāta—these bestow great accomplishment.
Where these three are united, that is declared to be a great parvan;
having bathed there, one obtains the great and auspicious eight-syllabled vidyā.
Having chanted according to his ability at dawn,
and having offered five hundred oblations into the consecrated fire with the auspicious eight-syllabled mantra beginning with "Om," he becomes pure.
With the Lakṣmī-hṛdaya mantra, one thousand and one hundred oblations should be offered using bilva leaves smeared with ghee and mixed with the three sweets (honey, sugar, and clarified butter).

Or, having offered oblations with the twelve-syllable mantra of Śrī, the Lord of Śrī, with his rays, having offered three times with cow’s clarified butter, and having performed the oblation of the offering unto Brahman (brahmārpaṇa); || 81 ||
The fee for the pair of the teacher’s feet is twelve niṣkas,
or six niṣkas, or three niṣkas, or even two niṣkas.
Or, having entrusted it to her, he should then give it to his wife with the thought that she is Kamalā;
likewise, he should give her ornaments or as much wealth as he can afford.
The triad of couples should be honored with delicious foods, sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā), and so forth;
and to a learned Brahmin who is poor, an excellent kūṣmāṇḍa fruit [should be given].
Having given it along with a sacrificial fee according to one's ability, one is liberated from all sins, attains great perfection, and is indeed glorified. || 85 ||
O King, on that day he should sleep on the ground and subsist on sacrificial food (haviṣya);
month after month, he beholds Hari himself in person.
Having obtained the fruit of the three types of *puraścaryā* and attained unsurpassed perfection, he shall acquire great fortune abounding in wealth, grain, and other riches. (87)
Having attained beautiful songs and delightful poetic skill,
as well as the increase of sons and grandsons, and even enjoyments that are very difficult to obtain.
Whether it be a woman or even a man, on the full moon day of Kārttika, they rejoice in the abode of the Lord of Lakṣmī; of this there is no doubt. (89)
Having given the Kūṣmāṇḍa oblation along with sacrificial fees according to one's ability,
one attains inexhaustible good fortune and a household abounding in prosperity, wealth, grain, and other riches.
Desiring the prosperity of her husband, as well as auspiciousness and delightful charm, she attains the complete growth of her lineage; of this there is no doubt. (91)
On the full moon day of the month of Kārtika, the Kūṣmāṇḍa fruit shall certainly bestow an increase of sons and grandsons, as well as wealth, grain, noble lineage, and prosperity.
One should perform the gift of a gourd (kūṣmāṇḍa) even when the sun is situated in Capricorn;
furthermore, I shall again fully describe the auspicious Navarātra vow.
Listen with one-pointed mind to this Navarātra Mahārātra vow, which bestows all perfections immediately and is the jewel among vows in the midst of the year.
It bestows success upon all sciences and shatters the multitude of sins; they know that even a single day spent there is equal to the Cūḍāmaṇi [tīrtha].
There, the Katañjatya rite was performed, which pacifies all suffering, delivers one from the ocean of existence, and bestows a portion of the mass of supreme bliss. (96)
It bestows longevity, increases wealth, wards off untimely death,
grants heaven and liberation, and immediately grants the fulfillment of all desired objects.
No other great vow has been declared equal to the Navarātra vow; having performed that vow there with the permission of the preceptor, a man becomes great. (98)
He becomes successful everywhere, capable of both subduing and favoring, when the auspicious first day of the month of Āśvina has arrived. (99)

Having bathed in the morning according to the prescribed rite in a river with the permission of his teacher, he should recite the Mother of the Vedas (Gāyatrī) one thousand times, or three hundred times.
Having attended upon Divākara and completed the daily fire-oblation (nityahoma),
one should [offer] into the fire duly consecrated according to the rules by means of the twelve-syllable mantra.
Having invoked Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa there and worshipped them with ritual offerings,
one should offer one hundred and eight oblations of clarified butter with the eight-syllable mantra.
Having offered one hundred and eight oblations with the *prasanna-lakṣmī* mantra, or with the twelve-syllable mantra of Śrī, or even with the six-syllable mantra of Śrī; || 103 ||
Having made a formal resolve (saṃkalpa), one should recite the glorious eight-syllabled mantra (aṣṭākṣarī-vidyā) one thousand times,
and likewise recite the twelve-syllabled Śrī-mantra one thousand times after making a formal resolve.

Having thus performed the vow for eight days, one should then recite the *Lakṣmīhṛdaya*, proclaimed in the *Atharvaveda*, which grants all desires, increasing the count by one each day up to one hundred and one recitations.
The wise one should recite [the mantra] either fifty times or forty times,
using bilva leaves accompanied by the three sweets and ghee in the Mahābhava [rite].
Having purified himself, he should offer milk-rice mixed with sesame seeds into the consecrated fire according to the rules,
accompanied by large ornaments and clarified butter, while remaining pure before it.
Having burned away the previously mentioned heap of sins with the glorious eight-syllable mantra one thousand and more times, and also with the twelve-syllable Śrī-mantra; 108.
Being pure, one should offer one thousand three hundred oblations of sin;
thereafter, one should offer clarified butter in three ways with the rays of the Blessed One.
Having performed the fire-oblation and subsequently the offering of water with recitations and other rites,
the observer of the vow should daily worship the Brahmavidyā five hundred times.
Day after day, having worshipped married women with the thought that they are Mahālakṣmī herself,
one should worship at least one woman with the thought that she is Vimalā.
O King, at the beginning, middle, and end, with the thought that she is the Earth herself,
one should worship a married woman and a Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas.

Having worshipped her with the thought that she is the Blessed One, one should constantly satisfy the married women of that family with food, drink, and other offerings, as well as with gifts and fees.

Whether eating sacrificial offerings (haviṣya), eating only a small portion (kalāśī), or eating but a single meal a day; whether subsisting on fruits, living on water, or sleeping on the ground—even one who is thus endowed with self-control [attains the goal]. || 114 ||
Then, having placed a single [coin] at intervals upon the two auspicious feet of the Ācārya,
he should present sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā), clothing, ornaments, and so forth.
Having offered oblations on the Mahānavamī day and having respectfully paid homage to the Fire-god,
he [worshipped] the two lords, Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa, with the twelve-syllabled mantra of Śrīśa.
Having worshipped according to the previously mentioned rite and gone to the teacher's residence,
[he should offer] a pair of earrings fashioned from gold and marked with the six signs.
Then, having given a pair of garments to that couple and having offered them,
one should thereafter worship them with golden rings and other such items.
Having given a single Śālagrāma stone accompanied by a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā),
he should also give a stream of wealth (vasudhārā) abounding with many kinds of grain.
Then one should offer a pair of oxen yoked for southward travel;
thereafter, four non-malevolent beasts of burden should be given.
A prince abounding in virtues should give ten villages;
this great ninth day of the month of Aśvayuja is thus proclaimed.
Each single day here, during this auspicious Navarātra vow, is said by the supreme sages to possess the brilliance of a thousand suns and planets. 122.
The ancient supreme sages have declared that the Ardhodaya is sevenfold [in merit];
the great Navamī is its vessel, and that which is equal to it bestows the perfection of the sacred festival (parva).
O illustrious one, I do not know where that inexhaustible perfection might be found;
yet, O trembling one, you desire the glory of victory on the day of Mahānavamī.
Having performed the worship of one's chosen deity and having daily offered a generous sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to him, one shall obtain the fortune of recitation.
Furthermore, by giving even a single morsel of food to one Brahmin,
one certainly obtains the same fruit as from feeding ten million Brahmins.
Having worshipped there even a single well-dressed woman with the thought that she is Mahālakṣmī,
one who is well-dressed obtains the fruit of thousands [of such women].
There, having offered the splendor of the earth at the lotus feet of the Ācārya,
he gave twelve portions of land abounding in wealth and jewels.
Whatever fruit a person enjoys from [giving] the earth endowed with its seven continents, he certainly obtains that same fruit in its entirety; of this there is no doubt. (129)
Having respectfully given two cows along with a calf as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), one attains the fruit of the gift of ten million cows in its entirety. || 130 ||

Having obtained the fruit arising from the gift of ten million cosmic eggs (brahmāṇḍas) through a Śālagrāma stone, the pure-souled one becomes liberated while living and attains the bliss of heaven. || 131 ||
On the ninth day of the month of Āśvina, the wealthy prince gave away two villages, a pair of horses, and a horse accompanied by an umbrella.
One should give even a noble elephant and offer a beautiful palanquin adorned with flowers;
one should then present one’s own daughter to one’s preceptor.
By honoring the teacher’s wife with abundant ornaments and garments, regarding her as Kamalā, one attains eternal perfection.
By offering even a single oblation on that day of Mahānavamī,
a person obtains the complete fruit of one hundred million offerings.
Whatever gold shines there at the feet of the Guru, the divine great sages say that constitutes a gift equal to Mount Meru. (136)
Having first prepared an auspicious, shining vessel measuring two palas,
the practitioner should place the seasonal materials therein for the preceptor.
O observer of noble vows, it is impossible for me to describe his merit in its entirety;
I shall grant him the lordship over this very world.

I shall lead his ancestors dwelling in hell to the world of Brahmā; and at the end, having rendered even the station of Indra and other gods as insignificant as a blade of grass, I shall establish them there.

One who possesses a form resembling that of the Blessed One rejoices in the supreme state; so too does one who possesses the glorious eight-syllable mantra, as well as the twelve-syllable mantra of Śrī. 140.
Having performed the preliminary rite (puraścaryā) together with its ancillaries (sāṅga), completed by means of gifts and fees (dakṣiṇā),
the fruit of that preliminary rite— performed a thousand times along with its ancillaries— is imperishable.
Having attained the Lord of the World, Nārāyaṇa, who is without beginning or end and who bears the conch, the discus, and other emblems, the Lord of Śrī beholds him indeed.
Here too, there is great sovereignty endowed with the qualities such as *aṇimā* and others, crowded with a flood of wealth, grain, cattle, and gold.
Having obtained horses and elephants, long life, flowers, and steadiness, as well as all forms of supreme welfare and great, auspicious knowledge. || 144 ||
Having enjoyed the increase of sons, grandsons, and so forth, as well as rare pleasures, he,
together with a thousand kinsmen, attains the supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
At the end of the body, he enters [the state]; there is no doubt in this matter.
Here, the specific distinction regarding the horse-headed Lakṣmī-vidyā will be explained.
On an auspicious day, beginning with the teacher and so forth, having bathed in the morning and purified his self, he should perform the daily twilight devotions (saṃdhyā). || 147 ||
Having recited the Gāyatrī many times and completed the daily fire-oblation (nityahoma),
one should offer a hundred oblations with the mantra consisting of eight syllables.
One should recite the Lakṣmīhṛdaya-vidyā one hundred and eight times;
one should daily recite the eight-syllable mantra five hundred times, for it bestows all spiritual accomplishments (siddhis).
Having made a formal resolve (saṃkalpa), a Śūdra should recite the Lakṣmīhṛdaya-vidyā one thousand times on the eighth lunar day; he should subsist on fruit or eat sacrificial food (vāhaviṣya).
Or else, having been cursed once, he shall eat excrement day after day;
inevitably, though adorned with ornaments, he shall become a consumer of filth.
On that day, having gratified with all necessary objects the preceptor, or his wife, or his son, he should respectfully seek the heart of Śrī.
A wise person should offer fifty-four oblations forty times,
O King, and auspicious women should be honored according to the previously mentioned ritual procedure.
On the Mahānavamī day, one thousand well-dressed women should be honored;
or else, one should worship twelve [images] who are the direct embodiments of the Mahālakṣmī-vidyā.
O King, one should feed twelve Brahmins with the thought that they are Nārāyaṇa himself,
and honor the wives of the preceptors with garments, ornaments, and other gifts, perceiving them as Śrī.
The wise practitioner, for the sake of fulfilling the vow,
should especially worship when the sacrificial fire has been kindled on the day of Mahānavamī.
One should offer twenty-eight oblations of cow-ghee into the fire with the Veda-dam mantra;
having invoked Śrī and Śrīpati there in the fire by means of the Brahmavidyā.
Having first offered a hundred oblations of clarified butter with the glorious eight-syllable mantra, he should then offer [oblations] soaked in the three sweets with the *Mahālakṣmī-prasannā* vidyā.
Having offered one thousand three hundred oblations of milk-rice mixed with sesame seeds and bilva leaves, together with cow's ghee, into the blazing fire; 159.
One should offer milk-rice (pāyasa) three times with the mantras of the Heart of Lakṣmī;
thereafter, one should offer ghee three times with the Vaiṣṇava rays (mantras).
Then, having performed the recitation (japa) and other rites, and having offered the oblation of Brahman-surrender (brahmārpaṇa),
he should respectfully circumambulate and bow down to Jātavedas (the Fire-god).
Having worshipped Śrī and Śrīpati three hundred times with the Brahmavidyā mantra, and having prostrated there before the two lotus feet of the Noble One (Ārya), [he performed the rites]. 162.
Having adorned either his wife or his son with perfumes and other ornaments,
he should place a pair of auspicious earrings upon the two ears of that person.
One should give away one's entire household wealth as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), or at least a pair of fine garments, or even food sufficient for a year. 164.
If one is unable even for that, twelve niṣkas are prescribed;
if one is unable even for that, O giver of honor, wealth amounting to ten niṣkas [is prescribed].
One should give wealth consisting of one niṣka or even five niṣkas,
or two cows accompanied by a calf that yields much milk.
By giving away the earth together with many villages, or even accompanied by wealth, one attains great perfection; there is no doubt in this matter. || 167 ||
Having performed the preparatory rite (puraścaraṇa) with full devotion and complete sacrificial fees—
even if only once— he becomes directly endowed with a portion of the Blessed One.
He attains great accomplishment, difficult even for the gods to obtain;
Mahālakṣmī protects him daily as if he were her own son.
Having thus performed this vow with devotion even during the Navarātra in the spring,
one becomes united with a portion of the Lord and is liberated while still alive.
Even the eight guardians of the directions, beginning with Mahendra, dwell there like servants; they grant all spiritual perfections directly to him.
In the vow associated with the twelve-syllable Śrīvidyā, as well as in that of the eight-syllable mantra,
one should likewise practice the eight-syllable Śrīmantra accompanied by Prasanna-Lakṣmī.
It is taught that the "all-own" (sarvasva) gift bestows all accomplishments;
alternatively, the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) is said to be an amount of wealth equal to one year's food.
Alternatively, the earth, provided with abundant crops and the like, joined by four bulls,
and accompanied by ritual fees (dakṣiṇā), is said to bestow all perfections.
One who desires this supreme bliss of Brahman-joy, which is free from old age and death, and this eightfold prosperity, should strive with a self-restrained mind.
In this manner, the *puraścaraṇa* must certainly be performed with devotion;
likewise, in every yoga of Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa, it should be done during the rising of the moon.
Having performed recitation, fire-offerings, and other rites, one attains eternal perfection when Jupiter is situated in the zodiac sign of Leo in the yoga named Puṣkara. || 177 ||
Even by performing recitation, fire-offerings, and other rites during the Govindadvādaśī conjunction, one beholds the Supreme Brahman directly. || 178 ||

Whether on the day of Puṣpārka, on the day of Puṣpasāsa, on the full moon, on a lunar festival, or during the rising of the moon in the month of Ārdrā, a thousand [other] gifts would not be equal to that [gift]. (179)
O King, the third day of the bright fortnight in Vaiśākha and the full moon day in Kārtika are declared to bring great accomplishment through recitation, fire-offerings, and other rites.
Great accomplishment is declared to be attained through the Bhṛguvāra vow, the Navarātra vow, and also the Dhanurmāsa vow. || 181 ||
Whether it be the full moon day of Vaiśākha or the full moon day of the month of Māgha—
these two days are most excellent and grant immediate accomplishment.
The period beginning from the eleventh day of the month of Māgha and ending on the seventh day is called Bhīṣmapañcaka; it is remembered as bestowing great spiritual accomplishments.
What is the use of saying more here? Listen to the essential word:
it is remembered that the practice of the *karu* and *śukra* [mantras] brings about the attainment of siddhi.
One may abandon even a devoted wife, one's father, mother, sister, or sons;
however, one should never abandon the pair of feet of the teacher, even at the end of one's life.
The word of the guru must always be carried out, whether it be auspicious or inauspicious;
service to the teacher should be rendered even at the cost of one's life and wealth. (186)
O Lord of the Earth, having understood this very thing to be the most formidable obstacle to the attainment of Brahman, one should always act accordingly. (187)
One attains the supreme abode, which is difficult even for yogins to reach;
yet by transgressing the command of the teacher even once, one is cast down to the earth.
Accompanied by his sons, grandsons, and others, along with his ancestors, he sinks into the dreadful hell for all time; of this there is no doubt. (189)
The pair of feet of the Teacher should be served daily with reverence;
having recited this Great Vidyā, it bestows enjoyment, heaven, and liberation.
Having spoken thus directly to Janaka, the all-pervading Lord, the great yogi Nārāyaṇa, together with Nara, did not vanish from sight.
Ṛṣyaśṛṅga said:
Thus was it spoken by Nārāyaṇa to the high-souled king;
Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, related it to Rudra when he questioned him. 192.
In the *Anuttarabrahmatattvarahasya*, the compendium of the Vedas, within the tantra known as the *Dāśarathīya*, the eastern quarter has been proclaimed. (193)
In this regard, even one who merely hears a single word from the lotus-like mouth of the Teacher, having heard it, is liberated from heaps of great sins. (194)
One attains that abode of glory which is difficult even for the gods to reach.
[Thus ends the fifty-ninth chapter in the venerable *Anuttara-Brahmatattva-Rahasya*, the *Dāśarathīya Tantra*, known as the *Vedārthasaṃgraha*. Śrī.
Salutations to Śrī Rāmacandra.
The sages said:
O most illustrious one, foremost among those possessing all-encompassing knowledge,
I have heard the greatness of the glorious eight-syllabled mantra, which contains the secret of the ocean.
Śrīvidyā, Lakṣmī, Mahālakṣmī, Triśaktikā, and Sāmrājyalakṣmī—these five are proclaimed as the glories of sovereignty (sāmrājyaśriyaḥ). || 2 ||
O ocean of compassion, you have not yet described that Sāmrā Lakṣmī Śrīvidyā; please speak of her full majesty.
Ṛṣyaśṛṅga said:
Having spoken thus to King Daśaratha, Rāma, the lord of the three worlds,
the Lord of the Universe laughed along with Sītā, the incomparable Rudrāṇī, and Auryāsā.
The illustrious Rudra said:

This secret of the direct realization of Brahman—which brings about the perfect attainment of identity with Brahman, which has been heard from the existent [teacher], and which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation—has come into being. || 5 ||
I have heard from the lotus of your mouth the entire majesty of the glorious eight-syllabled mantra, which instantly destroys all sins.
O Sustainer of the worlds, Śrīvidyā has been indicated but not yet revealed;
tell me her entire majesty here in this world.
The Blessed One said:
O Śambhu, while performing sacrifice and not consuming food for the sake of the Great-Souled Nārāyaṇa,
I shall declare the entire majesty of Śrīvidyā.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O King, to the *Śrībhagavadajanma*, known as the *Saubhāgyodaya*, which is contained within this *Nārāyaṇīya Tantra*; it is auspicious and bestows all perfections.
Having become the son of Daśaratha for the sake of the wise Pṛṣṭhaurudha,
I shall again respectfully proclaim the tantra known as Dāśarathīya.
O King, listen to this secret, the essence of the Lalitā-vidyā, which brings fame;
known by the name Saubhāgyodaya, it is highly honored.
Having heard, remembered, or even seen this Tantra which is for the welfare of the world,
one becomes the foundation of all fortunes and attains liberation.
He who is supreme over all the worlds, the eternal destroyer of the inner darkness,
the Supreme Self, the highest bliss, the omniscient Supreme Lord.
From his five faces, these Vedic traditions were brought forth:
the Eastern, the Western, the Southern, and likewise the Northern.
This collection of the *Ūha-āmnāya* and these others are proclaimed as the paths to liberation;
the *Pūrva-āmnāya* is the *Ṛgveda*, while the *Yajurveda* is the southern one.
The Sāmaveda shall be in the west, and the Atharvaṇa in the north;
the Ūrdhvāmnāya is proclaimed as the collection of all the Upaniṣads. || 17 ||
Indeed, I shall declare that which has been spoken in the remaining traditional lineages:
the body of the Lord of the Universe consists of thirty-six principles (tattvas). || 18 ||
The soul with its sheath is the transmigrating self; the soul without its sheath is the sustainer of the world, Śrīśa Nārāyaṇa himself. (19)
The eternal sounds, whose nature consists of phonemes, from which this entire universe is extended; through their inconceivable power, they constitute all mantras and the world itself.
From the tradition of the six [teachers], the supreme accomplishment of the noble Bhaga is remembered;
authority resides in the words that have emerged from the mouth of the Ācārya. (12)
O King, she is said to be the bringer of great accomplishment for all vidyās; one should always behave toward the teacher’s wife and sons exactly as one does toward the teacher himself. (13)
Having become steadfast in devotion, one surely ascends and descends;
one should always meditate with the intellect on the unity of the Guru, the Deity, and the Mantra.
One should proceed toward the supreme goal by following the pair of the teacher's feet;
for this alone is the established conclusion (siddhānta) declared by the proponents of Vedānta.
The Vedas, Shastras, and Puranas are like common courtesans; but this science, cherished by the illustrious one, is like the wife of a noble family. (24)
Possessing firm devotion to the two feet of the teacher, with his senses conquered, he should serve the teacher even at the cost of his body, life, and wealth. (25)
Devoted to Vedic conduct and dedicated to the path of dharma, he was superior,
turned away from worldly things, honorable, a speaker of truth, and free from malice.
To such a disciple—one whose self is free from egoism and who is intent upon the recitation of the Gāyatrī—knowledge should be given to one who seeks auspiciousness. (27)
The teacher should always protect his resident disciple on this earth like a son, instructing him in all the scriptures as well as the secret doctrines.
Having necessarily become initiated, the wise one, following the command of his preceptor, should mutter the Śrīvidyā for the attainment of the bliss of Brahman. (29)
There are three well-known initiations (dīkṣās) that destroy all sins;
the first is the Vaiṣṇava initiation, which is superior to the others.
The initiation into the city of Aya-rātri is remembered as bestowing great siddhi;
one who has been initiated there becomes perpetually pure. (31)
One who is joined with two initiations becomes a master of the assembly;
one who is joined with three initiations is the Blessed One himself, the triple-formed Lord.
Or even one initiated in a single [tradition], if he is today free from all [defects],
shall become pure and qualified for the state of possessing all vidyās.
I shall proclaim the ritual of initiation (dīkṣā-vidhi), by which the disciple becomes happy;
for through it, every object, including even one's own life-force, is bestowed upon the Guru.
This collection of garments, possessing the colors of the nine gems, gold, and so forth,
comes to ruin through a base recipient, one who is devoid of armor, one with defects in mantra, a slanderer, a fool, or one intent on hating sacred fords.

O King, it should not be given to one devoid of devotion nor to one who is impure; however, it may be given to one endowed with devotion, even if not yet purified, provided he is a soul who is a portion of Nārāyaṇa. (39)
To the king who walked the path of righteousness, who was devoted to the gods and the twice-born, who knew the meaning of all the scriptures and the Vedas, and who was firm in his vows; || 47 ||
Then, having constructed a pavilion and an altar adorned with flower arches, the portion for the king to be given at initiation shall be provided. (41)
Adorned with various ornaments and wearing a garland of lamps,
she was decorated with lines of vermilion and possessed a variegated appearance.
Then, O King, on the altar, one should draw a most enchanting, intoxicated wheel with saffron or with vermilion powder.
In the middle circle, one should draw a nine-cornered figure that is captivating to the mind, as well as a square, and nine golden jars.

[One should offer] vessels made of silver, copper, and so forth, as well as those fashioned from clay, filled with water, exceptionally rich [in offerings], and adorned with jewels, gold, and other precious materials. || 45 ||
One should worship the eight goddesses beginning with Vaśinī there, along with their auspicious fruits and flowers and fragrant substances, within the pitchers.
Having worshipped the entire sequence according to the rules in the consecrated fire, [he should do so] out of satisfaction with the Śrīvidyā, the Great Serpent (Mahīyāla), in the central pitcher.
Having performed the oblation once with the *raśmi* mantras and one hundred and eight times with the mantra of Śrī,
the pure teacher should then establish the disciple upon his own seat.
Having reached the end of all the peaks and ridges, one should worship that disciple;
one should meditate upon the Śrīcakra, which is the form of the sixfold sacrifice (ṣaḍadhvara), upon his head. || 48 ||
Having seen him, one should gaze at him; through that gaze, one should today unite with him.
One should effect the transmission of the command (ājñā-saṃkramaṇa) until the lineage becomes like a moving spider's web.
The body of Śambhu is free from all agitation, devoid of both void and non-void;
it is a reality consisting of the supreme void, the Puruṣa, the Supreme Lord. || 51 ||
It is non-empty because of the primordial power, for Prakṛti is the cause of all;
when there is a conjunction of Śiva and Śivā, grossness arises. (52)
At that time, it should be known as the state of dream, because of the predominance of the power of yoga;
it is celebrated as Śakti, Agni, and likewise as Śiva, characterized by immovability.
The wise declare that *suṣupti* (deep sleep) is so called because it is motionless;
however, it is said to possess the qualities of both waking and dreaming. (54)
(*** ) She, whose form is steadfastly devoted to Śiva, desires to serve him; know that she has become one who realizes the reality that transcends all qualities and is superior even to Śiva. 54.
When, through the union of Śiva and Śakti, there arises a preponderance of Śiva, then know that to be the state which destroys all impurities. 56.
