The sixteen digits (kalās), established in self-knowledge and merged within the seed-syllable of Śrīvidyā, one should cause to manifest within the body of the disciple. (57)
The Goddess Śrīvidyā, the life-sustainer of the worlds and sovereign of all thrones,
is called Umnānī because through meditation upon her, stability of mind is attained.

Śrī Dakṣiṇāmūrti said:

One finds that single reality named Śrīvidyā, which bestows great fortune upon the four castes, which delivers one from the cycle of worldly existence, and which is adorned by the two vowels *i* and *u*.
O lady of excellent vows, she is also called Brahman in the Vedāntas;

Obeisance to the eternal one, within whom the letters of the five mother-syllables (mātṛkā) are contained;

From this very source arose Śrī, who possesses fifteen syllables,

Arising from this very [source], adorned with the *vindunaya* and *avindunaya*,

O Daughter of the Mountain, even the science of Haṃsa, when joined with the Vidyunmālā,

The triad of consonants, the triad of worlds, the triad of feet of Hari, the triad of lotuses, the triad of phonemes, and likewise the triad of selves; || 28 ||

All the deities, born from portions and sub-portions of this [Being], as well as whatever beings have arisen in the forms of female, male, or neuter, are [contained within it]. (33)
It is certain that there is nothing whatsoever that does not consist of her alone;

She is Śrīvidyā, the Mother of Syllables (Annamātā), Sāvitrī, and Sarasvatī;

The Great Queen of all vidyās, the Sovereign of all lion-thrones, consisting of all knowledge, the destroyer of all sins—she is my auspiciousness. 36.
She bestows all prosperity and the attainment of siddhis upon the worlds accompanied by their queens;

O Śrīmān, this ten-syllable mantra is not obtained even by those who bow;

This ten-syllabled [mantra] of Śrī, which bestows prosperity, cannot be described by anyone;

Even sovereignty should be given, even the head along with life itself;

By the recitation of the Śatasaṃhitā a hundred thousand times, one obtains the merit of the Vedamātṛ;

She is the mother of Prajāpati and even of Viṣṇu, the Great Lord;

Having recited the eight-syllable mantra of Śrī known as Mṛtyuñjaya,

Even Kāmadeva, having recited this fifteen-syllable mantra of Śrī,
enchanted the three worlds, including men and women endowed with all virtues.

Those who desire to bring others under their control should daily recite the names of Śiva’s beautiful wives and the enchanting daughters of the gods and Gandharvas.

For one who desires to bring [others] under one's own control, this fifteen-syllable mantra is to be recited;
it is the Supreme Person himself, directly designated by names such as Brahmā and Rudra.
Nārāyaṇa is the leader of the three worlds, the Supreme Lord;
this Goddess is His power, the conscious aspect named Sundarī.
Even another who is devoid of power, if he were endowed with power, would indeed be capable;
for one is truly capable [only] to perform creation, maintenance, and dissolution.
O Daughter of the Mountain, Gāyatrī, Bhāratī, Vidyā, Sāvitrī, and Pārameśvarī—these, as well as Vedamātā, have arisen from her. 55.

you are all fourfold knowledge and the sovereign lord upon the throne of all learning.

This knowledge is equal to all knowledge; indeed, there is nothing superior to it.
It bestows the four aims of life eternally and grants the eight supernatural powers, beginning with *aṇiman*.
This [mantra] of Śrī, consisting of five syllables, bestows the status of Brahmā and other offices;

She consists of all yoga, she bestows the fruit of the recitation of the *sasala* and *urvavidyā*,

She is the embodiment of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśāna;

Therefore, this fifteen-syllable mantra, consisting of all vidyās,
having been obtained from her daily in solitude through the grace of one's own teacher, O Śivā, [one attains] thousands of crores of yoginīs.
He is worshipped even by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśa, and others;

Even the thousands of crores of Yoginīs, the venerable Bhairavas, the immortals beginning with Śakra, and millions of great sages [are present].

The fifteen-syllable Vidyārāja, which possesses the splendor of being grasped, bestows heaven upon this earth for those who undertake the recitation of Lalitā.

A thousand measures of gold given at a meritorious tirtha on the day of the moon's conjunction (Amāvāsyā) do not equal even a sixteenth part of the merit of reciting this Vidyā once.
Because it is inexpressible and devoid of the nature of being an object, it is incapable of being described through qualities or letters;

Indeed, she is like one mute to those who merely see; yet the Madhyamāmadhyamādhyamā becomes the very nature of the knowledge of Brahman, bestowing the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.

In the great yoga of Śiva and Śakti, whatever action arises, it becomes the object of knowledge; this is the fifteen-syllable mantra of Icchā. 75.
Without the instruction of a teacher, that fifteen-syllable vidyā which has been seen by the hosts of yogins is recited by Prajāpati himself. (76)
Bestowed through the grace of the Teacher, she bestows the nectar of the essence of all the Vedas;
she grants the good fortune of the three worlds and abundant prosperity. (77)
Possessing the charm of a hundred Kamadevas, capable of attracting even the gods through counsel,
she possesses the force of a river of nectar and bestows the skill of a virtuous woman.
Bestowing a multitude of arts endowed with good fortune and prosperity, she grants absorption into the Supreme Brahman to one who bows before her with reverence. 79.
She whose supreme power draws forth the radiance from the depths of the ocean, and by the flicker of whose sidelong glance the fourteen worlds are impelled. 80.
Women, men, and others become subject to his will;
he shall rule over the empire of the earth as far as the four oceans. || 81 ||
O Śivā, because you are supported by the conduct of the lineage of Śrīvidyā, you shall become the elephant of the lioness of Śrīvidyā;

Furthermore, O beloved, the creation of gods, humans, and so forth is not impossible for a man who performs the recitation of the Śrīvidyā, O dear one. (83)
O Beloved, for a person who has accomplished the Śrīvidyā, powers such as entering another's body and the siddhis beginning with aṇimā are not difficult to attain in this world. (84)
Listen to this great secret which was spoken by Brahmā in ancient times, and which was not even told to Nārāyaṇa; having heard it, become a guardian of its secrecy.

At the end of the three sections, having joined the seed-syllable of Śrī—which consists of fire (ra), wind (ya), and the sun (ra), combined with honey (m) and conjoined with lightning (u)—the yogi [should employ it]. 86.
He recites the sixteen-syllable Great Vidyā, which bestows all spiritual accomplishments;
he should give away his beloved wife and take back his sons and daughters. (87)
Even an empire may be given away, but the sixteen-syllable mantra must not be bestowed;
for whatever instruction is given to someone else, that very fruit is lost.
If the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) is complete, then [the deity] enters that very body;
through the giving of a full dakṣiṇā, [one attains this] even without preliminary rites (puraścaryā) and the like.
The success of the vidyās occurs, producing immediate conviction; here, these four [mantras] constantly bring about security and well-being. (90)
O Daughter of the Mountain, the Ṛgvedic verses proclaim the sixteen-syllabled Śrīvidyā;
she is declared to be Nityā, while the sixteenth is Mahānityā.
She alone is the supreme one, whose nature is consciousness and who consists of all knowledge;
she is the cintāmaṇi and other jewels, as well as the kalpavṛkṣa and other celestial trees.
There is no doubt that they reside in the home of one who chants the Śrīvidyā;
indeed, the supreme practitioner who constantly recites the Śrīvidyā [is graced by them]. (93)
O beloved, blessed is her mother who has seen the world fulfilled, and blessed is her father whose lineage has attained its purpose;
pure are those born of that family, and purified are her friends and kinsmen.
By recollecting the chanting of the Śrīvidyā, one obtains the fruit of a horse-sacrifice;
by not bowing to the chanting of the Śrīvidyā, one does not obtain the fruit of the tulā-dāna gift.
O my beloved, even by merely conversing with one who constantly recites the Śrīvidyā, one obtains the enjoyment resulting from the Vājapeya sacrifice and attains liberation. (97)
That divine field where the reciter of the Śrīlalitā-vidyā observes his vows is declared to extend for a hundred yojanas on all sides.
The treasures, such as Śaṅkha, Padma, and others, indeed reside at his gate;
Dharma, Artha, Kāma, and Mokṣa constantly abide in his hand.
The majesty of the goddess Sundarī is like a treasure-trove that must be constantly guarded with effort by one who desires his own welfare. 100.
Even Agni, Bhṛgu, Dakṣa, and others who possess the power of creating the world, as well as Vasiṣṭha, Vāmadeva, and the rest, are worthy of being gladdened by the divine [sight]. 101.
Even the great siddhas such as Kapila and others are of the nature of Nārāyaṇa,
as are Sanaka and the other lords of yoga, Mārkaṇḍeya and the rest.
O my beloved, having meditated upon the goddess Śrī who is seated gracefully, those who have observed the vow of recitation have attained all their desired objects and continue to recite even today.
This alone is the deity, this alone is the name, this alone is such a great vow;
this alone is the supreme yoga, this alone is the supreme fruit. || 104 ||
"This alone is the supreme initiation; this is the path higher than the highest"—thinking thus, O Śivā, one should recite the Vidyā of Śrī every day.
This very Mahāvidyā, which is a compendium of the essential meaning of all the Vedas and Vedāntas, has been proclaimed by the supreme sages as nothing other than this. (106)
Furthermore, [he attains] the state of a Siddha, or the state of a deity, or even the form of a Kinnara;
as well as the status of a great seer (maharṣi), power, and the state of being a creator. || 107 ||
O fair-faced one, by one who desires the state of Viṣṇu or the state of Rudra with a self-restrained mind, the Śrīvidyā alone must be recited; no other vidyā [should be used]. 108.
O fair-faced one, O Śrīnidhi, by one who necessarily desires even the unattainable power of subduing the sleeping [Śeṣa], this [mantra] must be recited. 109.
Having recited the great vidyā of sixteen syllables, or else that of fifteen syllables,
one becomes like the god Ādhorāṇa, the master of all fortunes.
One who constantly recites the Śrīvidyā becomes the lord of the dull-witted, free from all fear and endowed with every prosperity. 111.
I have thus related to you something of the greatness of Līlā; it is a merit that destroys all sins from the very beginning. What more do you wish to hear? 112.

[Thus ends the second chapter in the latter part of the Saubhāgyavidyodaya, within the Vedārthasaṃgraha, the Tantra of the Ten Sons of Daśaratha, the secret essence of the supreme and unsurpassed Brahman-reality. || 2 ||
The venerable Ṛṣyaśṛṅga said:
Having heard this, the Great Goddess, the Daughter of the Mountain King, with her palms joined in reverence, spoke again to the Lord Dakṣiṇāmūrti.
The Goddess said:
O Blessed One, Lord of the Gods of Gods, this fifteen-syllable mantra of Śrī, most secret among sciences and auspicious, has been heard by me; it bestows all prosperity. (2)
Thereafter, O ocean of compassion, the Lord who bestows prosperity, whose form is the nectar of the eyes, spoke to Akhilavada regarding its performance.
Listen, O Goddess, I shall respectfully proclaim the secret of Śrī.
Having heard which, even the gods are not able to obstruct its worship;
therefore, the glorious eight-syllabled lore is indeed the supreme Śrīvidyā.
This alone is the supreme bestower of great siddhis,
existing even within the Vedāntas and the Vedas as a most wondrous secret.
O beloved, listen with focused attention to the majesty of Lalitā:
having risen during the Brāhma-muhūrta, [one should meditate upon] one's own Guru in the Brahma-randhra.
The all-pervading Lord, whose nature is Śiva, possesses the hands of granting boons and fearlessness; he has the luster of pure crystal and is accompanied by his own power, Kṛttivāsas.
Having recollected [the Guru] and meditated upon oneself as being bathed by the streams of nectar flowing from his pair of feet, one should then contemplate the sandals of the Ācārya.
Then one should meditate upon the supreme consciousness, blazing from the base (mūlādhāra) up to the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra),
having the form of light and possessing the brilliance of a thousand rising sapphires.
Having first caused him to recite the Brahma-vidyā, which is a garland of rays of the Blessed One, his body was rendered aged even by that mass of her splendor.
O Daughter of the Mountain, having recollected Traipurī and the garland of rays, and having remembered the twelvefold Vidyā of Śrī, which bestows all perfections. (11)
Having gone outside, one should then perform the ritual dismissal (visarjana) starting from the base;
having carefully performed the washing of the face and other such rites, one should proceed with the *campa*.

Having restrained the breaths, made a formal resolve, and bathed in a river with a composed mind, one should offer three handfuls of water toward the further shore while reciting the root mantra over one's head.
Having drunk the water consecrated with the root-mantra three times, and thereafter having sipped it three times with the root-mantra, one becomes composed of food (anna) for Lalitā.
Having cleansed himself in three ways and wrapped his lower garment around him, he should perform the daily twilight ritual (nitya-sandhyā) and then utter: "Drāṃ Hrīṃ Drāṃ Saḥ. || 15 ||
One should utter "to Mārtāṇḍabhairava," followed by "to the Radiant One" (prakāśāya),
then "endowed with devotion and so forth," and finally pronounce the wife of Fire (svāhā).
With this Ravigāyatrī, one should offer three oblations to Savitṛ;
then, having meditated with reverence upon the Śrīcakra within the solar orb— 17.
O beautiful lady, having uttered the word *vāgbhava-bīja*, one should then utter the word *vidmahe*; after that, the *kāmarāja* [bīja]. (18)
Then, after reciting the word *pīṭhakāmini* and *dhīmahi*, one should utter the seed-syllable of Śakti, followed by *tannaḥ klinne pracodayāt*. (19)
With this [verse], one should offer the *arghya* three times to the goddess Lalitā;
then, [one should worship] the pair of lotus feet of the Preceptor, which grant all desires.
Having meditated upon the Brahman in the thousand-petaled aperture (sahasrāra) and having bowed again and again,
one should first recite the Kumārī-mantra according to one's capacity, O Daughter of the Mountain King.
Then, having recollected Annapūrṇā and the Aśvāsanā-vidyā,
one should subsequently recollect the sandals (pādukā) of the root preceptor, which bestow spiritual accomplishment.
Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, is remembered as the family preceptor of Sāmī-vidyā;
he alone is the Lord Ācārya, the blissful master of Being-Consciousness-Bliss (Saccidānanda). || 23 ||
If one recites the Śrīvidyā continuously without first having recited its pādukā-mantra, no accomplishment shall arise for him even in a hundred crores of kalpas. (24)
Remembering the sandals of that Lord who is directly the son of Daśaratha, the husband of Jānakī, and the master of yoga, one should daily recite the Śrīvidyā mantra. || 25 ||
Seated properly on a seat, having restrained the breath and controlled his speech,
one who is firm in his vow should first perform the ritual manual (kalpa) for the worship of Śrīvidyā.
The sage of this [mantra] is said to be Dakṣiṇāmūrti, the Lord;
they call the meter Pāḍu, and the deity is the supreme, consisting of consciousness.
She who is called Śrī Mahātripurā is the beautiful Supreme Deity.
Lalitā is the venerable Great Goddess, whose nature consists of the form of Lakṣmī. || 28 ||
The goddess Maheśvarī is declared to be the mother of the entire world. || 31 ||
The first seed-syllable, Vāgbhava, consisting of the three Vedas, has been declared. || 29 ||
The primordial power, the fragment of power, and power itself are called the glories of Śrī.
Kāmādya, Kāmarāja, and Kīlaka are thus proclaimed.
The application (viniyoga) is declared for the pleasure of the illustrious Goddess Lalitā;
then, with the [mantras] of Śrīkaṇṭha and Ananta, it is repeated twice over the fingers.
One should place [the fingers] on Śivā, beginning from the middle finger and ending at the palm;
this is declared to be the application (viniyoga) for the propitiation of the goddess Lalitā, whose essence is the Śrīvidyā.
[The application is likewise prescribed] for the mantras of the Śrīcakra, for Vāṅmāyā, and for Kamalā. (32)
One should place the Ācārya in the maṇḍala and perform worship as well;
one should perform the placement of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa) by repeating the Kumārikā mantra twice.
Thereafter, one should perform the placement of the internal and external Mātṛkās;
then, with undistracted mind, one should continuously perform the placement of the eight maidens beginning with Vaśinī.
Having uttered the two syllables "tā-raṃ," then the sixteenth vowel [au] followed by the sky [kha], one should utter the final part situated on the earth [bha], conjoined with the left ear [u]. (35)
O lady of excellent hips, having uttered the seed-syllable of Vaśinī joined with the bindu, one should then utter the word "Vaśinī. || 36 ||
Or else, one should place the word "Vāgdevī" followed by the fourth [vowel] and joined with "Hṛdaya";
having assigned this to the head, one should then utter the group of letters.

Then [the mantra] for Kāmeśvarī, the mistress of the abode of the world of Brahman; then the word for Vagdevatā; and afterwards the word for Hṛdagdevatā, ending in the dative case and followed by "namaḥ. || 38 ||
Having placed the [first] group on the forehead, one should then utter [the mantra] which has ascended to the plane of Māta, joined with the letter *vidru* (va) and the eye (*ī*). (39)
One should place "Modinī Vāgdevatāyai namaḥ" at the center of the eyebrows.
[Then one should place] the letter Ṭa, along with the syllable Dha, mounted upon the Earth (Va), and conjoined with the sixth vowel (Ū), representing Vāyu.
One should then place "vimalā-vāgdevatāyai namaḥ" on the throat; furthermore, one should place the *tavarga* (the dental class of consonants) ending with *cakravākī* as mounted upon Vaikuṇṭha.
Then the left eye together with the letter *vi*, followed by the word "aruṇā," then the word for the Goddess of Speech (*vāgdevatā*) ending in the dative case and joined with "namaḥ. (42)
Having placed the supreme *yavagaṃ* [mantra] in the heart, one should place the victorious water-deity, "Oṃ, salutation to the deity of water," at the navel. 43.

Then [the mantra] beginning with the letter *ya*, joined with the four vowels, endowed with the *yuta* and *indra* [syllables], together with *saviṭharuvākarṇa*, followed by the word *sarveśvara*. (44)
Afterwards, having placed the word for the Goddess of Speech (Vāgdevatā) in the dative case followed by the syllable *oṃ* upon the *liṅga*, one should place the seed-syllable *śakrādi-ṣaṭka-kṣmī*.
One should then place the Kaulinī Speech-Goddess at the root with the mantra "namo";
this aforementioned placement of the eight goddesses beginning with Vaśinī bestows all perfections.
By means of this yoga of ritual placement (nyāsa), one who remains diligent for a year shall attain perfection of speech and become a repository of all riches.
Then, on the two breasts, at the base of the navel, in the heart, and also in the three eyes;
then on the two ears, the face, and the pair of arms.
Having placed the syllables preceded by the seed-mantras and ending with "namaḥ" on the back and the pair of knees,
and having placed the final syllable of the root-vidyā on the anus, one becomes directly composed of Brahman.
In the ritual of placement (nyāsa) or in the worship of Vakrā,
all the mātrās should be uttered together with the supreme Vāṇī for the sake of attaining the state of the deity.
Having performed the placement (nyāsa) of the two *ghātṛkās* and the eight deities of speech (*vāgdevatā*),
and having performed the placement of the syllables of the root-mantra (*mūlavidyā*), the Lord of the World appeared in person.
The worshiper of the Supreme Brahman may take the form of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, or Rudra;
having performed the sixteen-fold assignment (ṣoḍhānyāsa), he should then perform the assignment of the ears (śrotranyāsa).
Whether one has performed [the ritual] or not, one should meditate upon the supreme Goddess whose form is consciousness;
the installation of the sixteen-fold Śrīcakra is difficult to obtain within the three worlds. (53)
Having performed this even within a month, one undoubtedly becomes the embodiment of Brahman;
this daily rite, when recited, bestows the attainment of all fruits. (54)
Having first performed these three daily nyāsas at the beginning of the day and having recited [the mantra], one passes this night as the manifest embodiment of the Supreme Brahman. (55)
One who has directly assumed the form of Śiva and Viṣṇu shall become the Supreme Lord himself.
Having thus performed the entire network of ritual placements (nyāsa) according to the rules day after day, [one attains this state].
Then one should meditate upon the goddess Śrī, the most excellent, who consists of the three Vedas and is composed of light;
she is like a lotus, with a complexion as ruddy as the rays of the rising sun.
Resembling the hibiscus flower, comparable to the pomegranate blossom,
resembling a ruby, and like the essence of saffron.
Adorned with a shimmering crest-jewel and a network of tinkling bells, she possesses beautiful,
curly locks that rival the swarm of bees.
Her lotus-like face was like the rising sun,
and the curved forehead-plate upon her brow was slightly furrowed with a frown.
The Supreme Goddess, whose creeper-like eyebrows are shaped like the Pināka bow,
whose eyes are swayed by the playful movement of blissful joy and delight.
Wearing a shimmering peacock feather with its tail, adorned with a resplendent golden crest and earrings that conquered the nectar of the serpent’s coils; || 61 ||
Her eyebrows are well-defined like a painted thread, her nose is perfectly straight,
and her lips have the luster of copper, coral, and the bimba fruit— serving as the means for attaining the nectar of redness.
Her tongue, which speaks sweetly, shines with teeth resembling pomegranate seeds; glowing red, it illuminates the world.
She surpassed the sweetness of smiles with her own sweetness; she was an ocean of aesthetic flavor (rasa), endowed with incomparable virtues, and graced by the region of her chin.
The Great Goddess Kaṃbugrīvā has arms as graceful as lotus stalks,
and her lotus-like hands are as delicate as the petals of a red lotus.
The surface of her chest was overspread by the moonlight of the nails of her lotus-like hands;
she was adorned with a string of pearl necklaces and possessed full, elevated breasts.
Adorned in the middle with three folds, beautifully graced by ten [lines],
she was embellished with a navel shaped like a beautiful whirlpool.
Her hips were adorned with a girdle inlaid with priceless gems;
she wore excellent garments as fine as the hair of a young elephant.
The Sovereign Lady possesses thighs as delicate as the graceful trunk of a plantain tree,
and she is adorned with a pair of shanks resembling the plantain stems of the God of Love.
Her ankles were hidden, her two feet were joined at the foreparts, and her heels were well-concealed; her toes were slender and long, and they shone with nails as beautiful as the moon.
Her lotus feet were rubbed by the crest-jewels of Brahmā and Viṣṇu;
her continuous radiance, resembling hundreds of moons, was filled with smiles.
She is red as the Lauhitya river, vermilion, and the Japā flower, possessing the hue of a pomegranate;
she is clothed in red garments, and her hands hold a noose and a goad.
Seated upon a red lotus, adorned with jewel ornaments, four-armed and three-eyed, she holds a bow and an arrow. (73)
Her mouth was filled with betel-leaf mixed with pieces of camphor,
and her face was reddened by the intense saffron of great musk.
Adorned with all manner of horns, poisons, and flesh as her ornaments,
she brings joy to the world and causes delight to the eyes.
She who attracts the world, she who creates the world, she who possesses form;
the Goddess who consists of all mantras, beautiful with every auspicious fortune. (76)
I salute her who consists of all prosperity, who is eternal, who bestows supreme bliss, and who holds a noose, a goad, the gesture of granting boons, and a bow in her hands.
The Supreme Goddess, seated upon a lotus, is richly adorned with a peaceful appearance and red limbs;
she possesses the luster of the orb of the rising sun and has four arms and three eyes. (78)
Holding a noose, a goad, an arrow, and a bow, she takes refuge in Śiva.

O Mother who sustains the world, salutations to you who have four arms, who are adorned with a digit of the moon, whose high breasts are red with the hue of saffron, and who hold in your hands a lotus, a sugarcane bow, a goad, a noose, and arrows.
One should meditate upon Bhavānī as being dawn-red, her eyes rippling with compassion, holding a noose, a goad, a lotus, an arrow, and a bow,
surrounded by rays of light like the sun itself.
Seated upon a golden lotus in the midst of a Kadamba forest, dwelling within a six-petaled lotus, she is the lightning of eternal perfection;
she possesses the luster of two uplifted breasts, bears the pure moon as her crest-jewel, and is the consort of the three-eyed Lord.
I take refuge in Tripurasundarī. || 82 ||

In the rite of recitation, he [visualizes her] smeared with saffron paste, adorned with *amlaka* fruit and *cūṅka*, and fragrant with musk; her eyes glancing with gentle smiles, accompanied by her sister Kuśā; enchanting all people, radiant with red garlands and ornaments, and shining with the brilliance of the *japā* flower.
I remember Ambikā. || 83 ||
I bow to Mahātripurasundarī, who holds a sugarcane, a bow, flowers, a noose, and a goad, and who resembles the rising sun. 84.
I worship her who dwells in the midst of the jewel-pavilion in the Sudhāccaukalpaka garden, through union with the mass of the bliss of nectar. 85.
Having thus meditated upon Mātṛkā, Lakṣmī, and Mātṛpurasundarī,
and having performed the *yava* and *oṃ-cāra* rites, one should then display the ten mudrās.
One should recite the mantra a thousand times; then, one should recite it five hundred times daily, or even one hundred and thirty-two times.
Having attained great success through one hundred and eight recitations, one becomes truly composed of the vow itself.

In a temple of Śiva where the western door is present, or in a shrine containing a liṅga, a bull, or an empty space; or likewise in a temple of Nārāyaṇa, or on a mountain, or by a fire—being pure [one should perform the rite]. || 88 ||
Or, in the presence of the teacher, one should recite [the mantra] three hundred thousand times for the sake of prosperity.
The wise one should offer libations ten times over with *kiṃśuka* flowers soaked in clarified butter. || 89 ||
One should offer one-tenth of that amount into the fire with oblations mixed with the three sweets;
then, having offered a great quantity of grain at the lotus feet of the preceptor, [one should proceed].
Yoked with four bulls and accompanied by many sacrificial fees, she bestows the fruit of Śrīvidyā upon one who gives a pair of earrings. 91.
Having attained great perfection, you shall become a treasury of all good fortune;
or else, when the eclipse of the sun or the moon occurs, [you shall attain it].
Having consumed food for only three days and having recited the mantra one thousand and twenty times,
he should, with a concentrated mind, bathe in a river at the time of touching that [object].
With water that has washed the pair of the teacher’s feet, [the offering should be made] in the presence of the teacher, into the auspicious fire duly consecrated according to the rules. (94)
With a concentrated mind, one should offer one thousand three hundred oblations with devotion,
using clarified butter mixed with honey and the three sweets, along with *kiṃśuka* flowers.
Alternatively, one should offer oblations into the fire through recitation and other rites;
having offered the oblation of the breath of Brahmā, one should respectfully pay homage to the fire. (96)
And having prostrated with eight limbs before the pair of the teacher’s feet,
[he offered] sixty gold coins and a pair of auspicious golden earrings.
Having placed divine jewels upon the ears of the Ācārya,
and having given him the entire earth together with a complete sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), || 98 ||
One attains success in a lore that is difficult even for the gods to obtain;
it is a treasure-trove of all sciences and the foundation of all prosperity. (99)
Having attained great prosperity accompanied by sons, grandsons, and others,
that leader, the lord of the world, [attained] the eight supernatural powers beginning with *aṇiman*.
Having become Virāyu, Vijaya, Sarvajña, Subhagā, and Sukhī, she resided as the wife of the Ācārya, Śrībuddhi, adorned with ornaments and other fineries. (101)
The wise one must certainly perform worship for the sake of attaining success in the *puraścaraṇa*;
having thus completed the *puraścaryā* for Lalitā, O my beloved. (102)
Resembling Kandarpa in splendor and equal to the Giver of Wealth (Kubera) in fortune,
he eventually attained supreme absorption in the intellect, endowed with profound self-control.
[Thus ends the third chapter in the latter portion of the Vedārthasaṃgraha, within the illustrious Anuttarabrahmatattvarahasya Dāśarathīya Tantra. || 3 ||
The venerable Dakṣiṇāmūrti said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the supreme sādhana of Śrī, by performing which even an ordinary man becomes a unique treasury of good fortune and prosperity. (1)
By this procedure, the practitioner recites day by day the fifteen-syllable Lalitā-vidyā of Śrī.
Having respectfully worshipped the wheel three hundred times according to the rule, and having bathed and honored the wheel— or indeed the central wheel— [one should proceed].
Or, when he has not arrived in this land, agitation arises in the world;
their minds are scorched by the intense heat of the blazing fire of desire. (4)
With their hearts concealed by mantras, the women approached from afar with their hips throbbing according to the manner of the *pililikā* and other such gestures.
O Great Goddess, by the sight of that, all women are born;
O my beloved, having performed even a single *puraścaryā* rite, she becomes dear to me.
Having recited the fifteen-syllable mantra of Śrī three hundred times with fixed concentration,
one should worship either the central wheel or the sacrificial fire, Jātavedas.
Having heard it once with the Raśmi-mantras, and thereafter with the Nityā-mantras, and having heard it once with the Guru-mantras, one should hear it twenty-eight times with the Śrī-mantras.
For the practitioner who constantly practices in this manner on the surface of the earth, his body becomes like that of Kandarpa, free from all impurity.
Even those aged eighty years remain perpetually youthful;
their heads are covered by crowns adorned with the nine precious gems.
Or those lords of men, tormented by the blazing fire of desire and arrogant with the pride of their beauty, serve them even while they are bestowing [favors]. || 11 ||
Then many women also came there for the sake of sport; they brought with them all kinds of divine splendors as well as human riches. (12)
Even the perfections of Kauberī reside constantly within him;
though he may be dull, slow-witted, or even devoid of wisdom. (13)
Through the grace of the teacher, one becomes the manifest treasury of all knowledge;
the abundance of his speech unfolds like the flow of the Ganges.
He who receives this grace shall become a treasury of knowledge;
he becomes like Vyāsa and Vālmīki, a true possessor of Sarasvatī.
He obtains rare enjoyments, both divine and human;
moreover, his lineage prospers as long as he worships Caṇḍatāraka.
Having attained long life and great health, one becomes like one free from pride;
he brings the three worlds under his control for as long as he lives—of this there is no doubt. (17)
At the end of the body, one goes to the supreme abode, which is difficult even for the gods to attain;
when this *kṣamātreya* is recited, the Lord of Beings (*bhūteśvara*) is agitated.
If even beautiful young women, intoxicated with passion and possessing eyes like those of a doe, do not slightly disturb the mind of the practitioner, [then he has attained success]. 19.
Then all the Naga maidens in Patala were agitated;
yet even for them, he did not cause even the slightest agitation.
Then the celestial women dwelling in heaven fled,
as did the beautiful and captivating daughters of the Gandharvas and Kinnaras.
Having thus recited it one hundred thousand times with a steady mind, the practitioner agitates the Mistress of the Universe; he attains oneness with all that is moving and unmoving.
Having performed three hundred thousand recitations, he fashioned a pair of excellent divine earrings made of sixty gems, joined with celestial jewels.
Having given a field abounding in grain to the ears of the preceptor,
and having bestowed the earth accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā), he then departed.
The teacher’s wife should present these ornaments, including earrings;
having given a pair of fine garments, whether made of linen or cotton. (25)
He will certainly attain great supernatural power, difficult even for the gods to obtain;
there is no doubt. I speak the truth, the absolute truth. (26)

Alternatively, having performed the preliminary rite (puraścaryā) as previously described during the lunar month of Āśvina, and having attained great perfection, one shall become a treasury of all good fortune. || 27 ||
Now, O beloved, I shall fully declare another unsurpassed vow, which has been taught in all the scriptures of all the gods. (28)
It is the destroyer of the multitude of great sins, the abode of prosperity, the immediate bestower of all accomplishments, and the grantor of the perfection of great good fortune. (29)
In the month of Āśvina, there is a very great vow called Navarātra;
in Caitra as well, there is a most excellent vow known as Navarātra. (30)
Having performed the preliminary rites (puraścaryā) for that vow, the preeminent practitioner attains unsurpassed perfection and is honored even by the gods.
Beginning from the first day of the lunar fortnight until the ninth,
the Navarātra vow is proclaimed as the destroyer of sin today, bestowing the fulfillment of all desired objects.
O beloved, on the day of the Pratipad, having prostrated like a staff with all eight limbs before the pair of feet of the teacher, and preceded by his permission—
Having bathed in the morning, the self-possessed one, and having performed the daily twilight worship (saṃdhyā),
he bowed at the pair of feet of the teacher in the auspicious aperture of Brahman (brahmabila).
Having sat properly upon his seat, being restrained in his vows, he should first offer oblations twenty-eight times— or four times— to the Kumārīs and the other Manūs.
Having performed the threefold breath control (prāṇāyāma), one should then, preceded by a formal resolve (saṃkalpa),
perform the recitation of the Thousand-Name [Hymn] during the nine nights according to the prescribed number.
Having performed the previously mentioned nyāsas, meditated upon the glory of the Blessed One,
and recited the mantra together with all its syllables, one should worship the wheel.
Having offered oblations once with the *raśmi* mantras and once with the eternal *guru* mantras,
one should daily offer one hundred and eight oblations into the fire with the *Śrīvidyā*.
One should always worship an odd number of married women, beginning with one; or, O beloved, one may always worship a single married woman here.
Eating only once a day, always adorned with ornaments, devoted to chewing betel-leaf, and constantly wearing sacred ash while performing worship; ||| 40 ||
When the Mahānavamī has arrived, one should, keeping the command of the preceptor foremost,
shake [the vessel] once with the Raśmi-mantras over the fire consecrated according to the rules.
Having offered the daily oblations with heavy [substances], thereafter, he should offer only once more with *kiṃśuka* flowers mixed with sacrificial wood, or with lotuses soaked in clarified butter.
With blue lotuses, or with various flowers, or with pure ghee alone;
or else with milk-rice (pāyasa) accompanied by honey and clarified butter in the fire.
Having offered one thousand three hundred oblations mixed with sesame and bilva fruits with the Śrīvidyā mantra, and one hundred and eight oblations with the Lakṣmīvidyā mantra; || 44 ||
Then, one should offer one hundred and eight oblations with the mantra of Prasannalakṣmī, followed by the mantra of Triśakti, and subsequently with the mantra of Sāmrājyalakṣmī.
Then, having offered one hundred and eight oblations with the glorious eight-syllable mantra,
and having performed the homa through recitation and other rites, he should perform the oblation with the realization that it is an offering unto Brahman.
Having circumambulated and paid homage to the blazing fire,
he respectfully prostrated himself with all eight limbs before the pair of feet of his own teacher.
Having fashioned a pair of earrings weighing two karṣas of gold, adorned with sixty marks or endowed with divine jewels. || 48 ||
Having given much [wealth] to the two ears of the preceptor, one should present it to the preceptor along with abundant sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā). || 49 ||
Having respectfully given a pair of cows along with a calf and a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā),
one should then offer a fine silk garment or a very delicate cloth.
Having meditated with the intellect upon the beloved of the Ācārya as the manifest Śrī Lalitā herself, [adorned] with earrings, golden cintāmaṇi gems, and other most beautiful ornaments; ||51||
Having worshipped with perfumes and other offerings, one should worship the Discus along with its ancillaries;
even by a poor person who is unable [to provide more], five gold coins must certainly be offered.
O Daughter of the Mountain, one should give a pair of sandals to the feet of the preceptor,
or one should offer a gold coin or fine gold to the preceptor’s wife.
Then, one should gratify the auspicious married women with desirable gifts, such as sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) and other offerings;
having thus performed the preparatory rite (puraścaryā) during the auspicious Navarātra vow, [one proceeds].
He will certainly attain great accomplishment, there is no doubt;
[using] a silver vessel measuring two palas, or indeed six palas. (55)
Having prostrated before the two lotus feet of the preceptor,
he who offers the sacrificial materials is indeed the Supreme Lord himself.
Even those belonging to that lineage, numbering hundreds of thousands,
though existing in the world of Brahmā, are submerged in the ocean of hell.
The merit of one who offers sacrificial materials at the pair of feet of the preceptor on the Mahānavamī day cannot be described.
By him a hundred horse-sacrifices have been performed with complete sacrificial fees;
by him a thousand Tulāpuruṣa gifts have been made—of this there is no doubt. (59)
On the day of the new moon, by giving wealth for the sake of a Śrotriya’s marriage—who is a dwelling place of poverty—one obtains the fruit of donating a thousand cows. || 60 ||
As many as are the particles of dust on the earth, and as many as are the drops of rain, for so many thousands of hundreds of kulas shall he be honored.
Accompanied by a thousand divine maidens, he rejoices in Vaikuṇṭha;
indeed, the gift of land together with a pair of earrings [is the cause].
On the Mahānavamī day, the rite should be performed accompanied by its constituent parts and ritual fees;
the giving of ornaments to the preceptor’s wife is traditionally recorded as mandatory.
O beloved, having performed this *puraścaryā* during the *navarātra* vow,
one obtains the fruit of a hundred *puraścaryās*, which bestows all spiritual perfections (*siddhis*).
By giving away the earth consisting of the seven continents, filled with wealth, jewels,
and grain, one obtains that same fruit by [offering it] at the two feet of one's own teacher.
By giving the earth on the Mahānavamī day, one obtains that fruit;
or else, one should offer a substance as a substitute for the earth to the preceptor.
Accompanied by the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) and provided with a pair of earrings,
the substance representing the earth is declared to be one hundred niṣkas.
Or half of that, or half of that again, or even half of that half; O Daughter of the Mountain, the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) should likewise consist of appropriate material wealth.
O Teacher, by placing a pair of earrings upon the two ears, one attains prosperity equal to that of Mahendra; of this there is no doubt. (69)
Having given ornaments and other gifts to the teacher’s wife by Śrībudhā,
he becomes fortunate, handsome, eloquent, and the son of Fortune.
Having thus performed the preliminary rite during the nine nights, O my beloved, one becomes a perfected being (siddha) who is manifestly composed of Brahman; of this there is no doubt.
One shall indeed obtain eternal, unshakable prosperity abounding in wealth, as well as a hundredfold beauty and fortune that brings auspiciousness to the world. (72)
Having attained mastery over all branches of knowledge,
he lives for a long time like a living being, remaining free from passion toward worldly objects.
O beloved, this god is worshipped by the Siddhas, yogis, and sages,
and he is prayed to day and night by celestial maidens.
He who is devoted to the worship of the Śrīcakra, he who is intent on the recitation of the Śrīvidyā—he alone is I, of this there is no doubt; he indeed is Hari, the Infallible One. 75.
He alone is liberated, he alone is Brahmā, and he alone is the lord of the world, whose firm devotion to Śrīvidyā is constant. (76)
He is the very image of Brahmā, he is indeed the Blessed Lord Hari;
such is the perfection of knowledge attained through the Navarātra vow.
O Dear One, one attains success through a hundred *puraścaryās*, even [if one has committed the offense of] reviling one's own father or one's guru. (78)
He alone should be punished; otherwise, he would partake in the sin.
By hearing the censure of the teacher, he becomes a partaker of the deity’s curse.
Without hesitation, one should punish the person who reviles his father, mother, brother, husband, son, or teacher.
"O beloved, one should proceed while covering the ears, or otherwise go elsewhere if unable;
having thus performed the preliminary rite (puraścaryā), one should recite [the mantra] a thousand times every day. (81)
Having performed the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) every year,
the practitioner should daily recite [the mantra] one thousand times, or three hundred, or four hundred times.
By seeing [this], one makes even Vāgīśa dull-witted and slow-minded;
by sight alone, one makes even the Lord of Fortune (Kubera) possessed of poverty. 83.
Even by merely gazing at women, even those divine and captivating, he draws them to himself;
and without even such a gaze, he swiftly destroys fevers and other terrible diseases.
By his mere glance, he destroys poison, whether stationary or mobile;
having become a perfected master (siddha) throughout the three worlds, he possesses the power of death at will everywhere. 85.
"He wanders as the leader of the eight supernatural powers, beginning with *aṇimā*";
thus it issued from the lotus-like mouth of the illustrious Lord of Jānakī. (86)
O beloved, this most secret teaching has been declared by me to you.
Beyond this, O Goddess, what more do you wish to hear? (87)

[Thus ends the fourth chapter in the *Śrīmadanuttarabrahmatattvarahasya*, the *Dāśarathīya Tantra*, which is a compendium of the essential meaning of the Vedas, in its latter portion, titled *Saubhāgyavidyodaya*.]
The Goddess said:

O Maheśa, O omniscient one, O treasure-house of compassion, I wish to hear the procedure for the sixteen-fold placement (ṣoḍhānyāsa) as well as the ritual for the placement of the wheels (cakranyāsa). || 1 ||
"O Lord, [please explain] the extraction of the *cakra* as well as the worship of the *cakra* along with its ancillaries.
Śrī Dakṣiṇāmūrti said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall explain that which you ask of me.
I shall tell you of a merit even more secret than those [previously mentioned]:
the Guru’s sandals, O Maya, without knowing the conduct of the observance (samayācāra). III.
In that [state] wherein this [practice] proceeds for the destruction of the gods,
it is the cause for the attainment of identity with Brahman, bestowing both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
I shall now tell you the secret convention of worship regarding honey;
by the mere knowledge of which one becomes liberated while living and dies [as such].
In that regard, the eternally manifest worship is determined to have three divisions:
the supreme (parā), O Gaurī, the intermediate (aparā), and the third is the supreme-supreme (parāparā).
The first state exists in duality; it moves toward all things.
But the second is indeed the supreme worship, which is always performed by me.
O Goddess, the third [state] consists of pure knowledge and is the primary source;
she is declared to be the supreme and most excellent. Now hear the procedure.

And a supreme worship of great renown is always performed for her; O Goddess, within that *vāgbhava* [syllable], one should nourish the sandals of the Guru, which consists of pure knowledge and is the third, the primary and most excellent power (*parā*). Now hear the procedure. || 8 ||
And upon the great lotus petal, one should place the Guru’s sandals,
which consist of the essence born from that [mantra], nourishing and raining down supreme nectar.
Having reflected upon the intoxication of the contemplation of supreme non-duality,
he did not look beyond the interior of the fire for the light of all-knowing wisdom.
Averse to conceptualization and volition, always inward-turned, with the contraction [of the mind] shattered by the waves of consciousness, you are exceedingly beautiful. (11)
Having performed self-worship with substances that gratify the senses,
I shall now perform the ritual placement (nyāsa), preceded by the sixfold placement (ṣoḍhānyāsa).

The first is the placement of the fingers; the second is that which consists of six counts; the third is called the internal and external placement of the Mātṛkā—thus the ritual placement (nyāsa) is described.
The fourth is the nyāsa of the eight goddesses of speech, which bestows all accomplishments;
the fifth is the nyāsa of the syllables of the root-vidyā, which grants the fruits [of practice]. || 14 ||
This fivefold nyāsa must certainly be performed on the day;
or else, having performed the nyāsa of the six wheels and so forth, it may be done every single day.
Having performed the fivefold assignment (nyāsa), one should always recite the root mantra.
I shall now describe the sixfold assignment (ṣoḍhānyāsa), which bestows the fruit of the nature of Brahman. (16)
One should perform the sixfold ritual placement (ṣoḍhānyāsa), which yields the fruit of all merit and destroys every sin, by means of which one becomes a leader of the universe. || 17 ||
Virāṭ, whose nature is that of the individual soul (vaśyātman), is Śiva himself; of this there is no doubt.
The first assignment (nyāsa) is by means of the Gaṇeśas, while the second is considered to be by means of the Tumburu [Gaṇas]. (18)
The third [placement] is with the net of rays, the fourth with the yoginīs, the fifth placement is with the zodiac signs, and the sixth is said to be with the sacred seats (pīṭhas). || 19 ||
This sixfold deposition (ṣoḍhānyāsa) has been proclaimed as invincible by all;
thus, one whose limbs are established through this [deposition] becomes worthy of worship by all yoginīs.
In this world, no one other than a father or mother is worthy of worship among all people;
he alone is the one to be honored by all, for he himself is the Supreme Lord.
If this practitioner bows down to anyone who is devoid of the sixfold deposition (ṣoḍhānyāsa), he shall soon meet with death and fall into hell. || 22 ||
Having uttered "Salutation to the Gurus," one should bow down constantly in all circumstances;
having meditated upon the pair of feet of the Teacher, one should always perform prostration. (23)
And I shall now describe the method of the sixfold deposition (*ṣoḍhānyāsa*),
by the mere hearing of which all perfections (*siddhis*) arise for one who is pure.
Resembling the rising sun, with the faces of elephants and three eyes,
they held nooses and goads that inspired fear, and were endowed with spears.
One should perform the Mātṛkā-nyāsa according to the rules upon the body for the sake of prosperity;
likewise, Vighneśvara with Śrī, and Vighnarāja with Hrī.
Likewise, Vināyaka is endowed with contentment and peace, being most auspicious;
he is joined with the removal of obstacles and the destruction of impediments, as is Sarasvatī.
He is endowed with the invocation of the Lord of Obstacles (Vighnarāja), and he is the leader of various forms of wisdom;
he is the Single-Tusked One (Ekadanta) and the Radiant One (Cakrānti), and he is united with the Wielder of the Trident (Aḍidanta) and the Desirous One (Kāmin).
O Dear One, [the faces] are Gajavaktra, Agnodinī, as well as Nirañjanajaṭha, Kapardabhṛt, Tīvra, and Dīrghavaktra. (29)
Then follows Jvālinī along with Manthāna and Amarṣaṇa; thereafter Pṛṣadhvaja together with Subhagā and Gaṇanātha.
Kāmarūpiṇikā with Pañcagajendra joined by Śubhrayā;
Sūrya and Karṇa, Jayinī accompanied by Trinetra and Satyā. || 31 ||
Then there are Laṃbodara, Vighneśa, Mahānanda, Surūpiṇī, Caturmūrti, Kāmadā, and Sadāśiva. (32)
Then there are Madavihvalalā, Āmodavikaṭā, Durmada, Ghūrṇī, Sumukhā, and Bhūtimat. (33)
Pramoda, likewise Bhūmi, Ekajaṭā, Satī, Dvijihva joined with Caramā, Śūra, and Mānuṣī. (34)
Then Vīreṇā, Sahitā, Śailajā, Karabhā, Ṣaṇmukhī, Vivarṇā, Varadā, and Bhrukuṭīlatā [followed]. (35)
Likewise Vāmadeva, Lajjā, Vakratuṇḍa, Niśā,
and thereafter Dīrghaghoṇānvitā or Viraṇḍā [worship] the wielder of the bow.
Senānī is joined with Yāminī; Agni is conjoined with Atri;
Mata is joined with Candrikā; and Vimala is [conjoined] with Śaśiprabhā. (37)
He was mounted on a rutting elephant, wore matted hair, and had restless eyes;
he was shaven-headed, carried a staff behind him, and was possessed by a terrible fear.
Vaṇya and Subhaga, Vṛṣaketu and Śivā, Bhakṣyapriya and Durgā, Meghanāda and Kālikā. (39)
Gaṇeśa and Kālakujā are the two Gaṇas who remove obstacles;
O Goddess, O beloved, one should place these [deities] according to the letters of the Mātṛkā.
Now I shall describe the letters of the Mātṛkā in their proper order:
red, white, likewise red, dark-blue, yellow, and pale-white. (40)
One should meditate on [the attendants] as smoke-colored, black, and smoky; they are the foremost among the Dravidas, able to assume any form at will, and adorned with all ornaments. (41)
Having assigned the Sun to the heart with the vowels,
and then the Moon with the *ka*-group, one should assign Mars to the middle of the ears with the *ca*-group and to the three eyes.
One should place Budha in the heart with the *ṭa*-group of consonants, Bṛhaspati with the *ta*-group;
O Goddess of Gods, one should place Bhṛgu in the throat with the *pa*-group.

Then, O fair-faced one, one should place the Moon with the labial class (pavarga) at the navel, Rāhu with the ka-group (kavarga) in the mouth, and Ketu with the two lakṣas (the sibilants and ha) in the anus; thus [it is done].
Then one should perform the placement (nyāsa) of the host of constellations, which bestows happiness;
they resemble the blazing fire of time (kālāgni) and are adorned with all ornaments. 45.
Nati, Pāṇi, Aśvinī, and Mukhyā have hands that grant boons and protection;
likewise, there are pairs, pairs, pairs, pairs, and pairs, along with Rohiṇī.
In this manner, one by one, each pair is released at the end of the sixth [breath]:
after the two eyes, then the left and right ears. || 47 ||
One should place [the syllables] on the two shoulders, the left throat, and the right throat in sequence;
having thus assigned them up to the end of the flowers, one should then assign Sāryaka with the two letters of the sky (kha) and the ocean (ga).
On the right shoulder, with the two syllables *dhaṃ*, there is the second joint;
on the right elbow, one should place *pūrvāphalgunī* preceded by *icchaja*.
O Dear One, one should place Uttarā-phalgunī on the left elbow;
then, one should place the hand situated in the syllables *jha* and *ña* upon the right wrist.
O Dear One, one should place Svātī, joined with the syllable *kā*, on the left wrist at the base of the thumb;
one should then place it on the right hand.
One should place Viśākhā, conjoined with the letter *ḍha*, on the left hand;
likewise, O Pārvatī, one should place Anurādhā, situated in the letters *tha* and *da*, on the navel. (52)
O Dear One, one should place Jyeṣṭhā, joined with the syllable *dhvākāra*, on the right hip;
likewise, O Dear One, one should place the root-mantra of Tapa-yūṣinī on the left hip.
One should place Pūrvāṣāḍhā on the right thigh;
immediately thereafter, one should place Uttarāṣāḍhā on the left thigh.
One should place Śravaṇa, conjoined with the letter *ma*, on the right knee;
one should place Dhaniṣṭhā, situated beyond it, on the left knee.
Then, O Goddess, beloved one, one should place Śatatārā with the letter *la*;
thereafter, one should place Pūrvābhādrapadā located on the right shank.
Having placed [the syllable] *va* established in the *vaśavaṇa* [position], or alternatively, having placed it sequentially on the shanks;
[one should place] the *uttarā-bhādrapadā* star, situated between *ṣa* and *sa*, on the right foot.
Having placed the letter *kṣa* at the beginning of the *visarga*, and the two *visargas* at the end of *ārevatī*,
the Yoginī performs the internal placement (*nyāsa*) upon her left foot.
One should contemplate [the goddesses] as white, black, dark-red, smoke-colored, bright, and yellow;
they have four arms and faces with unblinking eyes, and are adorned with all ornaments. (59)
O Dear One, having uttered the two seed-syllables Ḍāṃ and Ḍīṃ, followed by "ḍākamalāvarayā," enriched with the crescent moon and the nāda in the left ear, one should also say "ḍākinyai namaḥ. (50)
O Dear One, at the end of the vowels, one should utter the two protective words;
one should then place [the mantra] "to the self of the skin" in the region of the throat, in the Viśuddhi [cakra].
In the Kaṭha recension, however, Rākinī consists of the syllables beginning with *kaṃ* and the *yakṣas*, in sequence;
one should speak of them as being joined with the seed-syllable as before, according to the measure of the blood.
One should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) upon the Anāhata [cakra], and then again and again with the letters beginning with 'pha' and ending with 'kha', O Goddess;
likewise, one should place Lākinī and the one whose essence is flesh (Māṃsātmā) upon the Maṇipūraka.
One should place Kākinī with the syllables *vala* in the *khādhimāna* [location] in that same manner;
likewise, Yākinī, whose nature is differentiation (*bheda*), is to be placed with the syllables *vasa*.

One should likewise address the goddess Dakṣā, whose form is unstable and whose seed-syllable is as previously stated; one should place the syllables Ha and Kṣa, situated there, upon the two petals of the Ḍākinī.
O Great Goddess, one should likewise place Yākinī in the Brahma-randhra with the sound "haṃ"; this is the placement (nyāsa) accompanied by the Yoginīs.
One should constantly perform the Rāśinyāsa, which always effects all forms of protection;
one should visualize [the deities] as red, white, yellow, pale, variegated, and black.
One should comfortably arrange Piśaṅga, Piṅgala, Vabhru, Karvura, Asita, and Dhūmala within the four vowels beginning with 'A' on the right side.
One should place a ram on the right ankle; then, with two [verses], a bull on the knees; and then, with the *nivedana* verses, a pair [of twins] on the testicles.
By two [consonants] comes Cancer; by two [consonants] each, the two Aśvinīs and the Shoulder (Revatī);
by the Anusvāra and Visarga comes Leo; and by the Śa-group comes Virgo.
O you who are praised by heroes, one should place [the syllables] on the right and left sides of the head;
likewise, the cord should be placed on the head with the *ka*-group, supported by the letter *la*.
O beloved, one should always worship Vṛścika in the Varṇa-group, likewise in the Arga-group, and likewise in the Skandha-group.
O Dear One, one should likewise place the archer in the belly with the *ṭa*-group;
then, one should place the crocodile in the testicles in due order with the *ta*-group.
Likewise, one should place the pitcher with the labial class [of consonants] upon the left knee;
and with the letter *kṣa*, which belongs to the final class, one should place the fish upon the ankle.
O Goddess, one should again place the seats (pīṭhas) in the locations of the Mātṛkās;
their names shall be told, so listen attentively, O beloved. (72)
Kāmarūpa, Raṇasonaipāla, Pauṇḍravardhana, Varasthira, Kanyākubja, Pūrṇaśaila, and likewise Arbuda. || 73 ||
Āmrātaka, Cairaikāmra, Śrīsnāta, Kāmakroṭaka, Kailāsa, Bhṛgunagara, Kandāra, and Candrapūjaka. || 74 ||
The Śrīpīṭha, the Ekārapīṭha, Tālāghra, and likewise Mālava; Kulūttha, Devakūṭa, Gokarṇa, and Ārukteśvara. (75)
Aṭṭahāsa, Vaviraja, Rājagṛha, Mahāpatha, Kollāpura, Melāpura, Oṃkāra, and Svajayāntika. || 76 ||
Ujjayinī called Avicitra, Kṣīraka, Hastināpura, Uḍḍīśa called Prayāga, and likewise Vilva at Māyāpura. (77)
Jaleśa, the Malaya mountain, Meru the best of mountains, as well as Mahendra, Vāmana, and Hiraṇyapura; || 78 ||
Mahālakṣmī, Puroḍyaṇa, and thereafter Chāyāchatra—these seats (pīṭhas) designated by us have assumed the form of the Mātṛkās. (79)
The sixteenfold deposition (ṣoḍhānyāsa), which bestows the attainment of identity with Brahman, has been described.
Having performed this sixteenfold deposition, one becomes Hari himself, whose nature is the Virāṭ.
One truly becomes the manifest form of Paraśiva; of this there is no doubt.
Having performed this sixteenfold installation (ṣoḍhā-nyāsa), one should perform the installation of the Śrīcakra.
O Dear One, one should first place that which is called the "Nine Yoginīs," by the placement of which the Lord of the World becomes identical with the form of Brahman.

One should place [the syllables] on the two ears, the two *śruvuka* [joints], the two temples, the two eyes, the nose, the two *hṛṃsa* [breasts], the heart, the two elbows, and the two sides of the abdomen.

One should place the three seed-syllables, known as the nine wombs, consisting of the letters ja, ya, and ha, in the feet, the private parts, the two sides, the heart, the two breasts, and the throat.
Having again recited the Vālā mantra, one should place the Śrīvidyā around it;
having again recited the Vālā mantra, one should contemplate the square.
That maiden of the *golaka* lineage should, through yoga, meditate upon the *śrīcakra* within the six *cakras*, at the forehead, and at the hairline (*sīmanta*), all free from impurity.
Thereafter, O Goddess, having meditated upon them in nine locations, one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa);
then, one should place Śrīvidyā in the aperture of Brahmā (the crown of the head), and the Gurus behind it in sequence.
O Goddess, one should place the lunar-day goddesses (tithinityās) there, joined with the mother-syllables (mātṛkās) and the vowels;
by placing them on the mouth during the vowel-parvan, one bestows all good fortune.
Thereafter, the knower of mantras should place [the syllables] beginning with *Prakaṭā* upon the supports (*ādhāra*) and so forth;
this internal arrangement of the Śrīcakra is said to bestow all perfections. (89)
O Dear One, even by performing the practice of the Śrīcakra just once within [the heart], one is honored in the worlds even by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśa, and the others. (90)
O beloved of my life, hear now the external arrangement of the Śrīcakra;
by the mere knowledge of which one becomes the very embodiment of Brahman. 91.
O beloved, listen to the wheel-assignment (cakranyāsa) of Mahānipurasundarī;
it is declared to be the supreme means for accomplishing all siddhis. 92.

One should perform the placement [of mantras] starting with "Obeisance to the line of the eastern side" on the first [side] of the square; then, with the right hand, one should proceed to the back and the front, ending at the tip of the forefinger.

O beautiful one, [one should perform the placement] on the left thigh, the fingers, the feet, the hands, the face, and the sixth [part], as well as the root, the soles, and the back, by way of pervasive expansion.
In these very ten locations, O beautiful one, one should duly install the Siddhas beginning with Aṇimā; and at their conclusion, one should place [the mantra] as pervading the body.
O Beloved, having also placed [the mantra] "Salutation to the central line of the square" in its locations, as well as Brāhmī and the others in the eight [corners].
On the two big toes, on the sides of the chest, on the other side [of the chest], on the left and right knees, and likewise on the two outer shoulders. (97)
Then, one should perform the placement (nyāsa) upon the square with the mantra "Obeisance to the Line" (rekhāyai namaḥ),
applying it pervasively according to the previously mentioned method upon his body.
One should place ten maidens upon his ten bones;
then, one should place the eight goddesses beginning with Brahmāṇī, stationed in their respective locations.
One should deposit [the mantra] at the end of the eyebrows, at the end of the twelve [fingers], and at the big toe;
and also [deposit it] with "Salutation to the sixteen-petaled lotus within that. (100)
One should place Kāmākarṣiṇī and the others upon the petals;
the petals are on the right ear, the back, the shoulder, and the elbow. (101)
The back of the hand, the two thighs, the two ankles, and likewise the two soles of the feet;
starting from the sole of the left foot, these are considered the eight deities in this same manner. (102)
In the meantime, one should also perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) with the mantra "Salutation to the eight-petaled lotus" upon these petals,
on the right temple, and on the collarbone.
One should place the eight Śaktis, beginning with Anekusumā, on the left side at the ankles, the shanks, the thighs, the collarbones, and the temples. || 104 ||
Then, one should also place a fourteen-spoked wheel within that; one should place fourteen Śaktis in its corners.
Sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī is the principal [deity] of that [maṇḍala]; its corners are as previously described.
Lalitā is on the right side, and Dakṣagaṇḍī is in the middle.
O Pārvatī, if one moves from the left side of the waist, the thighs, and the shanks toward the left, then [one touches] the left thigh, the left side, and the left cheek. (107)
O Pārvatī, one should likewise [worship] the left side of the forehead and also the back, saying: "Salutation to the discus of the ten directions. (108)

For this [mantra], the *doṇa* and so forth are placed on the right eye, the root of the nose, and the two eyes; the *kukṣīs* on the southeast and northwest corners; and the pair on the anus and the two testicles. (108)
Likewise, one should place the ten Śaktis who bestow all accomplishments, beginning with Kakṣiṇī, in the two corners of the triangle today. || 109 ||

Then, at its end, one should also place "Obeisance to the wheel beginning with the ten spokes" (daśārādicakrāya namaḥ); furthermore, one should duly place [the mantras] beginning with "All-Command" (sarvājñā) in its corners.
The right nostril, the right cheek, the breast, and the testicle are Śivā;
the left testicle, the breast, the left cheek, and the nostril are Śivani. (111)
The tip of the nose should be known [as the center], and likewise the ten sheaths;
in the space between them, one should worship the corners and so forth, saying, "Obeisance to the wheel. (112)
Having again placed the group of eight beginning with Vaśinī in its corners,
[one should place them] on the chin, throat, heart, navel, and the right [side].
The four sides are to be known as Maṇighūrā and so forth on the left;
there are likewise four sides, and then again the eight corners.
The arrow, bow, noose, and goad are placed externally in the four directions of the triangle situated in the heart; likewise, obeisance to the triangle. || 115 ||
Having placed [the deities] in its corners— namely in the southeast and so forth— one should place the goddesses beginning with Kāmeśvarī, and place the central Goddess in the middle.
Thus has been taught the arrangement of the goddesses, the most secret sequence;
because this must be kept even more secret, O beloved of my life, I have spoken thus. (117)
It should never be given to a disciple who does not abide by the commitments;
today, that which is most secret and well-guarded has been revealed to you. (118)
One should again install the goddesses beginning with Mūladevī and ending with Śamaṇī;
then, one should install Kāmeśvarī and the others in the triangle of the head, starting from the east.
One should place two arrows on the eyes and eyebrows, and two nooses on the ears;
one should then place two goads on the nose and the region starting from the right.
Or, O fair-faced one, one may place the eight deities by means of the *muhurmālā* sequence; the wheels, beginning with the *dava*, are to be placed as well. (121)
At the root of the eye, on the body, and again on the ear, the east, and the north;
at the crest-lock and so forth, in the lower and upper parts, and on the top of the tuft and the back of the ear. (122)
One should place "Karṇapūrve" on the shoulder and "Tasya mūle" at its base;
and those [mantras] beginning with "Sarvasiddhi" should be placed while proceeding in a clockwise direction.
One should also worship the Śaktis situated in the corners within the heart;
[then] on the eight-petaled lotus at the navel, in the Tuvaṃśa, and on the left side.
One should place the first four [syllables] on the belly and the left side;
one should place another four, beginning with *vaṃśa*, *bhava*, *māṃ*, and *antarādi*, on the other [side].

The best of practitioners should place the eight Śaktis, beginning with Kāmākārṣiṇī, in the eight-petalled Svādhiṣṭhāna [cakra], starting from the east and ending in the south. Then, he should place the ten Mudrās in the Mūlādhāra.
Furthermore, on the right, the left, and in the intermediate space, there are ten mudrās above and below; however, [the two] at the very top and bottom are again excluded.
Therein, the group of eight beginning with Brahmaṇyā is as before in those [lines]. || 128 ||
Starting from the left calf, one should proceed in order, beginning with the left side.
One should place the eight Siddhis upon them, and place two at the soles of the feet;
this placement, which has issued forth from the Cause, stands like a lamp lit from another lamp.
Having thus performed the ritual placement, O Goddess of gods, one should contemplate [the deity] as non-different from oneself.
Then, being composed, he should perform the placement of the purifiers (śuddhi-nyāsa) on the head, the private parts, the heart, and the three eyes. 131.
Then, O Goddess, one should perform the placement of the Vidyā (vidyānyāsa) upon the pair of ears, then on the face, and again thereafter on the back, the knees, and the navel.
Furthermore, there is the purification of the hands, as well as the sixfold ritual beginning with the seat (*āsana*), the [mantras of] Śrīkaṇṭha and others, Vāgdevī, and Rādhā and so forth. (133)
One should indeed place the Śikhā-āryā in the position of the Vaiṇava, as well as the Agnicakra and the others;
together with the three movements, it is endowed with the entire Vidyā-vīṇā-traya.
Having performed the pervasive placement (vyāpakanyāsa) from the feet up to the navel, and likewise from the throat to the head, one should then render the mouth empty and exhale.
Furthermore, O Goddess, that gentle one should satisfy [the deity] with the juices of nectar;
O Beloved, there is the sixfold placement (ṣoḍhānyāsa), beginning with the powers such as atomization (aṇimā) and starting from the Root Goddess.
The practitioner should quickly perform the placement of the *khaḍga* and other weapons for the sake of swift accomplishment;
this placement of the *Śrīcakra*, joined with the sixteen-fold placement (*ṣoḍhānyāsa*), bestows all desired fruits. (137)
Or even by doing it just once, the person, becoming directly composed of the Supreme Brahman and possessing a body of light, shall become liberated while living and happy. || 138 ||
Furthermore, having attained the eightfold perfection (siddhāṣṭaka) in all three regions, he wanders through the three worlds accompanied by yogins and great seers. || 139 ||
Whether every month, or every six months, or even once a year,
having performed the ritual placement known as ṣoḍhā-nyāsa, one should then perform the placement of the Śrīcakra.
One attains a great perfection difficult even for the gods to obtain;
having become a body composed of splendor, one possesses the glory endowed with the eight qualities.
Having attained the eightfold yoga, he is honored in all the worlds;
he is the performer of these two nyāsas, whether toward his teacher or his father.
If one should bow [to another], one certainly incurs an equal death within a month;
nor should one bow to fate or even to the Lord (Īśvara) without one's own preceptor.
Wherever another practitioner of this [path] dwells, that place is designated as a field of accomplishment (siddhakṣetra) for three yojanas in every direction. || 134 ||
O beautiful lady, wherever another virtuous companion of this [man] resides, there are Gaṅgā, Gayā, Kāśī, Kurukṣetra, and Dhanaiṣṭha. (135)
The Siddhas together with the deities reside there perpetually;
this pair of Nyāsas, which grants the perfection of command, is exceedingly difficult to attain.
One whose self is purified attains accomplishment at every step through this six-month practice; he becomes identical in nature with Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva. (137)
He is the agent of the creation, maintenance, and destruction of the world;
this should not be spoken of otherwise, O Nyāsa, for this pair bestows all perfections.
Even for a fallen practitioner who is hostile toward the true Guru, the recitation of the Śrīvidyā and the constant performance of the prescribed conduct [are required]. 139.
The two nyāsas and the entry [into the heart] are the fruit of intense austerity;
having performed the two nyāsas of the heart daily, one becomes pure even if one has committed some impurity.
Having meditated upon the untainted reality, the leader of the entire Brahmāṇḍa, who is the supreme abode in the form of consciousness, she made her own body a vessel for that [divinity]. || 141 ||
Having recited the Great Vidyā of Śrī, one becomes directly composed of Brahman.
This [practice] born of Nyāsa has been told to you, O Daughter of the Mountain. (1)
The sacrifice of the great goddess Śrīsundarī shall now be fully described.
[Thus ends the fifth chapter in the Uttara-bhāga of the Saubhāgyavidyodaya, within the Veda-sārārtha-saṃgraha, the Daśarathi-tantra, the illustrious Anuttara-brahma-tattva-rahasya. || 5 ||
The illustrious Dakṣiṇāmūrti said:
Whether one has performed other rites or not, this is the essence of prosperity;
having meditated upon the Lord, the seed of the universe, one attains Śrī, the goddess of fortune and auspiciousness.
O Sovereign Goddess, having thus designated these fifteen-syllable Śrīs, one should enter the sacrificial ground in silence for the sake of the supreme mantra.
One should diligently utter the mantra "Vāgbhava-bhuvaneśānī-Śrīyam," and then recite: "Obeisance to the Support-Power (Ādhāraśakti), who has a lotus-seat. (3)
By this mantra, one who is well-seated on a firm seat, or on a seat of grass, becomes auspicious;
however, misfortune arises from a wooden seat.
One brings suffering upon oneself by using a stone; a multitude of diseases arises on the ground.
Success in various powers comes from a hide, and liberation and prosperity come from a tiger skin.
If one sits upon a deer-skin, liberation arises; on a garment, fortune becomes unshakable.
On a seat of kusha grass, there will be song; on a jeweled throne, the desired supernatural powers (siddhis) are attained.
Having sat upon the seat with the mantra of the pure pedestal (piṭha),
the practitioner should recite the triad [of mantras] ten times, or [visualize] the Red Goddess from the path.
Having recited the lords of the islands together with their respective powers according to their capacity,
and having recited the Heart-mantra, one should scatter handfuls of flowers upon the ground.
With his limbs smeared with fragrant sandalwood paste, adorned with all types of ornaments,
or even decorated with a garland of *mānasa* flowers, he should be pure, wearing white garments.
One should draw the wheel on gold, silver, copper, or birch bark—
a beautiful wheel consisting of the five Śaktis and the four forms of Śambhu.
Having first drawn the circle of the bindu, thereafter a triangle should be made;
then, having fashioned an eight-cornered figure, one should then draw two sets of ten spokes.
Then, having made a square in the center, one should draw a circle provided with eight petals;
thereafter, one should also draw sixteen petals joined by circles.
Then, one square should be drawn, followed by three concentric squares;
this destroys all calamities and bestows the attainment of all fruits. (13)
It bestows the eight supernatural powers, beginning with the power of attracting matter;
it is the enchanter of all worlds and the giver of the fruits of all sacred pilgrimage sites.
It bestows the fruit of all sacrifices, grants the reward of every gift,
produces eternal bliss, and bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon its devotees.
The support of all worlds, the bestower of the fruits of all desires, consisting of all dharmas, and the giver of the fruits of all jewels and wealth. || 16 ||
It is the source of all knowledge, the unsurpassed creator of all protection, and the dispeller of all fear from spirits, ghosts, and demons. (17)
The eternal cause for the destruction of all poisons, the bestower of long life and health, and the source of well-being and the increase of sons and grandsons. (18)
It bestows the fruit of all sovereignty, including wealth, grain, elephants, horses, and the like;
it destroys the fear of worldly censure and annihilates the illusion of death.
It bestows victory in all battles, crushes all enemies,
destroys misfortune, brings prosperity, and grants the attainment of the Cintāmaṇi and other such powers.
It bestows the fruit of all good fortune, grants the bliss of Brahmananda, constitutes the essence of the Vedas, Vedanta, and the scriptures, and brings about glory. (21)
Moistening, parching, as well as agitating, deluding, performing all types of attraction, paralyzing, and likewise causing yawning. || 22 ||
It pacifies disease and poverty, shatters all miserable rebirths, and is the supreme means for bringing about peace, rain, wealth, health, and the accomplishment of mantras. (23)

It bestows the state of moving through the air (khecaratva), accomplishes all undertakings, is supreme, grants all perfections (siddhis), brings about the highest good, and is free from obstacles. || 24 ||
It consists of all mantras, bestows the fruit of all yogic accomplishments, comprises all knowledge, and grants mastery over all speech. || 25 ||
O Goddess, it consists of all reality, bestows all auspiciousness, grants the perfection of sacrifices, comprises all vows, and likewise consists of all nectar.
O Goddess, it is the pacifier of all suffering, the warder-off of disease and grief, the inducer of all madness, and the peerless source of delight for all.
It pacifies all misfortunes, destroys all obstacles,
acts as a staff against fierce malevolent spirits, and devours the flood of supreme mantras.
It effects the attraction of others' magical sciences (paravidyā) as well as the attraction of others' commands;
it causes the immobilization of enemy armies and brings about the neutralization of weapons.
O Goddess, it brings about great prosperity, impels great intelligence,
removes great fever, and destroys great death.
O Goddess, it always causes the agitation of great cities, brings about great auspiciousness,
consists of great prosperity, and bestows the accomplishment of great welfare.
Bestowing the fruit of great power and granting the abundance of great bliss—thus has the power of this wheel been described by me. (32)
This has been declared by the forest-dwellers;
today this very thing called Ayodhyā is said to be the Śrīcakra, known by the name Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa.
The great seers declare that very [reality] to consist of Śiva and Śakti; having again pierced through Śakti and Śaktimat, it indeed enters the city of fire.
Having gathered all the upward-moving power (śakti), one should expand it downward;
one should pierce the power below the wheel of names (nāmādicakra) with fire from above.
Again, as before, one should expand the first line and divide it;
[it should be] with the upward power above and fire below, excluding the middle fire.
Having expanded it, one should cause the Śakti to split below by means of the primordial fire;
then, from the middle onwards, one should cause half of the Śakti to expand the Śakti downwards.
In that very same way, O Sovereign of the Gods, one should form the *saṃpuṭa* for the entire wheel;
O Great Goddess, with the *vācata* [mantra], one should pierce the eye of the fire-wheel.
O Dear One, by the very process of breaking the knots, [the consciousness] moves from the very top and the very exterior toward the middle and upward, reaching the limit of the beginning.
Then, O Lord, one should cause the power situated outside to expand upward within at the end of the night;
thereafter, O Lord, one should cause even that primordial power to expand upward.
Then, O Dear One,
having extended the external power (bāhya-śakti) from the top of all [the channels] down to the knot at the lower part, one should pierce it from below.
One should draw an eight-petalled lotus with its stalks;
O Goddess of the gods, beyond that, one should then draw a sixteen-spoked [wheel].
Then, O Agni, the third great wheel was created, provided with a surrounding enclosure and adorned with four gates. || 43 ||
The second [wheel] of the middle eight is the first of the three [wheels] of withdrawal;
thus has this great wheel of the goddess Śrī been described. 44.
This wheel of the sovereign fortune of the entire empire has been proclaimed;
it consists of fire and moon, O beloved, and is composed of all knowledge. (45)
