This very [reality] is the cause of the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the universe;
it is to be worshipped as possessing the phonemes of Mātṛkā, or indeed as being devoid of them.
Since there are four hundred million yoginīs of great power in this wheel, they indeed hold the sādhu in special esteem.
A quadrangular [mandala] adorned with the letters of the Mātṛkā for the sake of attaining success, shining with a level surface set with pearls and rubies. || 48 ||
Named Trailokyamohana, it bestows the fruits of the wish-fulfilling tree;
it has sixteen spokes, possesses the form of the lunar orb, and is the abode of all.
O Maheśānī, it fulfills all desires, rains down a shower of the nectar of non-duality, possesses eight petals, and resembles the Japā flower.
That which is named Sarvasaṃkṣobhaṇa, and that which fulfills all desires—O Great Goddess, these three constitute the Wheel of Emanation (Sṛṣṭicakra), which bestows happiness. 51.
O auspicious lady, the second lotus-petal, which resembles a hibiscus flower, bestows infinite fruit and the perfection of all good fortune. (52)
Adorned by the goddess Pūrvāmrāyādhī, it grants all desires;
it has fourteen spokes, is brilliant like a flower, and is presided over by Deveśī and others.
O beloved, this wheel which produces all protection consists of great gnosis;
O Great Goddess, these three constitute the wheel of maintenance, which bestows maintenance.
Facing south, it should be cultivated; it bestows desired fruits, O lady of excellent hips, and has eight petals, as red as the rays of the rising sun.
Resembling a ruby gem, it always removes all diseases;
it possesses the brilliance of a thousand rising suns and the luster of the bandhūka flower.
O Īśvarī, beyond the wheel that bestows all accomplishments lies the abode of the Kalās;
it is the triangle, which is eternally the source and the cause of the manifestation of all things.
O Varārohe, the bindu-cakra is supreme, consisting of universal bliss;
O Parameśvarī, it is the leader of the cakras and consists of Sadāśiva.
This wheel, which is of the nature of withdrawal and consists eternally of Brahman,
is to be cultivated through the Western Tradition (Paścimāmnāya) and is worshipped as the highest among the three.
O Goddess worshipped by heroes, the six paths (ṣaḍadhvan) exist within this wheel;
O Queen of the Gods, the path of words (padādhvan) is said to reside in the petals of the wheel.
The path of the worlds (bhuvanādhvan) is established within the three-fold divisions of the wheel;
I shall now describe the path of phonemes (varṇādhvan), which consists of the Mātṛkā, to you, O Nandin.
O Dear One, since the eight groups of the Mātṛkā are established in the directions,
know that the earthly [element] consists of them, having sixteen parts and being triangular in shape.
An eight-petaled [lotus] with the consonant groups beginning with 'ka' ending in 'kṣa' is placed in the cardinal and intermediate directions;
the letters from 'ka' to 'śa' occupy the petals of Indra, situated in the corners of Indra.
One should write the letters beginning with *ṇa* up to *bha* on the first ten-spoked wheel;
likewise, those beginning with *ma* and ending with *kṣa* on the second ten-spoked wheel.

The eight groups [of letters] are in the eight corners; the three-cornered [triangle] is said to be within the [figure] beginning with A-Ka-THa and ending with the triangle. The pair of H and Kṣa is situated in the center.

O Goddess, the path of phonemes (varṇādhvan) has been described as the form of the Mātṛkā-pīṭha; the wheel [of phonemes] exists in accordance with the root [text] in order to sustain the thirty-six principles (tattvas). 66.
She who possesses five lion-thrones, whose path is the digits of bliss (nanda-kalā), and who rules over the wheel (cakra-śāsana);
she is Mahātripurasundarī, joined with Kālā and Bhairavī.
O sinless one, these two, which are rich in the threefold merit and full of splendor, are always certainly declared to be the path of mantras (mantrādhvan) that pervade the wheel of the universe. 68.
Thus, the Śrīcakra, pure with its six paths and bestowing all accomplishments, is intended for worship in two forms—as Mount Meru and as the Earth. (69)
One may write it with powdered vermilion or with saffron;
when it has been written with a golden pen, one should worship it.
One should always worship the Wheel-King (cakrarāja), the city of Ayodhyā, whether it be made of gold, silver, copper, precious gems, or crystal. || 71 ||
O Goddess, one should worship the wheel facing the western direction;
it should be known as Śrīmā, while the eastern direction is declared to belong to Śiva. (72)
The northwest direction is likewise to be known as Īśāna, and the southwest as Rākṣasa.
O Goddess, facing the southern direction, one should worship the Cakra in this manner.
That [direction] is declared to be the East, while the corner of Rasaka possesses the Fire [direction].
O Goddess, one should worship according to the wheel (cakra) in the primary Northern direction. 74.
Then that [direction] should be known as the north, and that very one as the east—of this there is no doubt.
O Goddess of gods, then the northeast corner is the southeast—of this there is no doubt. (75)
O Goddess, saluted by heroes, this wheel, which is the form of Meru and the ocean of the syllables of the Śrīvidyā, consisting of all the Āgamas, has been described. (76)
When the King of Wheels (cakrarāja) is constantly worshipped with all ritual offerings, the entire universe—both stationary and moving—is thereby worshipped; of this there is no doubt. 77.
Then, having worshipped the pair of the Teacher’s feet with abundant jewels and wealth, he took this wheel which bestows all perfections.
From that time forward, one should worship with services arranged according to one's means;
having become free from old age and death, one attains eternal perfection. || 79 ||
[Thus ends the sixth chapter in the *Vedārthasaṃgraha*, in the latter portion of the *Anuttarabrahmatattvarahasya* of the *Dāśarathīya Tantra*, titled "The Arising of the Science of Saubhāgya"].
Śrī Dakṣiṇāmūrti said:
I have proclaimed the extraction of the wheel (*cakroddhāra*), which bestows the desired accomplishments upon the practitioner.
Listen, O Goddess; hereafter I shall explain the procedure for worship (*pūjāvidhi*).
Having installed this Śrīcakra, known by the name Ayodhyāpura, which belongs to the Supreme Lord, the wise practitioner of pure mind should worship it.
All the mantras to be extracted are joined with the triad of Tāras;
first is Amṛtāmbhonidhi, and after that is Ratnadvīpa.
There was a great garden of various trees, then a grove of Kalpa trees; after that, a grove of Saṃtāna trees, and then a grove of Hari-candana trees.
The Mandāra grove, the Pārijāta grove, and thereafter the Kadamba forest grove—
these are celebrated as the five groves.

The mantras of all the deities, preceded by the three *tāras* and joined with the fourth *āhṛt*, should be recited for the sake of granting success in recitation, fire-offerings, worship, and so forth.
The first is said to be the wall of great jewels, Puṣparatha; and after that is the wall of great rubies, Padmarāga.
There is also a rampart of gomedha jewels and a rampart of vajras;
likewise, there is a rampart of vaiḍūrya jewels and one called indranīla.
The great wall of pearls and rubies, as well as that of emerald,
and the great jewel-wall known as coral is recorded as the ninth.
Behind the Māṇikya-maṇḍapa is the Sahasrastambha-maṇḍapa;
then there is the garden called Mṛtā, and after that, the Ānanda-vāṭikā.
Then follows the *Tapoddhāra*,
after which, O Daughter of the Mountain King, one should worship the *Candrikoddhāra*.
Then there is Mahāśṛṅgāra, followed by Mahāryaghnāravī;
after that is the Cintāmaṇi, the great jewel, and beyond that the Gṛharāja.
First, one should worship the eastern gate, which consists of the Pūrvāmnāya;
then, likewise, the southern gate, which has the form of the Dakṣiṇāmnāya.
Then one should worship the form of the Western Āmnāya at the western gate,
and likewise the form of the Northern Āmnāya at the northern gate.
Then one should worship the circle of jewel-lamps, the great lion-throne, and thereafter the honey-foot consisting of Brahman. 15.
Then, O my beloved, one should worship one leg of the couch as consisting of Viṣṇu;
thereafter, one should worship one leg of the couch as consisting of Rudra.
One should worship a single foot of the bed as being with Īśvara;
then likewise [the other feet] as Sadāśiva; and thereafter the frame and the board.
Having diligently worshipped the seat known as *haṃsatūla*,
one should worship the great footstool made of *haṃsatūla* for the sake of wealth.
Afterwards, there was a safflower-colored carpet, then a great canopy, and after that a large curtain;
then the goddess Medirā and her worshippers [arrived]. (19)
I have declared forty-four mantras;
meditating upon the temple of the Goddess, one should worship it here with these.
Having placed flowers, unbroken rice grains (akṣata), and other offerings on his own right side,
and having offered lamps all around, he should worship the Cakra with the root mantra.
O Dear One, one should first worship the triangle with the three sections of the root mantra,
accompanied by instrumental music, fire, and water, along with three breath-control exercises (prāṇāyāmas).
Having performed the drying and burning, one should then perform the flooding;
having recited the root mantra and performed breath control (prāṇāyāma) three times.

Having then assigned the Ṛṣi, the metre, the deity, and the seed-syllable (bīja) and so forth, [one recites]: "Whatever beings there are that creep, and whatever beings are situated upon the earth... (24)
"O Daughter of the Mountain, by the command of Śiva, may those beings who create obstacles be destroyed"—
with this mantra, O Daughter of the Mountain, [he should perform the rite] by stepping with the heel of his left foot.

O beloved, having diligently dispelled all obstacles even by means of the *karatalatrapaṇa* [hand-clapping], and being endowed with the contemplation that "I am the Goddess," while still possessing a body; ||| 26 ||
Then one should perform the ritual placement known as the Vajrapañjara;
having first performed the purification of the hands, one should then recite the Kumārī mantra.
Having repeatedly uttered "Śrī Mahāpada" and then "Tripurā," and having placed his joined palms at his heart while saying, "Protect me! (ātmanaṃ rakṣasva), [he should proceed]. || 29 ||
Having diligently uttered *māyā*, *kāmarāja*, and *śakti*, one should [utter] the name of the Goddess ending in the dative case and followed by *namaḥ*. || 30 ||
Then, having recited this mantra, one should offer a seat;
having uttered Śrī, Māyā, and Kumārī, with this following mantra: || 31 ||
Having uttered the word "Śrīcakrāsana" joined with the fourth [case-ending] and the heart-mantra,
one should utter Bhuvaneśānī, the Parā-bīja, and Kumārikā.
Having uttered "Sarvamantrāsanāya Thenama," one should recite [the mantra]; thereafter follows Trilokeśī, Kāmarāja, and the syllable Kla. (33)

Having uttered the name of the one to be accomplished (sādhya), followed by the word "siddhāsana" in the dative case and joined with the heart-mantra (hṛd), the practitioner [should perform this] with these three mantras.
Having offered a handful of flowers (puṣpāñjali), one should perform the six-limbed assignment (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa);
then, having performed the Mātṛkā-nyāsa, one should subsequently perform the Viśinyāsa.
O my beloved, having first performed the placement of the syllables of the root-vidyā,
one should then perform the two types of placement known as the sixfold wheel-placement, which bestows all spiritual accomplishments.
Having performed the ritual placement (vinyāsa) for himself or another, and having meditated upon the digit of consciousness (citkalā) with the Dhyānasūkta,
[he should prepare] a circular and square area on his left side with pure water.
Having prepared and honored the vessel along with its base,
and having then established it, one should worship it further with the six-limbed rite (ṣaḍaṅga).
Then, having filled [the vessel] with pure water and touched it, one should recite the root mantra three times;
with that [water], one should sprinkle the image, and likewise oneself and the ritual site.
Some here perform a special *arghya* offering that bestows fruit;
having performed that special *arghya* there, one should also worship Śrī with devotion.
With *tajjailena* one should draw a circle intersected by three hexagons and a square;
with *tvāmalena*, the *vidyā* is in the center and within a triangle. (41)
Having worshipped that hexagon by repeating it twice, O beloved, [worship] Samavallabhā; or else, having uttered "Bhava" ending in the dative case, [worship her]. (42)

Then, for the vessel of the arghya water, which consists of ten kalās, one should utter the word "agnimaṇḍala" followed by the sixteenth vowel (Ā), joined with the fourth case-ending and a salutation.
Having established the support there with this mantra, O Śivā,
[one should invoke] Dhūmrārcis, Ūṣmā, Jvalinī, Jvālinī, and Visphuliṅginī.
The auspicious one, whose nature is form, is thus designated by the metaphorical usage of "form";
she is declared to be the ten digits of fire, arising from the primordial phonemes.
There, having worshipped Madana and uttered [his name] thereafter, one should then utter the word "Sūryamaṇḍala" accompanied by the dative case-ending (caturthī). || 46 ||

First the word "dvādaśa" (twelve), then also the word for the self of the digit (kalātman), then the word for the arghya vessel, followed by the dative case ending conjoined with the heart-mantra. (47)
Thus, having established the vessel, [the powers] Tāpinī and Tāpinī follow;
then Dhūmrā, Arciḥ, Jvālinī, and Ruci.
Suṣumṇā, Bhogadā, Viśvā, Vodhinī, Dhāriṇī, and Kṣamā—
these twelve digits (kalās) of the Sun are proclaimed to be the bestowers of desired boons.
O Daughter of the Mountain, at that time we were honored as the Kābhāyakṣas;
thereafter, we attained the supreme state of Soma, and after that, the highest [state] for the sake of the maṇḍala.
The word "sixteen" was stated later; in that regard, when the nectar of the sacrificial offering belongs to the nature of the *kalās*, it should be accompanied by some form of salutation. (51)
Therein, O Śivā, are Amṛtā, Madhukṣīrā, Madhvī, and the others;
likewise Amā, Anasūyā, Pūṣā, Tuṣṭi, Puṣṭi, Rati, and Dhṛti.
Śaśinī, Candrikākānti, Jyotsnāśrī, Prīti, Aṅganā, Pūrṇā, Apūrṇā, and Mṛtākā— these sixteen bestow desired boons and grant eternal bliss.
The sixteen digits (kalās) of the Moon are renowned as arising from the essence of the [sixteen] vowels;
therein they are to be worshipped and saluted, consisting of the nature of the letters of the *akatha* group.

Then, one should plant the three [syllables] at the corners: a triangle accompanied by the color of the *halas* (consonants), with the syllable *haṃ* in its center, and the syllable *kāma* (the letter *ka*) together with the *śakti* (the letter *ī*) at each corner. 55.
Having worshipped with the mantra known as Haṃsa, having drawn a hexagon outside the circle,
and having meditated upon it, one should then worship it thoroughly with the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga).
O Śivā, having consecrated [the vessel] seven times with the root mantra,
one should then recite the ninety-four mantras while touching the [vessel] made of clay.
O Daughter of the Mountain, the Kalās of Mercury, Venus, and the Sun are joined with three, two, and one respectively;
they are said to be thirty-eight in number. 58.
Creation, intellect, memory, fortitude, splendor, fortune, radiance, stability, persistence, and accomplishment—these are said to be the ten kalās of Brahmā. (59)
Jarā, Pālinī, Śātirī, Ācārī, Ratikāmikā, Varadā, Andrādinī, Prīti, and Dīrghā— these are the portions (kalās) of Viṣṇu.
Tīkṣṇā, Raudrī, Bhīmā, Nidrā, Tandrā, Kṣut, Krothinī, Kriyā, Utkārī, and Mṛtyu— these are said to be the ten kalās of Rudra.
Yellow, white, reddish, and black—these four, born from the syllable *ca*, are said to be the *kalās* that bestow all fruits. (62)
These thirty-four digits (kalās), beginning with 'ka' and ending with 'kṣa', arise from the syllables:
Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, Vidyā, and likewise Śānti.
Rodhikā, Dīpikā, Recikā, and then Mocikā; after that, Sūkṣmā, then Sūkṣmāmṛtā, and beyond that, Jñānā. || 64 ||
Jñānāmṛtāpyāyinī, Vyāpinī, and Vyomabhīti—
these are the sixteen digits (kalās) that arise from Sadāśiva.
There, the three Taras, who are to be worshipped and saluted, should be honored with prostrations; having recited "saḥ śuciṣad" and then "vasurantaḥ samudre," [one should proceed]. (66)
Having uttered "sadvotā" and "vidiṣatu," one should also say "padam atithisat.
Then, "uroṇasat" is declared, followed by "nṛṣat" and "varasat. (67)
Then "sat vyoma," "satyaś cādajvāgojā," and "ataṃ vahat";
at the end of the mantra, "pratad viṣṇuḥ," then "srāpyam vakaṃ," and thereafter the *manu*.
The mantra "tad viṣṇoḥ," the mantra "tad viprāsaḥ" following that, and then the root-vidyā—these are declared to be the forty-four mantras. (69)
Then, certain perfected great seers (maharṣis) [consecrated him] with mantras beginning with "Akhaṇḍa" and others;
they proclaimed this consecration consisting of ninety-four mantras.
O Unbroken Supreme Bliss, O Embodiment of Joy, O Soul of the Heart, O Mistress of the Akula Forest, bestow upon me the mere manifestation of the power of will! 71.
Abiding in the non-family (akula), having the form of nectar, O Supreme One who produces pure gnosis, you who know all things and possess the form of light—bestow immortality upon this [being]. 72.
Having attained oneness with Your form within this [mouth], become one whose nature is identical to Yours;
then, being composed of the form of supreme nectar, bring about the vibration of consciousness.
The syllables are *praṇava*, *vāgbhava*, *llūṃ*, *snauṃ*, *mlūṃ*, *jūṃ*, and *sa*; then, having uttered the word *amṛte*, the word *amṛtodbhave* [should follow]. (74)
O Amṛteśvarī, O showerer of nectar, [grant] the state of being deaf to sound;
cause the nectar to flow for a yuga, joined with fire and the known.
This vidyā of Uccaraidamṛteśvarī has been proclaimed:
[it begins with] Vāgbhava, followed by a pair of Vads, and then the word Vāgvādinī. (76)
Vāgbhava and Kāmarāja, then "klinne" and "kledini," followed by two instances of "kledaya," and finally two instances of "mahākṣobhaṃ kuru. (77)
Recite "mādakadanaṃ śaktim uccārya mokṣaṃ kuru," joined with the *yuga* [mantra], followed by "anaṃtaṃ candram avanaṃ" combined with the sound of *manu*. || 78 ||

Then, accompanied by the bindu, followed by the moon (the letter *i*) and Viṣṇu (the letter *k*), and endowed with the human vowel (the letter *a*) and the visarga—one should utter this as the fifth [syllable]. (79)
This illuminating vidyā, which bestows the accomplishment of all desired objects, has been declared.
With all these vidyās, Śivā should consecrate the immeasurable [space].
Then, having prepared the supreme nectar consisting of light and consecrated with mantras,
the Guru [places] the sandals of the triad [of gurus] at the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra) by means of its drops.
Then, having offered libations to the teacher (ācārya), one should offer the sandals of the teacher and that drop (bindu) which bestows the perfection of awakening into one's own kuṇḍalinī.
"O Mother of the World, the moist [substance] blazes when consecrated by mantra;
having thus prepared the special arghya, [one should offer it] every year. (83)
Having worshipped Catūrāja, the Lord of the World becomes a sovereign of the whole earth;
he becomes omniscient, one who has accomplished all that was to be done, and is liberated while living—of this there is no doubt. (84)
O Śivā, by constantly performing the ritual for the special arghya offering again and again,
and having quickly worshipped the Śrīcakra, one becomes the master of all fortune.

[Thus ends the seventh chapter in the *Śrīmadanuttarabrahmatattvarahasya*, the *Dāśarathīya-tantra*, which is a compendium of the essential meaning of the Vedas, in its latter portion, titled *Saubhāgyavidyodaya*.
Śrī Dakṣiṇāmūrti said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall explain with reverence the worship of the limbs of dissolution (layāṅga),
by performing which even a pure person becomes free from sin and endowed with good fortune.
Then, O Daughter of the Mountain, having meditated upon the goddess Mahātripurasundarī— who consists of pure consciousness— with the hymn beginning "tataḥ padmanibhāṃ dīptām," [he should proceed].

Having meditated upon the Goddess Śrī, who resides in the center of the heart-cakra, who consists of the three Vedas, and who is capable of piercing through the interior of the Suṣumṇā, the lotus, and so forth; || 3 ||
The eternal splendor of Śiva, the Lord of the universe and the lamp of all the worlds, dispels the darkness of delusion. || 4 ||
Having caused that primordial, pure, and conscious power— worshipped by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Īśa—
to emerge through the cavity of knowledge, she performed an act fashioned by her divine play.
Saubhāgyasundarī is the manifest, supreme Śrī composed of splendor;
she is accompanied by the triple-sectioned mudrā, with hands joined in añjali and filled with flowers.
Having brought together Mahāmāyā and Lakṣmī, one should utter the Śakti;
then, having joined [the name] Śrīmahātripurā, the word "Sundarī" follows thereafter.
Afterwards, O Śivā, [one should utter] the word "amṛta" and the word "caitanya";
then, O Śivā, with this [mantra], "namas te mūrtikalpaṣāyai," [one should worship].
O Daughter of the Mountain, having again uttered these three seed-syllables, one should fashion the supreme form of the illustrious Goddess within the mandala by means of the mantra.
In the midst of the cries of "hasara" and "hasa," there were the sounds of kalari-drums and swans;
[I beheld Him] whose infinite form is the cause, situated within the great forest of lotuses.
"O Mother, benefactor of all beings, come, come, O Supreme Goddess!"—with this mantra, [he invokes] the Supreme Will, whose form is imagined [by the mind]. (11)
Having established [the Goddess] within the center of the Śrīcakra, situated in the heart-cakra,
one should thereafter perform the sixty-four types of offerings for the Deity.
Having received the water for the feet (pādya) from the goddess named Tritārī according to the ritual manual,
he then said, "I shall go," accompanied by salutations and the highest offerings.
Thus, having recited all [the names] of those who possess constant glory within the Śrīcakra, one should say: "I offer water for the feet to the venerable Goddess; homage! (**) 14.

Having said, "I offer this arghya to the Śrīdevī," one should recollect the mantras beginning with "namas tataḥ" and so forth, along with their respective families and the names of the ritual services (upacāras). || 15 ||
Anointing with fragrant oil, entry into the bathing hall, and then seating upon a throne in the bathing pavilion. || 16 ||
Then one should perform the auspicious application of fragrant unguents for a divine bath;
thereafter, the bath with scented water, followed by the word "kanaka. (17)
Then follows the sprinkling with water from all sacred fords (tīrthas) accompanied by the sound of the *kalaśa* vessel;
thereafter, having uttered the verse beginning with "O cloth," the ritual purification (*mārjana*) is performed.
Beyond this, a reddish-white silk garment is prescribed for the lower robe;
one should likewise fashion an upper garment from reddish-white silk. (19)
Then, following the word "anointing" (ālepana), there is the entry into the pavilion;
then, following the word "anointing," there is the seating upon the jeweled throne within the pavilion.

After the words "sandalwood" (caṃdana) and "agallochum" (agaru), one should then say the word "saffron" (kuṅkuma); then, having said the word "oyster-shell" (śaṅkhamada), one should then say the word "musk" (mṛgamada).
Then, camphor, musk, sandalwood paste, gorocanā, and other such substances—divine fragrances used as an ointment for all the limbs. || 22 ||
Then there was black agallochum, great incense, and a mass of hair;
and from the words "mallikā," "mālatī," "jāti," "campaka," and "aśoka" [the flowers were offered]. (23)
The word *śatapatra* denotes a lotus; likewise, *pūga*, *kuharī*, *punnāga*, *kahlāra*, and so forth, are used as primary terms according to their respective seasons.
"I fashion a garland of flowers; obeisance to the mantra of the wreath.
Then, at the conclusion of the word "ornament," there is the entry into the pavilion.
Furthermore, after the sounds of ornaments have ceased and at the conclusion of the pavilion,
one should then seat [the deity] upon the pedestal and perform the ritual services (upacāras).
Then there was a crown of nine jewels, followed by a fragment of the moon; then the vermilion of the parting line, and then the jewel for the tilaka mark.
Then Vālī should offer black collyrium, a pair of earrings,
a pair of jeweled ear-rings, and a nose-ornament.
Alternatively, one should fashion for him a necklace of beads as his primary ornament,
and thereafter a crown fashioned from molten gold.
After that, the *sumahatvadaka*; then the *muktāvali*, and after that the *valimata*;
then the *ekāvalī*, O Goddess, and after that the *channavīramata*.
Beyond that, one should fashion four pairs of *devikās*,
and here also, having fashioned a series of bracelets, a row of *omikās*.
Then one should fashion a girdle-string and other threads as auspicious ornaments, followed by an anklet for the feet and jeweled foot-bangles.
Thereafter, he saw the ring on his foot, then the noose in one hand,
then the goad in the other hand, and finally the manifestation of the Apradrakṣu.
One should then fashion two beautiful sandals with the word "Māṇikya" at their end, and [imagine] her holding a bow in one hand and flower-arrows in the other.

Then, having said "with those equal to oneself," "with garments," "with footprints," "even in the enclosure," and "together with the deities," he should offer [the oblation] into the heart of the Great Wheel.
After that, Kāmeśvarī, Kapardī, and Kopaveśanā;
then the vessel called Sudhāsava, and thereafter Ānamanīyakā. || 36 ||
Afterwards, there was the sound of camphor-flavored betel being offered;
then followed the auspicious night-rite with playful laughter and supreme charm.
One should offer an umbrella, a pair of chowries, a mirror, a palm-leaf fan,
as well as perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, and food offerings.
Having offered sixty-four types of services to the Lord of the Mandala, and having displayed the nine mudrās to the Śrī Devī; || 39 ||

Then, having satisfied [the deities] three times with the root mantra, one should worship the sandals (pādukā) of the Śrī Devī upon the Lord of Mountains in the directions of Agni, Īśa, Asura, Vāyu, and the center, and so forth.
O my beloved, one should worship the six limbs of the Śrīcakra of the Goddess;
now I shall describe the daily worship—listen with one-pointed minds.
Even by hearing it, one becomes a practitioner possessing all accomplishments;
and she who is the totality of sound is considered the Supreme Bhuvaneśī.
One should then utter the mantra "nityaklinne madadrave sauḥ.
This is the Vidyā of Kāmeśvarī, which bestows the fulfillment of all desires. (43)
This first lunar day is eternally the manifest heroine of direct realization;
having first uttered the Vidyā, one should then [utter] the word "Kāmeśvarī. (44)
One should utter the mantra: "I worship the eternal Śrīpādukā," at the end of each Nityā-vidyā, appending the specific name of that respective Nityā. 45.
Having recited the eight-syllable mantra of the sandals, one should worship her with the words:
"Bhaga-bhug-e, O Bhaginī, O Bhagodari! (46)
"Bhagamāle," then "pada," then "padadevi," "bhago vahe," "bhagaguhye," having uttered "bhaga," and then the Yoginī is "bhaga. (47)
*Nipātanī*, *sarvā*, *bhagā*, then *darśakarī*; *bhagarūpā*, then *nityā* and so forth, *klinne*, followed by the word *bhaga*. (48)
Then [utter] the word *svarūpe*, then the word *sarvāṇi bhagāni*, then the word *me hyānaya*, and afterwards [the word] *varade* for the sake of removing sins. (49)

Then, having joined the words *rete* (semen), *surete* (good semen), *bhaga* (vagina), *klinne* (moistened), *klinnadrave* (moistened fluid), *kledaya* (moisten!), *drāvaya* (cause to flow!), and *yuktvā* (having joined), as well as the word for exertion (*śrama*) and the word for rising (*udya*). 50.
After the words *bhagaviccikṣubhekṣuktrākṣobhaya*,
one should utter *sarvasarvān* and then the word *bhageśvari*.
Having uttered the voice as the eighth [syllable] *krū*, [and] having pronounced *kṛcabhūtsacavlūmodhūmataḥ* from the smoke,
and then having uttered *parayektadom*, all [the syllables] become moistened by sound.
Bhaga herself brought me here from behind; beyond this, she is known as Strī.
She is the one who takes away the foot and the fruit, the eternal Māyā, Bhagamālinī.
Having uttered the mantra *vācaṃ māyām*, and having spoken the eternal [mantra] *nityaklinne madadrave* followed by *vahnijāyai*, she is known as the supreme one named Nityaklinnā.

The Praṇava, the seed-syllable of the noose (pāśa), then *caṃ*, *mrau*, *krauṃ*, *drauṃ*, followed by *aṣṭrā*, then *jrauṃ* and *svāhā*—this fourth [mantra] is known as the Rudrā, which bestows all accomplishments (*sarvasiddhi*). || 55 ||
Having first uttered the Praṇava, one should then recite "Lokeśī," followed by the word "Vahnivāsinyai" conjoined with "Namaḥ. (56)
This Vahnivāsinī is declared to be eternal and the bestower of all accomplishments;
having uttered "hrīṃ klinne" or "vā," one should then utter the seed-syllable named Aṅkuśa.
One should utter the syllable "hrīṃ" at the end of the word *pada*, as well as after the liquids;
this is the sixth [mantra], the eternal Mahāvajreśvarī, who bestows all knowledge.
After "Oṃ," "Bhuvaneśānī," and "to the messenger," [the name] "Śivādūtī" is uttered; this is proclaimed as the seventh eternal [goddess]. (59)
Then follows the armor (*kavaca*) mantra: *trayī bhayī*; then the word *khecarī*; then *kṣu śrīṃ hūṃ*; and thereafter the weapon (*astra*) mantra: *kṣetrilokeśī*. || 60 ||
This Nityā is declared to be Tvaritā, the bestower of all fruits;
thereafter she is called Kumārī, and then Nityā Kulasundarī.
Having uttered "haseti kalare," one should utter the syllable "da" joined with the nasal bindu;
having uttered "hasāyakatrāre," one should utter the syllable "da" accompanied by the bindu and the god of love (smara).
Having uttered "hasa," "kalara," and "iti," one should pronounce the syllable "duṃ" conjoined with the *manu* (seed-syllable).
This is declared to be the mantra named Nityā, which bestows all auspiciousness in this manner.
Having first uttered the seed-syllable named Aṅkuśa as "Hrīṃ Prestu Mi," one should then utter the Kāmarāja syllable "Vācya Glūm. (64)
In a liquid substance devoid of the sounds of the first letters of the vowels and so forth, one should recite the Kavaca mantra:
"Pre jrauṁ, this Nīlapatākā is the Nityā who bestows all fruits. (65)
At the end of "Bhramara" (bhramara) is the seed-syllable of the Wind (ma), adorned with the left ear (ū) and marked with a bindu;
this Nityā Vijayā quickly bestows the fruit [of one's desires]. 66.
When the Moon has ascended Varuṇa and is joined with Manu,
this Nityā, who bestows all fruits, is declared to be Sarvamaṅgalā.
The seed-syllable of the Trayī (the three Vedas) joined with *namas*, then the word *bhagavati*, followed by *jvālāmālini* and *śakrānte*, and then the words *devadeva*. (68)
The word for "all beings" (sarvabhūta) is followed by "at the time of withdrawal" (saṃhārakāle), and then "to the one who produces sound" (śabdakāriṇe).
Then, after "Jātavedas" (jātavedasi), there is "the end of sound" (śabdānte), and then the pair "blazing" (jvalat) and "two" (dvitaya). || 69 ||
Afterward, having uttered the two blazing [syllables] and Māyā accompanied by the three births,
and having pronounced the Rāpha-samakam, one should then [place] Jvālāmālinī upon the mountain.
Then, from the Kaca weapon, the eternal Jvālāmālinī emerged,
bestowing the fruit of all sovereign powers and cutting away disease and sorrow.
The mantra joined with the fire-syllable (Ra), adorned with the Manu (Oṃ) and the Bindu (M), is known as Klinnā, the fifteenth eternal [vow], which bestows great siddhi. || 72 ||
The Ṣoḍaśī is the mother of the entire world, the bestower of all accomplishments;
she alone is Śrīvidyā, the Great Knowledge (Mahāvidyā), Lalitā, the Supreme Goddess. (73)
O Daughter of the Mountain, these goddesses, beginning with Svarā and ending with Lalitā, are to be worshipped; they are the fifty Nityās previously mentioned. 74.

She who shines as the deity presiding over the New Moon and Full Moon observances, she who is the sixteenth digit, the eternal Great One, the primordial nature (Mūlaprakṛti), and the Sovereign Goddess. 75.
She is the mother of all worlds and the leader even of the eternal ones;
[she is worshipped] on every single day from the first of the lunar fortnight until the full moon.
Worshipping each of the Nityās individually with twenty-four types of offerings,
one should diligently recite the mantra until the worship of the fifteen Nityās is complete.
Having worshipped the eternal Tīrthī three times, one shall obtain incomparable good fortune;
he who performs the recitation of the Nityā mantra, fire-offerings, and worship on the day prescribed [for her]. (78)
The practitioner performs this on the ground; he is that Supreme Lord himself, having worshipped the fifteen Nityās who bestow the fruits of the daily rites. (79)
Or else, one should worship Mahānityā with three or five verses;
thus one attains great fortune, which is difficult even for the gods to obtain.
Having worshipped the fifteen Nityās daily, thereafter one should worship the supreme Śrī Lalitā, the highest Goddess, either daily or on specific lunar days (nithi).
Having worshipped Mahānityā in five ways or even in three ways,
and having worshipped the sandals of the Guru, one shall obtain a mass of auspiciousness.
O Śivā, listen attentively as I shall proclaim the lineage of gurus:
without having worshipped the lineage of gurus, one does not attain prosperity on this earth. (86)
At the end of the word *parameśvara*, one should append *parameśvarī* and *yathāmbikā*, followed by *śrīpādukāṃ pūjayāmi*; this eight-syllable mantra should be joined for a woman.
By this very Mahāvidyā, she became renowned upon the surface of the earth;
he worshipped her in the form of a Guru as the Supreme Lord and the Supreme Goddess. 88.
Then Mitreśa, then the sixth [is] Śamodbhīśa;
then Paracaryānātha, and then Lopāmudrā and the one known as Vāgastya. (89)
These are remembered as the teachers who bestow the playful initiation (dīkṣā) of the gods;
everywhere, I worship the venerable sandals (śrīpādukā) of Nandanātha. 90.
By this very procedure, one should worship the lineage of gurus;
however, the term "Ānandanātha" is not used for Lopāmudrā, nor is it used for the Guru Śiva.
By the power of Lopāmudrā, the goddess attained the state of sexual union;
she obtained from the mouth of Brahmā the sciences that bestow all supernatural powers.
To one who is devoted to her husband, Śiva is eternally present day after day;
for such a person, daily blessings and all forms of prosperity increase.
Therefore, O Śivā, a man who constantly worships the preceptor’s wife—who is virtuous and has sons—with the thought that she is Śrī herself, shall possess all perfections. 94.
One should not treat even the wife of the teacher with disrespect regarding her clothing, ornaments, and so forth;
rather, one should approach her with the thought that she is the mother of the world, especially during a great festival.
The foundation for good fortune arises both in this world and the next;
having first worshipped the Divine Current (divyaugha), one should then worship the Siddha Current.
After worshipping Kālatāpana, the teacher of Dharma,
one should thereafter worship Muktakeśīśvara and Dīpakalānātha.
The four gurus of the Siddhas are said to be the granters of desired boons;
having worshipped them with the mantra "Siddhauyaṃ," one should then worship the Mānavaugha.
Having first worshipped the deity Viṣṇu, and thereafter Prabhākara,
and then having worshipped the deity Tejas and Manoja, O beloved.
Beyond Vāsudeva, one should worship Kalyāṇa, Ratnaveva, and the supreme teacher of the worlds known as Śrī Rāmānandanātha. 100.

Then, reciting the *pādukā* mantra five times at the aperture of Brahma (*brahmaraṃdhra*), one should especially worship it three times; thereafter, [one should worship] the *pādukā* of one's own guru.
"O Śivā, I have thus declared that one should worship [the deity] through the process of dissolution (layāṅga);
or else, the best of practitioners should perform the worship of the dissolution-yoga every day. (102)
One attains omniscience and achieves the unsurpassed accomplishment.
[Thus ends the eighth chapter in the Uttara-bhāga of the Saubhāgyavidyodaya, within the Vedārthasaṃgraha, the Śrīmadanuttarabrahmatattvarahasyadāśarathīya-tantra.]
The venerable Dakṣiṇāmūrti said:
Now, O Great Goddess, I shall fully describe the worship of the goddesses of the enclosure,
known as the "limbs of enjoyment," which bestows worldly enjoyment, heaven, and liberation.
Atomicity, levity, magnitude, lordship, thereafter control, the perfection of will, the perfection of irresistible desire, and thereafter the enjoyment [of objects]. (2)
Then, O my beloved, these— namely Icchāsiddhi, Prāptisiddhi, and Sarvakāmābhidhā— are to be worshipped by me in the first square.
And on the second square, one should worship Brāhmī and Māheśvarī,
then Kaumārī and Vaiṣṇavī, and after that, Vārāhī.
One should also worship Māheṃdrī, Cāmuṇḍā, and Mahālakṣmī;
then, in the third square, one should worship the Saṃkṣobhiṇī mudrā as well.
The mudrā that drives away all, the one that attracts all,
the mudrā called "subduing all," and likewise the one that intoxicates all.
Then, O maiden, one should worship the Mahākuśa mudrā, the source of all sky-farers (khecarīs),
and the Sarvatrikhaṇḍa mudrā at the entrance.

Aṇimā and the others are to be worshipped in the directions starting from the west and also in the intermediate directions; Brāhmī and all the other Mothers are to be worshipped in order starting from the east.
The goddesses beginning with Kṣobhiṇī are to be worshipped in the directions starting from the west and also in the intermediate directions.
One should worship these [deities], preceded by the three-star seed-syllables (stritārī-bīja) and ending with the word "pādukā."
"tritāraitāḥ," then the word "padaṃ," then "prakaṭeti padaṃ," then addressing the word "yoginyaḥ," and the word "trailokyamohanai. (10)
Having said "The oceans [are] the wheels," he should utter "the accomplishments";
having pronounced the word "with weapons," after the word [he says] "with powers."
"O beautiful one, let them, together with their vehicles, retinues, and attendants, be worshipped by you with this mantra: 'May they be honored by the planets. (12)
In the Trailokyamohana-raśmicakra, one should abandon the Prakaṭā-yoginīs;
having uttered the three Tāras, one should perform the Karaśuddhi-kara-mantra.
Having uttered the word "Tripurācakreśvarī" followed by "namaḥ," or having uttered "Tripurācakreśvarī" followed by the word "śrī," [one should proceed]. (14)
"O Śivā, one should worship the sandals with the mantra 'I worship the sandals' and sacrifice to the Mistress of the Wheel (Cakreśvarī);
one should then display the all-agitating mudrā preceded by its seed-syllable. (15)
Thus has been described the first enclosure, which bestows all accomplishments.
Now, regarding the great lotus of the petals of the *kalā*s, I shall explain the ritual procedure for worship; listen.
Having uttered the three *tāras* and each individual vowel as well,
one should worship the sixteen digits (*kalās*) of the goddess Sakalānityā, O Daughter of the Mountain.
Then follow Kāmākarṣiṇikā and Vudhyākarṣiṇī.
The Attractor of Ego, likewise the Attractor of Sound, the Attractor of Touch, and the Attractor of Form thereafter. (19)
O Daughter of Himavat, [the mantras] are Rasākarṣaṇikā, Gandhākarṣiṇī,
Cittākarṣaṇikā, and thereafter Dhairyākarṣiṇī.
The one named Smṛtyākarṣiṇī and Ākarṣiṇī are dear to me;
then follow Bījākarṣiṇī and Ātmākarṣiṇī.
Amṛtākarṣiṇī, and likewise Śarīrākarṣiṇī—these sixteen deities, ending with Kalā, are the presiding deities of the spokes. || 22 ||
At the end, they should be worshipped with effort together with their seed-syllables (bījas) and colors;
these Yoginīs are at the end of the secret words, and one should utter the word "pada."
Then, the word "sarvāśāpariśabdāntapūraka" (the fulfiller of all hopes ending with the word 'pari') follows;
then "cakre samudrāḥ" and so forth—the remainder should be recited as before.
At the end of the three *tāra*s and the word *kumārī*, one should utter the word *tripureśī*, followed by the word *cakreśvaryai namaḥ*. Then, after that—
After the word *Tripureśvara*, one should say *Cakreśvaryai* or the word *Padāt paraṃ*, and having said *Śrīpādukāṃ pūjayāmi*, one should worship the Mistress of the Wheel (*Cakreśvarī*).
Having thus worshipped with devotion the wheel that fulfills all desires,
one should display the Sarvavaśīkaraṇa mudrā preceded by its seed-syllable.
Then, one should worship the deities in the Sarvasaṃkṣobhaṇa-cakra;
having uttered the three *tāra*s, one should then recite the eight [syllables] beginning with the *ka*-group.
Having uttered [the mantra], one should thereafter worship Anaṅgakusumā and the others:
first Anaṅgakusumā, then Anaṅgamekhalā, and after that—
Anaṅgadā, Menā, and then Anaṅgamadanāturā, Anaṅgarekhā, Anaṅgaveginī, and Yamalocanā. (31)
Then, O Śivā, one should join [the mantra]: "I worship Anaṅgā, Kuśā, Anaṅgamālinī, and the goddess Śrīpādukā. || 32 ||
"O you three who are worthy of worship, O most secret Yoginīs, this is the station"—thus one should recite the remainder as before in the wheel that agitates all. (33)
Then [worship] the Self, the seat, and Nescience; then Tripurasundarī; then "Obeisance to the Mistress of the Cakra," and again Tripurasundarī. (34)
Then follows Cakreśvarī and Ambikā, and after that the eight syllables; thus is Tripurasundarī, the sovereign of the third enclosure.
Having worshipped, one should then show the seed-syllable of the Attractor (Ākarṣiṇī);
afterwards, one should entreat the deity who bestows all good fortune.
Beginning with the letter *ka* and ending with *ḍha*, there are the powers starting with Saṃkṣobhiṇī in sequence:
Sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī Śakti, and likewise Sarvavidrāviṇī. (37)
Next is the one who attracts all, and also the one who gladdens all;
then the one who deludes all, and after that, the one who paralyzes all.
O Śivā, [the powers] are Sarvajaṃbhanikā-śakti, likewise Sarvavaśaṃkarī, Sarvaraṃjanikā, and then Sarvonmādinī. (39)
She is the power that accomplishes all aims, the fulfiller of all prosperity;
she is the power consisting of all mantras, the destroyer of all dualities.
Having uttered "Śakti Śrīpādukām," one should join it with "pūjayāmi. Then, following this, [one should utter] "Tritāra" and "etāḥ saṃpradāyayogibhyaḥ. (41)
One should utter the word *sarvasaubhāgya* for the child;
having pronounced the remainder as before, [one should place it] in the wheel of the collection of good fortune (*saubhāgyaka*).
Then, having uttered the great vidyā of Cakrāsana, [one should utter] the word "Tripuravāsinī," followed by the term "Cakreśvarī" joined with the word "namaḥ. (43)
Having uttered the word *Tripurāmbāsinī*,
one should then utter the word *Cakreśvarī* followed by the eight syllables (*vasuvarṇa*).
Thus, having praised the Mistress of the Wheel (Cakreśvarī), one should certainly display the mudrās;
now the worship of the deities in the wheel that accomplishes all aims shall be explained. (45)
The Goddess is the bestower of all accomplishments, as well as the bestower of all prosperity;
she is the Goddess who makes everything dear and the performer of all auspiciousness. || 46 ||
The Goddess who bestows all desires, who liberates from all suffering, who pacifies all death, and who wards off all obstacles. || 47 ||
One should worship these goddesses, beginning with the letter ṇa and ending with the letter pha: the goddess Sarvāṅgasundarī, who bestows all good fortune.

Having recited these three *tāra*s (*oṃ āḥ hūṃ*), followed by *kuralottīrṇayogipurā*, and then saying "I worship the state of the Sovereign of the Śrīcakra" (*śrīcakreśvaryai vā padaṃ*) and "I worship the venerable sandals" (*śrīpādukāṃ pūjayāmi*), one should worship the Mistress of the Cakra (*cakreśvarī*).
Preceded by the seed-syllable (bīja), one should then display the mudrā of all-enlightenment;
thereafter, one should worship the deities in the wheel that effects all protection.
She is all-knowing and all-powerful, likewise the bestower of all sovereignty;
the Goddess consists of all knowledge and is the destroyer of all diseases. 53.
She is the very essence of all conduct, likewise the remover of all sins;
she is the Goddess consisting of all bliss, whose nature is the protection of all.
One should worship these [goddesses] ending with Dakṣāntā, who bestow all desired objects;
then the Yoginīs beginning with Garbhā, as well as the Tretā and Āryā, and also the Padas.
One should recite the *sarvarakṣācakra* as before;
then, having performed the collective worship (*samaṣṭipūjā*), one should proceed beyond the *sādhyāsana* and *siddhāsana*.
Having uttered the name of the Mistress of the Wheel, Tripurāmālinī, joined with "namaḥ," and having then joined it with "Tripure" and also the word "Mālinī," [one should worship]. (57)
Having uttered the sound "Cikā," the mistress of the wheel, conjoined with the mantra of the sandals,
one should worship Tripuramālinī, the queen of the wheel.
Having formed the great goad mudrā (*mahāṅkuśa*) preceded by the seed-syllable on the peak of the mountain,
O Hare, one should then worship all the deities in the circle.
O Daughter of Himavat, the eight deities of speech, preceded by their respective seed-syllables and joined with the worship-mantras, should be used with "namaḥ" in place of "svāhā."
These are the secret yoginīs, the state of all kings and serpents;
having then uttered the remainder in the wheel, one should worship them preceded by the three tāras.
One should worship Tripurasiddhā preceded by the Mūrti-vidyās;
then one should perform the Vīramathodya-mudrā and the Khecarī.
One should perform the worship of Bāṇa and the others in the four directions on the exterior of the triangle;
having first uttered "drāṃ drīṃ klīṃ ṣṇū," one should then utter the word "sarva" (all).
One should utter "jaṃbhanebhyaḥ" followed by "padaṃ," and then "vāṇebhyo namaḥ.
Then, at the beginning and end of the three-syllable enemy-mantra, there is the word "sarvasaṃmohanīya."
Having uttered "namas" for the bow, followed by the seed-syllable *māyā*, then the word "vaśīkaraṇa" (subjugation) joined with the dative case-ending and the heart-mantra (*hṛdaya*). || 65 ||
Having uttered "Oṃ Aṅkuśāya" for the purpose of paralyzing all sounds, he should fill the four directions with arrows and other weapons.
Now I shall describe the triangle: in front is Mahākāmeśvarī, behind is Mahāvajreśvarī, and [in the third corner] is Mahāśrībhagamālinī. (67)
One should offer these to Vāgvāmaśaktikhaṇḍā;
thereafter, [one offers] Mahāśrīsuṃdarī preceded by the three sections.
Then, one should worship Kumārī-pūrvikā in the center;
likewise, the ninth is Yoginī, and the ninth is Cakradevī.
Among the eternal [goddesses] here are Ṣoḍaśī and likewise Mahāśrīsundarī;
then there is Lalitā, the supreme deity, situated in the Vaidava-cakra.
O Pārvatī, it is declared to be one alone; no distinction exists.
O beloved, there is no difference between the mantra and the deity in that knowledge.
These secret names are also for the yogis;
furthermore, even a single word [should be used] in the wheel that bestows all accomplishments (sarvasiddhi), while the remainder should be recited as before.
Having thus completed the collective worship (samaṣṭyarcā), one should then invoke the Vidyā;
having uttered "Tripurāvāñcakreśvaryai namaḥ," one should recite it.
Having said, "I worship Tripurā, or the state of Cakreśvarī, or even the state," one should worship Cakreśvarī with the [mantra] "Śrīpāka. || 74 ||
Then, having displayed the seed-mudrā preceded by the syllable of the seed (bīja),
one should worship the Sovereign Consciousness (Sāmrājī Saṃvid) within the great wheel of the Veda-path.
The three *tāra*s (oṃs) in the root mantra, then "Śrī Mahātripura," then "Sundari," then the word "Śrī Mahā," and then "Parameśvarī. (76)

Then, having uttered the eight-syllable mantra, "I worship the auspicious sandals" (śrīpādukāṃ pūjayāmi), and having worshipped and offered the libation, she thereafter attains the state that is both supreme and non-supreme.
After that, in the Cakra of All-bliss (Sarvānandamaya), there is the Rahasyayoginī;
along with her mudrās and the sound, there is the Siddhi together with her weapon.
Having addressed the word "with the spear" (saśaktiḥ), then the word "with the vehicle" (savāhanā),
and then the word "immediately destroying enemies" (sadyarivārā), [one should worship] with all the ritual offerings (sarvopacāraiḥ) beyond this.
Having said, "May you be fully honored," he then spoke the root-mantra (mūlavidyā) once more,
followed by the word "Śrīmahā" and then the word "Tripurā."
Having uttered "Sundarī Śrī Mahācakreśvaryai" followed by the word "Śabdada," Sundarī then spoke the great word "Śrī Mahāśabda Tripurā. (81)
Or else, one should worship the autumnal deity with the mantra: "I worship the lotus feet of Śrī Mahāūrva Cakreśvarī," or "I worship the venerable sandals (śrīpādukā). || 82 ||
Having first displayed the Yonimudrā beginning with Vāgbhava,
one should thereafter present incense, lamps, and the food offering (naivedya), and then display the nine mudrās.
Having diligently recited the root mantra five times or three times,
one should then offer libations and present the food offering (naivedya) to the Blessed Lady.
Then, having offered water for drinking in the middle, and thereafter the *uttarāpośana* water,
and having provided water for washing the hands, one should offer betel leaf.
One should meditate on the cakra with a single bindu at the heart, and not with two bindus at the breasts;
having visualized the yoni, one should contemplate the dhenu-mudrā facing downwards. (86)
Having meditated upon Darpakāma as the embodiment of aesthetic beauty (kalā), which bestows all fortune,
one should recite the Saubhāgyahṛdaya mantra, which grants the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.

Salutations to that supreme, most venerable Light, which consists of the mountain-dwelling serpents, which is composed of the fifteen-fold collection [of the Vedas], and which has shattered the malevolent power of Māra.
That supreme glory is marked by the five acts;
it is the auspicious one whose self is the essence of the entire universe, whose heart is full, and whose nature is the Self.
Salutations to that Great One, the eye of all, who is divided threefold according to the sequence of the object, the subject, the eulogizer, the eulogy, and the act of praise.
I remember that supreme Speech, which exists in the sequence beginning with Paśyantī and so forth,
and which is the cause of the experience of various kinds of great forms.
Whatever object—be it place, time, substance, self, or property—appears in whatever form and by whatever path, may I resort to that very form as a portion of my own consciousness. (92)
O Mahātripurasundarī, that body which extends from the base to the crown is renowned as the Adit; one should worship her who is endowed with the power of existence.
In the *yoni*, O Maheśvarī, it has the luster of the color of gold; in the *ādi*, it is radiant with wisdom; and in the *ājñā*, it resembles the moon—thus is the Great Splendor.
O Bhavānī, O Immortal Sovereign, I meditate upon you, who have brought peace to worldly existence, having satiated all things moving and unmoving with a vast flood of flowing nectar-food. 95.
O Goddess of gods, the phonemes, the divisions of time (kalās), the categories (tattvas), the mantras, and even the worlds— these sixty shine forth within the Self that is consciousness.
Everything from that which is dependent on others up to Kāla and Ārudra is variegated and wonderful;
yet even you, O Uśrīlayasimāt, possess a body of pure light.
Whatever shines here—whether as deity, name, form, or the nature of action—all that does not exceed you, whose very essence is light. (98)
O Goddess, from the eyes and other senses at the root of the anger, up to the heart, you repeatedly indulge in the honey of forms and so forth through the play of your seat. 99.

Having completely overcome the goddesses of consciousness and the objects of the senses, [the yogi] always offers them as an oblation of nectar for the sake of the worship of the noble state of the yogis. 100.
This secret Heart of Good Fortune was remembered by the yogi Śivānanda for the purpose of propitiation, granting all desires. (101)
Thus has this hymn to Tripura been composed here, revealing the supreme truth, honored by the best of yogis, and dedicated through the Yajurveda;
it has no purpose other than the destruction of all sins and diseases—let it be served with devotion according to the ritual injunctions for those endowed with power.
After the offering of food (naivedya), one should mutter the root-mantra according to one's preference;
thereafter, one should mutter the Saubhāgyahṛdaya mantra on the left side.
Having made it square and well-proportioned, one should then make it circular and beautiful; thereafter, at the edge of the two [circles], one should fashion the speech-mandala. 104.
Salutation to the Maṇḍala; there one should fully worship the Maṇḍala.
Having established the vessel there, [one should invoke] the Praṇava and Bhuvaneśvarī.
Then, having uttered "To all those who cause obstacles, to all beings" three times, and thereafter [the mantra] "O radiant one, O flame," (106) |||
O Śivā, having first given the *bhūta-pada*,
one should afterwards offer the *nīrājana* while reciting the root mantra (*mūla-vidyā*) and then the three *tāra*s.
O Goddess, sovereign of all the wheels, endowed with the ninefold nature, accept this lamp for the waving of lights (ārātrika) for my spiritual accomplishment. 108.
Having thus performed the lustration rite (nīrājana) while reciting the root mantra,
and having offered a handful of flowers, one should properly perform the circumambulation three times.
Having prostrated with the eight-limbed *daṇḍavat* salutation and having praised her many times with hymns,
the married woman (*suvāsinī*) worshipped Śrīvidyā with perfumes and other offerings, including betel leaf.
Or, even without performing the mudrā, having displayed the khecarī mudrā and said "Forgive me," one should then perform the ritual dismissal (udvāsana) of the goddess Śrī into oneself.
O Śivā, by performing the worship of the Wheel-King even once in this manner,
one attains eightfold prosperity and becomes of the nature of Brahman.
[Thus ends the ninth chapter in the glorious *Anuttarabrahmatattvarahasya*, the *Daśarathīya Tantra*, which is a compendium of the essential meaning of the Vedas, titled *Saubhāgyāvidyodaya*.]
The venerable Dakṣiṇāmūrti said:
Listen, O illustrious Goddess, to the auspicious fruit of the worship of the Cakra,
by the mere hearing of which even the eight siddhis, beginning with aṇimā, shall be attained.
The supreme [form of] worship is the daily offering; the middling is the fortnightly worship;
the lowest is said to be the monthly worship, which destroys the rising of sins.
Whoever desires even the prosperity of Mahendra or that of Kubera,
[should perform] the auspicious worship of the Cakrarāja with devotion every day for six months.
Having brought [the deity] under control, he attains prosperity equal to that of the Giver of Wealth (Kubera),
provided he performs the daily worship with nine enclosures for the duration of a year.
By his own splendor, he indeed acts as a lord over the realm of Kubera;
even the sciences such as the Vedas, Shastras, and Puranas are very difficult for him to attain.
From his mouth and other [limbs] emerge, even without being studied, the objects of the four aims—dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa—which are very difficult to obtain. (6)
The radiant ones remain eternally at his command by the order of the Triple Guru;
first there shall be the worship of the temple, and after that, the worship of the limbs of dissolution (layāṅga).
The third part of this [practice] is called Bhāgāṅgā; it is said that one should worship it in three ways.
Or, having performed the Layāṅga worship, the best of practitioners should do so constantly. (8)
Having recited the mantra known as the Devīvaṃdanamālā and being intent upon that supreme [state],
one who offers the arghya water shall become endowed with all auspiciousness and attain perfection.
One may perform either the worship of the entire wheel or the worship of the central wheel;
having invoked [the deity] twenty-one times, one should utter the ten-syllable mantra that generates supreme splendor.
Having offered twenty-eight oblations of cow-ghee into the Jātavedas fire,
he became the leader of the eight supernatural powers, beginning with atomization (āṇimā), upon the surface of the earth.
O Goddess, even the gods along with the ṛṣis shall suffer destruction in that place,
whether it be a country or a city, where the wheel-throne [is established].
Wherever this practitioner performs worship according to this ritual—whether in his own home, in a forest, or in a village—a disturbance of the world arises. (13)
Their minds scorched by the heat of the blazing fire of passion,
women approach from afar according to the analogy of ants.
O Great Goddess, upon seeing him, all women become bewildered at heart by his mantras, their hips quivering with desire. (15)
For one who daily worships that discus suspended upon copper,
great accomplishment arises here before long.
A crystal discus inscribed with gems, which subdues the mind,
bestows all desired objects upon us for the duration of a year.

Where the written, radiant wheel, along with the sacrificial oblation (caru), is worshipped together with its ancillaries by the command of the preceptor, that place becomes filled with wealth, grain, and other riches.
In his temple, even the fickle Mahālakṣmī shall become stable;
his intellect attains a likeness to that of Bṛhaspati, and he becomes perfected through various branches of knowledge.

A splendor like that of the god of love, a mass of auspiciousness at every step, and the attainment of wealth consisting of sons, grandsons, and so forth—these shall be accomplished for him before long. (20)
The bliss of Brahman will manifest for you in this very birth;
of this there is no doubt. Have faith, O beautiful lady. (21)
By the grace of the teacher, a golden disc inscribed [with mantras]—whether containing seed-syllables or devoid of them—is constantly worshipped by him. (22)
The eight Siddhis, beginning with Aṇimā, will certainly reside in his abode; at my command, they shall serve him in embodied form. (23)

It was completely filled with wealth, grain, and the like; crowded with heaps of pearls and gems; provided with elephants, horses, and chariots; and accompanied by multitudes of cattle and servants. || 24 ||
In your palace, there shall remain a supreme and pervasive prosperity that is difficult even for the gods to attain. (25)
Even if he were dull-witted, he would become a master of all branches of knowledge;
through the increase of sons and grandsons, he shall become equal to Kaśyapa himself. (26)
By her splendor, even those devoted to their husbands quickly became lax in their fidelity;
so too did kings, princes, their servants, and even ministers.
Even for those who stand like servants in the house of one who is possessed of the thought of what must be done, a man [who disregards them] goes [to ruin]. (28)
A terrible affliction, like that of being trodden upon by serpents, shall befall them;
even those who are under their control will meet with death at their own will.
He who casts off his body in the presence of the Golden Wheel has sown [the seed of merit] in the house of an outcaste; indeed, it is said that Badarīvana is like that. || 30 ||
The constant presence of the Cakrarāja is said to be Kāśī;
one who performs the worship of the Cakrarāja properly and with devotion every day [attains that state]. || 31 ||
Having performed the daily worship of the golden discus with devotion every single day, he treats even the gods as mere blades of grass, let alone those on the surface of the earth.
Having recited the fifteen-syllable mantra of Śrī three hundred times,
one gains a kingdom or a city that is twice the size of two mandalas.
He who worships the leader of the wheel of letters for six months will certainly bring the country, the village, and its people under his own control. (34)
He [overcame] even the gods, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Kinnaras, and Rākṣasas;
even the Brahman-sages, the divine sages, the Apsarases, and the Asuras.
He indeed makes them his slaves; there is no doubt about this.
By worshipping the golden Śrīcakra daily, along with its constituent parts and colors, [he attains this]. (36)
To kings he is like a preceptor, and to women he is the god of love;
he brings under his control the three worlds, including gods, asuras, and rākṣasas. (37)
He [beheld] the kinnaras, the gandharvas, and the lords of the yakṣas;
and the celestial women, such as Rambhā and Urvaśī, who were enchanting even with their divine speech. (38)
The daughters of the Nāgas and the maidens of the gods and Gandharvas become subject to his will like female servants; of this there is no doubt. (39)
Great indeed is the flower [of this practice]: health, sovereignty, the powers beginning with *aṇimā*, lordship over all sciences, and the turning back of old age and death. (40)
There shall be an increase in sons and grandsons, prosperity through the abundance of wealth, an opulence of pearls and gems, and an ever-increasing excellence day by day. (41)
O my beloved, there is no doubt that he attains success after one year;
now, O Maheśānī, I shall describe the great worship of Śrīvidyā.
O Maheśānī, by worshipping the Śrīcakra with its ancillaries daily using Brahma-flowers, one brings about the supreme and immediate destruction of faults such as the killing of a Brahmin. (43)
Having worshipped for just one month, he is liberated from millions of great sins and attains great fortune, abounding in wealth, grain, and other riches.
Having attained mastery through all branches of knowledge,
the beloved of Aṅgiras worshipped the venerable Krama along with its limbs every day with hibiscus flowers.
He is liberated from the defects of killing a Brahmin, even those committed in other births;
of this there is no doubt, and he becomes a wise man endowed with wealth. (46)
By constantly and respectfully worshipping with the reddish petals of the *ketakī*,
one shall destroy even the multitudes of minor sins within a single month.
By worshipping the Śrīcakra along with its ancillaries every day using Karavīra flowers, one attains fortune equal to that of Kāmadeva; of this there is no doubt. (55)
Within a single month, he was liberated from the flood of great sins and minor evils;
he became like Kubera in wealth and appeared like the Lord of Wealth himself.
Within three months, he indeed becomes equal in splendor to Kāma;
by worshipping with beautiful lotuses for half a month, he attains this state.
Freed from heaps of great sins within merely a month, and having attained incomparable good fortune, he obtains unshakable prosperity. (58)
By constantly worshipping the Śrīcakra with Campaka flowers, which are most delightful, one is liberated from great sins and minor offenses within a single month. (59)
Having attained great fortune, crowded with floods of wealth and grain, and having become preeminent among all branches of knowledge, he became equal in splendor to Kāma himself. || 60 ||
Having enjoyed all pleasures here in this world, he goes at the end to the supreme state,
by constantly offering bandhūka flowers for the duration of one month.
By worshipping [the deity] continuously for just one month with bilva leaves, one brings the three worlds under one's control and is liberated even from the hosts of sins. (62)
Liberated from all sins, one attains imperishable prosperity by worshipping [the deity] with bilva leaves together with lotuses.
One is liberated even from the multitudes of sins committed over a hundred lifetimes;
one attains great health as long as life lasts and exceedingly great prosperity. (64)
Having obtained liberation while still alive (jīvanmukta), he will certainly attain death [only] after a month,
having worshipped the King of Wheels (cakrarāja) with great devotion using jasmine flowers.
Released from heaps of great sins after only a month or so,
and having attained abundant prosperity, he reaches the supreme state in the end.
Day after day, he worshipped the Discus with jasmine, Arabian jasmine, Jātī, Kunda, and Śatapattraka flowers, or with white lotuses, or with various combinations of these.
Freed from the heaps of sins committed over a hundred lifetimes, he attains within a month prosperity and knowledge that are difficult to obtain. (68)
Having worshipped the King of Wheels (the Śrīcakra) for a month with garlands from the Mallikā family mixed with Tulasī leaves, along with its ancillaries, one whose mind is serene— (69)
O Jīva, live by your speech; through our power you shall become like Kubera, the giver of wealth, resembling the sun in brilliance, and freed from all sin.
Having attained great prosperity, he becomes liberated while living (jīvanmukta),
by worshipping the King of Wheels (cakrarāja) day after day with rose-apple sprouts.
One is liberated from the multitude of great sins (mahāpātaka) within just one month;
having attained the goddess Śrī, one is endowed with sons, grandsons, and friends. || 72 ||
Having enjoyed all pleasures for a long time, he shall attain liberation in the end;
likewise, by worshipping the King of Discuses (Cakrarāja) with Śamī wood, Dūrvā grass, or Kura grass.
One is liberated even from the sins accumulated over a thousand births;
having attained incomparable good fortune and wealth, one attains the imperishable state after death. (74)
Having worshipped with red lotuses or blue lotuses for a month,
one is liberated from all sins and attains the riches of Kṣaya.
Having worshipped the Cakrarāja day by day with *pāṭala*, *vakula*, or *nāgakesara* flowers for one month with a serene mind, [one attains success]. || 76 ||
Freed from the afflictions of misfortune, he attains unstable prosperity by constantly offering fragrant flowers or fragrant sprouts. || 77 ||
Having worshipped the Cakrarāja daily with devotion along with its ancillaries,
one is liberated from the entire mass of sins and attains imperishable prosperity.
Having attained even this fleeting excellence, one is glorified in the world of Brahmā;
and now I shall describe to you the ritual for the worship with jewels. || 79 ||
Even by worshipping him with various fragrant flowers, camphor powder, and sandalwood, one shall become endowed with all auspicious fortune.
For twenty-one nights, she indeed makes twenty kings her servants and destroys great diseases.
The reciter of the mantra becomes a lord of celestial chariots (vimāna); of this there is no doubt.
O beautiful one, he should fashion golden flowers adorned with pearls and gems.
The worship of the wheel (cakrapūjana) should be performed over a period of twenty-one nights;
behold, by means of these twenty-one nights, [the goal] will be attained—of this there is no doubt. (83)
The minister, possessing a luster like that of the moon, attains imperishable prosperity while worshipping the Śrīcakra with golden flowers set in coral. (84)
O Great Goddess, by performing this threefold concentration, one shall destroy the hosts of enemies;
even wicked kings will become submissive—of this there is no doubt. (85)
Likewise, by worshipping with golden flowers set in emeralds, one destroys Śakra and brings the gods under one's control. || 86 ||
O Goddess of the Gods, one should worship the Cakra with flowers made of gold and set with great gems such as topaz for twenty-one days.
Even the immortals, though they are independent, become granters of boons to him;
by means of this knowledge, he becomes equal to Jīva—of this there is no doubt. (88)
With flowers fashioned from gold and adorned with diamond filaments,
one should worship the leaders of the mandala for twenty-one nights.
Even the gods and the Daityas are undoubtedly under his control;
he brings the three worlds—gods, asuras, and humans—under his sway. 90.
Worshipping with golden flowers joined with sapphire gems, one undoubtedly paralyzes the three worlds through the triple concentration (*trisamādhi*). || 91 ||
Within twenty-one nights, one shall destroy hosts of enemies;
even women who are proud of their youth, though they be arrogant, shall become like female slaves.
One should worship the discus with golden flowers fixed upon a support;
within seven days, even kings will be brought under control by one's enemies—of this there is no doubt. (93)
By performing these three acts of concentration, even a great mass of sins is destroyed;
one who worships the wheel with golden flowers set in lapis lazuli [achieves this]. (94)
The three worlds indeed become subject to him; there is no doubt that they are cast down from their pride.
All beings become submissive, and he is liberated from the multitude of sins. 95.
O Goddess, one should not worship with flowers that have been used for eight nights, nor even with those made of gold;
O Supreme Goddess, [one should not worship] with flowers that have become *nirmālya* or with those that are defiled.
If one should worship Śivā with golden flowers made of the nine precious gems, then gods, asuras, humans, serpents, and even rākṣasas [would be subdued]. (97)
All these become submissive within seven days, O Agni, without a doubt; even from the sins committed over ten million lifetimes, one is liberated in a month. 98.
Constantly worshipping with flowers made of the syllables *svarāri* (sa), *ra*, and *ma*, one obtains the unsurpassed fruit attained by those born at Daśāśvamedha. 99.
Now listen to these words concerning the complete fulfillment of the jewels and so forth;
with those very flowers, the worship and other rites should be performed by the best of practitioners. (100)
O Goddess of the Gods, having offered whatever flower or leaf is available, it should be given in each respective place; it must not be given according to one's own whim.
By worshipping with his own flowers, such as oleanders and others,
one is liberated from the sins committed even over ten million lifetimes at the beginning of the month.
Or else, one should offer oblations mixed with *tulasī* leaves, or mixed with *bilva* leaves,
or with fragrant flowers, or even with the tender sprouts of the *vasu* tree.
Having worshipped the King of Wheels with auspicious golden flowers joined with fresh leaves, one is liberated from all sins.
Having obtained this great and auspicious knowledge from Śrī Aṣṭamuṇḍā,
he attained eternal prosperity, along with flowers and the fortune of having sons and grandsons.
Having attained all enjoyments, he attains union with Brahman,
whether in the month of Kārttika, Mārgaśīrṣa, Māgha, or even Phālguna.
In the month of Vaiśākha, or Āśvina, or Śrāvaṇa, on an auspicious day,
one should repeatedly entreat the preceptor for the Śrīcakra, which bestows all perfections.
One should receive from the hand of the preceptor the worshiped golden Śrīcakra, which bestows all spiritual accomplishments, accompanied by his benediction. (108)
They know that city of Ayodhyā to be situated on that very ground;
it is said to be the peak of Mount Meru and the abode of Kailāsa. (109)
By the grace of the Ācārya, on whichever day he receives the beautiful King of Golden Wheels from the lotus-like hand of his own teacher, [he attains success]. (110)
Then, with a pure mind, one should give two karṣas of gold as an auspicious ornament marked with sixty [signs] to the wife of the preceptor.
And worship a golden image of Trirāccihnuka for the teacher’s wife according to your capacity;
likewise, honor your own preceptor with ornaments.
He attains the great siddhi of Śrīvidyā as well as unshakeable prosperity; the Yoginīs and even the Mothers protect him like their own son. (113)
Holding lotuses in their hands and beautifully adorned. || 51 ||
When the son of the Sun was intent on washing his feet, [the two attendants] stood before him;
having honored the two treasures, Śaṅkha and Padma, they held chowries.
Having worshipped Varuṇa, the lord of aquatic creatures, on both sides,
one should subsequently worship Svarṇa, who holds a staff and a parasol, at the rear.
Having fully honored the signs beginning with Aries and worshipped them, thereafter [he should worship] the Sun, the Moon, Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, and Venus.
One should worship these nine planets: Śani, Rāhu, and Ketu;
and one should honor the lords of the directions, adorned with four types of ornaments, in their respective quarters.
Airāvata, Puṇḍarīka, Vāmana, Kumuda, Añjana, Puṣpadanta, Sārvabhauma, and Supratīka, in this order.
Then one should worship the eight guardians of the directions, beginning with Mahendra, in their respective eight directions; one should place Brahmā in the upper direction and Viṣṇu below.
Then one should worship the weapons, such as the vajra and the śakti, in the ten directions;
thus [one worships] Mahālakṣmī, the beloved of Hari, together with her retinue.
Having worshipped with incense, lamps, and so forth, as well as with drums, conchs, and other instruments, one attains great and eternal fortune; of this there is no doubt. (59)
Alternatively, having fashioned an image with the Lakṣmīhṛdaya-vidyā,
and having offered the lion-throne and other items, one should then worship it with the vidyā.
Thereafter, one should perform the worship of the [twenty-eight] forms in twenty-eight ways:
Śrīdhara, Hṛṣīkeśa, Vaikuṇṭha, and Viśvarūpaka; || 61 ||
Having worshipped Vāsudeva, Saṃkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha at the bases of the petals, one should thereafter worship them in the middle of the petals.
Gāyatrī, Pārvatī, Cāṇḍī, Īśvarī, and Damakārikā—
know these to be the syllables of Mahālakṣmī in their respective order.
[He should worship] Anurāga, Visaṃvāda, Vijaya, Vallabha, Mada, Poṣa, Cala, Tejas, and the lords of the directions beginning with Mahendra. (64)
Having worshipped those weapons in the directions, one should worship them in the outer directions;
by this very rite, those who worship the goddess Mahālakṣmī [attain success].
In these [places], the best of practitioners should dwell daily by whatever means possible, remembering his own abode. || 66 ||
Having become the abode of all learning and the source of even those things difficult to obtain, he was a treasury of all prosperity, with his fortune clearly manifest. 67.
Having enjoyed all pleasures here in this world, one goes at the end to the supreme state.
Or else, O beloved, hear of another great enjoyment, which is worship. (68)
The auspicious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇī, consisting of twenty-eight syllables, is the foremost;
it is kept secret in all the Vedas and Tantras by those who know the true meaning of reality.
O Śivā, having uttered the Mahānnapramī and Mahānārāyaṇī mantras three times, one should then recite this Lakṣmī mantra.
Having invoked the Lord of Śrī upon the beautiful Śrīcakra joined with a Śālagrāma stone, by means of the twelve-syllable mantra; 71.
One should perform twenty-four services with devotion to the All-pervading Lord by means of the twenty-four names beginning with Keśava.
Having worshipped Nārāyaṇa with the garland known as *namaḥ-śakti*,
one should thereafter worship the Vidyā of Mahālakṣmīvrata.
Having recited [the mantra] one hundred and eight times daily, or even twenty-eight times, and having performed worship and offered the food offering (naivedya) with devotion, || 74 ||
Worshipping with all the royal services every day, he enjoys daily the fruit of a hundred horse-sacrifices. || 75 ||
He attains the sovereignty of qualities such as *aṇimā* and other powers, the rare perfection of speech, great fortune, and imperishable longevity and health. (76)
Having obtained sons and grandsons, and even the most difficult-to-attain enjoyments upon her head, she reaches the eternal abode at the conclusion of her vow; of this there is no doubt. (77)
O auspicious one, this Vedic worship of Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa, though extremely secret, has been revealed by me; do not reveal it anywhere. 78.
O Daughter of the Mountain, by means of this [mantra], even the Brahmavidyā and other such [practices] are not difficult to attain; indeed, even the secret twenty-eight-syllable Vidyā is [attained].
Remembering Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇī ten times every day,
one who is pure day by day attains the great lore of royal fortune.
A thousand Tulāpuruṣa sacrifices performed with gold, together with the prescribed ancillaries and fees, certainly yield their fruit every single day. || 81 ||
A thousand horse-sacrifices, accompanied by the prescribed ritual fees, were performed by him;
there is no doubt about this, as was also the circumambulation of the earth.
O Daughter of the Mountain, always maintain constant faith;
or else, being pure, worship the Śrīpīṭha individually every single day.
Having remembered the twenty-eight-syllable mantra of Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa and the gracious Lakṣmī, [one should worship] in association with a Śālāgrāma stone. (84)
Having worshipped the two lords, Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa, in the pure Kamalāyantra every day, the best of practitioners becomes purified in soul. (85)
Having meditated twenty-eight times upon the twenty-eight-syllable vidyā named Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa, and [upon] the vidyā named Śrī-hṛdaya; 86.
Having subsequently performed twenty-eight recitations daily for Śivā,
it is equal to a thousand great gifts and a hundred horse-sacrifices.
Having obtained the fruit of giving a thousand elephants and ten million cows, and having become purified, she became equal to Dhanada, O beloved.
Equal to Vācaspati in all branches of knowledge, he was like Kaśyapa in his sons and grandsons, and resembled Kandarpa in his splendor. (89)
Equal to Mahendra in enjoyments and like Brahmā in lifespan,
he shall attain death at his own will, endowed with a multitude of kinsmen.
The embodied soul, beloved of the Blessed One, goes into the presence of the Blessed One;
therein lies the greatness of the Lakṣmī-vidyā, which is the seat of splendor today. (91)
Indeed, it cannot be overcome even by the gods and asuras led by Indra;
wherever that Lakṣmī resides, there alone is perpetual happiness.
There shall be an increase of sons and grandsons, as well as prosperity in wealth, grain, and other assets;
