and there shall be constant growth in righteousness. Therefore, one should always worship Lakṣmī.
The greatness of the worship of Lakṣmī when she is pleased has been briefly described; it is conducive to welfare both in this world and the next. What more do you wish to hear? (94)

[Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Arising of Saubhāgyā," in the latter portion of the *Śrīmad-Anuttara-Brahma-tattva-rahasya*, the *Daśarathi-tantra*, which is a compendium of the essential meaning of the Vedas.]
The Goddess said:
Śrī herself is declared to be Tripurā, Lalitā, and the Mother of the Universe;
having attained Lakṣmī, one obtains eternal auspiciousness as well as enjoyments that are otherwise very difficult to obtain.
Together with a thousand of his kin, he attains the supreme state. || 114 ||

[Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Arising of the Science of Good Fortune," in the latter portion of the *Vedasārārthasaṃgraha*, within the *Dāśarathīya Tantra* known as the *Śrīmadanuttarabrahmatattvarahasya*.]
The venerable Dakṣiṇāmūrti said:
Listen, O you whose limbs are entirely free from defect, to the supreme worship of Śrīvidyā,
through the realization of which one becomes the direct creator and destroyer of heaven.
By this method, wherever the Śrīcakra, which bestows all perfections, is worshipped, there one shall undoubtedly bring everything under control. || 2 ||
O Adrijā, the entire city, the region, and the circle of the country come under his control; all women, nourished and tormented by the blazing fire of desire, become subject to him.
With hearts utterly deluded by worldly knowledge and their minds fixed upon the practitioner,
all women there become filled with doubt upon seeing him.
Relying upon the rosary, which is the Mother (Mātṛkā) in her full form,
one who desires the highest good must certainly recite the Śrīvidyā, the Mother of the Universe.
Now, this [mālā] made of pearls bestows the fruits of speech, mind, and senses;
it eternally grants all perfections and brings all kings under one's control.
Just as one made of pearls, so too one fashioned from crystal;
a rosary of rudrākṣa beads bestows liberation and the fulfillment of all desires.
The coral garland bestows all perfections, granting both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
it is the enchantress of the entire world, providing the abundance of all prosperity.
A rosary of rubies bestows the fruit of universal sovereignty;
a rosary of putrajīva beads grants knowledge and the fortune of prosperity.
By means of a rosary of lotus seeds, great prosperity is born;
however, a garland of red sandalwood is said to bestow all enjoyments.
Having worshipped the rosary made of kuśa-grass knots, which bestows eternal auspiciousness, and having anointed it with sandalwood paste; || 11 ||
When a wise man, relying upon this, recites the vidyā exactly one hundred thousand times,
he surely captivates the minds of women, even if they are perfectly steadfast.
Then the best of practitioners should recite a second hundred thousand;
the daughters of the lords of the nāgas from the depths of the underworld will agitate him.
If he is deluded by the net of their sidelong glances, then the practitioner, with a steady mind, should perform three hundred thousand [recitations]. (14)

When it has been consecrated with one hundred thousand recitations for the third time, celestial nymphs— possessed of pride and intoxicated by the intoxication of their own beauty and good fortune— will speak these words.
It truly causes the practitioner to melt away; one should remain firm-minded in all states of existence.
By its recitation, the three-fold [impurity] is instantly destroyed, and there is a shattering of the accumulation of great sins.
Bestowing great accomplishment and immediately granting the attainment of all sovereign powers, the practitioner with a steady mind should thus recite [the mantra] three hundred thousand times. (17)
O beloved, he agitates the inhabitants of the earth-world and the dwellers of the nether regions; he brings under his control all men and women, whether moving or stationary, throughout the universe.
One should draw the sovereign wheel with substances such as gorocanā and others;
in its center, one should depict the supreme image, exceedingly beautiful and pleasing.
One should meditate upon her, blazing and interlaced with the Kāmarāja mantra,
even from a distance of more than a hundred yojanas.
O Goddess of gods, she who has never been seen before is difficult to find even by mere hearing;
yet she may be a princess or a wife, entirely devoid of fear and shame. (21)
O beloved, if the practitioner, having become situated in the center of the wheel, contemplates the mantra correctly while she is deluded, he becomes a successful adept.

Having visualized oneself as the dawn-colored Aruṇa, shining like the sun with outstretched hands, and likewise having meditated upon Sādhya who has become Aruṇa, one should recite the mantra for Śrī.
By this sequential yoga, one becomes personally like the god of love (Kandarpa) in form, possessing all beauty and charm, and becomes beloved by women. (24)
Fortunate in all worlds, he brings beauty to all the world;
he indeed makes men, women, kings, and others his servants.
One who, with all red offerings and body bound by mudrās, should worship the wheel whose name is interwoven [with the mantra]. (26)
Whether it be one who has mastered all the Vedas or a lord of the earth skilled in all dramatic arts, he should place the name of whichever woman he desires in the center of the wheel. || 27 ||
Even if she has not been seen before, O auspicious one, if one who wears the mudrā recites [the mantra],
then the Yakṣiṇī quickly brings a princess.
Whether it be a princess, a woman of the Akṣaras, a celestial nymph, a Vidyādharī, a divine maiden, or the wife of an enemy—(one should not look at her). || 29 ||
The divine beauty was tormented by the heat arising from passion, her circle of cheeks quivering, and her inner heart pierced by the arrows of Love.
O giver of bliss through the yoga of meditation on the Mahākāmakalā,
you cause agitation in the world of mortals, the netherworld, and those dwelling in the matted locks [of Śiva].
O Goddess, the wise one should take one part of rocanā and the like, one part of saffron,
and two parts of sandalwood from the mountain.
If one recites [the mantra] one hundred and eight times and applies the *tilaka*,
one shall bring under one's control the three worlds, including all men and women of every lineage.
Betel leaf, incense, water, leaves, flowers, fruit, curd, milk, ghee, red lead, cloth, and camphor—these as well. (34)
O Goddess, having recited it one hundred and eight times, whomever one gives it to—be they man or woman—they become submissive; there is no doubt about this.
Indeed, all women become submissive and like female slaves;
this is declared to be the rite of attraction, which certainly deludes the world. (36)
In a secret place, the practitioner should write upon the ground with yellow pigment (rocanā) a beautiful diagram, richly adorned with garlands and beautified by the syllable *Savarkilāra*.
Having painted a beautiful image of a most enchanting woman,
[he drew] the hair, neck, heart, navel, and the circle of the vulva of that woman.
One should write the syllable of Madana at all the joints of the body, interlaced with the Great Vidyā known as Janmanāma-muṅkuśa.
One should not contemplate pomegranate flowers at the joints of the body;
rather, facing toward that [direction], one should oneself become the very form of the Goddess. (40)
Having bound the Saṃkṣobhiṇī mudrā, one should recite the Vidyā one hundred and eight times;
then, having applied it to burning coals which consist of the digits of the moon and the sun.
Then she, with all her limbs distressed, pierced by the arrows of desire,
with no other thought in her mind, was made to wander by love, her very soul absorbed in him.
In this manner, one may attract a woman even from a distance of a hundred yojanas.
O Dear One, one should write the entire Mātṛkā along with the external [elements] within the wheel.
O beloved, one should wear that [amulet] on a golden plate, a silver plate, or a birch bark, or on a copper ring, either on the throat or on the right or left arm.
He shall be invulnerable to all creatures, especially to tigers and the like;
likewise, by worshipping the wheel daily according to the Mātṛkā, he shall be so.
Having become free from old age and death, he dwells among the worlds;
by this method, O King, with *rocanā*, *agara*, and saffron.
O most excellent one, the name of the person to be accomplished (sādhya) should be written using the wheel-arrangement;
it may even be interlaced with another name, situated within whichever [wheel] it may be.
O Great Goddess, one shall bring under control the entire circle of living beings, whether stationary or moving, by treading upon them with one's feet; of this there is no doubt. (47)
By means of the radiant Kāmakūṭa of Mahātripurasundarī, having grasped the single and the many, one should [grasp] the beloved syllables of the name of the target. 48.
One should also cause the Mātṛkā to enter [the body] from the outside with all the phonemes;
having placed gold in the center, one should wear it on the crest-lock or on both arms.
I shall wear this mantra, which brings the three worlds under its control, wherever I may be;
for it indeed makes even Indra, the lord of the gods, a servant. (50)
Indeed, kings, common people, serpents, elephants, wicked great crowds, tigers, and even ferocious lions become submissive [to him]. (51)
Having first prepared that clay according to the prescribed sequence,
one should place it in the center, or alternatively, one should deposit it in the four directions.
A great agitation arises among women, among common people, and even among the great;
likewise, it arises for all those who stand before the wicked. (53)
Within this [egg] was the earth, together with its mountains, forests, and groves,
blazing and adorned by all the lords of kings, along with the excellent oceans.
O beloved, he who meditates for sixty months upon her whose form is like that of Kāma himself— she becomes subject to him by the mere casting of a sidelong glance.
O Goddess, from the king come the Brāhmaṇas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, animals, and the entire world; having merely seen him, he would beautify the three worlds, including all things mobile and immobile.
One should kill even those with their companions by means of the gaze; no deliberation is required here regarding spirits, ghosts, piśācas, or even quartan fevers. (57)
O beloved, this auspicious sindūra, when worshipped at night, destroys diseases such as abdominal tumors and swellings by its mere sight in an instant.
O Īśvarī, when one has thus performed the rite according to the rules in all directions and intermediate points, one shall correctly attract a beloved person from even a thousand yojanas away.
Having written [the name] on birch bark with yellow pigment (rocanā), agallochum (agaru), and saffron (kuṅkuma), one quickly brings under control that son, along with his cattle and kinsmen.
In the midst of that, one should properly worship even a mere morsel of meat, thoroughly infused with the name of a city, a country, a mandala, or a region.
One brings the three worlds under one's control for as long as one lives; of this there is no doubt.
Alternatively, one should wear it on the neck, on the crest-lock, or on both arms.
O auspicious lady, wherever you may be situated, you should agitate the city of Dīpa with the juice of the *dhuttūra* plant combined with the milky sap of the sun-plant (*arka*).
Then, having combined together rocanā with saffron, lac with saffron, and musk with camphor; || 64 ||
Having drawn that wheel and worshipping it with the name of anyone, one protects them from the fear of tigers, elephants, flowers, stones, serpents, and so forth. (65)
O Great Goddess, no fear arises from thieves, planetary afflictions, water-demons, śākinīs, or ḍākinīs, nor from the malevolent incantations of supreme mantras. (66)
The wheel, revolving constantly, shall destroy timely death;
or else, O Goddess, it should be situated in the center, with the triangle on both sides.
Furthermore, having placed his name joined with *rocanā* and marked with *kuṅkuma*, one should bury it for seven days; from that, what cannot be accomplished? (68)
Having drawn [the diagram] with yellow substances, one should worship it with yellow flowers;
facing the eastern direction, one should overcome the arguments of opponents.
Through respect for consensus, the assembly becomes mute at that very moment. || 70 ||
O Goddess of the Gods, having inscribed the wheel with the juice of great sapphire, that person who possesses this becomes like a stone, mute and motionless.
The wise man, having joined the name [of the deceased] according to the prescribed rule, should face the southern direction.
O Maheśānī, O beloved, having burnt [the enemy] in fire,
one should kill the adversary by drawing together the excrement of a buffalo and that which is produced from a Śūla.
Having drawn the diagram in cow's urine and not applying the seal as before,
but casting it into the middle of a lotus stalk, it will become a means for inciting enmity.
Having written the name with yellow pigment (rocanā) in the middle of a crow’s wing-feather,
while that [feather] was suspended in the sky, she uttered words of incantation for the purpose of summoning Śakra.
Having drawn [the figure] with mahānīla and rocanā, and with milk and lac juice,
the practitioner who wears it shall bring all castes under his control.
Having drawn [the diagram], the practitioner holding the mantra shall bring all castes under his control;
by this very procedure, he should place it in the middle of the water.
Bathed with that water and having drunk it, one gains complete mastery; there is no doubt that good fortune arises for him through whatever [means] he employs.
O fair-eyed one, having then concentrated on the earth or the city situated in the middle of this [fire],
one should meditate upon it as being completely ablaze.
Having worshipped the golden wheel with flowers, roots, fruits, and sacred texts,
one is freed from both great sins and minor sins within a month.
Having attained a fortune equal to that of Mahendra, filled with wealth and sounds of prosperity, as well as a long life and glory endowed with the eight qualities; || 80 ||
Having attained the eightfold yoga, he was honored even by the gods;
endowed with the prosperity of sons, grandsons, and more, he enjoyed divine pleasures.
Having worshipped the Night-Cakra, he dwells with unimpeded movement throughout all worlds, possessing the steady fortune of sovereignty.
Having attained long life and even the most magnificent knowledge,
as well as the abundance of sons and grandsons, he shall attain the supreme state.
By worshipping the Copper Discus (Tāmracakra), one obtains a hundred lineages; there is no doubt about this, and one is liberated from all sins.
The lord of wealth (Kubera), endowed with great intelligence and accompanied by his sons and others, having renounced all enjoyments here, shall attain the state of Brahman in the end. || 85 ||
Having worshipped daily this wheel made of jewels, which bestows abundant success,
one attains here a mass of welfare with a splendor equal to that of the Giver of Wealth (Kubera).
Living as one equal to Vāc, endowed with the happiness of sons and grandsons,
long-lived, and having enjoyed abundant pleasures, he shall attain liberation at the end.
Facing the eastern direction, one should draw [the diagram] with sandalwood paste;
having worshipped it with yellow substances, one shall paralyze all disputants.
Facing the northern direction, the wise man should draw the lion-king;
by worshipping him according to the prescribed rite, he shall bring all the world under his control.
Facing the western direction, the wise man should draw [the diagram] with sandalwood paste;
having worshipped it according to the rules, he shall become beloved by women.
If one faces a direction other than that which one has intended while worshipping the black discus, the loss of the mantra occurs for whichever name is inscribed upon it. || 91 ||
Furthermore, O Rākṣasa, a pillar worshipped in the corners of Śambhu causes hatred, disease, and the eradication of enemies. (92)
A wheel inscribed with a golden stylus using yellow pigment, saffron, and other substances, when worshipped daily, is said to bestow great accomplishment (mahāsiddhi). || 93 ||
A wheel drawn with yellow pigment (rocanā) should be placed in the midst of milk;
O Goddess, it brings about the subjugation of all—of this there is no doubt.
The King of Wheels (cakrarāja) properly situated in cow urine causes the subjugation of Indra; however, when situated in oil, it causes enmity and piercing of the enemy. || 95 ||
Standing amidst blazing fire, it shall bring about the destruction of enemies;
when one writes [the mantra] with vermilion on a path in a secluded place, it becomes effective. (96)
O Goddess, the practitioner becomes a sky-walker (khecara); of this there is no doubt.
Likewise, one who contemplates the king of wheels (cakrarājaka) within either of the two mountains [Girīśa and Eka-śṛṅga]. || 97 ||
Having become free from old age and death, the wise one, being happy,
should worship the wheel of the great elements in the cremation ground on the day of Budha.
At midnight, by means of bilva leaves and even with these excellent flowers, one immediately obtains the *cuṭikā* and the sandals of the people. (99)
The accomplishment of the sword, the great accomplishment of mercury, the accomplishment of the great chasm, and also the accomplishment of the yakṣiṇī. (100)
One attains this; there is no doubt here. This is the truth, the truth, spoken by me in truth:
on the day of the great element (earth), conjoined with the day of Mars (Tuesday) and joined with the moon. 101.
There, having observed the fast for a thousand, three hundred, or even one hundred days,
and having subsequently recited [the mantra] three hundred times and performed the twilight devotions (saṃdhyopāsana), he attains the goal.
And having recited [the mantra] one thousand and one hundred times there again for Śivā,
one should then lift up the Śrīcakra along with its pedestal, using fragrant leaves and flowers.
Having installed the Jātavedas fire according to the ritual rules in its presence,
one who is pure should offer one hundred and eight oblations before it with the Gāyatrī mantra.
Having offered oblations with the rays of Lalitā just once,
thereafter one should offer clarified butter just once for each of the goddesses of the new enclosure.
Then, having reverently offered one thousand three hundred oblations of pure cow-ghee into the fire with the Śrīvidyā mantra, followed by the four Śrīmanus; || 106 ||
Having offered oblations twenty-eight times individually into the fire (jātavedas),
one should then offer oblations with recitations and other rites, and perform the oblation of dedication to Brahman (brahmārpaṇa).
Having circumambulated the fire and prostrated like a staff with eight limbs at the two feet of his own preceptor, he honored him with garments, ornaments, and other gifts.
Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, whatever and however much has been continuously provided, he should offer his entire wealth as a gift at the two feet of the preceptor.
Having offered whatever wealth has been prostrated before Yaśīśa, or before the feet of the Ācārya,
one should present a collection of ornaments to the Ācārya’s wife.
Having immediately obtained the hundredfold fruit of the *puraścaryā*,
the practitioner attains a sword, a pair of sandals, and a supreme, divine person.
Having attained the supreme accomplishment of base metals, as well as the accomplishment of the *ghurikā* pill, or the accomplishment of flight, or even the great accomplishment; (112)
Having pervaded himself with the powers such as atomization (āṇimā) and being freed from old age and death,
he became twenty-five years of age, resembling the god of love (Kandarpa).
With this very body, he sports in the Nandana and other groves with celestial maidens, enjoying pleasures as he desires.
An object equal to the Śrīvidyā is not seen anywhere;
nor is there anything worthy of worship like the Śrīcakra even within the three worlds. (115)

[Thus ends the eleventh chapter in the *Śrīmadanuttarabrahmatattvarahasya*, the *Dāśarathīya Tantra*, a compendium of the essential meaning of the Vedas, in its latter portion, within the *Saubhāgyavidyodaya*.]
The Goddess said:
This Śrīvidyā, known as Trikūṭā and proclaimed as Lalitā, is the venerable Rudrā;
O Lord of the World, tell me the means of accomplishment for these three seed-syllables.
The venerable Dakṣiṇāmūrti said:
Listen, O Goddess, to this great knowledge, the most supreme of all;
by the mere performance of which one does not sink into the ocean of worldly existence.
O Dear One, Tripurā is the supreme primordial power,
the mother of the three worlds who transcends them through her division into the gross and the subtle, and whose path is knowledge.
She is the very nature of the swallowing of all principles without remainder;
when she has undergone transformation, nothing else whatsoever is perceived.
Even another, being devoid of power, is unable to do anything;
O Supreme Goddess, he would become capable only when he is endowed with power.
In the subtle Śiva, who is the bearer of names, there exists no power or the like; even when known, it brings neither great splendor nor any worldly fruit.
But at the time of supporting oneself through meditation, there is neither thought, nor perception, nor stability;
having entered the supreme guest, she exists in the form of a subtle nature.
Having swallowed everything without remainder, she exists as the sprout of the seed;
thus Vāmā is Śivā, and likewise Jyeṣṭhā has attained the state of the Śṛṅgāṭikā.
But Rauvadrī, O Supreme Goddess, is the embodiment of the essence of the universe;
thus, she alone is the one supreme power, the Supreme Goddess. (8)
O Goddess, Tripurā is threefold, having the forms of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Īśa;
she consists of the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti), the power of action (kriyā-śakti), and the power of will (icchā-śakti), O beloved.
The one Tripurā, celebrated as supreme, creates the three worlds when she,
in her crooked form, shines forth from the Śṛṅgāṭa seat.
Having pierced the solar orb of Śiva and causing the grove of trees to melt away,
she was delighted by the supreme bliss of tasting the nectar produced therefrom.
A woman who is said to belong to a noble family goes to another man—
one who is without distinguishing marks, devoid of virtues, and bereft of lineage and beauty.
Then, having wandered through the world in her own free form,
she, the solitary one, being satisfied, returned by that same path.
The unmanifest Tripurā herself delights [in this state], having attained manifestation;
she is designated as the three principles (tattvas), the power of the phonemes (varṇa-śakti) whose essence is Śiva. 14.
Vāgīśvarī is the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti) in the Vāgbhava [bīja], whose form is liberation;
in the Kāmarāja [bīja], she is the digit of desire (kāma-kalā), whose nature is action (kriyā) and whose form is desire.
In the seed-syllable of Śakti, the Supreme Power (Parāśakti) is indeed Will (Icchā) in the form of Śiva;
thus the Goddess, the three-syllabled Śrī Mahātripurasundarī, [is established]. 16.
When understood through the transmission of the lineage, it liberates one from the bonds of existence;
when remembered, it pacifies sins; and when recited, it destroys death.
When worshipped, she destroys suffering, misfortune, disease, and poverty;
when offered oblations, she pacifies calamities; and when meditated upon, she accomplishes all goals.
O Goddess of the gods, hear now the method for accomplishing the three seed-syllables (bījas) of this [mantra]:
wearing white garments and anointed with pure sandalwood paste. (19)
A man devoted to celibacy, wearing ornaments of shimmering pearls and bearing white garlands, should worship with offerings of flowers and unhusked grains.
Having offered white food offerings such as curd, milk-rice, and so forth, or even having mentally conceived white food offerings for Śiva; 21.
One should worship Vāgīśī with beautiful fragrant flowers;
she is white as camphor and adorned with bright flowers and ornaments. || 22 ||
Wearing exceedingly white garments and adorned with ornaments of diamonds and pearls,
her hands were radiant with a rosary made of pearls and excellent gems.
O Maheśānī, one should meditate thus upon her holding a book, a boon-granting gesture, and a vessel that bestows fearlessness; thereby one shall become a sovereign of all sciences.

One should meditate on [the goddess] at the tip of the tongue, in the form of a lamp, consisting of the light of Brahman, raining down nectar, and flowing from the base up to the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra). 25.
Reciting the Vāgmaṇḍala-khaṇḍa a thousand times while pure,
one becomes like a stone, or even mute, or like a beast.

Whether one is a villager, a fool, or a sinner, or even one devoid of the Vedic path, or one whose mind is lost and whose intellect is dull—such a person is called a villager, a fool, or a sinner. (27)
Whether he be deceitful, unable to speak even a single clear syllable,
dull-witted, mute, like a beast, blind, extremely foolish, or one whose intellect and livelihood have perished— (28)
He too becomes eloquent in speech, like Vācaspati or even superior;
he speaks words of truth, is skillful in debate, and his brilliance remains unassailed.

Being vigilant and knowing the meaning of words and sentences, as well as all poetic figures of sound, he should compose [the work] with the same skill as one would describe the garlands of waves on an ocean struck by the wind. (30)
O Goddess, one who possesses the ornaments of form such as *isphāra* and the like, and who is skilled in the *pradagu* meters, becomes a composer of great poetry (*mahākāvya*). || 31 ||
He was a knower of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences (vedāṅgas), one who had reached the further shore of the knowledge of the established doctrines (siddhānta),
and a master of the science of astrology, history, the Mīmāṃsā, and the declarations of the Smṛtis.

He was an expert in the Purāṇas, the Rāmāyaṇa, the Mahābhārata, and the Gāruḍa; he was a knower of the rituals of the Atharva Veda, a master of the Pātālaśāstra, and one who understood the essence of the Tantras.
He was an expert eye for many crafts such as variegated painting and other arts; he was a master of the great grammars and a knower of the essential principles regarding the blending of words.
He possesses knowledge that surpasses all languages, performs all types of rites, understands the meaning of various scriptures and their training, and is renowned throughout the world. (35)
O Goddess, one becomes a knower of all speech and omniscient;
O Goddess, the majesty of Vāgīśvarī has thus been recounted to you. (36)
Thereafter, I shall proclaim the majesty of Kāmarāja;
then the practitioner, devoted to the expansion of desire, becomes the Supreme Lord. (37)
Adorned with red ornaments, beautiful due to the application of red sandalwood paste,
and properly clothed in red garments, he is the very essence of the arts of love in his central form.
One should worship with various red flowers, saffron,
and other offerings [the Goddess] who has the nature of a shimmering lamp, extending from the root center to the aperture of Brahma.
Adorned with ornaments possessing the luster of the *vaṃdhūka* flower,
she holds sugarcane stalks and flowers in her hands, which shine with the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
O Supreme Goddess, meditating upon the three worlds filled with the vermilion of His form, one should then recite the Kāmarāja mantra.
O Lord, the practitioner instantly deludes the three worlds;
kings, serpents, rākṣasas, and gods all come under his control.
O Goddess of the lords of gods, she who steals away one's pride through the power of passion— she shall become a servant submissive to one's will, even if she has merely been thought of in the mind.
One who follows that view may be a male practitioner or a female practitioner, a Vidyādharī, a Kinnarī, or even a Yakṣa or Nāga woman. (44)
The daughter of the fierce king of men was a Naga maiden,
her heart scorched by the blazing fire of love.
O Goddess, she becomes moist, agitated, offering herself, bewildered, overwhelmed by intoxication, having surrendered her entire being, and comes under his control. (46)
Resembling moving water and reddened by the rays of the rising sun, she was instantly agitated by the sight of Citrāṅgadā’s body.
This very [mantra], when meditated upon, instantly draws from the right [side] one who has the luster of vermilion—be it a man or even Tilottamā herself; of this there is no doubt. 48.
Having meditated upon Śrī, who is red in color, and being enveloped by her splendor,
one should remember the seed-syllable (bīja) upon her head, raining down a shower of nectar.
Chanted, it indeed causes delusion even to the beautiful celestial women;
through the two channels (nāḍīs), it may delude even the entire three worlds.
Moreover, O fair-faced one, through meditation on the arts of love, the five objects of desire delude the entire world; listen now to the ritual application [of this].

O Goddess of the gods, the previously mentioned five-fold desires are to be understood; having performed the *vidarbha* [interlocking] with the first desire, place the mantra within that very desire. (52)
O fair-faced one, having formed the Kaṃdarpa-sampuṭa, all of that which is situated in the middle of the corners is known as the Makaradhvaja. 53.
One should make the mind wander and delude this world;
this yoga is proclaimed as "Mohana" (the Deluder) throughout the three worlds. || 54 ||
Listen, O Goddess, I shall explain the practice of the seed-syllable of Śakti:
one should contemplate the Supreme (Parā) within the body, from the base (mūla) up to the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra). 55.
Flowing with streams of nectar, she rains down the destroyer of poison;
possessing the luster of gold, she is measured by the month and has a radiance equal to lightning.
She holds a jar filled with the digits of the moon and displays the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, as well as the gesture of knowledge; she is the very embodiment of nectar.
A practitioner of mantras, meditating upon her, can remove poison existing in various forms;
O Goddess, by the mere remembrance of her, even Śiva attained the state of having a blue throat.
Having become a conqueror of death, I shall indeed wander among the three worlds;
there is no practitioner of mantra equal to you, who can dispel thousands of burdens of poison.
It shall destroy the multitude of diseases caused by bhūtas, pretas, and piśācas;
it shall eliminate quartan fevers, chronic fevers, and those fevers that recur every eighth day.
Merely by the sight of the Nāgas, it causes paralysis; when burning, it has the appearance of nectar and is remembered as being like a stream of milk. || 61 ||

It is the destroyer of poisons and secondary poisons known as "stable" and "artificial," as well as [the afflictions caused by] evil diseases, hosts of seizing spirits (grahas), and the groups of Śākinīs and Rūpikās.
To the bhūtas, pretas, and piśācas, she appears as the three-eyed goddess;
then, she is the Mahātripurasundarī who completely fills the Trikūṭa mountain.
Once consecrated, it quickly destroys all the sins of the practitioner;
it bestows the fruit of all merit and brings all the worlds under one's control. (64)
Situated in the center of the navel-mandala, she resembles a hundred rising suns;
when chanted in the morning, she possesses a reddish luster, residing in the heart-lotus at midday.
Thereafter, at the time of evening, she, resembling molten gold,
established the luster of a ruby in the center of her facial orb.
O Śivā, by remembering and reciting [this] even before the three watches of the night,
the practitioner attains the eightfold sovereign powers and exceedingly great good fortune.
In that darkness, even by merely remembering her, one becomes dear to the Yoginīs; for him who possesses compassion for his own self in the contemplation of the Śrī-vidyā, [this occurs]. (68)
O lady of pure smiles, for him there is no fear of birth-impurity (sūtaka) or the like; he is eternally pure.
One should constantly engage Mahātripurasundarī in the practice of *tipata*. 69.
In that very way, the command from the Mother’s mouth is transmitted into his body;
he shall become beloved by all the Yoginīs who abide in every form.
O beloved, if Śrī is constantly recited in its entirety, that practitioner becomes like another son to you, O Sāṃsākṣat, as if he were your own.
The supreme success of Khecarī and the incomparable Yoga are swiftly accomplished by him,
for there are sixty-four crores of Yoginīs of great splendor [who reside therein].
Having resorted to that [mantra], she remained there, O Adored One; and having fully recited the Trikūṭī, she became Mahātripurasundarī. (73)
During her fertile period, on the sixth, eighth, tenth, twelfth,
or even the sixteenth day, he should approach his emaciated wife at night.
O Pāṇi, we obtained a son equal to Nārāyaṇa, named Āpuṣmanta Paśīkhana,
who was enriched with all branches of knowledge, possessed of great wealth, and endowed with good fortune.
Having attained this, he shall always be endowed with all that is most auspicious;
O Goddess of the Gods, there exists no knowledge whatsoever equal to this.
Having propitiated this very Vidyā, which deludes the three worlds, the Blessed Lord Hari assumed a form that deludes the three worlds. (77)
O Goddess of the gods, even Kāmadeva, having propitiated Mahātripurasundarī, became the most beautiful one in the world, endowed with all auspicious fortune. 78.
O lady of excellent vows, even now, while established in this very vow, I perform the recitation of this [mantra] at both twilights for the sake of attaining all fruits. (79)
By the daily worship of the limbs of dissolution (layāṅga), one attains wealth, good fortune, and eloquence;
having become a treasury of great fortune, one reaches the supreme state at the end.
Whether at midday or at the end of the day, one who casts off the cycle of rebirth by casting it aside attains all auspicious blessings and is honored even by the gods.
By worshipping him alone, one becomes a creator of the world like Brahmā;
even the moon and the sun are the agents of the creation and destruction of the universe.

[Thus ends the twelfth chapter in the *Śrīmadanuttarabrahmatattvarahasya*, the *Dāśarathīya Tantra*, which is a compendium of the essential meaning of the Vedas, in its latter portion, within the *Saubhāgyavidyodaya*.]
The Goddess said:
O you who possess ten auspicious hands, O observer of noble vows, please tell us the procedure for japa so that obstacles may be destroyed for the benefit of practitioners.
The venerable Dakṣiṇāmūrti said:
Listen, O Goddess, my beloved; I shall explain the procedure for recitation and fire-offerings (japa-homa), by the mere hearing of which the practitioner shall partake of the nature of Brahman.
O Goddess, one should worship the Cakra daily with all its limbs;
thus, one obtains daily the inexhaustible fruit of the horse sacrifice along with its ancillaries. || 3 ||
Having performed the *sayoga-pūjā* daily with his senses subdued,
the husband and wife obtain the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice and are liberated from all sins.
Having worshipped a copper discus and, being pure, having recited the Śrīsūkta daily,
one who is liberated from all calamities attains great and inexhaustible prosperity.

Having attained this great knowledge, one becomes a possessor of prosperity through sons and grandsons; at the end of his life, he truly dwells in the world of Brahmā along with ten ancestors and ten descendants.
Having worshipped the discus at night and recited the Śrīsūkta day after day,
one is liberated even from most terrible major and minor sins.
One attains royal fortune and becomes a master of all branches of knowledge;
having attained great prosperity accompanied by sons, grandsons, and others.
Having enjoyed all pleasures here on earth, he shall always be long-lived and victorious;
like Viṣṇu himself, he shall uplift hundreds of lineages.
Having worshipped the golden disc daily with devotion,
the practitioner, day by day, obtains the complete fruit of the horse sacrifice along with its ancillary rites.
He was liberated from terrible sins committed even over ten million lifetimes;
[he beheld] a city completely filled with pearls and gems, and abounding in wealth and grain.
Having attained here itself a splendor equal to that of Mahendra, the practitioner gains health, flowers for his heart, and a beauty resembling that of Kandarpa.
Having attained the mastery of all branches of knowledge, he, radiant with wisdom, shall be endowed with long life, prosperity, and fame, together with sons, grandsons, and other progeny. (13)
Having attained great prosperity and enjoyed pleasures difficult to obtain,
he rejoices in the station of Yama, accompanied by a thousand kinsmen.
Having constantly worshipped the wheel made of jewels with purity and devotion,
one becomes like Kāma in the auspicious world, possessing the splendor of a sovereign through this knowledge.
Endowed with the splendor of wisdom through the Vidyā along with Lakṣmī and Dhanada,
one enjoys all pleasures here in this world and, at the end, proceeds to the supreme state.
Having propitiated the King of Mandalas (cakrarāja), the bestower of fruits, with all ritual services,
one should constantly recite [the mantra] a thousand times, or otherwise five hundred times.
One should recite [the mantra] four hundred times daily, or three hundred, or two hundred; otherwise, one falls into a lower state of existence. (18)
Having exhausted the entire fruit [of his actions], he eternally attains that which bestows perfection,
facing westward in the southern region, when the sign of Taurus is empty, for the sake of Śiva.
Alternatively, whether in the presence of the Ācārya or even in the temple of the Lord,
wherever the presence of the Ācārya is, there is the presence of half of the Cakrarāja.
A divine field has been designated there, level and extending for a yojana;
on the eleventh or twelfth lunar day of the month of Māgha, one should remain pure, O auspicious lady.
Beginning from [the day of] Śivarātri until its conclusion, the practitioner, firm in his vows,
should bring the Preceptor into proximity and worship the King of Mandalas (Cakrarāja).
Eating fruits, or eating sacrificial offerings, or eating milk, with his senses subdued, O Goddess, he should eat but one meal a day while reciting the Gāyatrī many times.
Having worshipped the Cakrarāja with devotion, along with its limbs and enclosures,
one should daily recite the fifteen-syllable Śrīvidyā mantra one thousand times.
Then, having offered more than a hundred oblations, one should daily offer one hundred and eight;
likewise, one should always maintain three female residents (vāsinīs), each being a virtuous resident (vāsuvāsinī).
Then, having fed them with delicious foods and gratified them with sacrificial gifts (dakṣiṇā),
he remained fasting for the remainder of the month of Māgha, restrained by his vow.
Having bathed in the evening, he then worshipped the desired Cakrarāja at the outskirts of the city of Ayodhyā and respectfully set out on his journey.
Then, during that night, once Nala had been consecrated according to the rules, the practitioner, having worshipped the goddess Śrī upon the sacrificial fire, [proceeded].
Having first melted the ghee once with the *raśmi-vidyās*, one should reverently offer the ghee to each of the goddesses of the nine enclosures one by one. (29)
Then, having offered one thousand three hundred oblations of pure cow-ghee with the fifteen-syllable mantra in the presence of the preceptor for the sake of Śrī; || 30 ||
Having offered ghee twenty-eight times with the four Lakṣmī-mantras, one should then perform oblations by means of recitation and other rites. (29)
Then, having offered one thousand three hundred oblations of pure cow-ghee with the fifteen-syllable mantra of Śrī in the presence of the preceptor, [one should proceed].
Having offered ghee twenty-eight times with the four Lakṣmī-mantras,
and then having offered oblations through recitation (japa) and other rites, he should perform the Brahmārpaṇa oblation.
O Daughter of the Mountain, having circumambulated the fire and withdrawn Śrī into oneself,
one should again worship the Cakrarāja along with its limbs.
Having respectfully prostrated with eight limbs before the pair of feet of the Teacher,
[he offered] a golden vessel adorned with sixty marks and joined with a drop of jewels.
Then one should give a pair of earrings for the ears of the preceptor,
or else gold as a substitute offering, or a pair of auspicious garments.
One should offer excellent ornaments such as rings,
give many houses, and bestow inexhaustible wealth and food.
One should give a cow endowed with abundant milk and accompanied by its calf;
or else, one should offer wealth equal to a year's worth of food at the lotus feet of the preceptor.
One who is strictly observant of the vow should offer a pair of garments;
the wealth [to be given] is said to be measured by the annual food-ration, which is declared to be one hundred niṣkas.
One should abandon greed for even a single cowrie or half of one;
or else, [one should give] twenty-one *niṣkas* or even a single *niṣka* according to one's caste.
Or one may offer a golden coin to the Sun; having thus performed this formidable and most excellent preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) according to the rule, one attains great success.
He certainly attains success that is difficult to obtain and most exalted;
[he should give] a golden coin weighing one karṣa to the wife of the preceptor.
One should offer thirty golden ornaments for the neck and present a very fine garment made of linen or cotton.
Having kept a vigil at night and worshipped Śrī while remaining pure,
one attains eternal perfection as well as exceedingly great prosperity.
If that fourteenth day is joined with Mars at midnight,
having performed the preliminary ritual (puraścaryā) for this vidyā one thousand times there, [one attains success].
The practitioner certainly attains the fruit; there is no doubt in this matter.
Even sins such as the killing of a Brahmin perish for him at that very moment.
Then, at dawn, the practitioner obtains the complete fruit of a thousand horse-sacrifices and of the Vājapeya sacrifice. (45)
Having first performed with devotion the ritual of the boat along with its constituent parts and coverings,
and having worshipped the King of Mandalas (cakrarāja), one should [worship] a milch cow together with her calf and its limbs.
Then, having offered it to the preceptor and given him a sacrificial fee at night,
the observer of the vow should satisfy fifteen married women with food containing the six flavors.
When he has the means, the practitioner, being pure, should offer garments, sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā), and so forth,
along with the water used for washing the pair of feet of the Preceptor.
Having drunk [it], he should then respectfully consume the food remaining from his meal;
in that very forest, he beholds the Goddess, the sovereign of his own prosperity.
If the practitioner offers the highest sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) at the lotus feet of the Ācārya,
he beholds Śrī herself directly with his own eyes.
Having given a middling gift or even a small gift, she beholds prosperity upon prosperity and her beloved husband in a dream on that day. (51)
From that time forward, his day becomes one of great fortune;
there is inexhaustible and vast prosperity, abounding in wealth, grain, and other riches. (52)
Having become his servant, she remains by that water without a doubt;
the goddess of speech herself becomes present in his speech without a doubt. (53)
During the Navarātra of Āśvina or the Navarātra of Vasanta, having recited the fifteen-syllable mantra of Śrī one thousand times; 54.

Having offered oblations according to the previously stated rule and having given the aforementioned great sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), one attains supreme success and indeed becomes like this [the deity]. || 55 ||
Beginning from the third day of the Akṣaya [fortnight], one who is firm in his vows,
with the permission of the preceptor, should recite the Śrīsūkta, which bestows desired prosperity, a thousand times.
Having performed the recitation until the end of the full moon, thereafter, on the day of the full moon,
[one should offer] boiled rice mixed with curd, honey, and clarified butter, along with the products of the *yava* plant.
Having performed more than one thousand oblations according to the ritual procedure with fruits devoid of seeds but accompanied by parched grain (lāja), preceded by the Raśmividyā mantra; 58.
Then, having offered oblations with the Jaya-mantras and others, and having performed the Brahmārpaṇa oblation,
one should daily worship the King of Wheels (Cakrarāja) together with its limbs and enclosures.
Then, being pure, he should worship fifteen women with the thought that they are the Goddess Śrī,
offering them jaggery-water, curd-rice, and also charming fruits.
Having satisfied them with those [required] fees and ritual offerings,
one should thereafter prostrate like a staff before the Preceptor in the presence of the Śrīcakra.
Having given two cows accompanied by plenty of milk, having adorned them with ornaments, and having offered a pair of garments; || 62 ||
The wealth [obtained] as the measure for the rainy-season seat, or half of that, should be set aside;
it should be stored later and not kept like a staff.
Having given two milch-cows accompanied by abundant milk, having adorned them with ornaments, and having offered a pair of garments; || 62 ||
One should give as the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) wealth amounting to one year’s worth of food, or half of that, or even a quarter of that, or even five niṣkas.
Having offered a golden ornament according to her preference and also a garment to the preceptor’s wife, the observer of the vow should then feed those remaining from that [offering].
Having performed this, one attains great and eternal perfection;
there is great flowers, health, and prosperity endowed with the eight qualities.
There shall be abundance of wealth and grain, as well as great prosperity; there shall be good fortune equal to that of Kāmadeva, and also various kinds of knowledge. (66)
He attains success within this very year; of this there is no doubt.
The wise have declared that without such success, there is no accomplishment of any rites whatsoever.
One should accomplish one's desired goals immediately after attaining perfection,
by whatever swift means possible, through the full grace of the Guru.
Then his knowledge is perfected, and even divinity is not difficult for him to attain,
provided he meditates upon the King of Mandalas (cakrarāja) accompanied by mental worship.
A wise person should undertake the commencement of the recitation; even one who has committed great sins is liberated from them.
One should always perform the recitation either audibly, in a whisper, or mentally.
O Supreme Goddess, *nigada* is clearly articulated with distinct speech;
that which vibrates from the unmanifest (*avyakta*) is proclaimed as *upāṃśu*, O lady of radiant countenance. (71)
But that which is recited by means of the tongue while contemplating Your form during the ascent [of the breath] is also called mental (mānasa). || 72 ||
O fair-faced daughter of the mountain, a hundred thousand recitations performed aloud are equal to a single whispered recitation.
O beautiful one, even a hundred thousand recitations performed in a single moment with the *upāṃśu* method in the heart-lotus are not equal to a single recitation performed mentally. (74)

Meditating with the intellect upon the imperishable, from syllable to syllable and from word to word, that which is recited is declared to be mental *japa*; it bestows the perfection of destruction [of sins]. (75)

One who, with his body bound by mudrās, worships the Cakra along with its limbs, and recites [the mantra] one hundred thousand times while worshipping the King of Chakras (Cakrarāja), [attains success]. || 76 ||

Whoever recites this mantra one hundred thousand times is freed from terrible and great sins, whether committed in old age, youth, or childhood, and whether during waking, dreaming, or deep sleep. (77)
Whether committed through mind, action, or speech, and even those performed through knowledge or ignorance, one is liberated from the collection of minor sins; there is no doubt in this matter. (78)
One who recites the fifteen-syllable mantra of Śrī two hundred thousand times is liberated even from the sins of killing a Brahmin, consuming liquor, stealing gold, and so forth. (79)
One is liberated from the great sins (mahāpātaka) along with heaps of minor sins (upapātaka), even those committed over ten million lifetimes; of this there is no doubt. (80)
Having worshipped the Cakrarāja and having recited the fifteen-syllable mantra of Śrī three hundred thousand times, the practitioner of mantra obtains the fruit of a thousand horse sacrifices.
Having attained the fruit, the one whose self is purified is honored even by the gods;
he who recites four hundred thousand times while worshipping the King of Mantras (Yakṣarāja) [attains this]. || 82 ||
Even though he is insentient, all branches of knowledge shine forth from his discus.
He who, being self-restrained, recites this five-hundred-thousand-fold [mantra] shall undoubtedly become a great poet and a master of great speech, and he shall obtain the desired prosperity. (85)
This treasury of all knowledge, resembling Vyāsa and Vālmīki, becomes like Kubera and is constantly endowed with prosperity. (86)
Having become undecaying, he attains the inexhaustible fruit.
He who recites the mantra six hundred thousand times while worshipping the King of Mandalas (cakrarāja) [attains the fruit]. || 87 ||
Having become a master of the sciences and the sovereign of the Vidyādharas,
he attained omniscience after a long time, which is the greatest of flowers.
Having obtained this, one enriched with divine enjoyments attains everything desired;
one acquires great sovereignty abounding in pearls, gems, and other treasures. (89)
He who recites seven hundred thousand times this Śrī-vidyā, which bestows its fruit, shall be endowed with elephants, horses, chariots, and male and female servants.
Having become free from old age and death at the age of twenty-five,
and having attained supreme good fortune, he possessed an abundance of wealth, grain, and other riches.
She is perpetually worshipped even by Śakra and the other eight guardians of the quarters;
he who recites the mantra of Mahātripurasundarī eight hundred thousand times [attains this].
Having attained the eightfold yoga along with its three constituents, and being endowed with the eight supernatural powers, he conquered timely death and became free from old age and mortality.

Having attained the state of moving through the air (khecaratva), he ascends a celestial chariot (vimāna) filled with clusters of wish-fulfilling gems (cintāmaṇi) and endowed with the cow of plenty (kāmadhenu).
Residing within a grove of wish-fulfilling trees in the palace of the king of the gods and other celestial abodes,
he sports with divine maidens, as beautiful as the god of love himself.
Having become twenty years of age, Tripurasundarī, the presiding deity over all the Siddhas, should employ [the mantra] measuring nine hundred thousand [recitations].
Freed from old age and death, devoid of wrinkles and grey hair,
he attains the eightfold sovereign powers beginning with *aṇimā*, as well as the state of moving through the sky.
O Lord of the gods, he who constantly recites the fifteen-syllable mantra of Śrī one hundred thousand times sports forever with divine maidens. (98)
He alone is the creator, the destroyer, and also the protector of the worlds;
he is omniscient, fortunate, eloquent, and has reached the further shore of all branches of knowledge. 99.
With this very body, free from old age and death,
he shall enjoy for twenty-five years a splendor endowed with the eight qualities.
Having attained [this state], he was honored by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Īśa, Śakra, and the hosts of Maruts;
and having acquired the eightfold yoga, he even attained the power of moving through the sky.
He is sought after by divine maidens, he understands the speech of animals, he enters the bodies of others, and he becomes a possessor of divine enjoyments. (102)
Constantly worshipped even by the Brahman-sages headed by Vasiṣṭha,
he perceives with his eye everything within a range of a hundred yojanas.
In the divine worlds, foremost among which is Mehanḍrapura, he constantly sports, being praised by Gandharvas and throngs of Apsarases.
And having ascended a celestial chariot crowded with hundreds of divine maidens,
he enjoys great pleasures for a kalpa and, attaining perfection, becomes one with Brahman.
O Śivā, from the moment that the Sun enters the *āmaka-rasakrānti*, one should daily perform [the rite] with the permission of the preceptor.

Eating only one meal a day, reciting the mantra a thousand times every day, sleeping on the ground, having conquered the senses, and being devoted to the service of the guru—[by these means] he [attains] knowledge. || 107 ||
Until the end of the Kumbha-saṃkrānti, on that day, with the permission of the preceptor,
one should [offer oblations] according to the rules into the consecrated fire with auspicious Palāśa flowers.
One should offer one thousand three hundred oblations with [substances] that have been thoroughly ground;
O Śivā, having become as before through the rays and the vidyās, one should offer the desired oblation.

Having subsequently offered oblations one hundred and eight times with four *śrīmanu* mantras, and having performed the fire-sacrifice through recitation (*japa*) and other rites, one should perform the *brahmārpaṇa* oblation.
In the absence of *palāśa* flowers, [one may use] those resembling them, mixed with ghee and honey;
in the absence of lotuses, [one may use] bilva leaves or simply ghee alone.
Having offered [the oblation], one should give wealth sufficient for a year's sustenance at the lotus-feet of the Lord;
or else, free from desire for a year, one may give five niṣkas.
Having presented [the vessel] to the preceptor, one should give him a garment and ornaments;
having satisfied the women of the same number as the grains with food and other offerings, [one should proceed].
One should eat together with one's kinsmen in the presence of the preceptor himself;
having thus performed the great accomplishment arising from a hundred purascarana rites. (114)
Having sent forth the Mother of the worlds, the Goddess beholds for the sake of prosperity one who possesses the beauty of a hundred Kandarpas and the Fortune endowed with the eight qualities.
[He obtained] knowledge equal to that of Vācaspati, the supreme recollection of past births, yoga together with its eight limbs, and prosperity abounding in wealth and grain. (116)
O King, in his presence, one attains the state of a celestial maiden, as well as equality with the highest, honor, and even the state of being honored by the gods themselves. (117)
Having obtained divine enjoyments difficult to attain during that year,
at the end he goes to the supreme abode accompanied by a thousand of his lineage.
The kings shall become slaves, and the women indeed shall be slave-girls;
yet prosperity, pervasive and consisting of elephants, horses, and a multitude of chariots, shall remain. 119.
In his house, a woman adorned with pearls and gems, and surrounded by gold and silver, shall be born; of this there is no doubt. (120)
In this very body, one attains the state of a seer, or immortality, or even the state of a gandharva; or else, one attains the state of a perfected being (siddha) or the state of a deity.
O Daughter of the Mountain, this preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) has been described to you;
hereafter, I shall declare the specific materials required for the oblation (homa).

[Thus ends the thirteenth chapter in the *Śrīmadanuttarabrahmatattvarahasya*, the *Dāśarathīya Tantra*, which is a compendium of the essential meaning of the Vedas, in its latter portion, within the *Saubhāgyavidyodaya*.]
The venerable Dakṣiṇāmūrti said:
Now, the injunction regarding the specific substances for the oblation will be declared;
by hearing which even one who is not wise is liberated from the hosts of misfortunes.
Relying upon a lamp-stand, the best of practitioners should perform recitation, fire-oblations, worship, and so forth, for all vidyās, so that they may attain success. || 2 ||
O Goddess of beautiful eyes, one should fashion a circular diagram in the shape of a tortoise;
having divided its center into nine compartments, one should inscribe the syllables therein.
One should write the name of the field in the central square, and then one should arrange the eight vowels in pairs in sequence within the eight [surrounding] squares, beginning with the letter 'ka'.

O Goddess, one should write the 'a' group in sequence, followed by the 'ka' group and the others; then, in the northeast corner of Śambhu, one should inscribe the two letters 'la' and 'kṣa', which are known as the Kūrma [yantra].
O Pārvatī, know that the name of the field [indicates] the face of whichever square it occupies;
O Pārvatī, know that on both sides of the face are two hands.
Thereafter, O lady of beautiful smiles, know that the region of the belly is indeed situated there;
then know the two feet, and at the end of that, the tail is said to be located.
In the mouth, even hundreds of desires and undertakings are accomplished;
in the hand, there is great suffering that brings about the destruction of all tasks.
In the belly there is excessive suffering, and in the feet there is certain loss; moreover, O beloved, loss of wealth occurs in the tail—it shall not be otherwise.
I have proclaimed this site for the lamp, which is very difficult to find even throughout the three worlds;
whether in a city, a sacred field, a village, or a district, such is the site for the lamp.
O Daughter of the Mountain, know that by performing recitation, fire-offerings, worship, and so forth anywhere at all, one shall obtain infinite fruit. 11.
The daily fire-oblation (nitya-homa), which destroys all sins, has been previously described by me;
now I shall explain the rites of the optional fire-oblation (kāmya-homa) which grant specific fruits.
On the full moon day of the month of Caitra, one should offer three thousand oblations of Mallikā, Mālatī, and Jātī flowers mixed with honey.
O lady of excellent hips, even one who is dull-witted becomes a master of all sciences, possessing vitality as if he were alive, and indeed becomes a great orator and a great poet.
Having offered three thousand oblations with hibiscus flowers mixed with clarified butter, or else with oleanders, along with cow's milk and the "three sweets" (trimadhu), || 15 ||
As fortunate as Kāma himself, he might delude this entire world with his splendor, whether in the royal palace of a wealthy man, at the entrance of a cave, or even in the forest. (16)
And Hanumān constantly attains the glory of victory through good fortune, charm, and capability, O lady of virtuous vows.
Having offered the previously mentioned flowers, one can enchant even young women filled with passion, as well as the captivating daughters of kings.
O Goddess, having offered one thousand three hundred oblations of camphor, saffron, and musk mixed together in a quantity equal to a small jujube fruit, [one attains success].
A man obtains royal fortune that extends through his progeny by offering *caṃpaka* and *pāṭala* flowers mixed with the three sweets (*trimadhu*). || 20 ||
The pure-souled one, with great reverence, gave three hundred and thirty-three villages,
abounding in wealth, grain, and noble families, and filled with heaps of pearls and gems.
If one offers oblations of śrīkhaṇḍa, guggulu, candana, and nāgara, one attains great and eternal prosperity that is free from sin. || 22 ||
Each one, resembling Kandarpa in splendor, brought the cities of the kings, lords of men, and gods under his subjection, one thousand at a time. (23)
All the worlds come under his control; of this there is no doubt—having offered oblations by the thousands of ghee mixed with the three sweets and lac.
Having attained royal fortune, one is liberated from poverty;
having recited this three thousand times with purity, one becomes like Indra himself. (25)
Being liberated from the state of being bound by the nest [of worldly existence], one attains the power of moving through the sky;
having separately offered milk, honey, curd, and clarified butter thousands of times.
One shall obtain long life, great freedom from disease, and supreme prosperity, by offering three thousand oblations each of milk, honey, and ghee. (27)
Having completely conquered time and death,
the practitioner attains the great flower, liberated from all mental and physical afflictions.
By performing three thousand oblations for each with curd and honey, one shall attain great good fortune and acquire inexhaustible wealth. (29)
Then, having offered ten thousand oblations with ghee and white sugar,
one attains great prosperity and paralyzes one's enemies.
By performing oblations with curds, honey, milk, and parched grain while praising the heroic one, he shall be liberated from all diseases and attain death at his own will. || 31 ||
Having offered three thousand red lotuses mixed with the three sweets,
the pure-souled one shone like a second king of the yakṣas.
One should offer oblations of red lotuses smeared with the three sweets and soaked in ghee for seven days;
indeed, all beings will then become her servants.
O Daughter of the Mountain, from this [gift] of one thousand three hundred, he obtains his desired wealth every day; of this there is no doubt. (34)
Having offered more than a thousand oblations of blue lotuses and water lilies smeared with the three sweets, even cruel kings and leaders will be subdued in just one day.
Even women who are difficult to subdue become his slaves;
[this is achieved] by [offering] one thousand and one hundred white *palāśa* flowers smeared with the three sweets (*trimadhu*). (36)
Having offered [the oblation] with just one *samāhū* measure, he will certainly attain great and inexhaustible prosperity and become a master of all branches of knowledge. || 37 ||
Having offered more than a thousand oblations of white lotuses smeared with honey for a period of one month, one attains a splendor resembling that of Kandarpa.
Having attained great fortune,
the practitioner of mantras obtains a splendor equal to that of Indra by performing a thousand and three hundred oblations of white water-lilies (kahlāra).
Within seven days, one shall obtain all good fortune and inexhaustible wealth by offering one thousand three hundred fruits of the citron (mānuluṅga).
From one who is thus composed, Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas indeed arise here; of this there is no doubt.
By means of a thousand and three hundred oblations of orange fruits, [the same result is attained]. (41)
Within three days, all Vaiśyas indeed become one's servants; there is no doubt.
This is accomplished by performing a fire-oblation (homa) of three thousand and three hundred Kushmāṇḍa fruits.
Within five days, one shall obtain all good fortune and inexhaustible wealth by offering one thousand three hundred *mānuluṅga* fruits as oblations.
From that state of concentration, Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas arise here; of this there is no doubt.
By offering one thousand three hundred nāraṅga fruits as oblations, [the same result is attained]. || 41 ||
Within three days, she will undoubtedly become the entire retinue of servants for a Vaiśya,
by means of an oblation of one thousand three hundred kūṣmāṇḍa fruits.
Within five days, all Śūdras will undoubtedly be brought under one's control, O venerable one, by offering one thousand three hundred grapes smeared with the three sweets (trimadhu). || 43 ||
By performing oblations for twenty-one days, one shall attain the eight supernatural powers (siddhis);
by a hundred thousand oblations of plantain fruit, one becomes a sovereign of the earth.
Indeed, these ten [faults] remain throughout one's life; there is no doubt about this.
One who eats dates does not become a king even by means of a hundred thousand [meritorious acts]. || 45 ||
"The command of the Supreme Lord is that there are twenty [deities] to be brought under control;
having offered one hundred thousand oblations of *rikela* and *yūla* mixed with the three sweets (*trimadhu*), [one achieves this]. (46)
O beautiful one, by performing a hundred thousand oblations of cooked rice cakes (*pakvānnapūla*), this king shall become the sovereign of the seven islands for as long as he lives.
By means of jackfruit seeds devoid of kernels, soaked in the three sweets, one is always born as a lord of the earth who rules over the four oceans. (48)
Having offered a hundred thousand oblations, one attains Mahālakṣmī, whose splendor is equal to that of Indra;
she constantly brings all beings under his control, like servants.
Having offered one thousand three hundred oblations continuously for one fortnight with black sesame seeds mixed with fragrant ghee and the three sweets (trimadhu), || 50 ||
O beautiful one, by offering the smoke of guggulu resin with the *ṣaṭhasta* mantra, one attains the fulfillment of one's desires, even those difficult for the gods to achieve. (51)
There shall be the cessation of all suffering, and one attains imperishable happiness.
[This occurs when] saffron and other substances are combined with honey, mixed as a triad. || 52 ||
Having offered five thousand oblations, one who possesses a beautiful form like that of Kāyava will bring the three worlds under his control for as long as he lives; of this there is no doubt.
Having offered three thousand oblations of sandalwood mixed with ghee and combined with the three sweets, one shall bring about the pacification of enemies.
By offering one thousand three hundred oblations of red sandalwood,
women as well as men will constantly come under his control.
O Īśvarī, he who offers camphor mixed with ghee and the three sweets one thousand three hundred times for each of the three [mantras]— 56.
Having attained a long lifespan, resembling Kandarpa in splendor,
he is born even here with knowledge equal to that of Vācaspati himself.
By performing one thousand three hundred kuṣṭhūrī oblations correctly,
not even a single king's minister will remain unsubdued on that day.
By performing a thousand oblations of sesame seeds and rice for seven days, there shall be the cessation of all sins and the pacification of diseases shall arise. (59)
By performing one thousand three hundred oblations of sugar mixed with ghee, honey,
and the three sweets for seven days, the excellent practitioner becomes auspicious.
If one offers oblations of milk-rice mixed with ghee and the three sweets, one brings the three worlds under control and shall obtain even unshakable prosperity. (61)
O lotus-eyed one, having brought the three worlds under his own control for ten days, he possessed a thousand and three hundredfold prosperity endowed with the eight supernatural powers.
O beautiful-faced one, there is no doubt here regarding the truth;
by offering various kinds of food and oblations month after month, one attains a hundredfold [merit]. (63)
In this regard, one attains a heap [of merit] and enjoys inexhaustible grain; with condiments and pungent spices, one gains a thousand and three hundred [units].
Within merely seven days, he was afflicted by a multitude of diseases—
sharp and incurable by means of mantras, medicines, or therapeutic remedies.
There is no doubt here even regarding consumption, leprosy, and other such ailments;
if one performs oblations for seven days with hibiscus flowers mixed with the three sweets (trimadhu), [the result is achieved].
Having obtained unshakable prosperity amounting to one thousand three hundred [coins], and having become a treasury of all sciences, he shall become as beautiful as Kāmadeva. (67)
By offering three thousand one hundred flowers of the Vakula tree,
even an old man attains great good fortune and becomes like a youth.
By means of the offering of ten-ingredient incense, he shall become a possessor of good fortune;
likewise by offering three thousand one hundred jambu fruits smeared with the three sweets. (69)
By performing the homa for four days, even young women proud of their beauty—
and certainly even princesses— will surely become one's female servants.
By performing three thousand one hundred oblations of kūṣmāṇḍa fruits for seven nights or half that time, maidens indeed become female slaves.
By offering three thousand one hundred bilva fruits, purified and soaked in the three sweets (trimadhu), into the fire for five days,
one attains great royal fortune.
In that temple, there shall indeed be an abundance of wealth and jewels today;
it shall contain fourteen hundred and one thousand pieces of sugarcane.
Having offered oblations mixed with the three sweets, one beholds Śrī herself;
this should be done daily, either one hundred and eight times or twenty-eight times. (74)
Having offered oblations day after day with pure cow-ghee alone, one attains mastery over the vidyā as well as many other auspicious benefits. (75)
By means of an oblation of clarified butter alone, offered individually into the fire, one attains the complete fulfillment of all desired objects; of this there is no doubt.
Listen, O Goddess, I shall declare the measure for the oblation that grants success:
one should offer flowers, or *magra*, or *ūtīla*, or a lotus. (77)
One should offer whatever flowers and blossoms are desired to Śrī;
the number of sesame seeds is said to be one hundred, and the same applies to rice grains.
A handful of parched grain is prescribed as the measure; likewise, a māṣa of ghee submerged in fire is recorded [as a standard];
half a handful of milk is considered equal in essence to the recitation of a mantra.
O Maheśānī, O Manalocanā, one should offer a sacrificial cake made of *sthālī* fruit, *kūṣmāṇḍa*, and *mātuluṅga*, along with pieces of sugar-candy that are pleasing to the mind.
If the plantain fruit is small, it should not be cut into four pieces;
O beautiful woman, in the scriptures it is stated that the coconut must be divided into four parts. (81)
On every festival day, grapes are said to grant the perfection of all parts in every direction, while the orange is remembered as being of two kinds throughout the entire [world].
There should be one part each of dates, betel nuts, and guggulu resin;
along with an equal amount of gunja seeds, camphor, musk, and saffron. (82)
One should offer other fruits dear to the mind as individual oblations—
lac, guggulu, saṅkhyāśya, and whatever else is most enchanting.
O lotus-eyed one, having offered the oblation dear to the mind, you should perform the fire sacrifice;
this measure of oblations has been declared as the remover of all obstacles.
By whatever means possible, through the grace of one's own teacher,
one should constantly satisfy Śiva with recitation, fire-offerings, worship, and other such rites.

[Thus ends the fourteenth chapter in the *Saubhāgyavidyodaya*, the latter portion of the *Dāśarathīya-tantra*, which is the *Śrīmadanuttarabrahmatattvarahasya* and a compendium of the essential meaning of the essence of the Vedas.]
The venerable Dakṣiṇāmūrti said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim this supreme and special procedure:
first, having prepared a quadrangular sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) endowed with excellent characteristics. || 1 ||
Endowed with all auspicious marks, it should be half a cubit long for a hundred oblations;
for a thousand, it should be one cubit; and for two thousand, it should be two cubits.

For ten thousand oblations, a pit of three cubits is prescribed; for one hundred thousand, four cubits; and for ten million oblations, eight cubits—having thus established the characteristics of the sacrificial pit.
For pacification (śāntika), it is square; for subjugation (vaśya), it is indeed a half-moon; for paralyzing (staṃbhanā), a hexagon is prescribed; and for killing (māraṇa), it is exactly like that.
A triangle is for attraction, and likewise a circle is for eradication; O Maheśvarī, a lotus-shaped figure with many angles is said to grant various supernatural powers (siddhis).
In the north, the rite of pacification (śāntika) should be performed; in the northeast, there shall be the rites of paralysis (staṃbha) and subjugation (vaśīkaraṇa).
The south is declared for the rite of killing (māraṇa), and the west for the rite of attraction (ākarṣaṇa).
In the rite of burning, or even when [the enemy] has been consumed by fire, there is enmity;
likewise, there shall be eradication (uccāṭana) in the southeast (vāyavya), while in the northeast (īśānya) it bestows all accomplishments.
Facing the eastern direction during the rite of fire-oblation brings about the accomplishment of knowledge;
Kṛttikā is declared for attracting, and likewise Mṛgaśirā for killing.
Svātī is for subjugation as well as eradication; Jyeṣṭhā is for the rite of immobilization;
Śatabhiṣaj is for causing enmity; and Āśleṣā bestows peace.
Attraction should be performed on Monday, and likewise, killing on Tuesday;
subjugation should be done on Wednesday, and nourishing rites on Thursday.
In the Bhārgava [day], there shall be all success; on the day of the Vasus, it shall be auspicious.
For the purpose of paralyzing, the fuel-sticks of the Rājavṛtta tree should be offered into the fire for the sake of welfare.
The oblation performed by a mahiṣī brings the three worlds under one's control;
pomegranate wood is recommended for the oblation in rites such as killing.
An oblation of goat's ghee shall bewilder the three worlds;
likewise, for the purpose of inciting enmity, fuel-sticks of the *unmatta* plant should be offered.
Combined with linseed oil, these are great producers of enmity;
they bring about the accomplishment of all goals and purposes and the warding off of all obstacles. || 14 ||
O Daughter of the Mountain, by offering oblations daily with cow’s ghee,
or on a Saturday, or on the ninth lunar day, or on full moon days— 15.
O Goddess, one must certainly worship beautiful young maidens, beginning from their fifth year until they reach their twelfth year. (16)
From the worship of unmarried maidens, all perfections are attained;
by him who has worshipped maidens, the three worlds have been worshipped. (17)
Even those who have been married are declared to be "maidens" as long as they remain free from the appearance of menses for twelve years. (18)

With a mind endowed with auspiciousness, young maidens should be worshipped for the attainment of all fruits; likewise, married women whose husbands are living should also be honored with ornaments, clothing, and food. (19)
The teacher’s wife should be worshipped daily with the thought that she is Lakṣmī herself;
for she alone is born as the mother, she alone is Gaurī, and she alone is Sarasvatī. (20)
If the teacher’s wife is a widow, she who is accompanied by her son should be worshipped by the devotees with the thought that she is Mahālakṣmī herself. || 21 ||
There is no doubt that his wife also was similar to the other [Sītā];
and for the benefit of practitioners, I shall describe the ritual of binding the girdle (damanāropaṇa).
O Daughter of the Mountain, when you were given as a gift by Yama, who possesses the power of asceticism, the worship performed over a year became complete for him.
Then, having become Lakṣmī, Rati and Prīti were distressed;
with a satisfied mind, I granted a boon to them both for the sake of attaining me.
O Daughter of the Mountain, from the tears produced by his eyes grew the *damanaka* creeper;
O fair-eyed one, from its fragrance arose great happiness.
Therefore, for the sake of passion (rati) and delight (prīti), Madana is proclaimed;
one who possesses the mantra should worship him with Damana within the armor (varma). || 26 ||
"Her annual worship shall be for the sake of intoxication;
thus was the boon granted by me to her, O Sukhandikā. (27)
Therefore, the worship of Damana must indeed be performed by the best of practitioners—those devoted to the worship of Śrī-Śrīśa and those who worship Gaurī and Śaṅkara. (28)
Also by those devoted to the worship of the Sun, those intent on the adoration of Gaṇeśa, those engaged in the worship of the Śrīcakra, and likewise those who worship the Śālagrāma; || 29 ||
They were devoted to the worship of the Liṅga and intent on the adoration of Śiva;
they had sacrificed to Mahendra and their minds were occupied with the worship of the guardians of the quarters.
Whoever has devotion toward [a particular deity], they should perform the worship of Damanaka every year, even if they are otherwise occupied with the worship of that deity. || 31 ||
Otherwise, the fruit of that desire performed during the year arises [in the following manner]:
the three months beginning with Caitra consist of two fortnights each, the bright and the dark. (32)
Among these, each preceding period of time is the most excellent of all;
and [the worship should be performed] on the eighth, the fourteenth, the full moon day, or even at midday.
One should perform the preliminary mental cultivation (vāsana) either during the first part of the night or immediately;
having oneself uprooted the [obstructive] amana along with its root, it should be joined with the previous time-period.
O Goddess, O Bhadrakālī, O Vujā, one should place [the vessel] on the left, whether it has been brought by another or obtained for free from its price. || 35 ||
Having established the vessel for the bestowal of wealth (*vasvare dāmana*) behind the *prastha*, O fair-faced one, the eight-syllable *vidyā* should be recited.
In the place where "I declare my love" (*prītiṃ vade*) occurs, the wise man should describe the eight-syllable mantra of love: *vāgbhava*, *bhuvaneśānī*, *śrī*, and *kāma* thereafter. (36)
To Kāmadeva is the heart-mantra; this is the knowledge described by Rudra. Having extracted the seed-syllable as before, one should utter "pra" and then "are ātmane. (37)
"O fair-faced one, 'Ravyai namaḥ' is the eight-syllabled Vidyā;
in place of the word 'prītim', the eight-syllabled mantra for affection is 'vade'. (38)
One should worship that subduer, divided into nine types, in due order upon the lion-throne in the southern direction as previously described. (39)
One should perform protection with the *jatra* mantra and concealment with the *kavaca*;
having bound the trident and the *kundī*, one should whirl them over the *damana* plant.
One should perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) enriched with sandalwood paste and camphor;
one should carry out this excellent preliminary consecration on the first day.
