Whether by day or by night, for the sake of obtaining the fruit of the annual worship, one should perform the great worship at the proper time in the city named Ayodhyā. 42.
Then, having fashioned a nine-cornered [mandala] of great splendor with a lion-pattern,
one should place nine jars filled with gold, gems, and other precious substances.
Or the best of teachers should always place a single water-pot after drawing a mandala on the right side, adorned with saffron and other powders.
One should draw a triangular mandala at the foot of an Aśoka tree;
in its center, one should worship Kāma, who is youthful and of reddish-golden luster.
O Dear One, he is adorned with red garlands, garments, and ornaments on his left and right sides;
he is enriched by the splendor of Rati and Prīti, and he holds the bow and five arrows.
One should properly worship Kāma, accompanied by Vasanta and situated in the midst of a Kadamba forest,
with the previously mentioned mantra for the sake of attaining success.
Gaura and Śyāmā, Rati and Prīti, adorned respectively with jewels, holding lotuses and betel leaves in their hands, and resplendent in red garments. || 48 ||
Immediately thereafter, one should meditate upon Kāma on the left and right [sides], adorned with divine ornaments and resplendent with divine garlands.
Thereafter, one should worship Vasanta, who stands in the midst of a grove of Kadamba trees,
fair-complexioned and holding in his left hand a jar filled with nectar.
Having worshipped Kāma along with his limbs, holding a collection of various flowers in his right hand, one should then worship Mahātripurasundarī.
One should duly worship the two feet of the preceptor in the proper sequence,
with thousands of bhāras of gold, and with divine garlands, garments, and ornaments.
One should worship with jewels, pearls, and wealth for the sake of attaining one's desired goal;
that ritual in which the teacher is honored is declared to be fruitful.
Without the worship of the preceptor, it is fruitless; of this there is no doubt.
If he possesses virtuous qualities, one should entrust him with the preceptor’s son or his wife.
One should worship the teacher’s grandson, or his son, or even his disciple; in their absence, one should worship his brothers.
Afterwards, the maiden should worship the married women with eight types of food;
then, she should reverently offer clarified butter three hundred times with the Śrīvidyā mantra.
Having offered an oblation with the *brahmārpaṇa* mantra, he should then feed the Brāhmaṇas;
having thus performed the vow of the "proper mounting of the goad" (*damanāropaṇa*), the man [attains the fruit]. || 57 ||
Year after year, by properly performing the fire-oblations, worship, and other rites along with their constituent parts, one obtains the fruit; there is no doubt about this.
O Kanyaka, whatever worship, recitation, fire-offerings, and so forth are performed for Śiva throughout the year, if done otherwise, they would go only to Madana. (59)
Devoted to the supreme knowledge of the great queen Lalitā Śrī,
one should eat pieces of sugarcane and should not be harsh toward women.
One should not be a hater of the world, nor should one ever be impure; one should never speak untruth to anyone, and especially not to a guru, O Śivā.
One who desires his own welfare should avoid hearing disparagement of the teacher, whether he be poor or wealthy, foolish or even learned. (62)
The Teacher alone is the Blessed One, Hari, Brahmā, the shoreless, and Śiva; what is the use of much speaking here, O Supreme Lord, for he is the Infallible?
Know that the one in the form of the teacher is Truth itself, not untruth; of this there is no doubt.
One who possesses devotion toward the knowledge [of him] [attains] even Lakṣmī and other excellent mantras.
A wise person should recite it according to their ability; they shall attain unsurpassed perfection.
The majesty of that Śrī Devī is like a mere mouthful of water in the ocean.
Something has been said by me, O Goddess; what more do you wish to hear?

[Thus ends the fifteenth chapter on the Science of Saubhāgya in the latter section of the *Śrīmadanuttarabrahmatattvarahasya*, the *Dāśarathīya Tantra*, which is a compendium of the essential meaning of the Vedas.]
The Goddess said:
O Blessed One, Dakṣiṇāmūrti, omniscient one, ocean of compassion! This Vidyā, attended by the four Lakṣmīs, is the very embodiment of glory. 1.
"O Lord, please describe the ritual procedure for the jewels of knowledge, such as Lakṣmī and the others.
Śrī Dakṣiṇāmūrti said:
The illustrious Goddess Lalitā, whose form is the cause of the entire universe.
She is served by the fourfold Lakṣmī and is remembered as the manifest source of all desires.
Śrīvidyā, Lakṣmī, Mahālakṣmī, and thereafter Triśakti and Sarvasāmrājyalakṣmī—these five are proclaimed. || 4 ||
She is the most venerable root-vidyā of Śrī, the Mother of the three worlds.
The auspicious Siṃhāsenaśvarī, who consists of all vidyās, has been proclaimed;
now I shall speak of the single-syllabled great vidyā, Lakṣmī.

The seed-syllable of Lakṣmī is declared to be that which ends with Vāruṇa (the letter va), is situated in Vahni (the letter ra), is adorned with the left eye (the vowel ī), and is joined with Bindu and Nāda.
This Lakṣmī, who consists of the triad [of the Vedas], is the sovereign of the eastern direction;
she bestows all prosperity and happiness, and was worshipped by the Creator in ancient times.
O Dakṣa, from the Brāhmaṇa [Brahmā], Kaśyapa and the other lords of progeny were born;
having propitiated this seed of Lakṣmī, they attained the lordship over the worlds. (8)
The sage is Bhaśu, the great yogi; Nichchaṃda is declared the meter;
the deity is said to be Śrī Lakṣmī, who bestows all self-restraint and prosperity.

The seed-syllable (bīja) and the power (śakti) are in the fourth [position], and the pin (kīlaka) is said to be the letter *ra*. By means of the second, third, and sixth letters, it is thus [established].
Having united the mantra with Indra and the digit of the moon, the beautiful practitioner of the mantra should place the six limbs: first the heart and head, and then the crest-lock (śikhā).
One should join the armor (kavaca), the eye (netra), and the weapon (astra) mantras with "namaḥ," "svāhā," "vaṣaṭ," "huṃ," and "vauṣaṭ" at their ends respectively, in due order.
One should draw an eight-petaled yantra and write a *bhūbimba* (earth-circle) around it;
having placed a flower in the center, one should worship the powers of the pedestal (*pīṭhaśakti*).
One should worship Vibhūti, Runnati, Kānti, Puṣṭi, Kīrti, Satnati, Vyuṣṭi, Utkṛṣṭi, Ṛddhi, and Vasu in the various directions.
O beloved, having worshipped the lion-throne in the center, which consists of all powers,
one should then meditate upon the beautiful Śrī, who is saluted by all the gods.
Shining with the luster of molten gold and adorned with divine jewels,
she was being sprinkled with nectars as well as with the liquid essence of pearls and gems.
O beloved, with her pair of bright white parasols, she repeatedly shines today with many jewels upon her crown and pure sandalwood paste as her body ointment.
I worship this lotus-eyed goddess who is seated upon the left lap of Manobhava;
having meditated thus, one should always worship the Goddess as she holds a pair of lotuses.

One should display the gestures (mudrās) for invocation and so forth in their proper sequence—[the deity] who grants boons, who abounds in the splendor of [dispelling] fear, who has four arms and three eyes. || 19 ||
If one places the raised palms facing downwards, this becomes the invocation;
if, however, it is the reverse, then it is indeed the installation.
With the fists joined and the thumbs pointing upward, this is the *sannidhāpanī* [mudrā];
likewise, with the thumbs placed inside the fists, this is the *nirodhanī*.
By rotating [the hands] with the two index fingers, the sakalīkaraṇa (totalization) occurs;
and by forming the añjali mudrā as in the arghya offering, the paramīkaraṇa (transcendentalization) occurs. || 22 ||
Having turned the two hands over, one should place the two index fingers and the two little fingers as the leaders, and the two middle and ring fingers together, interlacing them with one another.
This mudrā, which has the form of a cow, is called Amṛtīkaraṇa;
O Dear One, having displayed these common mudrās, one should perform the recitation (japa).

With perfumes, flowers, and other offerings for the sake of accomplishing all desires and goals, one should perform the worship of the limbs in the directions of Agni, Īśa, Asura, Vāyu, and the center. (25)
Vālākā, Vimalā, Kamalā, Vanamālikā, Vibhīṣikā, Mālikā, Śāṅkarī, and Vasumālikā. || 26 ||
O Goddess, one should worship them in order, starting from the east and proceeding clockwise:
those known as Indra, Agni, Yama, Rakṣas, Varuṇa, and Anila.

One should first abandon the earth-element for the sake of solitude; then one should worship Kuvera and Īśāna as the lords of the world, and subsequently worship Brahmā and Viṣṇu as the lords of the world, starting from the top in due order.

The practitioner should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times, and then perform the fire sacrifice (homa) with ten thousand lotuses weighed against clarified butter, using the three metals [gold, silver, and copper] in accordance with the rules.
Having offered twelve thousand [oblations] at the two feet of the Teacher, he fashioned a beautiful, auspicious lotus from gold weighing one pala.
Having given [this], one attains perfection and obtains all prosperity;
or else, the most excellent practitioner [obtains it] by twenty-four thousand [recitations]. || 31 ||
On the eleventh day of the month of Kārttika, the wise man, fasting,
should recite [the mantra] three thousand times and offer oblations into the fire three thousand times with cow-derived ghee measured by weight.
Alternatively, one may offer a pala of gold or twelve thousand cows;
or, one should offer thirty-one thousand oblations of bilva leaves soaked in ghee into the consecrated fire. (35)
By worshipping married women on the auspicious occasion of Śiva’s wedding with the five mountains,
one obtains for years great fortune abounding in forests.
Having recited it twelve thousand times every day for four months, or even five thousand times, or indeed three thousand times; || 37 ||
Having offered one hundred and eight oblations with cow-ghee,
the practitioner attains great and unshakable prosperity, abounding in wealth, grain, and other riches.
One attains this here; there is no doubt. I speak the truth, the absolute truth:
by reciting this single-syllable Lakṣmī mantra with devotion, one attains it. (39)

If one who is devoted to the guru personally attains the glory of sovereignty, then since wealth and knowledge are both contained therein, what more need be said? This which has been spoken by me is the pacifier of great poverty; what else do you desire? (40)

[Thus ends the sixteenth chapter in the *Śrīmadanuttarabrahmatattvarahasya*, the *Dāśarathīya-tantra*, which is a compendium of the essential meaning of the Vedas, in its latter section, titled *Saubhāgyavidyodaya*.]
The sages said:
O highly fortunate Ṛṣyaśṛṅga, possessor of divine knowledge, the Supreme Lord [bestowed] the science of Prasannalakṣmī upon Pārvatī. || 1 ||
O Lord, we wish to hear further that auspicious account which the Blessed One spoke concerning Mahālakṣmī and Manu. (2)
"Please tell me once more that majesty which destroys all sins.
Śrī Ṛṣyaśṛṅga said:
Having heard the ritual procedure for the Lakṣmī-vidyā, Girijā was delighted in her mind; then Dakṣiṇāmūrti spoke these words, which are esteemed by the world.
The Goddess said:
O God of gods, salutations to you, O Maheśa, the supreme receptacle of compassion.
I have heard from Lakṣmī herself the majesty of Lalitā,
as well as the ritual procedure for Mahālakṣmī, the Great Vidyā, which bestows all perfections.
"O Guru of the worlds, please tell me out of compassion, even though it is a well-guarded secret.
Śrī Dakṣiṇāmūrti said:
Well asked, O highly fortunate one, [is this question] which brings benefit and illuminates the world.
The majesty of Prasannalakṣmī, which instantly destroys all sins,
was formerly told by Nārāyaṇa to the high-souled Janaka.
Then the son of Daśaratha spoke with reverence to Vasiṣṭha and the others:
"O lotus-eyed one, I too shall speak here to you."
Now I shall describe the majesty of Prasannalakṣmī, which is more secret than the secret, meritorious, the essence of essences, and supreme.
The three Vedas, the syllable *vijaṃ*, Śrī, Bhuvaneśī, and that which is beyond them;
the elements beginning with touch, preceded by Brahman, and the Earth accompanied by Rudra. || 10 ||
Then one should place Smara, whose belly is the color of gold and whose face is circular;
next, Vāyu, the younger brother of Vala, endowed with the Rudra-svara. ||11||
Be gracious; [the mantra consists of] the couple (Yugala) again, followed by Śrī, Uddhā, Bhuvaneśvarī, Mahālakṣmī, and the fourth [syllable] at the end of the feet. 12.
This twenty-seven-syllable mantra is declared to be that of Mahālakṣmī;
she is the sovereign of the throne of Dakṣa and was worshipped by Viṣṇu in ancient times.
With her forelocks raining down a stream of pearls, she is the sovereign of the universe;
Ayodhyā-pura is the mistress of the entire empire of Vaikuṇṭha.
She is renowned as Mahālakṣmī, praised by the Vedas and the Upaniṣads;
she is celebrated as Prasannaśrī by those who know the Vedas and the Upaniṣads.
She is the auspicious one who bestows the wealth of the treasures, such as the conch and the lotus, upon her devotees;
she grants the prosperity of Mahendra to the Brahmins who worship her.
She is the bestower of sovereignty over the city of Alakā, the showerer of wealth, and the one who grants mastery in speech regarding the Vedas, Vedāṅgas, Vedānta, and the Purāṇas. || 17 ||
She consists of all sacred fields, she is the embodiment of all yoga scriptures,
she comprises all holy fords, and she is the destroyer of the multitude of sins.

Through the grace of the Blessed One, the hosts of deities beginning with Brahmā, the practitioners of yoga, those who discourse on the seven topics, and the great seers headed by Vasiṣṭha [attained this]. || 19 ||
Puraṃdara and the other guardians of all the directions, the nectar-consuming Vasus—eight highly fortunate ones—and also Ekāśā; (20)
Likewise, O Pārvatī, even the twelve divine [Ādityas], having propitiated Mahālakṣmī, the beloved of Hari,
attained the eightfold sovereign powers (aṣṭaiśvarya) and remain so even today.
Those who, being self-restrained, constantly recite this mantra which grants the attainment of all fruits,
[attain] the sovereignty of the city of Alakā and the splendors of the city of Mahendra.

Whether she desires the sovereignty of the qualities such as *aṇimā* and the rest, or the status of Brahman, this Mahālakṣmī— who grants the accomplishment of all fruits— should be constantly recited by one who is self-controlled.
By one of restrained mind, she bestows the imperial sovereignty of the city of Alakā and the splendors of the city of Maheṃdra.
Neither by the Vedas, nor by the Āgamas, nor by the Śāstras, nor by the very extensive Purāṇas can the auspicious Mahālakṣmī be known without the grace of the Preceptor.
If one who possesses a clear fortune beholds this vidyā established in a book and recites it,
he will be devoured by the hosts of yoginīs within six months.
By constantly reciting this *Mahālakṣmī* mantra through the grace of the teacher,
one attains the eightfold sovereign powers (*aṣṭaiśvarya*), beginning with *aṇimā*, as well as imperishable and unsurpassed excellence.
Incomparable perfection in great speech, an inexhaustible heap of wealth,
many intoxicated elephants, numerous horses, and even many cattle.
Having attained divine enjoyments and even being blessed with sons and grandsons,
and having obtained great prosperity, she shall attain the state of Satī in Vaikuṇṭha.
This [hymn] is to be recited by those desiring prosperity before dawn; O Śivā, it brings forth this very prosperity.
It should always be recited by one who desires the fortune of universal sovereignty, and by one who seeks both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
This Mahālakṣmī [mantra] should be recited; it bestows the abundance of great prosperity, as well as unshakable great sovereignty and unswerving great accomplishment.
O Auspicious One, this [mantra] of radiant glory should be constantly recited by one who desires [success];
it destroys the gods, the enemies, and the sleepless [obstacles], and it enters the very heart. 31.
From Varuṇa he obtained mastery over the waters, from Vāyu the power of the wind,
from Savitṛ brilliance, and from the Moon swiftness of action.
Through Kuvera he obtained mastery over treasures; through his preceptor [Bṛhaspati] he gained the respect of Śakra;
through Agni he acquired the power of burning heat; and through the Moon he attained lordship over medicinal herbs.
The sovereignty of Pātāla was obtained by the Nāga, and the lordship over the worlds by Śakra and the other guardians of the quarters; it is immovable and free from fear.
The son of Īśvara attained the leadership of the divine army;
Gaṇeśa attained lordship over the Gaṇas, and Nandin attained equality with Śiva.
O Goddess praised by heroes, this is not otherwise; it is through the power of Mahālakṣmī that great fortune was attained in various places in the past by gods and sages. (36)
This is undoubtedly due to the grace of Śrī herself who is well-pleased;
even Brahmā, the lord of the worlds, [acknowledges] the majesty of the gracious Lakṣmī.
Even Nārāyaṇa, the Lord, is not able to describe it by his power, since even Śakra became a leader of men due to the curse of Urvaśī. (38)
O Śivā, having lost your fortune, you then entreated the preceptor Aṅgiras;
by his grace, you obtained this Mahālakṣmī.
From the churning of the ocean, the supreme Śrī was seen directly;
the lord of the gods attained unsurpassed and great fortune. (40)
From that time forth, having become endowed with immovable glory, the Lord of Śacī attained the sovereignty over all the three worlds.

In his intoxication, he seized the three worlds as if they were a mere recitation; he took possession of Mātaṅga, who had gone to Airāvata, and the jewel among horses, Uccaiḥśravas, who was equal to Manovega.
Indeed, King Śravaṇa, having performed difficult austerities in the past,
attained the sovereignty over the Rākṣasas for a fortnight and reached the auspicious city of Alakā.
Then, having been reviled by Rāvaṇa, he again, through the grace of Pulastya,
chanted the propitious Mahāvidyā and thereafter performed oblations.
O Daughter of the Mountain, having attained my friendship and unsurpassed sovereignty over wealth,
he obtained the imperial rule of the city of Alakā.
This royal fortune is known as the Vidyā Mahālakṣmī;
she is celebrated as Prasannalakṣmī, the bestower of all desired perfections.

This Great Lakṣmī is said by tradition not to be spoken of to one who delights in misconduct, nor to a slanderer, nor to one who is prone to anger, nor to a fool, nor to a greedy person, nor to one who speaks falsehoods.
To one who reviles his father, mother, or teacher; to one who acts with malice, who is intent on the destruction of the Vedas, and who is devoted to censuring others—48.
One who is intent on union with another's wife, greedy for the wealth of others, dull-witted, inert, foolish, and likewise devoted to wicked conduct; || 49 ||
One should avoid, for the sake of discipleship, a person of evil soul who is outside the Veda, devoted to reviling the Veda, and devoid of the conduct prescribed by the Śruti.
One who possesses firm devotion to the pair of feet of the teacher, has conquered the senses, is averse to the wealth and wives of others, and is free from sloth; || 51 ||
One who is constantly devoted to Vedic conduct, always speaking the truth,
peaceful, stainless, pure, and dedicated to the worship of Hari.
O Supreme Goddess, having examined the disciple for three years,
one should bestow this Great Lakṣmī-vidyā, which grants all perfections, beginning with compassion.
In former times, Sarasvatī, the mother of the Vedas, assuming a physical form,
arrived and spoke to a Brāhmaṇa, being pleased with him and bestowing desired prosperity.
I shall give this to you; keep it secret always, O twice-born one!
Do not give it to one who is envious, nor to one who is dishonest, nor to one who is dull-witted, nor to one who speaks untruthfully. (55)
If you do not ask for the reasons, I shall then be full of vigor;
she who must always be protected from the arrival of an evil-doer shall remain so. 56.
"O twice-born one, if this knowledge of Mahālakṣmī has been guarded by you, then I shall grant you a station equal to that of Mahendra. (57)
This was spoken of old by Sarasvatī to Viṣṇu, the best of gods;
therefore, this Mahālakṣmī should not be revealed anywhere at all.
O Śivā, even a Brahmin on this earth who desires prosperity equal to that of Mahendra should recite this Mahālakṣmī mantra through the grace of his preceptor.

Service to the pair of feet of the teacher’s guru must always be performed with reverence, even at the cost of one’s entire possessions, for the sake of attaining the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation. (60)
Those of restrained mind should remain in the presence of the teacher, honoring the two lotus-feet of the teacher day after day. (61)
The teacher alone is to be honored even more than the king in assemblies;
one should abandon even one's father, wife, mother, and sons for his sake. 62.
One should never abandon the bestower of great fortune even at the end of one's life;
rather, one should serve the two lotus-feet of the preceptor day after day.
When recited, the Prasannaśrī [mantra] bestows enjoyments, heaven, and liberation;
it grants the attainment of the essence of Brahman-bliss and the glory of the eight supernatural powers, such as *aṇimā*.
One who desires the royal fortune must certainly recite this day after day;
for this alone is the supreme good, and this alone is the highest austerity. (65)
This alone is the supreme sacred ford; this alone is the supreme fruit;
this alone is the great sacrifice; this alone is the highest goal.

Thinking thus, and being pure through the recitation of mantras, he should daily seek the royal fortune of knowledge by traveling a thousand *yojanas* to find a preceptor who is the best among the twice-born.
O lady of excellent vows, having served her for a hundred years with one's life-force and wealth,
one should then recite the mantra of the gracious Kamalā through her grace.
Kārtravīrya, Sagara, Māndhātṛ, Purūravas, Raudrāśva, King Daśaratha, Duṣyanta, and Bharata as well; || 69 ||

The Manus beginning with Svāyambhuva, as well as the universal sovereign kings, having chanted this Royal Fortune (Rājyalakṣmī) and having served their preceptor with reverence, [attained their status]. (70)
This supreme welfare, difficult even for the hosts of gods to attain, has been obtained by you—whether it be the sovereignty over Śvetadvīpa or the splendor of the Golden Mountain. (71)
He who desires royal splendor should perform this recitation day after day;
for even Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśa, and the other leaders of the three worlds [are attained through it]. (72)
Indeed, no one is capable of describing the majesty of Prasannalakṣmī;
even the great ṛṣis lack the power to recount her greatness.
What need is there to speak of men on this earth who possess dull intelligence?
This science of the Goddess Prasannalakṣmī was [attained] by those born in the lineage of Nimi.
Released from there by Gautama through the power of his incanted nectar,
you were born into his lineage as the daughter of Janaka, with Lakṣmī herself manifesting in her grace.
From that time forward, all those born in his lineage became renowned as Janakas; they were liberated even while still living.
She alone is the supreme Gaurī, Himavat’s daughter, and Śivā;
she alone is Mahāvāṇī, Sāvitrī, and Sarasvatī. (77)
The Vedas and the Vedāntas have emerged from my mouth;
after that, the even more extensive Purāṇa emerged in ancient times.
Even all the treatises on Dharma proclaimed by the sages—no science superior to this has been seen or heard of anywhere. (79)
Even sages wander here in this world, afflicted by the misery of great poverty;
they do not obtain royal fortune, which bestows enjoyments, heaven, and the supreme goal.
This is the wish-granting tree of the world for men, bestowing the fruit of all desires; this is the manifest Kalpa-creeper, which grants the fulfillment of one's intentions.
What is this supreme jewel, which visibly bestows the fruits of one's desired goals,
such that even the perfected sages here are endowed with divine enjoyments?
Know them to be intent day after day upon the Mahālakṣmī-vidyā;
the first word consists of four syllables, and the second is called Parā. (83)
Know that Jālandharīśvara alone is the master of these three stages of the all-encompassing [Śakti]: the second called Paśyantī, the third called Madhyamā, and the first called Vaikharī.
Even the great sages, endowed with the grace of the Blessed One, know [this];
thereafter, the omnipresent Lord [bestowed] the fourth [son], Vāmadeva, named Vaidavari.
The four steps of speech are Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśvara, and even the great sages whose sins have been burnt away by austerity; they too know them. (86)
O Goddess, Daughter of the Mountain, that fourth form of Viśvarī which I have described as my own state is well-established among the gods, but not upon the surface of the earth. (87)
It is well known among humans, as well as among birds, animals, ants, serpents, and all deceased beings. (88)
Through the grace of the teacher, the royal fortune of knowledge arises from constant recitation;
this entire web of knowledge issues forth from his mouth. (89)
What is the use of saying much more in this regard? There is no object whatsoever—whether superior or even equal—that possesses the threefold nature of Mahāmanu’s royal fortune.

The sages of ancient times, possessed of great majesty, having worshipped Dharma—which bestows all objects of desire and possesses a gracious splendor—attained neither worldly enjoyment nor liberation, nor even the most exalted station of heaven. (91)

[Thus ends the seventeenth chapter in the Uttara-bhāga of the Saubhāgyavidyodaya, within the Śrīyadanuttarabrahmatattvarahasya, the Tantra of Daśaratha, which is a compendium of the essential meaning of the Vedas.]
The illustrious Dakṣiṇāmūrti said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall fully declare the procedure for the ritual practice of the great Mantra of Rājyalakṣmī,
by performing which one shall attain perfection.
The seer (ṛṣi) is declared to be Brahmā or Dakṣa Prajāpati;
the meter (chanda) is said to be Gāyatrī; she is the Mother of the entire universe. || 2 ||
O Śivā, Mahālakṣmī, the mother of the world, is declared to be the deity who is the sovereign of the great lion-throne of empire over the three worlds.
Śrī, U, and Bhuvaneśānī are proclaimed as the seed-mantras (bījamantra);
the heart is declared to be Śakti, and its application (viniyoga) bestows all desired objects.
The heart is said to be "kamale," the head "kamalālaye," and the crest-mantra (śikhā) is "prasīdade"; the armor (kavaca) consists of three syllables.
Or, at the end, one may separately recite the Netra-weapon mantra encapsulated by the Śrī-bīja.

I worship the lotus-born Mother of Hari, who is like a wish-fulfilling Pārijāta creeper; she is eternally bathed by the waters from jeweled jars held in the trunks of four tall, ruby-like elephants, and she holds in her lotus-hands a pair of lotuses that grant boons.
It stood amidst the ocean of nectar, wondrous with its fresh blossoms,
and was beautifully adorned with *putrāga*, *pāṭala*, *aśoka*, and *campaka* trees.
It was adorned with flowers stirred by a gentle breeze and water,
and graced with *sameru*, *ādhavī*, *bilva*, *devadāru*, and *lavaṅga* trees.
With *saṃtāna* trees, *pārijāta* and others, which are like celestial wish-fulfilling trees adorned with blossoms, as well as with *mātuluṅga*, *karṇikāra*, sandalwood, and *vuñjula* trees; || 9 ||
It was beautifully adorned by *aṅkola*, *dāḍima*, and *pūga* trees, as well as by *kuravaka* trees,
all of which were laden with flowers of every season and bent low under their weight.
In the midst of that [place], there were lotuses, heaps of pink and blue water-lilies,
fragrant kahlāras, and blossoming blue lilies as well.
In the midst of that, on a sandy bank surrounded by bees, hamsas, kāraṇḍavas, cakravākas, and other birds, and beautifully adorned with great white lotuses, [he saw her].
The jeweled pavilion was adorned on all sides by pārijāta trees and others,
provided with four gates, and beautified by a divine golden enclosure wall.
Resplendent with the brilliance of a thousand rising suns, yet as cooling as the moon;
adorned with divine jewels and beautified by eight door-panels.
It was enclosed by lofty gate-towers (gopuras) adorned with divine rubies,
and embellished by rows of learned twice-born men who were like golden sacrificial posts.
It was adorned with rows of pillars joined with the nine precious gems,
and it shone brilliantly, resplendent with thousands of divine, glowing columns.
It was endowed with windows resplendent with refined gold,
and further adorned by tens of millions of golden ornaments set with variegated silks.
It was adorned with golden tinkling bells, radiant like a jewel-mansion,
and [scented] with mālatī, kaṅkeli, jātī, and the filaments of yellow lotuses.
The surface of the earth was adorned with Tulasī, Mallikā, Savāsī, Nandyāvarta, and Kadamba flowers, as well as other divine blossoms of various kinds.
The quarters of the sky were made fragrant by Kāśmīra saffron, musk, tamālaka leaves, sandalwood, aguru, and camphor.
Having thus reflected in his mind, he beheld the vast jeweled pavilion and,
situated in the center of that pavilion, the Pārijāta, the celestial tree.
Below that was an unsurpassed throne of nine rubies;
there sat the Lord of the World, possessing the luster of a dark blue cloud.
Resembling the pinnacle of desire, it was draped in a pair of yellow garments and adorned with drops of great rubies,
diamonds, and rubies.
Wearing two earrings set with refined gold,
he was adorned with a crown, necklaces, armlets, bracelets, and other ornaments.
His chest was illuminated by the Kaustubha gem, he was adorned with a garland from the Tulasī grove, and he shone, resplendent with flower garlands such as those from the Pārijāta tree.
With a serene countenance and peaceful, he has eyes as long as lotus petals;
he holds the conch, discus, and the gestures of fearlessness and granting boons, and is served by yoginīs. || 26 ||
Adorned with a golden girdle set with divine rubies,
it was incomparable, beyond even the reach of the words of the ancients.
I bow to Nārāyaṇa, the ancient bliss, the forest of true consciousness, the infallible one, who is saluted by the elders among the gods and praised by the supreme sages.
On her lap was Mahālakṣmī, resembling a hundred rising suns,
with a complexion like the pomegranate flower and a radiance equal to the hibiscus.
Then she beheld her, who resembled refined gold, who was like a thousand flashes of lightning,
whose feet were adorned with anklets and shone brightly.
She was resplendent with a ring upon her toe of the lotus-foot that surpassed milk-white lac,
and she was graced by a pair of lotus-feet resembling land-growing lotuses.
Her lotus feet are resplendent with the luster of the rubies that are Brahmā, Rudra, Maheśvara, and the other lords; she is held by the remover of the afflictions of her devotees.
Adorned with a girdle-string of refined gold and jewels, she possessed a slender waist, broad hips, and was endowed with a deep-set navel. (35)
Resembling a golden pitcher, endowed with full and lofty breasts,
possessing broad and expansive thighs, and resplendent with the shining Kaustubha gem.
Divine, adorned with musk and saffron, chewed upon by the feet [of the Lord],
and beautified by an array of gems, pearls, and gold.
It was joined with large beads, adorned with small beads,
combined with strings of pearls, and beautified by a single-string necklace.
Adorned with divine jewels, wearing a golden ring upon her finger,
she was equipped with golden armlets and graced by a series of bracelets.
She was resplendent with golden bracelets and shining lotuses,
and her neck was graced by the first of ornaments.
Adorned with a bodice fastened with gold and pearls,
she has a smiling face, large eyes, and lips like the ripe bimba fruit.
She was adorned with a row of teeth as brilliant as a diamond-dust mote,
and graced by the tip of her tongue, which was red as a lotus and the abode of the play of speech.
Adorned with a nose-ornament set with pearls and gems,
she was graced by a pair of earrings made of refined gold.
She had lotus-like eyes and golden flower-dust upon her silver [complexion],
and the expanse of her two eyebrows surpassed the beauty of the god of love’s bow.
Her forehead shone, marked with an applied tilaka,
and she was adorned with garlands of jasmine, campaka, and punnāga flowers.
Adorned with a mass of hair resembling blue bees, her head was covered by a crown set with fresh rubies. || 46 ||
She bears a beautiful vessel filled with lotuses, gold, and jewels, possessing the luster of a lotus-womb, as well as a garland made of pearls and gems.
She who causes the delusion of the world and brings the three worlds under her control;
her face is like the stainless, full orb of the autumn moon.
[He saw her] consisting of all knowledge, worshipped by the entire host of great sages, with Vāṇī, Gaurī, Indrāṇī, and others serving her on both sides. (49)
She was not ascended by the sun and other [planets], but was surrounded by virtuous women;
she was graced by a white parasol dripping with gold upon her head.
Then [he saw her] surrounded by two female companions holding chowries in their hands,
her lotus feet resplendent with the rubies from the crowns of Indra and the other gods.
Praised by all classes of yogis, served by hosts of Brahman-sages, worshipped by the multitude of deities, and saluted by the assembly of great Siddhas; || 52 ||
The eternal one, who is the cause of prosperity for the three worlds, who attracts the three realms, and who brings delight to the three realms. (53)
She who causes delight to the three worlds, whose form enchants the universe,
the receptacle of powers such as atomization (aṇimā), and the bestower of the perfection of universal sovereignty.
She was beautiful with divine ornaments, adorned with celestial garlands and garments,
her limbs anointed with divine sandalwood paste, and she was praised by divine maidens.
She who dwells upon the lap of Nārāyaṇa, who is enchanting to Nārāyaṇa,
who has three eyes and four arms, and whose lotus-face is exceedingly serene.
I eternally worship Mahālakṣmī, the sovereign of the great lion-throne of imperial dominion over the three worlds, the bestower of all spiritual perfections.
Thus one should meditate upon Mahālakṣmī, who embodies the three Vedas, as the beloved of Hari;
or else, from the mūlādhāra to the brahmarandhra, she resembles the rising sun.
One should meditate upon the blazing, eternal Mahālakṣmī, the beloved of Hari, who consists of radiant energy, whether she be devoid of attributes (nirguṇā) or possessed of attributes (saguṇā). 59.
Having meditated upon and extracted from his heart the Vidyā named Śrīhṛdayā,
one who is pure in soul, by reciting it daily, shall become the foremost among those possessing prosperity.
Or if the disciple, having conquered his senses, [should behold] the teacher’s wife— who is Mahālakṣmī herself, the embodiment of the three Vedas, and adorned with divine ornaments— (61)
Having meditated upon her limbs anointed with divine sandalwood paste and adorned with divine garments and ornaments,
one should meditate upon the preceptor as Acyuta, with the thought that he is Nārāyaṇa.
The teacher’s wife, through meditation and with the thought that she is Mahālakṣmī,
becomes the beloved of Hari and the bestower of all desired fruits for him every day.
By this very authority, know the wife of the Guru to be Mahālakṣmī, who consists of the three Vedas; perform the sacrifice here, for there is no doubt.
Therefore, one must certainly and respectfully provide for the teacher’s welfare;
he should be honored with ornaments, clothing, and food, regarding him as Mahālakṣmī herself.
In all auspicious vows and supreme meritorious rites performed by practitioners,
one should honor the preceptor’s wife with ornaments, clothing, and food.
Let the practitioner behold with his very eyes the goddess Śrī herself, adorned with a pair of excellent earrings and a double-stringed necklace. 67.
Then [he gave] a beautiful golden nose-ornament set with gems,
as well as excellent finger-rings and other divine ornaments.
O Daughter of Himavat, by giving a pair of soft, smooth garments every month, one attains great success that is as difficult to obtain as a fly-whisk (cāmara). || 69 ||
Having prepared it anywhere at all, even year after year,
one should offer the collection of ritual procedures to the wife of the preceptor with a mind focused on Śrī.
If she beholds Mahālakṣmī, the beloved of Hari, with her own eyes, the wives of the preceptors shall indeed become blessed with sons. (71)
She herself is Mahālakṣmī manifest; do not entertain any doubt in this matter. The other wives of the preceptors should be understood as being like her, appearing as if they were Tṛpti.

O Daughter of the Snow-Mountain, O Śivā, if the wife of a guru is killed even by her own husband, or if she is situated at a great distance, yet within the range of [the killer's] illusory power (māyā), [he is guilty]. || 73 ||
Having offered the ornaments and other items, the best of practitioners should then give them to the hands of the preceptor’s son or to the preceptor’s wife. (74)
Even during festivals such as weddings,
one who is free from blemish should honor the teacher’s wife with ornaments and other gifts while standing before her.
Having also honored the teacher, one should then perform a great festival;
thus having meditated upon Mahālakṣmī, the Vidyā named Śrīhṛdaya.
Having recited the mantra five hundred times daily, or even four hundred,
or having performed the recitation three hundred times, one should offer oblations of clarified butter day after day.
He shall always obtain only auspicious things and is liberated from his afflictions;
all misfortunes shall never touch him because of that.
Misfortune and strife shall not dwell in that house where the Navacakra is installed;
in that home there shall be an increase of cattle and an increase of forest produce day by day. (79)
Every day there shall be an increase of grain and a constant growth of prosperity; it shall be filled with pearls and jewels today, and abounding in wealth and grain. (80)
The elephants were crowded together, and the assembly of servants was likewise thronged;
the goddess Lakṣmī remained upon that mountain for as long as the moon and stars endure.
Even those born into that lineage shall be endowed with prosperity, filled with a multitude of blessings, and possessed of long life and good health. (82)
O Goddess, you are the abode of all prosperity, like the moon and the stars;
wherever he dwells, O Goddess, or whichever field he protects, [may it be blessed by you].
That very Kollāpura is called Lakṣmī-kṣetra, the bestower of desired objects;
here and even in the hereafter, it grants prosperity, whether one possesses the three qualities or is endowed with virtues.
He obtained enjoyments, both divine and human, as well as the state of a Yakṣa;
likewise, for us two born of his lineage, O Śivā, may there be eternal liberation. 85.
This hymn on meditation, spoken by Akṣmī, bestows all perfections, removes all suffering, and is auspicious; now its worship shall be described. (86)
[Thus ends the eighteenth chapter in the Uttara-bhāga of the Saubhāgyavidyodaya, within the Vedasārārthasaṃgraha, the Dāśarathīya Tantra, the illustrious secret essence of the supreme Brahman.]
The venerable Dakṣiṇāmūrti said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the supreme procedure for the worship of Śrī;
by performing which, even one of dull fortune or ill-fortune becomes possessed of great fortune. (1)
Having risen during the *brāhma-muhūrta*, the practitioner, while still on his bed,
[should meditate upon] the pair of lotus feet of the Guru, which bestows all spiritual accomplishments.
The practitioner should join his palms at the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra) and recite [the mantra] twelve times;
likewise, he should recite the Vidyā of the Preceptor’s sandals ten or twelve times.
Having remembered his own great sin, having seen with his own eyes the pair made of gold—whether heated or melted—and having bowed down with devotion; || 4 ||
Or, being devoted to Viṣṇu, even while seeing the Tulasī or the lamp,
he should first look at the face of the teacher and then at the teacher’s feet.
One should perform purification in the presence of the preceptor and nothing else;
then, having bathed, one should perform the twilight devotions and recite the Mother of the Vedas (Gāyatrī).
Having worshipped the Sun-god, one should then diligently recite, according to one's capacity, the glorious eight-syllable mantra and the vidyā known as Śrīharayā.
Having recited [the mantra] five hundred times daily, or even four hundred times,
and having praised [her] with the *Prasannalakṣmī-stotra* or with the *Śrī-hṛdaya*, || 8 ||
The eight verses on the heart of Prasannalakṣmī have thus been proclaimed. || 8 ||
In ancient times, at the auspicious and delightful city of Kollāpura, Agastya [revealed] the great secret of the Atharvaveda, the *Lakṣmīhṛdaya*, which bestows all that is desired.
O fair-faced one, in ancient times, the Bhārgava beheld that which is the form of the mantra; then, having completed the daily fire-oblation, it blazed forth in the sacrificial fire.
Having offered oblations twenty-eight times with the Lakṣmī-hṛdaya-vidyā,
and having entered the sacrificial hall, he then remembered the two feet of the preceptor.
Having performed the worship of the Guru’s sandals with all the ritual offerings,
one should respectfully present milk, sugar, or clarified butter as the food offering (naivedya).
One should always give wealth according to one's capacity—whether it be a *niṣka*, or less than a *niṣka*, or half of that, or half of that again, or even a *cihnuka*, or half of that. || 13 ||
A wise person should offer half of that to the two feet of the preceptor,
using either vermilion, or according to one's capacity, copper, or even betel leaf.
Having offered [the image] into the presence of the pair of the teacher’s feet,
the wise one should then remove Mahālakṣmī and worship her in the [mandala] diagram.
She who was previously described as the sovereign queen Śrī-Vigrahālokanāyikā—that which was spoken of is known by the name of the city of Tanmallakramayodhyā. 16.
It brings about the attainment of the bliss of Brahmananda, bestows all perfections (siddhis),
and grants the fruit of the primordial form that destroys all evils.
It attracts the world, brings the three worlds under its control,
bestows the attainment of qualities such as *aṇimā*, and deludes the three realms.
It is the foundation of all prosperity, the subduer of all sciences, and that which always brings about the increase of sons, grandsons, great-grandsons, and their descendants. (19)
The sandals and collyrium for the body and so forth are supreme, bringing about great supernatural powers (mahāsiddhi); they remove all calamities and destroy all fears. || 20 ||
It pacifies all obstacles, bestows the accomplishment of all auspiciousness, removes all inauspiciousness for men, and shatters all primordial ignorance. || 21 ||
It bestows all good fortune through recitation, crushes all enemies,
pacifies untimely death, and increases beauty and intelligence.
This great secret among the worlds bestows long life and flowers and fruits;
it generates health for men and wards off disease and sorrow. || 23 ||
Having worshipped day after day that great and secret Śrīcakra, which bestows the fruits of all the years and grants the fruits of all desires; 24.
One shall obtain the complete fruit of the worship of all deities along with their ancillaries, because the Śrīcakra consists of all vidyās and bestows all perfections (siddhis). || 25 ||
In the presence of the Śrīcakra, the attainment of all vidyās occurs twice over, provided that one performs worship with constant devotion. (26)

Having recited the *Lalitā* three hundred times, and having purified himself, he should recite five hundred times the *Śrīdevī*, the bestower of all accomplishments, as well as the *Lakṣmīhṛdaya-vidyā*.
Freed from old age and death, he shall attain for a long time the supreme state hereafter,
as well as the sovereign powers such as atomization (aṇimā) and inexhaustible wealth.
One who practices this [rite] today shall obtain good fortune like that of the God of Love, the wealth of sons, grandsons, and so forth,
as well as divine and great enjoyments.
By the grace of the Lord of Lakṣmī, accompanied by a thousand families, he shall dwell in the city of Ayodhyā at the end; there is no doubt about this.
O Brahman, through the worship of the Śrīpīṭha, [are worshipped] Brahmā, Nārāyaṇa, Maheśvara,
the eight guardians of the quarters beginning with Śakra, as well as you, Lakṣmī, and Sarasvatī.
The Mothers, Caṇḍikā and the others, as well as the nine planets beginning with the Sun,
when worshipped, become satisfied and bestow their fruits upon him.
This supreme Śrī Devīcakra is named Ayodhyāpura;
by him who worships it constantly, the three worlds are worshipped.
The beautiful Śrī Devī, the mother of the worlds and the embodiment of the three Vedas, is constantly worshipped by him; he is the omniscient Lord of the universe. (34)
Or, day after day, one should worship the goddess Lakṣmīprasannalakṣmī, known as the Threefold Power (Triśakti), or the Sovereign Fortune (Sāmrājyalakṣmī).
One attains great accomplishment, difficult even for yogins to obtain;
Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa, together with their limbs and faces, are joined [therein]. 36.
Those who seek welfare should especially worship Bhavānī and Śaṅkara with reverence, or rather, them together with their limbs and retinues.
When worshipped, O Śivā, they shall both bestow all fruits; there is no doubt in this—whether by worshipping Mahālakṣmī alone or each [deity] individually.
In this Śrīpīṭha, one obtains great and unsurpassed merit;
however, if one is unable to do so here, one may worship Mahālakṣmī in another pīṭha.
I shall also describe that pīṭha; listen with a one-pointed mind.
It is a triangle, then a hexagon, and beyond that, a twelve-spoked [wheel]. (40)

One should draw a circle with sixteen petals, accompanied by two outer enclosures (bhūpuras); one should write the Praṇava in the center, interspersed with the name of the person to be accomplished and the ritual action.
In the three corners here, one should write the Śrī-bīja and the Śakti, as well as Bhuvaneśvarī;
then, one should write the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) in the six corners starting from the southeast corner in successive order.
Then, one should draw the twelve-spoked [lotus] of Mahālakṣmī with twelve syllables;
one should fashion sixteen petals joined with the sixteen vowels.
One should cause the Bhūpura (the city of the earth) to be known through the mantra of Tvaritā;
likewise, one should encircle the second earth-house in two ways.
In the corners of the two Bhūpuras (outer squares), the letters Ha and Kṣa should be carefully inscribed.
This Yantra of Mahālakṣmī, which destroys all misfortunes, has thus been described.
It bestows the fruit of all sovereign powers, shatters all poverty, pacifies all suffering, and grants the accomplishment of all that is auspicious. (46)
Enough has been said here; there is nothing superior to this:
here, before us, is the one endowed with form, the flower-bowed god accompanied by the goddess Rati. (47)
One should worship Kāma, who forms a handful of flowers, O Daughter of the Mountain;
one should worship him duly in the previously mentioned locations that have been prepared.
O Lord of the Universe, Dharā, Śrī, Sarasvatī, Durgā, Cāndrī, Gāyatrī, Devī, Uṣā, Iḍā, and Mahālakṣmī—these are known as the Three Powers (Triśakti). || 1 ||
You have stated that the sovereign fortune (sāmrājya-lakṣmī) is indeed Śrī herself; and you have declared that Maya is the source of all [delusion], while Maya is known by the name Dhyānagaṇa.
O Lord of the worlds, the Śrīcakra is Your very form upon this earth;
O Compassionate One, if You have mercy, please describe it out of Your grace, O Protector.
The venerable Dakṣiṇāmūrti said:
O Daughter of the Mountain, I shall proclaim the sacred seats (pīṭhas) of the Goddess Śrī; listen to their names upon the surface of the earth and remain attentive. || 4 ||
O Daughter of the Mountain, Mahālakṣmī is to be known at Kollāpura;
likewise, Mahālakṣmī, the beloved of Hari, resides at Sannati-pīṭha.
On Śrīśaila she is known as Āmara, the bestower of the glory of victory;
in Pāṇḍuraṅga she is called Triśakti, the beloved of Lakṣmī and Viṭṭhala.
Known as Saptā, Droghaka, Vīrā, Reṇukā, Rūpiṇī, and Ramā,
she is celebrated as the Yoginī Alaṃpurā, the bestower of the perfections of yoga.
The city of Kāñcī is proclaimed as Kāmākṣī, the beloved of Śaṅkara;
she is likewise known as Mīnākṣī in the southern city of Mathurā.
O Daughter of the Mountain, she who is famous as Śivakāmā and others is renowned even in Cidambaram; the remaining one is the great Lakṣmī, famous in Cāle.
The victorious Mahākālī, the beloved of Mahākāla, is eternally worshipped in the city of Laṅkā; she is Śāṅkarī, the dear consort of Śaṅkara.
In the great seat (pīṭha) of Kāmarūpa is Kāmākṣī, who possesses a form at will;
on Mount Mahendra is Durgā, the crusher of the demon Mahiṣāsura.
She is known as Padmākṣī by the sages on Siddhaparvata;
she is celebrated as Gaṅgāsāgarasargopā and Kamalālayā.
In that very place is she known as Pārvatī, who shares half the body with Śaṅkara;
on Nīlācala she is celebrated as Subhadrā, the bestower of worldly enjoyment.
Known as Māyādevī in Āgāyā, she is Śrī Haripriyā;
in Vārāṇasī she is Viśālākṣī, and there she bestows the perfection of pure food.
Right there resides Mahālakṣmī, who eternally bestows imperial sovereignty and spiritual perfection;
she is known as Mādhavī and Tāmrā, the beloved of Nārāyaṇa. (15)
Jānakī, the beloved of Rāma, is renowned as Citrakūṭā;
and Rukmiṇī, the beloved of Hari, is Mā at Dvārakā. (16)
In the city of Mathurā she was the daughter of Devaka and the mother of Kṛṣṇa;
in Gokula she is called Yaśodā, and in the forest of Vṛndāvana she is Rādhā.
In Hastināpura she is Subhadrā; on the Vindhya mountains she is Śubhanivāriṇī; and she who dwells auspiciously upon the peak of the Vindhya mountain is renowned as the goddess Durgā.
In the hermitage of Tārā, Vaidehī, the beloved of Rāghava, was proclaimed;
at Gaṅgādvāra, in the great field (Mahākṣetra), she is Sītā, the daughter of Janaka.
The illustrious Goddess Lalitāmbikā, whose chariot is the Himavat mountain,
is renowned as Mahātripurasundarī herself in Śrīpura.
On Mount Tārākiṃdha, she is renowned as Sarasvatī;
on Mount Mataṅga, she is celebrated as the Śrī-devī Maṃtriṇī. (21)
On Mount Varāha she is renowned as Bhūdevī, whose abode is the lotus;
in Kurukṣetra she is likewise celebrated as Pārvatī, the beloved of Śaṅkara.
In the city of Ayodhyā, she is renowned as Jānakī, the beloved of Hari;
on Śrīraṅga Mountain, she is renowned as Śrīdevī, whose abode is the lotus.
She is known as Sītā, the beloved of the son of Daśaratha, manifest at Siddhavaṭa;
she is known as Rudrāṇī, the beloved of Śaṅkara, on Tryambakagiri.
In the city of Tulajā, Bhavānī is renowned as Rūpiṇī-Ramā;
O Daughter of the Mountain, their sacred seats (pīṭhas) consist of the Cakrarāja.
Even by remembering this, a heap of sins is destroyed;
these are the perfected sacred fields (siddhakṣetra), though there are others as well upon the earth.
By remembering these names here, O beautiful one, one becomes cleansed of all impurities; all these are seats of radiant prosperity.
The forms of the Śrīcakra have been described, which are fully capable of bestowing all supernatural powers (siddhis).
One should be pure, always having the senses subdued, and devoted to the service of the Guru. (28)
Having recited the great spell of royal fortune while observing his vows, one shall attain great accomplishment in just three days. (29)
O Śivā, listen attentively as I shall describe to you those other pīṭhas on the surface of the earth that bestow spiritual accomplishments (siddhi), which are equal to the truth itself.
Kumbhakoṇam is a great village, and from there is Setubandha;
beyond that is the meritorious Anantaśayana and the bank of the Candraprakāriṇī.
Then there is the most purifying sacred field of Vīrarādhāvadhā,
and beyond that is the great sacred field of Alāpura, known as Āhovala.
The place named Gomana, Dhāmamūka, or Kṣetra, as well as the great village of Kanyākubja and thereafter Vedāraṇya. || 33 ||
The sacred field of Kālahastīśvara, the mountain named Maṅgalācala,
Varāhaśikhara, and then the meritorious Vedāriśikhara.
The sacred field named Dharmapura is known as Ākāśeśvara;
beyond that is the meritorious Ratnādriśikha, and then also the field of Lakṣmīśa.
Then there is the field named Jānakī, Vāsiṣṭhā, and the confluence of the Sindhu;
next is the field called Dākṣāṇya, and beyond that is Brahmeśvara.
The field named Nārāyaṇa, likewise Siṃhāghriśikhara, Śrīkūrmapada, and that which is called Mārkaṇḍeyapada. || 37 ||
Ānandeśa, Kṣetramoka, Kṣetra, Pañcaprayoga-kṣetra, and also Kedāra-kṣetra—these are the [five] fields. || 38 ||
Govardhana and other peaks, the supreme sacred site of Prabhāsa, the great field of Jaṃjūmārga, and the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean. || 39 ||
O Bharatas, the holy place named Kāpila is without a name;
the field known as Nandigrāma is exceedingly great and supremely purifying. (40)
The sacred Badarī forest is greater than all others, for there dwells the Blessed Lord himself, established in yoga, the husband of Śrī. (41)
For the welfare of all three worlds,
the lord of the earth protected the entire world while acting for the benefit of the virtuous.
He is the Lord who is the agent of creation, preservation, and destruction;
and that sacred field is attained through the dawning of fortune by those of virtuous soul. (43)
Even one afflicted by the consequences of killing a Brahmin or other such sins shall be liberated immediately upon seeing that sacred field, even if he is a perpetrator of a great crime (mahāpātaka).
There, the great yogi Hari himself, who is beyond Nārāyaṇa,
came from the world of Vaikuṇṭha to bestow spiritual perfections.
I shall fully describe the sacred fords (tīrthas) upon the surface of the earth that bestow spiritual perfection.
The Jāhnavī, the best of rivers, the Yamunā, and the Sarasvatī; the Godāvarī, the Kṛṣṇaveṇī, and the Kāverī, the foremost of rivers. (48)
The Narmadā, the highly meritorious Candrabhāgā, the Śatadrū, the Yoṣṇī, and likewise the river Sindhu, which is supremely purifying.
The Tuṅgabhadrā, the Bhīmarathī, the lake known as Yākhyam, the presence of Bhadrādri Śikharasvāmin, and the bank of the Gautamī. || 50 ||
You shall reach the bank of the Saptagodāvarī, Jānakīkuṇḍa,
the highly meritorious Rāmahrada, and the unsurpassed Rāmatīrtha.
The great holy site named Puṣkara on the bank of the Suvarṇamukharī,
the meritorious Lakṣmīsarovara, and also the Phalgunī-tīrtha.
The bank of the Sarayū is supreme, and beyond that the bank of the Tāpī;
then there is the Mandākinī, that holy pilgrimage site known as Vāsiṣṭha.
Gokarṇa, Naimiṣa, and Āṇaya; beyond that is Gaurītīrtha;
then the highly meritorious Śivagaṅgā, and after that Dhanuṣkoṭi.
The Gautamī river, the confluence of the Sindhu and the Gaṅgā (Veṇī), the sacred grove of Tulasī, and the seed of the Bilva tree are supreme. (55)
The bank of the Gaumati is also mentioned, as well as the celebrated Gaṇḍakī-tīrtha;
furthermore, the Kamalālaya-tīrtha and the excellent Sāvitrī-tīrtha.

Beyond that, the presence of these [deities] has been described; O Śiva, the presence of the Ācārya is said to be the most excellent of all sacred sites (tīrtha). They know that this glorious power resides in the presence of the stone discus (śilācakra). || 59 ||
The midst of a Tulasī grove is declared to be a great sacred site (tīrtha);
a grove of Bilva trees is remembered as meritorious and a bestower of great spiritual accomplishments (siddhi).
O beautiful one, all these forms possess a serene splendor;
by merely seeing them, eternal perfection shall be attained.
The seats of Lakṣmī, which consist of the sovereign wheel (cakrarāja), have been described;
or, by reciting even for a single day the Vidyā known as the Śrīhṛdaya, [one attains the goal].
One certainly attains great success; there is no doubt in this matter.

[Thus ends the twentieth chapter in the Uttara-bhāga of the Saubhāgyavidyodaya, within the Śrīmadanuttarabrahmatattvarahasya, the Dāśarathīya Tantra, which is a compendium of the essential meaning of the Vedas.]
The venerable Dakṣiṇāmūrti said:
O Śivā, I shall now declare the rite of *puraścaraṇa*, by performing which a person never fails to attain perfection in the mantra. (1)
One hundred thousand is prescribed for the Kṛta age, two hundred thousand for the Tretā,
three hundred thousand for the Dvāpara, and four hundred thousand for the Kali age.
In the Kali age, mortals will always be prone to physical ailments, possessed by wicked thoughts, and greedy for the wives and wealth of others. (3)
Therefore, O my beloved, the accomplishment of these mantras does not arise from a small number of recitations, even when performed during the previously mentioned auspicious times.
One who performs the *puraścaraṇa* rite on such ground attains unsurpassed success,
whether in the midst of a grove of *tulasī* plants or even in a forest of *viṇva* trees.
Whether at the foot of a tree, O Blessed One, or even in a temple of Śiva, or in a temple of Bhavānī, or even in a lotus-pool; || 6 ||
Whether in the temple of Śaṅkara or in the shrine of Gaṇeśa, having brought the preceptor into close proximity, perform the *puraścaraṇa* rite.
Even in the Kīkaṭa regions, if the presence of the venerable Guru exists,
that very place is declared to be Vadarīkānana, swiftly bestowing its fruits.

Remaining in the presence of the teacher, devoted to his daily duties, pure, with a slender body, self-controlled, having conquered anger, observing silence, and well-restrained during the twilight prayers; ||| 9 ||
Having become free from desire for fruits and avoiding conversation with heretics,
he never engaged in discourse with atheists or those outside the Vedic fold while in the forest.
He regards the wives of others as his own mother, is not greedy for the wealth of others, and is intent on not conversing with women in their menses or with those of the lowest castes.
Whether one is observing the Cāndrāyaṇa vow, or the Prājāpatya, or even another penance, or intent on the Tapta-kṛcchra, or subsisting on the five products of the cow (pañcagavya). || 12 ||
Whether subsisting on milk, or eating fruits, or consuming vegetables, or even eating roots and tubers; whether eating fruits or likewise sacrificial oblations (havir-anna). || 13 ||
Or, O Śivā, eating but a single meal a day and being pure with a stainless mind, one should recite this mantra for Mahālakṣmī after having informed one's own teacher.
With a serene mind, one should daily recite [the mantra] for three watches of the night, avoiding unwholesome company, idle talk, and slander. (15)
A wise man should avoid gambling with dice, as well as betting, association with wicked people, and devotion to scriptures that do not lead to liberation.
Listen to the censure of the Blessed One, which is a censure of the Vedas; it is found in the censure of the Teacher, and nowhere else is there a censure of sacrifice that bestows such evil. (17)
His heart was always intent on non-violence even toward a mere blade of grass, and he maintained an equal attitude toward all, whether friends, enemies, or their offspring. (18)
One should also converse with those who are disciplined while performing rites such as recitation and fire-offerings;
constantly worshipping the King of Mandalas (cakrarāja), one remains firm in one's vows.
Having consecrated the great vidyā, which has the eye as its mark,
the wise and supreme practitioner should satisfy it with ten parts of clarified butter, milk, sugarcane juice, or water.
O Goddess, one should satisfy [the deity] with jaggery-water or with water;
then one should offer oblations into the fire ten times that amount, using lotuses mixed with ghee.
Or else, with bilva fruits combined with the three kinds of honey, one hundred married women (suvāsinyas) should be honored, as should an equal number of Brāhmaṇas.
Upon the lotus-feet of the teacher, [one should offer] a thousand bhāras of gold,
or a thousand niṣkas, or even a hundred niṣkas.
Having granted a great accomplishment difficult even for the three worlds to attain,
one obtains the fortune of sovereignty and reaches the ultimate goal even at the end of the body.
This great preliminary rite (puraścaryā) is auspicious and brings about great accomplishments;
it overcomes even that which is unattainable for the gods, even if it be situated in another continent.
O lady of excellent vows, by means of this rite of *puraścaraṇa*, the goal is accomplished;
however, one who is unable to perform it here should perform a brief *puraścaryā* while remaining restrained in his observances.
I shall proclaim its ritual procedure; listen attentively, O auspicious one, to this most purifying vow performed in the month of Āśvina at the beginning of autumn. (27)
Known by the name Navarātra, it destroys all misfortunes and sins,
cures all diseases and impurities, and shatters all forms of suffering.
This purifying vow, which destroys great poverty, bestows enjoyment, and grants the great vidyā of royal fortune, should be undertaken by one who desires success. || 29 ||
O my beloved, one must certainly perform the Navarātra vow;
O blessed one, it is the destroyer of suffering and the supreme bringer of contentment and nourishment. (30)
O Śivā, I shall now describe the procedure for the Navarātra vow, which generates all that is auspicious; listen attentively, O Śivā.
O Goddess,
those learned in the meaning of the scriptures declare that beginning from the first lunar day (pratipad), each successive day is equal to a solar festival (raviparva).

In that regard, those learned in the Vedas and Vedānta declare that one should perform [the rite] every day, beginning from the root asterism (Mūla) and ending with the Viṣṇu asterism (Śravaṇā), at the time of half-rising.
Even there, the ninth [tithi] is equal to a hundred solar parvan festivals;
it is celebrated as "Mahatī" (the Great), bestowing the fruit of great siddhis.
The Vijayādārī [cave] is there, which bestows the fortune of recitation;
it is said to grant all perfections and to bestow enjoyment, heaven, and liberation.
On the first day of the lunar fortnight, having risen early in the morning,
one should remain silent and first perform an auspicious bath preceded by the command of the Noble One.
Or, having likewise meditated upon the Lord of the Gaṇas, one who is pure should recite [the mantra]. || 38 ||
Having visualized the serene Śrī Mahāvidyā, one should daily recite her mantra a thousand times,
or perhaps a hundred times and so forth.
O Daughter of the Mountain, having worshipped the Cakrarāja (the King of Discuses) together with its limbs and enclosures, or else the Sālagrāma stone discus; 40.
One should worship it daily twenty-eight times according to the prescribed rite, together with the *Laghuśrīcakra*, using the venerable eight-syllabled mantra (*vidyā*).
Having offered clarified butter and pure ghee with a tranquil mind,
he should then offer one hundred and eight oblations while bowing with the fifteen-syllable mantra.
Having offered oblations twenty-eight times with clarified butter using the four *Śrīsūkta* mantras, and having offered them one by one, he should recite the auspicious *Ārṣeya-stotra*.
In the nine-night rite, one may perform fifty-five repetitions, or even forty repetitions, according to the sequence of increasing by one each day.
With the knowledge of Brahman, the wise man should worship one hundred and twenty, or two hundred, or even one hundred [deities] of Śrī-Śrīśa, and he should also feed married women.
O Śivā, one who is firm in his vows should daily feed five, three, or even one couple with the thought that they are Śrī and Śrīpati.
O Śivā, one should always offer water for the feet at the lotus-feet of the Ācārya according to one's inclination,
or else, with the thought that he is directly Mahālakṣmī herself, who is dear to the Ācārya.

One should constantly worship [the deity] with garlands, ornaments, clothing, and food; even one who is weak or unfortunate should, at least occasionally, offer these, even if they are of the Śūdra class.
On the Mahānavamī day, having especially honored the preceptor’s wife with garments and ornaments, one should then worship the preceptor.
One who is firm in their vows should daily worship the Goddess of Speech (Vāṇī) within books;
and when the Mahānavamī day arrives, one should perform the worship in the morning with great fortune.
Having bathed and performed the purificatory rites, being modest and pure, he should offer oblations twenty-eight times into the kindled fire with the Gāyatrī mantra dedicated to Jātavedas.
Then, having offered one hundred oblations of ghee with the glorious eight-syllabled mantra,
he should subsequently offer one thousand three hundred oblations to Prasannalakṣmī.

Having offered oblations of honey mixed with the three [sweet substances], combined with sesame and bilva leaves, and saturated with cow's ghee, into the clarified butter [consecrated] by the rays of the Lord; 53.
Then, having become pure once, one should respectfully offer ghee fifteen hundred times with devotion using the Lalitāraśmi-vidyās. (54)
Then, having offered one hundred and eight oblations of cow-ghee for the sake of Lakṣmī, Prasannalakṣmī, and thereafter for Triśakti; || 55 ||
One should zealously offer oblations twenty-eight times for the sake of imperial sovereignty;
having performed the recitation (japa) and other rites, as well as the fire-oblation (homa), one should then perform the expiatory oblations (prāyaścittāhuti).
Having offered the oblation with the "brahmārpaṇa" mantra and bowed to the fire thereafter,
one should then worship Lakṣmī and the Lord of Lakṣmī (Viṣṇu) five hundred times with flowers.
O Śivā, having performed the worship of the Wheel-King (Cakrarāja) along with its ancillaries in its presence, he,
being composed, prostrated before the pair of feet of the Preceptor.
One should offer two earrings made of sixty *sauvarṇas* of gold, fashioned with the color of *yama*, and joined with *vajra* and *bindu*. (59)
Then, O Śivā, one should give a load of gold as a fee to the Guru,
or a thousand *niṣkas* of gold, or even a hundred *niṣkas*.
Or half of that, or half of that again, or twelve niṣkas;
one should give a pair of fine garments, and the disciples should receive them with auspiciousness.
He gave to the teacher’s wife an auspicious ear-ornament known as the *śrī-budhyātāṭaṅka*,
fashioned from gold, and also a nose-ornament.
The practitioner must certainly wear ornaments such as these:
either earrings as an ornament, or a necklace made of gold.
The practitioner, being unattached, should offer a single ornament to Śivā;
or, having first offered something subtle, he should then offer it with the thought that it is Mahālakṣmī herself.
One hundred married women should be fed, or half of that, or half of that again;
or fifteen should be honored, or even none at all. (65)
One should worship pairs of lotuses with the thought that they are Śrī and Śrīpati; one should also cause Brahmins to bathe them along with their wives using sacrificial fees.
In this way, by what has been performed, there is no doubt; the vow would be declared complete.
Even a poor person, having performed the vow, [attains it] through the two-fold selection of his own preceptor.
Having first given two cows that yield much milk along with their calves,
he should offer a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) while remaining restrained in speech.
Having thus performed the preliminary rite (puraścaryā) during the auspicious Navarātra vow, || 70 ||
One attains the unsurpassed success of great knowledge and royal fortune,
equal to that of a thousand Agniṣṭoma sacrifices and an unimpaired Vājapeya sacrifice.
Having obtained the fruit arising from a hundred great sacrifices such as the Tulā and Hiraṇyagarbha, the purified soul attains union with Nārāyaṇa.
In that year, he will certainly behold Mahālakṣmī,
despite the terrible great sins accumulated over ten million births.
Having obtained this great gift, which is vast, long-lasting, and beyond comprehension—filled with pearls and jewels like a field of grain—he is liberated. (74)
And having obtained great fortune, which is fickle yet pervasive through progeny and crowded with elephants and cattle, he becomes endowed with all auspiciousness. (75)
Having become beautiful in body, resembling the life-force of a master of spells, and having attained great prosperity crowded with sons, grandsons, and so forth; || 76 ||
Having attained the eightfold sovereign powers on earth and the ability to die at will,
he then enjoys divine pleasures that are exceedingly difficult to obtain.
Having rescued a hundred families submerged in the hells,
he shall obtain a beautiful celestial chariot that moves at will and is accompanied by a hundred divine maidens.
Having ascended the vehicle of the Blessed One, one attains the supreme state; of this there is no doubt.
This auspicious Navarātra vow bestows all perfections.
Thus has been briefly stated that which brings about accomplishment; another [method] shall now be declared:
when the sun’s transit (saṃkrānti) occurs on the seventh lunar day in conjunction with a Sunday.
The one named Jayakṛḍāmaṇi is declared to be attainable through yoga;
if the sun’s transit (saṃkramaṇa) should occur there during the Brahma-muhūrta, [it is most auspicious]. || 81 ||
"O beloved, the great sages declare that the Mahāyoga conjunction occurs when the constellation presided over by Bhaga is present here."
Neither I, nor even Brahmā or Hari, would be able to describe its fruit;
furthermore, there is the Uttarāyaṇa Saṃkrānti occurring on a Monday in conjunction with the seventh lunar day (Saptamī).
If this [time] at midday is obtained together with the Sāvitra-tārā, the great sages call it the supreme, great yoga named Vijayā. || 84 ||

In the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, during the time sacred to Brahmā, on the seventh lunar day falling on a Sunday, there occurred the sun’s transit into Sagittarius (Dhanus), which was joined with that very yoga.

The wise call this yoga "Rājarāja" or "Mahendra. If, on the seventh lunar day of the month of Puṣpa, conjoined with the asterism Indu (Mṛgaśīrṣa), there occurs the transit of the Sun at midday conjoined with the asterism Savitṛ (Hasta); || 86 ||

They call this "Trailokyacintāmaṇi-yoga" the bestower of great siddhis, the most excellent, the cause for the attainment of all prosperity, and the cause for the destruction of the multitude of all sins. (87)

They declare this Yoga to be auspicious, glorious, the destroyer of the impurities of the Kali age, the eradicator of suffering, pure, a wish-fulfilling gem, and the divine cause for the attainment of dharma, artha, and kāma. (88)
O Śivā, when the sun, joined with the [appropriate] lunar day (tithi), transfers its rays to the other heap [of days], that entire month is said to be conjoined with Yoga.
The divine great sages have declared this yoga to be the bringer of the fortune of victory;
it shall first be explained as lasting until the transit of Hṛṣa.
O auspicious one, when the sun enters the zodiac sign at the time of Brahma (dawn),
the pure-souled one should rise there and [recite] the twelve-syllable mantra of Śrī-Śrīśa.
Then, having constantly remembered [the Lord], bathed, and performed the twilight prayers (saṃdhyā) and other rites,
[one should worship] at the Śālagrāma stone-circle endowed with the king of discs (cakrarāja).
The wise one, fulfilling the command of his own teacher, should worship Śrī Śrīśa;
he should worship Him daily three hundred or one hundred times with the Brahmavidyā mantra.
With excellent bilva leaves, or with flowers, or with tulasī petals, or with rose-apple sprouts, dūrvā grass tips, or even with śamī leaves. (94)
Having worshipped and offered services such as incense and lamps,
[he should offer] krisara mixed with sugar, along with fresh ginger and immersed in cow's ghee.
Then, having offered that same auspicious *kṛsara* separately to Śrī, Śrīpati, and Śrīdevī, he [offered it] according to the rules into the consecrated fire. || 96 ||
O Śivā, one should offer oblations twenty-eight times with honey mixed with cow’s clarified butter, using the Veda-mantras as the starting point.
Thereafter, one should perform twenty-eight oblations with the Śrīmadaṣṭārṇa mantra using pure ghee, or else with the Lakṣmī-hṛdaya-vidyā.
Having offered one hundred and eight oblations with the fifteen-syllable mantra of Śrī, and then having offered twenty-eight oblations with the four Śrī-mantras; || 99 ||

Then, one should offer clarified butter with the *arkāvṛtti* [recitation]; thereafter, one should recite the mantra of the Heart of Śrī a hundred times daily, having first recited the eight-syllabled mantra.

O Daughter of the Mountain King, by performing a sacrifice with the *vidyā* of the Lord of Prasadālakṣmī using arka flowers as the oblation, one obtains day after day the merit of ten million cows and ten thousand sacrifices performed daily. 101.
O Śivā, by performing this daily practice through the great yoga of Vijaya-śrī in this month, the sun enters Capricorn just as it does [at the winter solstice].
Having risen there at dawn and performed the morning rites,
one should offer three hundred oblations into the fire with the *Ramā-hṛdaya-vidyā*.
Having worshipped as before with the glorious eight-syllabled mantra,
and thereafter having offered three hundred oblations of clarified butter, [one should worship] with the rays of the Lord.
Having offered ghee individually for each [deity], one should offer ghee once for the Śrī-devī;
then, having offered it one hundred and eight times with the mantra of the Śrī-devī.
Having offered [the oblation] twenty-eight times, or even twenty-one times, O illustrious one. || 107 ||

One should recite the *Hṛdayavidyā* five hundred times for the sake of clear fortune; at the time of the transition of the sun [at the equinox], one should bathe and worship the two feet of the Teacher (*Ācārya*). (108)
Having bowed and drunk the water from the feet [of the preceptor], he is liberated from all sins; thereafter, having established the sacred fire in the presence of the Ācārya... (109)
At the beginning, one should offer ghee twenty-eight times with each of the Veda-mantras;
one should also offer ghee twenty-eight times with the Brahmavidyā.
One should offer clarified butter individually with each of the Bhagavadraśmi-mantras;
thereafter, one should offer three hundred oblations of clarified butter with the Śrīmad-aṣṭākṣara-mantra.
Then, having invoked Mahālakṣmī into the blazing fire, || 112 ||
Having worshipped the goddess Śrī, the beloved of Hari, with all ritual offerings,
Mahālakṣmī became pleased and [bestowed] one thousand three hundred [verses].
Having offered oblations in the presence of the preceptor with sesame seeds mixed with clarified butter, accompanied by bilva leaves, and combined with the three kinds of honey; 114.
One should offer ghee individually with each of the Lalitā, Raśmi, and Vidyā mantras;
and one should offer ghee one hundred and eight times with the fifteen-syllable Śrī mantra.
Then, O Goddess, having offered clarified butter with the Lakṣmī-mantra, the Śrīdevī-hṛdaya, the Triśakti-lakṣmī, and the Sāmrājya-lakṣmī; || 116 ||
Having offered oblations twenty-eight times, having offered them individually into the fire (jātavedas),
and having subsequently performed the recitation of mantras and so forth, one should perform the oblation of "Brahmārpaṇa."
Having circumambulated the fire and bowed with devotion by prostrating with all eight limbs,
he indeed paid homage to the pair of lotus feet of the preceptor.
Having adorned [the image] according to one's ability with a pair of fine garments,
one should thereafter offer a pair of earrings upon the two ears.
Having offered another ornament upon the pair of ears,
wealth equal to a year's worth of food should be given at the two feet.
Or he may offer twenty-one [pieces], or half of that in their absence, or even half of that; the wise man should avoid greed for wealth. || 121 ||
One āḍhaka measure of pearls should be sent to the house of the Guru;
and five āḍhaka measures of ginger should be offered, O Śivā.
Or half of that, or even half of that, one should abandon there as well;
two cows yielding much milk should be given for the duration of a year.
If one is unable and poor, O Goddess, one should respectfully offer five gold coins (niṣkas) at the pair of feet of the preceptor for the sake of attaining success.
Then, O Śivā, one should offer as an arghya to the teacher’s wife a beautiful and auspicious ear-ornament (āṭaṅka) known as the Śrī-budhyā, along with a shimmering kunaka and a cintāka.
There, being unable [to give it directly], he should place a nose-ornament fashioned from a coin into a cloth,
conceal it, and then feed the married women.
The wise one should offer a pair of excellent golden bracelets, fashioned from two *pala*s of gold, upon his two hands. (127)
One should offer an image fashioned from a pala of gold to Śivā;
if one is unable to do that, then one should fashion it from very bright silver.
One should give two palas in measure, or even just one pala;
furthermore, one hundred married women (suvāsinīs) should be fed, or fifty, or twenty-five.
Or else, with a mind of serene faith, one should diligently offer as food to a learned Brahmin (śrotriya) a pumpkin (kūṣmāṇḍa) rich in many seeds.
Having placed it upon a heap of grain, one should offer it at that time;
O my beloved, at that time, a very long gourd (kūṣmāṇḍa) is dear to me.

If one’s own wife or oneself should give it with a one-pointed mind upon the ground, accompanied by a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), then even instantly [the merit] is attained by those who eat from the hand.
O Daughter of the Mountain, for as many seeds as one who is liberated casts there,
for that many thousands of kalpas does he dwell in Vaikuṇṭha.
There, one endowed with abundant wealth should bestow the earth along with many sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇās),
give twelve cows, and offer a heap of sesame seeds with a liberal fee.
One may give even a great gift or a kingdom for the sake of attaining compassion;
