whatever is given at that time of the Great Yoga, O Maheśvarī, [is of supreme merit]. (135)
The ancient supreme sages, having constructed sacrificial altars equal to Mount Meru,
performed the fire-oblation in this manner with devotion for a thousand years.
O Mīnālau-dhana, whatever fruit is obtained by one who stands in the midst of the five fires through austerity, that very fruit you shall obtain; there is no doubt in this matter.
He who, having conquered his senses, performs the *puraścaryā* rite during this month according to the aforementioned procedure, obtains the merit of giving away thousands of horses.
O Śivā, the radiant one obtains twice that fruit by doing this;
moreover, Lakṣmī becomes gracious toward him.
O Daughter of the Mountain, on the occasion of the Śrī-Budhāda yoga, one should offer a golden ornament along with fine garments to the wife of the preceptor.
"Thus, having performed the *puraścaryā* here in this rare conjunction, he shall become a son of Fortune, a being of splendor on earth endowed with good luck. (141)
Though burdened by heaps of sins accumulated over ten million births,
one is liberated [from them] and attains the fruit produced by a thousand horse-sacrifices.
Having obtained inexhaustible merit from a thousand great gifts, O auspicious one,
the pure-souled person shall always possess great and imperishable health.
Having attained a long life,
he shall enjoy great and inexhaustible prosperity, crowded with bees and filled with elephants, horses, and chariots.
Having attained a splendor resembling that of Indra, appearing as if distinguished by sacred knowledge,
and having achieved the eightfold supernatural powers, he obtained the glory consisting of sons and grandsons.
Having attained the eightfold yoga and become one who remembers his past births for a long time,
he [attains] that which bestows all enjoyments together with a thousand divine nymphs.
At the end, having ascended a celestial chariot accompanied by thousands of his kin,
he becomes free from old age and death, remaining at the age of twenty-five.
O Śivā, this Yoga-rāja is obtained after thirty-six years; it remains in the presence of the Blessed One as the ultimate oblation unto the Blessed One.
O lotus-eyed one, it is truly not possible for me to describe the fruit of the gift given, the oblation offered, or the deed performed here. 149.
Now, even on a single day, the [rite] of Mahālakṣmī will be proclaimed twice;
having heard which, the practitioner on earth will have accomplished his purpose. || 150 ||
In the month of Bhādrapada, during the bright fortnight, on the eleventh lunar day conjoined with the asterism Śravaṇa and joined with Monday. || 151 ||
Or when joined with a Saturday, or likewise conjoined with a *sukarman* [auspicious] day, or even when joined with an *ati-ṣaḍa*, whether by day, at twilight, or at night. (152)
The great yoga known by the name Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa has been proclaimed;
it is said to be unattainable in this world, yet it bestows the accomplishment of all auspiciousness. || 151 ||
In this [state], what is muttered, offered in sacrifice, and given is said to bring about all accomplishments;
no yoga equal to this is described by the supreme sages. (152)
When this essence of yoga has been attained, Mahālakṣmī becomes gracious toward those who perform recitation, fire-offerings, and other such rites, together with the Lord and the Self. 153.
I shall now describe the *puraścaryā*, which grants success in the Yoga-rāja; when an unattainable conjunction (*alabhyayoga*) has arrived, whether by day, at the twilights, or at night. (156)
Having first performed auspicious ablutions, or having bathed in a river, O Śivā,
one should prostrate like a staff with eight limbs before the pair of feet of the preceptor.
Then, placing that command upon their heads, the two lords, Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa,
worshipped him with twenty-four types of ritual offerings.
Having worshipped five hundred [mantras] beginning with "Śrī Śrī," consisting of ten syllables, into the consecrated fire in the presence of the lotus feet of the Guru; 159.
With sesame seeds mixed with cow-ghee, using the glorious eight-syllable mantra,
and combined with the three kinds of honey, one should perform more than a thousand oblations.
One should offer sesame seeds and *revaha* flowers into the fire along with *bilva* leaves mixed with ghee,
while reciting the twenty-eight-syllable mantra of the Blessed One's Vidyā.
Having offered oblations twenty-eight times with the rays of the Goddess Śrī using ghee,
one should then offer oblations individually with the mantra of Śrī consisting of ten syllables.
Then, having offered one hundred and eight oblations with the four Śrī-mantras,
he should offer them twenty-eight times each into the sacrificial fire.

Then, having offered oblations with clarified butter alone, and having performed the expiatory oblations through recitations and other rites, one should perform the oblation of "offering unto Brahman" (brahmārpaṇa).
Then, having prostrated before the pair of feet of the teacher in the presence of the fire,
[he offered] sixty gold *cihukas* adorned with rubies.
A pair of beautiful earrings, necessarily marked with diamond-like spots, should be respectfully placed upon his two ears.
Then the teacher’s wife should be diligently adorned with collections of ornaments for the sake of auspicious intellect, or having offered her fine garments. 167.
And sesame seeds, measuring either five āḍhakas or four āḍhakas, should be offered at the lotus-feet of one's own teacher.
Alternatively, pure rice equal in weight to a *droṇa* should be given;
or gold weighing one hundred *niṣkas*, or half of that, or half of that again.
Gold must necessarily be given, either twelve *niṣkas* or whatever wealth is appropriate as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), accompanied by a pair of earrings.
One who desires the attainment of mountains should certainly give to the pair of the teacher’s feet a vigorous cow with her calf, O Mountain. (171)
One should give twelve villages and a hundred [gold pieces] along with sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā);
having respectfully gratified the preceptor with gifts of reward, one should honor him with devotion.
O Maheśvarī, in the absence of that Guru, having given the prescribed sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) along with a pair of earrings to his son, [he departed].
One should keep a vigil at night, intent on the worship of Śrī and the Lord of Śrī;
for he who has performed the Paurāṇika vow there, O my beloved, [attains my favor]. (174)
By that act, a hundred Vājapeya sacrifices would have been performed; of this there is no doubt.
On that day, one should remain without food, or subsist on milk, or eat only fruit. || 175 ||
Having kept a vigil at night with twelve kinds of pure foods,
one who has risen in the morning, bathed, performed his daily rites, and honored the illustrious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa— 176.
The observer of the vow should feed twenty-four Brahmins and married women, or else twelve, with polished, four-cornered plates.
Having personally satisfied [the preceptor] with betel, sacrificial fees, and other offerings according to the rules, and being pure,
he should receive the blessings of the preceptor and eat together with his kinsmen.
O Śivā, whoever of pure soul performs this *puraścaryā* in the *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-yoga*, he certainly becomes a perfected one (*siddha*). || 179 ||
By the heaps of great sins accumulated over ten million births—
whether committed through body, mind, or speech, and whether done knowingly or unknowingly— (180)
One shall be instantly liberated from the collection of minor offenses (upapātaka);
likewise, that which arises from a hundred repetitions of the preliminary rite (puraścaryā), when performed with its constituent parts and accompanied by the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). || 181 ||
In the Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa yoga, one obtains the supreme fruit;
in this case, an auspicious Śālagrāma stone must certainly be offered. 182.
Through the offering of a Śālagrāma stone during the Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa yoga, one obtains the eternal fruit of giving away ten million cosmic eggs (Brahmāṇḍas). || 183 ||
By offering even a single oblation of sesame seeds during the Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa yoga,
one enjoys the inexhaustible fruit of a thousand million homas.
One hundred niṣkas of wealth, measured by a year's worth of food, is prescribed;
one should abandon greed for wealth by giving half of that, or even half of that again. (185)
In the Yoga named Lakṣmīśanāmūka, one should give wealth equal to a year's worth of food,
or even twelve niṣkas, at the lotus-feet of the preceptor.
Having obtained the fruit born of giving, which is as vast as Mount Meru, moving, and golden, what would a pure-souled person do, O Blessed One? (187)
In the Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa yoga,
having given a pair of golden earrings to the ears of the preceptor, one attains the merit of offering gold equal to Mount Meru.
Whatever fruit one obtains on earth, one attains that same fruit here in an inexhaustible form. || 189 ||
Moreover, having rescued his thousand ancestors who were submerged in the ocean of hell,
he causes them to reach the eternal Satyaloka.
Having offered such ornaments as these to the teacher’s wife,
she beholds with her own eyes Śrī herself, accompanied by the Blessed Lord.
Having given a cow during the Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa conjunction, the ascetic woman attains the complete fruit of giving ten thousand cows.
Having performed the *puraścaraṇa* rite with devotion during the *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa* yoga in the presence of the preceptor, one attains prosperity endowed with the eightfold qualities. (193)
Having obtained a city resembling that of Mahendra, abounding in wealth, grain, and the like,
and filled with pearls, gems, and other riches, he was equal to Kandarpa in splendor.
Having reached the further shore of all branches of knowledge, and having become the repository of all prosperity, he was joined with sons and other kin. (195)
Having attained a mass of excellence and auspiciousness day by day, and having obtained a long life, he shall be endowed with all enjoyments. (196)
Having long remembered his past births and having perceived Brahman, he reaches at the end of the body that eternal, supreme abode which is difficult even for yogins to attain. || 197 ||
Where there is no doubt as to where one should proceed, I have spoken the truth, the absolute truth:
a yoga equal to that of Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa does not exist. 198.
Whatever action is performed here is said to yield infinite fruit;
thus, the attainment of the mantra (vidyāsiddhi) is not declared to occur in a single day alone.
O Śivā, I shall further explain that which brings about the attainment of the mantra.

[Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Arising of the Saubhāgya-Vidyā," in the latter section of the *Vedasārārthāgraha*, the *Dāśarathīya Tantra*, which is the illustrious secret essence of the unsurpassed Brahman-reality.]
The illustrious Dakṣiṇāmūrti said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the great ritual of the Mahālakṣmī-mahāmantra, which bestows success; by performing it, one shall attain perfection. || 1 ||
At the beginning of the year, in the month of Caitra, starting from the first day (pratipad), there is a great wound in your city called Vāsanta, which is known as Night. || 2 ||
It brings about the highest good, destroys great calamities, grants desired objects,
bestows the fruit of prosperity such as sons and grandsons, and grants success in recitation (japa).
It is the cause of all prosperity, the bestower of the fruits of Vedic rites,
and that which brings heaps of wealth such as pearls, gems, and gold into the home.
It is conducive to dharma, bestowing glory, providing nourishment, and increasing fame;
this should be performed from the first day of the month when Caitra arrives.
O Mahodaya, as long as that excellent rice-offering for the birth of Śrī Rāma lasts, each single day there shall possess equal splendor.
The ninth lunar day (Navamī) of Śrī Rāma’s birth always bestows the fruit of a hundred sacrifices;
its presiding deity is Tāraṇa, Aditi, or likewise Bṛhaspati.
If [the rite] is performed on that ninth day, it bestows great supernatural power (mahāsiddhi);
its fruit cannot be described even by me or by the Creator himself.
That day is proclaimed as Sītārāma Jayantī, which bestows all perfections;
the fruit produced there by recitation, fire-offerings, and other rites is most exalted.
It cannot be described even by me, nor by Brahmā or Hari;
for as long as the birthday of Śrī Rāma exists on earth, it renders [all other auspicious days] fruitless.
O Daughter of the Mountain, on this earth, he alone has accomplished all his duties who offers even a small amount of gold on the birthday of Śrī Rāma.
Having bestowed the great gift upon the lotus feet of the preceptor, and having obtained the fruit born of a thousand [such acts], the purified soul attains union with Brahman.
On the birthday of Śrī Rāma, one should certainly offer either a piece of sugarcane or even a plantain fruit at the lotus feet of the preceptor.

At the end of the body's life, one shall attain residence in a delightful forest of wish-fulfilling trees on the day that the glorious eight-syllable mantra is bestowed by the Goddess of Royal Fortune.
Having offered a single oblation into the fire, one obtains the fruit of a hundred sacrifices;
I shall describe the procedure for that, O best of men, with the utterance of "vāṣaṭ."
When the Navarātra of Vasanta, which bestows all perfections, is proclaimed, it is for the sake of the eight-syllable heart-mantra of Prasannalakṣmī. || 16 ||
On that first day of the lunar fortnight, having bathed there in the presence of his own preceptor, he, with a purified soul, performed his morning rituals.
Having mastered one thousand Gāyatrīs, or five hundred, or four hundred,
or three hundred, while the sacrificial fire is blazing, || 18 ||
Whether in a Vedic or worldly rite, having offered twenty-eight portions of clarified butter from cows with the Veda alone, and twelve with the Brahmavidyā; 19.
Afterwards, one should offer one hundred and eight oblations with the *Śrī-aṣṭākṣarī* mantra;
then, one should also offer one hundred and eight oblations with the *Prasanna-lakṣmī* mantra. (20)
Afterwards, one should offer clarified butter with the Śrīvidyā mantra one hundred and eight times,
and then recite the glorious eight-syllabled mantra five hundred times.

O Śivā, beginning from the first day of the lunar fortnight, one should devotedly recite the *Śrīhṛdaya* mantra eight thousand times every day for eight days, accompanied by a formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*).
One should daily recite three hundred and twenty-eight times the fifteen-syllable mantra of the Goddess who dwells on the lion-throne, the Daughter of the Mountain. (23)
One should daily recite one hundred and eight, or even twenty-eight times, the Rājarājeśvarī-vidyā known as Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa.
Having recited the Śrī-hṛdaya-stotra, the unsurpassed hymn of the Atharva-veda,
one should respectfully recite it forty-five times according to the prescribed practice.
One should worship the Śrīcakra daily together with a Śālagrāma stone, and one should always feed married women with the thought that they are Mahālakṣmī herself.
Or, the observer of the vow may satisfy even a single person who is prone to causing dissension with delicious foods;
thereafter, having risen in the morning on the ninth day, he should worship Śrī Rāmacandra.
Having bathed, recited the Gāyatrī, and completed the daily fire-oblation (nityahoma),
he should afterwards [perform the rite] in the presence of the preceptor before the consecrated Jātavedas (sacrificial fire).
One should offer cow’s ghee twenty-eight times at the beginning of each Vedic mantra and so forth;
having offered it twenty-eight times, one should [offer] the ten-syllable mantra beginning with "Śrī Śrī."
One should offer five hundred oblations of clarified butter with the glorious eight-syllabled mantra;
then, having invoked Mahālakṣmī, who consists of the three Vedas, into that fire.
One should perform twenty-four supplementary offerings;
then, one should offer a single oblation for each of the deities of the enclosure.

Having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the Ṛṣis, meters, and other elements, the self-controlled practitioner, being serene, meditated upon the Goddess who destroys the obstacles of sacrifice, remaining fixed in her abode. || 32 ||
Mixed with the three sweets (madhuparka), accompanied by sesame seeds and bilva leaves,
combined with plantain fruit, and endowed with tawny-colored clarified butter.
Or, having offered one thousand three hundred oblations of pure cow-ghee,
he should then proceed with that same ghee for the sake of attaining a serene splendor.
One should offer one oblation for each of the Bhagavadraśmi-mantras;
then, [one offers] up to ten with the Raśmi-mantras of the Great Queen Śrī.
Having offered one oblation for each [syllable] with the fifteen-syllable Śrīsūkta mantra,
he should then offer one hundred and eight oblations of clarified butter from a cow.
Then, one should offer oblations one hundred and eight times, or twenty-eight times, to Rājarāja, Mahālakṣmī, and Nārāyaṇa.
O you of pure vows, one should offer even a single oblation of clarified butter during a festival time to Rājarāja Mahālakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa.

He shall obtain the imperishable fruit of a thousand-fold ten-millionfold oblation (sahasrakoṭi-homa) by offering oblations with the twenty-eight-syllable mantra at the conclusion of the preparatory rite (puraścaraṇa).
One immediately obtains the fruit of a hundred *puraścaryās* without a doubt;
therefore, for the mantra of twenty-eight syllables, the conclusion with *homa* must certainly be performed. (40)
Then, having offered oblations through recitations and other rites, and having performed the *brahmārpaṇa* oblation,
he circumambulated the fire and paid homage to the Daughter of the Mountain King.
And having prostrated with eight limbs before the pair of feet of the teacher,
he offered two golden earrings fashioned by the artisan Cihnuka.
The preceptor should certainly place the vajra, joined with the vidyā and accompanied by the lotus, into the pair of ears of the disciple while the fire is present.
The all-pervading Lord Rāma, son of Daśaratha, whose essence is the Narayana of sacrifice,
together with Jānakī, performed a hundred-fold preliminary rite for him.
It bestows great accomplishment immediately, without a doubt; or else, a pair of fine silk garments (dukūla) should be offered, or even a pair of cotton cloths. 45.
One should request a pair of garments and a ring, performing many recitations;
or, having given wealth, one who is affluent may further offer a thousand pieces of gold.
Or else, one may offer as much wealth as is consumed in a year, or twelve *niṣkas*; even if unable to afford that, one should offer six *niṣkas*, or three, or even a single *niṣka*.
And there he should offer a fresh plantain fruit to the venerable Guru,
along with a multitude of stalks of sugarcane and accompanied by coconut fruits.
Even a poor man of meager fortune must certainly offer [the gift] at the two feet of the Vīmanācārya, having begged from members of all castes.
Having given gold or a coin to the lotus-feet of the preceptor,
one should give a beautiful maiden endowed with the qualities of virtue and nobility.
If one is unable to give even a pair of earrings, one may first offer a maiden or even a small amount of wealth; beyond that, it is considered a heap of fruit.
One must certainly offer a substance worth five niṣkas to the guru;
if one gives less than that, one does not attain success.
One who desires the greatest success should not harbor greed for the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*);
rather, one should regard the wife of the preceptor as Mahālakṣmī herself, honoring her with an abundance of offerings throughout the entire kalpa.
The wise man must certainly worship with a very fine cloth;
thus should one act on the birthday of Śrī Rāma. 54.
Having attained the great perfection of the Lakṣmīhṛdayavidyā through the grace of Jānakīśa, [he obtained] the fickle fortune of Indra.
O long-lived one, having attained right here a wealth of riches and jewels abounding today, as well as an abundance of sons and grandsons, may auspicious things increase day by day. 56.
At the end of the body, he goes to the supreme abode, which is difficult even for the gods to attain;
on that day, he should remain without food, or subsist on milk, or eat only fruit.
Or, having become one who subsists on bulbs and roots, the preeminent practitioner, on the following day,
should worship women with auspicious marks with choice foods, perceiving them as Śrī herself.
Then, having caused the Brahmins to recite [the mantra] with the thought that they are Śiva and Jānakī,
the practitioner should respectfully eat the remnants of the food from the Brahmins together with his kinsmen.
O Rāma, he who performs this supreme *puraścaraṇa* during the nine nights of spring shall, through the grace of Candrānugraha, become [successful] on earth.
He will be a master of all sciences, equal to Mahendra in splendor,
endowed with the prosperity of sons and grandsons, and possessed of long life.
Endowed with all enjoyments and always possessed of auspiciousness,
he shall subsequently become one who remembers his past births and, having seen the village, shall traverse the world.
Having ascended an excellent celestial chariot that moves at will and is auspicious, he rejoices in the presence of Hari at the end of his body, accompanied by thousands of noble families.
Now, O Daughter of the Lord of Mountains, I shall further proclaim another [mantra] which brings about immediate success on earth and serves as the cause for universal sovereignty and all prosperity.
The third lunar day in the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha is known as Akṣayā;
it is especially auspicious when conjoined with Mercury, Venus, or the Sun.

Or even when joined with Prajāpati (Ma), it bestows the accomplishment of all fruits; when joined with Samasta (Sa) at the beginning, it pacifies all afflictions and grants the fruit of all merit. (66)
And on earth, during the year numbered as the third Dṛṣṭi,
there is no lunar day equal to this one, which bestows all perfections.
O Vakra, merely by reciting [the mantra] or offering oblations here, everything bestows imperishable success;
for here the Lord of Lakṣmī, the ocean of compassion, is ever awake.
Nārāyaṇa, the great yogi, who does not dwell within even the Badarī tree,
beheld people of supreme righteousness who were eager for his vision.
Thus spoke the great yogi; listen as I speak those words:
"O Akṣaya, on the third lunar day, whatever elephant-herd comes here to me," (70)
Having bathed in the river named Ākanda, one of pure vows beholds [the deity] and thinks:
"I shall certainly grant him union with me; of this there is no doubt. (71)
On this day called Akṣaya, wherever on earth one may be,
those who, firm in their vows, recite the glorious eight-syllabled mantra (Śrīmadaṣṭākṣarī-vidyā), [attain the fruit].
One should offer a single oblation with the Lakṣmī-hṛdaya-vidyā;
having bestowed upon him inexhaustible great accomplishment here, [the mantra] says "Maha Āṃ."
And for those born in that lineage,
I shall grant an eternal and supreme state within my own abode, Vaikuṇṭha, in my presence.
This lotus-foot of the Teacher bestows one's desired object;
and by His command, He grants her steady sovereignty over the ear. (76)
Alternatively, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) with the single-syllable mantra of the Lakṣmī-hṛdaya-vidyā;
having performed this here at the Akṣayavini tree on the earth, [one is freed] from the planet Madana.
"Having attained great perfection, one is honored even by the gods," so said the blessed Lord Yogī, the all-pervading Hari-Nārāyaṇa. (78)
Accompanied by Nara, in the presence of all the gods, he [spoke] on that very day in Vaiśākha known as Kṣaya. || 79 ||
The best of the twice-born should perform special recitations, fire-oblations, and other rites if he desires great supernatural power (mahāsiddhi) here on this earth among men. 80.
On the third day of the month of Vaiśākha, which is known as Akṣayā and designated as Kṣaya,
the best of the twice-born should certainly perform special rites such as recitation and fire-offerings (japa-homa) if he desires great, inexhaustible success here on earth. (80)
On the third lunar day known as Akṣayā, one must certainly observe the vow;
there is no other vow equal to this that bestows the fruit of protecting [the world]. 81.
Because it bestows desired objects that are imperishable, they know it to be imperishable among all things;
and because it bestows union with Brahman (*brahmasāyujya*) which is imperishable, it is therefore imperishable.
On the Akṣaya Tṛtīyā, when the minds of Brahmā and the other great-souled ones are pleased, this day is proclaimed by the virtuous as the day of Kamalā. (83)
O Mahāsiddhiṣka, I shall now describe the supreme *puraścaraṇa*:
having risen at the hour of Brahmā and having recited the *brahmavidyā*, || 84 ||
Having recollected the *Raśmimālā*, bowed to the lotus feet of the Teacher,
and performed purification, he then bathed and completed the rites of the twilight prayers (*saṃdhyā*) and recitation (*japa*).
Having prostrated with all eight limbs before the pair of feet of the teacher,
and having completed the daily fire-oblation, [he should then recite] the glorious eight-syllabled mantra.
Having obtained the royal fortune of five hundred [years], and thereafter the knowledge;
being pure, he should mutter [the mantra] five hundred times in the presence of the lotus-feet of the Guru. (87)
Having established Vaiśvānara and recited the Veda-measure thereafter,
one should offer twenty-eight portions of clarified butter into the fire, O daughter of the Lord of Mountains.
O Goddess, having offered five hundred oblations of rice mixed with curd from cow’s milk using the glorious eight-syllable mantra, and [another five hundred] using the Lakṣmī-hṛdaya mantra; || 89 ||
One should offer into the fire one thousand three hundred oblations of ripe *pāṭala* fruits, devoid of seeds, mixed with honey and saturated with ghee.
Then, having offered clarified butter individually with the fifteen-syllable Śrī-mantra,
one should subsequently offer one hundred and eight oblations of cow's ghee.
Having performed the oblations with recitations and other rites, and having subsequently offered the *brahmārpaṇa* oblation,
one should circumambulate the fire from left to right and pay homage to it with reverence.
Having worshipped the Cakrarāja and also the Sālagrāma stone,
O Śivā, one should recite the twelve-syllabled mantra of Śrī-Śrīśa five hundred times.
O Goddess, having crushed the jackfruit along with other fruits, one should offer this food-offering (naivedya) together with curd-rice. 96.
There, having honored the teacher and prostrated before him with reverence, one should give a pair of cows accompanied by much milk, O child. (97)
Having given wealth equal to a year's worth of food, or half of that, or half of that again, or even three niṣkas, to the preceptor’s wife with the thought that she is Lakṣmī; 98.
Having given fine garments and ornaments, he should feed the twice-born;
and by feeding married women, he attains unsurpassed perfection. 99.
Accompanied by the Blessed One, Mahālakṣmī becomes gracious to him,
bestowing a lineage-expanding fortune abounding in wealth, grain, and other riches.
Inexhaustible great health and very long life, as well as inexhaustible perfection of speech and an inexhaustible lineage of sons. (101)
The beloved of Hari bestows inexhaustible and unimpeded enjoyments here in this world,
and at the end of his body, she grants him imperishable union with Brahman.
For the sake of attaining the grace of Śrī, this unsurpassed vow must certainly be performed at the end of the day in the month of Vaiśākha. (103)
Or, O Daughter of the Mountain King, having performed it in this manner on the third day of the waning moon, one should offer a single gold coin (niṣka) at the two feet of one's own preceptor.
One desiring the greatest perfection should perform the vow until the end of the full moon;
having thus performed the fire-oblation with devotion on the Akṣaya Tṛtīyā, [one attains success]. (105)
Having given two *niṣkas* at the feet of one's own teacher, and having offered a *niṣka* to the teacher’s wife with the thought that she is Lakṣmī herself, || 106 ||
The glorious food, mixed with ghee. || 108 ||
Having offered one hundred and eight oblations with the *vidyā* of the Heart of Ramā,
one should offer as oblation only curd-rice mixed with the clarified butter of a pure cow.
One should offer clarified butter individually with each of the Bhagavadraśmi mantras;
having offered it twenty-eight times, one should then offer it with the twenty-eight-syllable mantra.
One should offer oblations one by one, consecrated with the *suṃdarī* and *raśmi* vidyās;
having offered twenty-eight times, one should then offer with the fifteen-syllable mantra of Śrī.
For the pleasure of Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa, one should also feed a married couple;
having performed this according to the system ending with the full moon (pūrṇimānta), it should be continued from the full moon onwards.
Having bathed in the morning, with his soul purified and having performed the rites of the forenoon,
he completed his obligatory duties at the consecrated sacrificial fire.
One should offer ghee, as well as rice mixed with curd and ghee, twenty-eight times into the mouth and other [orifices] of the Veda, using the glorious eight-syllable vidyā.
Having first offered five hundred oblations with the *vidyā* of the Heart of Ramā, one should offer curd-rice, which is endowed with the fruits of all desires.
O Daughter of the Mountain King, one should offer more than a thousand oblations mixed with ghee,
offering each individual oblation with the Bhagavadraśmi mantras.
One should offer oblations with cow's ghee twenty-eight times, reciting the mantra twenty-eight times;
thereafter, one should likewise perform [the rite] twenty-eight times with the rays of Śrī.
One should offer oblations of clarified butter one by one with the fifteen-syllable mantra;
O Daughter of the Lord of Mountains, having offered one hundred and eight oblations with ghee alone, [one should proceed].
Then, having performed the recitation (japa) and other rites, as well as the fire-oblation (homa), they declare that even those who have transgressed [the rules] are purified;
having offered the oblation of "offering to Brahman" (brahmārpaṇa) and having bowed to the purifier (pāvaka), [they are cleansed]. || 119 ||
Having adorned the preceptor with perfumes, flowers, and unbroken grains of rice,
one must certainly and respectfully offer him a pair of earrings.
O holy one, if he is unable to give a pair of earrings,
he may instead give an ornament of pearls or an ornament of gems.
Having given ornaments to the teacher according to his capacity, he should give one pala of gold, or half of that, or half of that again, into the teacher's ears.
If one is unable to do that, one should offer three *niṣkas* at the lotus feet of the Guru;
furthermore, a cow accompanied by her calf must certainly be given as a gift for the sake of abundant prosperity.
One should then [offer] five fruits, or three that are suitable for the vehicle; they should be many, large, long, and endowed with a collection of fruits. || 124 ||
And one should offer a plantain fruit, resembling a bud, to one's own guru, O Śivā.
One should present sandals and umbrellas to those learned in the Vedas (śrotriya),
and one should feed women who have recently given birth with curd-rice, cakes, and various kinds of edible foods.
One should honor the teacher’s wife with offerings such as betel, fragrant powders, and garments, or otherwise present these in the presence of Lakṣmī.
One should send that wealth to the guru, or to his son, or to his wife, or to his daughter, or even to his grandson. || 125 ||
Having received blessings from the preceptor, one should eat while maintaining silence;
O Pārvatī, this is the vow of *puraścaryā* to be performed in the month of Vaiśākha.
The one of pure soul who performs this attains a great accomplishment, difficult even for the gods to obtain, which is immediate and provides manifest proof.
Even one who is devoid of vows, or is dull-witted, foolish, poor, or even miserly, attains prosperity abounding in wealth, grain, and jewels through the grace of Ramā. (128)
Even those with new learning will certainly obtain prosperity through the grace of Śrī, as well as sovereignty;
O Vatsa, in this year he shall find the full glory of kingship, abounding in chariots and horses, yet terrifying to his enemies.
Those born in her lineage obtain royal glory and prosperity, as well as long life, health, an increase in wealth, and an expansion of their family equal to that of Mahendra. (130)
Having attained incomparable prosperity and enjoyments, and likewise having reached the eightfold yoga, he subsequently,
at the end of the body, becomes stainless and attains divine equality by the side of Hari.

Even thousands born in his lineage, having attained the grace of Ramā, though once submerged even in hell, ascend to the feet of the Creator, endowed with supreme enjoyments, O Daughter of the King of Mountains. (132)
O Daughter of the King of Mountains, there is no vow equal to this, which brings about the complete attainment of all perfections,
nor is there anything in the Smṛtis or the collection of Purāṇas that bestows such fierce grace.

O Daughter of the Lord of Mountains, by beginning the vow known as Akṣaya-vaiśākhī on its full-moon day and completing it on the following day, one obtains every kind of excellent and desired object through the grace of Śrī. 134.

Dakṣa, Pulastya, Pulaha, Vasiṣṭha, Śukra, and Garga—the lamp of the Kauśika lineage—having performed their vows and attained the accomplishment of the great goal, wander through the three worlds, freed from all bonds. (135)
This vow of *puraścaryā* performed in the month of Vaiśākha bestows success; by performing it, a man brings others under his control and beholds Mahālakṣmī herself. (136)
When the mother of the world has been quickly subdued, what remains unachievable in the three worlds?
[Even] the Brahman-sages such as Vasiṣṭha and others, and the lords of the gods such as Śakra and others. || 137 ||
Brahmā and the others also, having performed that vow with extreme devotion,
[attained their goals] through the grace of Mahālakṣmī and also through the favor of Lakṣmīśa.
Having attained uncommon power and prosperity endowed with the eightfold qualities, you shall remain eternally happy in equality with the Blessed One.
I shall now describe another vow for the preliminary practice (puraścaryā) which bestows success, destroys the accumulation of great sins, and grants the fruit of a hundred sacrifices. (140)
O Śivā, when the preceptor of the gods enters the zodiac sign of Leo under the guise of a mendicant,
there, on a Sunday coinciding with the Puṣkara yoga at its conclusion, [one should act].
The great merit of the Godāvarī has been declared by the sages;
it contains thirty million holy sites (tīrthas) together with an additional half-million.
When the preceptor of the gods is situated in Leo, the twelve days arrive at Gautamī; there, Puṣkara, the leader of holy places, is present.
At the beginning and at the end, one encounters the destruction of all the hosts of sins by giving even the food of a mendicant at Gautamī during the arrival of Puṣkara. || 144 ||

One obtains the eternal fruit of giving food equal to that of the Maruts; even one who has killed a Brahmin, a drinker of liquor, a thief, or one who has violated the teacher’s bed [is purified]. 145.

Whether he be one who associates with such people, one who is bound by the fetters of ignorance, a killer of children, a thief, a giver of poison to those who trust him, or one who causes abortions in thousands; || 146 ||
Whether one has killed an embryo, slain a hero, or even killed a mother or a father,
by undertaking a restriction from food at the yoga known as Puṣkara, [one is purified].
Having risen early in the morning at Gautamī and performed his daily purifications,
he shall be liberated from all sins after twelve days and freed from the misery of worldly existence.
Or, by reciting there day after day a mantra composed in the vernacular language,
he attains their grace and reaches his desired perfection.
Furthermore, by giving even a small amount of gold to a teacher or another worthy person, one obtains the unsurpassed fruit equal to that of giving a thousand Meru mountains.
O Daughter of the Mountain, by performing even a single oblation there, the preeminent practitioner always obtains the fruit of ten million homas. (151)
O Śivā, this Yoga-rātra is obtained in twelve years on the beautiful bank of the Godāvarī; it is not found elsewhere on earth, O Purifier.

In that regard, I shall describe the practice known as *puraścaryā*, which bestows great spiritual accomplishments (*mahāsiddhi*); listen well with a concentrated mind, O Daughter of the Mountain. (153)
On the day when the preceptor of the gods enters the zodiac sign of Leo,
you shall go to the bank of the Godāvarī and perform the rites for Gautamī.
Having prostrated like a staff before the pair of feet of the teacher,
and having bathed in the Godāvarī river, he performed his morning rituals.
Having again prostrated before the pair of feet of the teacher,
one should offer clarified butter with the Gāyatrī mantra one hundred and eight times day after day.
One should also offer one hundred and eight oblations with the glorious eight-syllable mantra, using parched grain mixed with honey and saturated with the ghee of a tawny cow. (157)

Having offered even five hundred oblations of sesame seeds and bilva leaves accompanied by the Lakṣmī-hṛdaya-vidyā, one then becomes endowed with fortune and attains the eight perfections (aṣṭasiddhi).
Having offered oblations twenty-eight times with the mantras of the Bhagavad-raśmis, and then having offered ghee individually with the Suṃdarī-raśmis; 159.
Then one should offer clarified butter individually with the fifteen-syllable mantra;
having offered twenty-eight oblations, one should then offer the expiatory oblations.
Having offered the oblation with the mantra "brahmārpaṇam" and having bowed to the fire with devotion,
he should then feed couples by reciting the Śrīsūkta five hundred times.
On the twelfth day, one should perform the vow that brings about great accomplishment;
now I shall explain the sequence of gifts for those twelve days.
On the first day, one should provide five [measures] accompanied by a large fee for the laborer;
on the second day, one should cause the ground to be thoroughly ploughed.
On the third day, one should give a heap of sesame seeds measuring five āḍhakas,
or as prescribed, a thousand-fold dakṣiṇā along with the annual ritual materials.
On the fourth day, one should offer a pala of gold,
or else a pair of fine silk garments, or even two pairs.
On the fifth day, O auspicious one, he should give a gift accompanied by a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā),
consisting of twelve khārīs of grain, or alternatively, four khārīs.
On the sixth day, the observer of the vow should give a cow along with a sacrificial fee;
on the seventh day, he should give molasses accompanied by a sacrificial fee.
One should give either five āḍhakas or one āḍhaka of jaggery,
along with twelve palas of silver or four palas.
On the eighth day, one should give salt and also aścala;
or alternatively, on the ninth day, one should give five ācchakas.
On the ninth day, one should present a beautiful palanquin accompanied by many sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā), fully equipped with elephants, horses, and chariots.
On the tenth day, one should give a new house, measuring one karṣa in size, along with wealth, clothing, and a vehicle.
On the eleventh day, one should give pearls and gems;
on the twelfth day, one should give gold by the thousands.
A wealthy prince should likewise undergo initiation in this manner;
or else, he should offer wealth increasing by one unit at each step upon the lotus-feet of the preceptor.
Alternatively, the wise man should give a single cow every day;
he should also offer earrings and other ornaments during that yoga.
On the twelfth day, one should honor the preceptor with gold weighing one *niṣka* for each lotus at the Gautamī riverbank, or with double that amount of gold.
If one is unable even for that, one should offer half a *niṣka* daily to the Guru;
if one is unable even for that, one should abandon greed for wealth.
Even after bestowing upon the Preceptor the earth consisting of the seven continents, teeming with wealth, grain, and so forth, one would still remain a debtor daily toward Śiva. (177)
Having given away the entire earth, abounding in wealth and jewels, as well as [services] such as washing clothes and massaging the feet; || 78 ||
A wise man, being self-restrained, must necessarily perform service every day by sweeping away leftovers and by cleaning the house and so forth. (179)
This is indeed the Mahāpuṣkara yoga; furthermore, with the thought that she is Lakṣmī herself, one should honor the preceptor’s wife with garments and divine ornaments.
On the twelfth day, twelve couples should be fed with delicious foods;
having performed [this] in this manner during this Puṣkara-yoga on the bank of the Godāvarī, [one attains the fruit]. || 181 ||
Through the vow of *puraścaryā* for Lakṣmī, one shall obtain the greatest success;
when joined with its constituent parts and the prescribed sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), the *puraścaryā* yields the fruit of a thousand repetitions.
One certainly attains the fruit; there is no doubt in this matter.
[The land] shall be filled with wealth, grain, elephants, horses, and so forth, and crowded with jewels. (183)
Having attained great and unshakable prosperity even before a year has passed,
the practitioner regards the splendor of Indra, Kubera, and others as no more than a heap of straw.
Though aged, he acted like a youth due to his splendor, which was like that of the god of love;
his radiance was doubled by the crest-jewel of fresh passion.
Even while bestowing their entire wealth, those wise rulers serve them;
for even one of dull intellect or a fool may possess knowledge in all eighteen branches of learning.
Having become directly equal to Vācaspati at his very feet,
and having attained the power to die at will, what could he not accomplish for Yama and the ancestors?
At the end of his body's life, he attains the state of the Lord of Śrī;
whereas the wife of a father or mother sinks into the ocean of hell. || 188 ||
Having uplifted a thousand of his kin, he does not fail to reach the eternal Brahman;
having fully increased his lineage, he attains prosperity endowed with glory.
Thus, this preliminary rite (puraścaryā) for the Puṣkara yoga has been described by me;
it is a bestower of grace, and there is no other like it found in the Śruti or the Smṛti.
[Thus ends the twenty-second chapter in the latter part of the *Śrīmadanuttarabrahmatattvarahasya*, the *Dāśarathīya Tantra*, which is a compendium of the essential meaning of the Vedas.]
The venerable Dakṣiṇāmūrti said:
O Mahālakṣmī, daughter of the Lord of Mountains, I shall once again proclaim that which brings about all perfections on this earth; be disciplined and listen.

The new moon (Amāvāsyā) and the full moon (Paurṇamāsī) are recorded as the two great festivals (mahāparvan). If the sun is eclipsed by Rāhu at the junction between the new moon day and the first lunar day (pratipad), [it is a special occasion]. || 2 ||
Furthermore, they know that an eclipse occurs when the moon is seized by Rāhu or even by Ketu at the junction of the full moon and the first day of the lunar fortnight (pratipad). || 3 ||
If the Moon, being eclipsed, is swallowed by Rāhu, it is called a lunar eclipse;
this occurs when it is conjoined with a Sunday or conjoined with a Monday.
That which was spoken by the ancient seers, beginning with Cūḍāmaṇi,
is auspicious for all people to hear and difficult to grasp.
It bestows immediate nourishment, grants the fruit of merit instantly,
pacifies untimely death, and yields the fruits of victory and prosperity.
There is nothing on earth like this which brings success so quickly;
for whatever little is chanted, offered in sacrifice, or even given as a gift [by means of it], [that very thing becomes effective].
They know that the merit at an eclipse of the sun or moon is multiplied by tens of millions upon tens of millions;
here, whether for a birth or a death, there is no need for a thread ceremony (sūtraka).
Or, during the auspicious eclipse of the moon or sun, one who performs a bath in the great ocean or in a river is instantly freed from heaps of sins.
Even a Brahmin who has been bound by the karmic results of ten million births is liberated if he bestows there a piece of land the size of a cow-hide, accompanied by a smile.
On this earth, she was endowed with abundant crops and accompanied by sacrificial fees;
she possessed the earth consisting of seven continents, teeming with wealth, grain, and other riches. (11)
Whatever fruit one obtains on this earth by giving [gifts] a hundred times, a mortal who performs the *visādhana* certainly obtains that same fruit. || 12 ||
Even from the mere act of giving a small token of gold, one obtains the fruit of a gift of gold as vast as Mount Hemādri, by the power of this mantra. (13)
Whoever gives here a single cow that yields much milk and is endowed with all auspicious qualities, obtains the merit of giving ten million cows; of this there is no doubt.
Gold is the first gift of Agni; cows are the offspring of the Sun and daughters of Viśvakarman;
these three have been bestowed upon you. He who would give gold, a cow, and land—these three worlds are his. (15)
O Pārvatī, it has been declared by the knowers of Brahman that this time yields a great fruit for gifts such as the Tulā-hiraṇyagarbha and others.
Or, having offered any mantra whatsoever preceded by the command of the preceptor, and having recited it here at the pair of auspicious lotus feet of the preceptor; 17.
Even by giving just anything at all, though one be poor, one obtains great fruit;
one attains the perfection of the Ācārya and also reaches the grace of Śrī.
Whether it be a king, a prince, or one wealthy in riches on this earth—whatever and however much of their entire possession [is given] during an auspicious solar or lunar eclipse. (19)
One should offer it at the lotus-feet of the preceptor; one directly perceives Brahman, even by dedicating it for the sake of deceased fathers or mothers. (20)
O Śivā, wherever a practitioner gives a cow that yields much milk and possesses its own calf,
even one's ancestors who are burdened with great sins [attain liberation].
And those great ones, liberated from the terrible hell and freed from the fear of hell, immediately go to the eternal Satyaloka. || 22 ||
Even in all the scriptures, nothing has been declared that brings immediate success like the seizing of the lunar phases; therefore, it shall be explained here.
For five days, or at least three days, prior to the solar or lunar eclipse, one should diligently remain self-restrained, observing celibacy and subsisting on fruit.
Or one may subsist on milk, or on sacrificial food (haviṣya), or on bilva fruits soaked in ghee;
or else, with bilva leaves soaked in ghee and combined with sesame seeds. || 25 ||
Having offered one hundred and eight oblations with the glorious eight-syllable vidyā,
one should then also offer one hundred and eight oblations with the mantra of Royal Prosperity (rājyalakṣmī).
O beautiful one, even by means of the Lord’s vidyā, having bathed twelve times or more,
one who is weak and afflicted by disease should prostrate like a staff upon the ground before the pair of the Guru’s lotus feet.
Having established Vaiśvānara according to the prescribed rites with purity,
one should offer oblations into the fire with blue lotuses mixed with sesame seeds, cow products, and clarified butter.
First, one hundred and eight [recitations] were performed with the eight-syllable Vidyā of Śrīmad;
then, with Prasannalakṣmī as well, more than a thousand [recitations] were completed.
One should offer oblations into the consecrated fire with blue lotuses mixed with ghee;
in the absence of blue lotuses, one may use bilva leaves soaked in ghee.
O Daughter of the Mountain King, one should offer oblations into the fire with sesame seeds mixed [with other ingredients];
in their absence, one should offer pure sesame seeds alone, mixed with ghee and the three sweets (trimadhu).
One should offer ghee individually with the mantras of the Bhagavadraśmis;
one should offer each individual oblation of ghee with the mantras of the Lalitā-raśmis.
Having offered oblations with the fifteen-syllable mantra, one should offer twenty-eight oblations to Śrī;
having performed the expiatory oblations, one should perform the oblation of "offering unto Brahman" (brahmārpaṇa). || 35 ||

Having circumambulated the fire clockwise and prostrated like a staff with eight limbs before the two feet of his own preceptor, he should offer twenty-eight oblations to Śrī using the fifteen-syllable mantra as an atonement; then, having bowed, he should proceed with the collection of ritual implements for the duration of the rite.
Having adorned it with water-pots and other vessels, and having offered a pair of garments,
one should offer a single village endowed with abundant grain and wealth.
One who gives even a single Śālagrāma stone, or two stones accompanied by milk, or even a small iron needle, shall be born with horses and cattle.
One should also offer a swing, palanquins, a white umbrella, and chowries,
as well as gifts such as the Tulā and Hiraṇyagarbha.
O Goddess, O Sovereign, I shall now describe the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) for one who is capable:
having given a pair of earrings to the ears of the Guru, O Śivā... [40]
O Daughter of the Mountain King, one who is unable to do that should give pearl ornaments,
or else ornaments of gems, or even ornaments of rudrākṣa beads.
One who possesses a Śālagrāma stone must certainly give land measuring a gocarma, provided with abundant crops. (42)
It must certainly be given, measuring one hundred āḍhakas;
in its absence, its value is recorded as one hundred and fifty paṇas.
One should give twenty *niṣkas*, or twelve *niṣkas*, or even one *niṣka* every day, abandoning all greed for wealth. (44)
O daughter of the mountain, two cows must certainly be given;
or else, one should give their value, thereby [worshipping] Rāmā herself with devotion.
One should give earrings, ornaments, and so forth to the preceptor’s wife;
thereafter, twelve couples should be fed with food mixed with black gram.
Then, having received the embrace of the teacher and grasped it, the disciple attains a great perfection that is difficult even for yogis to obtain. (47)
Within a year, he shall surely obtain stable prosperity, abounding in wealth, grain, and the like,
strewn with clusters of pearls and gems.
Kings, princes, and his ministers become his servants and grant him whatever he desires. (49)
He is constantly honored in all the worlds and shall be ever victorious;
he enjoys all manner of pleasures, including sons, grandsons, and great-grandsons.
Having attained great perfection of speech, equal in splendor to the preceptor of the gods,
and having achieved long life, he was liberated from the accumulation of diseases and passions.
Accompanied by his family and endowed with divine enjoyments,
having become undecaying and immortal, he shall possess a form similar to that of the Blessed One.
Having ascended a celestial chariot that grants all desires and is accompanied by hundreds of divine maidens, he will surely attain the state of Bhaga; of this there is no doubt. (53)
O Goddess, having performed this *puraścaraṇa* during two eclipses, or even during a single eclipse, one attains Mahālakṣmī, the beloved of Hari.
And with his two eyes, he directly beheld Nārāyaṇa endowed with [the powers of] aṇimā and the other qualities, having remembered his former birth.
Equal to Mahendra in splendor, endowed with the happiness of sons and grandsons, and accompanied by Hari, you shall constantly behold the immortals, beginning with Brahmā and Indra. (56)
Having attained death at his own will and having acquired yoga endowed with its eight limbs, he certainly attains union with Brahman; this is most assured.

When the sun is situated in a Vaiṣṇava asterism, and that same Vaiṣṇava asterism is conjoined with the first day of the lunar fortnight (mādya) and the new moon (amāvāsya), and further joined with Sunday; 58.
When conjoined with Vyatīpāta, it is known there as Ardhodaya;
this rare conjunction is said to be obtainable only after many years.
When joined with a Monday, it is known as Mahodaya;
these two yogas are said to be unattainable and rare on earth.
It instantly destroys the multitude of mortal sins, eradicates all diseases,
pacifies all miseries, and enables one to cross the ocean of saṃsāra.
When this yoga has arrived, the preceptor, preceded by the king,
shall bathe in a great lake, a river, a pond, or even at home.
Having completed the daily obligatory rites according to the rules,
he offered one hundred and eight oblations of clarified butter from a cow into the consecrated fire while reciting the Vedic meters.
One hundred and eight offerings of milk-rice for the venerable Aṣṭāṅganātha, combined with the three sweets and mixed with cow’s clarified butter; (64)
Having offered one thousand three hundred oblations with the Lakṣmī-hṛdaya-vidyā,
he should then perform the vow by offering oblations with the Bhagavad-raśmi-vidyās.
One should offer clarified butter individually with each of the Lalitāraśmi vidyās;
one should offer clarified butter one hundred and eight times with the fifteen-syllable Śrī mantra.
Having offered [the oblation], one should offer ghee twelve times with the four glorious *anubhavas*,
and then twenty-eight times with the *sundarī* and *bhagavatī* vidyās.
Having offered oblations with recitations and so forth, having offered the expiatory oblations in sequence,
and having offered with the Mahāvyāhṛtis, one should perform the oblation of dedication to Brahman (brahmārpaṇa).
Having circumambulated the fire and then respectfully prostrated at the two feet of his own preceptor, he [honored him] with auspicious golden ornaments.
Then, having adorned it and placed gold weighing one śatamāna, half of that, half of that again, or even half of the latter, into a bronze vessel, he should cast it into the water.
Having abandoned stinginess regarding wealth and having placed it at the lotus feet of the preceptor,
one should give a cow that yields good milk along with her calf.
A bronze vessel weighing sixty-four palas, or twenty palas,
provided with a new cloth and accompanied by ornaments and other such items.

O Śiva, one should offer [the remains] to the wife of the preceptor with the thought that she is Mahālakṣmī; furthermore, one should satisfy the married women and the widows according to one's capacity.
He attained the supreme perfection of the Lakṣmī-hṛdaya-vidyā, of the illustrious eight-syllabled mantra (Aṣṭākṣara), and of Mahātripurasundarī. || 74 ||

When the arising of supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) has been attained, or when a great yoga of supreme success (*mahodaya*) has been reached, the practitioner should perform the *puraścaryā* according to this procedure. (75)
Having obtained the fruit of a hundred sacrifices, accompanied by a lofty sacrificial fee,
and having attained great prosperity arising from a hundred cities, [he dwelt there].
Liberated from all origins of evil, he shall become composed of all the gods;
through sovereignty, health, and progeny, he shall possess a splendor equal to Kaśyapa.
Having attained great sovereignty endowed with qualities such as the power of the *maṇi*,
he rejoices in the abode of the Blessed One for two thousand kalpas of his lineage.
When the rising of the moon occurs, or when a great festival arrives, one who is able should always give all kinds of gifts to the Brahmins with reverence. || 79 ||
One must certainly offer milk-rice placed in a bronze vessel to a Brahmin,
as well as either a sesame-cow, a curd-cow, or even a jaggery-cow.
Or one should give a milch cow, or a two-faced cow (a cow with two udders), along with a monetary gift;
a wealthy person should likewise perform the gift of salt and other such items, or the gift of a mountain.
One should also offer a balance, the Hiranyagarbha [image], and other gifts;
likewise, gold, a colored cow, salt, and sesame seeds.
One should give clothing and even molasses during the lunar eclipse and at the time of great prosperity;
these gifts one should offer to Brahmins who are learned in the Vedas.
Having offered a silver vessel measuring two *palas*, or one *pala*, or a vessel fashioned of gold, if one is wealthy. (84)
He who should offer sacrificial materials at the lotus-feet of his own teacher—whether a thousand, three hundred, or even one hundred and twelve—[attains the fruit]. (85)
The merit that the supreme practitioner attains by bestowing [this] upon one who has attained great prosperity or who has abandoned [all worldly ties] cannot indeed be described. (86)

Having offered the entire wealth of sacrifice along with its constituent parts upon the pair of feet of the Teacher, regarding them with the thought that they were Nārāyaṇa himself, he was accompanied by ten million members of his lineage.
One who rises during the Brāhma-muhūrta and [recites] the twelve-syllable mantra of the Lord of Śrī will certainly rejoice in the abode of the Blessed One; there is no doubt in this matter. (88)
Having recited [the mantra] three hundred times, or even one hundred and eight times, and having recollected the garland of rays, one should perform the twilight rituals and other duties. (89)
One should daily recite the auspicious eight-syllabled mantra of Śrīnātha a thousand times;
or, O Śivā, having recited it five hundred times, or even three hundred times.
The best of the Bhrigus, performing the vow of the fifteen-syllable Śrīsūkta— the great lore of royal fortune— worshipped the Cakrarāja.
Having attained a steady prosperity equal to that of the Lord of Wealth and the King of the Gods, as well as long life and exceedingly great health, [he shall remain] for a long time. (92)
Resembling Kandarpa in beauty and like a preceptor in learning, he was always honored like a teacher in the presence of the king. (93)
Requested by young maidens full of desire, O ornament, enjoy both divine and human pleasures together with your sons, grandsons, and others. (94)
Having eaten at the proper time at the end of the excellent [period], he shall rest in the abode of the Blessed One;
he who recites the Śrīhṛdaya mantra one hundred and twenty thousand times. (95)
O Daughter of the Lord of Mountains, why is it that these twice-born ones do not achieve through devotion the auspicious yoga of moving through the sky, which consists of the eight limbs? 96.

The imperishable remembrance of the powers such as atomization (aṇimā) and other qualities of sovereignty, as well as the state of being a seer (ṛṣi), the state of a perfected one (siddha), the state of a gandharva, and the state of a yogin; || 97 ||
Then, by means of this very body, he attains the state of a god, the state of Rudra, and even the state of Brahmā,
resembling hundreds of Kandarpas.
Having become ageless and immortal, appearing as a youth of twenty-five years, his body composed of splendor, he was sought after daily by divine maidens.
He rejoices in worlds such as Śvetadvīpa, possessing divine enjoyments.
Ṛṣyaśṛṅga said:
In ancient times, the Praśannalakṣmī-vidyā was [taught] by Dakṣiṇāmūrti.
Thus have the means of accomplishment been declared out of a desire for the welfare of devotees;
other yogas as well have been fully expounded right here. (101)
One who, being pure, recites this single Great Vidyā of Mahālakṣmī every day, becomes like another Nārāyaṇa manifest before one's eyes. (102)
He is always worshipped like a god both here and in the hereafter;
in his lineage, no one is born unfortunate or poor. (103)
The great fortune pervading her lineage shall endure as long as the moon and sun;
it is true, truly true, there is no doubt that it exists within that very lineage. 104.
Thus has been declared the practice for the Lakṣmīhṛdaya-vidyā;
hereafter, I shall describe the practice for the Triśakti-lakṣmī-vidyā. (105)

[Thus ends the twenty-third chapter in the Uttara-bhāga of the Saubhāgyavidyodaya, within the Śrīmadanuttarabrahmatattvarahasya, the Dāśarathīya Tantra, which is a compendium of the essential meaning of the Vedas.]
The Goddess said:
The ritual procedure for the Prasannalakṣmī-vidyā has been heard with reverence;
now, please explain the ritual procedure for the Triśakti-lakṣmī-vidyā.
The illustrious Dakṣiṇāmūrti said:
O Śivā, I shall thereafter proclaim the Vidyā of Kamalā, who possesses the three powers; by the realization of which a person truly becomes identical with Nārāyaṇa.

The letter "va" mounted upon fire (ra), conjoined with the left eye (ī) of the moon (u)—this is declared to be the first seed-syllable. Then, the sky (ha) conjoined with the left eye (ī) of the moon (u). || 3 ||
The second seed-syllable is extracted, joined with the fire (ra) and the drop (m), combined with the sixteenth consonant (kṣa) and the earth (la), and conjoined with the fourth vowel (ī). || 4 ||
This third seed-syllable is said to be accompanied by the bindu;
this Vidyā is proclaimed as Mahālakṣmī, known as the Threefold Power (Triśakti). || 5 ||
This form, which bestows all perfections, is Lakṣmī, Girīndrajā, and Vāṇī;
it is the destroyer of the multitude of all sins and the bestower of the fruits of all merit.
Consisting of all branches of knowledge and comprising all sacred fords and sacrifices, she is supreme;
she is eternally worshipped even by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśa, and the others.
She who causes a rain of pearls, gems, gold, and other treasures in the homes of the virtuous;
she who bestows the attainment of universal sovereignty and grants the fruits of dharma, wealth, and desire.

The eternal [Lakṣmī], who is the cause for attaining the bliss of perpetual joy, is established within the threefold power (triśakti) of Lakṣmī; when she is perfected, there is nothing unattainable even for the three worlds.
O Sovereign of the Great Lion Throne, you are the protector of the treasures of devotees and the bestower of royal fortune; you reside on the western side of Śrī Devī.
The seer of this [mantra] is declared to be Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds and the great-grandfather; or, it is stated by those most proficient in the Veda that Sammohana is its seer.
The meter (chandas) is declared to be Gāyatrī, or else, O Śivā, it is Yajus;
the deity is Mahālakṣmī, known as Triśakti, who has the luster of Hari’s horse (or is greenish-yellow).
Inertia (jādya) is said to be the seed-syllable, and Śrī Bhuvaneśvarī is the power (śakti).
The Kīlaka is the Kāmarāja-mantra, and its application (viniyoga) is for the sake of accomplishment (siddhi). || 13 ||
Repeating [the mantra] twice, the wise one should perform the six-limbed assignment (ṣaḍaṅga) using the very same heroic syllables.
[He should meditate on the deity] on a charming island situated in the middle of an ocean of nectar.
In a ship upon a floor shimmering with gold, within a courtyard paved with jewels, situated amidst a grove of Pārijāta trees and adorned on every side.
In the center of the Great Lotus Forest, upon a beautiful jewel lion-throne,
she dwells as the abode of Nārāyaṇa, possessing a radiance equal to ten million flashes of lightning.
She has the luster of molten gold and resembles hundreds of rising suns;
her head is covered by a golden crown shimmering with radiant jewels.
Adorned with jeweled earrings, a necklace, armlets, a pair of bracelets, earrings, golden rings, and a girdle of gold threads; || 20 ||
Adorned with various ornaments inlaid with many jewels,
she bears a boar-tusk, a goad, a pair of lotuses, a noose, and a bow.
On both sides, she was being fanned by two female companions holding beautiful chowries in their hands,
while celestial women fanned her with fans made of mani-jewels and pearls.

She was surrounded by two female companions holding golden vessels filled with betel leaves in their hands, while with both hands they held beautiful whisks made of divine jewels; she herself was adorned with golden anklets, bracelets, and a golden girdle-string.
She is inlaid with many jewels, adorned with various ornaments,
and holds a young elephant goad, a pair of lotuses, a noose, and a bow.
She was being fanned on both sides by two female companions holding beautiful whisks,
while celestial women fanned her with fans made of rubies and pearls.
Surrounded by [attendants] with golden vessels containing betel leaves in their hands, and respectfully holding golden drinking-cups made of divine jewels in their hands; 23.
She is served by the beloved couples of deities such as Brahmā and Rudra;
her feet are eternally worshipped, and she is the supreme refuge and protector of her devotees.
I bow to Mahālakṣmī, the mother of the three worlds, the supreme sovereign, who consists of the three Vedas and is compassionate toward those who have come for refuge. 25.
Having meditated upon Mahālakṣmī in this manner three times a day,
one should recite the vidyā three thousand times daily, or two thousand times.
Having recited it one thousand and eight times, or three hundred, or a hundred,
or even twenty-eight times, one shall attain perfection.
First, the wise one should draw a hexagon and write the Vidyā in its center;
he should then write the three seed-syllables in the six corners in succession, repeating them twice.
On the exterior, one should make an eight-petalled lotus adorned with the long vowels;
one should draw a mandala that is square, adorned with four gates.
The central deity should invoke Śrī while reciting this Vidyā;
having worshipped her with ritual offerings (upacāras), one should then worship the limbs and the surrounding deities (aṅgāvaraṇa).
O Supreme Goddess, one should then worship the attendants starting from the eastern corner, beginning with Mahālakṣmī, who is dear to Hrī.
Thereafter, one should worship Girijā and Śaṅkara, then Rati and Kandarpa;
furthermore, on the two sides of the hexagon, one should worship the two treasures, Śaṅkha and Padma.
O Great Goddess, on the eight-petaled [lotus], one should place Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, Vaiṣṇavī, and then Varāhī and Madanā.
Or alternatively, one may worship Māheṃdrī; beyond that is Mahālakṣmī.
Then, Maheṃdra and the others, with equal divisions, are situated in the eight directions within a square.
The practitioner of the water offering (arghya) should constantly worship Lakṣmī, who embodies the three powers,
and recite the great vidyā of the three seed-syllables for the sake of attaining all that is unborn and immortal.
Or else, O Śivā, by worshipping the King of Wheels (cakrarāja) in the western part of Mahātripurasundarī, one attains the desired perfection.
O auspicious one, who is the support of the entire world, whose nature consists of the four Vedas, who is worshipped by all gods, and who is the sovereign of the Śrī Devīcakra! || 37 ||
By worshipping the three forms and the three powers daily, along with their constituent parts, one certainly attains the fruit in the presence of the King of Mandalas (cakrarāja). || 38 ||
Or, having constantly recited even a single mantra while remaining restrained in his vows, he will certainly attain great success; of this there is no doubt. || 39 ||
By whomsoever the worship of the Śrīcakra is performed daily, [they are honored by] Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśa, and the others, as well as Indra and the other lords of the directions. || 40 ||
O Śivā, when he has thus worshipped [the Lord] along with his limbs (attendants), Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, Gaurī, Śacī, and the Muravī Śaktis become pleased every single day.

One who is a constant worshiper of the Śrīcakra should perform worship through the Cakra; however, if one worships even a single [deity] within it while the others remain unpropitiated, that worship is in vain.
O Daughter of the Mountain King, one should always perform worship within the Śrīcakra itself, which is the presence of all, rather than in another vessel.
The Goddess Lalitāmbikā, the Śrīdevī, consists of all the gods;
the Śrīcakra has been described by the wise as consisting of all the seats of knowledge (vidyāpīṭha). || 44 ||
Therefore, being pure, you must certainly worship the Śrīpīṭha every day;
thus, you shall attain the merit of all the teachers of the deities together with their limbs.
Having thus worshipped the triple-powerful consort of Hari according to the prescribed rite,
one who has conquered the senses and the mind should recite the mantra three hundred thousand times.

The wise one should perform the *tarpaṇa* rite with ten parts [of the total] using either *kṣurasa* or *kiṃśuka* flowers offered into the fire with cow’s clarified butter mixed with the three sweets (*trimadhu*). (47)
Having given a solid hundred gold coins (niṣkas), one shall attain the perfection of knowledge;
this occurs when the first Sunday falls on the first day of the month while the Sun is situated in Capricorn.
With devotion, one should offer twenty-five thousand oblations on the eleventh day, using clarified butter mixed with the three sweets on that eleventh day.
One should offer three thousand oblations into the fire of conditioned existence with lotuses or blue water-lilies,
or else with bilva leaves or milk-rice.
Having given wealth equal to a year's worth of food at the feet of the preceptor’s lotuses, one attains the perfection of knowledge; there is no need for deliberation on this matter.
She who causes the delusion of all, bestows the great accomplishment of speech, grants the sovereign power of qualities such as *aṇimā*, and destroys the multitude of sins. 52.
This *Lakṣmī-vidyā* of the three powers (*triśakti*) brings all kings under control;
standing in water reaching the navel, one should gaze at the solar disk.
Having recited it three thousand times daily with a restrained mind,
one beholds Mahālakṣmī herself on the final day of the maṇḍala rite.
[He saw] prosperity that was complete with wealth, grain, and so forth; crowded with elephants, horses, and chariots; accompanied by streams of pearls and gems; and pervasive throughout his lineage.
To him, that Lakṣmī, accompanied by the Lord, will certainly grant her favor,
provided he offers six thousand oblations of sesame seeds soaked in clarified butter while remaining firm in his vow.

One shall become free from disease and long-lived; even one whose life is destined to end will certainly find it prolonged by consuming milk-rice mixed with honey and the three fruits over a blazing fire.
Having offered five thousand oblations into the blazing fire,
he shall become a treasury of all knowledge and a treasury of all sovereignty.
Having recited the mantra three thousand times on the full moon day,
one should offer three hundred oblations of milk-rice (pāyasa) soaked in the three sweets into the fire.
Having offered even a small amount at the pair of lotus-feet of the Guru,
and eating only what remains from the oblation, one becomes a practitioner of the vow for that entire night.
Having performed this vow of preliminary practice (*puraścaryā*) for three years, two years, or even for one year, the preeminent practitioner [attains success]. (61)
Attended by the personified treasures, Śaṅkha, Yamā, and the others, who stood before him, he was directly served by a multitude of excellent men showering him with offerings worthy of his status.
Having commenced on the Uttaraphalgunī asterism, one should reverently recite the Śrīcakra along with its ancillaries three thousand times and offer three hundred oblations; this constitutes the vow.
On the fifth lunar day, one should offer one hundred and eight oblations of clear foods;
on the full moon day, one should offer three hundred oblations of red lotuses into the fire.
Having thus performed the preliminary rite (*puraścaryā*) and the vow for one year, the wise man attained great fortune, possessing the splendor of Mahendra and Kubera. (65)
Having attained a fortune equal to that of Kāmadeva, as well as supreme longevity and health,
he shall prevail over all people, including men, women, and kings.
One could bring even the gods under one's control for as long as one lives, let alone human beings;
such an abundance of eloquence is attained that it is like the flow of the Gaṅgā.
Even while living, he becomes liberated and attains union with Brahman,
provided he remains concentrated during the Navarātra of Āśvina or during the spring season.
Having recited this vidyā of Śrī twenty-five thousand times,
[one should offer oblations] soaked in honey and ghee into a blazing fire during the great month of Mādhava.
Having offered three thousand oblations of milk-rice mixed with sesame seeds,
one should honor the preceptor and his wife with the Bharaṇī and other [constellations].
The teacher was equal to Vālmīki in learning and in the abundance of his wealth.
Having become equal to the Giver of Wealth (Kubera) in prosperity and resembling Madana (the God of Love) in splendor.
Having enjoyed abundant pleasures here in this world, one endowed with daily devotion to the triple-powerful Lakṣmī-vidyā goes to that supreme state at the end of the body. (73)
Having recited it three thousand times, or indeed two thousand times.
Having recited it three hundred thousand times, or else daily, being pure; || 74 ||
He is liberated from the entire mass of sins and becomes the possessor of good fortune and prosperity. || 75 ||
He was the foundation of all sciences, O grandson, and endowed with happiness.
Having attained supreme fortune and brought the three worlds under his control,
he enjoyed divine and human pleasures for a long time until they were exhausted.
At the end of the body, one who is free from delusion goes to the supreme, eternal abode.
Thus has the majesty of Lakṣmī, the power of the three-fold energy (triśakti), been recounted by me;
now the majesty of the Sāmrājyalakṣmī-vidyā shall be declared.

[Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter in the Uttara-bhāga of the Saubhāgyavidyodaya, within the Śrīmadanuttarabrahmatattvarahasya, the Daśarathīya Tantra, which is a compendium of the essential meaning of the Vedas.]
The illustrious Dakṣiṇāmūrti said:
O Daughter of the Mountain, I shall describe the majesty of the knowledge of the Fortune of Sovereignty, which bestows the accomplishment of all aims and destroys every misfortune.
Having extracted the seed-syllable of the Moon (Caṃ), then the Sky (Ha) and Mādana (Ra),
the seed-syllable of Forgiveness (Kṣa), and the seed-syllable of Śiva (Hrīṃ) adorned with Fire (Ra) and the left eye (I).
O lady of beautiful hips, when joined with the *viṃva*, she is proclaimed as the Fortune of Sovereignty (*sāmrājya-śrī*).
O wide-eyed one, this great knowledge (*mahāvidyā*) is Śrī, consisting of seven syllables.
This Vidyā, worshipped by the Vicchus, is the Mistress of the Water-Simhāsana;
she bestows imperial sovereignty upon her worshippers and grants both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
She is the devourer of heaps of great sins, the destroyer of great poverty, the bestower of great Sarasvatī, and the granter of the perfection of great good fortune. || 5 ||
O Daughter of the Mountain, this Vairadarī bestows even upon a bird the splendor of Śiva; a worshipper of her shall likewise attain such glory on this earth.
When worshipped, she bestows all good fortune and grants the attainment of enjoyments;
when recited, she is like a wish-fulfilling cow that milks forth the fulfillment of every desire.
When offered, she bestows all speech and increases prosperity, granting every kind of abundance;
she grants dharma, artha, kāma, and even the state of Kaivalya as well as the powers beginning with aṇimā.
This great vidyā should certainly be recited with devotion by one who desires [its fruits];
Nārāyaṇa is the seer (ṛṣi), and the metre is declared to be Gāyatrī.
The enchantress of the three worlds, the bestower of the fruit of universal sovereignty, Mahālakṣmī, the Mother of the Universe, is declared to be the deity of food. (10)
The seed-syllable is declared to be the peak-syllable (kūṭa), and Śakti is said to be the syllable of Śrī.
One should perform the ritual of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) using the syllable of Śrī conjoined with the six long vowels.
In the midst of the ocean of milk, upon an auspicious island made of jewels,
which was surrounded by forests of the Saṃtāna, Pārijāta, and other celestial trees.
Beneath the wish-fulfilling tree, upon an auspicious golden pedestal inlaid with fresh rubies and adorned with pearls and coral; (13)
She was seated on the left lap of the Supreme Lord, the Lord of Śrī, the Supreme Soul, who was sitting there; she possessed the luster of a blooming blue lotus.
Resembling a blue lotus, or possessing a luster like molten gold,
she shines with the brilliance of a hundred rising suns and is adorned with various ornaments.
Divine and yellow in hue, bestowing boons, anointed with divine sandalwood paste, and resplendent with fresh garlands from the Pārijāta and other celestial trees. || 16 ||
Holding in her hands the conch, discus, mace, lotus, arrow, and bow,
she bestows fearlessness and grants boons while bearing the [other] weapons.
[He saw] Śrī herself, eight-armed, the sovereign leader of all empires,
being reverently attended by [goddesses] holding chowries and mirrors, and others holding parasols.
She was served by celestial maidens who spoke with smiles;
her lotus feet were resplendent with the rubies from the crowns of Śakra and the other gods.
I worship Mahālakṣmī, the mistress of the lion-throne, who consists of the three Vedas and is adorned on both sides by beautiful celestial women.
Having meditated upon and constantly worshipped Śrī, the sovereign mistress who is the embodiment of all prosperity and imperial sovereignty, within the beautiful Cakrarāja; ||| 21 ||
One should constantly worship the Sovereign Lady (Sāmrājyanāyikī) in the presence of the Śrīdevī;
or, if one is unable to do so there, the best of practitioners should worship her within this yantra.
One should draw a triangle, an octagon, and a square, provided with four gates; this yantra bestows the attainment of universal sovereignty.
Having recited the root-vidyā and visualized the form,
the practitioner should invoke [the deity] and worship with all the charming articles of service.
Then, O Goddess, one should worship the six limbs as before; thereafter, having respectfully worshipped the Goddess of Imperial Sovereignty in the center of the triangle.
One should protect the three corners with Sāvitrī, Gāyatrī, and Sarasvatī;
these, joined with the eight long vowels, are the eight Mothers beginning with Brāhmī.
These should be worshipped in the eight corners, granting all perfections to the devotees;
then, one should worship Indra and the other guardians of the directions in the eight directions of the square.
