Having worshipped her, one should perform the ritual service (puraścaryā) three hundred thousand times to obtain the fruit of imperial sovereignty, which bestows the glory of universal empire.
The wise man should satisfy the ten directions with honey or even with water;
then, according to that proportion, he should offer oblations into the fire with *kiṃjuka* flowers mixed with clarified butter.
O Śivā, by giving twelve cows as a sacrificial fee to the preceptor,
one attains mastery over the mantra and obtains the desired fruit.
Alternatively, during the nine nights, having recited twenty-five thousand [times],
one should offer palāśa flowers weighed against three parts of honey.
Having offered three thousand oblations at the lotus-feet of the preceptor and having presented ten cows as a fee, one shall attain perfection in the vidyā.

Having recited this mantra one hundred thousand times and having offered oblations with red lotuses mixed with ghee and the three sweets, one will certainly become a sovereign ruler of the earth, possessing jewels.
Having offered twelve thousand oblations of milk-rice mixed with ghee and the three sweets into a blazing fire, one attains the unshakable fortune of sovereignty.
Even one of meager fortune, having attained this, shall become a king of kings;
he who constantly recites it one thousand and eight times along with the *śālibhṛt* hymn. (35)
Even having obtained the sovereignty over the seven continents as the most excellent of men,
he would not become equal to the Giver of Wealth (Kubera) within his realm.
Having recited [the mantra] a thousand times every day and offered a hundred oblations of ghee, one attains the glory of sovereignty and becomes a master of all sciences. || 37 ||
Having offered ten thousand *kadaṃbīka* flowers for ten days, one becomes like Kandarpa (the god of love) and captivates kings, men, women, and others. (38)
One may bring [them] under control for as long as one lives, or even beyond that, including the gods;
what need is there for much speaking in this matter? One shall obtain everything from this armor-mantra.
There is no science like this one in the three worlds.
This brief exposition of the ritual procedure for the four sciences has been told;
what more do you wish to hear? Speak, O you who are unagitated by the arrows of passion. (40)
[Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter in the Uttara-bhāga of the Saubhāgyavidyodaya, within the Vedasārārthasaṃgraha, the Dāśarathīya Tantra, known as the Śrīmadanuttarabrahmatattvarahasya.]
The illustrious Goddess said:
O Blessed One, you have spoken of the garland of rays (*raśmimālā*) of Śrī that is to be recited;
O Lord, please proclaim to me this hymn (*sūkta*) of Śrī known as the *Raśmimālā*.
The illustrious Dakṣiṇāmūrti said:
Listen, O auspicious Goddess; I shall proclaim the *Raśmimālā* of Śrī, by the mere recollection of which one who is composed should always [recite it] in the morning. (2)
One shall be liberated from all sins and become possessed of all good fortune;
she is the primordial mother of all the Vedas and the bestower of all perfections.
The second is proclaimed as Māhendrī, the bestower of fearlessness;
the third is the eight-syllabled Sāvitrī lore, which increases one's splendor.
The great vidyā known as Praṇava bestows the accomplishment of union with Brahman;
thereafter, the leaf residing in the fourth state yields the fruit of union.
Cakṣuṣmatī, when practiced, bestows the fruit of far-sighted vision;
Gandharvarājavidyā yields the fruit of marriage.
Since knowledge (vidyā) protects one from the perils of the narrow path of existence,
Tārā is therefore remembered as the Great Knowledge (mahāvidyā) that pacifies the ocean of worldly existence.
The Great Vidyā of the Three Names, which divides the assembly of diseases; the Vidyā of Mahāgaṇeśa, which destroys the hosts of obstacles. || 8 ||
Then there is the Umāmaheśa-vidyā, which bestows the accomplishment of all desired objects;
and the ten-syllable Mṛtyuñjaya mantra, which wards off the fear of death.
Then there is the Śrutadharī-vidyā, which bestows the fruit of all vidyās;
and the great vidyā known as Mātṛkā, which bestows the fruit of omniscience. || 10 ||
The Great Vidyā of Kāmeśvarī bestows the accomplishment of identity with Śiva;
the Vidyā of Saṃpatsarasvatī grants great self-restraint. || 11 ||
The Kālasaṃkarṣiṇī-vidyā is long and bestows flowers and fruits;
the supreme Śambhu-mahāvidyā eternally bestows bliss and happiness. || 12 ||
Then follows the Parakalā-vidyā, which bestows the perfection of great speech;
after that, the Kumārikā-vidyā, which grants the accomplishment of all desired objects.
The Vidyā known as Annapūrṇā bestows abundant fruit;
the Mahāvidyā Aśvārūḍhā brings all the worlds under her control.
Then follows the Śrīpādukā-vidyā, which bestows the siddhis of Śrīvidyā;
it is the root-vidyā of the Śrīdevī, granting the enjoyment of all fruits. (15)
Then follows the Laghuśyāmā Vidyā, which brings men and women under one's control;
and then the Vāgvādinī Vidyā, the supreme bestower of perfection in speech. (16)
The Nakulī-vidyā bestows the fruit of all vidyās;
thereafter, the Śyāmalā-pādukā-vidyā bestows its own fruit. || 17 ||
Then there is the Rājaśyāmā Vidyā, which bestows the fruits of one's desires;
and then the Laghu-Vārāhī Vidyā, which cuts down all enemies.
Vidyā, she who is her own stream of discourse; she who proclaims both the auspicious and the inauspicious;
Tiraskaraṇā Vārāhī, the one who effects concealment. || 19 ||
Vārtālī is the sandal (pādukā), and thereafter Vārtālī is the bestower of supernatural powers (siddhi);
she is the Vidyā known as Rājavārtālī, who bestows grace upon her devotees. || 20 ||
Then follows the one known as Śrīpūrtividyā, which bestows prosperity, grants liberation,
is the great Pādukā, and subsequently bestows the fruits of the four aims of human life.
Afterwards, the six obstacle-removing deities who bestow the fruits of Śrīdevī are:
Rājaśyāmā, Mahāvidyā, and Vighnadevī; beyond that [are the others]. 22.
Next is Vārtālī, the deity of obstacles who pacifies the flood of impediments;
she is proclaimed as Raśmimatī, the bestower of all accomplishments by the illustrious Goddess. (23)
The practitioner who, day after day at dawn, recollects this garland of mantras once, twice, or even thrice; || 24 ||
O Śivā, being liberated from all fears arising from sins day after day,
he shall attain great fortune as well as incomparable perfection of speech.
Having enjoyed great good fortune and all desired pleasures today, one attains union with Brahman at the end of the body; of this there is no doubt. (26)
If one recites even a single great vidyā-mantra daily, that person of great fortune shall obtain all desired objects. || 27 ||
One who desires the accomplishment of the Śrīdevī should daily recollect the Raśmimālā mantra— whether once, twice, or thrice— as it bestows all accomplishments.
Here, only the names of all the sciences have been revealed; their respective greatness has been proclaimed by the sages in those various tantras. (29)
All these sciences are declared to be the queens of the Goddess; because she is the sovereign of all, these are remembered as having become her rays.
The devotee of the Śrī Devī, constantly intent on the worship of the Cakrarājñī,
should daily recollect the Raśmimālā mantra once at the beginning of the day.
One attains mastery over all sciences here; of this there is no doubt.
She is the sovereign empress of the three worlds, the illustrious Goddess, the Supreme Sovereign.
To him for whom all things are accomplished and for whom nothing in the entire world is unattainable—to that Ācārya who bestows the garland of rays, the supreme Guru. (33)
O Śivā, one should always worship [the deity] with the direct realization of Brahman, and not otherwise;
for even the venerable Goddess Tāṇḍikā is the giver of the *Raśmimālā*.
The elder brother, the father, his father, and even one who nourishes him—he alone is the kinsman, the friend, the teacher, and the great preceptor. (35)
"He alone is the Creator, he alone is the Sun, and he alone is the Supreme Lord"—thinking thus, one should constantly [revere] the Guru who bestows the garland of rays. (36)
The wise man should worship the Teacher day after day with jewels and wealth;
for you, who are bowed at my feet, the true nature of Śrī has been described as being like a garland of rays.
O Daughter of the Mountain, what more do you wish to hear beyond this?

[Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Arising of the Saubhāgya-Vidyā," in the latter part of the *Śrīmadanuttarabrahmatattvarahasya*, the *Dāśarathīya Tantra*, which is a compendium of the essential meaning of the Vedas.]
Salutations to Śrī Sītā-Lakṣmī and Rāma-Nārāyaṇa.
The Goddess said:
O Lord of gods, O omniscient one, O Lord of the Gajīs, this has been well-guarded by the Blessed One even within the Vedas, the Upaniṣads, and all the Purāṇas.
"What you have spoken has been related to me by you, and it has been heard by me with great respect;
now I wish to ask something that dwells within my heart. (2)
For those who are devoid of Vedic study, brahminhood does not exist;
and those Brahmins who are devoid of the performance of sacrifices are considered commoners.
Even those who have reached the further shore of the meaning of the *Arthavādha* and the *Naya*, as well as the *Śruti* and *Smṛti*,
are declared to be common [to all], O Brahmins, even though they are knowers of the Vedas.
Having entered this saṃsāra, which abounds in suffering and is crowded with various calamities,
they do not indeed turn back even after hundreds of births.
The worship of the eight-syllable mantra has been declared as that which carries one across the ocean of worldly existence;
therein also, the Raśmividyā, the Mālā, and the Sūkta have been proclaimed.
The network of nyāsas has been taught, as well as the worship of the wheels and the limbs;
the Śrīdevyuyāmana has been proclaimed together with the Raśmimālā.
Combined with the worship of the Śrīcakra, she is the one who carries across the ocean of worldly existence;
[she is the power] for the dull-witted and the intoxicated in their grasping and retaining of knowledge.
"Since no such power exists at all, how can you have such a supreme destination?
You are devoid of Vedic study and abandoned by the performance of sacrifices."
And what, O Lord, is the destiny of those who are devoid of knowledge of the meaning of the Vedas—the eternal Being who is the means for crossing the ocean of worldly existence? (10)
The complete study of all four Vedas bestows its fruit;
it has the fruit of understanding the meaning of the Vedas and bestows the fruit of all sacrificial rites. || 11 ||

O Śaṅkara, by the mere recollection of this eight-syllabled Vidyā that bestows prosperity, as well as of the Śrīdevī mantra, one obtains the fruit produced by the complete performance of the ritual along with its ancillaries.
"O Dakṣiṇāmūrti, if you exist, then grant me that vision.
Śrī Ṛṣyaśṛṅga said:
Thus addressed by the goddess Girijā, Śaṅkara, the benefactor of the world, [replied]. (13)
For the benefit of all the worlds, Śrī Dakṣiṇāmūrti spoke this according to reality. Śrī Dakṣiṇāmūrti said:
Listen attentively, O Goddess, O auspicious one, O blessed and beautiful lady. || 14 ||
Although this which you have asked is a secret even within the Vedas, out of compassion for you I shall declare that which was uttered by Rāma. 15.
Formerly, in the city of Sāketa, which was adorned with celestial palaces, there was a most beautiful temple, exquisitely decorated with gold and jewels.
In the midst of that enchanting [palace], upon a beautiful, divine golden lion-throne made of nine jewels, like a celestial *pārijāta* tree, [he sat]. (17)
[He saw] the lord Rāma, the son of Daśaratha and the husband of Jānakī, seated there, adorned with a crown, necklaces, armlets, earrings, and other ornaments. || 18 ||
Wearing yellow garments, his chest radiant with the glorious Kaustubha gem,
his face smiling, and his eyes possessing the luster of a lotus, he sat in the heroic posture (vīrāsana).
[He beheld] the Moon-like Lord, possessing the beauty of ten million Kandarpas, accompanied by Jānakī,
and whose lotus feet were served by the son of Sumitrā, Bharata, and others.
He was served by the eight ministers, beginning with Añjaneya and others,
as well as by great sages such as Vasiṣṭha, Vāmadeva, and the rest.
Though consecrated by all the earthly and divine lords, his playful form was not that of a human being; he was the Lord intent upon protecting the three worlds.
Brahmā, the creator of the three worlds and heaven, approached to see him,
accompanied by his mind-born sons, Sanaka and others, who were great yogis and leaders.
He was surrounded by the Prajāpatis, headed by Marīci and Dakṣa,
and was accompanied by the Vedas in personified form and by the Goddess of Speech herself.
Recognizing that he had arrived while Brahmā was present, the lord of the earth rose up—
out of his illusory human form— and offered him the guest-offering (arghya).
Then, embraced by the Creator, he gave a beautiful divine gem-studded throne to Hiraṇyagarbha and to his sons as well, according to what had been prescribed.
Then the Creator, the leader of the worlds, was saluted by Vasiṣṭha and other stainless Brahman-sages, as well as by Lakṣmaṇa, Bharata, and others.
He praised the powerful Rāma, the son of Daśaratha and husband of Jānakī.
Brahmā said:
That which is formless, the supreme abode, devoid of qualities, and stainless.
That which has the form of truth, bliss, and consciousness, established beyond darkness, known through the Vedāntas, and stainless, is called the Supreme Brahman. || 29 ||
O Lord of the Universe, that very reality which is established even within the secret caves sleeps;
it is the eternal fire and moon whose nature is the sun.
You are the wondrous cause even of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and the others;
consisting of the three Vedas and known through the three Vedas, you are the cause of the universe.
The Puruṣa with a thousand heads, a thousand eyes, and a thousand feet;
the Virāṭ, the Svarāṭ, and the Samrāṭ—you are He, O son of Aditi. 32.
O son of Virbha, all the Vedas and Vedāntas,
as well as the Purāṇas and the Dharmaśāstras, are merely the exhalation of your breath.
O mighty-armed one, you alone are that which is expressed by the syllable *praṇava*, the deliverer from *saṃsāra*, and the Brahman; you are the supreme form of the Lord, higher than the highest.
This Sītā, the mother of the world, is the ninefold power consisting of the three Vedas; you are the father of all worlds, and by your own nature, this entire universe is pervaded by you.
The senses perceive their objects because you are the great one even among the great;
from you as the primary source, Agni, Indra, and the Moon have arisen from the mind.
From your eye the fire emerged, and from your head there was the terrible [Rudra];
the Brāhmaṇas were born from your mouth, and likewise the Kṣatriyas from your two arms. (37)
Likewise, from his thighs were born the Vaiśyas and Śūdras, as they have been declared;
but I am born from your navel, O Rudra, arising from your wrath. (38)
All the powers, beginning with Gaurī, have arisen from you;
so too have the Vedas, the Upanishads, and even I, Rudra, and the gods. (39)
And even the highly fortunate ṛṣis and the siddhas, O Lord of the World, have truly sought to know your greatness and your purpose through tens of thousands of years. (40)
O Indra among kings, they do not understand this; how much less so on earth, even by men?
For you have been entreated by Śaṅkara, Śakra, and the other gods as well. || 41 ||
Having assumed a human form for the sake of benefiting the worlds,
you have descended from King Daśaratha through the womb of Kauśalyā.
O Lord, by whom could the web of your virtues be described?
You are Rāma, the delight of all the worlds upon the earth. (43)
Since all yogis always delight in that form of yours which is of the nature of consciousness and bliss, you are Rāma, the sustainer of Brahman.
For the sake of subduing the wicked and for the protection of the virtuous,
you became the son of Daśaratha and [slew] crores of night-stalkers.
Having seized all the worlds and having dispelled fear, he was consecrated in Ayodhyā; yet he was not endowed with the goddess Śrī.
The primordial Nārāyaṇa himself, the Lord of all elephants, became manifest:
"Be ever gracious to me, O Lord, Leader of Jānakī. (47)
Satisfied by all this, the Blessed One, the Lord of Jānakī,
the Supreme Sovereign, spoke to Brahmā, the self-born Creator.
The Blessed One said:
"O Brahmin, is all well with you?
Does the ninth month appear [favorable] for your Agnihotra sacrifices, and for your high-souled sons? (49)
"Even though you are engaged in the study of the entire Veda along with the eightfold yoga, for what purpose have you come here with these sons of yours who are devoid of self-control?"
"Or what desired thing shall I grant to you, O Brahmin? Speak, O Lord.
Thus was Brahmā, that treasure-house of austerities, urged by the Blessed One.
The Supreme Soul spoke these words to the infallible Rāma;
Brahmā said:
These perfected ones are highly fortunate, having conquered anger and mastered their senses.
O Lord, my mental sons—Sanatkumāra and the others who are foremost in their bodies—as well as the celestial sages beginning with Nārada and even the Likhitas, [are all present]. (53)
They ask me about their doubts for the benefit of the entire world—those who are devoid of the performance of sacrifices and abandoned by Vedic study. (54)
Many Brahmins remain devoid of the Agnihotra sacrifices and abandoned by Vedic conduct, even though they are capable of performing ritual acts. (55)
The poor, the wretched, the deluded, and those devoid of the duty of charity—
for them, liberation from hell does not exist even at the end of a kalpa.
The Vedas must always be studied, and Vedic dharma must also be practiced;
sacrifices accompanied by complete sacrificial fees must certainly be performed.
Gifts must certainly be given upon this earth;
likewise, the great yoga endowed with eight limbs must be practiced constantly. (58)
One should also undertake pilgrimages and bathe in millions of sacred fords; by these virtuous deeds, there arises a means for crossing over the ocean of worldly existence.
O Lord of the World, how is it that those who are immersed in saṃsāra remain unattached?
What is the means for crossing over saṃsāra, and how is there liberation from hell? (60)
It is declared in all the Vedas that liberation is attained in a single birth, whether by means of the glorious eight-syllabled mantra or the fifteen-syllabled Śrī-mantra.

Therein also exists the very extensive hymn known as the *Raśmimālā*, as well as the collection of ritual placements (*nyāsajāla*), the sacrificial session of worship (*pūjāsatra*), and the manual of liturgical recitation (*vākulya*). (62)
If, through the grace of the teacher, one attains all these goals—dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa—as well as others—by means of the worship of a single Vidyā; || 63 ||
O illustrious Lord, if these are indeed effective, then please tell me how knowledge is attained through service to the guru and even by mere remembrance.

If the fruit of the sacrifice were to be accomplished through the mere study of the Vedas, as would likewise be the fruit of the preliminary ritual service (*puraścaryā*) of the seventy million great mantras. (65)
O Lord of the Universe, if it is possible, please graciously impart to me and my sons that royal science which bestows all perfections.
Thus questioned at that time by Bhṛgu, Rāma, the Lord of Indirā,
remembered Kapila, the all-pervading sovereign of all the Siddhas.

One is liberated by [meditating on] the son of Kardama, the sovereign lord of all perfected beings (siddhas), who is devoted to the practice of yoga, tranquil, and desirous of the welfare of the three worlds. || 68 ||
By the mere recollection of him, that master of Sāṃkhya and great yogi arrived there just as he was, accompanied by his host of perfected yogis.
Resembling the twelve suns, the infallible Acyuta was a treasury of splendors;
seeing him, they were all struck with wonder and rose up suddenly with joined palms.
They all bowed down to the sage Kapila, whose wisdom pervades all beings; there, he was honored with water for the feet and offerings by Jānukīyatī.
The teacher of Sāṃkhya, a great yogi, said to Rāma, the Lord of the world:
"O Nārāyaṇa, O best of the Raghus, I have been summoned by you in person. (72)
"I am born from a portion of you alone, O best among the knowers of Yoga.
What more need I say, O Lord? Command me, O Master of the World. (73)
Thus addressed by Kapila, the powerful Rāma, son of Daśaratha,
spoke to Kapila, who was born from his own portion and whose essence was Kardama.
The Blessed One said:
You are Nārāyaṇa, the omniscient Supreme Lord, the teacher of all yoga, and one who is devoted to the welfare of all worlds. || 75 ||
The highly fortunate Sanaka and others, sons of Brahmā who were firm in their vows,
as well as Atri, Bhṛgu, and these others, were together with the Grandfather (Brahmā).
They ask this Lord of the entire world about their doubt;
I am situated in a human womb, seated upon the royal throne. (77)
O you who are eternal, you are the omniscient one even among all the perfected ones;
you are Nārāyaṇa, the cause of all branches of knowledge, O observer of vows.
"O Great-minded One, because you possess the sovereignty of a king, I do not instruct these [beings] myself;
in my presence, you should speak to them, for you are their guru. (79)
Thus addressed by Rāma, the supreme self and master of yoga, the Lord, having smiled slightly, spoke to the powerful Rāma, the son of Daśaratha.
The venerable Kapicārya said:
You are Nārāyaṇa, Viṣṇu, the omniscient Supreme Lord;
you are devoid of beginning, middle, and end, and consist of truth, bliss, and consciousness.
You are the direct deliverer from saṃsāra, the stainless one whose form is Brahman;
you are formless yet possess all forms, the Puruṣa who transcends Prakṛti.
You are the object of meditation for yogis, a great yogi, the destroyer of the ordinances of Vidhi, and the one who completely envelops the three worlds;
you are the preceptor even of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa. (82)
O Lord of the World, having assumed a human body through illusion for the sake of establishing the Dharma, you are born into a lineage of supreme majesty. 83.
Seated upon the royal throne, you have taken recourse to the dharma of mortals;
yet these gods, sages, and perfected beings, including Brahmā and the others, [are also here]. (84)
O Lord, O King, we are the servants of your command; if you have given the order, then by the very fact of its occurrence, I am the eternal omniscient one.
O Indra among kings, by your command, I shall relate this secret even to these sons of Brahmā, who are protected by all the Vedas.
Having heard the Blessed One’s reply, the sons of Brahmā and the great sages were satisfied and filled with wonder; they bowed down before the all-pervading Kapila.

[Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter in the *Śrīmadanuttarabrahmatattvarahasya*, the *Dāśarathīya Tantra*, which is a compendium of the essential meaning of the Vedas, in its latter portion, titled *Saubhāgyavidyodaya*.]
For those on this earth who are powerless, impoverished, and dull-witted, will there not arise a boat for crossing the ocean of saṃsāra, born from the unborn? (13)
If even here the attainment of all good fortune and every desired object can be accomplished effortlessly,
then tell me the means for that spontaneously.
Thus addressed, the great yogi Kapila, the ascetic of the worlds,
the lord Kapila, spoke to the highly fortunate Sanaka and the others.
The venerable Kapila Ācārya said:
Well asked, O illustrious sons of Brahmā, you who are rich in ascetic merit;
for you have reached the further shore of all sciences and possess far-sighted vision.
This Lord, the husband of Sītā, is the Supreme Self and the Lord of the universe;
one should worship Him, who is known as Brahman and is the deliverer from the cycle of existence. 17.
The Lord Mahāviṣṇu, the husband of Śrī, whose back is supported by Nārāyaṇa, is he;
the eternal Vedas with their secret doctrines are his very breath.
Prakṛti, the source of the world's transformations, arises from a ten-millionth part of this;
by a mere fraction of its glance, the entire universe emerges.
Even a mere fragment of his fire of wrath would dissolve the entire universe;
yet the Supreme Lord remains seated within the secret chambers of all living beings.
Having entered the solar orb, he was even the progenitor of Time;
having studied all the Vedas, he completed them with the final sacrificial fees.
Having recited the king of mantras and having respectfully satisfied the guru,
even the great sages pray for this service to be accomplished.
Through sacrifices such as recitation (japa) and oblation (homa), accompanied by complete sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā),
yogins pray for this very state of union (sāyujya), which is the most eminent of all perfections (siddhis).
That which is the formless Supreme Brahman, characterized by truth, bliss, and so forth—
that very same infinite reality, assuming a human form, is this one named Rāma.
He is to be known by all the Vedas and indeed by all the Upanishads; He is to be worshipped with all sacrifices accompanied by complete and excellent sacrificial fees.
This is the object of meditation for those devoted to yoga within the center of the heart-lotus;
he is composed of the Vedas, the embodiment of mantras, and the all-pervading Lord consisting of sacrifice.
He who is expounded by the Gāyatrī, assuming the form of the venerable eight-syllabled mantra—
this is the limit, the highly fortunate Power of Consciousness (Cicchakti), as proclaimed by Śrī.
The eternal Veda, which takes the form of the three Vedas, is known by those who know the truth of all the Vedas;
from a minute fraction of this [Veda] was born this Brahmā, the creator of the universe. (28)
Born from a portion of that wrath, he is Rudra-Saṃkarṣaṇa by nature;
[those who are] performers of sacrifice accompanied by sacrificial fees, and those devoted to the study of the Vedas. (29)
For the sake of accomplishing this service, he constantly desires on earth to study all the Vedas and to perform all the desired sacrifices. (30)
Without worship, union with Brahman does not exist;
nor is the attainment of identity with Brahman possible without the grace of the teacher. (31)
Having worshipped with the permission of their teacher that great abode named Rāma—which is supreme Brahman and identical with Nārāyaṇa—the wise ones [attain liberation]. 32.
Some indeed attain union with Brahman not through birth alone;
on this earth, karma is said to be of two kinds: merit and demerit. (33)
Merit bestows the happiness of heaven, while sin brings the suffering of hell;
the study of the Veda is merit, as is the contemplation of the meaning of the Vedas. (34)

The perfection of conduct prescribed by the Vedas, the avoidance of what is forbidden therein, and the performance of sacrificial rites accompanied by complete sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) bestow the fruit [of one's actions]. || 35 ||
The daily recitation of the Vidyā of the Mother of the Vedas (Sāvitrī), which destroys all impurities and bestows infinite happiness in heaven, is the perpetuator of one's lineage. 36.

In this world, which is called the truth and the cause of dwelling, he who bestows eternal happiness [attains] the constant victory of Śrīvidyā through the daily recitation of the Brahmavidyā. || 37 ||
Bestowing happiness upon Satyaloka until the end of the time of the great dissolution,
it is endowed with the placement (nyāsa) and radiance of the glorious eight-syllable vidyā.

When all sins have been exhausted through many births and conquered, the practice of recitation, fire-offerings, and other rites, along with their constituent parts, bestows the enjoyment of the city of Vaikuṇṭha.
O best of the twice-born, an unwavering intellect regarding the dharmas alone arises.
Established in his own duty, at the end of a hundred births he attains the state of Dhātṛ;
from there he attains the state of Śiva, and thereafter he reaches Nārāyaṇa. || 41 ||
The supreme, eternal state of non-falling away. || 41 ||
The killer of a Brahmin, the drinker of liquor, the thief, the violator of the guru’s bed, and one who associates with these—these five are renowned as the great sinners (mahāpātakin). 42.
Janaka, Dyota, Mātṛghna, Bhrātṛghna, Goghra,
Viśvastaviṣadātṛ, Vālaghra, and Garbhapātaka— 43.
These are declared to be swift-acting and indeed terrible slayers of Brahmins;
there are eleven types of intoxicants on this earth, beginning with those derived from the palm tree.
These are declared to be equal to *surā*; by drinking them, one is considered a drunkard.
Likewise, the wife of the preceptor, his daughter, one’s own mother, and even one’s own sister [are forbidden]. (45)
"The wife of a brother, the wife of a son, the wife of a king, or one's own daughter—these are called 'mother' by the wise; therefore, one should avoid union with them. [46]
O twice-born ones, the stealing of gold, pearls, gems, and so forth by means of theft, as well as the theft of knowledge and the theft of fine garments, is declared to be *steya* (theft). (47)
Now I shall describe the sins that are equal to the killing of a Brāhmaṇa:
listening to the censure of one's teacher, and personally showing hostility toward one's teacher. (48)
O best of the twice-born, disobeying a command, stealing a preta’s knowledge, and anything beyond that would be sins equal to the killing of a Brahmin. (49)
Such a multitude of evils, as enjoined by the scriptures, exists;
the fruit of these actions is the suffering of hell for a kalpa.
O twice-born ones, that medicine which is prescribed in the Dharmaśāstras is indeed a remover [of sin]; only by performing it may one be liberated from sins, and not otherwise.
When the cessation of all evils occurs upon the earth,
at that very moment supreme knowledge shall arise within the body.
Through the grace of the teacher and by means of the recitation of the venerable eight-syllabled mantra and other practices,
there will arise a great destruction that bestows liberation.
On this very point, O bulls among the twice-born, they cite this ancient history, a dialogue between a father and a son concerning sin in the Kali age.
A certain highly intelligent descendant of Bhṛgu among the Brāhmaṇas brought his son, who was peaceful, wise, yet appearing dull-witted, for the purpose of instruction.
O Sumati, study the Vedas from the beginning according to the proper sequence;
be intent on serving your teacher, and take your meals consisting of food obtained as alms.
Then, having performed sacrifices accompanied by ritual fees according to the tradition of Gārhasthya,
and having produced the desired offspring, you should thereafter resort to the forest.
Therefore, my child, you should become a recipient of the Brahmanical wandering life;
having gone to such a state, one does not grieve. || 58 ||
The venerable Kapilācārya said:
Thus addressed many times, he said nothing at all like one who is dull-witted;
but the father spoke again and again with affection to his son. (59)
Thus, having been repeatedly urged by his father with words sweet with affection and enticement, the son laughed and spoke as follows.
"Father, that which is taught here should be practiced;
likewise, other scriptures and various arts [should be mastered]. (61)
More than ten thousand births have come to my memory,
as well as those states of weariness, full of longing, and likewise those that arose from growth.
Enemies, friends, time, fortune, and the like, as well as unions and associations;
likewise, there are many mothers who are joyful, and many fathers. (63)
Thousands of sufferings and joys have been experienced;
various kinsmen have been encountered, as well as diverse fathers. (64)
Having dwelt within the womb of women, which is smeared with feces, urine,
and mucus, one experiences manifold sufferings of the fetus during both childhood and youth.
In my old age, I remember all those instances of being insulted within the wombs of Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras.
And at dawn, [the slaughter] of cattle, insects, wild animals, and birds, as well as of the king's servants and of kings distinguished in battle, [occurs]. (67)
And having been born in houses as well as in lowly dwellings, I have repeatedly entered into the state of servitude and even slavery to men. (68)
I have experienced lordship and sovereignty, as well as poverty;
I have seized wealth, others have seized it from me, I have caused it to be seized by others, and I have likewise been pursued and driven away.
Many times I have given to others what was given to me by others, and for the sake of my father, mother, son, brother, wife, and so forth. (70)
Dejected, wretched, and with his face washed by tears—thus does he wander in this cycle of existence, which is full of essential suffering and fraught with peril. (71)
This knowledge, which is the cause of liberation and perfect accomplishment, has been attained by me;
when this is realized, all this that is designated as Ṛg, Yajus, and Sāman [is known].
The collection of ritual acts does not appear correctly when devoid of its proper qualities;
therefore, for one in whom awakening has arisen, what purpose do the Vedas serve? (73)
O Brahman, I shall describe that supreme state which is free from the sixfold activities, devoid of pleasure, pain, and desire, and which is itself bereft of the qualities (guṇas) and flavors.
Craving for tastes, fear, agitation, joy, and the snares of other [passions], it is a net that captures the deer of discernment; it is entangled with hundreds of fetters of attachment. (75)
Therefore, has she abandoned this heart of his, this very seat of suffering, which is like the ripening fruit of the threefold dharma known as merit and demerit? (76)
Having heard those words of his, the father, his voice faltering with joy and wonder, spoke with a delighted mind to his illustrious son: || 77 ||
"What is this that you speak, my child? From where has this knowledge of yours arisen? By what means was this splendor previously attained, and how has awakening come about now? (78)
However, O divine sage, this is a transformation caused by a curse, whereby your knowledge, though obscured, has now become manifest.
The son said:
Listen, therefore, to how this rod of mine, which bestows both happiness and suffering, has functioned;
and from whomsoever it was taken away in this or another birth, by whomsoever, and for what reason.
In the past, I was a brahmin who had surrendered his self to the Supreme Self, having reached the highest state of firmness in inquiries concerning abidance in the Self. (81)

For one who is constantly engaged in yoga, through the union with constant practice, through association with the virtuous, through the nature of the virtuous, and through the awakening of the understanding of the path of discernment. || 82 ||
In him alone was my supreme devotion; thereafter, I attained the state of a teacher, the best at removing the doubts of his disciples.
Then, after a long time, being severely afflicted by disease,
the great yogi Prahā, a direct disciple of Vivasvat, arrived there.
Thus addressed as "Yājñavalkya," the best among all knowers of Yoga,
the high-minded one saw that sage Yājñavalkya approaching on the lunar day.
Although I was afflicted by disease, I offered him water for his feet, the guest-offering, and other honors;
and for the sake of attaining union with Brahman, I made this request.
Wealth, grain, and other such things; likewise female and male servants; cattle, buffaloes, and the like; and heaps of pearls and gems situated within the house—[all these he gave]. (87)
Having offered that lotus-foot which grants the perfection of the vision of Brahman, I prayed thus: "Tell me the knowledge of non-duality. || 88 ||
Then, having shown favor, the Blessed One, the great sage Yājñavalkya,
[taught] the supreme knowledge of Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa, the sovereign of the lords of kings.
The great yogi bestowed upon me the causeless mantra of the Goddess;
on that very day, he taught me that supreme Vidyā of the Lord.
Having attained that one supreme reality and recollecting it alone,
he whose heart was previously ignorant of the true state of things and who had met with calamity, became restored through grace.
On this single day, through the recollection of the royal science and the worship of my guru, may there be no loss of memory for me from the time of my departure [from the body] onwards. (92)
"O Father, because the memory of as many as ten million births has come back to me through that very same former practice, I have conquered my senses. (93)
I shall strive to act in such a way that this fruit of the gift of knowledge—namely, the recollection of my births—shall not occur again for me. (94)
Indeed, this is not accomplished by men who rely on the three Vedas;
therefore, having departed from my former stage of life, I have now attained this dharma.
I remember that very teacher, the most excellent one, within my heart;
resorting to solitude, I shall strive for the liberation of the self.
"I shall go to that very place where my guru, the yogi, resides. O highly fortunate one, tell me that which is firmly established in the heart of that ascetic. (97)
By this much, one attains joy and, having risen, reaches the state of non-attachment. 98.
Then the father, placing faith in those words, said to his son:
"That which you have perceived is the refuge within the thicket of saṃsāra. (99)
The son said:
Listen, my dear, to how this wheel of saṃsāra—which is difficult to cross and wherein no stability is found—was once experienced by me. (100)
Therefore, I declare all this, having been sent by your very command;
from the time of my departure until now, no one else shall speak. (101)

[Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Majesty of the King of Kings' Knowledge," in the latter portion of the *Śrīmadanuttarabrahmatattvarahasya*, the *Dāśarathīya Tantra*, which is a compendium of the essential meaning of the Vedas.]
The son said:
Listen, dear one, I shall relate that great fruit of karma which was experienced by me alone in ten thousand other previous births; listen to that.
The heat, provoked within the body and accompanied by a violent wind, blazes forth without fuel, piercing the vital points (marmas). || 2 ||
That which is called *udāna* arises from the very moment one becomes angry;
it prevents the downward movement of water and food that have been consumed. (3)
Then,
by means of those meritorious deeds performed through food and drink, she attains joy in that state.
He by whom food was given with a mind purified by faith attains satisfaction even then, despite the absence of food.
He who has not spoken falsehoods, who has caused no breach of affection,
who is a believer, faithful, and generous— he meets death with happiness.
Those men who are devoted to the worship of gods and Brahmins, who are handsome, pure, and eloquent, are said to be modest; such people meet with a happy death.
He who would not abandon the Dharma out of desire, nor out of passion, nor out of hatred;
he who acts according to what has been taught and is gentle—he attains death with ease.
When death has arrived at that time, men experience the burning of a house and the hunger of one who receives no food. || 9 ||
In the cold, clouds bring [suffering], while in the heat, they are averse to water;
others cause painful agony that destroys living beings and produces great distress.

Those who strike down wisdom with delusion, who take away the light of darkness, who give false testimony, who speak falsehoods, and who fail to instruct those worthy of instruction—[these are the ones to be avoided]. 11.
All those who revile the Vedas likewise become fearful,
foul-smelling, and carry deceptive mallets in their hands.
The evil-minded messengers of Yama likewise approach;
when they have reached the wrong path, his own path becomes manifest.
Then, remembering his brothers, mother, and sons, he moves toward them;
consequently, that speech of his is perceived as indistinct and consisting of only a single syllable. (14)
The vision becomes confused due to terror, and the mouth withers from gasping for breath;
thereafter, overcome by agony, he abandons that body.
When the form is carried away by wind and fire, another body is attained;
that karma arises from the practice of *japa*, occurring together with the mother and the father.
Then, according to his previous conduct, he is bound with extremely cruel nooses by the messengers of Yama, who seize him at the stage of his departure and his particular age and physical condition.
Agitated by blows from sticks, they are dragged toward the southern direction across ground as rough as kusha grass, thorns, anthills, stakes, and stones.
Likewise, in some places there were blazing fires, fierce with hundreds of flames,
and scorched by the burning sun, where they were being tormented by those very rays.
He is dragged by those who observe the vow of non-violence, while he himself is terrifying with his cries;
being dragged by those fierce ones, he is devoured by hundreds of jackals.
This person of evil deeds goes to his abode on a path difficult to traverse;
however, men who give gifts of umbrellas and vehicles go to their own home.
Men travel the path with ease, but the giver of food does not fare so;
thus, becoming emaciated and helpless, he suffers from the affliction of his own sins.
The man is led by the twelve-day rite to the city of the King of Dharma;
while his body is being burned, he undergoes a great burning.
While being devoured and likewise being cut into pieces most cruelly, the living being experiences incessant suffering as it is being cooked. (24)
Even though he has entered another state of existence due to the ripening of his karma, whatever water with sesame seeds your kinsmen offer there [to him], [that reaches him]. || 25 ||
Whatever rice-ball they offer, that is eaten by Nīlamātā;
as for the oil massage and the massaging of the limbs belonging to the kinsmen— || 26 ||
By that [offering], the living being is nourished, as well as the kinsmen who offer their own oblations;
and by those kinsmen sleeping upon the ground, the deceased does not undergo excessive suffering. (27)
Likewise, by those giving gifts, a deceased being is nourished;
therefore, food should be given with devotion for the sake of satisfying the departed spirits.
Carried away by his own group, he sees himself for twelve days as a wealthy man possessing garments and other such things according to his own desire. (29)
In that same manner, he enjoys on earth the water, the funeral cakes (piṇḍa), and other offerings given to him;
after twelve days, however, he assumes a terrible and fearsome form.
Then the creature, being dragged here and there, beholds the realm of Yama—
possessing eyes that are excessively wide, and having a luster like crushed collyrium.
In the midst of Mṛtyu, Kāla, Antaka, and others, he beholds one who is peerless,
with a face made terrible by fangs and a form distorted by knitted brows.
With hideous and terrifying faces, surrounded by hundreds of diseases,
with great arms grasping a staff and a noose in his hand, he was most fearsome.
Thereupon, the living being goes to a state of existence, whether auspicious or inauspicious, as indicated therein;
however, a man who gives false witness out of deceit subsequently goes to the Raurava hell.
Listen as I describe its true nature:
Raurava also measures two thousand yojanas in extent.
And there was a pit there, knee-deep and very swift-flowing,
filled with heaps of glowing coals and made level with the surrounding ground.
And there, in the midst of that excellent ground heated by an exceedingly fierce fire,
the followers of Yama cast down the evildoer.
Being scorched by that intense fire, he runs;
at every step, his foot is destroyed and then born again.
In a single day and night, he traverses the removal [of the distance] between his two feet;
in this manner, he is liberated after a thousand extended yojanas. || 39 ||
Thereafter, for the sake of purifying other sins, he undergoes a similar hell;
then, having emerged from all of them, the sinner is born as a lower animal.

Having passed through worms, insects, and moths; through beasts of prey, solitary jackals, and the like; and likewise through elephants, trees, and so forth, as well as through cows, horses, and asses. (41)
And even after attaining human birth among other sinful and painful wombs, one may become hunchbacked, despicable, or even a dwarf. (42)
Endowed with the remaining merit and sin, a man is born into the wombs of Caṇḍālas, Pukkasas, or Ugras. || 44 ||
Thereafter, he obtains a more auspicious birth immediately following that;
then he enters the wombs of a Śūdra, a Vaiśya, a Kṣatriya, and so forth. (45)
And sometimes Rohiṇī even descends to the state of a brahmin or the lord of gods;
for thus do those of evil deeds fall downward into the hells.
Listen now from me as to how those who perform meritorious deeds attain their destination; hear how those men, as designated by me, go to a meritorious state. (47)
The hosts of Gandharvas sang forth, the throngs of Apsarases danced,
and the spotless [palaces] were adorned with the sweetness of necklaces and anklets.
Celestial chariots, radiant with divine fragrances and garlands, quickly departed;
and from those [chariots], she fell before the king and that other great-souled one. 49.
Those who protect virtuous conduct are born with bodies free from disease;
they attain the highest enjoyments and likewise proceed upward, whereas otherwise it is the opposite.
Or, having reached the Avarohiṇī [path], human beings proceed as previously described. All this has been told to you, regarding how a living being perishes.
Therefore, O brahmin-sage, listen to how that embryo enters [the womb] when the seed has reached the menses of women during the period of conception.
Immediately upon being liberated from hell or even from heaven, one attains stability in the Nābhisūla; for that consists of two seeds.
The state of the *kalala*, the state of the *budbuda*, and likewise the state of the *peśī*—just as the atom of a seed is within the fruit, so too is it said to be. (54)
Then the production of the five limbs occurs according to their respective proportions:
the thumbs, the fingers, the eyes, the nose, and the mouth. || 55 ||
In the same way, nails and hair grow from those limbs;
from the skin, body hairs arise, and after that, the head-hairs.
It attains equal growth; by that very means, the sheath of the sprout reaches growth, just like the sheath within the fruit of a coconut.
In that same way, that [wind], situated at the mouth, increases along with its treasury; however, by placing it upon the sole, the knees, or the sides, it grows even more excellent. 58.
Having placed the two thumbs upon the knees, one should extend the other fingers;
likewise, the eyes are on the back of the knees, and the nose is in the middle of the knees.
The two shoulders develop on both sides, and the arms gradually emerge from the outside;
in this manner, the creature situated within the woman's womb attains its form step by step.
Just as a creature within the womb of a woman remains in accordance with its form, so too does [the body] attain solidity through fire; it does not live on what is eaten and drunk alone.
The state of a living being within the womb consists of merit and demerit;
likewise, the channel named Āpyāyinī is bound to its navel.
In the same way, a very subtle aperture is produced within women;
through it, the food and drink consumed by women pass into the womb.
Once this living being has been brought to a body by them, it indeed attains growth;
there, the various states of worldly existence (saṃsāra-bhūmi) serve as its abode.
Being tormented here and there by them, he comes to utter despair:
"I shall never again do this once I have been released from this belly. (55)
I shall act in such a way that I shall not conceive a womb again,
[so that I may see] Acyuta, who holds the conch, discus, and mace in his hands and is dressed in yellow garments.

"By meditating upon Nārāyaṇa, who is not the [limited] self and who is the consciousness of creation, preservation, and dissolution, I shall be liberated from the arising of the miseries of worldly existence. (67)
Thus the living being reflects, remembering indeed hundreds of sufferings which occurred in the past and which are truly of the nature of destiny.
Then, in the course of time, the creature turns head-downwards;
thus, in this tenth month, it is born from the womb.
Or, while being expelled by that Prājāpatya [wind], he is tormented;
trembling and dissolving, he is then afflicted by suffering. (70)
Having emerged from the stomach, it falls into a swoon lasting for seven nights;
or, through the touch of the wind, it regains consciousness once again.
Then the deluding Māyā of Viṣṇu overcomes him;
his mind being thus deluded by austerities, he suffers a fall from knowledge.
Or, having fallen from right knowledge, that creature then attains the state of a louse;
weeping and afflicted by the torment of bedbugs and the like, it is intensely distressed. (73)
Then, having reached the state of youth following childhood— a state as fickle as it is— [he] became constantly tormented by desire and greedy for union with young women.
Even upon reaching old age, afflicted by phlegm and wind and other ailments, he did not recall the Dharma pertaining to the next world even in his mind. (75)
Having heard this, one meets death; then again birth, and then again death.
Thus, in this wheel of saṃsāra, one is whirled around like a water-wheel.
Sometimes one attains heaven, and likewise sometimes hell; and sometimes one experiences both heaven and hell together. (77)
Sometimes he is born again right here, or [he is reborn] according to his own karma as heard in the scriptures;
sometimes, having abandoned his karma, he departs from here after a very short time.

O best of the twice-born, sometimes, through even small auspicious and inauspicious deeds, one is born as if anew; and having mostly experienced [the fruits] in the heavenly world and in hell, [one returns]. 79.
The great suffering in the hells is this: that those dwelling in heaven are seen rejoicing while being cast down by the denizens of hell. (80)
Even in heaven, there is incomparable suffering; from the very moment of ascending, the thought persists in the mind: "I shall fall. (81)
Having beheld the hells, one experiences great suffering;
thinking "I shall go to this great [hell]," one remains restless day and night.
There is great suffering in dwelling in the womb, and even greater when being born; for one who has been born, there is suffering in the absence of gain, and likewise suffering in old age. (83)
In youth, there is supreme suffering in the connection with desire, passion, and anger;
old age consists mostly of suffering, and death is the supreme suffering. (84)
Being dragged by the agents of Yama into the hells, he wanders there;
then again into a womb, then birth, and likewise death and hell. (85)
Thus, in this wheel of saṃsāra, living beings are bound by material fetters and revolve like a waterwheel, returning again and again. (86)
"O father, there is no happiness whatsoever here, which is crowded with hundreds of sufferings;
thus, for one striving for liberation, how can the threefold Veda be followed? (87)

[Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Majesty of the King of Kings' Vidyā," in the latter portion of the *Śrīmadanuttarabrahmatattvārahasya*, the *Dāśarathīya Tantra*, which is a compendium of the essential meaning of the Vedas.]
The father said:
O virtuous one, you have well crossed the most profound thicket of saṃsāra by relying upon the great fruit arising from the gift of knowledge. || 1 ||
In that regard, O Mahāmati, all those hells are indeed like Raurava; I shall describe them to you in detail.
The son said:
Raurava has been described by me to you as the first hell;
now hear, O father, of the hell named Mahāraurava.
Extending four or five thousand yojanas in every direction,
its ground there consists of copper, and beneath it is fire.
Therefore, this entire sevenfold [world], shining with rising lightning,
will blaze forth as something extremely terrible, beyond sight and touch.
Bound by both hands with the Yamī and Vamśī [nooses] by the attendants,
the evildoer is released from the midst as he rolls along.
Being devoured by crows, cranes, wolves, owls, scorpions, and mosquitoes, as well as by vultures, he is dragged along the path of teeth.
Being burned, O father, mother, brother—distressed by these [thoughts] and agitated, he speaks repeatedly and does not attain peace. (8)
Why, then, is liberation not attained by men who are deluded by *kuśa*, and who—possessing wicked intellects—have committed sins for tens of thousands upon tens of thousands of years? (9)
Likewise, another is named Tama, which is cold by its very nature;
it is as long as Mahāraurava and is enveloped in great darkness. || 10 ||
Afflicted by the cold, men run there toward the red glow of the fire; having reached one another, they embrace each other for refuge. || 11 ||
Their teeth are gnawed away as they are tormented by the affliction of cold; likewise, others are afflicted by hunger, heat, and the loss of their strength.
The wind, carrying fragments of snow, is harsh and breaks their bones;
therefore, those possessed by hunger weep, their marrow and blood having been drained away.
Unable to endure it, they wander upon meeting with others;
likewise, even there in that darkness, men experience great suffering.
O best of Brahmins, the destruction of many misdeeds is attained there;
beyond that is another hell known as Nikṛntana, the most excellent of hells. (15)
Then, as the potter's wheels revolve incessantly,
men are placed upon them and dragged through the Kālasūtra hell.
O best of the twice-born, by the hand of the followers of Yama, from the soles of their feet to the crown of their heads, no loss of life occurs for them.
Even hundreds of their diverse fragments come together as one;
thus do the evildoers wander for thousands of years.
Listen as I speak: until that evil has been entirely exhausted and gone to destruction, he shall dwell in the Apratiṣṭha hell. (19)
Those very things where human beings dwelling [there] experience unbearable suffering are the wheels, as well as the water-wheels and machines in that place. (20)
Some men who have committed evil deeds are mounted upon wheels as the causes of their suffering and are made to whirl there.
Their duration does not last even for thousands of years; their stability is like a water-clock within a machine, or like a vessel of water [emptying] from another.
Human beings wander about, vomiting blood again and again,
with entrails hanging from their mouths and eyes fixed upon the intestines.
Listen now to another [description] of the hell named Asipatravana, where living beings encounter the seven kinds of sufferings for many yojanas.
A thousand [fires] blazed upon the ground strewn with sacrificial grass, covered by the rays of seven suns, as terrible as the fire at the end of an aeon. (25)
Then, living beings dwelling in excellent abodes arrive there;
and in the midst of that, even a cool forest is perceived as a mere leaf. (26)
O best of the twice-born, there are sharp-pointed iron spikes fixed there,
and brindled dogs bark there by the tens of thousands.
Having large mouths, large fangs, and great claws like those of tigers,
they then beheld that forest, which offered cool shade at its edge.
There, tormented by that [heat], living beings go forth, crying out "O father! O mother! in extreme distress. (29)
Their pair of feet were measured by the ghee, while the fire remained on the ground;
even as they had gone there, the wind blew away their leaves.
Having been driven forth and led away, their swords likewise fall above them;
then they fall upon the ground into a blazing heap of straw.
There, while they are being licked by dogs remaining on the surface of the earth,
those embodied beings are then swiftly torn apart by the dogs.
Their many fragments, as they were being cut, were exceedingly terrifying;
where the sword was brandished, there it has been described by me to you.
Beyond this, learn of the even more terrible Taptakumbha hell.
There, those jars are all equal in size and completely enveloped in flames of fire.
Filled with blazing fire, heated oil, and powdered iron,
those wicked-doers are cast head-first into them by my attendants.
Their brains, dripping from split skulls, are boiled in turbid water amidst terrifyingly bursting eye-sockets and bones. (36)
Furthermore, they are said to be devoured by vultures as they fall;
again, they shriek with a *śimi-śimi* sound as they become one with the oil.
With their heads, eyes, sinews, flesh, skin, and bones liquefied,
they were then scorched by the messengers of Yama from afar, like dense clouds.
In Kṛtāvarta, sinners are boiled by great whirlpools;
in Pṛṣata, as described at length, the heated cauldron has been cast by me.
I was born into a Vaiśya family; in this birth, however, when that [previous] life had passed away, I formerly obstructed cows at a watering hole.
Due to the ripening of that karma, I have reached this most terrible hell, which is filled with jackals and other beasts of prey, O Śiva. || 41 ||
A stream of blood flows from mouths crushed by machines;
it drags along a mire of living beings, agitated by the thundering roar of evil karma.
As I was being driven along, more than a hundred years passed for me,
who was tormented by the pain of great heat and scorched by the forest fire of thirst.
Then Adṛka said: "O Sadyaḥpava, you who possess a pleasant seat, you have arrived standing in the midst of burning sand that feels like the heat of the sun's rays. (44)
Through contact with that [place], there shall be the destruction of all sins for men;
and for me, too, there shall be supreme liberation in heaven, just as it is for the dwellers of heaven. (45)
"What is this? they asked, their eyes wide with joy and fixed in a steady gaze; for we have beheld the unsurpassed jewel among men drawing near. (46)
And the formidable servant of Yama, the powerful lord with a noose in his hand, showed me the path in front of him, saying, "Come here, O giver of honor! (47)
Then, seeing that man afflicted by hundreds of torments in the hell of Yama, he was filled with compassion and asked, "What have you done? (48)
The man said:
"O man of Yama, tell me: what evil deed was committed by me, because of which I have reached this supreme hell, heated with torments? (49)
I am well-known as Vipaścit, born in the lineage of the Janakas; I was born in the territory of Videha as a perfect protector of men.
I have performed sacrifices with Vedic rites, and the earth has been protected according to dharma;
I have never abandoned battle, nor have I ever retreated with my back turned in flight. (51)
I have performed service to my ancestors, gods, and sages,
and I have never harbored desire for the wives of others, whether they be of noble birth or otherwise.
At the times of the sacred festivals, the ancestors come to a man of their own accord, and at the time of spiritual attainment, the gods come,
just as fish rush toward fresh bait.
Since those householders turn away having made a firm resolve,
therefore both types of merit— the sacrificial (iṣṭa) and the charitable (pūrta)— perish.
The exhalation of the Pitṛs destroys the merit acquired over seven births;
the exhalation of the Deva destroys that which arises from three births—of this there is no doubt. (55)
Therefore, one should always be diligent in rites for the gods and the ancestors;
how then have I reached this most dreadful hell? (56)
The son said:
Thus questioned by him at that time, while we two were listening, the great being—
the terrible messenger of Yama— then spoke these relevant words.
Kiṅkaṇu said:
"O Great King, you are exactly as you have said; there is no doubt about this. However, a small amount of sin was committed by you, and I shall remind you of it. (58)
All sacrifices have been performed by you with full and excellent sacrificial fees;
great gifts have been bestowed by you with devotion upon those learned in the Vedas.
The teachers and the foremost of fathers have been constantly honored by you;
the glorious eight-syllabled mantra has been perfectly practiced by you.
Accompanied by the rays of the Blessed One, she bestows grace upon the earth from time to time,
during the transits of the moon, the sun, and the planets, and on Fridays.
Having performed especially the recitation and fire-oblation, he gave to the preceptor a sacrificial fee consisting of thousands of gold pieces, animals, and jewels.
Month after month, you have personally worshipped her with divine ornaments and garments bestowed by the Preceptor, regarding her as the embodiment of Mahālakṣmī herself.
The sons of the preceptors were constantly served by you with abundant jewels and wealth, as were your grandsons, even though they were not the faces of the gods.
Everything was given by you daily with the permission of the teacher;
you have properly performed compassion and instruction, avoiding all censure of the teacher. (65)
On one day there, O King, the Guru said to a poor brahmin, "Give me five thousand dīnāras. (66)
"You yourself have said that even three things given to him with devotion [are sufficient];
yet, by that sin, he has seen a terrible hell. (67)
O observer of noble vows, if there were even the slightest trace of sin in him, then someone else might [speak];
therefore, O King, go now to enjoy the fruits of your merits, for your life is at its end.
The king said:
"O follower of the gods, you will go where you will not lead me;
therefore, I ask you this—please deign to tell it to me exactly as it is. (69)
These crows with diamond-like beaks captivate the eyes of men;
moreover, their eyes likewise become [fixed] again and again.
Tell me what loathsome deed they have committed,
such that their tongues are being torn out as they are being reborn again in that manner.
What karma did they perform by which they are partakers of this suffering? Because they are cut down with a saw, they are therefore distressed. (72)
Tell me, what [merit] is there in this ritual, that they are boiled in oil over sands of hell and dragged by iron-beaked birds? (73)
The excellent birds, crying out with great and terrible shrieks, were pained by wounds on all their limbs from the striking of the beaks and talons. || 74 ||
Why do these old women burn with such certainty day and night?
These and other such women are seen [suffering] as a result of their sinful deeds.
"Tell me in brief by which ripening of karma that occurred.
Kiṃkara said:
O protector of the earth, as for what you ask me regarding the arising of the fruit of sinful karma—
I shall therefore explain that here to you briefly and exactly as it is:
a person experiences both merit and demerit in their respective turns. (77)
While one is experiencing [the results], merit as well as sin comes to exhaustion;
yet, without experience, no karma—whether sinful or meritorious—endures until the end of existence.
Understand that one renounces enjoyments through merit alone;
likewise, famine becomes a divine abundance, and suffering becomes non-suffering, as well as fear and the like.
From death they go to death, and likewise from poverty, those who commit evil deeds;
from festival to festival, from heaven to heaven, and from happiness to happiness [they go].
Those who are self-controlled, generous, wealthy,
and performers of auspicious deeds [overcome] the terrible fears of wild beasts, elephants, and difficult terrains.
Sinner struck by their own evil go [to hell]; what could be more than this?
[Yet they receive] fragrant garlands, fine garments, excellent vehicles, and auspicious seats. (82)
Even in empty forests, the noble ones always hear it being recited—this merit which has been accumulated through the collection of many thousands of births. (83)
In the same way, for men, merit arises from merit, and likewise pleasure and pain arise from their actions (kuru);
for just as a seed observes the earth, the rain, and the seasons. (84)

One should observe that even a very small sin committed by men becomes [grave] through the influence of merit, merit, as well as time, place, and so forth, when brought about by the circumstances of time and location. (85)
The placement of the foot causes suffering arising from thorns;
that which arises from a thick stake or pin is far more intense.
That which bestows suffering is the cause of headaches and other ailments;
it brings about distress through unwholesome eating, exposure to cold, fatigue, and heat. (87)
Likewise, one should consider other sins as well when there is a conjunction of planets;
in this manner, great sins [are determined] according to the sequence beginning with long-term diseases and so forth.
Indeed, hundreds of austerities and difficult penances are for the sake of fruit;
[but] merit grants a small amount of auspicious fragrance with ease. (89)
Whether it be touch, or sound, or form, or even taste—whatever is more formidable than the Virāj, or even as great as that which is born of Time (Kāla). (90)
And thus, experiencing pleasures and pains arising from merit and demerit, he remains here, being born again and again in the manifold cycle of existence. || 91 ||

Those [impressions] which are not contradicted by birth or place, and those produced by knowledge or ignorance, remain there; what else is there? In them, the Self is established merely as the witness. (92)
Never, at any time or place, does a person remain without performing either a sinful or a meritorious deed by means of action, mind, or speech. (93)
Whatever happiness or even suffering a person obtains—
whether it be abundant or very slight— it is merely a modification of the form of the mind.
To that same extent, once a person has experienced the suffering resulting from their sin—or whatever else—it goes toward the exhaustion of its consequences, like food being consumed. (95)
Thus, these men dwelling within the various hells exhaust their terrible and great sin through agonies day and night.
In the same way, O King, meritorious deeds are enjoyed together with the gods in the heavenly world by Gandharvas, Siddhas, and Apsarases through songs and other delights. (97)
In this state of divinity, humanity, and the intermediate state of animals, one experiences the auspicious and inauspicious arising from merit and demerit, characterized by pleasure and pain. (98)
As for what you ask— regarding that sinful woman Mīrājanyā—
and by what various ripenings [of karma] it occurred, I shall explain that to you thereafter.
The wives of others were gazed upon with evil eyes by the lowest of men,
and the property of others was looked upon with longing minds.
Those birds with diamond-tips snatch away their eyes;
moreover, the regeneration of these eyes occurs again and again.
For as many times as these men have closed their eyes while committing evil,
for that many years shall they suffer from eye disease, from which there is no escape.

Even when questioned thoroughly by men who are devoid of destruction and incompleteness, [the results] are determined by those who have been instructed by the teachings of false scriptures and by those who are crooked in conduct.
Those by whom the scripture has been proclaimed otherwise, and those by whom improper speech has been uttered,
shall repeatedly fall from the summit of that mountain.
Blaspheming the gods, the Vedas, and the twice-born, as well as reviling one's guru—
these sins cause their tongues to be born again and again.
For that many years, extremely fierce Vajratuṇḍas [will protect] the high-souled Ācārya of the glorious six-syllable vidyā.
For as many *ghaṭikās* as [the slander] was heard, seen, or committed, for that many thousands of *kalpas*, this tongue of theirs shall [suffer] again and again. (107)
They take away the excrement from one's mouth and even thrust it into one's ears;
[but they cannot harm] the eight-syllabled lore of Śrī-yad and the fifteen-syllabled [mantra] of Śrī.
Those who, having accepted him as their teacher, do not honor him day after day—
even Śiva shall cut open his belly with sword-blades and divide it into portions.
O father, for as many hundreds of kalpas as there are nāḍikās,
one who lives as a householder should daily attend upon the teacher.
He who eats during these occasions undoubtedly eats excrement for a thousand kalpas, even in matters such as marriage, sacrificial rites, and the performance of *puraścaryā*. (111)
Having begged for a complete sacrificial fee at the auspicious pair of lotus-feet of the Preceptor, he was nevertheless led away by various stratagems along with his wife, sons, and dependents.
With parched throats, lips, and tongues, and afflicted by hunger and thirst,
they wallow in the ocean of hell for a thousand kalpas.
Likewise, the alienation of friends, as well as of father and son, of kinsmen, of the sacrificer and the teacher, of mother and son, and of companions; 114.
Those lowest of men who would create any dissension between wife and husband—see how they are cut at the end by the king with a saw. 115.
Those who cause distress to others and obstruct their joy, even if they possess palm-leaf fans and carry sandalwood, ushira-root, and fragrant garlands; || 116 ||

This [suffering] which causes the end of life is for those who have committed evil; as for those who have not committed evil, it increases their merit. Those situated on the sands of the Karaṃbhava river are these consumers of the fruits of their sins.
If one who has been invited to a Śrāddha feast for either the gods or the ancestors fails to eat,
he is torn asunder in two by birds.
And those who cut into the vital spots of the virtuous with their words— being thus devoured by birds, they remain there unrestrained.
But he who commits slander or holds a contrary opinion toward others is cut into two pieces of heart and tongue by razors hurled at him. 120.
Those who act with arrogance toward their mother, father, and teachers will wallow head-first in a pit of pus, feces, and urine.
Those who eat while the deities, guests, dependents, and beings who have arrived are still unfed, eat their sin to the ancestors, the sacrificial fire, and the Yakṣas.
Those wicked ones eat from vessels of pus with mouths like needles;
behold what kind of men they become—possessing the massive bodies of mountains. (123)
Those who feed a Brahmin from another row, or one born of a different caste, or those who eat unequally, are just like these fire-eaters (demons). || 24 ||
O Lord of Men, those by whom cows, Brahmins, and fires were touched while they were impure—into their fire-pits, hands were cast that were blazing with flames. 125.
For those who have willfully looked upon the sun, the moon, or the stars while impure from eating remnants,
the fire consecrated by mantras blazes even more intensely when struck by the messengers of Yama.
A cow, fire, a mother, a Brahmin, an elder brother, a father, a paternal aunt, female relatives, teachers, and elders—whoever has touched these with their feet; || 127 ||
Their feet are bound with iron shackles produced by Agni Prajāpati; they remain standing in the midst of heaps of glowing coals, their bodies burning up to the knees.
The meat of goats emaciated by sin, as well as those sacrificial foods for the gods which have been consumed by them without performing the purificatory rites— these are the portions of such sinners.
As they lie cast upon the surface of the earth, watching the extinguished fire,
their mouths are then drawn open by the messengers of Yama with hooks.
Those by whom even a single word of censure against the teacher has been heard shall have iron spikes driven repeatedly into their ears.
These most terrible messengers of Yama arrive without fail, even on a single day, when the command of the Teacher has been issued. (132)
The evil-minded one who transgresses against him, Yama’s servants shall pierce with spears his mouth until it is filled to the very brim, and he shall lie upon the earth.
O Gurudeva, [this was done] by the lowest of men, who, through the power of their sins measured by the night of destruction, were intent on reviling the twice-born, the virtuous, and the holy ones.
O Mother, for those who lament, the messengers of Yama repeatedly fill their ears with iron spikes the color of fire.
Indeed, O Brahmin, because of their departure, the auspicious temples and assembly halls were brought to ruin by those who followed anger and greed. || 36 ||
With these sharpened weapons, those extremely cruel servants of Yama repeatedly flay the skin of those who lament,
separating it from their bodies.
Those men who void urine or excrement upon cows, Brahmins, the sun, or the path—
their own entrails shall be devoured from the anus by crows.
Having given his daughter to one man, he who gives her to a second is split asunder like a tree cut once and for all, and is driven away by the river of caustic brine.

But he who is intent on nourishing himself alone, who abandons his own caste and family, and who leaves behind his son, wife, and other circle of kinsmen, possessing nothing—[he is truly destitute]. (140)
Even during a famine or a state of great distress, he likewise had his own months of flesh placed into his mouth by the servants of Yama, as his hunger remained unsated.
One who is devoted to sons, friends, wife, and other kinsmen—
even during a famine or a time of great turmoil— should [never abandon] his own teacher, who is identical with the Blessed Lord.
O King, for that man who abandons the wife and children of his teacher,
his servants shall place excrement and urine in his mouth for an entire kalpa.
They fill his stomach and then tear it apart again and again;
he who abandons that which has come to him for the sake of greed is called "living dead. (144)
Even he who is thus tormented by the tortures of Yama’s servants is [rescued] by those men who bestow their own merit, performed throughout their entire lives, upon him. || 145 ||
These evildoers, who have misappropriated deposits, shall be crushed like stones being ground,
their entire bodies bound with fetters.
Day and night, men are devoured by worms, scorpions, and crows; their tongues and palates are scorched by hunger and thirst, and they are overwhelmed by agony.
Behold the Śālmalī tree, where those who indulge in sexual intercourse during the day and those who take pleasure in the wives of others are pierced by sharp iron thorns. 148.
Behold these [demons], their limbs pierced and mangled, with profuse blood flowing from their wounds,
being placed even within the crucibles while they are meditated upon and sacrificed by their followers.
O tigers among men, by means of every man, one should cast down those who violate the wives of others, having made that study of theft their own lesson. (50)
Or if he takes up a craft, even then, bearing a burden on his head,
he encounters suffering and, being tormented, goes along the path of Yama.
Emaciated by hunger, his head afflicted day and night by the pain of a heavy burden, he discharged phlegm, urine, and excrement into the water. (52)
Having gone to hell, they are afflicted by foul odors of phlegm, feces, and urine;
tormented by hunger, they devour one another's flesh. (153)
Having fallen into the state of a worm, they are even devoured by gadflies;
this results from accepting gifts from the fallen, from taking what is not given, and from serving as a servant to a Kṣatriya.
A man attains the state of an insect within a stone while his circle of relatives, friends, and guests look on. (155)
He shall eat alone from the remains of eight [others], amidst a heap of glowing embers, surrounded by wolves;
this ungrateful man, who does harm to his friends, is of very wicked mind.
He is boiled in a cauldron and then dissolves;
from there he goes to the Karaṃbha-vālukā hell, and from there he is crushed by a machine.
Then there is the Forest of Blades, where one is torn apart by saws;
likewise the Black Thread, the Severance, and many other tortures. || 160 ||
Having obtained atonement for that [sin], how will he not tremble?
Thus the Brahmins who had gathered for the Śrāddha, having come together with one another, [spoke]. (161)
Having touched the *sṛdmiśriṃ* [river], they then drink this water for a thousand years;
likewise those who have stolen gold, those who have killed a cow or a Brahmin, those who have drunk liquor, and those who have violated the bed of their teacher.
Burning on all sides in a blazing fire below and above,
they remain there for many thousands of years again and again.
These human beings are born marked by diseases such as leprosy and consumption; having died, they go again to hell, and being born once more, they are seen to suffer those same [afflictions]. 164.
O lord of men, those who kill a Brahmin, those who kill their father, those who drink liquor, or those who violate the teacher’s bed, suffer diseases for a duration equal to the end of a kalpa. (165)
Expiation has been proclaimed in the treatises on dharma by Manu and others;
however, for one who betrays his teacher, there is no expiation in the Vedas or the treatises on dharma.
It is declared by Manu and others who have mastered the Dharma that those who commit treachery against their teacher shall dwell in hell until the time of the great dissolution.

[The cow-killer goes to a lower state in the hells for three births— thus ends the thirtieth chapter in the *Dāśarathīya Tantra*, which is the secret essence of the unsurpassed Brahman-reality, a compendium of the essential meaning of the Vedas, in its latter portion, concerning the majesty of the Royal-Royal Knowledge.]
The servant said:
Listen, O highly fortunate King, to this dharma which destroys the multitude of sins today;
it is established in the Vedas and Śāstras by those foremost among the upholders of dharma. (1)
Desiring happiness in this world and the next, one who practices the supreme dharma declared in the Vedas becomes liberated from all evils and attains happiness.
Having constantly offered perfumes, flowers, unbroken grains, and other such items to a twice-born man,
one is liberated from minor sins and rejoices with the Gandharvas.
Having given plantains, jackfruit, and other such fruits, as well as sugarcane juice,
to those learned in the Vedas, he was freed from all sins.
She shall dwell among the worlds of the Vidyādharas for four sets of four yugas,
she who gave food every day to guests who had arrived.
Having reached the world of Śakra, he shall dwell there for as long as a manvantara,
provided that, being pure in soul, he gives garments to those learned in the Vedas day after day.
Having reached the city of Alakā, one shall enjoy pleasures until the end of the kalpa,
after having bestowed ornaments and moving riches upon those learned in the Vedas (śrotriyas).
Having obtained half of Kuvera’s throne, he rejoices until the end of time;
